What Amit taught us: How the Bonzel family keeps the legacy of a fallen soldier alive
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
19:51:23 UTC
04:51:23 KST

Noa Bonzel is very proud of her three children, Nadav, Amit, and Adi. “Nadav is now on reserve duty in Lebanon, Amit is on Mount Herzl, and Adi is a casualty assistance officer in the Engineering Corps.”
Her matter-of-fact description of Amit’s location, where he is interred in the military cemetery in Jerusalem, sounds jarring at first. But as our discussion continues, it becomes clear that, though Amit is no longer alive, the lessons he exemplified during his life continue to inspire his family, compatriots, and Israeli society at large.
Amit, 22, a member of the Paratroopers Brigade, fell on December 6, 2023, in Gaza. Since his death, Noa and her husband, Yitzhak (Itzik), have kept his memory alive by sharing the legacy of his accomplishments in his all-too-brief life.
On a recent late-summer morning, I visited Noa and her husband at their home in Shoham to discuss Amit’s legacy and why it matters. Outside their home stands a large banner emblazoned with the verse from the Book of Samuel – “How the mighty have fallen in the midst of the battle” – next to a photo of their smiling son.
“Amit Street” in Shoham is named in his memory, and Noa admits that she sometimes finds it difficult to drive down that road. “It’s crazy. I never dreamed that there would be a street named after my son in Shoham,” says Noa, who grew up in Petah Tikva.
The synagogue in Shoham that they attend has a cabinet where holy books are kept, with a prominent sign displayed in Amit’s memory, and a synagogue – B’Darkei Amit (In the ways of Amit)– was established in his memory in Kiryat Gat.
“Amit was a very special son,” says Noa. “He was the middle child, and whenever Nadav and Adi would argue, he would say, ‘Stop. I’m begging you not to argue. We are a family.’”
Noa recalls that Amit’s sensitivity manifested at a very young age. “When he was six, I had just finished our Shabbat preparations one Friday afternoon, and for some reason, I was a bit sad. Amit smiled at me and didn’t say a word. Before he left for the synagogue with his father, he said, ‘Ima, listen. I have a surprise for you.’”
Shortly after Amit and his siblings had left for the synagogue with their father, there was a knock at the door. “It was my best friend,” says Noa. “She said that Amit had called her a few minutes before Shabbat and said, ‘My mother is a little sad. Could you please come over to visit, to make her feel better?’ That was Amit.”
Amit valued service in the IDF above all else
GROWING UP, Amit valued service in the IDF above all else, Noa says. He was not an outstanding student, but he always wanted to learn more about military life. As a student at the yeshiva high school in Petah Tikva, the city where Noa grew up, he refused to attend classes taught by a teacher who had not served in the IDF, and spent most of his time with teachers who had served as company commanders in their units.
“Amit did not have the best grades in school, and he was not the fastest runner, but he always aimed high when it came to his army service,” Noa shares.
Performing meaningful service in the IDF is a family tradition. Itzik, who grew up in Jerusalem, served in the paratroopers, as did Amit’s uncle and his brother, Nadav.
In Amit’s room in Shoham, a large flag of Israel hangs. Underneath, Amit had written: “Many people say they want to succeed, but not everyone is willing to pay the price required to achieve success.”
When Amit turned 16, he asked his mother to register him for a course in Shoham that prepared teens for tryout days for military and commando units. “I asked him what unit he wanted to try to prepare for,” recalls Noa. “He said that he wanted to join the General Staff Reconnaissance Unit, considered the most elite special unit.” In response, Noa quipped, “And I want to become prime minister.”
Amit was just 1.68 m. tall (five feet, six inches), not the ideal height for the unit, but he begged his mother to register him for the unit’s tryout day. He said, “If I do not protect the country, who will do it?” Not paying much attention to his comment, she signed him up for the course.
After being turned down twice, Amit wrote a letter to the army requesting a final chance to try out for the Reconnaissance Unit. This time, they accepted him for the screening. Despite his best efforts, Amit was not accepted. Other military units contacted him and expressed interest in recruiting him, and he decided to join the IDF Paratroopers Brigade’s elite reconnaissance unit.
Amit was accepted into the unit, and after he completed his post-high school army preparatory program at Keshet Yehuda in the Golan Heights, he joined the paratroopers and spent a year and two months training.
“There are some soldiers who give up because the training is very difficult, both physically and mentally,” says Noa. “But whenever Amit came home for Shabbat, he was so happy. He had a great deal of motivation.” The training was not easy for him because of his diminutive size, but he succeeded.
Noa also discusses the great respect that he had for his parents. When Amit finished his paratrooper training, he prepared a photo of himself standing next to his parents and left it in their room, with the inscription, “Thank you very much for your support.”
'Amit was the only one who stayed behind'
NOA RECOUNTS a story from Amit’s training, which illustrates these qualities. “There was an incident when they were training at the Wingate Institute. Their commander told them that they had to scale a wall, and that anyone who completed the exercise could go home for Shabbat.
“Itzik and I drove to Wingate and waited for Amit to finish training. We waited and waited, but he didn’t come out. We began to worry. What had happened?
“One of the soldiers on his team couldn’t scale the wall. Amit was the only one who stayed behind. He set up a portable speaker and played music, climbed to the top of the wall, and kept encouraging the soldier. He refused to give up on him, and went home only after the soldier had succeeded in scaling the wall.”
At the ceremony in Beit Lid marking the end of paratrooper training in May 2023, Amit’s commander appointed him staff sergeant over a younger group of paratroopers because of his leadership qualities and willingness to help others.
After the ceremony, Amit and his family were inching toward the exit in their car; Amit and his two siblings sat in the back seat. Shortly before they reached the main exit, Amit told his parents to stop the car. Looking through the window, he noticed someone pushing a visitor in a wheelchair. He jumped out of the car, helped push the wheelchair, and assisted the disabled person into their car.
“All the time, Amit would say, ‘How can I help another person? How can I volunteer? Who needs my help?’ When I speak to the army now, I tell everyone that I follow in Amit’s path.
“When I went to work, I was always in a hurry,” notes Noa. “But now, when I go, I look ahead and say to myself, ‘Perhaps someone needs me, as Amit would think.’ Whenever I see the street cleaner, I go back into the house, bring him a piece of cake and a cup of coffee.”
'He never came back home'
THE SOLDIERS under Amit finished their training on Thursday, October 5, 2023, during Hol Hamoed Sukkot. Amit’s soldiers came to Shoham, and Amit prepared a barbecue for them. On Friday, Amit’s parents returned from a vacation abroad, and Amit, together with friends from Shoham, went to a villa in the North near the Kinneret for Simchat Torah.
On the morning of Oct. 7, Amit returned home and told his parents that the war had started, which surprised Noa, since they had not heard any sirens in Shoham. He organized his gear and, after 20 minutes, left the house. “He never came back home,” says Noa wistfully.
Amit fought with his soldiers in the kibbutzim being attacked by Hamas terrorists. On November 19, his 22nd birthday, his unit was in the Rimal neighborhood in Gaza City, and his soldiers threw him a surprise party. He said it was his happiest birthday, because they appreciated and respected him.
He then returned to the army base at Lachish. Noa and Itzik visited Amit there at the end of November. The last time they spoke to him was at the end of November; afterward, Amit reentered Gaza with his unit, commanded by Ariel Malka.
On December 5, 2023, Ariel’s brother, Yehonatan Malka, fell in combat against Hamas in the Gaza Strip. Ariel Malka was granted temporary leave and returned to Israel to attend his brother’s funeral, held the next day, on December 6.
Amit was appointed to command the unit in his absence, though he had not completed his officer’s training course. His commanders trusted his ability to lead the soldiers effectively in combat.
Noa and Itzik had not heard from Amit in some time, and Itzik decided to attend Yehonatan Malka’s funeral, where he would see Ariel and find out how Amit was doing.
While Itzik was attending the funeral of the brother of Amit’s commander, Amit fell in Saja’iya, a large neighborhood in Gaza City. Noa recounts that when the IDF representative arrived at their home in Shoham to break the tragic news, only Adi was home. Noa was at work in Modi’in, and Itzik was on his way home from the funeral.
When he returned home from Yehonatan Malka’s funeral and saw the officers, he realized that they had come to inform him about the death of his son. He asked, “Which one? Nadav or Amit?”
Over 1,000 people attended Amit’s funeral, says Noa, and each day of the shiva saw visits from hundreds of people from all walks of life – religious, secular, haredi. Noa and Itzik were astounded to hear the stories that people told about Amit’s kindness and consideration for others.
At the conclusion of the shiva, Noa and Itzik went to Amit’s grave and saw the nearby grave of Eyal Meir Berkowitz, a 28-year-old IDF soldier from Susya, who was killed in action in the Gaza Strip on December 7, 2023.
They decided to pay a shiva visit to the family in Susya that evening. While they were there, they learned of another family who had lost a son from the nearby community of Asa’el. Soon, they went there and comforted them. Noa and Itzik continued to visit many bereaved parents and wounded soldiers in hospitals.
NOA OPENED a WhatsApp group for bereaved mothers, where they communicate and speak about their needs, both emotional and otherwise. When the Jewish community in Bondi Beach, Australia, was reeling after the terror attack during Hanukkah in December 2025, Noa and Itzik traveled privately to comfort the bereaved families.
“They thanked us for coming from so far away to visit them. We visited each family and gave them practical tips on how to get back on their feet after what happened,” Noa recounts.
The couple traveled to the US, France, Italy, and Australia, where they delivered talks about their son. They frequently speak at Bahad 1, the IDF’s officer training center, and at schools and workplaces, focusing on the values Amit lived by, and how others can put them into practice.
“What really stands out is what the children say afterward: One said, ‘I didn’t believe in myself, and now I realize I can achieve great things,’” recalls Itzik. “Another girl wrote, ‘I live in the periphery, and my dream was to become a paramedic. I gave up on that dream, but after the lecture, I won’t take ‘no’ for an answer.’”
How do Itzik and Noa cope with their loss? Noa explains that they keep busy with work – she is an import manager and he is a lawyer – and by talking to others about what Amit did during his life. “We cry several times a day,” says Itzik, who grew up in Jerusalem. “It can be for a second or two, or it can be longer. It catches you in the throat or the heart, but it shows that you are normal.”
They are certain that Amit’s death was not in vain. “When we walk down the street and see people sitting in cafés, you think, ‘They must be on vacation, or they’re just idle,’ or whatever.
“We go to shows and weddings – which are the hardest things. But then we realize, when we see people out on the streets, at celebrations and at shows, that we’re seeing victory.
“Everyone asks, ‘What is victory?’ We see victory in the fact that our people keep going to the beach, keep celebrating their children’s weddings with great joy, and keep sitting in cafés, instead of sheltering in safe rooms. That really is our victory. What seems normal to you is a victory for us. It’s thanks to Amit and all the soldiers that we’re here.” ■
Heshbon nefesh
These are the words of Amit Bonzel, of blessed memory, who fell in Gaza. His family found his notes among his belongings.
The kind of person I want to be
• Committed all the time
• Give everyone the benefit of the doubt
• First to volunteer
• Happy to give, and want to give without compromises
• Don’t complain
• A person that people share everything with
• Responsible – someone people trust
• Always know what to say, and when not to
• Don’t get upset by what people say about me
• Talk to everyone at eye level
• Lead everyone in the right way
How do I become this person?
• Always be positive
• Say hello to everyone in the unit, even to those with whom I connect less or people I don’t know
• Always say thank you, even if it’s embarrassing sometimes
• Don’t get offended if I’m not included in something – need to understand not everything revolves around me
• Give people the benefit of the doubt
• Count to three before I react
• Understand that not everyone here has the same motives
• Not everything revolves around me
• See how I can bridge the gaps in a respectful and beautiful way
• Be the first to volunteer
• Always say “I will,” even if it’s not the most comfortable at that moment
May we be worthy – Am Yisrael chai.
A mechina (pre-army preparatory program) has been established in Amit’s memory in Lod, home to both Jewish and Arab communities. Named “Bedarkei Amit” (the path of Amit), the mechina now has 150 students and is a growing presence in the city.

Northrop’s Talon Blue drone wingman makes first flight
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
19:45:19 UTC
04:45:19 KST

- Northrop Grumman's YFQ-48A Talon Blue completed its first fully autonomous flight, including taxi, takeoff, maneuvers and landing, in Mojave, California.
- The company-funded drone is competing for the U.S. Air Force's Collaborative Combat Aircraft program after Northrop lost the first round.
Northrop Grumman’s YFQ-48A Talon Blue, the company’s self-funded entry for the U.S. Air Force’s drone wingman program, has made its first flight, flying entirely on its own from taxi to landing in Mojave, California.
The company announced the flight on Oct. 3. It said the aircraft taxied, took off, flew a series of maneuvers and landed without a pilot steering it remotely. Northrop Grumman did not say on what date the flight took place, how long it lasted, how high or fast the aircraft flew, or what the next steps in the test program are.
Talon Blue is designed to fly alongside crewed fighters as a Collaborative Combat Aircraft, the U.S. Air Force’s term for uncrewed jets that can scout, jam or carry weapons for pilots in F-35s, F-22s and the future F-47. The aircraft has an internal weapons bay, a high-mounted engine intake and a wide-set landing gear, which Northrop Grumman said allow it to handle a range of missions for the United States and allies.
“Our customers made it clear they need autonomous systems that can be fielded faster and more affordably without sacrificing mission effectiveness. We listened,” said Craig Woolston, vice president and general manager for research and advanced design at Northrop Grumman.
The company has focused its pitch on cost and production speed. It said design and manufacturing changes cut both the number of parts and the aircraft’s weight, which it says makes the drone cheaper and faster to build. Northrop Grumman has previously said Talon uses composite structures and roughly half as many parts as earlier designs.
Northrop Grumman built Talon Blue with its own money after losing out in the first round of the U.S. Air Force’s Collaborative Combat Aircraft competition. The program, first known as Project Lotus and later renamed Project Talon, was unveiled in December 2025. Later that month, the U.S. Air Force gave it the YFQ-48A prototype designation, calling it “a strong contender” in the program. The designation does not come with a contract.
The two Increment 1 winners are already moving ahead. In June, the U.S. Air Force ordered both General Atomics’ FQ-42A Dark Merlin and Anduril’s FQ-44A Fury into production, and both companies announced in late July that production aircraft were coming off their lines. Those drones first flew in August and October 2025, respectively.
Talon Blue’s realistic target is the next round, Increment 2, for which the U.S. Air Force has not yet chosen a design or set production plans. A service spokesperson said in December that nine companies were working on Increment 2 concepts but declined to name them or confirm whether Northrop Grumman was one.
Talon Blue is one part of what Northrop Grumman calls its Project Talon portfolio. The other is Talon IQ, a flying testbed based on Scaled Composites’ Model 437 aircraft that runs the company’s Prism mission autonomy software. Northrop Grumman uses it to test and mature autonomy software before it goes on combat aircraft. Scaled Composites, which builds experimental aircraft in Mojave, is a Northrop Grumman subsidiary.

OpenAI safety leader quits, warning AI company’s culture is ‘broken’

A safety leader at OpenAI has quit the company, warning that its culture was broken and that AI firms were not “being nearly careful enough” about developing the technology.
David Robinson, who led the writing of safety reports that accompanied the ChatGPT developer’s product releases, explained his resignation in an essay headlined, “I quit OpenAI because its culture is broken”.
Robinson wrote that a cultural overhaul was needed at cutting-edge AI firms and incidents such as a “swarm” of OpenAI agents – AI programmes operating autonomously without human oversight – attacking the AI startup Hugging Face were “typical of the industry, given the speed and flexibility with which people operate”.
Writing in The Atlantic magazine, Robinson wrote: “I agree with other recently departed staff that the companies building this technology aren’t being nearly careful enough. But I believe that we need to look deeper than specific rules or new laws. We need to talk about culture.”
Referring to OpenAI’s pace of development, he wrote: “As the company sprints from one launch to the next, it is failing to achieve the level of care that I believe is needed.”
OpenAI has, however, shown signs of caution in recent weeks following the Hugging Face incident and the revelation that it has notified more than 100 organisations about rogue agent activity. This week it announced it was scrapping the release of a next-generation AI model after researchers raised safety concerns during internal testing. OpenAI has also paused training of its most advanced models.
Geoffrey Irving, who worked at OpenAI and DeepMind before becoming chief scientist of Resolution, also joined the warnings on AI on Saturday.
Writing in Time, he said: “Recent warnings about the potential destructive power of AI are understating the severity of the situation.
“I believe there’s about a 50% chance we all die because of the development of smarter-than-human AI systems, and that our actions over the next two to 10 years will determine the outcome.”
Robinson’s essay also follows the resignation of Jacob Coxon, a researcher at OpenAI rival Anthropic, who quit the Claude chatbot developer last month. He warned AI “could kill us all by the end of the decade” – and was followed by Anthropic warning there was a more than 10% chance AI would wipe out humanity within the next decade. Critics of such warnings have cautioned, however, that they are unscientific because they cannot be verified or falsified.
Robinson wrote Silicon Valley lacked an awareness of “how to handle dangerous technology” and “what it means to care for people”. Warning that OpenAI had “unimpeded optimism” about solving problems as they arose, he wrote that this internal culture meant safety failures would only grow as systems become more capable.
“Imagine ‘rogue’ agents that work like teams of hackers (for example, holding hospital computer systems for ransom) but never need to sleep,” wrote Robinson.
Robinson called for two safety changes: that AI firms rely on safety expertise in other fields such as nuclear and aviation and develop “new science” that ensures powerful systems in the future are capable of being reined in when they are operating autonomously.
“Given today’s risks, frontier labs need to run like nuclear-power plants or busy airports, with layers of redundancy and careful, time-consuming planning, so that the occasional and inevitable human error does not open a door to disaster,” he wrote.
An OpenAI spokesperson said the company was continuing to “strengthen our safety and security practices to address the risks we see today”, while working on dealing with the risks that might be created by future AI breakthroughs.
“We’re making sure our models don’t become more capable than we can safely manage and secure, and we pause training or hold back models when we need to slow down,” said the spokesperson.

'We’re biscuity people': The traditions being kept alive in Australia’s suburbs
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
19:34:30 UTC
04:34:30 KST

This audio is voiced by AI and may occasionally mispronounce words.
Share your feedback and help us improve this feature. Read more about how we use AI at SBS here.
There's something about food that makes us feel cared for and at home.
For Michelle Raguz, the biggest compliment she can receive is being told her food tastes just like baka's (Croatian for grandmother).
"That was my aim, to get that nostalgia back," the mother-of-three tells SBS News.
Raguz, who lives in Austral in Sydney's south-west, is one of a growing number of people running small businesses from their home kitchens, often supplying niche cultural foods to families who may not have the time or skills to devote to make them, but still crave the taste of home.
While Croatian-style biscuits are available to buy in certain shops, the 41-year-old says "anything that comes out of a machine is not going to taste the way a homemade biscuit does".
News that makes sense
Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
During her busiest periods ahead of Easter and Christmas, Raguz easily makes 1,000 biscuits for sale through her Instagram account.
The NSW Food Authority tells SBS News that "anecdotal feedback from local councils indicates home-based food businesses have grown in number", although it does not specifically collect data on these businesses.
Driven by a mix of nostalgia, convenience and a desire for supportive communities, these micro businesses have also become a way for people to stay connected to their culture, share food traditions and recreate a sense of home.
Not everyone can bake mum's biscuits
Among the Balkan community in Australia, including those of Macedonian and Serbian heritage, it's traditional to enjoy treats like madarice (a chocolate layer cake) and oblatne (wafers) with coffee at social gatherings.
But Raguz says many older members of the Croatian community can no longer make the traditional biscuits and cakes she sells.
"Even my mother-in-law, she's got arthritis in her hands [so] they can't stand there and bake anymore," she says.
During the COVID-19 pandemic, she was spurred to start her business by a desire to help her community, which didn't have the option of having traditional foods delivered.
[During lockdowns] if you wanted to reach out to somebody, the only option people had were … donuts or flowers.
This was not appealing to Croatians, Raguz says, who love having small portions of a variety of homemade cakes and biscuits.
"We're biscuity people. You have a slice of this, or a piece of that."
About 90 per cent of her customers are of Balkan heritage, but she also has other customers who have found her sweet treats after friends or neighbours shared her biscuits with them, for example.
"I actually get a lot of Asians — once they try it, they love it."
Raguz says she loves recreating the warm memories she had growing up and is lucky to have inherited a love of cooking from her mum.
"All of our friends still talk about my mother's hospitality," she says, adding that she always wanted to carry that on with her own children.
I don't want the way we grew up to be lost.
'Cooked by people that care'
Home cooking can create a sense of care that sets it apart from restaurant meals, says Carol Perdigao, a former chef who moved to Melbourne from Brazil six years ago.
She regularly orders food such as feijão tropeiro (bean stew) and empadão de palmito (palm heart pie) from a home cook via WhatsApp.
"It's something I miss from home," she says of the dishes, which she adds can be difficult to find in Brazilian restaurants in Australia that often focus on meat.
She says that when she began ordering the food she was mainly motivated by the desire to support the Brazilian community in Australia but says it is also "one of the best foods flavour-wise because it's cooked by people that care".
"A lot of people work in hospitality because they end up there and it's a very busy-paced life," Perdigao notes of restaurant cuisine.
"[You don't] necessarily get that sort of care with the food."
The meals have also helped Carol to continue the Brazilian tradition of having a large warm meal for lunch.
"It's an important part of the day for me," she says. "It's a habit that I really wasn't able to get rid of."
I basically don’t feel satisfied if I don’t eat a home-cooked lunch.
Cultural sociologist Sian Supski, a research fellow at Monash University, says food can be used to make people feel at home. She says women migrating to Australia in the 1950s used it as a way to become part of the Australian suburbs.
"They would give food to their neighbours and then their neighbours would ask for the recipes," she says.
Migrants must also find local substitutes for some ingredients and Supski says this creates a lot of "cultural traffic" between the place they now live and where they came from.
"So I think that food helps the placemaking [that helps people feel connected to spaces]."
'I feel like people appreciate me'
Sarah (not her real name) says the thing she values the most about selling her homemade dumplings is that it gives her a chance to meet her neighbours, and a topic to talk about.
"My job [in Australia is] pretty boring and not so many people talk [with me]," she tells SBS News.
"[But] I love chatting."
Sarah sees her dumpling business as just a hobby, which is why she doesn’t want her name to be published. She sells one or two bags of dumplings in Sydney each week, mostly through posts on a local community Facebook page.
"Back in China you have a good income; here you [are] basically nothing," she says.
Doing this just give me confidence. I feel like people appreciate me. I feel good for myself.
Sarah's jiaozi (northern Chinese-style dumplings) are a blend of how her grandma cooks and the preferences of her non-Chinese husband and two children.
The pork and prawn filling is minced by hand chopping, just like Sarah's grandma's, but she wraps them using store-bought dumpling pastry, which is thinner than handmade dough, and steams them rather than boiling them.
This also suits Sarah's customers as the majority of them are not Asian. Regular buyers include a woman who orders dumplings every Valentine's Day, and a man who buys them monthly to serve to his mates during a regular catch-up.
Once her children finish their education, Sarah says she may start a small dumpling bar because she loves having a drink and chatting with friends while eating dumplings.
"You know Chinese, we love sharing food," Sarah says.
"The way we show love [to] neighbours or that, we just keep feeding them. That's the Chinese."
Mother-of-three Asma Khalaf would also like to build up her business selling Middle Eastern treats in Sydney.
Khalaf arrived in Australia from Gaza two years ago and the 39-year-old says she wanted to find a way to talk about her background.
How can I show other people, who [are] in different culture, about my culture?
"Then I start thinking about food, because food is the main language to talk about your country."
A former teacher, Khalaf says she used to enjoy making pastries in her spare time before the war.
She's now selling these using Palestinian recipes inspired by her mother through an Instagram account. Eid is the busiest time for her and last year she made 13kg of fragrant treats like maamoul (date cookies), kaak (ring-shaped pastry) and baklava (layered filo pastry dessert).
While most of her goods are sold to those of Middle Eastern background, about 30 per cent are bought by people from other cultures.
Demand can be quite unpredictable but Khalaf hopes to eventually open her own shop, to help support her family in Australia and Gaza.
Supski says food can hold an important role for migrants from countries that have experienced societal upheaval and seen their cultural and literary heritage destroyed.
"They have lost their loved ones, or their connection because records have been lost, as well as people.
"The re-creation of food and the feeding of community is this very direct connection straight back to family or to the place that people grew up."
Concerns over food safety and commercialisation
But the Food Safety Information Council has warned Australians not to buy or sell food through social media sites that is prepared in unregulated home kitchens.
Chief executive officer Lydia Buchtmann says food prepared in a home kitchen or backyard barbecue is unlikely to meet the food safety regulations that apply to businesses selling food.
A NSW Food Authority spokesperson tells SBS News home-based food businesses must meet the same requirements as all food businesses in NSW.
"Home-based businesses must notify the appropriate authority, their local council or the NSW Food Authority, with their business details so their food safety compliance requirements can be assessed," the spokesperson says.
Sukhmani Khorana of the University of NSW, whose research looks at how migrants use food cultures to foster belonging, says food safety verification is important, although she questions whether it's always accessible to the people starting these businesses.
"Sometimes it also doesn't matter a great deal to customers from the same community if they know the family," she tells SBS News.
She says she's also noticed an increase in supper clubs, where people host guests in their homes, which can allow for specific foods from certain regions to be experienced in place of cuisines often served in restaurants catering to broader tastes.
But Khorana notes there is always a potential downside to commercialising any cultural product.
Australia has a long history of multicultural foods starting off as operated and owned by independent families or from ethnic backgrounds, and then becoming cool … [and] too homogenised and commercialised.
She is concerned social media algorithms may also limit access to foods and businesses to those who are already searching for them.
"Opportunities we had before [may have] extended that knowledge and awareness to other communities as well."
Selling food and posting recipes on social media may help provide access to food that is not commonly available — especially to younger generations — but Khorana points out that platforms like Instagram rely heavily on visual aesthetics.
"Not all ethnic food is going to be visually appealing."
Supski acknowledges concerns around the reliance on social media but says it appears to have played a positive role for some people amid concerns about what some say is a loneliness epidemic.
These online communities … bring a lot of connection and support to the people who are selling the food.

Details
It is reported that on the morning of October 2, a car exploded on Druzhby Street in Novomoskovsk, killing the driver.
Russian National Guard personnel and vehicles with Defense Ministry license plates arrived at the scene. It was reported that an explosive device had been planted under the vehicle's floor on the driver's side, and that a participant in the war against Ukraine was behind the wheel.

At the end of November 2024, he returned to Tula region for treatment.
In September 2025, the Office of the Prosecutor General of Ukraine notified Syromyatnikov of suspicion of torturing Ukrainian prisoners of war at Penal Colony No. 1 in Tula region. According to the Ukrainian investigation, he worked there in 2022.
Ukrainian law enforcement officers believe that Syromyatnikov may have been involved in the torture of at least 50 Ukrainian prisoners. According to the Ukrainian investigation, during morning and evening checks, the prisoners were beaten with hands, feet, rubber batons, plastic pipes, and hammers, and stun guns were also used.
In addition, according to the investigation, contacts from a TA-57 field telephone were attached to the prisoners' bodies and electric current was passed through them. These allegations formed the basis for notifying Syromyatnikov of suspicion in Ukraine.

Valdai 2026: The search for a new world order has only just begun
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
19:29:52 UTC
04:29:52 KST

Valdai 2026: The search for a new world order has only just begun
Journalists and public figures from nearly 40 countries gathered at this year’s Valdai Club conference to discuss how the world is responding to a growing number of crises, and one conclusion stood out – the world has become more complex and there will be no return to an age of simple solutions.
The 20th century gave humanity a great deal, but it also encouraged the belief that fundamental political and social questions can be settled by choosing the correct ideology. Capitalism and communism competed to provide the answer, and after the Cold War, liberal globalism made its own attempt to reduce international affairs to a common set of rules and assumptions, but this has also failed.
We are therefore learning to live in a world where even the most dangerous developments need not produce panic or despair. This was reflected in the agenda at Valdai as participants discussed issues that would have seemed extraordinary 15 or 20 years ago about how societies withstand prolonged war, the increasingly impersonal nature of modern warfare, the military use of AI, and the uncertain future of nuclear deterrence.
Yet these discussions took place without a sense of panic, and without attempts to frighten participants with the prospect of a world in which the US and Europe can no longer set the rules. As Russian President Vladimir Putin argued in the closing session, the global situation under these circumstances could instead change for the better.
This explains why, despite the dangers facing the world, the tone at Valdai was constructive. Yes, the risks are real, but they were discussed as conditions in which future development must take place, rather than as signs of inevitable catastrophe.
One reason is that the overwhelming majority of participants come from countries outside the West, and their perspective is often quite different from that which prevails in Europe, as rather than seeking to restore an international order that is disappearing, they’re trying to understand what will replace it.
In this respect, Valdai provides a useful snapshot of the intellectual debate taking place beyond the Western world.
For Russia, this matters enormously, given new ideas and alternative approaches to development are increasingly being debated in China, India, Iran, and the Arab world, and across Africa, Asia, and Latin America, and Russia has much to learn from these discussions.
It’s equally important to understand the thinking of countries that have resisted pressure from the US and Europe and maintained relations with Russia during the past four years. These countries constitute much of the ‘global majority’ with which Russia hopes to build a multipolar international order.
The exchange also gives Russia the opportunity to explain its own perspective, not only on the Ukraine conflict but on broader questions that will shape international affairs for decades, and the first is war.
International law is playing a diminishing role in restraining countries, as conflicts in some regions have become exceptionally violent, while new technologies are changing the nature of warfare, and unmanned systems and AI create possibilities that scarcely existed a generation ago. Far from eliminating human responsibility, these technologies make questions of responsibility, error, and human judgment even more important.
The second question is how international rules will be established and maintained as Western influence declines.
Russia, China, and other countries have long promoted multipolarity as an alternative model of international order. Putin used his Valdai appearance to call for reform of the UN system and a greater role for developing countries and the Global South in making important international decisions.
The third challenge is older but no less pressing because climate change, environmental degradation, inequality, and poverty have not disappeared, and while the struggle by the US and Europe to preserve their international position has increasingly pushed these questions into the background, they will eventually have to be addressed.
This raises two difficult questions regarding the role China and other Asian powers will play, and which institutions will be capable of coordinating international action.
There is still no clear answer to the first, and Asian countries show little enthusiasm for simply replacing the West as global leaders, but on the second, BRICS increasingly appears capable of playing an important role.
The attraction of BRICS is that it does not operate through one member issuing instructions to the other, and that its members have different interests and political systems but share an interest in stable development and greater freedom in determining their own policies.
Its weaknesses should not be ignored, because BRICS lacks the internal discipline characteristic of traditional Western alliances, and two of its members, Iran and the UAE, came dangerously close to conflict this spring, yet the organization is increasingly discussed as a source of mutually beneficial ideas and practical solutions.
Another challenge is AI, and this goes far beyond its military uses. Fundamental questions concern the ethical limits of AI, the preservation of humanism, and the danger of what Putin calls “digital totalitarianism.” Technological progress is moving faster than the political and social institutions that are expected to regulate it.
For Russia, perhaps the most important lesson is that the economic and social problems it faces aren’t uniquely Russian, given that countries everywhere are struggling with economic imbalance, technological disruption, and rapid social change, and this is both good and bad news.
It’s good news for Russia because it demonstrates the failure of Western attempts since 2022 to isolate the country from the wider world, but it’s bad news because nobody has discovered universal solutions to these problems.
Economic and social resilience will therefore be critical, as the international system is undergoing changes on a scale rarely seen in modern history. An era lasting more than 500 years, during which Western civilization progressively acquired the ability to determine much of humanity’s political and economic development, is coming to an end, and this transformation coincides with extraordinary advances in technology, medicine, and genetics.
Every major civilization is searching for answers, but the fundamental disagreement concerns how these answers should be found, as Western countries are attempting to preserve the international positions they have accumulated over centuries, while Russia and its partners in BRICS argue instead for an order based on sovereign choice and mutual benefit.
The clash between these two approaches may prove to be the defining conflict of our time.
This article was first published by Vzglyad.ru, translated and edited by the RT team.

‘He prayed, then hit me’: Flydubai captain recounts cockpit attack
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
19:27:43 UTC
04:27:43 KST

Indian flydubai captain Smit Machchhar has given his first detailed account of the seconds before his Omani co-pilot allegedly tried to crash a Tel Aviv-bound passenger jet, saying the man prayed in the cockpit for several minutes before suddenly attacking him from behind.
Speaking with Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, Machchhar said co-pilot Hamam al-Hammami asked to pray shortly before the attack. The Sept. 30 incident aboard flydubai Flight FZ1073 from Dubai to Tel Aviv is being investigated by authorities in several countries. The United Arab Emirates has described it as an attempted terrorist attack, while investigators have so far found no established connection between al-Hammami and a terrorist organization.
“It was just a normal flight,” Machchhar told Netanyahu. “The co-pilot wanted to pray. A lot of the locals, they do pray, which is not out of the ordinary. While he was praying, out of respect, I was just looking at the front and not at the back — and suddenly after about four, five minutes, there was a big blow to the back of my head.”
Machchhar said his first thought was that the aircraft had suffered a catastrophic malfunction.
“But after that, the blows kept coming, one after the other. That's when I realized that it's not the aircraft — it's the other guy who was in the cockpit with me,” he said.
“I did try to stop him, but because of his initial blows, my vision was almost nothing. I was completely blurred out. And at that point, the next feeling that I had was that the aircraft was sharply going down.”
Flight-tracking data showed the Boeing 737 rapidly lost more than 16,000 feet during the incident. Al-Hammami is accused of attacking Machchhar with an emergency ax kept in the cockpit and attempting to seize control of the aircraft.
Machchhar, seriously wounded and struggling to see, said he tried to open the cockpit door to summon help.
“I did try and manage to open the [cockpit] door once, but I think he shut it back closed,” Machchhar said. “At this point, I remember I was lying down on the cockpit floor, and I felt the aircraft and the whooshing sound, and people screaming.”
He said he realized he had one final chance to act.
“I had that one last fight left in me,” he said. “Call it personal or call it for people, but I did it; if I don't do it, I'm going to die. And that's when I pushed against everything. I gave everything that I had, and just went for the door and opened the door. And thankfully, people were waiting to pounce back, took over the control, and the rest is what you know, sir.”
Machchhar has separately said he knew as he lay wounded that the aircraft was plunging and that he could not allow the passengers to die. The veteran pilot has 17 years of flying experience, including 11 as a captain.
Netanyahu asked Machchhar how he had managed to open the cockpit door.
“The door, from the inside, has a twist-to-open mechanism,” Machchhar said. “From the outside, you can only open [the door] with a code. My colleagues from outside were trying to put in the code, but the guy was not allowing to open [using] the code.”
“The only way to open the door was to reach the knob, and like any other knob, just to twist it open, and it opens on its own,” he continued. “The issue was to reach to that point. Once I had my hands on the knob, I guess I twisted it and I opened it.”
Opening the door proved decisive. Israeli passengers rushed into the cockpit and subdued al-Hammami, while others helped stabilize the aircraft until off-duty pilots aboard the flight could take control. The jet diverted to Tabuk in northwestern Saudi Arabia, where it landed safely. 
Machchhar was hospitalized with serious injuries and was later transferred to Abu Dhabi. In a separate video call with Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi, he said he recited the Hanuman Chalisa, a Hindu devotional hymn associated with strength and courage, as he struggled to get off the cockpit floor. 
Netanyahu, who has met several of the Israeli passengers credited with helping thwart the attack, told Machchhar that he wanted him honored at Israel’s annual Independence Day torch-lighting ceremony.
“It's our highest honor that we give on our Independence Day,” Netanyahu told him. “It's usually reserved for Israeli citizens, but I think here, in this case, all the citizens of Israel will embrace you. We hope to see you very soon in Israel.”
Netanyahu also said he would like Modi to participate in the ceremony. The proposal comes months before the event, and the composition of Israel’s government at the time remains uncertain.
Meanwhile, Dr. Shota Musaev, an Israeli dentist who treated Machchhar after the cockpit attack, was the guest of honor Saturday evening at Simchat Torah celebrations organized by the Chabad Jewish outreach movement in the Nahalat Yehuda neighborhood of Rishon LeZion in central Israel.
“The greatest gift we received is that we are alive, and today I can dance with the Torah scroll,” Musayev said.

Azerbaijan, Turkey and Uzbekistan join forces in major military exercise
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
19:26:46 UTC
04:26:46 KST

Thousands of military personnel from Azerbaijan, Turkey and Uzbekistan, as well as other nations participating as observers, including Iran, joined forces in the “Power of Unity, 2026” military exercise for the first time, in the Hojavend district of Azerbaijan’s Karabakh region.
Mass drone attacks, cyberattacks, disinformation and attempts to seize a vessel were among the simulations that Azerbaijan, Turkey and Uzbekistan's troops rehearsed for the first time together in Azerbaijan over the past few days, designating the current threats that the military forces of these countries are facing in the current geopolitical shifts.
More than 3,500 troops from the three countries took part in the “Power of Unity-2026” exercise, held for the first time in the Hojavend district of Azerbaijan’s Karabakh region.
Turkish Defence Minister Yaşar Güler highlighted the need for military readiness saying “we will prepare in the best possible way, but we will live in peace,” hailing the success of the exercise “in both its planning and execution”.
The simulated training ranged from drone warfare and electronic attacks to border incidents and operations at sea in a new approach to military preparedness.
In the Qızılqaya military training area troops used more than 130 unmanned vehicles, alongside over 70 armoured vehicles, more than 90 artillery systems and over 20 aviation assets.
Drones featured heavily in the training as a sign of evolving warfare, with troops training to repel drone swarm attacks, strikes on advancing military columns, surveillance and the delivery of ammunition and supplies.
The drills combined unmanned systems with artillery, armoured vehicles, aviation and electronic warfare. Troops also practised breaching defensive positions and anti-tank trenches, clearing minefields and advancing with armoured vehicles.
Beyond the conventional battlefield
The training also focused on the new challenges that have not been part of traditional military scenarios until now.
Troops responded to simulated cyberattacks and online disinformation, carried out operations against "terrorist" positions in mountainous terrain, practised clearing settlements and setting up checkpoints.
Training also involved using drones to detect and stop attempted border crossings.
Azerbaijan’s Defence Minister, Colonel General Zakir Hasanov, said the exercise included land, naval and air operations which help raise the combat readiness of the participating armies.
Uzbekistan’s Defence Minister, Lieutenant General Shukhrat Kholmukhamedov, said the participating personnel had demonstrated “high combat readiness” and the ability to carry out missions together.
From the border to the Caspian Sea
The scenarios extended beyond land operations, into the Caspian Sea, with forces practising freeing a vessel and an offshore facility, rescuing hostages and landing on the ground to neutralise a simulated terrorist base.
This exercise was held at training areas in Baku, the Karabakh region, Nakhchivan and Azerbaijan’s part of the Caspian Sea.
Azerbaijan and Turkey describe their defence relationship as an alliance under the 2021 Shusha Declaration. Azerbaijan and Uzbekistan have also expanded cooperation in military, defence-technology and military education.
Kyrgyzstan, Pakistan, Serbia, Slovakia, Tajikistan, Georgia, Turkmenistan and the United Arab Emirates, as well as Iran, attended the exercise as observers.
From Qızılqaya to Shusha
The military exercise was followed by a trilateral meeting of the defence ministers of Azerbaijan, Turkey and Georgia in Shusha.
Azerbaijan’s Defence Minister Colonel General Zakir Hasanov, Türkiye’s National Defence Minister Yaşar Güler and Georgia’s Vice Prime Minister and Defence Minister Irakli Chikovani took part in the 13th trilateral defence meeting, which focused on military cooperation, regional security and trilateral ties.
Hasanov described Azerbaijan-Georgia-Turkey cooperation as “an important platform for regional stability, security, and development”.

Unknown

India, which has recorded the maximum road deaths since such global data compilation started, registered 1.74 lakh such fatalities in 2023, and this was a little over 14% of the 12.2 lakh people who lost their lives in road crashes across the world.
NEW DELHI: ‘Road injuries’ was the eighth leading cause of deaths among males in India in 2023, and in the case of females, ‘falls’ was the eighth biggest cause of deaths, as per the latest WHO Global Health Estimates (GHE). Overall, road traffic injuries ranked the 10th leading cause of death for both males and females in India, while fatalities due to falls ranked 9th.India, which has recorded the maximum road deaths since such global data compilation started, registered 1.74 lakh such fatalities in 2023, and this was a little over 14% of the 12.2 lakh people who lost their lives in road crashes across the world. This has only increased in the past two years to reach 1.83 lakh in 2025. The figures underline the continuing scale of the road safety challenge in the country, where road crashes claim 500 lives daily.Falls in India claimed 25,150 lives, as per the National Crime Records Bureau (NCRB) data, which was around 3% of the total 8.42 lakh lives lost in such incidents. Most of the deaths due to road crashes and falls are preventable. The data also highlights the significant burden of injuries that can result in loss of life and have wider social and economic consequences for families.
As per the WHO report, globally, road traffic injuries were the 8th biggest cause of death in low-income countries and the 10th biggest in middle-income countries. Globally, it was ranked 11th, indicating that the high number of such deaths not only has a huge burden on low- and middle-income countries but also a major concern for the global community, despite many developed nations having been successful in bringing down fatalities due to road crashes.
The differences in rankings across income groups also reflect the varying burden of road injuries across countries and regions.Road safety experts have maintained that low- and middle-income countries need to find solutions to this “avoidable disaster” taking into account the local conditions, including heterogeneous road users and poorly sensitised authorities about the concept of safety of all users. They said addressing the problem would require greater attention to the safety needs of different categories of road users and a stronger focus on preventing crashes and reducing their consequences.

Remains of Bulgaria’s Czar Samuel return ‘home’ after 1,000 years
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
19:14:43 UTC
04:14:43 KST

Remains of Bulgaria’s Czar Samuel return ‘home’ after 1,000 years
The emperor is a symbol of Bulgarian national identity whose repatriation stoked tensions with Greece.
More than 1,000 years after his death, the remains of medieval ruler Czar Samuel have arrived in Bulgaria.
A symbol of Bulgarian national identity, Samuel was a warrior emperor who battled the Byzantine Empire to expand his kingdom before suffering defeat and dying soon after in 1014. His supposed remains were discovered in a Greek border area in the 1960s.
The coffin and remains were flown on Saturday to the Bulgarian capital, Sofia, on board a military aircraft that was surrounded by air force fighter jets.
Thousands of people poured into a public square to honour the czar’s arrival, which capped years of fraught negotiations between Bulgaria and Greece until an accord was reached this week.
Bulgarian politicians across the spectrum paid tribute to the medieval ruler, listening to the national anthem and a 21-gun salute.
“Today, we Europeans are learning to read history with a desire to belong not only to our homeland, but also to the culture that unites us across the entire European continent,” Bulgarian Prime Minister Rumen Radev said.
“That is why Europe must not reopen old wounds but must work for peace as the supreme good,” Radev continued, referring to the centuries-old rivalry between neighbouring Greece and Bulgaria.
Crowds cheered as fighter jets performed a flypast.
Martin Nestorov, a 42-year-old software engineer, told the AFP news agency he attended the ceremony “to welcome Czar Samuel back to Bulgaria, where he belongs”.
“I am here because I am Bulgarian, and a Bulgarian is returning to his homeland,” added Tsanka Zlatkova, 65, a retired art historian.
A procession brought the remains to be laid in the Church of Saint Sofia, a sixth-century basilica that is the capital’s namesake and where church officials say Samuel was baptised.
Competing claims
The handover of Samuel’s remains is part of a broader accord between the Greek and Bulgarian culture ministers.
In exchange, Greece is slated to receive 48 objects that Bulgarian troops pillaged from churches and monasteries in Greece during World War I.
Speaking before the handover, Greek Prime Minister Kyriakos Mitsotakis said he hoped the ceremony would boost Greece’s campaign to repatriate the Parthenon Marbles, a collection of 2,500-year-old marble sculptures taken from the Acropolis in Athens and later displayed in the British Museum.
“The global community is essentially re-evaluating its longstanding stance on protecting cultural heritage,” Mitsotakis said, adding that historical heirlooms “cannot be treated as the spoils of war”.
Bulgaria is not the only country to have claims on Samuel. A huge statue of the czar stands in the North Macedonian capital of Skopje, with Macedonians claiming him as “their” ruler.
In 2022, a bilateral commission recommended presenting Samuel as the head of a state that “most contemporary historiographers consider to be the Bulgarian Empire”, based in what is currently North Macedonia.

The G7 Is Releasing Emergency Fuel Reserves. How Much Will It Help Americans?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
19:13:51 UTC
04:13:51 KST

The Group of Seven (G7) countries said Friday that the nations would release 100 million barrels of oil and fuel products in the coming months, starting with “substantial” amounts of diesel. The move comes amid a global shortage largely attributed to slowdowns of the passage of oil through the Strait of Hormuz.
A joint statement from the G7 nations—Canada, France, Germany, Italy, Japan, the United Kingdom, and the U.S.—confirmed that the International Energy Agency (IEA) will coordinate the release over the next four months.
It calls the move a part of “decisive, coordinated measures to stabilize immediate energy supplies” amid record-high fuel prices driven by the war in Iran and the recent escalation of fighting between Russia and Ukraine.
Read More: Once Again, Energy Is Power
“Europe has just agreed to release a massive amount of their heavily stocked Diesel Oil,” President Donald Trump wrote on Truth Social on Friday. “The process will begin immediately.”
In talks leading up to the announcement on Friday, Trump had been pushing European partners for the release, citing high fuel prices for Americans. Last month, the Trump Administration threatened to temporarily suspend its exports of diesel—earning immediate backlash from countries that rely on it, including Canada, Mexico, and much of Europe.
European leaders and oil executives at the time said that such a ban would be disastrous for long-term oil flow. For that reason, experts believe the threat helped pressure those nations to release their fuel reserves.
The agreement could offer some relief for Americans even if the released diesel stays in Europe, because Europe buys some of its diesel from the U.S. Releasing European reserves could ease competition for U.S. diesel and potentially reduce prices for American buyers.
This is especially critical as the cost of Brent crude oil sits at $102 per barrel as of Oct. 3 and on-highway diesel hit a high of $6.529 per gallon as of last month, according to the U.S. Energy Information Administration.
But how much relief consumers will actually see—and how quickly—will depend on what type of fuel is released, how much reaches the market and when, and whether supply disruptions persist.
What is actually being added to the market?
Although the G7 shared how much fuel it would release, it did not specify the full breakdown of the release by fuel type. Its statement did say, however, that there will be a “frontloaded” and substantial release of diesel fuel within the first 20 days.
While crude oil must be refined into products like gasoline before consumers can use it, diesel is already a finished fuel. That means a diesel release could address the immediate shortage more directly.
The planned release could help ease shortages of both crude oil and refined fuels, with supplies disrupted by the wars in Iran and Ukraine.
The supply of crude oil has been heavily disrupted this year after the U.S. and Israel launched joint strikes that ignited a war with Iran in February. In response, Iran effectively closed the Strait of Hormuz in March. More recent negotiations to end the war have largely failed to address differing opinions on ownership and control over the Strait. This has critically restricted the passage of oil-carrying vessels through the waterway, with daily shipping traffic in the single digits last month, down from pre-war averages of roughly 138 to 140 daily transits.
Diesel, meanwhile, is essential to U.S. transportation, agriculture, and manufacturing: Most goods, food, and manufacturing supplies across the country are transported by heavy-duty trucks and trains running on diesel engines. The war in Iran has driven diesel prices up and lowered supply, but Russia and Ukraine’s targeting of one another’s energy infrastructure has further exacerbated the issue.
While the U.S. in particular does not heavily rely on Russian diesel, America is vulnerable to the volatility caused by Russia removing it from the global market. Trump has claimed outright that Ukraine’s targeting of Russian oil infrastructure is to blame for diesel shortages.
What could Americans feel, and when?
Jason Bordoff, founding director of the Center on Global Energy Policy at Columbia University, says it’s difficult to predict the consumer impact given the scarce details shared so far.
“It makes a big difference if the release is in the next two weeks or if it's four months from now,” Bordoff says.
“I think if we saw some announcement tomorrow from Germany or France that gave concrete, specific numbers for a substantial amount—50 million barrels or so—of diesel, then it could have a real impact if this release actually happens in a timely fashion,” Bordoff says.
At the same time, Jeff Colgan, a professor of political science at Brown University, cautions that American consumers may see limited benefits.
“Releasing diesel could make a difference on price, especially in tight markets in Europe,” Colgan says. “But American consumers are unlikely to see much of a price drop from this policy move unless the diesel share of that 100 million barrels is very large.”
With a timely release of diesel, Bordoff predicts that Americans could see a drop by as much as 25 cents per gallon after a few weeks—but, he adds, the markets seem pretty unsure that that will actually happen.
And market perception is central to whether or not prices drop in the short term.
“I think they’re saying: Show me the barrels, so I have confidence this is real, and it's going to happen quickly,” he says.
David Bieri, an economist and associate professor of urban affairs and planning at Virginia Tech, tells TIME that international interventions like this help “signal” to markets that governments are a credible safety net in prolonged periods of uncertainty.
“That's the main mechanism, because they want to influence market sentiment,” Bieri says. “Then, futures markets begin to price more optimistically, and then eventually the hope is that prices will come down.”
The effect Bieri is describing has already begun: The price of diesel futures in the United States fell 8% on Friday morning, a sign of more optimism in the market.
Bordoff adds that they are also, in part, a response to Trump dropping his threat of a diesel export ban—a threat that was lifted as a condition of the G7 agreement.
The release itself may not impact the markets “an awful lot,” Bieri says, given the broader context of the war with Iran.
“In fact, consumers might not necessarily notice it, ever. That's how insignificant the quantity itself is,” he says of the 100 million barrels. “But it's the importance of the cooperative signal that hopefully will make things better this fall.”
Bieri also cautions that any savings could take time to reach consumers, as carriers and other distributors may use lower fuel costs to rebuild their margins.
“[They] have been bleeding on increased fuel costs,” he says. “This is going to be, if anything, a welcome reprieve for their profit margins, and they're not going to pass that on immediately to consumers.”
What happens if the supply gap is still there when releases taper off?
This October announcement is not the first of its kind: Following the initial market shock of the war in Iran, IEA member countries announced a 400-million-barrel release in March—80% of which has already been released. Notably, the latest announcement did not clearly establish how much of the forthcoming release would be additional to earlier commitments.
In March, the IEA said that the majority of the barrel release would be crude oil; however, reports show that Europe has primarily contributed refined oil, like diesel—which could suggest more of the same in this latest round.
In either event, such fuel releases are just a matter of sticking a bandage over the larger issue of two unresolved wars and continued global energy disruption, says Bordoff.
“We're going to continue to have oil, gasoline, and diesel price shocks until that conflict comes to some sort of resolution, and energy flows can get going again,” he says. “Inventories, and stocks and other schemes like waiving state fuel taxes or something can help on the margin for temporary disruptions, but at some point this isn't temporary anymore.”
Michael Noel, economist at Texas Tech University, agrees with Bordoff, telling TIME that “unless something dramatic happens to end the Ukraine and Iran conflicts, the supply shortage will persist.”
Negotiations between Iranian leadership and the Trump Administration have stalled multiple times in the last six months. Trump said on Sept. 9 that he expected a resolution to come after the midterm elections, which take place in the U.S. on Nov. 3.
“I think the war's going to end immediately after the election because they can't hold out any longer,” he said last month. “Right after the election, oil prices are going to be tumbling downward.”
Axios reported, however, that senior Trump Administration officials met at Camp David to discuss the war on Friday. The talks come as the U.S. last week added economic pressure in the region with a series of sanctions aiming to curtail funding streams and stymy industrial lifelines for Iran.
Experts argue that the fuel crisis and volatility exposes the need for the U.S. to adapt to a changing energy ecosystem. Notably, Colgan says that would include “the national security advantages of clean technologies like EVs, batteries, and renewable energy.”

This is shown by the results of a survey conducted by the INSA polling institute for the Bild newspaper, reports UNN.
Details
Over the past week, support for the CDU/CSU across Germany fell by one percentage point to 18 percent

The rating of the Social Democratic Party of Germany (SPD), which forms the governing coalition together with the CDU/CSU, has not changed since last week and stands at 14 percent. The opposition party Alliance 90/The Greens has the same level of support, but its rating fell by one percentage point over the week. The Left Party remains at 10 percent. ‘There’s a lot of silence’: have we created a new ‘Lonely Generation’?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
19:00:07 UTC
04:00:07 KST

In September, a Reddit user identifying themselves as a 25-year-old man turned to the r/ForeverAlone subreddit with a question: How do you deal with touch starvation? “It’s becoming obvious to me that I’ll probably be alone forever,” he wrote. He used to be worried about missing out on sex, but now he just misses hugs. Cuddles.
“I don’t have many friends and none with that kind of physical relationship. I don’t really hug family either anymore. Some days, I feel so desperate for a hug with someone I love.”
On another thread, a user identifying as a 20-year-old woman took to the platform to ask if anyone else had experienced university as one of the loneliest times in their lives. “I eat lunch alone, go to class, drive home, study, and repeat,” the user wrote. “Evenings and weekends are the hardest because I crave social connection, but there’s no one to go out with or even talk to.”
Another user, on another subreddit thread, expressed that they had tried to ease their unwanted solitude, but failed. “The loneliness is unbearable,” they wrote. “Is anyone else experiencing this” No question mark. No full stop.
The answer is yes.
Around the world, young people, according to the 2025 World Health Organization Social Connection Commission report, “feel the loneliest”. Between 17 and 21% of 13-to-29-year-olds report feeling lonely, a greater proportion than any other age group, the report found. Another study, based on a survey of more than 1 million young people from 38 countries, found that youth loneliness had increased in many regions between 2002 and 2022. From Germany to Australia to the UK, studies are showing an uptick in loneliness and social isolation among teenagers and young adults.
That much of the world has produced a generation in which so many regularly feel unable to meet their needs for social connection is a curiosity which has propelled years of work for Dr Michelle Lim.
The act of learning to be one human among many has always been a lonely, discombobulating exercise in parts, she says. But in her new book, The Lonely Generation, the loneliness researcher and clinical psychologist examines exactly what has happened over this century to make many young people even lonelier.
In short, she writes, “It must be said that the nature of childhood has changed dramatically over the past few decades.”
The list of aggravating factors Lim identifies is long: our hyper-competitive education culture, digital technology, the long tail of Covid (“they’re grieving”), the shift towards smaller families, the decline of third spaces, the high cost of living, hybrid working, hybrid learning, the decline of religion, and the rise of automation which means a trip to the supermarket can be conducted entirely without speaking to another human. Young people, she argues, are being offered fewer and fewer opportunities to form meaningful connections.
“What I fear is social atrophy,” she writes. “People are getting used to being alone.”
‘Being very busy didn’t protect me’
Lim is one of the world’s pre-eminent loneliness scholars. Alongside her work as a psychologist and researcher, she leads the University of Sydney’s School of Public Health’s Social Health and Wellbeing Group, is CEO of the Australian Ending Loneliness Together campaign, is on a loneliness advisory panel to the World Health Organization and in 2020 cofounded and led the Global Initiative on Loneliness and Connection, which has since expanded to six continents.
In The Lonely Generation, she seeks to dispel myths around loneliness and expound on its many individual and societal consequences. But it is in diagnosing the cause of the “crisis” levels of youth loneliness that she spends the most time. And the first among the culprits she identifies is education.
“The current education systems are built to prioritise academic excellence from children and adolescents,” she writes. And this focus entails “hidden costs”.
After-school tutoring, high-stakes testing and well-intentioned enrolments in extensive extracurricular activities are the hallmarks of a 21st-century education. Lim says that parents tell her: “If I stop, then [my child] will fall behind and I’m not doing the best job I can.”
However, children need rest, free play and empty time in order to practise organic social interactions, says Lim – interactions which are essential to developing their fledgling social skills and a sense of identity outside their family.
“The more time you spend studying, it will come at the expense of [other] important skills,” she says. “We run the risk of raising them to be academically strong, but not socially well-equipped to manage the challenges of adulthood.”
The idea resonates with Usha Makkena, a 22-year-old student at university in Sydney.
“I think when you’re growing up with school, extracurricular activities and then later study and work, a lot of your time can become very structured and goal-oriented,” she says. “Something I realise as I’ve gotten older is that meaningful connection often develops in quite unstructured and almost unproductive times.
“And for me, being very busy certainly didn’t protect me from loneliness.”
Makkena, who is now a national reference group member for Australian youth mental health charity headspace, first started experiencing loneliness in her late teens, around her last year of high school. She did a lot of extracurricular activities and had an active social life, but she had a persistent feeling of disconnection. “What I was missing wasn’t necessarily having more people around me, but that deeper sense of feeling understood and genuinely connected to people.”
Her life did not have the contours of a lonely life. “And I think that can make it harder to recognise,” she says. “When you look at your life and you see all this happening, sometimes it makes you think ‘I shouldn’t be lonely.’”
Awkward anyway
At the high-rise campus of the University of Technology Sydney, in the centre of the city, students wander through chatting in pairs, threes. Some, solo, walk or sit with earbuds in and eyes fixed on their phones. Across the flight of stairs in the foyer of the main building are cast the words “MAKE NEW CONNECTIONS”.
Nenyasha Dongo has struggled to do as the stairs advise.
The Zimbabwean 18-year-old was excited to move to Sydney for her studies. She is a friendly person. She doesn’t want for a huge group of friends, or for parties. Three good friends would do it. But at the end of a day of classes where she didn’t really establish relationships with peers, she would return home to where every one of her five housemates were either out or had retreated to their bedrooms. “There’s a lot of silence,” she says.
“When I do get home, the loneliness,” she shakes her head. She would watch movies and TikTok to fill time until she could call family or friends back home. She carried on like this for six months. “You just have to get used to it.”
Dongo sits with Mihindi Pathinyake at a table in the sun outside a campus cafe. Around them, students and staff mill in and out. Often what the pair describe might have been a situation transplanted from university halls decades ago; the trepidatious step into a lecture hall, scanning to see who might be open to a greeting by a stranger, watching the one big group of old high school friends chat together in the front row, wondering whether the person you just spoke to might like you, might be interested in hanging out one day.
“Just to be clear, young people are just generally awkward,” laughs Lim. “They’re really awkward.”
And the transition from school to university, vocational training or work has always been an inflection point for loneliness, Lim says. Individual young people leave their highly structured environment of high school, with a set cast of characters with whom they are familiar and enter a new world populated by new – and often a vastly greater mass of – people. It is also a time when, often, the desire for a great deal of social interaction and a volume of connection is at its highest. Add to this their prefrontal cortex is still developing and adolescence has yet more years to run its course, the period can be one of flux, confusion, self-questioning and, of course, loneliness.
But this awkward rite of passage is now charged in a new way, says Lim. “Our young people in this generation are living in a world that is very different.”
‘Digital is not the enemy’
“You meet new people every day,” says Pathinayake, an exceedingly bright-eyed 20-year-old student from Sri Lanka. But she describes a new social script to developing friendships in 21st century adolescence and young adulthood.
“They take your Instagram and then you never talk to them again.”
Due to the hybrid online-real life attendance structure to many tutorials and lectures which has proliferated since Covid, it can be difficult to be sure that you may run into the same people with the frequency needed to establish organic connection.
“Sometimes following someone or reacting to something that they post can almost be a substitute for reaching out, even though those interactions don’t meet the same need,” says Makkena over a video call in late September. “And then there’s also that element of comparison.
“For me, when I was already feeling lonely, constantly seeing other people’s friendship groups or social lives could sometimes create the impression that everybody else had found their people and I somehow hadn’t.”
She is, however, wary of narratives which pit technology as the silent assassin of social connection. “It also helped me maintain relationships.”
“Social media has not been an entirely negative development”, writes Lim. While the professor is concerned about the dopamine hit from social media blunting the rewards we feel from other interactions and that, for people who are already lonely, it can embed an aversion to real-life connection, her own research has shown it can fortify young people living in communities that don’t accept them, or help others to learn about the world. “Digital use is not the enemy.”
However, she openly imagines (not happily) a future in which her own daughter might tell her that her best friend is an AI avatar. It does not feel like a big leap from what she already sees in her clinical practice, where she might be helping a young person navigate problems in their romantic relationship only to realise they have never met their boyfriend or girlfriend in real life. “It’s really common,” she says.
These virtual relationships, whether remote between human beings on separate continents or between human and AI avatar, are lower in the friction typical of in-person relationships, and entirely absent of touch.
“Humans are hard,” says Lim. “But that’s actually the beauty of relationships as well. We are being challenged, we are being pushed. Our ability to think more diversely, be empathetic are challenged by other humans.”
“Do we run the risk of getting de-socialised with real humans?”
The ‘loneliness loop’
Anxieties about the decline of social fabric and interaction – particularly for young people – have abounded for decades. Telephones and televisions were derided for their antisocial powers long before the term the “antisocial century” was coined by US writer Derek Thompson.
“But there is a sense of feeling unsafe right now, generally, whether it’s political safety around the world, or the lack of community,” says Lim. “It affects the way we see our relationships, the way we relate to people, what we choose to do.”
Lim writes about the “loneliness loop” – a particularly nasty trap for young people – by which experiencing loneliness causes the lonely person to perceive social interaction as more threatening, and so they retreat, reduce their social interaction and in doing so become more lonely.
But there is a bigger, community-wide loop too. We have settled, she writes, into a social disconnection crisis.
In The Lonely Generation, Lim imagines a world where social interaction becomes something like exercise has become today: something we once did as part of daily life, but which now we need to make a concerted effort to schedule in our diaries.
“We already see this,” says Lim. Paid-for services coming on to the market as apps or activities in order to facilitate human interaction and combat loneliness. Lim herself receives “so many” requests to endorse different offerings.
“People are capitalising on that,” she says. “This is not to say that they are not a good thing, but I think that it’s really reflective of the erosion of other kinds of social life that we once had.”
Loneliness, particularly youth loneliness, writes Lim, is a signal. A sign that we need to reassess our social world. “There is an ‘us’ problem here.
“People just go, ‘well, it’s not my responsibility’. But the problem is, actually everyone’s responsible,” she says.
“If everyone says that, then we are going to be living in a world, and raising kids in a world, where healthy social connection is ‘a nice to have’.”

The moment I knew: As a reality TV contestant, I was allowed one 15-minute call a week. Even at 3am, Chris would always pick up
Unknown
