Iran army says prepared to face any scenario
TEHRAN– Iran’s Armed Forces are closely monitoring developments and remain fully prepared to respond to any scenario, the spokesperson for the Islamic Republic of Iran Army said on Saturday, as he referred to repeated threats by the country’s adversaries.
Brigadier General Mohammad Akraminia made the remarks during a visit to the Army’s 65th Airborne Special Forces Brigade, a unit widely recognized for its specialized capabilities and role in missions requiring a high degree of operational readiness.
Highlighting the brigade’s position within Iran’s defense structure, Akraminia said its personnel, combining commitment, specialized training and operational capabilities, have turned the unit into an important asset for both the Army and the country.
He stressed that the missions assigned to the 65th Brigade extend beyond conventional tactical operations, arguing that the unit’s activities can produce consequences at the strategic level and affect Iran’s national security interests as well as the wider regional and international environment.
Against the backdrop of continued tensions and threats, the Army spokesperson said Iran’s military capabilities have been undergoing continuous development and that the Armed Forces are prepared to confront whatever circumstances may arise.
Akrami-Nia also addressed the calculations of the United States and Israel in the conflict with Iran, saying the resilience of the Iranian Armed Forces, coupled with the steadfastness of the Iranian people, had disrupted the adversaries’ calculations.
According to the Army spokesperson, the United States and Israel had initially anticipated that Iran’s defensive capabilities could be dismantled and their objectives achieved within a matter of days. He said those calculations did not materialize.
Akraminia further argued that the objectives pursued by Iran’s adversaries went beyond the country’s nuclear and missile programs or their confrontation with the Resistance Front. He said the broader objective was to undermine the Islamic Republic and fragment Iran as a country, but that none of those objectives had been achieved.
The remarks come as Iranian military officials have repeatedly emphasized the importance of maintaining a high level of readiness amid continuing regional tensions and threats of renewed confrontation. Iranian authorities have also stressed that the country’s defense posture is based on deterrence and the ability to respond to threats against its territorial integrity and national security.
The Army spokesperson attributed the Armed Forces’ ability to withstand the pressure to their faith, motivation and spirit of resistance. He also pointed to the role of public solidarity in sustaining the morale of military personnel.
Akraminia said the nightly presence of people in public squares during the conflict was not merely a manifestation of national unity and cohesion, but also had a direct psychological effect on servicemen stationed on the frontlines, strengthening their morale and determination.
His comments underscored the Iranian military’s continued emphasis on preparedness, national cohesion and the integration of specialized military capabilities into the country’s broader defense posture.

Investing in brain health
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
16:38:04 UTC
01:38:04 KST

Artificial Intelligence (AI) has spread faster than any technology in modern history. Within three years of ChatGPT’s release, generative AI has been adopted by 53 percent of the world’s population — faster than the PC and the Internet — while organizational adoption hit 88 percent last year. Global corporate investment in AI has more than doubled, with much of that money going into physical infrastructure such as data centers and power grids.
Skepticism about AI is rising almost as quickly. A survey by S&P Global found that 42 percent of companies abandoned most of their AI initiatives last year, up from 17 percent the year before, and in a recent PwC poll, 56 percent of chief executive officers reported that AI has brought their firms no measurable benefit. Communities around the world are mobilizing to prevent data centers from being built in their backyards, while documented incidents of AI harms rose by more than 55 percent last year.
However, even as governments rewrite their industrial strategies around a technology whose value they cannot yet quantify, and as investors, insisting that this time is different, drive valuations reminiscent of the dot-com boom, calls for more responsible and ethical AI are growing louder. Everyone is trying to divine the future of AI in the hope of mastering whatever comes next.
Illustration: Tania Chou
The utopian and dystopian camps suffer from the same myopia. Both assume that the future of humanity depends primarily, perhaps exclusively, on the future of AI. It does not. While optimists and pessimists alike have trained their focus on the rise of AI, they have ignored the rapid decline in brain health and brain skills.
That decline is eroding the human capacity on which every system, including AI, depends. Mental and neurological conditions, substance-use disorders, strokes and self-harm account for about one-quarter of the global disease burden. The number of people who are 65 or older living with dementia rose to 49 million in 2021 from 18.7 million in 1991 and continues to climb. Governments allocate just 2 percent of their health budgets to mental health, even after the WHO declared loneliness a “pressing health threat” in 2023.
Brain skills are in freefall too. A majority of business leaders surveyed last year by the skills training company General Assembly said entry-level employees were less prepared for their jobs than they had been five years ago, especially when it came to soft skills. Likewise, the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development’s (OECD) 2024 Survey of Adult Skills, the largest direct assessment of adult cognitive proficiency ever conducted, recorded declining or stagnant literacy across most participating countries. About 18 percent of adults in OECD countries lack basic proficiency in literacy, numeracy and problem-solving. Even among university-educated adults, proficiency fell or flatlined in most of the countries surveyed. New data from the Programme for International Student Assessment (PISA) show that student performance in reading, math, and science is declining across the OECD.
AI is fueling these trends. Emerging research suggests AI can reduce cognitive engagement, with studies finding less critical thinking and weaker neural connectivity during AI-assisted work. It can also foster over-reliance, as users sometimes accept incorrect AI outputs despite conflicting evidence or their own judgement.
Think about what this means. Just as humanity developed machines capable of taking on complex cognitive tasks, humans themselves have become less capable of performing them. The Global Brain Capital Index, which measures cognitive health and related skills, suggests that brain capital is declining at a time when trillions of dollars are being spent on AI infrastructure without a clear idea of what those investments should achieve. While a recent McKinsey Health Institute analysis estimated that the US spends about US$2.6 trillion a year on brain capital, from education to neurological care, less than 1percent of that spending goes toward disease prevention. Early intervention and research are underfunded, too.
Technological progress by itself does not make people healthier or more capable. However, the AI boom plays out, humanity would not fare well without a civilization-wide effort to rebuild brain health and cognitive skills. If AI becomes as powerful as its boosters predict, the premium on human intelligence would increase. As AI agents take over routine cognitive tasks, the value of human work would depend on qualities that machines cannot replicate, such as judgement, ethical reasoning, empathy and curiosity.
As the World Economic Forum’s employer survey last year showed, many of these human qualities are among those most in demand today and are expected to remain so through 2030. The survey also suggests that 59 percent of workers would require retraining, making investment in natural intelligence essential if human workers are to remain valuable in an AI-powered economy.
The current debate is largely focused on whether AI would save humanity or destroy it, but it could also turn out to be another technological fad. Even if the AI hype fizzles out like the metaverse craze of 2022, social and economic progress would still depend on rebuilding brain capital.
We do not need to start from scratch. Much of the necessary infrastructure already exists, thanks to those trillions of dollars already being spent on it. The challenge is to treat such investments as part of a larger system. Scaling interventions available today could give people around the world a combined 267 million additional years of healthy life by 2050 and add up to US$6.2 trillion to global GDP. Quality early-childhood programs can generate annual returns of 7 to 13 percent, while proactive investment in employee health could boost global GDP by as much as 12 percent.
That means investing in maternal and early-childhood development and shifting primary care toward preventing neurological and psychiatric disorders later in life. Workplaces can protect mental health without eroding cognitive skills, while education and professional training can be overhauled to promote lifelong learning. These are not moonshots, and there is plenty of evidence that they work.
AI itself can be part of the solution. It can enable early diagnosis of brain disorders and accelerate drug discovery. By democratizing knowledge, it can also feed curiosity and make lifelong learning easier.
The returns on brain capital do not hinge on the fate of the AI industry. Human ingenuity has economic value no matter which technology dominates the next decade. Investing in it is always a winning bet, because it is the one technology that will never become obsolete.
Harris Eyre is executive director of the Global Brain Economy Initiative. Lenny Mendonca, former chief economic and business adviser to California Governor Gavin Newsom, is senior partner emeritus at McKinsey & Company. Remington Tonar is cofounder of Cart.com.

He is an exceptional storyteller, with an ability to present a vision

Paris Fashion Week  illuminates the City of Light

Saint Laurent sent out a river of gold, as giant chandeliers bathed a glossy black outdoor runway in golden light and the Eiffel Tower shimmered in the background.
The extravagant show was attended by Catherine Deneuve, Kate Moss, Hailey Bieber and Rami Malek, while elsewhere at Paris Fashion Week Jennifer Lopez watched from Stella McCartney’s rain-soaked gardens. Rihanna turned out for the upstarts at Matieres Fecales, a conceptual fashion house whose name translates as “fecal matter.” There, the finale sent a woman in a gold lame gown across a Paris protest square carrying two slumped dummies of white men in suits.
Whatever luxury’s financial troubles, Paris retained its ability to assemble stellar front rows and social media-ready staging.
Photo: Reuters
Midway through next year’s spring-summer season, shows crystallized into three stories: glamour on a grand scale; a great undressing that stripped all the way down to a pale pink thong beneath a coat that can top US$33,000; and an industry working couture technique into T-shirts and jeans — all while asking itself, nervously, who all of this is for.
SAINT LAURENT
“Was it an adieu?” one front row guest asked.
With a decade at the house, designer Anthony Vaccarello dispensed with his customary interviews and let a retrospective-tinged collection carry the occasion.
No departure was announced — but the guessing fit the mood of an industry swapping designers at a frantic clip in search of growth.
Last month, cosmetics giant L’Oreal overtook LVMH as France’s most valuable listed company. It is the first time since 2017 that a non-luxury company has topped the Paris bourse.
Saint Laurent’s parent Kering has returned to growth after a bruising downturn, but Balenciaga remains under pressure behind the runway gloss.
Saint Laurent on Tuesday night featured gold — and it was almost the whole story: brittle, fluid, translucent or densely worked.
Gold, of course, is exactly what Kering wants from this house.
Saint Laurent, the group’s second-biggest label, is growing again on strong US and European demand, hauling the load while Gucci struggles to reverse years of falling sales.
Safari jackets and trenches came in crinkled metallic cottons. Cocktail dresses featured glinting lace, cropped jackets in brocade. Stilettos stood on serpent-shaped heels.
Then came the black finale, led by model Anja Rubik — a reversal of Yves Saint Laurent’s all-gold closing sequence in 1991.
CHLOE
Two days later, Chloe approached excess through texture.
Chemena Kamali piled broderie anglaise with lace, pearls and tassels, and sent out rainwear and long-brimmed fishermen’s hats in vivid colors.
The question was how much decoration Chloe’s promise of easy dressing could carry.
McCartney’s show rewarded its damp audience with easy tailoring, coral-like knitted forms and airbrushed dolphins on denim.
Sculptural hems and peplums gave the clothes an underwater buoyancy, while naturalist David Attenborough’s voice supplied an ocean-conservation message.
The peplum was one of the week’s quiet constants, turning up sculpted here and stitched into shirting at Balenciaga.
Air was the week’s other quiet constant, and Issey Miyake built a collection on it: dancers opened Satoshi Kondo’s show on Friday by billowing a vast cloth to live piano, before balloon-twisted dresses and nylon forms that inhaled with every step floated past — what the house calls ma, “the space in between” body and garment.
UNDERGARMENTS
Underwear was doing an increasing share of the dressing.
At Tom Ford, Haider Ackermann staged a particularly playful display: sharp tailoring accompanied by bare chests, fishnet, severely reduced swimwear and silk robes. Black swimsuits were more geometry than garment.
A male model in a sweater and pale pink thong carried a vicuna coat — the world’s most expensive wool, which can cost more than US$33,000 a coat — draped over a weekend bag.
CORSETS AND CAGES
At Balmain, Antonin Tron built a stronger second outing around midcentury backstage photographs and their air of glamorous half-dress: corset bodices, garters swinging from miniskirts, bras under shrunken satin bombers, eel skin and animal-patterned jacquards.
Simulated rain lashed the covered windows of Karl Lagerfeld’s former mansion. Printing, embroidery and sequins gave the surfaces depth, although their richness sometimes competed with the sensual draping.
Even Rick Owens went boudoir, on his own terms: On a ramp across the Palais de Tokyo’s reflecting pool, he sent out stone-colored column gowns, spiked tulle, crystal-laden footwear and full-body constructions of tulle and elastic.
The cages turned literal at Courreges, where Drew Henry’s debut broke up its neon tailoring with floral bra tops, flower-dotted cage jumpsuits and hotpants.
LUXURY TRIMMINGS
The question beneath it all was harder to stage: in a downturn, how does luxury justify itself?
Pierpaolo Piccioli’s answer at Balenciaga was technique.
Dense rows of stitching shaped a white shirt into a fitted waist and flaring peplum.
A T-shirt received a similar treatment. Jeans were cut on the bias — diagonally across the fabric — to change their fall.
The collection made a persuasive case for putting couture knowledge to everyday use.
Loewe, entering its 180th year, answered more plainly still: fewer technical fireworks, more supple leather and glass-bead dresses — clothes made to be worn rather than talked about.
Luxury’s answer to the squeeze? Not lower prices — but craft moved into the clothes people live in, so the cost feels earned.
MATIERES FECALES
The new it-brand took over Paris’ protest area, Place de la Republique, for a show titled “The 99 Percent.”
The collection brought together sari-inspired draping, shredded denim and figures styled to evoke masked demonstrators.
While public access was part of the idea, the irony was hard to miss: 99 percent of the world cannot afford Matieres Fecales’ clothes.
The 99 percent have been voting with their wallets: Pinched by inflation and prices up some 20 percent in two years, about 60 million customers have abandoned luxury since 2022, said consultancy Bain & Company — which said that even the wealthy clients who remain feel “betrayed.”
Paris had demonstrated how to make people look, but it is the clothes, the industry hopes, that could persuade them to spend.

IEA says 325m oil barrels released by members’ reserves
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
16:38:03 UTC
01:38:03 KST

The International Energy Agency (IEA) yesterday said member countries had so far released 325 million barrels of oil and oil-derivative products from strategic reserves, up from 400 million barrels promised in March.
The update came a day after G7 countries, in coordination with the IEA, agreed to immediately release 100 million barrels of diesel and crude oil to ease global energy supply concerns caused by the fallout from the US-Iran war.
The G7 did not say whether the 100 million barrels included the outstanding 75 million barrels from the March IEA commitment, or came on top of that.
Photo: AFP
The government of US President Donald Trump has been pressuring allies to release diesel reserves to ease a spike in prices for the fuel, being felt in the US and elsewhere.
Restricted diesel supplies is one of the consequences of the war in the Middle East, where Iran has been throttling ship traffic through the Strait of Hormuz in retaliation for US and Israeli attacks.
Ukrainian strikes on Russian refineries, part of the fightback against Moscow’s strikes, have also affected the market.
“Around 325 million barrels of the IEA collective action announced on 11 March have so far been released, representing over 80 percent of the 400 million barrels originally pledged in the action,” the IEA said.
The March pledge was offered up by the IEA’s 32 member countries, a grouping that includes all the G7 nations.
The G7 countries on Friday agreed to release over the next four months 100 million barrels of oil and oil-derivative products, “including a frontloaded substantial diesel release within the first 20 days.”

China overtakes US in Latin America influence
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
16:38:02 UTC
01:38:02 KST

China’s influence in Latin America is now viewed more positively than that of the US, a major poll conducted in 17 Latin American countries showed on Friday.
China overtook the US in terms of influence for the first time since the annual Latinobarometro survey began in 1995.
It showed 57 percent of people in Latin America considering the US to be a positive influence, down from 60 percent in 2020.
Photo: AP
Meanwhile, China was considered a positive influence by 65 percent of respondents, a jump from 48 percent six years ago.
Costa Rica and the Dominican Republic were the only countries in the region where US influence was deemed more positive than that of China.
The report partly attributed the shift to Washington’s “almost complete absence” from the region after the 2003 Iraq War.
During that time, Latin America “drew closer to other powers, to China, to the EU, to Japan,” Latinobarometer director Marta Lagos said.
China had won over Latin American populations by allowing them to access cheaper imports, Lagos said.
“The void that China fills is the void in people’s pockets, more than anything else,” she added.
The growing disaffection for the US comes nearly halfway through US President Donald Trump’s second term, during which he has openly asserted his desire for hegemony over Latin America.
The US remains more popular than China, with 63 percent saying they had a favorable view of the world’s top economy, compared with 58 percent for its arch-rival, but its popularity was markedly down compared to 2024, under then-US president Joe Biden, when 73 percent had a favorable view of the US.
Trump’s push to restore US dominance in what Washington calls “our hemisphere” was in evident in January when the US overthrew then-Venezuelan president Nicolas Maduro.
Majority of people in all but one country — Argentina — approved of Maduro’s capture by US special forces, the poll showed.
However, only 35 percent believed it benefited Venezuela, compared with 28 percent who said it harmed the Caribbean country, the poll showed.
Venezuelans were among those who viewed US influence most positively.

Drones developed by US-Taiwan collaboration unveiled
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
16:38:01 UTC
01:38:01 KST

US-based AEVEX Aerospace on Friday showcased two drones developed in collaboration with Taiwanese drone maker Coretronic Intelligent Robotics (CIRC), and said it planned to expand operations in Taiwan.
The two companies are technology-transfer partners collaborating to develop products for export, CIRC president Wu Hsiu-hui (吳秀蕙) said.
The two models, named Vandal and Onyx, have been tested in Ukraine, AEVEX said.
Photo: Wu Che-yu, Taipei Times
AEVEX is best known for its Phoenix Ghost one-way attack drones, which have been supplied to Ukraine and used in combat since 2022.
The drones are manufactured using 3D printing and can be produced quickly in large quantities, the company said, adding that their capabilities could attract interest from the military.
The Vandal is designed for intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance missions, but can also be used as a one-way attack drone. It has an operational range of 486km, an endurance of more than 3.5 hours and a payload capacity of 4.5kg.
The Onyx has an operational range of 270km and an endurance of more than 2.8 hours. It has a payload capacity of 13.6kg and can also be used as a one-way attack drone.
AEVEX’s strengths included not only its systems’ performance, but also its innovation and ability to quickly develop and manufacture products using technologies such as 3D printing, Wu said.
The partnership combines US technology with Taiwan’s manufacturing capabilities to develop autonomous systems for export, Wu said.
CIRC is more than a supplier to AEVEX, she said.
AEVEX was particularly interested in CIRC’s optical payload designs, which are developed and manufactured in-house and meet international standards, she said.
The designs could be incorporated into products for export once mass production begins, she added.
The companies have completed the technology transfer in compliance with US export-control regulations, Wu said.
CIRC’s decision to announce the partnership to the public showed that the products were ready and that the companies had clear plans to bid for Taiwanese military contracts and seek customers overseas, she said.
CIRC has delivered 3,000 drones to the government in one year to support military operations, she said.
The company’s drone production facility in Miaoli County’s Jhunan Township (竹南) is planned to produce 4,000 drones monthly, with further expansion pending future market demand, she added.

EDITORIAL: Resilience, at home and beyond
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
16:38:00 UTC
01:38:00 KST

Harun Talha Ayanoglu, a visiting research fellow at the Institute for National Defense and Security Research (INDSR), usually writes about materiel and defense issues. In “What does resilience even mean?” published on this page on June 21 this year, he explored the concept of resilience from a wider perspective, and concluded that, at its most fundamental, it was about people.
Rather than offering solutions, the article was about broadening the scope of the debate to facilitating the participation of immigrant communities and migrant workers in the provisions for societal resilience in the event of natural disasters or national security crises. Just as national debate focuses on weapons procurement and whether US President Donald Trump would release a US$14 billion arms package to help the nation resist an attack from China’s People’s Liberation Army (PLA), other minds are concentrated on how the government can bolster resilience within local communities, through ensuring that systems, basic infrastructure and levels of morale are maintained.
Over the past week, this page has included articles discussing aspects such as medical and energy resilience, as well as how the government can take technologies such as drones into consideration in resilience planning. The article “Resilience comes from redundancy” by Yasuyuki Ishida, a Japanese scholar focusing on maritime security, published on this page today extends the idea of resilience further out into the region, along the First Island Chain. Together, these articles explore the complex, multi-layered approach to how we might answer Ayanoglu’s question.
In “Taiwan needs medical resilience” (Sept. 24, page 8), National Taiwan University graduate healthcare policy researcher Hanson Wu (吳宗翰) wrote about how medical resilience should be viewed not only as a healthcare issue, but as “a pillar of civilian resilience.” He imagines a society under pressure from attack or a sustained blockade from the PLA and how, just as defending the nation against missiles, ensuring that hospitals remain operational and medical supplies remain available when supply chains come under strain is essential.
Wu includes considerations of maintaining medical services, adequate supplies of medicines with a variety of storage requirements, and the logistics of distribution and access in challenging situations over sustained periods, but he also writes about how a system breakdown would weaken society’s willingness and ability to endure, as well as how cohesion and resilience could become vulnerable when people lose confidence in essential services. He adds that this potential vulnerability is exactly what a hostile external force would be seeking to exploit by extended blockades or “quarantining” Taiwan, stopping short of an actual invasion, but providing a route to its objective nevertheless.
As Wu says, “a coercive campaign succeeds when disruption turns into exhaustion and exhaustion becomes political pressure.” He also cautions that to ensure medical resilience, arrangements should be tested during peacetime, not improvised under pressure.
Part of these arrangements would necessitate building a degree of redundancy into the system, where shortages from one source or compromised system could be obtained from another.
In “We need civilian energy resilience” (Oct. 1, page 8), INDSR visiting researcher Phoebe Pham (范菲比) and policy analyst Lin Jun-rong (林均蓉) argued that energy resilience is a participatory process, not just a top-down planning problem, and requires cooperation from all levels of society — from government to industry and civil organizations to people on the ground, including careful consideration of how to facilitate communication and synergy between these groups. They write of the importance of clarity of who does what “when the grid goes dark,” and how trust could turn “local capacity into national endurance.”
Returning to his field of expertise, Ayanoglu explores in “Drone strategy beyond production” (Sept. 29, page 8) what must be done if Taiwan is to be able to effectively utilize the drones that it is manufacturing in the event of an emergency, including integration into operations and command structures.
Finally, Ishida proposes building resilience — not only in terms of military capability, but also in terms of disaster response and economic resilience — into the First Island Chain, through coordination with Tokyo and eventually Manila, regarding it as a collection of nodes within a coordinated network that creates resilience out of redundancy in the region, in the same way that Wu views the concept of redundancy to be crucial to medial resilience on the local level.
In 40 years of watching politics, I have never seen anything quite like Taipei mayoral candidate Puma Shen’s (沈伯洋) breed of politician. He has a presence that commands attention, and a combination of qualities that appear to be the result of powerful political currents. What is it that makes Shen different? Throughout the past decades of local elections, I have not seen anyone seriously discuss a long-term vision for urban planning, let alone with the kind of clarity and insight that Shen possesses that compels people to keep listening. He is an exceptional storyteller, with an ability to present a vision
If Taiwan falls, the true battle moves from the beaches into the concrete streets. Western analysts fixate on the invasion phase. They end wargames when missiles stop flying and submit policy papers after the fate of a beachhead is decided. This narrow focus ignores the grim reality of “the day after.” To address this blind spot, the Irregular Warfare Center (IWC) published a seminal study on March 5, 2026, titled China’s Way of Occupation: Implications for Taiwan. Authored by Jan K. Gleiman and others, the report analyzes Beijing’s actions in Tibet, Xinjiang (East Turkestan), and Hong Kong to expose a chilling playbook

The use of AI in creative and academic work has become increasingly common. NSYSU designated southern Taiwan’s national drone center
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
16:37:59 UTC
01:37:59 KST

National Sun Yat-sen University (NSYSU) has been designated by the Ministry of Education as southern Taiwan’s only national drone center as the government seeks to bolster domestic drone development and reduce reliance on Chinese supply chains.
The university recently won two three-year projects including key technologies and applications for commercial-grade military drones and the establishment of a national regional drone soccer center.
The projects aim to train domestic talent to address a shortage of specialists in advanced drone research and development, as well as practical drone operation and management, the university said on Thursday.
Photo courtesy of the Military News Agency
The university’s location gives it access to coastal, lowland and mountainous terrain, providing varied and challenging environments for drone testing and training, it said.
Students would learn to operate drones in complex terrain, gaining skills that could prove valuable in military applications, it said.
The programs would also train personnel in intelligent mobility, autonomous artificial intelligence (AI) systems and emerging defense technologies, it added.
The university’s research team has developed technology capable of transmitting 1080p high-definition video over distances of more than 100km, meeting military requirements for long-range communications.
The technology also features military-grade anti-jamming capabilities, AI-powered autonomous mission execution, and automatic takeoff and landing, the university said.
The technologies would be incorporated into courses and practical training, giving students experience with defense systems designed to meet industry standards and military requirements, it said.
National Sun Yat-sen University president Lee Chih-peng (李智鵬) said developing indigenous technologies and bolstering defense self-reliance were key priorities for Taiwan.
The university plans to combine expertise in information engineering, telecommunications, automatic control, AI, mechatronics and hydrogen fuel cells, while working with industry, government and research institutions to train specialists for Taiwan’s drone industry, Lee said.

====================================================================================================

Overstating credentials a lack of authenticity
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
16:37:58 UTC
01:37:58 KST

As the dust has yet to settle on the controversy over Taipei Mayor Chiang Wan-an’s (蔣萬安) supposed doctorate, the Legislative Yuan has chosen the perfect timing to amend Chiang’s educational credentials in his former legislator’s profile.
The label of Doctor of Juridical Science (S.J.D.) that persisted for years was subsequently amended to the lesser degree of Juris Doctor (J.D.) overnight. Chiang holds an Master of Laws and a J.D. from the University of Pennsylvania’s law school, and he and the Taipei City Government say the S.J.D. label was a translation error by a Legislative Yuan contractor. Obfuscation and blame-shifting really is the gift that keeps on giving.
It does not matter if a politician holds a doctorate, whether a legislator, mayor or even president. John F. Kennedy, Ronald Reagan and US President Donald Trump — US presidents of past and present — never earned a doctorate, and I doubt Americans felt ashamed of the presidents’ lack of one.
So one does wonder about where the Taiwanese obsession with political figures having a doctorate comes from. Never mind the large number of politicians brandishing doctorates of dubious veracity from Chinese universities; even a genuine, bona fide doctorate proves little.
Chinese Nationalist Party (KMT) Legislator Weng Hsiao-ling (翁曉玲) holds a doctorate in law from the renowned University of Munich in Germany. One would assume that someone with that background should possess a better grasp of the law than an undergraduate, yet back in 2024, she interpreted the legislators’ power to question the premier as a “top-down relationship.”
Anyone who has taken a close look at the shoddy bills Weng has proposed would hardly consider them to uphold the sanctity of the law, but rather undermining it. So much for being the holder of a prestigious doctorate.
What is intriguing is not whether Chiang holds a doctorate, but the more fundamental issue of whether he has been honest about his highest degree. Former US president Barack Obama holds a J.D. from Harvard Law School, which he received in 1991. Even though the word “doctor” appears in the title, the convention among US lawyers is that J.D. holders do not refer to themselves as “Dr.” While running for president, Obama did not style himself that way, and no news outlet ever called him “Dr. Obama.”
The “Silicon Valley lawyer” Chiang — who spent more than a decade in the US — should know that he cannot and should not parade his “Dr.” status in the Taiwanese political arena. Otherwise, it is inevitable that he would be suspected of a political chicanery. Even if the title was born from media attention, a politician of integrity would have jumped at the first opportunity to set the record straight.
Allowing the charade to continue is deception by omission, and the same applies to Chiang’s intransigence in the face of calls by Kuo Yi-hsi (郭貽熹) — son of the late army general Kuo Li-po (郭禮伯) — for a DNA test to settle whether Chiang’s father, former KMT vice chairperson John Chiang (蔣孝嚴), is in fact Kuo’s son rather than that of former president Chiang Ching-kuo (蔣經國), as he claims.
Honesty truly is the best policy. It does not matter whether Chiang holds a doctorate or descends from the Chiang bloodline, because neither has a bearing on his academic ability or competence as a politician. However, given that he has long cultivated the political persona of a “Dr.” and a Chiang descendant, the verdict on whether he is an upright and honest politician lies in the authenticity of these two identities.
Chang Kuo-tsai is a retired associate professor at National Hsinchu University of Education.
Translated by Wilson Ng

Philippines receives vessel donated by coast guard
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
16:37:58 UTC
01:37:58 KST

A patrol vessel donated by the Coast Guard Administration (CGA) to the Philippines was commissioned into the Philippine Coast Guard (PCG) on Friday, a Philippine non-governmental organization said.
The CGA on Sept. 16 confirmed media reports that Taiwan had donated a retired 500-tonne patrol vessel to the Philippines. The Manila-based We Protect Our Seas (WPS) foundation, which served as an intermediary in the transfer, said that the vessel was formerly the CGA’s 500-tonne petrol vessel Kinmen (CG123).
The WPS, in a statement issued on Friday, said the vessel, renamed as the BRP Sarangani, had been commissioned into the PCG the same day.
Photo: Screen grab from the WPS Foundation’ s Facebook page
The vessel is about 61m long and 11.7m wide, with a full-load displacement of about 688 tonnes, the foundation said.
“It gives the PCG an additional platform for maritime patrols, search and rescue, humanitarian assistance and disaster response, marine environmental protection, training, and other civilian missions,” it said.
The donation reflects how far maritime cooperation between the peoples of Taiwan and the Philippines has come since the “difficult” 2013 incident involving a Taiwanese fishing vessel, the statement said, alluding to the fatal shooting by the PCG of a Taiwanese fisherman aboard his vessel, which was operating in an area where the exclusive economic zones of the two countries overlap.
“Both sides have since worked to prevent similar incidents and to build cooperation in areas such as maritime safety, and search and rescue,” the WPS said.
WPS president and CEO Jeffrey Ordaniel said the parties involved “began discussing the possible donation and transfer in December 2025.”
“It took months of quiet discussions and coordination to get it across the finish line,” he said.
“One of the main challenges was navigating the political sensitivities surrounding the Philippines’ ‘one China’ policy,” he said, adding there had been no violation of the policy throughout the transfer.
The organization also had to work through funding issues related to the ship’s refurbishment, Ordaniel said.
“In the end, we were able to secure the transfer at no cost to the Philippine government,” he said.
He said the ship would be deployed in Mindanao to help secure shipping routes and the maritime environment in the area, adding that “the vessel transfer certainly advanced the friendship and shared values of the people of both sides of the Luzon Strait.”
The WPS Foundation on its Web site says that it seeks to advance “principled approaches” to resolving maritime disputes in the Philippine and South China seas through research and dialogue with academia, public policy, military and industry.
It is also the coordinating organization of the Manila Dialogue on the South China Sea and the Dialogue on ASEAN Maritime Security.

Smithsonian looks to AI to help tie back to past
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
16:37:58 UTC
01:37:58 KST

The distance in the march from the American Revolution to the age of artificial intelligence (AI) is a vast gulf. Now, leaders of the Smithsonian Institution are using AI to bridge the divide.
As the US celebrates its 250th anniversary of independence, Smithsonian leaders are turning to AI to better understand items in its collection tied to the war that led to the country’s founding.
The goal is to allow the public and scholars to search the institution’s collection and draw connections across the Smithsonian and other organizations, such as the Library of Congress, to gain a deeper sense of how communities formed and functioned at the nation’s birth.
Photo: AP
Since researchers on the project, known as Revolution Crossroads, began applying AI models in the spring, they have quickly drawn links that would have previously required extensive manual searches across multiple catalogs. For example, they located a silversmith who was running newspaper advertisements for a creamer around 1774, similar to one held at the Smithsonian’s National Museum of American History.
The ultimate ambition is to scour records and uncover new stories about people whose lives have faded away over the centuries.
“An ideal scenario is that we get to a place where we’re actually adding to the public record,” said Becky Kobberod, the chief digital and innovation officer at the Smithsonian. “Maybe they’re not Thomas Jefferson or George Washington, but they did live in a community and build that community, and that name is now known.”
Since its founding in 1846, the Smithsonian has curated the nation’s history and culture across an operation that spans 21 museums and galleries, including the National Zoo. It is a role that has taken on new significance as US President Donald Trump has questioned some of the institution’s portrayals.
Kobberod’s team has identified about 10,000 objects centered on people who lived during the 40-year period from 1770 to 1810. They have had to digitize — and in some cases redigitize — the objects to make them more accessible to AI. The public can search the records online.
For Natalie Buda Smith, the director of digital strategy at the US Library of Congress, the project is a reminder that these institutions are deeply engaged in rapidly evolving technology. This work can help people researching materials who do not know whether to begin at the Smithsonian, the Library of Congress or somewhere else, she said.
The creamer example “illustrates that there’s a richness out there and you might find part of the story at the Smithsonian and part of the story at the library,” she said. “Open up those doors to people so they can understand, because they found it in the Smithsonian doesn’t mean it’s the end of the story.”
The work is unfolding at a sensitive time in the debate over how to properly harness AI. Some of the industry’s top leaders have issued increasingly dire warnings about the technology’s ability to harm. Many were in Washington this week, where they met with Trump and signed a voluntary accord for reviews. Democrats and some Republicans are calling for a more robust response, including stronger regulation of AI.
Kobberod, the first person to hold her role at the Smithsonian, acknowledged a “healthy fear” of AI. She said the Smithsonian is not using any of the frontier models that have received much of the scrutiny in the past few weeks. She emphasized the importance of human oversight in the research, saying that trained historians review the data and can recognize nuance that would be lost on an AI agent.
“What they might say is, ‘actually that is a known nickname for so-and-so’ or ‘that is a generic term that’s used for X, Y, Z,” she said. “That is the nuance that a historian or someone who’s spent their whole career studying that time period is going to know that a machine is not.”
She said it is important to embrace the possibilities that surround AI.
“It’s not going away,” she said. “We do believe we need to lean in and figure out the part that this technology plays in our work.”

Unknown
Unknown Publisher

16:37:57 UTC
01:37:57 KST

North Korea yesterday said it test-fired an intermediate-range ballistic missile that it claimed has maneuverable flight capabilities designed to evade missile defenses in South Korea and Japan.
The latest test comes amid heightened tensions between the two Koreas over border land mine blasts.
Kim Yo-jong, sister of North Korean leader Kim Jong-un, said her brother supervised the test of the missile, which she described as strategic, implying it was designed to deliver nuclear weapons.
Photo: EPA
It could change its flight trajectory at low altitudes and was equipped with unspecified artificial intelligence capabilities that would make it highly difficult to intercept, she added.
Japan’s military said the missile landed in waters outside its exclusive economic zone.
The South Korean military did not immediately comment on Kim’s claims.
The South Korean Joint Chiefs of Staff early yesterday said it detected the North Korean missile being launched from the eastern coastal Wonsan area and flying more than 700km.
The Japanese Ministry of Defense said it detected the missile flying about 680km.
Kim Yo-jong said the differing flight details proved the two countries could not properly track the missile in flight.
“Whenever we applied the wavelike trajectory mode to missiles, the enemy failed to track the targets from their first skip points,” she said. “There is no way to avoid this attack.”
The launch came a day after she ridiculed South Korean demands for the North to apologize over the Sept. 21 land mine blasts, which occurred about 10m south of the countries’ military demarcation line, injuring three South Korean soldiers.
South Korea said a joint inspection of the site with the UN Command found the blasts were caused by mines planted by North Korea.
The command later determined that the North contravened the armistice agreement that ended fighting in the Korean War.
The South has also called on the North to halt its recent border fortification efforts, including the installation of mines and anti-tank barriers, which have accelerated after Kim Jong-un in 2024 abandoned his government’s long-standing goal of reconciliation with the South and declared Seoul a permanent adversary.
Kim Yo-jong dismissed Seoul’s demands over the mine blasts as “utterly pathetic,” saying the North intends to cut ties with the South forever.
Yesterday’s launch was the latest in a series of North Korean military displays over the past few weeks, including missile tests, live-fire exercises and the commissioning of a new warship.
South Korea said its military stepped up surveillance and vigilance for possible further launches from the North and was closely sharing information with the US and Japan.
Seoul called for Pyongyang to halt its ballistic launches, calling them a violation of UN Security Council sanctions and a “serious act that does nothing to help manage the current situation.”

====================================================================================================

Slow-moving wave threatens more damage to US West Coast
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
16:37:56 UTC
01:37:56 KST

Sea levels in California are set to rise by as much as a foot (30cm) in the coming days as an enormous wave washes up the US West Coast.
The huge surge of energy, known as a “coastal trapped wave” or a “Kelvin wave,” is part of El Nino, a months-long phenomenon in the Pacific Ocean that scientists say could generate powerful storms and floods in some parts of the world, while leaving others in drought.
The Kelvin wave is not anything like a tsunami; nor does it crash on beaches. Rather it is a sustained bulge of excess water up to 30km wide that should hug the coastline as it travels all the way up to Alaska.
Photo: AFP
Dillon Amaya, an oceanographer at North Carolina State University, said the elevated sea levels could combine with other natural phenomena to create problems for coastal communities.
“What this wave is doing is it’s raising sea states, and then when... you combine this wave with things like storm surge from passing weather, large swells, or things like astronomically high tide... [you] elevate your risk for things like flooding and also beach erosion,” Amaya said in a phone interview.
“The general rule of thumb is that every two to four inches [5-10cm] of sea level rise that we see in that background state essentially doubles your flood risk,” he said. “So it doesn’t sound like a lot, but because it’s over a huge volume of water, and it’s combined with these other factors, you start to get the flood risk.”
In the past few weeks parts of southern California have been hit by storm surges that have eaten away at beaches or damaged properties.
In Dana Point and Laguna Beach, south of Los Angeles, several houses have been rendered uninhabitable, and at least one has completely collapsed.
In Malibu, an enormous sinkhole formed in the driveway of a house belonging to actor Nicolas Cage when pounding waves from a hurricane eroded the coastline.
The Kelvin wave is both a cause and a symptom of El Nino, said Amaya, adding that it originates in waters near Indonesia when trade winds die down.
“Those trade winds hold up a ton of really warm water in the Western Equatorial Pacific because they’re pushing on the surface waters as they blow. “If they weaken for too long... water is then able to effectively slosh back along the equatorial strip from Indonesia all the way to South America.”
As this wave makes its way across the Pacific, it suppresses the cold water that usually comes up from the deep ocean, making the surface temperature higher.
It is this ocean warming that we call El Nino.
“So these Kelvin waves are, in many ways, the driving force of El Nino. They help El Nino grow and mature over the course of several months,” said Amaya.
As the equatorial Kelvin wave hits South America, the energy converts into a coastal Kelvin wave, and heads both north and south along the continents.
The wave going toward the US is somewhere north of Cabo, Mexico, and travelling about 6mph (10kph), said Amaya, who expects it to reach San Diego within the next week.
While Kelvin waves are common — there are five or six during every El Nino — this one arrives at a delicate time, said Amaya, with sea temperatures already elevated.
“When it gets really warm, that water expands... which causes sea levels to rise just because the water is warm, so you get an additional additive increase in sea level,” he said. “Southern California... just got battered by offshore tropical cyclones, which led to flooding events already and beach erosion, so there’s lots of anxiety about extra flood risk coming from El Nino and these waves.”

Photo courtesy the Ministry of Foreign Affairs

American Institute in Taiwan Washington Office Managing Director Ingrid Larson is scheduled to visit Phoenix to accompany the delegation, they said.

TSMC’s expansion in the US also proved that Taiwan’s advanced semiconductor industry is capable of proactively and strategically positioning itself globally, they added.
As Taiwanese enterprises expand into the US, they are steadily building up Taiwan’s manufacturing and supply chain integration capabilities, the source said, adding that combined with US innovation, capital and market scale, it would create local opportunities for employment, talent development and industrial collaboration.
The office in Phoenix marks Taiwan’s 14th diplomatic mission in the US, they said.
As Taiwanese businesses continue to expand their investments and footprint in Arizona, so must diplomatic services, extending beyond consular and overseas community affairs to encompass industry, trade and local government cooperation, the source said.
Taiwan can better respond to the needs of businesses through the overseas missions, they added.
Over the past few years, the US has also repeatedly encouraged state governments and businesses to deepen relations with Taiwan, which shows that Taiwan-US exchanges have moved from the federal level to state governments, cities, industries and civic society, the source said.

Unknown
Unknown Publisher

16:37:52 UTC
01:37:52 KST

A US senator has urged Washington to counter Chinese pressure on countries to restrict Taiwanese presidential flights, warning that such tactics could threaten international travelers.
At a US Senate Foreign Relations Committee nominations hearing on Wednesday, US Senator Tammy Duckworth questioned Marc Dillard, the nominee for US ambassador to Madagascar and Comoros, about Beijing’s efforts to isolate Taiwan.
She said that Madagascar, Mauritius and Seychelles in April revoked permission for President William Lai’s (賴清德) plane to fly through the airspace they managed, delaying his visit to Taiwan’s diplomatic ally Eswatini, and that the revocation was at China’s behest.
Photo: Reuters
Madagascar and Mauritius subsequently interfered with his return journey, she said, adding that the restrictions contravened International Civil Aviation Organization rules.
Duckworth said Taiwanese officials had repeatedly raised the issue during her recent visit to the nation.
“These reckless actions could endanger everyone who travels internationally,” she said, warning that Chinese President Xi Jinping’s (習近平) next target could be aircraft that carry civilians or critical supplies.
Dillard, currently serving as deputy chief of mission at the US Embassy in South Africa, said Madagascar’s withdrawal of clearance had a limited impact on Lai’s flight, but reflected Beijing’s broader intimidation tactics.
“And in this case, I believe [it] clearly undermined Madagascar’s sovereign foreign policy decisions,” he said.
Dillard added that if confirmed, he would engage Madagascar’s government on the risks of deepening ties with China and the advantages of working with the US as a trusted partner.
Duckworth challenged Dillard’s characterization of the disruption as “limited,” adding that Lai needed to change his flight path.
She said that her concern extended beyond the immediate consequences for one trip to whether countries honored international aviation arrangements.
“We can’t let that happen, because if it happens here, it’s going to happen in other places with territorial waters, with international trade,” she said.
In a statement on Thursday, Duckworth’s office said the episode underscored the urgent need for US support for Taiwan against Chinese pressure.

Manila, Taipei monitor China’s ships
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
16:37:49 UTC
01:37:49 KST

The Coast Guard Administration (CGA) yesterday confirmed that it had recently deployed three patrol vessels to waters in Taiwan’s overlapping exclusive economic zone with the Philippines to monitor three Chinese vessels.
CGA Deputy Director-General Hsieh Ching-chin (謝慶欽) said the agency regularly monitors Chinese vessels around Taiwan, and that the deployment south of Oluanpi (鵝鑾鼻), Taiwan proper’s southernmost point, was carried out in accordance with standard procedures.
He added that the waters fall within the overlapping exclusive economic zones of Taiwan and the Philippines, which extend 200 nautical miles (370km) from their coastlines.
Photo: CNA
Hsieh made the comments when asked about a statement on Friday by Philippine Coast Guard (PCG) spokesman Jay Tarriela that three Taiwanese vessels were operating near the BRP Teresa Magbanua while it was monitoring three Chinese vessels — a survey ship and two China Coast Guard vessels.
The Chinese research ship, Jia Hai Ke 7 (嘉海科7), has moved north from its loitering position toward the outer limit of the Philippine exclusive economic zone in the Luzon Strait, Tarriela said in a social media post.
The PCG has deployed the BRP Teresa Magbanua to shadow the three Chinese vessels, he said.
The three Taiwanese coast guard vessels were about 0.89, 1.18 and 5.45 nautical miles (1.6km, 2.2km and 10.1km) off the BRP Teresa Magbanua’s port bow respectively, he added.
Beijing sent two China Coast Guard vessels to escort a “supposedly private research ship,” Tarriela said. “This shows again that Jia Hai Ke 7 is not operating on its own.”
“A government law enforcement fleet does not escort a commercial survey ship unless that ship’s mission serves the interests of the state,” he said.
Jia Hai Ke 7, which “spoofed its automatic identification system position to hide its movement,” is a seabed-survey ship that held station for four days in waters crossed by critical submarine cable corridors, he said.
The presence of other maritime law enforcement vessels in the area shows that concerns over this vessel go beyond the Philippines, he said, adding the safety of undersea communications infrastructure in the Luzon Strait matters to the entire region.
The Chinese vessel did not ask for permission to conduct marine scientific research in the Philippine exclusive economic zone, he said.
The BRP Teresa Magbanua would remain in the area and continue to monitor the Chinese vessels, he said.
The PCG would continue to track Jia Hai Ke 7’s movements to “make sure it does not return to Philippine waters to resume unauthorized activities,” he added.
Asked whether the appearance of three Taiwanese coast guard vessels in the Bashi Channel indicated coordinated operations between Taiwanese and Philippine maritime law enforcement agencies, former Philippine Navy vice commander Rommel Jude Ong said the deployments should be seen as separate monitoring missions rather than a joint operation.
Conducting substantive coordination would pose significant logistical challenges for both sides, he added.
Speaking about the strategic importance of the Bashi Channel, he said that in the event of a Chinese attack on Taiwan, the Chinese People’s Liberation Army could seek to seize control of Port of Kaohsiung.
Doing so would require control of the Bashi Channel, while the Batanes Islands could serve as a strategic constraint on such an operation, he said.
That would help explain the Philippines’ increased military presence in the north and its decision to shift some military exercises toward the region, he added.
Tarriela previously said that undersea cables linking the Philippines with northeast Asia and the broader Indo-Pacific region run through waters near the Batanes Islands and the Luzon Strait.
Prolonged loitering by survey vessels in fixed locations could pose a risk to the security of undersea communications infrastructure, while data collected by such vessels could be used for military purposes, Tarriela said.
Military experts have also called the Bashi Channel a key chokepoint connecting the South China Sea and the Pacific Ocean, as well as a vital route to Taiwan’s east coast, with depths exceeding 5,000m that allow submarines to potentially transit undetected.

Taiwan, UK sign science, tech pact for three projects
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
16:37:48 UTC
01:37:48 KST

Taiwan and the UK have signed an agreement to pursue projects in satellite communications, silicon photonics and semiconductor talent development, the National Science and Technology Council (NSTC) said yesterday.
The Taiwan-UK Science, Innovation and Technology Arrangement (SITA) was on Friday signed in London by Representative to the UK Vincent Yao (姚金祥) and British Representative to Taiwan Ruth Bradley-Jones, the NSTC said in a news release.
The agreement marks an important step toward institutionalizing Taiwan-UK science and technology cooperation, allowing both sides to use their complementary strengths through concrete projects and bolster cooperation in key technology sectors, NSTC Deputy Minister Chen Bing-yu (陳炳宇) said.
Photo courtesy of the National Science and Technology Council
The three projects were agreed during a SITA roundtable co-chaired by Chen and British National Technology Adviser Dave Smith following the signing ceremony.
The first project will involve satellite communications, with the UK Space Agency and Taiwan Space Agency planning joint research and development in advanced satellite communications technologies. The project would serve as a flagship outcome of SITA, the NSTC said.
The second is the launch of a Taiwan-UK silicon photonics academic alliance backed by seed funding secured by the UK. With support from the Taiwan Semiconductor Research Institute (TSRI), the alliance would promote academic exchanges, talent development and industry-academia cooperation in silicon photonics.
The third is a semiconductor skills initiative, building on a memorandum of understanding on semiconductor talent development signed by former British Department for Science, Innovation and Technology and the Ministry of Foreign Affairs.
The two sides welcomed the results of the first group of UK master’s students who came to Taiwan for internships, the NSTC said, adding that it will work with TSRI to support the initiative, including programs for British research talent to visit Taiwan.
SITA is a legally non-binding framework between the UK and Taiwan to support cooperation in science, innovation and technology, the British government said.

Scientists investigate cause of rising baby whale deaths
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
16:37:46 UTC
01:37:46 KST

Investigators in Argentina are trying to solve the mystery of baby whales washing up dead in unusually high numbers along the country’s Patagonian coast.
Scores of the calf carcasses have been washing ashore around Peninsula Valdes, a major breeding ground for southern right whales in Argentina’s Chubut Province. Hunted to the brink of extinction in the 19th and 20th centuries, the whales now gather in the peninsula’s sheltered waters to give birth and nurse their young.
“We’re looking into the whale calf deaths based on 23 years of monitoring that we have of this same population. That’s what allows us to say that this is an unusual event,” said Marcela Uhart, a veterinarian with the One Health Institute at the University of California, Davis, who is leading the investigation as head of the Southern Right Whale Health Monitoring Program.
Photo: AP
The leading hypothesis is that the whale calves are getting infections from marine bacteria that can enter their bodies through injuries inflicted by kelp gulls, Uhart said.
For decades, the seabirds have pecked at whales surfacing to breathe, gorging on their skin and blubber. Adults learn to surface with only their heads exposed, keeping their backs underwater and out of reach of the gulls. Calves cannot do that maneuver, leaving them vulnerable to attacks.
The carcasses have been washing ashore around Puerto Madryn, including near the central waterfront where they alarm residents and tourists. Residents have reported hundreds of them, but researchers declined to give a death toll, saying that would become clear after the season ends late next month.
Uhart and a team of biologists, veterinarians and park rangers have been searching the area for the dead calves. The work is gruesome: They photograph and examine the bodies, racing against decomposition to collect skin and organ samples for testing at a veterinary school in Tandil.
Bacteria have already been detected in those tissues, but researchers are still culturing samples to identify the microbes and determine whether infection was the cause of death, she said.
Even if bacteria are to blame, researchers must still determine why they have become so deadly this year.
Changes in marine conditions such as warming sea temperatures could contribute to “this perfect storm where this bacteria is powerful enough to overcome the immunity of the babies and cause their deaths,” Uhart said.
“So to the extent that we can, we’ll try to identify at least what factors may be triggering this event and making it so massive,” she added.
Right whales got their name from whalers who considered them the “right” animals to hunt, because they swam slowly, stayed close to shore and floated when killed, according to the International Whaling Commission.
Although illegal hunting continued into the 1970s, southern right whales have gradually rebounded since gaining international protection in 1935, but their recovery remains threatened by the same pressures facing whales worldwide: declining food supplies, fishing gear entanglements, oil spills and ship strikes.
“If the cause relates to something that we are doing as humans, then we need to change that,” Uhart said. “We don’t want to endanger these whales again.”

People receive first flu vaccines as cases rise
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
16:37:45 UTC
01:37:45 KST

More than 601,000 people received a flu vaccine in the first two days since public-funded vaccination began on Thursday, the Centers for Disease Control (CDC) said yesterday, adding that flu activity is at a peak in Taiwan and increasing in Japan, a popular travel destination for Taiwanese, so getting vaccinated is encouraged.
The first phase of this season’s public-funded flu and COVID-19 vaccination began on Thursday, with elderly people, young children, students and several high-risk groups eligible for the vaccines.
More than 601,000 doses of flu vaccines and more than 209,000 doses of COVID-19 vaccines have been administered in the first two days, both higher than the first two days of the program last year, CDC Deputy Director-General Lin Ming-cheng (林明誠) said yesterday.
Photo courtesy of the New Taipei City Government’s Department of Information via CNA
The number of flu and COVID-19 vaccines given was 9 percent and 19 percent higher, respectively, than those given on the first two days last year, he said.
On Friday alone, more than 335,000 people received a flu vaccine. That is the highest daily number since the program began offering the vaccines in two phases in 2021, he said.
Meanwhile, the CDC last week said that flu cases in Taiwan are still in the epidemic stage and weekly cases are predicted to remain at high levels in the next few weeks. Lin yesterday said that the latest data from Japan’s Ministry of Health, Labor and Welfare last month show that flu activity is also rising in Japan.
Japan’s data showed that the average number of flu-like illnesses reported per sentinel site (designated hospitals and clinics) was 8.48 during the week between Sept. 14 and Sept. 20, which was 53.1 percent higher than the week before, and 10 times the number of the same week last year, he said.
Among the cases reported that week, patients aged 70 years or older accounted for 47.5 percent, he said, adding that 98 percent of the cases were caused by the influenza A (H1N1) virus, which is also the current dominant strain spreading in Taiwan.
The data also show that 44 prefectures among Japan’s 47 prefectures reported an increase in flu-like illnesses, with the highest average case numbers in Okinawa, followed by Tokyo, Aichi, Kanagawa and Chiba, Lin said.
Weekly cases have increased for nine consecutive weeks until Sept. 20 in Japan, he said, adding that aside from Japan, flu activity in other countries, including China, Hong Kong, South Korea, Singapore and the US, are also rising.
The CDC encourages people to get vaccinated as soon as possible for better protection, either locally or if while traveling abroad, Lin said.

India defeat Pakistan in rare cricket rivalry match
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
16:37:44 UTC
01:37:44 KST

One of sport’s fiercest rivalries descended on a sleepy corner of Japan yesterday as India and Pakistan clashed in the men’s cricket final at the Asian Games on a converted baseball field, which India won 211-6 over 192-6.
The neighbors only meet in international tournaments because of long-running political tensions and matches between them typically attract television audiences of hundreds of millions back home.
The gold-medal encounter in a suburban park in Nagoya was a once-in-a-lifetime opportunity for Indians and Pakistanis living in Japan.
Photo: Reuters
They lined up hours before the game to get into the cozy 2,500-capacity purpose-built Korogi Athletic Park Stadium.
“I think this is never going to happen again, India against Pakistan in Japan,” long-time Nagoya resident Umer Dar, draped in a Pakistan flag, said in an interview. “I’m crazy about cricket but I never have the opportunity to watch it live because I’ve lived here for 26 years.”
The last time India and Pakistan collided was at the T20 World Cup in February, where they played in front of a sell-out 35,000 crowd in Sri Lanka.
The Asian Games setting was significantly more modest, with trees and a baseball pitcher’s mound just beyond the boundary.
The atmosphere was as passionate as ever though, with fans waving flags and cheering every ball from the temporary stands.
“We bought tickets three months back when they started selling them,” said Tokyo resident and India supporter Mohammed Kashim Raja.
“At the time it was easy but it became really difficult for others to get them,” he said.
“We heard that many people were selling them for high prices.”
Cricket is a niche sport in Japan and neutrals at the final appeared to be virtually nonexistent.
ALWAYS CRAZY
There was more of a casual crowd at the bronze-medal match between Sri Lanka and Bangladesh earlier, on a warm and sunny day.
Teachers Hiromi Niwa and Miki Kaede, both from nearby Gifu, said they knew nothing about cricket and had bought tickets out of curiosity.
After reading a free leaflet explaining the rules and watching some of the action, Kaede said it had been a “really fun” experience.
She was disappointed that their tickets did not get them into the final.
“We didn’t realize that India against Pakistan was such a big deal until we actually searched for it,” she said.
Cricket has a growing presence in Japan and the sport got a huge boost when India played their first-ever T20 international against Japan last week.
The historic match, celebrating 75 years of diplomatic relations, took place at Japan’s modest Sano International Cricket Ground outside Tokyo.
It was Japan’s first T20 game against a full-member nation, and they gave India a huge fright before losing by two runs in a rain-shortened match.
Kushal Gowda, an Indian fan living in Tokyo, said Japanese people were “trying to understand” cricket.
“We were trying to explain to our colleagues in our office and they were curious and keen to know what it was about,” he said. “They kind of compared it with baseball.”
The crowd for the Asian Games final overwhelmingly supported India, with only a few Pakistan flags and shirts dotted around the ground.
A cheer went up when the gates opened to let fans in, and the party continued when the game began under clear skies.
“Even if it’s in Japan, the craze of India versus Pakistan is always there,” said Tokyo-based India fan Afroz Khan. “Anywhere they play in the world, it’s always crazy.”

Some characters exist only in a fictional world, while others step into real life. These are the mascots people often see at sports events, in amusement parks, during marketing campaigns or even on busy shopping streets. They possess a magnetic charm that transcends age and language. Yet beneath every cheerful costume is a performer __1__ surprisingly demanding tasks.
A mascot performer is an actor, athlete and brand ambassador rolled into one. They bring energy to an __2__ lifeless costume entirely through their body language. Every wave, jump and playful gesture must be exaggerated enough to bring the character to life. However, the job is physically grueling. Heavy, poorly ventilated costumes make breathing difficult, while limited vision and muffled hearing can turn simple movements into __3__ ones.
To succeed in this role, performers must follow a strict code of practice. The golden rule is that faces must remain hidden and voices completely silent. Seeing a mascot without its head or hearing a voice that does not match one’s imagination can __4__. A mascot is expected to stay in constant motion. This relentless flow of energy is exhausting, which is why the performer needs frequent breaks behind the scenes. For safety reasons, a performer should always be __5__ at least one staff member to handle any unexpected situations. Most importantly, under no circumstances should a mascot pick up children, as limited vision and heavy costumes can make this unsafe.
Photo: AdobeStock I 照片： AdobeStock
By keeping reality out of sight, mascots allow imagination to take center stage and give their audience a brief escape from everyday life.
有些角色只存在於虛構世界，有些則會踏入現實世界。這些是人們常於運動賽事、遊樂園、行銷活動，甚至是繁忙商店街上看到的吉祥物。它們具有超越年齡與語言限制的致命吸引力。但在每個歡樂布偶裝下，都有一位執行著異常吃力任務的操偶師。
操偶師集演員、運動員和品牌大使於一身。他們全靠肢體語言為原本無生命的布偶裝注入生氣。每一次揮手、跳動，和活潑的肢體動作都必須誇張到足以讓角色活靈活現。然而，這項工作在體力上相當折磨人。厚重且通風不良的布偶裝會讓人難以呼吸，而受限的視野與模糊不清的聽覺會讓簡單的動作變危險。
要成功扮演這個角色，操偶師必須遵守嚴格的行規。重要原則是：不得露臉、不得出聲。看到沒有頭的吉祥物或聽到不符合想像的聲音都可能會打破幻想。吉祥物應該要不停活動。不間斷保持源源不絕的活力很累人，這就是為什麼操偶師需要在幕後頻繁休息。為了安全起見，操偶師應全程由至少一位工作人員陪同，以處理任何突發狀況。最重要的是，吉祥物在任何情況下都不能把小孩抱起來，因為受限的視野和沉重的布偶裝可能會讓這樣的動作不安全。
透過把現實隱藏起來，吉祥物讓想像力成為焦點，並帶給觀眾短暫逃離日常生活的機會。
What Did You Learn?
1. (A) settling down (B) warding off (C) breaking up (D) carrying out
2. (A) unless (B) anyway (C) otherwise (D) instead
3. (A) risky (B) graceful (C) slight (D) cautious
4. (A) delight the audience (B) break the illusion (C) hide the disappointment (D) preserve the image
5. (A) composed of (B) accompanied by (C) guided toward (D) isolated from
答案： 1. D 2. C 3. A 4. B 5. B
Words in Use
1. fictional a. 虛構的
Several fictional creatures in the movie were inspired by animals that live deep in the ocean.
這部電影中幾種虛構生物的靈感來自深海動物。
2. campaign n. （宣傳、社會）活動∕運動
A social media campaign helped the animal shelter receive donations.
一場社群媒體宣傳活動幫助該動物收容所獲得捐款。
3. a magnetic charm 強大的吸引力∕魅力
magnetic a. 有吸引力∕磁性的
The old cafe possesses a magnetic charm that keeps customers returning.
那間老式咖啡廳具有強大的魅力，讓顧客不斷回訪。
4. costume n. （特殊裝扮用的）服裝
The dinosaur costume looked so realistic that it frightened many kids.
這套恐龍裝逼真到嚇壞了很多小孩。
5. demanding a. 吃力的
? Climbing the mountain was a demanding task for my parents.
我爸媽來說，爬山是一項吃力的任務。
Practical Phrases
1. (all) rolled into one 集於一身，融於一體
The smartphone acts as a phone, computer and camera all rolled into one.
智慧型手機集電話、電腦與相機於一身。
2. bring. . . to life 賦予……生命，使……活過來
Emma’s storytelling brings every character to life.
艾瑪的說故事能力讓每個角色都栩栩如生。
3. in motion 在移動∕運動中
The dancers remained in motion throughout the performance.
舞者們在整個表演中都持續在移動。
4. behind the scenes 在幕後
Many people behind the scenes contributed to the film’s success.
許多幕後人員為這部電影的成功做出了貢獻。
5. under no circumstances + 倒裝句構 在任何情況下∕無論如何絕不
circumstance n. 情況（常用複數）
Under no circumstances should passengers open the emergency door mid-flight.
乘客在飛行途中絕不能打開緊急出口。

Akhilesh Yadav asks SP leaders to keep seat-sharing concerns internal amid friction with Congress
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
16:37:31 UTC
01:37:31 KST

Akhilesh Yadav reins in SP leaders amid seat-sharing differences with Congress
NEW DELHI: Samajwadi Party (SP) president Akhilesh Yadav on Saturday asked party leaders to keep their views on seat-sharing negotiations with the Congress within internal party channels, amid public differences between the two INDIA bloc allies ahead of the 2027 Uttar Pradesh Assembly elections.Yadav's intervention came after SP MP Shiv Pal Singh Patel publicly criticised the Congress' reported demand for 150 seats and said allocating too many constituencies to the party could affect the alliance's electoral prospects.
Addressing reporters at an event in Lucknow, Yadav said, "I would like to tell all our leaders that whatever opinions or concerns they have regarding seat-sharing should be shared with us. Whenever the discussion takes place, we will discuss and consider their suggestions."
SP MP questions Congress' reported demand
Patel had said the Congress' reported demand for 150 seats was "highly unreasonable", pointing to the parties' performance in the 2022 Uttar Pradesh Assembly elections.
"They currently have two MLAs, whereas we have 125. Based on this ratio, they should receive seven or eight seats… We can give them even 50 seats; anything beyond that would simply mean wasting seats and risking defeat," Patel told news agency ANI.
He said the Congress' "realistic capacity is around 25–30 seats" and stressed that the final decision on seat allocation rested with the SP national president."Congress should demand seats based on their actual numbers and standing, rather than making arbitrary demands. Their realistic capacity is around 25–30 seats… Everyone knows that only Akhilesh Yadav can provide good governance, ensure justice for all, and work for the welfare of everyone. That is why the public stands with Akhilesh Yadav; the Congress has no contribution in this regard," Patel further said.The reported demand for at least 150 seats had also been raised by Uttar Pradesh Congress in-charge Rajendra Pal Gautam, who said earlier that the party had candidates available for all 403 Assembly constituencies and would not contest fewer than 150 seats under an alliance arrangement.
Congress says top leadership will decide
Newly appointed Uttar Pradesh Congress president Aradhana Mishra said the decision on seat-sharing would be taken by the top leadership of the INDIA bloc and its constituent parties, rather than at the state level."Let me clarify one thing: the INDIA alliance was not formed specifically for Uttar Pradesh. It was formed in Delhi. This is not a state-level arrangement; it is a national-level alliance. Decisions regarding this will be taken by the top leadership of the alliance and the top leadership of the constituent parties," Mishra said.
She said the Congress leadership would decide both the number of seats and the timing of any alliance."As for the Congress party, our top leadership will decide on the number of seats and the timing of the alliance, and I am fully confident that they will do so while keeping in mind the faith and trust of Congress workers," she said.Mishra also said Raebareli and Amethi held special significance for the Gandhi family, describing them as the family's "home".
The Congress and SP contested the 2024 Lok Sabha elections together in Uttar Pradesh as part of the INDIA bloc. The two parties had also allied for the 2017 Uttar Pradesh Assembly elections.The next Uttar Pradesh Assembly elections are due in 2027, with the BJP and SP among the major parties in the state.In the 2022 Assembly elections, the BJP won 255 of the 403 seats, while the SP secured 111. Congress won two seats and the Bahujan Samaj Party (BSP) won one.The BJP's vote share was 41.29 per cent, compared with 32.06 per cent for the SP, 12.88 per cent for the BSP and 2.33 per cent for the Congress.SP chief Akhilesh Yadav had earlier indicated that his party would contest the 2027 polls with largely the same allies with which it fought some recent elections and said the alliance would be declared soon.
