The winter war: Ukraine is prepping for another season of Russian attacks before the cold sets in
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
15:59:11 UTC
00:59:11 KST

On Sept. 23, Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov once again voiced Moscow’s rejection of a Ukrainian proposal to halt fighting along the current front line. Now Kyiv is preparing for another series of strikes on its critical infrastructure that appear intended to freeze the country during the upcoming winter and result in a humanitarian disaster. Ukraine’s military and civilian institutions have already begun preparing for what they expect to be an especially difficult Russian campaign, with energy companies inspecting equipment and stockpiling fuel while apartment associations buy up generators.
In September, air raid alerts have sounded in Kyiv every day — and almost continuously. Jet-powered Shahed drones circle over the city, disrupting the work of municipal services, shops, businesses, and public institutions. A new operating protocol took effect on Sept. 10, introducing a “yellow” alert level for Shaheds and a “red” level for missiles. Under a yellow alert, most businesses and institutions now remain open.
The changes do not apply to schools, which are still required to suspend classes during air raid alerts. Schools without underground classrooms have moved children to online learning. Across Ukraine more broadly, local authorities have been given discretion over how to respond to alerts.
In August and September, central government officials held a series of meetings with businesses. Entrepreneurs were advised to consider setting up air defenses on their own, to cooperate with existing volunteer territorial defense formations (known by the Ukrainian acronym DFTG), and to move warehouses underground.
Russian forces have been striking warehouses belonging to home improvement retailer Epicentr and delivery company Nova Poshta for years, but the logistical networks of supermarket chains recently started coming under systematic attacks for the first time. Strikes on warehouses reduced the range of goods available in stores in August, though the situation had largely stabilized by mid-September.
As fall begins, everyone in Ukraine seems to be asking the same question: how can the country make it through a winter of relentless strikes? It is already clear that the infrastructure responsible for heating and other fundamental civilian services will be among Russia’s targets.
The military shield and the front line
Ukraine needs interceptors to defend against ballistic and cruise missiles. But increasingly frequent attacks by jet-powered drones have created another challenge.
A volunteer (call sign Max) with a Kyiv Region DFTG told The Insider that his unit formed teams of interceptor-drone pilots in preparation for the winter campaign, alongside its regular gun and mobile fire teams. Training began in mid-spring, and by the end of summer, most volunteers had passed examinations and received certificates — along with combat interceptor drones.
But a problem emerged: older interceptor drones work well against conventional Shaheds traveling at speeds of up to 250 kilometers per hour, but new interceptors designed to take out jet-powered Shaheds have only recently completed testing. Russia is expected to use both conventional and jet-powered Shaheds during the fall and winter, meaning crews are expected to use different interceptors depending on the target.
Volunteer formations are part of Ukraine’s Territorial Defense Forces (TDF) and their supply system tends to lag somewhat behind those of the Unmanned Systems Forces, the Security Service of Ukraine (SBU), and the National Guard. Newer technologies only reach the TDF and volunteer groups after they have been tested by regular units.
By Sept. 20, videos had emerged showing jet-powered Shaheds being intercepted by high-speed fixed-wing interceptor drones and Sting S quadcopters.
“We have to remember that there is no such thing as 100% effective air defense. Some missiles and Shaheds will get through any defenses. That is why residents should always follow the recommendations of Ukraine’s Defense Forces. New Ukrainian interceptor drones are more maneuverable and can engage targets at greater distances and altitudes than the usual weapons used by ground-based fire teams. But they cannot offer a complete guarantee either. The same applies to Russia, where they are also technologically behind. So if power stations, thermal power plants, and combined heat-and-power plants burn here this winter, there is an even greater likelihood that they will burn in Russia as well,” Max said.
Ukraine’s new interceptor drones are more maneuverable and can hit targets at greater ranges and altitudes, but they cannot provide a complete guarantee against Moscow’s aerial attacks
A Kyiv volunteer territorial defense formation commander called Asgard said his unit has gun teams equipped with a wide range of weapons “from 5.45 mm up to 23 mm,” along with interceptor-drone crews. “The biggest target was probably a cruise missile we shot down in 2024. Believe it or not, we brought it down with a 7.62 mm Maxim machine gun manufactured in 1942.” Unsurprisingly, Asgard’s unit also engages jet-powered Shaheds.
There has been no particular need for “retraining” this year, the Kyiv DFTG commander said. “Every day we face new challenges and learn. Before, they were ordinary Shaheds. Those are very easy targets for us now. We still have work to do with the jet-powered ones.”
Ukraine’s small mobile air defense units shoot down conventional Shaheds in 95% to 99% of cases, but their success rate against jet-powered versions is no more than 40% to 60%. Volunteer formations hope that rate will increase soon as interceptor-drone teams receive more high-speed drones of their own.
At the front itself, winter could provide Ukraine with some advantages, according to Silver, an FPV drone pilot who flies fiber-optic-controlled drones.
“There will be more work in winter. First, the leaves will fall, which will make things easier. Even now we manage to fly fiber-optic drones through forests, but without the ‘greenery’ [the military term for dense seasonal foliage] we will create far more problems for the Russians. Second, we will rely on skill, quality, and careful planning rather than quantity. We are changing our approach, adapting technically and improving our skills. Everyone is talking about AI-equipped drones now, but artificial intelligence will not replace the person who still decides which target to send it toward. I’ve worked with AI-assisted terminal guidance, and it works!”
Even if Russia carries out another mobilization, conditions will become harder for Russian soldiers in winter, according to a Nemesis bomber-drone pilot who has flown 1,000 combat missions over a year and a half.
“The Russian military is adapting too, changing tactics and infiltrating our lines. Maybe they have something new prepared for us. But overall, we’re ready. We’ll see how their mobilization goes and how many more targets we have along the line of contact,” the pilot said.
Front-line cities
About 127,500 people live in the Ukrainian-controlled portion of the Kherson Region — about a quarter of the prewar population. In the city of Kherson itself, 63,000 out of the prewar population of 283,000 remain — roughly 22%.
The situation there is difficult. Russian forces deliberately target energy and heat-generating facilities in an effort to deprive residents of basic services. Strikes take place around the clock, with explosions heard roughly every two minutes. Since the area was liberated in November of 2022, the regional administration has recorded 400,000 Russian attacks involving more than 900,000 munitions.
Elvina Osmanova, head of the Kherson regional administration’s domestic and information policy department, told The Insider that between three and 10 guided aerial bombs (known by the Russian and Ukrainian abbreviation KAB) are dropped on Kherson each day. “They hit infrastructure sites one after another, including the combined heat-and-power plant, and essentially everything responsible for electricity, heating, gas, and water supplies.”
Alongside guided bombs, Russian forces make extensive use of conventional drones, a particular problem for Kherson, Nikopol, and other cities within a 20-kilometer range of the front line. Osmanova lists off the drone types that most frequently attack the city: “FPV drones, Mavics, cheap Molniya kamikaze drones, and other systems. Most of them use fiber-optic control, which makes them difficult to stop. As many as 5,000 drones can be launched at Kherson in a week.”
Still, food deliveries still make it to central Kherson, Osmanova said:
“The city has a sufficient supply of food. But the Russians deliberately destroy trucks and kill drivers transporting bread and other foodstuffs, so issues with deliveries cannot be ruled out. Due to constant shelling, some parts of Kherson are already effectively dead — riverside areas such as Antonivka, Voyenne, Korabel, and several others near the Dnipro. They haven't had normal municipal services for a long time.
Last winter, there were times when people went 10 days without electricity or water. Right now, one district of the city has been without power for 14 days. In other areas, electricity has been restored through the heroic efforts of utility workers. Many have unfortunately been wounded or killed. Drones deliberately target workers while they repair infrastructure.
We understand that the Russians will only increase their attacks in the fall and winter. The number and severity of enemy attacks are increasing every day. Kherson may end up without electricity and heating not just for hours or days but for prolonged periods, and we're preparing for that. We're adapting our anti-drone system — detection systems, electronic warfare, and mobile fire teams — and increasing physical protection for important facilities.”
Shelters are another major focus. Osmanova said 307 protective structures have been repaired and 439 mobile shelters installed in crowded public areas. Protection for critical infrastructure is also being strengthened through backup power, additional physical defenses, and alternative systems intended to allow facilities to continue operating after Russian attacks.
“The Russians attack any kind of transportation with drones: mopeds, passenger cars, trucks, ambulances, municipal vehicles, and public transit,” Osmanova said. “Last week alone, about 40 vehicles were damaged or destroyed. We are doing everything possible to protect the city’s supply routes, including covering roads and streets with anti-drone nets. About 270 kilometers of roads have already been protected that way.”
Zarina Zabrisky, an American journalist with Byline Times who lives in Kherson, told The Insider that residents are preparing for winter however they can. Residents with standalone, private houses were able to heat their homes with firewood in previous winters and are preparing to do so again — and many of them have generators. Zabrisky’s apartment has access to a supply of natural gas, which she used to heat her home last winter.
At the same time, the local administration is advising residents — particularly older people, those with limited mobility, and families with children — to seriously consider temporarily relocating to safer parts of Ukraine. The authorities say they are prepared to assist at every stage, including organizing evacuation, finding housing, providing humanitarian aid, and offering psychological and legal assistance.
Kyiv
Locals in Kyiv are not counting on an energy ceasefire. Instead, they are preparing for something resembling a repeat of last year. The main difference is that the upcoming winter is expected to be milder, with frequent thaws.
Vyacheslav Hryb, who heads three condominium associations in Kyiv, told The Insider how preparations are going:
“We’re buying additional inverters, checking the generators, and connecting elevators to them. If the power goes out, our calculations show the elevators can operate for five to six hours. Heating should also be fine. We have a large building and a 110-kilowatt generator that powers the cold-water supply, hot-water supply, and heating.
Last year, the unprecedented cold made everything harder, and after the strikes, many buildings had to drain water from their heating pipes. Restarting the heating at minus 22 Celsius [about negative 8 degrees Fahrenheit] was what you might call an advanced-level challenge. The instructions say it’s impossible, but we pulled together and managed to get it running.”
Kyiv’s energy situation is among the most difficult among Ukrainian cities not located near the front. Last winter, residents of several buildings on the eastern bank of the Dnipro went without centralized heating for around a month after heating pipes burst. Electricity schedules were largely maintained, with power generally available for four hours followed by four hours without it.
Kyiv’s energy situation is among the most difficult of Ukraine’s non-frontline cities
Residents are now buying batteries and inverters in order to be more self-sufficient. Buildings with condominium associations are generally better prepared, often with generators or high-capacity battery and inverter systems that can keep heat, water and elevators running during outages. But only about 2,000 of Kyiv’s more than 10,000 residential buildings have these associations.
Other buildings are serviced by municipal housing offices, commonly known by the Soviet-era abbreviation ZhEK. Their residents therefore often have to go to special “Points of Invincibility” set up by city authorities and Ukraine’s State Emergency Service to warm up and charge their devices.
The Zhytomyr phenomenon
The city of Zhytomyr is located less than 100 miles from Kyiv, but last winter it did not even suffer widespread short-term power cuts. Vitaliy, a Zhytomyr resident, told The Insider that while Kyiv spent days at a time without electricity, Zhytomyr experienced only a handful of outages, none lasting more than an hour:
“Specialists had told me before that Zhytomyr had inherited many military factories from the Soviet era. It was also an early adopter of power systems designed for wartime conditions. The city developed a distributed energy system, which is why, despite repeated attacks, we did not face major disruptions or prolonged power outages last winter or the winter before.”
In Ukrainian cities where power distribution has been managed effectively, utility services remain close to prewar levels. Residents of Kyiv — and perhaps soon Moscow and St. Petersburg — can only look with envy at Zhytomyr.
The overall state of Ukraine’s energy system
The risk of new large-scale attacks remains one of the most serious and unpredictable factors facing Ukraine this winter. DTEK, the country’s largest private energy company, is preparing for a range of possible scenarios.
“First and foremost, we are repairing and restoring thermal power plants around the clock after attacks,” the company told The Insider. “There is not a single DTEK generating unit that has not been damaged or destroyed during the years of the full-scale war, and some units have had to be rebuilt several times.”
At the same time, the company is carrying out scheduled equipment repairs in order to improve reliability during the winter. It is also stockpiling fuel and supporting the operation of mines, machine-building facilities, and repair businesses. DTEK spent more than 7.6 billion hryvnias ($170 million) on those efforts in the first half of 2026 alone. Since the start of the full-scale invasion, it has spent more than 51 billion hryvnias ($1.2 billion) restoring thermal generation, supporting its businesses, and preparing for wartime winters.
In the first half of 2026, DTEK invested 3.3 billion hryvnias ($74 million) in repairing and modernizing power grids. Since the start of the full-scale invasion, investment in that area has exceeded 15 billion hryvnias ($335 million). The company says its central goals are to restore as much available capacity as possible, maintain sufficient supplies for emergency repairs, and be prepared to respond as quickly as possible to new attacks.
DTEK is advising Ukrainians to use electricity carefully, particularly during periods of peak demand, and says it will do everything possible to minimize the effects of attacks. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky, meanwhile, said the government would prepare the country’s air defense network for the winter.
“This is extremely difficult, but it has to be expanded. Absolutely everyone is working on it: the Defense Ministry, the Foreign Ministry, and the Foreign Intelligence Service. The obvious challenge, as you know, is missiles for the Patriot system. But we are working on that as well,” Zelensky told reporters Sept. 25. “Separately, we are working on our own anti-ballistic air defense system. That is the FREYJA system. We will work on all of this so there is no collapse.”
Zelensky also said Ukraine would retaliate for attacks on its energy system by striking not only Russian oil refineries — but its energy facilities as well.

Roundup: Myanmar experts stress ecosystem conservation for migratory bird habitats, flyways
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
23:58:07 CST
00:58:07 KST

People visit a photo exhibition marking World Migratory Bird Day in Yangon, Myanmar, Oct. 3, 2026.(Xinhua/Myo Kyaw Soe)
YANGON, Oct. 3 (Xinhua) -- A series of photo exhibitions and thematic talks were held in Yangon on Saturday to mark World Migratory Bird Day, as Myanmar ornithologists and environmentalists urge global efforts to protect migratory bird habitats and migration routes increasingly threatened by human activities.
Of the world's billions of birds spanning over 10,000 species, some 18 to 20 percent are migratory, said renowned Myanmar ornithologist Thein Aung. He noted that human activities including illegal bird hunting for trade, wetland pollution, and large-scale infrastructure development near feeding grounds have posed growing risks to migratory birds along their flight paths.
This year's World Migratory Bird Day falls under the global theme "Every Bird Counts -- Your Observations Matter." Thein Aung, one of the event's organizing ornithologists, said the activity aims to disseminate popular science knowledge about migratory birds and mobilize public participation in conservation work.
During the event, Ko Phyo, a veteran bird photographer and environmental conservation practitioner as well as director of Myanmar's non-profit organization Wild Wings Group, exhibited bird photos taken across Myanmar over more than 15 years. "Bird observation requires systematic learning of bird habits, habitats, breeding grounds and chirps through both books and on-site observation," he said.
He stressed the importance of joint efforts to protect local vegetation and ecological environments. "Birds serve a vital role in ecological protection. For example, they prey on pests that damage rice and other crops, forming an interdependent ecological relationship with human agricultural production. This is why bird conservation matters greatly," he explained.
Daw Khin Khin Thaw, a Yangon-based teacher who brought nearly 50 students to the event, emphasized that bird conservation awareness should be cultivated among children from an early age. She said interactive activities such as bird observation and bird drawing based on the photo exhibition help students gradually build ecological and environmental awareness.
Thein Aung also called for strengthened international cooperation on transboundary bird conservation. He introduced that two major global migratory flyways, namely the Central Asian Flyway and the East Asian-Australasian Flyway, traverse multiple ASEAN countries.
Taking neighboring China as an example, Thein Aung said China has accumulated mature and extensive expertise in migratory bird protection. Advanced academic programs at the master's and doctoral levels in China offer valuable learning opportunities for Myanmar researchers.
He expressed the hope for future China-Myanmar cooperation, including joint research on cross-border migratory bird routes, to jointly advance regional conservation undertakings.
World Migratory Bird Day is observed twice annually, in May for spring migration departure and in October for autumn migration arrival. The official observance dates for 2026 are May 9 and Oct. 10. ■

Unidentified Object Entered Lithuanian Airspace From Belarus—Search Underway
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
15:57:27 UTC
00:57:27 KST

On the morning of October 3, Lithuania declared a yellow threat level due to an unidentified aerial object, likely a drone, that entered the country’s airspace from Belarus.
This was reported by Vilmantas Vitkauskas, Head of Threat Management and Crisis Prevention at the Prime Minister’s Office in Lithuania, according to LRT.
Due to the incident, the airspace near Vilnius Airport was temporarily closed, and operations at the airport were suspended. NATO fighter jets were scrambled.
A yellow-level alert was issued shortly before 10:00 a.m. Residents of the region received alerts on their cell phones urging them to find a safe place.
However, the aerial object could not be fully identified. According to Vitkauskas, the fighter jets took to the air and carried out the appropriate procedures.
Authorities also received reports from residents who claimed to have seen the object outside Vilnius in the direction of Jonava. However, these reports were not confirmed.
The air threat was lifted at 10:37 a.m. According to Vitkauskas, the object disappeared from the surveillance zone and no longer posed a threat. It is currently being searched for.
Vitkauskas noted that it is unknown whether the object was actually a drone. He said that certain parameters of the object indicated a speed slightly lower than what is typical for a UAV.
“If it crashed, if it was a drone, we’ll have to find it. But it wasn’t necessarily a drone,” Vilmantas Vitkauskas said.
The official also did not rule out that the observed phenomenon could have been related to an anomaly or bird migration. Lithuanian authorities are currently continuing to determine the nature of the object and the circumstances of its appearance in the vicinity of the Lithuanian capital.
As a reminder, on the morning of September 13, a drone flew from Belarus to the Kaliningrad region of the Russian Federation through Lithuanian territory. It was also initially identified as an unidentified aerial object. The UAV flew 60–70 km over Lithuania and remained in the NATO country’s airspace for about 20 minutes.
Amid the growing threat from drones in Lithuania, a pilot version of the Ukrainian SkyFortress system is being deployed, which is designed to help detect them at low altitudes using sound or radio signals.

Inside the UK Greens' debate over landmark anti-Zionism motion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
15:51:03 UTC
00:51:03 KST

Breadcrumb
Inside the UK Greens' debate over landmark anti-Zionism motion
UK Green Party members are debating the details of the "Zionism is racism" motion that will be put to a vote on Sunday at their annual conference, with its backers optimistic that the party will formally adopt an anti-Zionist position.
The motion, endorsed by leading advocates of the Palestinian cause, seeks to declare the party opposed to Zionism, which it defines as a racist, settler-colonial ideology.
It defines Zionism as a political ideology seeking the creation and continuation of an ethnonationalist Jewish state in historic Palestine through the exclusion or domination of its non-Jewish population, and says its material consequences have included the dehumanisation, displacement, dispossession and disenfranchisement of Palestinians.
The motion seeks to make opposition to Zionism an explicit Green Party position, while affirming Palestinian self-determination and liberation.
"As a Palestinian, second of all as a human being, thirdly because it's what's right, it's to oppose a racist root core of the ideology behind our erasure as Palestinians," Lubna Speitan, author of the motion, told The New Arab on the sidelines of the party's conference in Brighton.
The motion also calls for support for the Boycott, Divestment and Sanctions (BDS) movement and embargoes similar to those imposed on apartheid South Africa, as well as the release of Palestinian prisoners and recognition of the right to resistance under international law.
It also supports the establishment of a single democratic Palestinian state across historic Palestine, with equal rights and the right of return, a demand that has emerged as one of the main points of disagreement within the party ahead of Sunday's vote.
The motion was originally submitted to the party's spring conference but was not reached for debate before the conference ran out of time, meaning it was deferred rather than rejected. It has since returned with a record number of supporters and proposed amendments.
Call for a single Palestinian state
Deputy Leader Rachel Millward told The New Arab that while she does not believe the motion will derail the conference, she has reservations about its call for a single Palestinian state.
"It does sort of make really clear that the solution has to be a single Palestinian state -- that I really struggle with that," Millward told The New Arab on the sidelines of the conference.
"It feels a bit imperialist, if I'm honest, for us, the Green Party of England and Wales, to dictate what the outcome of a peace process would be."
While the motion has attracted a record-breaking number of supporters and co-proposers, party leader Zack Polanski called for two amendments, including one to explicitly safeguard Jewish members and another to remove the call for a single state.
Millward argued that the Greens already have a strong platform on Palestine, including being the first major UK party to declare Israel's actions a genocide, as well as backing the Palestinian right to self-determination.
Speitan rejected the suggestion that advocating a single Palestinian state amounts to imposing a solution, arguing that Britain's historical role in Palestine makes the description of the proposal as "imperialist" particularly misplaced.
"'Imperialistic' is the Balfour Declaration that imposed this racist, rogue, settler colony," Speitan said. "It was through the Balfour Declaration here in Britain that they imposed this rogue state upon us and we're simply here talking about the reversal of the wrongs that were committed and imposed upon us."
Jewish Greens said ahead of the conference that its members were divided over the motion, and that the group would not take an official position.
A survey published by Jewish Greens on Friday found that 81% of 108 respondents did not identify as Zionists, while 70 described themselves as anti-Zionist and 70 as non-Zionist, with some identifying as both. The group said there was nevertheless no consensus among its members over whether the motion itself should pass.
'The root of the problem'
For the motion's backers, formally opposing Zionism is central to the proposal rather than simply an addition to the Greens' existing policies on Palestine.
They argue that condemning Israel's actions without confronting the ideology they say has underpinned the dispossession, displacement and dehumanisation of Palestinians fails to address the root of the issue.
Kieran Andrieu, a British Palestinian political economist and supporter of the motion, said the Greens' longstanding commitment to anti-racism should therefore extend to opposition to Zionism.
"I think that it's important to recognise when something is racism and to call it as such. People in this party feel very deeply about Palestine," Andrieu told The New Arab.
"The problem is that we're going to be attending anti-genocide marches for a thousand years unless we're able to actually identify the root of the problem, which is that Palestinians have been systematically dehumanised over more than a century, and the ideology that's dehumanised them is Zionism," Andrieu added.
Not all prominent Greens agree that formally defining Zionism in this way would strengthen the party's position on Palestine.
Caroline Lucas, the party's first MP and its only MP until the 2024 general election, described the motion as "divisive", pointing to disagreements over how Zionism itself is defined.
"I think it's divisive because I don't think there is an agreed definition of Zionism, and I speak as somebody who has been a long-time supporter of the Palestinian cause," Lucas told The New Arab ahead of Polanski's speech at the conference.
"I just think this motion is a distraction; it's unhelpful, it's divisive, and if it does end up with Jewish people feeling unwelcome and feeling even worse, potentially even scared, then I don't think that helps our cause," she said, while acknowledging that for Palestinians, the term represents "the most appalling, colonial, extractive racism".
Supporters of the motion dispute the suggestion that opposition to Zionism should conflict with the party's anti-racist principles, arguing instead that their position is rooted in the historical and continuing Palestinian experience of dispossession.
Speitan also pointed to the record-breaking number of supporters and co-proposers as evidence of the strength of support for the motion within the party.
"The fact that the majority of the party have supported it, never in the party's history, has there ever been a motion that has garnered so much support," the author of the motion said.
For Speitan, the disagreement ultimately comes down to whether the party's anti-racist principles extend to rejecting an ideology that has enabled the dispossession of Palestinians.
"If there ever to be any division, then let it be clear, it's between the racists and anti-racists. There is no middle ground. You either stand with the occupier or the occupied. It is literally as simple and straightforward as that," Speitan added.

After decades of negotiations: the remains of Tsar Samuel returned from Greece to Bulgaria
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
18:49:13 EEST
00:49:13 KST

After decades of negotiations: the remains of Tsar Samuel returned from Greece to Bulgaria
Kyiv • UNN
Greece handed over to Bulgaria remains identified as those of Tsar Samuel, discovered in 1965. There is no genetic confirmation of the identification.
On October 3, Bulgaria received from Greece remains identified as those of the medieval Tsar Samuel, who ruled from 997 to 1014. This was reported by UNN, citing the governments of Greece and Bulgaria, BTA, and The Guardian.
The transfer took place following years of negotiations between the two countries במסגרת an agreement on the mutual return of historical and religious valuables. The remains have already been delivered to Sofia, where they were received with state honors and placed in a special marble sarcophagus.
Details
The official handover ceremony took place in the morning at the Museum of Byzantine Culture in Thessaloniki, attended by Greek Prime Minister Kyriakos Mitsotakis and Bulgarian President Rumen Radev. The parties signed the relevant protocols on the transfer of cultural valuables. The remains were then transported to Sofia aboard a Spartan military transport aircraft. After it entered Bulgarian airspace, it was escorted by MiG-29 and F-16 fighter jets. A state ceremony titled "Bulgaria Welcomes Tsar Samuel" was held in the capital's center, during which the national anthem was played and a 21-gun artillery salute was fired.
After that, the remains were carried in procession to the Basilica of Saint Sophia. There, Bulgarian Patriarch Daniil led a memorial service, after which the remains were placed in a specially made marble sarcophagus.
The transfer was part of an agreement signed by the two countries' culture ministers on September 29. In exchange, Bulgaria returned 48 historical and ecclesiastical relics to Greece, which had been taken to Sofia in 1917 during World War I. These included icons, crosses, church vestments, reliquaries, and a bishop's throne from the Panagia Eikosifinissa and Timios Prodromos monasteries, as well as from the Metropolis of Serres and Nigrita. Until November 5, the items returned to Greece will be displayed at the Museum of Byzantine Culture in Thessaloniki, after which they are to be handed over to the monasteries and church institutions from which they originate. Sofia and Athens also agreed to continue negotiations on other historical objects of mutual interest.
How the remains were found
The remains believed to be those of Tsar Samuel were found by Greek archaeologist Nikolaos Moutsopoulos in the Basilica of Saint Achillius on an island in Lake Prespa. The discovery dates to 1965. Other anthropological material was also found with them in four sarcophagi, which Greece likewise handed over to Bulgaria.
There is no definitive genetic confirmation of this identification. Bulgarian historian Professor Milko Palangurskiy stated that no DNA analysis of the remains had been conducted before their return. At the same time, a number of Bulgarian archaeologists and historians consider the available archaeological and historical evidence sufficiently convincing to link the burial specifically to Samuel.
Negotiations lasted for decades
According to Mitsotakis, negotiations on the mutual return of cultural valuables effectively began about half a century ago. The first discussions of the issue were held in the 1970s by then-Greek Prime Minister Konstantinos Karamanlis and Bulgarian leader Todor Zhivkov.
At the ceremony in Thessaloniki, Radev said that the return of the remains concludes a lengthy diplomatic process and could mark a new stage of cultural cooperation between the two countries. He stressed that historical objects should be accessible to the peoples with whose past they are connected.
However, the agreement also sparked debate. According to the Associated Press, some Greek scholars and church representatives expressed dissatisfaction with the specific items Bulgaria transferred to Greece. In Bulgaria, for his part, Professor Palangurskiy said that, in his view, a more comprehensive examination and cataloging of the relics should have been conducted before the agreement was concluded.
What the Parthenon Marbles have to do with it
Greek Prime Minister Kyriakos Mitsotakis also used the transfer of the relics as an argument in Athens' long-running dispute with the United Kingdom over the Parthenon sculptures, a significant portion of which is held by the British Museum.
According to him, the international attitude toward cultural heritage is gradually changing, and historic monuments should not be regarded as military trophies or objects detached from the cultural environment for which they were created. Mitsotakis said that the same principle underlies Athens's demand for the reunification of the Parthenon sculptures.
The Greek prime minister also reiterated that Athens would not agree to a solution that would mean recognizing another state's ownership of the sculptures or provide for their return to Greece only in the form of a loan.
Who Was Tsar Samuel
Samuel ruled the Bulgarian Empire from 997 to 1014 and fought the Byzantine Empire for decades. During his reign, the state's political center moved to the southwestern Balkans, to the area around Prespa and Ohrid. In 1014, Samuel's forces suffered a heavy defeat at the hands of the army of Byzantine Emperor Basil II. Shortly afterward, the tsar died. The Bulgarian Empire continued to resist for several more years, but in 1018 its territories came under Byzantine control.

Ukraine’s $33 veterans’ gym subsidy drew 800,000 uses. Now it is gone, squeezed by war and stalled reforms, holding up $20 billion in aid
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
15:45:48 UTC
00:45:48 KST

Ukraine has stopped paying veterans to go to the gym because of the economic crisis looming in the country, the war, Russian strikes, and the lack of reforms needed to receive extra funds from the EU. The Veteran Sports program, which provided veterans and combat participants with about $33 per quarter toward a nearly monthly gym membership, was suspended on 1 October after the state found no funds for it, the Ministry of Veterans Affairs said.
The suspension is a telling sign of Ukraine's budget squeeze, and the ministry puts it plainly: defense comes first, so the money for everything else runs short. It fits a wider government decision to freeze non-essential spending and fund only the army, pensions, and public wages.
The program proved far more popular than planned, drawing more than 800,000 users and costing over double its budget.
Defense takes the money
"The main priority of state spending remains the country's defense. Under these conditions, the state budget's ability to finance other areas is limited," the ministry said.
Launched in 2026 with about $13 million for an expected 100,000 recipients per quarter, and roughly 300,000 applications over three, the program instead saw more than 800,000 uses. Payments passed $27 million, more than twice what was set aside.
The crisis runs deeper
The squeeze has two main drivers. Russia's intensifying strikes on Ukraine's energy and infrastructure are pushing the war's cost higher and battering the economy.
And billions in Western money sit on hold: Kyiv has struggled to complete the reforms the EU set out before releasing roughly $20 billion in aid, and the prime minister has admitted that part of it is late because Ukraine missed commitments to its partners.
The ministry plans a 2027 restart
Ukraine intends to bring the program back in 2027, this time for good, said Deputy Veterans Minister Ruslan Prykhodko.
"We have to account for real demand, fix the shortcomings we saw this year, and make the use of funds more targeted," he said.
In next year's budget, Ukraine would provide significantly more funds, he added. In the meantime, the ministry says it is talking to the sports community and businesses about covering the gap for veterans, with concrete proposals to come.

Firefly High-Precision Guidance Kits are Already Being Supplied to Ukrainian Units
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
15:44:35 UTC
00:44:35 KST

Firefly high-precision guidance kits, which enable ammunition for bomber drones to be converted into high-precision bombs, are already being supplied to Ukrainian Defense Forces units.
A representative of the manufacturer discussed this in a Militarnyi video.
The module consists of a body, wings, and a tail section that corrects the munition’s flight path. The system is controlled automatically from a drone.
The Firefly is a system that was jointly developed by the Aerorozvidka NGO and a unit of the Ministry of Defence of Ukraine, while the company manufactures the modules under license and focuses on scaling up production and supplying ready-to-use factory-made products to military units.
Currently, the company offers guidance kits in two form factors—the smaller-diameter FF85 and the larger-diameter FF120.
The FF85 can be used with OGB-1 ammunition, 82 mm mortar rounds, and ammunition manufactured in-house by the company. The FF120 is compatible with a wider range of munitions, including the MOA-400, MOA-900, 105 mm artillery shells, and 120 mm mortar rounds. Among the manufacturer’s own ammunition is the KIL-9, a 9-kg penetrating high-explosive delayed-action round designed to destroy enemy field fortifications.
“The idea is that after being dropped, the munition gains a certain velocity, which allows it to destroy dugouts, penetrate, and breach the roofs of standard dugouts, which have two embankments and a layer of earth on top. The munition penetrates and detonates after a certain amount of time. Many units had similar solutions, but they were not mass-produced factory items,” said a company representative.
During the prototyping and small-batch production phases, a significant portion of the parts were manufactured using 3D printing. With the transition to mass production, the company began using injection-molded plastic parts produced on a thermoplastic injection molding machine.
According to a representative of the manufacturer, Firefly guidance kits are already being supplied to individual brigades. The military can order Firefly through the AOZ, the DOT-Chain Defence platform, or via direct contracts.
It is noted that the system costs about $200, and the price difference between the FF120 and FF85 is minimal. At the same time, the manufacturer is ready to adapt the product to ammunition already in the military unit’s inventory.
“Typically, interaction with units proceeds as follows. When a unit purchases or receives these products—homing modules—it provides us with a list of munitions it wants to use with them. We receive data on weight and dimensions, go to the firing range, conduct several test firings, and adapt the modules for ease of use, integration, and overall application,” the company explained.
According to the manufacturer, an assessment of the cost of use should take into account not only the price of a single drop but also the costs of zeroing in and flying the drone, including the risk of losing it.

Italy’s Ustica enigma: Can French files solve mystery crash blamed on stray missile?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
15:42:45 UTC
00:42:45 KST

Italy’s Ustica enigma: Can French files solve mystery crash blamed on stray missile?
France’s decision to share defence documents with the Italian judiciary has raised hopes of a breakthrough in investigations into the 1980 crash of a passenger jet near the island of Ustica, which a former Italian president claimed was mistakenly shot down by a French fighter jet. Sceptics caution that the files are unlikely to shed light on one of Italy’s most enduring mysteries, let alone reveal a culprit.
A rocky outpost of Italy in the Tyrrhenian Sea, the island of Ustica owes its name to the smouldering volcanic lava that gave its striking rock formations their dark hue.
For many Italians, however, the picturesque island is synonymous with a notorious plane crash that claimed 81 lives, and the intricate cover-up that buried its causes in a thick fog of lies, decoys and mysterious deaths.
The fate of Itavia Flight 870, which plunged into waters off Ustica on June 27, 1980, remains a subject of fierce debate after countless expert reports and judicial enquiries spanning several decades. The most widely accepted theory suggests the plane was caught up in an aerial dogfight and mistakenly shot down by a fighter jet, which a former Italian president has claimed was French.
News this week that French authorities would hand over defence documents to Italian investigators has been greeted as a potential gamechanger in Italy, where prosecutors and plaintiffs have long accused France and other Western allies of withholding evidence.
The 11th-hour twist led prosecutors on Wednesday to abort plans to shelve the latest investigation into the crash, throwing a lifeline to families of the victims who have relentlessly lobbied Italian governments and the judiciary to pursue the case.
Cover-up
The DC-9 plane operated by the now-defunct Itavia carrier was in the final stretch of its journey from Bologna to Palermo on a clear summer evening when it suddenly broke up and crashed into the sea, killing all 77 passengers and 4 crew members, all of them Italian.
The incident is known in Italy as the strage di Ustica, a term commonly used to refer to the deadly terrorist attacks that rattled the country in those years, many of which also remain shrouded in mystery.
Watch moreVictims of Italy’s deadly ‘Years of Lead’ demand justice
“At first, it was labelled an ‘accident’ or a ‘tragedy’. But as efforts to cover up the incident became apparent over time, people started calling it a ‘strage’ (massacre),” said historian Cora Ranci, who has written a book about the Ustica affair and the many smokescreens she says have hampered investigations.
Like other unsolved civilian massacres, she added, the Ustica affair “has contributed to the erosion of trust between citizens and institutions in Italy, fuelling the sense that those in power are bound by a code of silence and that their actions are shrouded in secrecy”.
Following the crash, officials hastily concluded that it had been caused by mechanical failure, precipitating the demise of the already struggling carrier Itavia. Judicial inquiries resumed only years later under pressure from victims’ families, spurred by an investigative journalist convinced that the plane had been shot down.
Progress was slow, hampered by the fact that tracking data and radar scans had been wiped clean at all but one of the various Italian bases within range of the incident, leaving investigators with little hard evidence to work on. Four air force generals were eventually tried on charges of treason and withholding evidence, though none were convicted.
The untimely deaths of at least 15 military personnel and others connected to the case – through transport accidents, shootings, stabbings and suicides by hanging – furthered muddied the waters, compounding the sense of a conspiracy to hide the truth.
In 2013, Italy’s highest court ruled that the plane had been brought down in an aerial battle, either by a missile or through a near-collision, without identifying a culprit. It ordered the state to compensate families of the victims, adding that cover-ups in the investigations were considered “definitively ascertained”. The ruling was in line with the conclusions of an earlier, decade-long inquiry, which determined that the intended target of the operation was a smaller aircraft travelling in the DC-9’s slipstream to evade radar detection.
“We’ve known for years that the passenger plane was downed in a combat operation,” said former senator Daria Bonfietti, the head of the association of families of the victims that lobbied the authorities to recover the wreckage and reopen investigations decades ago. But, she added, “we still don’t know who did it.”
The Libya link
Despite the court rulings, some remain deeply sceptical of the missile scenario, leaning instead towards the theory of a bomb exploding on board the plane. They point to the numerous terrorist attacks that shook the country in those years, including the strage di Bologna, a train station bombing that killed 85 people and injured score more just weeks after the Ustica crash.
Potential culprits cited by proponents of the bomb theory – which has never been upheld in court – include far-right activists, Palestinian militant groups and Muammar Gaddafi’s Libya.
The late Libyan strongman is also at the heart of the missile hypothesis, which gained further traction in 2007 when former Italian president Francesco Cossiga claimed that the passenger jet had been shot down by French military planes who were after Gaddafi.
Cossiga, who was prime minister in June 1980, cited Italian intelligence but offered no evidence to back up the allegation. He claimed Italian sources had tipped off Gaddafi, ensuring that he was not on board the smaller plane allegedly tailing the Itavia flight.
Proponents of the Libyan link say it is substantiated by the recovery, three weeks after the Ustica disaster, of the wreckage of a Libyan MiG fighter on a mountain in Calabria, which may have been chased and downed on the same night as the DC-9.
“We know from declassified documents that Italy at the time was covertly allowing Libyan aircraft to fly though its airspace to Yugoslavia for purposes of training and maintenance,” said Ranci, adding that it was common practice for those jets to evade detection by tailing commercial flights. On top of creating dangers for civilian planes, this tacit agreement infuriated the Americans and even more so the French, who were fighting a proxy war with Gaddafi’s Libya in Chad.
The Ustica crash came months after France’s embassy in Tripoli was ransacked and after a botched Libyan attempt to shoot down a French surveillance aircraft over the Mediterranean, which sent tensions spiralling.
Bonfietti, whose elder brother was on board the Itavia flight, said successive judicial inquiries had established that multiple military aircraft were operating over the Tyrrhenian on the day of the crash, including US, French and other NATO aircraft. “Now we need those countries to tell us what they were up to and why they kept quiet about it,” she said.
Watch moreGladio: NATO’s secret cold war operation in Italy
“If Gaddafi was indeed their target, it’s obvious that whoever carried out the operation could not openly claim it – not in a Cold War context,” Bonfietti added. “Instead, they decided to cover up what happened and pretend the plane experienced a mechanical failure.”
Locating the Foch
Allegations of French involvement resurfaced in 2023 when former Italian prime minister Giuliano Amato urged France to come clean on the mysterious plane crash, asking President Emmanuel Macron to look into the matter.
“If he shows that the allegation is unfounded, so much the better. If it is true, he should apologise,” Amato, who served as deputy PM at the time of the incident, told a news conference, suggesting it would be easier for someone Macron’s age to overcome old taboos.
Bonfietti said she had personally asked Italy’s current Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni to raise the issue with Macron when they met for a summit in June. According to Italian media reports, it was those talks that helped pave the way for the release of French documents.
The former senator said she hoped the new files would help expose what she described as France’s “past lies”, including about the whereabouts of a French aircraft carrier that Cossiga claimed was involved in the Ustica incident. Italian prosecutors say testimony from witnesses contradicts French claims that the Foch carrier was docked at Navy headquarters in Toulon on June 27 and that the Solenzara base in Corsica had closed and ceased all radar recordings hours before the Ustica crash.
“If the Foch was instead in the Tyrrhenian, as witness accounts suggest, it would have been in a position to detect and record what happened,” said Ranci, adding that the same applied to a US Navy carrier stationed in the Tyrrhenian – which US officials claimed had switched its radar off that night – and an AWACS mobile radar station believed to have been flying overhead.
Contacted by FRANCE 24, France’s defence ministry said it had “always responded to requests from the Italian judicial authorities” in connection with the case. It said it “recently confirmed (to Italian authorities) that a batch of documents could be used in legal proceedings”, adding that these documents “had been brought to the attention of the Italian authorities several years ago”.
The ministry did not say whether classified documents previously withheld would this time be handed over.
Analysts have voiced scepticism that the French documents would lead to any breakthrough, stressing that the decision to make them available to Italian prosecutors in no way constitutes an admission of guilt. According to Professor Gregory Alegi, a professor at LUISS University in Rome and a prominent critic of the missile hypothesis, France’s willingness to share more information “suggests they know they have nothing to fear”.
Some families of victims have expressed hopes that French cooperation might open new lines of investigation, urging prosecutors to also pursue the terrorism lead. All agree the French move will at least ensure the inquiry is not shelved.
“It’s quite possible the French sent us nothing new – their shopping list or something – but the important thing is they sent us documents and so investigations go on,” said Bonfietti. “We owe it to our loved ones to keep fighting for the truth.”

Russian Strike Hits Kyiv’s Northern Bridge, Blocking Traffic Across Dnipro
Russian forces struck one of Kyiv’s key Dnipro River crossings on October 3, damaging transport infrastructure and disrupting traffic between the capital’s left and right banks.
Russian forces struck Kyiv’s Northern Bridge on the morning of October 3, damaging the roadway and trolleybus infrastructure and forcing authorities to restrict traffic across the Dnipro River crossing.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko, the strike damaged the bridge’s road surface and overhead trolleybus power lines. Traffic from Kyiv’s left bank toward the right bank was subsequently blocked while emergency and municipal services responded at the scene.
The strike occurred shortly after an air raid alert was declared in the Ukrainian capital over the threat of Russian drones. Explosions were reported in Kyiv before officials confirmed the hit on the bridge.
Kyivpastrans said the closure disrupted several public transport routes, including buses No. 21, 73, 101, and 114, as well as trolleybuses No. 29, 30, 31, and 47.
Several bus routes were redirected through the Podilskyi Bridge crossing, Poshtova Ploshcha metro station, and European Square.
The Northern Bridge is one of the main road connections across the Dnipro in Kyiv and links districts in the northern parts of the capital.
The attack follows a series of Russian strikes on Kyiv’s Southern Bridge over the previous two days. Russian forces first struck the Southern Bridge on October 1, targeting part of its support structure before hitting it again later that day and damaging the road surface, bridge infrastructure, and protective structures used by the metro system.
Russian forces struck the Southern Bridge again early on October 2, prompting authorities to introduce restrictions on several crossings between Kyiv’s left and right banks. The bridge was subsequently targeted for a fourth time.
Following the repeated attacks, Kyiv police announced additional traffic restrictions during air raid alerts. The Southern Bridge is to be completely closed in both directions during alerts, while traffic on several other Dnipro crossings may also be limited.

‘Bordering on angry’: The state of play as US midterms enter final month
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
15:18:28 UTC
00:18:28 KST

‘Bordering on angry’: The state of play as US midterms enter final month
Democrats enter final stretch with surprisingly positive outlook as Republican money seeks to stem damage.
Washington, DC – Democrats have the momentum; Republicans are surging in defence and cash.
That narrative has emerged ahead of the United States midterm elections in November, as races across the country enter their final stretch.
With control of the US House of Representatives and the US Senate at stake, Democrats begin October with a surprisingly rosy outlook as more congressional seats are seen as in play.
Republicans, meanwhile, appear to be in damage control, pouring millions of dollars into races once seen as secure victories while injecting more funding into a handful of marquee showdowns.
The party’s standard bearer, President Donald Trump, who has embraced the notion of the election being a referendum on his leadership, enters the final month with staggeringly low approval ratings.
The most recent Associated Press-NORC polling, released on Thursday, showed Trump with 31 percent approval, the lowest during either of his two terms. Only 26 percent of respondents approved Trump’s handling of the economy, dipping two points below his predecessor, former President Joe Biden’s lowest rating on the topic.
Surveys continue to show voters rank the economy as their top issue, with topics like gas prices, made higher by the US-Israel war with Iran, dominating their concerns. Immigration and corruption have also regularly ranked high.
“The broad stroke is that Americans are disappointed, bordering on angry that President Trump hasn’t delivered on the core promises he made when he won re-election,” according to Henry Olsen, a senior fellow at the conservative Ethics and Public Policy Center in Washington, DC.
House looking solid for Dems
Political trackers have long projected Democrats will take control of the US House of Representatives in the November 3 vote.
Winning a majority in the 435-member chamber from Republicans would give the party renewed legislative power to assert leverage over Trump, while launching investigations into his administration’s dealings. Top Democrats have already signalled that probes into Trump’s family business dealings would be top priorities.
Two election non-partisan prediction authorities, the Cook Political Report and the University of Virginia’s Sabato’s Crystal Ball, have recently assessed that the likelihood of Democrats taking the House has only increased.
The Cook Political Report recently shifted 15 House races in the direction of Democrats, moving some considered “toss-ups” to “leans Democrat” and some previously considered “lean Republican” to “toss-ups”.
One such shift was for a Texas border district represented by Republican Monica De La Cruz. Her district was emblematic of a wider Latino shift towards Trump in 2024. Once seen as holding the advantage over her challenger, Democrat Bobby Pulido, Cook now rates her race as a “toss-up”.
All told, the political analysis clearinghouse now predicts Democrats are on track to win 5 to 15 House seats.
Senate in play
With 30 days left to go, “there’s much more drama in the Senate than the House races”, according to Kyle Kondik, the managing editor at Sabato’s Crystal Ball.
Once considered a pipe dream for Democrats, who need a net gain of at least four seats to win a slim majority, the 100-member chamber has moved within a more comfortable striking distance.
Unlike in the House, where every seat is up for re-election, only 35 Senate seats are up for grabs in this cycle, creating a far narrower pathway to control.
“The trajectory of the polling since Labor Day (September 7) has generally been that a bad Republican environment is just getting worse,” Kondik said, adding that “the Senate just seems to get more and more competitive as the cycle has gone on”.
To be sure, the quality of polling can vary across the country, with Kondik cautioning that gauging the political temperature of the Midwest has been particularly challenging for pollsters.
Still, in North Carolina, former Democratic Governor Roy Cooper is expected to trounce former Republican National Committee chairman Michael Whatley in the race for a Senate seat currently held by Republicans. Top conservative donors have already begun to divert funds from the contest.
Surveys have consistently shown Democrats leading in three other races for seats currently held by Republicans: Democrat James Talarico against Republican Ken Paxton in Texas; Democratic challenger Sherrod Brown against Republican incumbent Senator John Husted in Ohio; and Democratic Mary Peltola against Republican Dan Sullivan in Alaska.
Races for Republican held seats in Iowa, between Republican Ashley Hinson and Democrat Josh Turek, and in Maine, between Republican incumbent Susan Collins and Democratic challenger Troy Jackson, remain separated by less than one point, according to Real Clear Politics polling averages.
Democrats, meanwhile, have consistently led in polling in Senate races in Georgia, New Hampshire and Michigan for seats the party currently holds.
Big money in the race
For Republicans, salvation could be in the spending, with this year’s race continuing a US phenomenon of small fortunes poured into politics.
All told, at least $4bn had been spent on gubernatorial and congressional midterm advertising buys as of September 17, putting the race on track to become “perhaps the most expensive midterm on record”, according to Michael Franz, co-director of the Wesleyan Media Project.
Republicans entered September with a considerable funding edge. The Republican National Committee had $125.6m on hand, with the Democratic National Committee trailing far behind with $16.9m and $17.6m in debt.
When accounting for the three major committees associated with both groups, the Republican Party had $233.4m in cash, according to a CNBC analysis, while the Democratic Party had $130.4m.
Trip Yang, a Democrat strategist based in New York City, told Al Jazeera such spending can be deployed to help boost a candidate’s name recognition or to tear down a competitor.
According to AdImpact, Republicans and their allies were set to spend $888m on advertising from mid-September to election day, with Democrats and their supporters set to spend $666m.
The firm found pro-Republican ad spending would be particularly pronounced in the key Senate races in Ohio, Texas and Michigan, outpacing Democratic spending by at least $24m in each state.
Trump’s unpopularity, Yang said, means “Republicans spending millions or hundreds of millions of dollars improving their candidates’ images by itself may not be enough”.
“If you’re a little bit handicapped because your president is so toxic, you try to spend your hundreds of millions of dollars attacking the Democrats to make it more of a food fight,” he said.
A New York Times analysis estimated by the end of August at least $1bn in so-called “dark money” had been poured into the midterms. The term refers to spending where the donor’s identity is shielded, typically through nonprofit and shell-company donations to Super PACs.
Industry groups, including those supporting Crypto, AI and online betting firms, are expected to be top spenders in key races, although their support tends to cut across partisan lines.
Trump, meanwhile, has pledged to spend between $400m and $500m from his MAGA Inc Super PAC, though it has so far spent about $15m to support Paxton’s Senate bid in Texas.
Pro-Paxton ad reservations far outpaced Talarico in September, according to AdImpact data analysed by NPR, with $94m spent compared with $30m to support the Democrat.
The Trump factor
Trump has pledged to spend the final days before the election in non-stop campaign mode, after urging supporters during his Republican Midterm Convention in Dallas, Texas, to “vote like I’m on the ballot”.
His plan to criss-cross the country for rallies underscores a “base turnout” strategy meant to energise voters already loyal to the party, according to conservative analyst Olsen.
“But the Republican problem is a persuasion problem with people in the middle,” Olsen said. “[Trump’s campaigning] might help with some turnout … but their real problem is persuasion, and it’s not something that’s going to help with that in the slightest.”
Polls have spelt trouble for Republicans when it comes to swaying independents, with a PBS News, NPR and Marist poll from September 23 showing unaffiliated voters breaking for Democrats at 57 percent compared with 32 moving towards Republicans.
The scenario has created a dilemma for some top Republican candidates over whether to break from the president on his most controversial actions, according to Lee Miringoff, the director of the Marist University Institute for Public Opinion.
Senate candidates Ashley Hinson in Iowa, Jon Husted in Ohio and Mike Rogers in Michigan all recently put daylight between themselves and Trump on the war with Iran.
One Republican House candidate, Representative Maria Elvira Salazar, has criticised Trump’s aggressive immigration enforcement policies as she seeks to rally Latino voters in South Florida.
Trump, in turn, reposted a social media message calling Salazar a “backstabber”.
“You need to have, you know, something else going for you other than endorsement of Trump,” said Miringoff. “Some Republicans are starting to have self-preservation kick in because they’re concerned.”
What can change?
Achieving a wide-scale shift in public opinion remains a tall order for Republicans in the final stretch of the race.
Many of the defining issues are unlikely to change before November, with Trump signalling a possible escalation with Iran following the vote as he has downplayed the prospect of short-term affordability relief.
At the same time, the US president has also not ruled out actions that rights groups say could upend voter turnout. Most recently, he refused to commit to not invoking the Insurrection Act or declaring a state of emergency surrounding the vote during an interview with Time magazine.
Miringoff said he believed that the “potential for more than just a marginal shift is there”, as he assessed some Democratic candidates have struggled to present clear visions beyond opposition to Trump.
“The result isn’t formed in concrete,” he said, “to the degree that there’s going to be a lot of money still spent.”
Analyst Olsen saw less remaining wiggle room for the party.
“Republicans have the time and the resources to change the outcome with respect to a few close Senate races,” Olsen said. “But to change direction, they would need something that would be apocal.”

Spaniards protest housing crisis as Sánchez weighs snap vote
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
15:17:04 UTC
00:17:04 KST

Spain's Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez delivers a speech during an extraordinary parliamentary session to vote on a government housing decree on Octrober 2, 2026 at the Congress of Deputies in Madrid. | Javier Soriano/AFP via Getty Images
A wave of housing protests swept across dozens of Spanish cities on Saturday as Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez weighed calling a snap election.
The largest demonstration took place in Madrid, where four columns of protesters filled the capital’s main boulevards before converging on Cibeles Square. The Spanish Tenants Union, which organized the protests, said 500,000 people took to the streets, while the government’s delegation in Madrid estimated 70,000 protesters participated.
Spanish Tenants Union spokesperson Valeria Racu said the turnout reflected public exasperation with political leaders who have failed to tackle a housing crisis in which average rents have risen nearly 90% over the past decade.
Advertisement
“The people on the streets once again hold the power,” she said while addressing the demonstration, insisting that their movement would “no longer tolerate inaction.”
The protests were triggered after an investment firm evicted 87-year-old Maricarmen Abascal from the apartment where she had lived since 1956. Sánchez’s government sought to contain the discontent on Tuesday by unveiling two long-delayed bills aimed at curbing speculative practices, extending eviction protections for vulnerable tenants and automatically renewing existing contracts. But conservative lawmakers in parliament rejected both bills on Friday.
Amid the defeat, senior government figures indicated Sánchez — already under pressure over the ongoing migrant crisis in Ceuta and corruption cases involving members of his family and close political allies — was considering calling a snap election in a bid to capitalize on anger over housing.
Protesters hold a banner reading ‘towards the general strike’ along Gran Via street during a demonstration against the housing crisis on October 3, 2026 in Madrid. | Pablo Blazquez Dominguez/Getty Images
Saturday’s protests underscored the risks of that strategy. While demonstrators slammed the conservative opposition for voting down the bills, they also accused Sánchez of failing to tackle the housing crisis since taking office in 2018.
“Eight days of people power have achieved more than eight years of progressive government,” Racu said, adding that protesters would continue pressuring politicians “regardless of who governs this country.”
Calling for a general strike to force the adoption of urgent housing measures, Racu said “the feelings of disaffection, desperation, disillusionment and sadness have been replaced by a new energy on the streets.”
Advertisement
As the demonstrations took place, Sánchez remained out of sight, weighing his options. Emiliano García-Page, the Socialist president of Castilla-La Mancha, and the party’s leaders in Extremadura, the Basque Country and Castilla y León on Saturday urged Sánchez to call an early election, saying voters needed to be heard.
Meanwhile, the prospect of an imminent election is prompting Spain’s fractured left to scramble to regroup. With Deputy Prime Minister Yolanda Díaz declining to run for reelection, Health Minister Mónica García and Culture Minister Ernest Urtasun are seen as frontrunners to succeed her in the leadership of the Sumar party.
But Podemos leader Irene Montero is also positioning herself to lead a broader left-wing alliance. So, too, is longtime housing activist and former Barcelona Mayor Ada Colau, who has signaled a willingness to return to frontline politics at the head of a progressive coalition.
The center-right People’s Party leads in electoral polls with 34% support and is open to forming a government with the far-right Vox party, which is polling at 18%. Sánchez’s Socialists are backed by 26% of voters, and would need the fragmented left to unite behind a viable electoral alliance capable of winning enough seats in parliament to form a fresh coalition.
Spain’s housing protests have begun to spill beyond the country’s borders, with similar demonstrations held in Lisbon, Dublin, Potsdam and The Hague. The mobilizations reflect a bloc-wide crisis marked by the lack of affordable homes and governments under pressure to increase housing supply.

Thousands take to the streets across Spain as protesters call for a general strike after parliament rejects two government housing decrees.
Demonstrators are marching in several Spanish cities on Saturday, a day after parliament voted down two government decrees aimed at giving tenants stronger protection.
In Madrid, according to the organisers, around 500,000 people took part in the demonstrations, while the authorities put the number at around 70,000. Activists have been camped for about a week in Puerta del Sol, one of the capital's main tourist squares.
Participants could be seen carrying placards reading "General strike" and chanting slogans such as "Down with rentierism".
The protest remained peaceful, under a visible police presence. The president of the employers' confederation CEOE, Antonio Garamendi, says he respects the protests but warns that he will take action if a general strike is called, as he considers it "illegal".
The Tenants' Union, which is coordinating the protests, says in a statement, "There is an irreparable disconnect between what the people want and what the parties vote for."
The Tenants' Union is demanding a 50% cut in rents, open-ended contracts and the expropriation of homes from vulture funds. Its spokesperson, Valeria Racu, says there is still no date for the general strike, which is being negotiated with other organisations and which they want to be "historic".
Tensions in Valencia and protests across the rest of the country
In Valencia, protesters marched towards the Palau de les Arts Reina Sofía, where the Valencia Real Estate Summit 2026 property investment conference is taking place, with former Citizens leader Albert Rivera among the speakers.
Some protesters removed barriers and the police cordon and threw objects at officers. Police responded with rubber bullets and tear gas. Several people managed to reach the upper part of the building. The march had been called by four organisations, including the Tenants' Union and the Housing Union.
There were also demonstrations in many other cities. In San Sebastian, the protest entered its second consecutive day, called by the LAB union with the backing of the Tenants' Union. In Cádiz, where according to organisers the average rent is about 900 euros and buying a home reaches 200,000, the march ended at City Hall with the reading of a manifesto.
There were also marches in Las Palmas de Gran Canaria, with further rallies in Lanzarote, Fuerteventura and Tenerife. In Barcelona, Luana Rocha, a member of the camp, told 'TVE' that the intention is to stay indefinitely, "We are heading towards a general strike". Teruel will join in on Sunday with a demonstration at 18:30 starting from Plaza del Torico.
Sánchez begins a period of reflection as parties trade blame
On Friday, Congress rejected the government's two housing decrees, with votes against from PP, Vox and UPN and Junts refusing to support them. The first falls by 172 votes in favour to 178 against, and the second by 166 in favour to 184 against.
Sánchez ended his speech with a warning, "History will judge you sooner than you think and more harshly than you imagine". He now enters a period of reflection over whether to call early elections, a decision that rests solely with him. The opposition is again calling for elections, and some PSOE leaders and ministers now think so too, according to the original report.
Junts urges the PSOE to sit down and negotiate. Its spokesperson, Míriam Nogueras, described the decrees as "a poorly drafted law", and its secretary general, Jordi Turull, argues that they would have "discouraged" property sales. The PSOE replies that the texts already include Junts' proposals, "What more do they want?"
Vice-President Yolanda Díaz says that responsibility for evictions “has three names”: Feijóo, Abascal and Nogueras. Alberto Núñez Feijóo, for his part, pledges to look for a legal formula so that there is no further term without a budget.
Meanwhile, the camp in Sol reaches its seventh night, with around 2,000 people.
The protests begun after the eviction of Maricarmen Abascal, an 87-year-old woman who was carried out on a stretcher and is now recovering in hospital.
Housing campaigners say an investment company has bought the property where she lived for around seven decades and sought to raise her rent by 275 percent. After the backlash, the new owners have agreed to let her return at a low rent.
