Teaching is just the start: The crushing burden on India's college teachers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
14:18:24 UTC
23:18:24 KST

According to a survey on higher education, while recommended student-teacher ratio (STR) targets in higher education range between 15:1 and 20:1, the national average hovers between 24:1 and 27:1.
In a brightly lit classroom at an engineering college in Bengaluru, a fourth-year Computer Science lecture is underway. At the front, a professor moves through a technical lesson while also keeping track of attendance sheets and administrative requirements.In the middle rows, a student sits quietly, mentally calculating train schedules between Bengaluru and Pune. He is trying to work out how to explain to a corporate employer that a career-launching Pre-Placement Offer (PPO) could be at risk because of a mandatory offline attendance requirement for a single elective subject.The scene captures a growing tension inside India’s higher education system.For final-year students, college is no longer only about completing a degree. With competition for jobs intensifying, students are increasingly focused on internships, practical skills, early employment and mental health support. But the institutional framework around them remains tied to attendance thresholds, credit requirements, standardised evaluation and administrative compliance.Caught at the centre of these competing pressures is the college teacher.According to data from the All India Survey on Higher Education (AISHE), while recommended Student-Teacher Ratio (STR) targets in higher education range between 15:1 and 20:1, the national average hovers between 24:1 and 27:1.
In public and state institutions, that figure can rise to 35:1 or 50:1, with individual undergraduate lectures accommodating 80 to 120 or more students per section.The pressure is compounded by faculty shortages. Central universities report faculty vacancy rates between 29% and 34%, while senior professor vacancies frequently exceed 50%. Across technical institutions such as the IITs, NITs and IIITs, unfilled positions range from 30% to over 50%.This leaves teachers performing several roles at once: academic instructors, institutional policy enforcers, career advisers and, often, informal listeners when students are struggling.At the same time, they have to manage UGC Academic Performance Indicators, NAAC and NIRF documentation and heavy teaching loads.
Modern classroom: More than academics
For today's students, particularly those in their final year, the classroom is closely linked to the question of what happens after graduation.“A student may come because he is confused about an internship, worried about placements or simply doesn't know how to deal with something happening at home. We try to listen, but there is a limit to what a subject teacher can realistically handle,” Prakash, a college faculty member at an engineering college, says.From the student's perspective, the final year can feel like a race against time, with academic requirements running alongside internships, placements and preparations for entering the workforce.Pranav Vats, a final-year Computer Science and Engineering student in Bengaluru, describes what students prioritise:“Whenever a guy comes to a college, he eventually wants to get placed. He doesn't want to get a 9-plus CGPA every semester. He just wants to get placed in a good company and do well in his career financially and also growth-wise... I have been doing internships from the first year itself. And whatever interviews I have been going through, nobody asked me about what my CGPA is. Everybody just asked, okay, how much do you know, how much practical skills you have, and how well you understand the market and how well do you understand your business in which you are going to work now.”That shift creates a difficult balance for teachers. Students may see practical experience as more directly connected to employment, while faculty members remain responsible for ensuring that students complete prescribed courses, credits and attendance requirements.
When attendance collide with career
The tension becomes particularly visible during placement and internship season.Pranav describes a situation in which he had secured an internship opportunity in Pune after clearing an interview:“Two, three months back, I got an interview. I've cleared it. I went to Pune. And at that time, I got permission from college. They gave me this letter of acknowledgement that you can go and pursue your six months internship, and all. But all of a sudden, after two months, they are saying that no, you have to fulfil your academic requirements and all... This company is very good. I'm doing very well there. And they are giving me the PPO for it. I could have got placed. But right now, this company is not giving away. College is saying that you have to attend weekly once class. As a student, it is not possible for me to come from Pune to Bangalore every week to attend some stupid class that is not even relevant to my coursework, which is not even relevant to my computer science degree... It is just an open elective subject.”He says discussions with his mentor, department head and other authorities did not resolve the problem. Pranav says similar situations have affected other students, including those with jobs or internships in Bengaluru itself.He says, “A guy got placed in Bangalore itself. And he said, ‘Sir, I can't attend this class this week because I've got placed.’ They said, ‘You have to fulfill this academic thing’.”For teachers, however, understanding the student's situation does not necessarily mean being able to change the rule.“The final year is particularly difficult because everything seems to happen at once. Students are completing projects, dealing with attendance and examinations, and at the same time worrying about placements and what they are going to do after graduation. You can see that pressure building up, especially when a student's plans don't work out,” the faculty said.The faculty member explains the dilemma, “There are situations where a student gets an internship or an opportunity outside the college and genuinely needs flexibility. As a teacher, you may understand why that opportunity matters to him. But you are also responsible for implementing the academic requirements. That can put the teacher in an uncomfortable position because you may sympathise with the student without having the authority to change the rule.”
Teacher becomes institutional buffer
The teacher is therefore often caught between three sets of expectations.The administration expects attendance, syllabus completion and documentation for institutional requirements. Students expect empathy, career guidance and flexibility. Parents expect academic performance, safety and career outcomes.The teacher may have to explain an institutional decision to a student without having any authority over that decision.“Sometimes the student is upset with the institution, the parents are worried about the student's performance and the department is concerned about academic requirements,” the teacher explains. “The teacher ends up sitting in the middle. We are expected to explain one side to the other, even though we may not have control over the decision ourselves.”For students, this can reinforce the perception that teachers are primarily there to enforce attendance and award marks.Pranav puts it bluntly, “They don't care, they just want these things to attend classes, they want attendance, they want marks, that's it... If you go to an off-campus thing, where majorly everybody is applying right now, nobody asks you about your CGPA. They just want you to have your practical skills. But this CGPA thing or whatever coursework they are teaching us in college, it is not even relevant to what we will work in our offices.”
When personal problems enter classroom
The pressure is not limited to academics and placements.Teachers are also increasingly expected to recognise when students are struggling emotionally, even though they may not be trained to provide professional mental health support.“You spend enough time with a class to notice changes,” the faculty member observes. “If a student who is normally interactive suddenly stops speaking, misses classes or stops submitting work, you notice it. The difficult part is deciding whether to ask, ‘Is everything okay?’ because you don't know whether the student wants you to enter that part of his life,” Prakash say.The teacher describes the boundary involved, “There is a very fine line between being concerned about a student and becoming intrusive. If I ask too many questions, it may seem intrusive. If I don't ask anything, I may miss something important. Teachers are constantly trying to judge where that line is.”At the same time, faculty members recognise their own limitations.“I want my students to know that they can approach me, but I also have to be honest about my limitations. I can listen, I can help them think through a problem and I can direct them towards the right person. But I am not trained to provide therapy, and pretending otherwise can be harmful,” Prakash says.
Counselling gap, a stigma problem
Many institutions have counselling cells or mentor-mentee systems, but having a service does not necessarily mean students will use it.Pranav says his mentor-mentee system is largely focused on academic issues:“For every 20 or 30 sets of people there is assigned one mentor. So whatever the issues you have regarding the college, you can talk with them and they can get a resolution about it... [But] there is nothing like that through which we can discuss our career... They are strictly for the subject.”He says students also face peer pressure around seeking counselling.“We have one basically like they have hired a person... if you have any emotional issues or something like that, then you can go schedule a session,” Pranav says. “[But] if you suppose you go to a counsellor there is this peer pressure. If you go to a counselor, or maybe you're discussing things with the teacher, you would seem like a weak person.”“This thing is very very disturbing to the students and nobody talks about it because everybody feels that okay, if I talk about it I can feel weak about it and people will think that okay he's not mature enough to deal with his own problem on his own... I talk to some of my friends about it who are eventually on the same path... but majorly I work with my pressure on my own,” Pranav adds.When behaviour changes significantly, teachers also have to balance intervention with confidentiality.“If I feel that a student's behaviour has changed significantly, I cannot just say, ‘That's his personal matter.’ There are situations where you have to involve the appropriate support system. But you also have to be careful about confidentiality and about not turning a student's difficulty into a public issue,” Prakash says.
Emotional burden on teachers
While student stress receives increasing attention, the pressure on faculty can remain largely invisible.A teacher managing a class of 80 to 120 students may also have to deal with staff shortages, administrative work, evaluations, meetings and institutional documentation. A difficult conversation with a student does not necessarily end when the class does.The faculty member says teachers need institutional support if they are expected to take on these additional responsibilities.Prakash says, “I don't think teachers are unwilling to take on a larger role. Most teachers care about what happens to their students. But if the expectation is that we should identify emotional distress, provide career guidance, handle academic problems and support students through personal crises, then the institution also has to give teachers training and a proper support structure.”
Beyond the classroom
The experiences of both students and teachers point to a larger structural problem.When colleges rely on individual teachers to enforce academic rules, handle administrative requirements, guide students through careers and respond to emotional distress, the teacher becomes the point where multiple pressures meet.
The solution therefore cannot rest entirely on individual faculty members.As colleges respond to changing job markets and rising student pressures, the system would require clearer boundaries for faculty responsibilities, greater flexibility for final-year students navigating legitimate career opportunities, and stronger professional support systems.For the teacher standing at the front of the classroom, the challenge is no longer simply teaching the subject. It is managing everything that happens around it, often without the authority, time or institutional support required to do so.
Vijaya Srivastava is a journalist and feature writer whose expertise lies in covering human-centred developments. Her stories explore how policy, technology, economic shifts and social change influence people's everyday lives. Her work also focuses on bringing depth, context and a human perspective to complex issues.
Her reports primarily cover society, healthcare, safety, public policy and emerging trends, alongside other political developments.

Troubled Flydubai plane remains at Saudi airport for four days now
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
14:18:00 UTC
23:18:00 KST

MOSCOW, October 3. /TASS/. The plane from Dubai to Tel Aviv that made an emergency landing because of an internal personnel incident on board on September 30 has been at Tabuk Airport in Saudi Arabia for a fourth day, a source in a Middle Eastern air traffic control service told TASS on Saturday.
"The plane on board of which a cockpit incident occurred and which made an emergency landing en route from Dubai to Tel Aviv for that reason is still at the airport of Saudi Arabia’s Tabuk," the source said. On the day when that incident took place passengers from the troubled flight were taken to Tel Aviv on board another plane while the aircraft in question still stays where it landed, he recalled. The source found it difficult to say when the plane could possibly return. "It seems everything will depend on how the probe into the incident unfolds," he noted.
On September 30, a Flydubai flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv made an emergency landing at Saudi Arabia’s Tabuk Airport following a security incident. On October 1, the Saudi Ministry of the Interior confirmed that the incident was caused by the stabbing of the flight captain by his co-pilot which left the two of them with injuries of varying severity.
Both pilots departed for Abu Dhabi with an Emirati security escort once their condition had stabilized, while the other six crew members had earlier safely returned to Dubai, the Saudi ministry specified. The UAE has continued to look into the reasons and circumstances behind the incident, including operational aspects of it and safety measures. UAE Prosecutor General Hamad Saif Al Shamsi has said the incident is being investigated as a terrorist attack.

Donnyland abandoned: the last negotiations of the year
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
17:18:00 EEST
23:18:00 KST

Donnyland abandoned: the last negotiations of the year
In early June 2026, just as the St Petersburg International Economic Form was underway, Ukraine attacked the city with long-range drones. That attack effectively marked the beginning of a new phase of the war, described in Kyiv government circles as an attempt to force Russia into peace talks.
The two-pronged strategy of drone attacks and open letters, which Ukrainska Pravda covered in detail, consisted of striking Russia's critical infrastructure on the one hand, steadily increasing the range of attacks to 1,000-3,000 km, and offering to begin peace talks at any time on the other.
The general expectation was that in the second half of the summer Ukraine's defence forces would launch a drone blockade of Crimea and Ukraine's south, making the Sea of Azov and the Black Sea completely unusable for Russian shipping. This was supposed to take place in sync with increased sanctions pressure from Ukraine's partners so that in the autumn, after the Russian elections, they could jointly push the Russians to genuinely engage in negotiations.
Back in June, a source in President Zelenskyy's diplomatic team explained the logic behind Ukraine's actions to UP: "Taking together all the military, diplomatic and international factors, a certain window of opportunity for negotiations may open in October or November – sometime before the US elections and after the Russian State Duma elections."
As of early autumn, the Armed Forces of Ukraine have achieved most of their military objectives. In some respects – such as disrupting Russian logistics in the south and targeting the shadow fleet – they have even surpassed expectations.
Yet it cannot be said that Ukraine has moved any closer to achieving its main objective – the start of substantive negotiations. Quite the opposite.
The overall positive momentum began to fade in August. A sharp escalation in Russian attacks on Ukrainian cities in the rear – above all Kyiv, Odesa, Zaporizhzhia and Kharkiv – has left Ukraine practically alone in confronting Russia's relentless aerial attacks.
There are several reasons for the stark contrast between what had been planned and the actual outcome. And the infighting over control of the Defence Ministry, the government, the General Staff and the Armed Forces didn't help, giving the Russians a head start in the technology war.
The procession of corruption scandals also took their toll, as did the total ineffectiveness of Ukraine's international partners in terms of ramping up pressure on Moscow.
It was against this backdrop that Presidents Volodymyr Zelenskyy and Donald Trump held their latest meeting in the US on 22 September.
Could that meeting have given a new impetus to the negotiations and reversed the diplomatic momentum working against Ukraine? What do Ukraine and its partners realistically expect from the autumn window for negotiations? What might Putin theoretically be prepared to agree to, and why? And what should Ukraine be prepared for after its unsuccessful attempts to force the Russians into negotiations this autumn?
Ukrainska Pravda set out to tackle these questions.
Negotiations between two capitals
In August 2026, after months of attempts that never came off, promises, postponements and yet more promises, Donald Trump's special envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff finally arrived in Kyiv. They had just visited Moscow, where they held talks with Vladimir Putin.
That trip can effectively be regarded as the start of the final phase of this year's negotiation process.
This round had begun with the notorious Dmitriev-Witkoff "peace plan" draft at the end of 2025. The negotiations then intensified after Kyrylo Budanov and Davyd Arakhamiia joined the Ukrainian team in early 2026. There were several fairly productive rounds of talks and meetings in various jurisdictions.
Eventually the broad outlines of a potential framework for a deal emerged. People involved in the negotiations jokingly referred to it as "Donnyland" (it is an irony of fate that Donbas should have the same initial syllable as the US president's first name).
The idea was to have a ceasefire along the line of contact, certain restrictions on Ukraine's military capabilities, and most importantly, a kind of "free economic zone" in Donbas, to be administered by the United States.
Exactly where this so-called Donnyland was supposed to be – in the Ukrainian-controlled part of Donbas, proportionally across both Ukrainian-controlled and Russian-occupied territories, or within broader boundaries – was something the leaders themselves were supposed to decide.
But the process ground to a complete halt before a meeting could even take place, largely because the guarantees on offer were too vague and the risks for Ukraine too great.
Despite all this, Trump and his special envoys have continued to repeat the mantra that the war could be swiftly ended – if not within 24 hours, then at least in 2026. But members of Zelenskyy's team have said privately that Kushner and Witkoff's visits to Moscow and Kyiv left them feeling a lot less optimistic, to put it mildly.
"They finally made it to Kyiv, but the problem is that with the messages they brought, they could have saved themselves the journey. They didn't bring us anything new," one member of Zelenskyy's team complained to UP off the record in early September.
"Their entire approach came down to this: before, we used to discuss scenarios for Ukraine's victory, but these people don't even have a strategy for a dignified defeat. All they have to offer boils down to this: give the Russians what they want and then we'll shower you with money. But that doesn't look much like a workable plan," the UP source said, describing the general shift in the situation.
Especially not when you consider that the Russians have identified the weak point in Ukraine's defences: the shortage of interceptors to counter ballistic missiles, and of interceptor drones to down the new jet-powered Shaheds.
So the only issue on which a more or less realistic agreement might be reached this year is the energy ceasefire.
Negotiations between two elections
"Our oil refinery strikes are what really hurt the Russians," a senior member of Zelenskyy's team told UP. "And that's the only thing they're genuinely prepared to talk about right now. An arrangement where we don't hit their oil industry and they don't hit our energy infrastructure is, so far, the only thing that might be put together before winter."
In early September, UP learned that preparations were underway for a trilateral Ukraine-US-Russia meeting at adviser level in one of the Gulf states to explore the idea of an energy ceasefire.
"Trump's envoys came away from Moscow with the impression that the Russians weren't going to enter into any negotiations or make any concessions before their State Duma elections because that would be perceived as weakness in their society. After the elections they won't let up on their attacks either, because they'll need to demonstrate that they're strong and use that to strengthen their position. But they may well be willing to talk about energy," one member of Zelenskyy's inner circle said, sharing their impressions following the US envoys' visit.
The Russian "elections" ended on 20 September. The aforementioned meeting of advisers was supposed to take place sometime afterwards. But once again, Trump intervened.
With his own congressional midterm elections approaching, the US president, true to form, declared his willingness to hold a meeting of advisers almost as if a deal had already been signed.
This forced Ukraine to respond publicly as well, and President Zelenskyy announced Kyiv's official negotiating position: if strikes on energy infrastructure are to stop, the arrangement must cover the entire energy sector. Ukraine cannot be expected to stop striking Russian oil refineries while Russia retains the right to attack Ukraine's electricity infrastructure, for example, on the pretext that it "serves the defence industry".
Kyiv's position is clear: any energy ceasefire must be comprehensive and unconditional.
It was against this backdrop that Zelenskyy and Trump met in the US on 22 September on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly.
They had actually spoken by phone a few days earlier. That conversation, however, was mostly about diesel prices, which had surged in the US. For some reason Trump chose to blame the price fluctuations not on his failed campaign in Iran, but on Ukraine and its strikes on Russian oil refineries.
The face-to-face meeting on 22 September produced no breakthrough, nor even any tangible practical results. That much was evident from the presidents' brief joint press conference before the talks, Zelenskyy's briefing afterwards, and UP sources in the Ukrainian delegation.
The only achievement was that the Americans stopped saying no to requests to sell Ukraine Patriot missiles and grant licences to manufacture them in Ukraine – although they didn't give a definitive yes either.
Even on long-term issues such as licensing missile production in Ukraine – a process that would take years – Trump continues to avoid giving specific answers.
And this is despite the fact that ahead of the midterms, he badly needs to demonstrate at least some semblance of pressure on Moscow. Ultimately, Moscow's semblance of engaging in negotiations may be only an act to support Trump (whom it views favourably) ahead of the congressional elections.
The US administration hopes to make gains on the Russia front through the signing of the Graham Act, which provides for "bone-crushing sanctions" against Russia. But will Trump be willing to impose such sanctions on members of the Russian elite with whom, it turns out, his family has close personal ties? His meeting with Zelenskyy did not yield an answer to that question.
Perhaps an answer will emerge from talks between the US president and Chinese leader Xi Jinping. Zelenskyy has at least asked Trump to test Xi's willingness to put pressure on Moscow.
***
Following Zelenskyy and Trump's talks in the US, one conclusion can now be drawn: the campaign Ukraine launched at the start of the summer to force Russia towards peace has not achieved its intended result.
This is largely because Ukraine has been unable to secure a united front among all its partners on sanctions, or to persuade them to become genuinely engaged in addressing the problem of Russian aggression.
Ukraine's military actions aimed at seizing the initiative in the south and Crimea did work. Moreover, the combined pressure on the enemy enabled Ukraine's defence forces to conduct successful and effective counteroffensive operations in the south, near Kupiansk, and even in the area with the highest concentration of Russian forces – around Lyman in Donbas.
This proved once again that while Putin may claim to have captured Kupiansk or Sviatohirsk, saying so does not make it true on the ground. On the battlefield, Ukraine remains capable of defending itself effectively and even destroying elite Russian units such as Rubicon.
Ukraine's biggest problem may prove to be the disarray in its domestic politics.
This has been fuelled by a stream of major corruption revelations involving people close to Zelenskyy. It's also been compounded by months of instability at the Defence Ministry following Mykhailo Fedorov's dismissal and the departure of his team, which had been responsible for the aggressive offensive component of Ukraine's strategy.
The new leaders at the helm of the Defence Ministry, General Staff and Armed Forces have generally received positive assessments, but they need precious time to establish control over their respective agencies. Issues such as the still-unsigned contracts for the procurement of Patriot missiles are perhaps the clearest illustration of this.
As a result, some of Ukraine's military and media momentum has been lost, while Russia has launched a new wave of massive ballistic missile and drone attacks against the capital and western oblasts.
The overall level of frustration in Ukrainian society means the government has to deliver a clear and rapid course of action. With the budget stretched to breaking point and some allies going so far as to bargain over sanctions against Russian oligarchs, Ukraine faces serious risks unless it can restore its internal resilience.
We have to get back to the "spirit of 2022", when it wasn't just the president or a single political force fighting for Ukraine's survival, but the entire nation. Otherwise, our chances of holding out until the next window of opportunity opens for talks will diminish with every passing day.
Roman Romaniuk, Ukrainska Pravda

Spain: Massive protests after housing bills voted down
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
14:18:00 UTC
23:18:00 KST

Spain: Massive protests after housing bills voted down
October 3, 2026
Tens of thousands of people protested across Spain on Saturday to demand affordable housing.
The protests come a day after the Spanish parliament narrowly voted down two emergency bills designed to support renters and prevent evictions.
"It only proves that it is us the people who have to adapt to the political parties, and not the politicians to what the people want, and this can't go on like that," one 26-year-old protester in Madrid told the Reuters news agency.
They are the latest demonstrations in a week-long wave of actions that began in response to the eviction of an 87-year-old woman, Maricarmen Abascalin, in Madrid.
"What we are feeling in the streets is a new energy that we haven't seen in a long time, and energy that is showing that eight days of people's power can achieve more than eight years of progressive government," said Valeria Racu, one of the spokespeople of the Tenants' Union organizing Saturday's protest.
Protests in dozens of cities
Police said around 70,000 people took part in the demonstration in Madrid. Organizers put the figure closer to 500,000 people.
Additional protests were held in around 50 other cities.
In the eastern city of Valencia, police used tear gas and rubber bullets against protesters.
Dozens of protesters had managed to get inside Valencia's City of Arts and Sciences — a major landmark in the city — before they were ejected by police.
What's next for the Spanish government?
Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez's proposed emergency measures included automatic renewal of tenancy contracts and restrictions on evicting vulnerable tenants. However, bills were shot down by opposition parties on Friday.
This defeat infuriated those who had been protesting against the country's increasingly unaffordable housing market all week.
"We are demanding a fundamental right: decent housing, stability and conditions allowing us to construct a decent life project," another protester in Madrid, aged 31, told the AFP news agency.
Spanish media reported that Sanchez might call a snap election for November after the legislation failed to pass, adding that the government would be watching Saturday's protests closely before making a decision.
Sanchez's office declined to comment on the reports.

SYDNEY, Oct. 3 (Xinhua) -- The alleged teen driver of the car, which plowed into a crowd in the Australian city of Newcastle, 110 km north of Sydney, on Saturday morning, has been charged, the Australian Broadcasting Corporation (ABC) reported.
Indika Bambrick Samarasinghe, 18, has been charged with three instances of dangerous driving occasioning grievous bodily harm, three instances of negligent driving occasioning grievous bodily harm and three instances of causing bodily harm by misconduct, according to court documents viewed by the ABC.
Samarasinghe will appear in Newcastle Bail Court on Sunday, the ABC said.
The assistant commissioner of police in the Australian state of New South Wales, David Waddell, told reporters on Saturday afternoon that a car was driving erratically before the driver lost control and crashed into a crowd around 9:30 a.m. local time on Saturday.
He said that the crowd had gathered along the side of the road as part of an official farewell event for the local team, the Newcastle Knights, as they traveled to Sydney to play in the National Rugby League grand final on Sunday night.
Police said that 10 people were injured, including a five-year-old girl and a 67-year-old man who were hospitalized in critical conditions.
The remaining eight people, including a second five-year-old girl and a two-year-old girl, were taken to hospital with non-life-threatening injuries.
Samarasinghe, the driver of the vehicle, was arrested at the scene and taken to hospital for mandatory drug and alcohol testing. ■

TOKYO, Oct. 3 (Xinhua) -- Eight people, including a diving instructor and seven customers, were rescued alive after being reported missing in waters off Tokyo's Hachijo Island on Saturday, local media reported.
The captain of a diving boat made an emergency call at around 1:50 p.m. local time after the eight divers failed to return as scheduled, Kyodo News reported, citing the coast guard.
They had begun diving at around 11:30 a.m. and had been scheduled to surface about an hour later.
Following the report, coast guard patrol vessels and other ships searched the surrounding waters. At around 4:30 p.m., more than two and a half hours after the report was made, the eight people were found at sea about 10 km north of Hachijo Island, public broadcaster NHK reported.
All eight were rescued by coast guard aircraft by around 5:30 p.m. and were conscious, the report said.
Authorities are investigating the circumstances surrounding the incident. ■

ADDIS ABABA, Oct. 3 (Xinhua) -- Eritrean President Isaias Afwerki departed for Egypt on Saturday for a working visit amid heightened regional diplomatic tensions.
During the visit, Afwerki will participate in a summit of heads of state on collective security, stability, and partnership, Eritrean Minister of Information Yemane Gebremeskel disclosed on Saturday.
According to Gebremeskel, the current summit is a continuation of periodic forums on the wider neighborhood, namely the Red Sea Region, the Gulf of Aden, the Arabian Gulf, as well as the Nile Basin.
The Eritrean president left for the North African country upon the invitation of his Egyptian counterpart, Abdel Fattah El-Sisi. The two leaders will also discuss further enhancement of bilateral ties during the visit, it was noted.
The visit comes as the African Union (AU) has called on Ethiopia, Eritrea, and Egypt to exercise "maximum restraint," urging the three countries to de-escalate the situation amid mounting regional diplomatic tensions.
The AU called on "all three member states to exercise maximum restraint and refrain from actions or statements that could further escalate tensions and undermine regional peace and stability."
Ethiopia closed its embassy in Eritrea and ordered 10 Eritrean diplomats to leave within 48 hours, accusing them of hostile actions and threats to national security on Thursday. Eritrea, also on Thursday, rejected the claims and announced the severance of diplomatic ties with Ethiopia, accusing Ethiopia of supporting armed opposition groups that seek to destabilize its government.
Tensions also flared between Ethiopia and Egypt, with each country expelling a diplomat from the other's embassy recently. Analysts link the disputes to rising military tensions in Ethiopia's northern Tigray region. Allegations that Eritrea and Egypt support Ethiopian rebel groups have been denied by both countries. ■

====================================================================================================

Revolutionary base of China's Long March in Wuqi County sees ecological, industrial development
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
22:17:17 CST
23:17:17 KST

Farmer Zhou Xiaoqin picks apples at her orchard in Nangou Village in Wuqi County of Yan'an City, northwest China's Shaanxi Province, Oct. 2, 2026.
The year 2026 marks the 90th anniversary of the victory of the Central Red Army's Long March. Wuqi is the county where the Long March ended. Today, the county is home to many revolutionary sites.
The Long March was an epic military trek from 1934 to 1936, during which the Communist Party of China-led Red Army broke through encirclement by the Kuomintang forces. Red Army soldiers braved raging rivers, snow-covered mountains and treacherous grasslands, with some marching as far as 12,500 kilometers. The maneuver helped lay the foundation for the eventual victory of the Chinese revolution.
The spirit of the Long March has been passed down through generations in Wuqi, inspiring local people to forge ahead and pursue development.
In the past, the county had long suffered from fragile environment, severe desertification and natural disasters. Since launching large-scale ecological restoration efforts in 1998, the county has seen its forest and grass coverage rate rise from 19.6 percent in 1997 to 72.9 percent at present, bringing significant improvements to the local environment.
Meanwhile, Wuqi has actively developed its apple industry. The apple orchards now cover 120,000 mu (about 8,000 hectares), helping increase farmers' incomes and promote rural revitalization. (Xinhua/Zou Jingyi)

Since launching large-scale ecological restoration efforts in 1998, the county has seen its forest and grass coverage rate rise from 19.6 percent in 1997 to 72.9 percent at present, bringing significant improvements to the local environment.
Meanwhile, Wuqi has actively developed its apple industry. The apple orchards now cover 120,000 mu (about 8,000 hectares), helping increase farmers' incomes and promote rural revitalization. (Xinhua/Zou Jingyi)

when exhibitions become formats, what happens to the experience of art?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
14:15:23 UTC
23:15:23 KST

when exhibitions become formats, what happens to the experience of art?
a new generation of exhibitions is adapting the museum to the way we already consume media, raising questions about what happens to the artwork along the way.
A different kind of museum
Walk into a Museum of Illusions or a Museum of Ice Cream and the experience feels closer to an adult playground than to the kind of museum most people grew up visiting. Visitors move through optical illusions, mirrors, oversized objects and brightly colored installations, looking for the right position, the right gesture or the right moment to take a video. The spaces are made for participation, and their images are made to travel. The word ‘museum’ gives these places an institutional identity, while the experience itself is largely built around play, social interaction and the pleasure of being photographed inside an unusual environment.
There is nothing necessarily wrong with that. People have always gone to cultural spaces to have fun, spend time together and experience something outside their everyday surroundings, and a well-designed interactive installation can be memorable precisely because it asks visitors to participate physically. But what kind of experience these places are offering, particularly when the museum becomes a format for entertainment and the photograph becomes one of the clearest ways of communicating what happens inside? The Museum of Illusions is a useful example because the visitor’s body is essential to many of its optical effects. Perspective, scale and mirrors create situations that only become complete when someone enters the frame, while the photograph records an illusion that can be difficult to understand from an empty installation view. The whole experience is therefore designed around the exchange between space, body and camera. You enter the illusion, you perform within it, you photograph it and the image becomes part of the story that reaches the next visitor.
The Museum of Ice Cream works through a different visual language, using color, scale, playful environments and participatory installations to create a sequence of experiences that are easy to photograph and share. These places have become part of a broader category of attractions that borrow the language and spatial authority of the museum while operating primarily through participation and entertainment. Their popularity is interesting precisely because it suggests that the museum has become useful as a cultural format even when there is no ‘collection’ at its center. The distinction matters because the word ‘museum’ carries expectations. It suggests collections, preservation, research, education and encounters with objects that have a history beyond the visit. Places built around optical tricks or themed environments may offer a very different kind of value, based on social experience, play, spectacle and the opportunity to create images of oneself inside the space. That experience can be enjoyable and carefully designed, but it may leave less to investigate once the illusion has been understood and the photograph has been taken.
The rise of immersive exhibitions
There are many interactive installations where the situation is quite different. An artwork can be highly photogenic while also giving visitors something to think about, whether through an unusual material, a social question, an environmental proposition or a physical experience that changes the way they understand a space. In those cases, the photograph is only one trace of a larger encounter. The image may be what circulates most widely, but there is still another layer that remains after the visitor has left. The distinction becomes particularly important with the current wave of immersive exhibitions built around famous artists. Across different cities, touring experiences have taken works by Vincent van Gogh, Claude Monet and Frida Kahlo and transformed them into large-scale projected environments, surrounding visitors with moving images, music and animation. Paintings that most people already recognize from books, screens and reproductions are enlarged until they become architecture, while the visitor is invited to walk inside the imagery.
There is an obvious appeal to this approach. A city does not need to own a collection of Van Gogh or Monet paintings to host an experience based on their work, and visitors who might never travel to a major museum can encounter a version of an artist’s visual language much closer to home. The temporary and touring nature of these exhibitions also makes them relatively easy to distribute, with the same basic format appearing in one city after another. This format is familiar for another reason. Most people already encounter paintings through screens, where images can be enlarged, cropped, animated and accompanied by sound. Immersive exhibitions take this everyday form of looking and expand it to architectural scale. A painting becomes a screen, the screen becomes the room, and the visitor enters an environment made from images that they may already have seen hundreds of times. That familiarity is part of the attraction. There is little difficulty in recognizing Van Gogh’s The Starry Night, Monet’s Water Lilies or Frida Kahlo’s most reproduced self-portraits, and the immersive exhibition can build on that recognition immediately. The visitor does not have to spend time learning how to look at the work before the experience begins. The paintings are already culturally familiar, and the exhibition turns that familiarity into movement, atmosphere and scale.
What happens to the original
The transformation changes the experience in ways that can be genuinely engaging. A projected painting can become an environment rather than an object viewed from a distance, and the combination of sound, movement and changing imagery can produce an emotional response that a displayed painting might not create for every visitor. For someone encountering an artist for the first time, the experience may even become an entry point into the work, giving them a reason to find out more afterwards. Something is also lost. When The Starry Night becomes a moving projection across a wall, the physical qualities of the painting disappear. The brushstrokes, the thickness of the paint, the texture of the canvas and the small variations in color that become visible when standing close to the original are no longer available in the same way. The dimensions of the painting also change, and with them the scale that Van Gogh chose when he made it.
A painting also has its own sense of time. It stays still, and the viewer decides where to look, what to notice and how long to remain in front of it. An immersive projection, where the sky can move, details can appear and disappear, the light can shift across the room and music can guide the experience, changes that relationship completely. It can be absorbing, but it asks the viewer to experience the work through movement and atmosphere instead of the quiet act of looking at the painting. This can make the distinction between the original work and its digital interpretation easy to overlook. After spending half an hour surrounded by Van Gogh’s paintings, it is understandable that a visitor might feel they have experienced Van Gogh, even though they have encountered projections of his work, a totally different experience from the one of the paintings themselves. The experience is real, but it is an experience created around the work, using another medium and another set of tools to shape how we see it.
How the experience is shared
The touring model also fits naturally into the way these exhibitions circulate online. A photograph of a visitor standing beneath a giant projection of The Starry Night communicates the experience through a familiar painting that provides recognition, a person that gives the image scale and the room that provides the spectacle. The same image can work as a souvenir for the visitor and as an invitation to someone seeing the exhibition for the first time through a screen. That logic also influences the design of the exhibition. A room may be arranged around a particular viewpoint, an installation may depend on where the visitor stands, and an interaction may be conceived with the photograph or video in mind. The visitor is therefore experiencing the space while also producing its most widely circulated representation.
Standing inside a projected Starry Night can be striking, but it is still a different encounter from standing in front of Van Gogh’s painting. What we gain is immersion; what we give up is some of the specificity of the work itself. The same contradiction appears in the places that use the word ‘museum’ for experiences built around fun and participation. A Museum of Illusions can be understood on its own terms, just as an immersive Van Gogh exhibition can offer a compelling way into an artist’s work.
When very different experiences are presented as museums, the distinction between them becomes less clear. An immersive exhibition, an interactive installation and a playful attraction can all create memorable experiences, but they do so for very different reasons.
This article is part of designboom’s SPECTATOR AND SPECTACLE chapter, asking how wonder gets built, presented in partnership with SolidNature, and how it might return some mystery to a world that has measured most of it away. Discover more stories that turn onlookers into participants, alter perception and disrupt the everyday here.

More patients traveling outside home county for doctor visits across Estonia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
14:15:00 UTC
23:15:00 KST

More patients traveling outside home county for doctor visits across Estonia
Getting to a doctor increasingly requires traveling farther from home as services concentrate in larger centers. For example, residents of Võru and Põlva counties make nearly 70 percent of their doctor visits outside their home county.
Finding a suitable appointment time at the Tartu University Hospital has recently been a challenge for Olga Margulis, who lives in Tartu. In September, she searched for a pediatric ophthalmologist appointment, but because the issue required quick attention and no times were available in the coming months, she decided to go to a private clinic. Her family has also needed a pediatric surgeon, which meant traveling to a smaller county hospital.
"We had concerns about adenoids and needed a consultation to determine whether surgery was necessary. We couldn't get an appointment at Tartu University Hospital and found one at Põlva Hospital. I don't remember exactly whether the hospital had no times at all or the queue was extremely long. At Põlva Hospital, a surgeon from Tartu consulted us and referred us for surgery at the university hospital, where he performed it," Margulis said.
Many patients from Tartu and Tallinn also end up at Viljandi Hospital, where a doctor from Tartu may meet a patient from Tallinn — or vice versa.
"In the last four years, the share of patients with permanent residence in Tartu County has increased significantly. In 2022, we had about 500 such contacts per year; today it is nearly 5,000. So the mantra that regional movement from smaller hospitals goes only toward Tartu University Hospital does not hold. I cannot state it absolutely, but there are specialties where I know the waiting time at a large hospital is four to six months, while here you can get help in under a month," said Mart Kull, member of the management board of Viljandi Hospital.
The Health Insurance Fund explains the movement from big cities to smaller regions by noting that demand for certain specialists — such as dermatologists, gynecologists, and psychologists — exceeds the capacity to provide services.
"In most cases, demand quickly exceeds capacity in places with large populations. Mental health services in Viljandi County may be somewhat more accessible than in Tallinn," said Marko Tähnas, head of the specialist care portfolio at the Health Insurance Fund.
The fund also acknowledges that services are concentrating in larger centers. Traveling to another county for medical care has increased almost everywhere in Estonia. In Võru County, such visits make up two‑thirds of all doctor appointments.
"If service usage is not very high, it makes sense to concentrate it in fewer locations, because performing the service more frequently with the same team in the same facilities ensures quality," Tähnas said.

EU issues anti-corruption demand to Ukraine – FT
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
14:12:29 UTC
23:12:29 KST

EU issues anti-corruption demand to Ukraine – FT
The EU has rejected Ukraine’s plea to accelerate financial support needed to cover an unexpected $27 billion defense gap, instead pressing Kiev to speed up reforms needed to unlock the funds already available. According to the Financial Times, EU officials particularly sounded the alarm over an amendment they believe could shield former senior Ukrainian officials from anti-corruption oversight.
Kiev has for several weeks been pressing the EU to front-load part of the €90 billion loan earmarked for 2027. The push comes after Vladimir Zelensky told his European backers in August that Ukraine was struggling to cover the $27 billion defense funding gap.
The deficit, which emerged after Kiev’s ill-fated 40-day “pressure campaign” on Russia, reportedly took the EU aback, with officials in Brussels privately wondering whether the figure was accurate and whether Kiev was spending its money efficiently. Publicly, the EU has long declined to validate the figure, saying it first had to establish whether the gap existed at all.
On Thursday, following talks in Brussels, the EU and Ukraine issued a statement which conspicuously did not mention the $27 billion, saying only that the sides had “identified the means to cover Ukraine’s budget and defense needs for 2026” and “reconfirmed the steps needed to ensure their timely release.”
Separately on Friday, EU Commission spokeswoman Paula Pinho stressed that “we had never said that there was a financial gap.” Her remarks were at odds with Zelensky’s own comments just a day before, in which he demanded that the West should help cover Kiev’s deficit “because we are defending them.”
Access to much of the available money this year (€34 billion) remains conditional on Ukraine’s reforms, many of which have stalled. Among them are new taxation rules for digital platforms and changes to VAT treatment of low-value imports.
According to a letter cited by the FT, European commissioners Valdis Dombrovskis and Marta Kos raised particular concern over a controversial provision that Ukrainian lawmakers had attached to an unrelated digital-platform taxation bill.
The amendment would make enhanced financial scrutiny of former politically exposed persons (PEPs) mandatory for only one year after they leave office, thus raising concerns that it would weaken efforts to combat Ukraine’s rampant corruption.
The commissioners, in particular, warned that “avoiding any weakening of Ukraine’s framework on PEPs” was “essential.”
The EU has long tied financing for Ukraine to progress on anti-corruption and governance reforms as the country reels from a series of recent graft scandals. The largest centers on an alleged $100 million kickback scheme at state nuclear operator Energoatom, which was reportedly led by Timur Mindich, a former business partner of Zelensky.
Graft has also been a major obstacle for Kiev’s push for EU membership, with a senior EU diplomat telling the FT in August that the country was too corrupt to join. “You can’t bring a country of 40 million people that’s at 104 on the global corruption list into the EU. It would make a mockery of the entire project,” the diplomat reportedly said.

Three Banderol Missiles and Two UAVs Entered Moldova and Exploded: Damage Reported
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
14:12:06 UTC
23:12:06 KST

On the morning of October 3, Banderol missiles and unmanned aerial vehicles entered Moldova and subsequently exploded near a number of settlements in several districts.
This was reported by Moldovan President Maia Sandu.
“Five Russian air attack vehicles, including Banderol missiles and drones, violated our airspace and exploded on our territory,” she wrote on social media platform X.
Moldova’s national airspace monitoring system recorded the passage of five unmanned aerial vehicles between 7:45 a.m. and 8:00 a.m.
Subsequently, Moldovan Defense Minister Anatolie Nosatîi reported that there were three missiles and two drones, according to Newsmaker.
The Ministry of Defense of Moldova clarified that the incursion of Banderol missiles and UAVs occurred amid Russia’s massive strikes on Ukraine.
According to monitoring system data, explosions were heard near the towns of Krokmaz, Ștefan Vodă, Delacău, Puhăceni, Anenii Noi, Bozieni, and Hîncești, as well as near Dubovka, Konstantinovka, and Căușeni. Police officers and National Army soldiers were dispatched to the scene to investigate the incident.
The police added that reports of explosion sounds had been coming in since the morning from residents of the Kaushan, Ștefan Vodă, Anenii Noi, and Hîncești districts. On the outskirts of Căușeni, law enforcement officers discovered debris from a drone, from which smoke was rising.
Debris from drones was also found near Dubrovka in the Hîncești district, between the villages of Delacău and Puhăceni.
In Krokmaz, a drone crashed into a vineyard, causing dry vegetation to catch fire, and shattered the windows of a nearby house.
According to police, there were no casualties as a result of the incidents. Law enforcement officials are currently documenting all cases and determining the circumstances of the events.
The missile was developed by the Russian company Kronstadt. Its maximum speed is 620–650 km/h, and its cruising speed is 520–560 km/h. Banderol is equipped with an OFBCh-150 high-explosive fragmentation warhead with a total mass of 114.3 kg, of which 49.5 kg is explosive material.

China concludes Northern Sea Route container shipping season to Europe until summer 2027
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
14:10:23 UTC
23:10:23 KST

SHANGHAI, October 3. /TASS/. China has concluded its seasonal container shipping operations to Europe via the Arctic route, including the Northern Sea Route (NSR), with services set to resume in summer 2027, China Central Television (CCTV) reported, citing customs data from the port city of Ningbo.
"The route is seasonal in nature and will resume operations next summer," the broadcaster said.
Eight voyages were completed along the northern route this year, carrying nearly 8,000 TEUs (twenty-foot equivalent units) of cargo. Goods worth 5.33 billion yuan ($79.5 million) were shipped from China to Europe via the Arctic, primarily including energy storage systems, batteries, and electric vehicles.
In China, the route is known as the Ice Silk Road or the China-Europe Arctic Express. The journey takes approximately 18-20 days, about half the time required for the traditional route through the Suez Canal.
On August 15, Chinese shipping company Sealegend Shipping announced the launch of its first weekly service to Europe via the Northern Sea Route, which runs along Russia’s Arctic coast.
The Northern Sea Route is a major shipping corridor and the principal maritime artery of the Russian Arctic. It follows Russia’s northern coastline through the seas of the Arctic Ocean, stretching approximately 5,600 kilometers from the Kara Strait to Providence Bay.

‘I didn’t know it was goodbye’: Parents relive their children’s final Oct. 7 calls
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
14:07:33 UTC
23:07:33 KST

“Dad, I love you”; “Mom, they’re shooting on the road I’m on”; “I just wanted to tell you I love you, in case something happens.” On the morning of the October 7 massacre and in the hours that followed, parents received phone calls from their children. What was supposed to be the joyous holiday of Simchat Torah became a desperate effort to calm them, give instructions, offer hope and promise that everything would be all right. They did not know these would be the last words they would ever hear from them. Three years later, the recordings remain: the voices, the fear and the words the parents wish they had said differently.
'It was an unmistakable final goodbye'
“Dad, I love you.” Those were the first words the late Guy Illouz said to his father, Michel, when he managed to reach him by phone on the morning of October 7. “What happened? Where are you, Guychuk?” Michel asked. “I love you very much, Dad.”
“What happened, Guy?” his father asked, and Guy replied: “They killed Alon. I’m hiding in a tree. I was shot, I took a bullet. I’m lying here wounded, bleeding on the ground. Four people died in my arms, four. Dad, I just wanted to tell you that I love you.”
“Guy, don’t say goodbye to us. Stay with me on the line for a second,” Michel said.
Three years later, Michel still relives that conversation every day. “When I want to tell people who my son, Guychuk, was, I always start with that conversation,” he said. On Saturday, he hears it differently: “It was an unmistakable final goodbye. Guy understood what I refused to believe or understand.”
When the phone rang that morning, Michel still had no idea of the scale of the disaster. A siren had sounded and he was sitting at home with a cup of coffee. A blocked number appeared on his screen. On the other end was a Magen David Adom dispatcher who asked to connect his son to a conference call. Guy had fled the Nova music festival, was wounded by gunfire and was hiding among the trees near Route 232. His own phone had been left in the car, so he used the phone of his friend, the late Alon Verber, to make emergency calls and summon help.
Over the course of nearly an hour, Michel said, Guy made seven calls to emergency and security services. Even while wounded, he tried to explain where he was and ask them to come for him. During one of the calls, he said: “I also don’t understand why you’re not coming to save me. I can see IDF vehicles here, too. I can hear helicopters. Why aren’t you coming to save me?”
Michel tried to give Guy instructions and keep him alive. He told him to stay hidden and not try to be a hero. “I told Guy that I loved him, that he would get through it and that he had to be strong,” he said. “I think, ultimately, I told him everything. I instructed him to do what I thought was best.”
But there was one thing he did not do: say goodbye. “I regret that I didn’t understand quickly enough what was happening, that I was very confused about the situation. I regret that I didn’t say goodbye to him. I told him everything would be all right. I truly hoped and believed it would. I wanted to believe.”
The call ended amid the sound of gunfire. Michel was convinced his son had been killed and went out to search for him. Only later did he learn that Guy had been abducted to Gaza alive. According to the testimony of Maya Regev, who met him in captivity, he was wounded and hospitalized in a Gaza hospital. After 57 days of uncertainty, she told the family that Guy was no longer alive.
There is another sentence Michel has returned to ever since. “He told me, ‘Dad, tell my mom I love her and tell my sister Maya and my brother Ori that I love them.’ Saturday, I know he was really saying goodbye to everyone. Guy didn’t leave this world without getting the chance to say the final words that mattered most to him. At least that gave me some comfort.”
'I should have told her I loved her'
Ronit also did not understand that her daughter was saying goodbye. Just hours earlier, she had been certain that the late Nitzan Rahum had not gone to the party at all. Nitzan was pregnant, suffering from nausea and had told her mother she was not feeling well and planned to sleep at her parents’ home. In the end, she went with her partner, the late Lidor Levy. Shortly before 7 a.m., the phone woke Ronit. “Mom, you can’t imagine what a nightmare this is,” Nitzan said. “What happened?” she asked.
“There are rockets and chaos at the party, you have no idea. Thank God I went with him and not alone. Otherwise I’d be on the road alone right now. We’re at a party in the south. The Red Alert started, rockets are flying over my head.” Ronit asked where she was. Nitzan said they were heading to friends’ home in Beersheba. “Come home,” her mother told her.
“We can’t. They’ve closed roads, everything is chaos. Everyone is driving and fleeing. You don’t understand how crazy it is.” Then her voice changed: “I don’t want to be here. I don’t want to be on this road,” Nitzan can be heard crying and shouting. “Nitzan, Nitzan, calm down,” Ronit tried to tell her.
“Mom, they’re shooting on the road I’m on.” Ronit replied: “Sweetheart, take a deep breath. Calm down.” Lidor, Nitzan’s partner, could also be heard on the call. “Everything is OK,” he said. “Calm her down, she’s panicking right now,” Ronit told him. “Hug her, hold her.” Lidor said: “Everything is OK. Stay calm, everything’s fine.”
On Saturday, when she returns to that moment, Ronit hears things she was unable to understand then. That morning, she still thought the danger was rocket fire. She knew her daughter as someone who was very fearful even in ordinary circumstances and attributed some of her panic to her anxious nature and to her pregnancy.
“I tried to calm her down angrily,” she said. “That is something I deeply regret. I should have tried to calm her instead of getting angry that she was scared. More than once during the call she told me, ‘Mom, this isn’t nothing. They’re here. They’re shooting at us.’ And I didn’t understand. I didn’t understand the scale of what was happening. It eats me alive.”
There were no words of farewell
They spoke twice and Ronit later also spoke with Lidor. When she realized terrorists were in the area, she asked him not to tell Nitzan so she would not become even more frightened. Nitzan was nearing the end of her fourth month of pregnancy. Just a week earlier, she had undergone an anatomy scan and the family learned she was carrying a boy. Amid the disaster, Ronit was also thinking about the grandson who was supposed to be born. “Take care of her, calm her down,” she told Lidor. ““She needs to stay calm.”
There were no words of farewell. Nitzan told her mother she would call when she reached Beersheba. That next call never came. For six days, the family did not know what had happened to her. “My hope was that she had been taken hostage and not murdered,” Ronit said. Eventually, the family learned that Nitzan had been murdered. Lidor was murdered as well.
Three years have passed and Ronit returns to that phone call again and again. “Every day,” she said. “There are days when I go in just to hear her voice.” And what is hardest for her? “That I didn’t stay on the line with her. I would have stayed with her every second, so she could feel that I was there. I should have told her I loved her. That was the hardest thing for me.”
Since then, the loss has also changed the way Ronit speaks to her other children. “On the one hand, I’ve become anxious about them. I ask them to call me in the morning and evening, just to say hello. They don’t have to tell me where they are or where they’re going. I don’t want to pry. But I do want to hear them and know that everything is all right.”
Above all, she now says aloud the words she so desperately wishes she had said during that final conversation with Nitzan. “Now I say ‘I love you’ more. I hug more. I tell them I’m proud of them, that I love them. We used to say ‘I love you’ less often. Now I try to say it every day.”
Ronit now has a 10-month-old grandson, Neil, the son of Gil, Nitzan’s younger sister. His name also commemorates them: the Hebrew letter nun from Nitzan and lamed from Lidor. Ronit says he reminds her greatly of her daughter. “He even looks exactly like her at that age. Exactly. I show people and their mouths fall open,” she said. “It’s as though she left me a piece of herself in Neil.” She calls him “a light in the darkness”: “His smile makes me smile.”
'He knew this was the last call'
For Dikla, the call came after hours in which she had been convinced her son, the late Reem Meir Batito, would make it out alive.
On the morning of Simchat Torah, her parents were staying at her home in Netanya. When her sister, who observes Shabbat, called, Dikla realized something extraordinary was happening. She turned on the television and saw the images from southern Israel, but at that very moment, she said, she was overcome by an almost inexplicable sense of confidence.
““I can sense Reem,” she told her father. “He’s OK. I can feel it. He’s fighting. He’s a lion, he’s strong. There’s no way anyone can hurt him.” Reem was at the Kissufim military post and fought for hours. Toward evening, he called home.
“Reem, where are you?” Dikla asked. “I’m back at the post. Waiting for further orders,” he replied. “Are there other soldiers with you?” she asked. When her son answered, “Whoever’s left,” she replied anxiously: “What do you mean, 'whoever’s left'? Do we have a lot of wounded? Dead?” Reem did not elaborate: “Plenty. I love you and I’m sorry if I ever hurt you.”
“You didn’t hurt us. Everything is OK. You need to be strong,” Dikla replied. “I just wanted to tell you I love you, in case something happens,” Reem insisted. “Nothing is going to happen, Reem. Everything is fine. You’ve been preparing your whole life for a situation like this. You know exactly what to do.”
“You don’t understand what’s happening here ... never mind. There are things here no one should see,” he continued. “These are the moments when you have to believe in yourself. Reem, you can do this. I know who you are.” His sister could be heard in the background: “I love you. Good luck.”
Dikla now believes her son knew. “Looking back, I understand that he knew this was the last call,” she said. “At the time, it never crossed my mind.”
Only later did Dikla understand what he meant when he said: “whoever’s left.” “He said things very vaguely,” she recalled. “He knew me so well. If he had phrased things just a little differently, he knew that Mom Dikla would have gotten in the car and driven there, no matter what.”
The call lasted about seven or eight minutes, she said. Toward the end, the phone was passed to her husband, Ofir, who asked Reem about the equipment he had with him. Dikla continued shouting in the background: “Reem, take care of yourself. Please, take care of yourself.” Reem said he had to end the call because he was becoming emotional and talking to his family was bringing tears to his eyes. After hanging up, he sent his sister one final message: “I love you very much.”
About 10 minutes after the call, Dikla said, Reem was killed.
Three years later, her regret is not about something she failed to say but something she failed to do. “I’m not someone who believes in words. I’m someone who believes in actions,” she said. “More than anything, I regret not simply starting the car and driving. That is what I regret most — that I stayed where I was.”
'Through the calls, I understand how to fulfill his final wishes'
Dikla has more than 2,000 recorded conversations with Reem saved on her phone and every morning she returns to one of them. “Every morning, I listen to Reem and me talking on the phone,” she said. “I ask him for a message and try to draw some strength from it.” Once, while driving to the cemetery after Yom Kippur ended, she asked him aloud to give her a sign that he was all right. When her phone connected to the car’s system, one of their old conversations began playing and the first thing she heard was Reem’s voice telling her: “Mom, g’mar chatima tova,” the traditional greeting said at the conclusion of Yom Kippur. “I started crying my heart out,” she said.
Over time, she said, the recordings have also become a way for her to continue learning from him. “I listen to my conversations with him and realize just how mature, genuine and precise his perspective on the world was. Through these conversations, I learn how to conduct myself and how to fulfill Reem’s final wishes.” Things she once tried to temper in him have taken on a different meaning. “Now I listen to them and say, ‘How did I not tell him, Reem, you’re right?’ On the other hand, I know his soul is here and that he sees me, and I try very hard to make him proud of me.”
Three years later, the parents hear these conversations differently: the words they did not understand at the time, the fear they tried to calm, the things they themselves said and the things they never had the chance to say. “This is what remains of Guy,” Michel said. “The final conversation, the music he created, his dog Georgie. Nothing in life can prepare you for this.”

Israel election double standard: Arab leader forced out, far right cleared
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
14:06:47 UTC
23:06:47 KST

Israel election double standard: Arab leader forced out, far right cleared
A Palestinian Israeli politician forced to withdraw candidature while far-right Israeli leaders allowed to run in upcoming elections.
A prominent Palestinian Israeli politician has been forced to withdraw from the upcoming elections over his remarks about the Gaza war, while Israeli far-right leaders have remained untouched despite their incendiary rhetoric and calls for violence against Palestinians.
The Israeli political institutions, including the electoral body, have been accused of double standards for targeting Palestinian politicians and parties in Israel.
Sami Abu Shehadeh, the leader of the Balad party, withdrew his candidacy after the Supreme Court warned he could be disqualified from the race. He has described the decision to disqualify him from the upcoming elections as “a historical catastrophe for democracy”.
That court advisory came after Israel’s central elections committee barred him from running over comments he made about the war on Gaza.
The election, set for October 27, has renewed scrutiny of the challenges faced by Palestinian citizens of Israel seeking political representation.
Experts and critics, including Palestinian rights groups, have accused electoral system staff of applying a double standard in which Arab candidates have faced attempts to remove them from the ballot, while far-right Israeli politicians accused of repeatedly inciting violence against Palestinians have been allowed to run.
“It’s always been the case whether the Israeli political system, the political elite, has always designed the political system in a way to ensure that it’s a Zionist state, not just or even a Jewish state,” Zaidon Alkinani, founding director of the Arab Perspectives Institute, told Al Jazeera.
So, what happened, and what does the controversy say about Palestinian participation in Israeli elections?
Who is Sami Abu Shehadeh?
Abu Shehadeh is a historian from Jaffa and the leader of Balad, a Palestinian nationalist party that advocates equal rights for all citizens of Israel. He served in the Knesset from 2019 until 2022.
His candidacy was challenged by far-right Israeli National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir over an article published on October 8, 2023, the day after the Hamas-led attacks on Israel, which he described as “an important historical event”.
Attorney General Gali Baharav-Miara backed his disqualification, arguing the wording could amount to support for armed struggle.
Abu Shehadeh, speaking at the Supreme Court on Thursday, said he did not support “armed struggle”, but acknowledged that a paragraph in the article had been incorrectly worded. The Balad leader said his intention was to urge moving the conflict towards a political process.
What was the Israeli Supreme Court’s decision?
Last month, the Central Elections Committee voted to bar Abu Shehadeh, Hadash politician Ofer Cassif and the two main Arab-majority electoral lists – the Joint List, which includes Balad, Hadash and Ta’al, and Ra’am, or the United Arab List.
The Supreme Court overturned the bans on the two lists and Cassif.
Cassif is a politician from the left-wing, Arab-majority Hadash-Ta’al party. In the late 1980s, the pro-Palestinian Israeli spent time in jail for refusing to serve as a soldier in the occupied territories.
He claimed in 2021 that police beat him while he participated in a protest against an illegal Jewish settlement in occupied East Jerusalem.
Abu Shehadeh accused the Supreme Court of bowing to pressure from Ben-Gvir and questioned how a politician he accused of promoting violence and displacement against Palestinians could seek his exclusion from the election.
“Someone [Ben-Gvir] who was calling for starving people to death in Gaza, for preventing medicine, water and food, and supports the occupation and ethnic cleansing in the [occupied] West Bank … was able to disqualify me, a human rights activist for three decades,” Abu Shehadeh told Al Jazeera.
Adalah, the legal rights group representing him, called his withdrawal “a severe blow” to Palestinian citizens’ right to political representation.
“This entire process was a deliberate attempt to delegitimise Palestinian citizens and their parliamentary representatives and to turn racism against Palestinians into election propaganda,” it said in a media statement.
Have Israeli leaders used incendiary language?
Before the Supreme Court hearings, petitions were also submitted seeking to disqualify the parties of Ben-Gvir and that of another far-right cabinet member, Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich.
The Central Elections Committee rejected those petitions, leaving both parties on the ballot.
Section 7A of Israel’s Basic Law on the Knesset provides the legal grounds for barring candidates or electoral lists, including rejecting Israel’s character as a “Jewish and democratic state”, promoting racism, or backing an armed campaign against Israel by a hostile state or a designated “terrorist” group.
Attorney General Baharav-Miara found that the attempts to exclude the far-right parties lacked sufficient legal basis.
Ben-Gvir and Smotrich have repeatedly faced international backlash over their incendiary rhetoric towards Palestinians. In 2025, the United Kingdom, Canada, Australia, New Zealand and Norway imposed sanctions on both ministers, accusing them of repeatedly inciting violence against Palestinians in the occupied West Bank.
More recently, Ben-Gvir proposed a seven-year plan for Palestinians to leave Gaza through what he called “voluntary emigration”.
“Instead of illusions of peace now, we need actions of emigration now,” he said in September. “Instead of [them] digging tunnels, it’s time to pack suitcases.”
Smotrich has also advocated the displacement of Palestinians from Gaza and annexation of the occupied West Bank. Both he and Ben-Gvir have called for the permanent takeover of Gaza and re-establishment of Jewish settlements there, proposals Netanyahu has rejected.
Why are there accusations of a double standard?
The different treatment of Abu Shehadeh and Israel’s far-right politicians has led Palestinian politicians and experts to accuse the electoral system of applying a double standard.
Palestinian political analyst and playwright Ahmed Najjar told Al Jazeera that Abu Shehadeh’s case exposed what he described as the “two-tier nature of Israeli democracy”.
“This is not the equal application of the law,” he said. “It establishes one threshold for Jewish Israeli politicians and another for Palestinian citizens of Israel.”
Najjar pointed to the contrast between the court’s treatment of Abu Shehadeh’s October 2023 article and the continued eligibility of Ben-Gvir and Smotrich, despite inflammatory statements attributed to the two far-right politicians.
“Jewish extremism can be accommodated within Israel’s political system,” Najjar argued, “while Palestinian political speech is treated as an existential threat”.
“A democracy that selectively excludes Palestinian representatives cannot credibly call itself democratic.”
Alkinani, founding director of the Arab Perspectives Institute, argued the controversy reflected a wider problem facing Palestinian political participation rather than an isolated dispute over one candidate.
He told Al Jazeera that Israel’s political system had historically been structured to preserve its Zionist character, creating particular “intimidation” and “pressures” for Palestinian citizens seeking political representation.
Alkinani said those pressures had intensified since October 7, 2023, which he argued had given a “powerful symbolic push and confidence” to right-wing nationalist parties.
What are the difficulties facing Palestinians in Israeli elections?
Attempts to exclude Palestinian-led parties are not new.
Adalah has documented challenges to Arab candidates or lists in elections in 2003, 2013, 2015, 2020 and 2022. The Supreme Court has repeatedly overturned decisions by the Central Elections Committee, whose voting members are representatives of parties in the outgoing Knesset.
Palestinian citizens of Israel account for roughly 20 percent of the population, yet their turnout at the polls has traditionally been lower than that of Jewish Israelis.
Parties must also secure at least 3.25 percent of the national vote to enter parliament, encouraging smaller Arab parties to form joint lists to avoid losing representation altogether.
Arab Perspectives Institute’s Alkinani says the issue extended beyond Israel’s far right. Some parties considered centrist on domestic Israeli issues, he said, still supported “hawkish security actions towards the Palestinians”.
