Iran stone industry targets $5b exports as 18th intl. stone exhibit opens in Mahallat-Nimvar
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
13:31:35 UTC
22:31:35 KST

Iran stone industry targets $5b exports as 18th intl. stone exhibit opens in Mahallat-Nimvar
TEHRAN- Bahram Shokouhi, Head of the Iran Stone Association, said Iran’s stone industry has the capacity to generate at least $5 billion in foreign currency earnings and exports if its potential is properly guided and supported.
Speaking at a press conference for the 18th Iran International Stone Exhibition in Mahallat and Nimvar, he said this capacity, combined with job creation, could make the stone industry more prominent in the national economy.
The exhibition will be held from October 6 to 9, focusing on block stones and products from Iran’s stone industry. More than 600 domestic and foreign companies are participating. It covers about 120,000 square meters, with more than 45,000 tons of block stone offered. Trade delegations from Russia, Pakistan, Turkey, India, and Egypt have been invited.
Shokouhi said that for the first time a stone service desk will be set up with experts from the Deputy for Mining Affairs, the Trade Promotion Organization, the Mining Engineering Organization, and representatives of the Iran University of Science and Technology. Specialized panels, training workshops, cultural and artistic programs, the campaign “Behind Every Stone Is a Life,” and discussions on risks in the stone industry and family issues of activists are among other programs.
He noted that the Stone Headquarters, previously the Stone Policy Council, has been reactivated with the association’s follow-up and the cooperation of the Ministry of Industry, Mining and Trade. It examines exploration, extraction, processing, and export issues. The 14th meeting of the National Stone Desk and a joint meeting of the Mining Commission of the Iran Chamber with the Arak Chamber will be held on the sidelines.
Shokouhi, who also heads the Mining Commission of the Iran Chamber, pointed to new technologies entering Iran’s stone industry. One is cutting machines using wires as thin as dental floss, currently used for soft stones, which can increase extraction and processing efficiency while reducing waste. He said this technology can create about 35 to 40 percent more recovery from block stone and reduce finished costs.
He stressed the need to reduce the carbon footprint in the stone industry. Programs include training and developing environmental product passports, courses on carbon footprint, and active participation at the COP31 climate summit in Antalya. The goals are lower carbon emissions, lower production costs, and a competitive advantage for Iranian stone exporters.
Shokouhi also mentioned the formation of the World Stone Federation. With cooperation among stone associations from various countries, a global stone alliance and federation has been formed to strengthen natural stone’s position in global markets. One goal is to create a carbon passport or ID for stone, determining carbon emissions from extraction at the mine to destination, so the natural stone industry can strengthen its global position based on this data.
On production and export statistics, Shokouhi said that in 1403, about 10 to 12 million tons of stone were produced in Iran, but export value was only about $230 million. Compared with the approximately $42 billion value of global stone exports, Iran’s share is very limited. About 85 percent of produced stone is processed and consumed domestically, and nearly 15 percent is allocated to exports, of which about 5 percent is exported as block and 10 percent as cut stone. Turkey, by contrast, produced about 15 million tons of stone in 2025 and exported nearly 41 percent of its production.
Shokouhi said the Iran International Stone Exhibition can introduce the diversity of Iranian stones to foreign buyers. Instead of visiting different mines across the country, buyers can see, choose, and order products in one place. Offering stone blocks in global markets can pave the way for recognition and, later, development of processed stone exports.
He called fuel shortage one of the serious problems of mines. A significant part of mining machinery is old and high-consumption, and last year fuel distribution was announced about 25 percent less than stated need. As a result, some mines bought fuel from the free market and in some cases faced smuggling-related cases.
Referring to transportation problems under wartime conditions, Shokouhi said long truck queues at land borders and stopped shipments can cause exports to face penalties and loss of customers. Coordination with neighboring countries is needed to speed up truck passage, and special routes or a “green lane” should be considered for export shipments that have customers. During the exhibition, some stone shipments reached their destination late due to customs and transportation problems, and with coordination between the Iran Stone Association and Customs, part of these shipments were cleared and transferred out of turn.
Shokouhi emphasized that the main demand of economic activists is to reduce barriers and cumbersome regulations so producers and exporters can continue. In the current situation, the issue of the stone industry is no longer merely development; rather, it is maintaining existing production and employment, and removing barriers can help continue activity.
Ziba Yazdani, Secretary of the Iran Stone Association, said that if the goal is synergy, economic growth, and business development in the stone industry, no link in the chain can be ignored, and the Iran International Stone Exhibition can be the connecting link. She noted the difficult conditions of holding the 18th edition, saying that continuing the event when even some more ordinary exhibitions were not held shows its importance for the economy and related businesses. The association participated in planning and execution within its responsibility for coordination and paving the way for business development.
Yazdani said five specialized panels are planned: Iran’s stone industry in the carbon era, a stone block is not raw, multi-wire technology, social issues of miners’ families, and export development solutions. Booth layout began about a month ago, and more than 2,000 executive operations have been considered for preparing and holding the exhibition.
Ali Joudaki, Head of the Industry, Mine and Trade Organization of Markazi Province, pointed to the region’s capacities for hosting the exhibition. He said holding it in Mahallat is an important advantage because a significant part of the country’s stone mines is concentrated there. About 70 percent of Iran’s stone mines whose products are exportable are located within a 300-kilometer radius of Mahallat. The exhibition venue is next to the stone export terminal, allowing trade delegations and foreign buyers to view products and have suitable access to mines and production capacities.
Joudaki continued that the stone economy chain—from exploration and extraction to processing, supply, export, and sales—must be fully formed so the industry has economic justification. Given the region’s mining capacities, access to mines, export terminal, and existing facilities, the Mahallat exhibition can become a platform for introducing Iran’s stone industry and increasing the country’s share of global markets.
Hassan Khazaeipour, Governor of Mahallat, referred to the county’s diverse capacities in tourism, agriculture, and industry. With more than 150 active mines and about 300 stone processing units, Mahallat is one of the important hubs of the country’s stone industry, and the 18th exhibition is an important opportunity to introduce these capacities. With a population of more than 65,000, Mahallat is an important tourism area of Markazi Province and has capacities such as the Abgarm area, production of ornamental flowers and plants, and production and export of ornamental fish. More than 900 hectares of the county’s lands have been allocated to greenhouse cultivation and production of ornamental flowers and plants.
Khazaeipour said more than 14 percent of the world’s travertine stone is located in the Abbasabad area of Mahallat County, and holding the international stone exhibition in Nimvar is a valuable opportunity to introduce this capacity and develop export markets. So far, the presence of activists from about eight countries, including India, Portugal, Bangladesh, China, Turkey, Russia, and Armenia, has been announced. Last year, stone industry activists from 27 provinces attended. This year, the exhibition will also be held in an area of about 120,000 square meters.
Abbas Karbalaei, a private sector activist in the stone field, said the complex has been launched as the country’s first exhibition site with 100 percent private sector investment and the participation of miners and stone industry activists. Alongside the International Stone Exhibition, the country’s first export terminal in the stone field has also been launched in this complex so that necessary infrastructure for export development and a more active presence in international markets is provided.
Mohammad Hallajian, organizer of the 18th Iran International Stone Exhibition, said the brand of the Iran International Stone Exhibition, Mahallat–Nimvar, has been introduced in more than 10 countries over the past 12 years, and it is the only Iranian stone exhibition included in the global calendar of exhibitions in this field. With about 38,000 square meters of net exhibition space and about 45,000 tons of products, it has a notable record among specialized stone exhibitions worldwide in terms of stone brought in. More than 600 entities, including companies and mines from 27 provinces, are present.
Hallajian continued that considering about one thousand active building stone mines in the country, more than 400 mines are present. Service desks with the Deputy for Mining Affairs of the Ministry of Industry, Mine and Trade, the Mining Engineering Organization, the Iran Trade Promotion Organization, and the Iran University of Science and Technology are being held to provide specialized answers on exploration, extraction, export, foreign exchange commitments, and supply of machinery. He also announced the unveiling of Iran’s first quartzite mine at the exhibition, saying Iran has a special position in diversity of building stones, and the discovery and introduction of Iranian quartzite can help complete the chain of mineral diversity.
The Executive Director of the Exhibition referred to cultural and social programs. The campaign “Behind Every Stone Is a Life” will be unveiled to support and educate the families of miners who are away from their families for long periods due to work conditions, and it is planned to be developed nationally with the support of the Iran Stone Association. Artistic programs including music, calligraphy, painting, and sculpture with stone will also be held so that the cultural and artistic capacities of this natural material are introduced alongside its industrial and mining capabilities.

Pentagon’s new religious office faces watchdog challenge
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
13:29:54 UTC
22:29:54 KST

Pentagon’s new religious office faces watchdog challenge
The Freedom From Religion Foundation (FFRF) has announced plans to launch a probe into a new religious affairs office recently unveiled by US Secretary of War Pete Hegseth.
The Wisconsin-based nonprofit said on Thursday that it is seeking transparency into the office’s funding, operations and plans to assess troops’ “spiritual fitness.”
The announcement came shortly after Hegseth said the Pentagon was establishing the Office of Religious Affairs (ORA) to address what he described as a decline in religious community in the military following an era of “political correctness.”
In his State of the Force address on Wednesday at Marine Corps Base Quantico in Virginia, Hegseth said the new office’s head is expected to serve as the secretary and deputy secretary’s chief adviser on religious affairs.
Hegseth argued that the military had previously prioritized “political correctness and secular humanism” over religion, with “secular careerists in cubicles and lawyers running around with red tape” overseeing service members’ spiritual lives instead of military chaplains.
According to the memorandum signed by the secretary earlier this week, the office is tasked with aligning religious-affairs policy, overseeing the Armed Forces Chaplains Board, representing the department to civilian religious endorsing organizations, and sponsoring research and tools to “support and assess spiritual fitness, spiritual readiness, and spiritual resilience.”
The FFRF said it will use the Freedom of Information Act (FOIA), which allows the public to request records from US government agencies, to seek documents on the office’s funding, budget and staffing. The group also wants records on how the Pentagon defines and plans to assess “spiritual fitness,” “spiritual readiness” and “spiritual resilience,” including any technologies or tools being considered. The requests will also cover ties to outside religious groups and records concerning atheist, humanist and other nonreligious service members and potential First Amendment issues.
Americans United for Separation of Church and State President and CEO Rachel Laser said Hegseth’s new office would elevate Christianity’s role in shaping US military policy. She also accused him of using his position to advance what she described as a “Christian Nationalist agenda” in the military.
Hegseth’s personal Christian beliefs have previously drawn media attention, with some analysis arguing that they are increasingly influencing US military policy.
In March, The Washington Post cited former senior military officials and experts on religion and law as saying that Hegseth’s religious policies had challenged longstanding norms limiting the promotion of a particular faith. The war secretary reportedly held monthly evangelical services at the Pentagon at the time, while department employees were reluctant to discuss concerns related to his religious campaign.
Earlier this year, the Pentagon, at Hegseth’s initiative, cut the number of recognized religious denominations and belief systems for service members from 211 to 31. The department’s latest official breakdown from 2019 shows that about 70% of active-duty service members identified as Christian, 2% as atheist or agnostic, and 24% as having no religious affiliation or an unknown religious affiliation.

The CEO of the National Iranian Gas Company, referring to the upcoming difficulties in sustainably supplying the country’s gas after the recent incidents in the South Pars gas field, announced: “If I want to compare the performance of the first six months of this year with the same period last year, although the volume of gas delivered to the network was about 14 percent lower, the share of gas supply to power plants was maintained at approximately the same level. So that this year 85 percent and last year 86 percent of the fuel basket needs of power plants were supplied with gas, which indicates the high resilience of the country’s gas network under difficult conditions.”
Tavakoli emphasized: “These figures show that the country’s gas industry, by prioritizing the supply of fuel to power plants to prevent electricity imbalance, has used all its power to continue the flow of gas in production and industrial sectors so that the wheel of the country’s economy does not stop under difficult production conditions.”

Ukraine asks EU to increase bioethanol export quotas by volume of its consumption in imported gasoline
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
16:24:21 EEST
22:24:21 KST

Ukraine is proposing that the European Union increase the existing duty-free export quota for Ukrainian bioethanol of 125,000 tonnes per year to account for the volume of bioethanol that Ukraine imports from the EU as a component of motor gasoline, Minister of Agrarian Policy and Food Taras Vysotsky told journalists.
"We calculated that Ukraine currently imports about 10,000 [tonnes] of bioethanol per month in gasoline... This proposal is for the period of martial law, as long as security conditions do not allow Ukraine to blend gasoline with biocomponents, forcing us to import it," the minister explained.
He recalled that the mandatory requirement for a minimum 7% bioethanol content in A-92 and A-95 motor gasoline came into effect in Ukraine on July 1 of this year, whereas the 125,000-tonne quota was established last year when gasoline was imported without bioethanol content.
Vysotsky noted that the quota could be flexible: if, for example, gasoline containing 5,000 tonnes of bioethanol is imported in a given month, then an additional 5,000 tonnes [of export quota] appears; if 15,000 tonnes in another month, then 15,000 tonnes.
According to him, overall for the year, this could amount to another roughly 120,000 tonnes of bioethanol.
In the opinion of the Minister of Agrarian Policy, this Ukrainian initiative has a high probability of being received and implemented by European partners.

Grandmother and granddaughter killed by Russia in Kyiv home where three generations grew up

Grandmother and granddaughter killed by Russia in Kyiv home where three generations grew up
Yevheniia, 45, and her 94-year-old grandmother Mariia were killed in a Russian drone strike on a house in Kyiv on 30 September. The evening before the attack, Mariia took medication because she was worried about a possible missile strike.
Source: Yuliia Haharina, a relative of Yevheniia and Mariia, chemist and founder of the Laborantki scientific and creative association, on Facebook
Details: A Russian Shahed drone detonated in the bedrooms of the house where three generations of the family had grown up.
The evening before yet another Russian attack, Yevheniia, an aunt of Yuliia's, turned on the gas boiler and gave Mariia her medication. That evening, Mariia felt anxious after warnings of a possible missile strike.
At about 03:00, the family heard the sounds of an aerial attack. A Russian drone later struck their home, where the three women were staying. Only Yehor, a nephew of Yuliia's, was not at home: he had gone to a friend's house for a sleepover.
Quote from Yuliia: "Businka [Yevheniia's beloved dog – ed.] was hiding on grandma's bed. My aunt texted everyone for the usual roll call: 'How are you?', saw the replies and went to the toilet. She came out and the next thing she saw was a brick wall flying at her.
The Shahed detonated literally in Zhenia's [short for Yevheniia – ed.] and grandma's bedrooms. The bricks were scattered like Lego, you couldn't see the ground under them at all. The beautiful wooden ceilings, which our grandfathers were so proud of, caught fire, and the fire was still being put out the next day."
Details: Yuliia said the family home, damaged by the Russian strike, was built in the 1950s by her two grandfathers, who were brothers.
Quote from Yuliia: "They put it together from bricks, wood and, as they used to say, 'from bottles of vodka', which they gave in exchange for building materials."
Details: She says everyone lived peacefully in the house for the most part, recalling a funny childhood incident with her cousin Zhenia as an example of "discord".
Quote from Yuliia: "I was about seven years old. I ran to my aunt in the kitchen, shouting: 'Zhenia hit me right in the heart with a pig!' The 'pig' was a rubber baby doll that she threw at me. The adults told this story at family dinners for a long time."
Details: Her grandmother was the oldest resident on the street, where she helped locals as a family doctor. The woman left her profession after she turned 70 to take care of her great-granddaughter, and later her grandson Yehor.
On the evening of 29 September, Mariia had everyday worries: she was anxious that she might not have time to plant garlic before the cold weather set in. She did not dare to do it herself, fearing she would get into trouble with her relatives.
The family was worried that Mariia might fall again and break her hip. This had already happened a month before the full-scale war began. After a successful operation, the woman was even able to move around independently, although she needed a walking stick.
In those days, her granddaughter Zhenia, who had only recently celebrated her birthday, was happy because she had bought new curtain magnets, carefully chosen to match the newly redecorated room.
Quote from Yuliia: "She was a Virgo, she loved making the space around her beautiful. She used to tease me: 'How does your husband live with you?' (he is also a Virgo). I would reply that only my childhood with her allowed me to be understanding towards my husband. The secret to a happy life: respect your neighbour's neurosis as your own. She definitely had this match with her husband."
Details: A farewell ceremony for the women will be held on 4 October at 10:00 at the crematorium of the Baikove Cemetery.
Background: A Russian attack on 30 September killed two people and injured five others, two of whom had to be taken to hospital.

Russia struck Kyiv’s Northern Bridge on Saturday, damaging its road surface and trolleybus power lines as attacks on the Ukrainian capital’s transport network continued for a third day.
Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko said two people were injured and traffic from the city’s eastern bank to the western side was halted after the strike.
Emergency crews went to the bridge, one of the main crossings over the Dnipro River.
The attack followed repeated Russian drone strikes on the Southern Bridge since Thursday, which forced authorities to restrict traffic on several routes and caused long queues across Kyiv.
The two bridges link parts of a city where about three million people live. More than a third of residents lived on the eastern bank before Russia’s full-scale invasion in 2022, while much of Kyiv’s government and business activity is based on the western side.
The disruption has increased pressure on roads and public transport. Large numbers of residents use the metro to cross the river each day, while bridge closures affect cars, buses and trolleybuses.
Klitschko described the situation in the capital as “very dramatic” after a city security meeting on Friday. He said Russian forces were targeting infrastructure, logistics and residential areas.
Russia said its forces had struck bridges used to move Ukrainian troops and military cargo. Moscow also renewed a warning urging foreign nationals, including diplomats, to leave Kyiv.
Ukrainian officials accuse Russia of widening attacks on civilian and economic infrastructure. President Volodymyr Zelensky told the Financial Times that Moscow was seeking to damage bridges, communications networks, hospitals, schools and other services.
Russian President Vladimir Putin said this week that strikes on Ukrainian economic targets were a response to Ukrainian attacks on Russian oil refineries and Black Sea vessels. Ukraine says those operations target infrastructure that supports Russia’s war effort.
Kostiantyn Kryvolap, an aviation expert and former Antonov test engineer, told the Kyiv Independent that the drone warheads used in the bridge attacks were unlikely to destroy structures of this size. He said the attacks appeared aimed at interrupting traffic and logistics rather than bringing the bridges down.
Elsewhere, Ukrainian port authorities said a Russian strike on a Liberian-flagged civilian vessel in the Odesa region killed one sailor and injured three crew members. Twelve others were evacuated.
Russian-installed officials in occupied parts of Ukraine also reported deaths from Ukrainian drone strikes in Luhansk and Zaporizhia, while Russian media reported one death in the Belgorod region.

Ukraine fired its first FP-7 ballistic missile in combat. Its maker says next version will do what Ukraine needed since 2022
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
13:21:56 UTC
22:21:56 KST

- Ukrainian forces have fired a Fire Point FP-7 ballistic missile in combat for the first time
- The launch heralds a new phase of the wider war: the ballistic phase
- Soon both Ukraine and Russia will be able to bombard each other with hard-to-intercept missiles
Ukraine has fired its new Fire Point FP-7 ballistic missile in anger for the first time, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky announced on Thursday, 1 October.
Kyiv hasn't said what the missile targeted or how much damage it caused. The Wall Street Journal, citing an unnamed source, reported that it struck a target in Russian-occupied Ukraine. Zelensky was ecstatic on social media. "Thank you for the result," the Ukrainian president wrote. "Next up: production. Glory to Ukraine!"
The FP-7 can hit back at Russia, but it can't stop the Iskander ballistic missiles Russia fires at Ukrainian cities. Its twin is meant to. Fire Point is building an interceptor version, the FP-7.X, as the core of Freyja, its bid for a cheaper alternative to the American Patriot, and the company aims for a first ballistic missile interception by mid-2027.
Kyiv drone- and missile-maker Fire Point, most famous for its FP-1 and FP-2 one-way attack drones and FP-5 Flamingo cruise missiles, has been hard at work on ballistic missiles for at least a year. Ballistic missiles can cost millions of dollars per round, making them much more expensive than a $50,000 drone or $500,000 cruise missile.
But the extra expense buys a lot more destructive potential. An FP-1 packs a 60-kg warhead; an FP-7's warhead weighs about 200 kg. While an FP-1 might motor as far as 1,000 km, it's slow and fairly easy to shoot down. An FP-7 possesses less range—up to 250 km under the best conditions—but it streaks through the atmosphere at several times the speed of sound, making it extremely difficult to intercept.
The only Russian air defense systems that stand any chance of swatting down an incoming FP-7 are also among the most in-demand in the Russian inventory and thus the most over-stretched: the S-400 surface-to-air missile batteries.
Ukrainians know better than anyone the kind of damage and terror ballistic bombardment can inflict. Since effectively running out of Patriot surface-to-air missiles earlier this year, Ukraine has been unable to defend itself against weekly Russian bombardment that now usually includes several Iskander ballistic missiles.
The Russian bombardment threatens to disrupt commerce, throttle electricity generation, and grind down Ukrainian morale at a critical juncture in Russia's wider war on Ukraine. Ukrainian troops are holding their own along the 1,200-km front line, but behind the front line everyday Ukrainians are suffering under missile and drone impacts.
That suffering will only get worse as winter closes in, temperatures drop, and the Russians resume intensive attacks on the electrical grid, potentially depriving millions of people of household heating. Ukrainian batteries firing FP-7s can't directly prevent Russian attacks. But they can retaliate for the attacks.
Expect the ballistic tit for tat to intensify. It may not be the first Ukrainian ballistic missile fired in anger: in June, Russia said it shot down a Ukrainian ballistic missile over Moscow, and Kyiv never said what it was. But the FP-7 is the first Kyiv has confirmed using in combat, and it has the range and payload to inflict serious damage on targets inside Russia. But an even more powerful Ukrainian missile, the Fire Point FP-9, is coming soon. It reportedly ranges 850 km with an 800-kg warhead.
Trending Now
The ballistic phase
The FP-7 can smash Russian depots, air bases, and factories in oblasts bordering Ukraine. The FP-9 could wreak havoc as far as Moscow. The only major constraint on the Ukrainian bombardment will be Fire Point's production capacity, and Kyiv's ability to finance that production.
The Ukrainians will be incentivized to produce as many FP-7s—and, later, FP-9s—as possible. The same factories that produce surface-to-surface FP-7s will also churn out a surface-to-air variant, the FP-7.X.
That missile, which is overall similar to the standard FP-7 but includes a sophisticated seeker head, is the main munition for Ukraine's new mostly homemade air defense system being developed by Fire Point and various foreign partners under the auspices of the European missile defense program Freyja.
Ukraine has five ways to stop Russia’s Iskanders. Only one arrives before the strikes on the grid begin
If the FP-7.X works as advertised and Fire Point can scale production, it could bolster Ukraine's defenses against Russian ballistic missile strikes while the standard FP-7 and its bigger cousin the FP-9 retaliate for Russian ballistic missile strikes.
A new phase of the wider war is about to begin—the ballistic phase, where both sides can pummel the other with hard-to-intercept missiles.
The side that makes the most and best missiles, for offense and defense, will prevail in the coming ballistic fight.

Feature: "Auntie Basketball" brings Chinese culture to Utah high school
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
21:20:44 CST
22:20:44 KST

A member of "Auntie Basketball" talks with American students at Crimson Cliffs High School in Washington, Utah, the United States, Oct. 2, 2026.(Photo by Zeng Hui/Xinhua)
by Xinhua Writer Gao Shan
WASHINGTON, Oct. 3 (Xinhua) -- Forget the traveling call, just run with the ball. Forget about winning or losing, just enjoy the game.
Cheers, applause and laughter filled the gym at Crimson Cliffs High School in Washington, Utah, on Friday as a women's basketball team from Guizhou Province in southwestern China took on the school's team in a highly unusual game that brought together two groups of young people - and two cultures - on the same court.
The visiting team, known as "Auntie Basketball," comes from a grassroots sporting tradition that originated in the Miao villages of Leishan County in southeastern Guizhou.
In the Miao community, women who have married and returned to their hometowns are affectionately called "Gu Ma," or "aunties." What began as a recreational activity for women returning home has gradually grown into a showcase for Guizhou's ethnic culture and rural vitality.
Unlike conventional basketball, Auntie Basketball has its own playful rules: Players can carry the ball and run with it rather than having to dribble.
The result is less about the intensity of competition and more about fun, community and participation.
Before the game, the gym came alive with songs from the Miao villages and energetic traditional dances. Dressed in colorful ethnic costumes, the visiting players performed for hundreds of students and teachers, drawing enthusiastic applause from the crowd.
But the biggest excitement came when the players took the court.
The aunties faced Crimson Cliffs' Mustangs, whose mascot is the mustang, in what quickly became a lighthearted cultural exchange through basketball.
The American players initially struggled to adjust to the unusual rules, particularly the idea that they could run while carrying the ball instead of dribbling. But their solid fundamentals and teamwork soon kicked in.
Fast-paced plays, quick passes and accurate shots kept the game lively, with the two teams trading baskets and giving the crowd plenty to cheer about. The chants from the stands grew louder: "Go, Gu Ma!" in Chinese and "Go, Mustangs!" in English.
At one point, a tall Crimson Cliffs student dressed in a shirt and tie joined the aunties on the court. His exaggerated, "wild" and playful style of play sent the crowd into fits of laughter and pushed the atmosphere to another level.
Reagan Haws, a Crimson Cliffs player, said that she found the game "really fun," especially because of the unusual rules.
"It was just like a new experience. It was great to see the other cultures," she added.
Crimson Cliffs Principal Kim Monkres welcomed the Chinese team to the school and said the visit provided an opportunity for cultural exchange between the two countries.
"I'm just so thrilled that we have the opportunity to bring Chinese culture together with ours," she told Xinhua.
"The dual language program in our school has been such a blessing. It's one of my favorite classes to sit in to. I have no idea what they're saying, but the kids do."
Monkres said seeing how much the students have learned over the years and how fluent they have become in Chinese is "truly phenomenal."
Monkres also expressed enthusiasm about China's plan to invite 100,000 young Americans to visit China for exchange and study programs over the next five years, saying she hopes Crimson Cliffs will have an opportunity to participate.
Shen Xin, vice president of the Chinese People's Association for Friendship with Foreign Countries, who led the Auntie Basketball delegation to the United States, said the sport's grassroots and entertaining nature makes it an effective way to bring people from the two countries closer together.
"It can help American people get a closer look at the everyday lives of ordinary people in China and learn more about the country's diverse ethnic cultures and traditions," Shen said, adding that he believes such people-to-people exchanges can help strengthen the foundation of China-U.S. relations.
The Auntie Basketball team's U.S. tour, which began earlier this week, includes stops in California, Nevada, Utah and Washington state. ■
Members of "Auntie Basketball" pose for a group photo with an American student at Crimson Cliffs High School in Washington, Utah, the United States, Oct. 2, 2026.(Photo by Zeng Hui/Xinhua)

NAGOYA, Japan, Oct. 3 (Xinhua) -- Records have tumbled and new stars have emerged at the 2026 Asian Games, where a generation of young athletes has made its mark across sports ranging from swimming and athletics to skateboarding and eSports.
Of China's 815 athletes, 548 are making their Asian Games debuts, while nearly a third were born in 2005 or later. The youngest is 12-year-old skateboarder Cao Shiqi.
Cao finished fourth in the women's park final, just 1.63 points shy of the podium. The tears she shed afterward, her coach said, would only sharpen a talent whose composure belies her age.
In the pool, 19-year-old Zhang Zhanshuo emerged as one of the Games' biggest stars, winning seven gold medals from eight events to equal the record for the most titles by an athlete at a single Asian Games.
Zhang swept the men's 200m, 400m, 800m and 1,500m freestyle titles, breaking the Asian record in the 200m and Games records in the 400m and 800m. He added three relay golds, helping China set Asian records in the men's 4x200m and 4x100m freestyle relays.
Zhang was not the only teenager making waves at the Tokyo Aquatics Center.
Yu Zidi, 13, won three individual titles in four days. Victory in the women's 200m butterfly made her the youngest swimming gold medalist in Asian Games history before she broke the Asian record in the 200m individual medley and the Games record in the 400m individual medley.
On the track, Chen Yujie collected three golds and a silver on her Asian Games debut.
The Chinese sprinter won the women's 100m in a Games-record time, lowering the previous mark by 0.09 seconds. After taking silver in the 200m, she anchored China to victory in the women's 4x100m relay before producing a late surge to secure gold in the mixed 4x100m a day later.
Yan Ziyi needed only one throw to make her mark. The 18-year-old won the women's javelin with an opening effort of 70.46 meters, breaking the Games record by 4.37 meters and beating Japan's Olympic champion Haruka Kitaguchi.
But the emergence of a new generation has stretched well beyond China.
Japan's 17-year-old Shin Ohashi smashed the men's 200m breaststroke world record with a time of 2:04.83 and shared the 100m title with China's Dong Zhihao.
In eSports, 11-year-old Yuki Kurihara of Japan defeated South Korea's Kang Dong-shin 10-2 in the Puyo Puyo Champions final to become the youngest gold medalist in Asian Games history.
Chinese Taipei's Ku Yong-yan, 12, took silver in the men's skateboarding park with 87.33 points, finishing behind Japan's Izuru Nagahara.
Other delegations also found young athletes breaking new ground.
Thailand's Puripol Boonson, 20, completed the men's sprint double, winning the 100m in a Games-record 9.90 seconds before clocking 19.88 in the 200m to equal the Asian record held by China's Xie Zhenye.
South Korea's Kang Jun-i won the men's street skateboarding title at 17, delivering his country's first Asian Games gold in the sport.
His compatriot Hwang Seo-hyun, 16, also made history, winning the women's balance beam to give South Korea its first Asian Games title in the event in 40 years. ■

Thai team coach Jeelachat Permpoonprom said the tournament provided another platform for exchanges between Thailand and China.
"The close relationship between China and Thailand can be further consolidated through sports events, especially the increasingly popular pickleball competitions," he said.
Liu Xinrui, a student competitor from Wuhan University of Technology, said pickleball made it easy for Chinese and ASEAN players to compete and communicate.
"I hope that more multinational pickleball exchanges and competitions will be held in the future," Liu said. ■

UK-Iran national arrested over alleged bomb plot at RAF Fairford released on bail

A sixth man who was arrested in connection with a suspected terrorist plot at RAF Fairford has been released on bail.
The 25-year-old, a dual UK-Iranian national, was arrested on suspicion of preparing terrorist acts under section 5 of the Terrorism Act 2006.
He was detained on Thursday in the borough of Westminster, London, where searches of two properties have now concluded.
The investigation into the incident is still under way, counter-terrorism police said.
Last weekend, five British nationals, all in their mid-20s, were arrested on suspicion of explosives offences and terrorism and then bailed.
The arrests were made after three suspicious vans were spotted near the military site in Gloucestershire.
Vicki Evans, the senior national coordinator for Counter Terrorism Policing, previously said the investigation was “hugely complex”, adding that specialist teams were “interrogating multiple lines of inquiry”.
She said: “As we’ve made clear, we’re looking at all possible angles – including possible foreign state involvement.”
The prime minister, Andy Burnham, has said there were “strong indications” Iran played a part in the incident near the Gloucestershire military base.
RAF Fairford has been used in recent months by US bombers after former prime minister Keir Starmer granted Washington permission to use British bases for “defensive” strikes against Tehran.
Counter-terrorism police have said a quantity of petrol, but no explosive devices, was found in the vans that had sparked the security alert near the airbase.
On Thursday, the Israeli prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, claimed Israel handed Britain intelligence about the suspected terror plot.
Netanyahu said his country warned UK authorities about the “Iranian-sponsored attack” shortly before Britain’s announcement of a ban on trade with illegal Israeli settlements in the West Bank.

====================================================================================================

Britain’s military in Kenya: Allegations, immunity and a fight for justice
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
13:18:37 UTC
22:18:37 KST

When Noldonyo Piro and her older sister were growing up, they were inseparable. Just a year apart, Piro, then about 15, and Mantoi Lekoloi Kaunda, 16, spent most days grazing the family’s herd of about 250 goats and sheep across the vast plains that stretch for miles around their home in northern Kenya.
“We lived a very simple life,” Piro, now in her 40s, recalls, sitting outside her small home made of tin sheets and sticks, topped with a patchwork roof of plastic bags in Archer’s Post, a rural settlement in Samburu County.
“I remember we used to stand some distance away from each other, and then one of us would start singing, and the other would answer. We loved to play with each other and tell stories.”
As teenagers in the mid-1990s, their biggest fears involved the wildlife roaming the area — lions, cheetahs and elephants. The sisters had no reason to fear the British soldiers who had long trained on the outskirts of Archer’s Post. In fact, neither had ever seen a white man before — until, on one afternoon, everything changed.
Piro and Mantoi, who was about six months pregnant, were out herding livestock when Piro saw white soldiers approaching from behind.
“I felt scared and started running,” she tells Al Jazeera, staring at the thickets across the arid landscape. “One of them chased me and hit me on the back of my head.”
“I fell down, and the soldier stood on my arm until it snapped and broke.” She holds up the arm, still visibly indented where the bone broke.
Piro says the soldier then raped her until she passed out. When she regained consciousness, she was covered in blood. Nearby, her sister Mantoi lay with her eyes closed, lifeless.
Piro staggered home. “She was just shouting ‘problem, problem,’ and I could see she was having trouble walking,” her father, the late Kaunda Lekoloi, later told ITV. “She said the white men had attacked them.”
He went out to search for Mantoi.
“I found Mantoi covered in blood. I could see that she was dead. There were two sets of soldiers’ boot prints in the dust.”
He carried his daughter’s body home on a donkey and buried her the next morning.
“There was no one to tell,” Piro says.
No police post was within reach, and for a Samburu pastoralist in the 1990s, reporting an attack by men in foreign uniforms was unlikely to lead anywhere.
For years the family lived with the horror in silence, only whispered from household to household.
“After that day, I became more scared of white men than I was of lions,” Piro says, her eyes filling with tears. “Even now, when I think about what happened, it makes me sick to my stomach.”
No one has ever been charged over Mantoi’s alleged murder.
Her case is among decades of allegations against soldiers from the British Army Training Unit Kenya, or BATUK, that include rape, murder, abandoned children fathered by soldiers, deaths and severe injuries from unexploded ordnance, environmental destruction and fatal vehicle collisions.
The military arrangement dates back to a 1964 defence agreement, signed months after Kenya’s independence, that allowed United Kingdom forces to keep training on Kenyan soil.
Six decades later, BATUK remains embedded in northern Kenya, training around 10,000 soldiers a year in Laikipia and Samburu. There has been no known case in which British personnel accused in the cases documented by Kenyan communities and investigators have faced prosecution in Kenya.
The UK has repeatedly invoked sovereign immunity — the principle that one state cannot be sued in another’s courts — a claim that went untested for decades, keeping cases from reaching Kenyan judges.
Now, finally, that power imbalance is being challenged.
Unearthed, then buried again
Mantoi’s case might have stayed buried had hundreds of women from the Maasai and Samburu tribes not come forward in 2003, alleging decades of rape by British soldiers and suing for negligence under UK law, arguing commanders had known of issues since 1977 and failed to act.
The Royal Military Police launched Operation Tasker in March 2003 to investigate the allegations. By October 2004, it had logged more than 2,000 allegations of rape and sexual violence involving British soldiers over the preceding four decades.
Kenya’s Criminal Investigation Department handled Mantoi’s case, and her father allowed her body to be exhumed — a profound cultural taboo in Samburu tradition. The pathologist told ITV at the time that the rib fractures indicated that considerable force was sustained to her back, suggesting a blow from a boot. Experts also recovered hair from her lower body, including an unidentified pubic hair.
Gideon Kibunja, the detective chief superintendent leading the investigation, was direct.
“The findings so far tend to agree with the claim by Mantoi’s sister that they were attacked by a British soldier,” he said, noting that investigators hoped UK authorities would help them obtain DNA samples from soldiers training in the area at the time.
Piro says that when the investigators left, her father quietly buried his daughter a second time, hoping that, after all those years, he might finally get some answers. He died shortly afterwards without seeing justice served, and the investigation went cold.
Despite the allegations by 2,000 women, the UK Ministry of Defence (MOD) announced in 2006 that the three-year investigation, Operation Tasker, had found no reliable evidence to support a single allegation, and claimed much of the evidence provided by Kenyan police and medical authorities appeared to have been fabricated. No one was prosecuted.
The investigators also failed to conduct DNA tests on any of the 69 mixed-race children whose mothers say were conceived when they were allegedly raped by British soldiers.
Piro says the family has not heard from the police since the exhumation and has never been shown the autopsy report.
Declassified UK, a British investigative media outlet, filed freedom-of-information requests with the MOD for documents on Mantoi's case, including the pathology report, DNA results and the ministry’s correspondence with Kenyan police and courts surrounding the exhumation.
The MOD confirmed it held some material but refused to release the records, saying they were scattered across electronic files and archive boxes and that searching them would take at least 14 days — far beyond the statutory cost limit of three and a half days of work. It told the journalists there was no way to narrow the request to bring it within the limit.
Last year, after Piro supplied a letter supporting the request, the MOD eventually released a single, redacted Royal Military Police interim investigation summary.
The report, provided to Al Jazeera by Declassified UK, documents seven unhealed rib fractures consistent with injuries sustained at or shortly before death, and a British military-type battery recovered two feet above the grave’s surface. The report notes that Kenyan police “appeared to apportion significant relevance to this find”.
But the British officer who wrote it disagreed, reasoning that Mantoi had been buried some 9km (6 miles) from where she was attacked. “The importance of this find is not shared by the undersigned,” he wrote.
The section titled The Kenya Police Enquiries is blacked out. The forensic results were still pending when it was written, and nothing further has been released.
Al Jazeera asked the MOD whether the forensic testing was ever completed, and whether British soldiers’ DNA had ever been compared with samples from the grave. It replied that the investigation and exhumation “were led by the Kenyan authorities”, with the Special Investigation Branch, the RMP’s investigative arm, “fully” supporting both, and directed further questions to the Kenyan police. Kenya’s Directorate of Criminal Investigations, the Attorney General and the Office of the Director of Public Prosecutions did not respond to questions about the case.
Operation Tasker "is now a closed investigation with no official requests to reopen it”, the MOD said.
Piro, meanwhile, struggles to believe justice will ever be possible.
“Nothing ever happens except people coming here, asking me questions, taking pictures and then leaving,” she says with a tired shrug. “Those men should have been arrested many years ago.”
But a new generation has taken up the question Piro was never allowed to ask: whether the British Army can be made to answer under Kenyan law. At the centre of this effort is a lawyer whose grandfather was among the last anti-colonial Mau Mau fighters to emerge from the forest after Kenya’s guerrilla war against British rule: Kelvin Mugambi Kubai.
When history came full circle
Kubai, a 29-year-old advocate of the High Court of Kenya, was a child when investigators descended on Mantoi’s grave in 2004, 73km from his home in Meru County.
His late grandfather, Musa Mwariama, had fought British colonial forces in the forests of Mount Kenya decades earlier. A Mau Mau field marshal, he led fighters armed with a handful of guns and, more often, arrows and crude weapons against a better-equipped army.
While studying law at the University of Nairobi, Kubai encountered a pivotal 1913 case before the colonial high court in Mombasa: Ol le Njogo v. Attorney General — the first known case in which indigenous Africans in East Africa took the British Crown to a local colonial court.
A young Maasai man and seven other community leaders had challenged their forced eviction from Laikipia, arguing the agreements surrendering their ancestral land were invalid: Their paramount chief had no authority to give away communal territory.
Rather than contest the claim, the British Crown had the case dismissed on jurisdictional grounds: The agreements were treaties between sovereign powers, beyond the authority of domestic courts. Versions of that argument outlived the empire and were invoked repeatedly to shield Britain from legal challenges over colonial-era abuses.
“From that day, that case never escaped my mind,” Kubai tells Al Jazeera from his office in Nairobi. He did not know then that it would one day become his fight.
In 2021, a fire broke out during a UK military training exercise at the Lolldaiga Conservancy in Laikipia, scorching some 12,000 acres of grazing land and crops, killing livestock and blanketing nearby communities in smoke for days. Kubai and activists from the African Centre for Corrective and Preventive Action opened temporary offices to register victims.
Taking on the UK military was, in Kubai’s words, “uncharted waters”. Lawyers he consulted believed sovereign immunity made it unwinnable.
“When I brought up the case to my former professor, his answer was a blanket ‘No, you cannot sue the army; they have sovereign immunity,’” Kubai recalls.
Then a Swahili song came to mind: “I will not stand by while injustice reigns.”
“That’s something I share with my grandfather,” Kubai explains. “I can't cower from standing against injustices, and I can’t be silent in the face of evil.”
Despite the warnings, Kubai, then 23, filed a class-action lawsuit against BATUK at the Environment and Land Court on behalf of affected residents.
The British army responded much as it had a century earlier. BATUK was an organ of a sovereign state, its lawyers argued, and the Defence Cooperation Agreement governing its presence in Kenya — renewable every five years — was an accord between nations. Under sovereign immunity, Kenyan courts had no jurisdiction over a foreign power — the same argument used against the Maasai in 1913.
“It was shocking to me because I was facing the same defendant in essentially the same situation, and they came back with the same defence,” Kubai recalls, shaking his head.
“They were using a hundred-year-old trick on me,” he says. “But this time around, it didn’t work.”
Breaking the shield
Kubai's response was the text of the defence agreement itself. Under Article 6, Kenya has jurisdiction over criminal offences committed by British personnel — unless the offence arose in the course of “official duty,” in which case jurisdiction falls to the UK.
The agreement specifies that sexual offences, torture, slavery and robbery can never be treated as acts undertaken in the course of official duty. Murder, however, is absent from that list.
Article 11 goes further, giving Kenya jurisdiction over all civil claims arising in its territory and obliging Britain to pay “prompt and adequate compensation” where its forces are found liable. Article 23 requires the same for any death, injury, loss or damage caused to local communities.
Kubai argues that, despite the agreement’s provisions on civil claims and compensation, BATUK invoked sovereign immunity in the Lolldaiga litigation to challenge the Kenyan court’s jurisdiction.
“In this agreement, they expressly waived their immunity,” Kubai says of those provisions. “So you cannot waive something when it suits you, and then raise it again when it doesn’t suit you.”
In March 2022, the Environment and Land Court agreed. Justice Antonina Kossy Bor ruled that in signing the agreement, the UK had “waived their immunity to the extent stipulated”, giving Kenya jurisdiction over the Lolldaiga claim. She was not persuaded, she wrote, that starting “a massive destructive fire” could be considered part of military training or a sovereign act at all.
According to Kubai, it was the first time the British army had raised sovereign immunity in a Kenyan court and lost.
“This ruling broke through the ceiling and penetrated the shield of sovereign immunity that so many lawyers had been unwilling to challenge,” Kubai tells Al Jazeera.
But the victory came with a catch: The same judge ordered claimants to first exhaust a mechanism in the Defence Cooperation Agreement itself, the Intergovernmental Liaison Committee, a body of senior officials from both countries that meets roughly twice a year and, Kubai says, has no permanent office or published complaints procedure. The MOD says it is a forum and can meet virtually or in either country.
That process dragged on for years, and activists say around 50 elderly claimants died waiting. Last year, the UK agreed to pay 2.9 million pounds ($4m) to 7,723 claimants, some receiving as little as 22,500 Kenyan shillings — about $175 — and, under the confidential settlement, the UK accepted no liability for the fire.
But the case also established that, in certain circumstances, the British military could be held to account in Kenyan courts.
It wasn’t the only case shattering the perception that British soldiers were untouchable.
Agnes Wanjiru, a 21-year-old mother, was last seen in 2012 at a Nanyuki hotel with British soldiers. Her body was found two months later in a septic tank, and a 2019 Kenyan inquest — a fact-finding process, not a criminal trial — concluded that she had been unlawfully killed by one or more of the soldiers.
Last year, a Kenyan court charged Robert James Purkiss, the former UK soldier accused of killing her, with murder and issued an arrest warrant. Purkiss denies the charge.
Weeks later, he was arrested in the UK and is now contesting extradition in a London court. If extradited, he would, according to ITV News, be the first former or serving British soldier to face trial abroad for murder.
Ben Keith, a London barrister who specialises in extradition and whose colleagues at his chambers are representing Purkiss, tells Al Jazeera that the chances of Purkiss being sent to Kenya are “moderate to good”.
He expects the former soldier will be extradited eventually, but the process could take two to three years. One obstacle, Keith notes, is prison conditions in Kenya. UK courts have approved extraditions to Kenya after accepting prison-condition assurances in the past, but those precedents are old and may carry less weight in Purkiss’s case.
“There is now an awakening that is happening which was not there before,” Kubai explains. “Victims now see that justice is possible, and they are willing to pursue it.”
But that shift has been slow to reach the communities where the harm occurred. Across Samburu and Laikipia, most of those affected by BATUK are poor pastoralists, far from the courts, with no local office to lodge a complaint and few lawyers willing to take their cases.
“Get away with it”
Memusi Lochede sits on a bed as her 24-year-old daughter Chaula lies motionless on the floor of their home in Archer’s Post, in the shadow of the training grounds. A donated wheelchair sits in the corner. Her daughter’s right leg is gone; metal rods brace a body so badly injured that she struggles to hold up her head.
“I have so much pain in my heart seeing my daughter in this condition,” 46-year-old Lochede tells Al Jazeera, wiping the drool from her daughter’s chin. “I feel ashamed that she needs so much help, and I don’t know how to help her.”
In 2019, Chaula, then a teenager, says she was hit by a speeding BATUK vehicle while crossing the road. Her leg was amputated and, her mother says, she was left paralysed and spent nearly three years in hospital.
A BATUK representative later came to see Lochede, she says.
“He apologised for what happened and said they don’t want a court case and would take care of my daughter — anything she needs,” she recounts.
The MOD said it “has not located a record of an approach having been made by a BATUK representative to the family.”
When her daughter was discharged, BATUK paid the hospital bills — without receipts or disclosing the amount — and disappeared, Lochede says. For years, Lochede called its community liaison officer, the Kenyan official tasked with receiving complaints like hers, who never answered. Eventually she gave up.
The MOD told Al Jazeera in August that BATUK is aware of the claim that one of its drivers “hit and injured a minor” in 2019, “resulting in permanent injuries”.
It said legal representatives have been in contact with the Kenya National Commission on Human Rights about the case and that a compensation offer has been made but the commission has not responded.
In late September, Al Jazeera asked the MOD what had been offered, when, and through whom. It did not provide those details, saying instead that BATUK “remains willing to engage with the child’s family, through an appropriate representative and on a without-prejudice basis,” but that “to date, we have been unable to establish contact with the family or an authorised representative”. Any resolution would have to rest on “verified medical and factual information” and, because the claim concerns a minor, be approved by a Kenyan court.
Ruth Getobai Nchagwa, a deputy director at the commission, says it has “never engaged with BATUK directly as our letters to them went unanswered”.
Chaula’s case “has not been addressed to date,” she notes, and the commission is not aware of any discussions about compensation. Lochede similarly says no one has ever approached her about compensation.
Before the accident, Lochede supported her five children by making beaded necklaces and selling them in Nairobi. Now she cannot leave her daughter’s side, and Chaula’s care costs about 30,000 Kenyan shillings ($230) a month — more than Lochede usually earns.
“It’s a shameful feeling to pick up the phone and call so many numbers for help, and no one picks up your call,” she explains, her lips quivering as she fights tears. “In those moments where I can’t provide for my daughter, I just lock myself inside the room and lie in my bed and cry.”
Her daughter, once healthy and active, now barely speaks.
“There are some days she wakes up and says just one word, like ‘food’ or ‘bathroom,’” Lochede says. “Those are the good days. Other days, she refuses to eat. I can see that she’s depressed and lonely. Inside, her soul is shattered.”
“These soldiers do these things because they know they can get away with it,” she adds sharply. “They know we don’t have money. We don’t have power. It’s extremely difficult for us to fight them.”
Cases like Chaula’s are far from isolated. Last year, a landmark two-year inquiry by Kenya’s parliamentary defence committee put decades of alleged BATUK abuses on the official record.
The 94-page report gathered testimony from hearings across Laikipia and Samburu, including a herder allegedly shot by a British sergeant; the alleged gang rape of 30 women at knifepoint in 1997; a boy who lost both arms and an eye to unexploded ordnance; and women with children their British fathers had never acknowledged.
BATUK declined to appear, citing its status and immunities under the defence arrangements. The committee condemned the refusal as contemptuous, calling it “emblematic of institutional contempt for the authority of Parliament and, by extension, the sovereignty of the people of Kenya”.
It concluded that BATUK “is increasingly seen as an occupying presence rather than a development partner”, with affected residents drawing parallels to colonial injustices. Witnesses told the committee that “suspected BATUK abuses are not only unpunished but actively covered up” — that whenever a BATUK member is implicated, police files often “go missing” and complainants are “intimidated into silence.”
An MOD spokesperson told Al Jazeera the UK “deeply” values its relationship with Kenya, “which has long been the UK’s defence partner of choice in East Africa”.
The MOD is “addressing concerns raised by Kenyan authorities and communities, focusing on legal accountability, ethical standards, environmental stewardship, economic benefit and social responsibility,” the spokesperson said.
Regarding road traffic incidents, the spokesperson said BATUK “cooperates fully with the local authorities and Kenyan Police”, that all such incidents are “investigated thoroughly” and that “where claims are made, BATUK submits to the jurisdiction of the Kenyan courts”.
When asked what progress the MOD had made on the concerns raised by the committee, and whether it was investigating any of the specific cases, it referred Al Jazeera to the written statement it submitted to the inquiry, which said it was “not aware of any evidence to support any allegation of collusion with security forces to suppress or dismiss complaints, or intimidate, bribe or coerce victims into silence”, and that any such evidence “would be taken extremely seriously and investigated accordingly”.
For Awino Okech, professor of feminist and security studies at SOAS University of London, the parliamentary report points beyond individual abuses. “This is no longer a case of a few bad apples but reckoning with what many will interpret as accepted militarised institutional culture,” she tells Al Jazeera.
“The fundamental question the British government is being asked to reflect on is their responsibility when there is a documented pattern of malbehaviour by their employees in a foreign country.”
Okech says the pattern cannot be separated from race. “We cannot ignore the racialised element. In this case, it is visible when crimes committed in Kenya are taken less seriously.”
Among the cases recorded by the committee was that of Robert Swara Seurei, a 28-year-old BATUK worker who lived with his aunt, Irene Kipsage. He was killed in 2007, three weeks into his first job with BATUK.
He came home from the training grounds with a heavy metal object he mistook for a candle. When he tried to light it, the device exploded, killing him, destroying the family home, and injuring his grandmother and Kipsage.
According to the parliamentary report, BATUK’s own investigation found warnings not to remove objects from the training grounds had been issued in English, which Seurei did not understand. Kipsage says compensation for Seurei’s death was paid to his father, his legal guardian. Kipsage, who suffered hearing damage and lost her home, and his grandmother, who became permanently deaf, received nothing.
“BATUK never even apologised,” Kipsage tells Al Jazeera from her rebuilt home in Laikipia, where the blast occurred nearly two decades ago. “They treat us like we’re not human — like we don’t exist.”
The MOD confirmed that liability for the incident was admitted in March 2008. The claim was brought by his family and “was settled by agreement in November 2010”, it said, constituting “a full and final settlement”.
The MOD noted that it does not discuss the details of individual compensation claims. Based on its available records, it said, no further claim from the family has been identified since the 2010 settlement.
Charles Ngare was 17 in 2010 when British soldiers asked him and his friends to help free a vehicle stuck in a culvert. As the boys rocked it loose, it lurched back into the lorry towing it, crushing his leg between the two.
The soldiers drove him to hospital but, Ngare says, told staff they had found him injured by the roadside. The parliamentary report also notes that “BATUK personnel were [...] accused of providing false accounts to mislead investigators” in Ngare’s case. Sixteen years on, his leg still causes pain, preventing him from doing the manual labour that is the main work available where he lives.
In 2018, his compensation claim was dismissed as time-barred, according to correspondence he has kept from the case. Kubai says this is a tactic BATUK uses to let complaints languish unanswered until they are too old to pursue.
“My case may not be as severe as others, but I still deserve justice,” Ngare says, with letters to BATUK scattered across a table in his family’s home. “These British soldiers feel they can harm anyone and nobody will question them.”
The MOD said Ngare’s claim was filed in 2018, “after the applicable limitation period had expired”, and dismissed by the Kenyan courts as time-barred. “The MOD respects and complies with decisions of the Kenyan courts,” it said.
On the allegation that BATUK personnel gave false accounts, it said the materials currently available “do not substantiate” it, and that no witness statements, investigative findings or disciplinary determinations were identified establishing that its personnel deliberately gave false evidence.
The war remains
For Kubai, these cases follow a familiar pattern. “BATUK has been harming a class of persons with no resources to defend themselves,” he says.
“So they get away with it. Not because what they did was right, but because they harmed someone who has no capacity to litigate the injustices against them.”
Kubai works with UK lawyers and geneticists to identify British soldiers who fathered and abandoned children in Kenya, using DNA databases to trace them and press them to take responsibility. He is currently preparing four cases against BATUK, including those of Mantoi, Ngare and Chaula.
Much of the work is funded by his law firm or, at times, his own pocket. Kenyan organisations that could support it are reluctant, he says, because many depend on British aid.
But there are too many victims for one lawyer.
“It feels very disappointing when I have to turn people away,” Kubai explains. “I am just one person doing work that our government and the British government should be doing.”
“The cases themselves are very, very draining,” he adds. “My time, my effort — so much of it goes uncompensated. But you have to be okay with it, because there is a bigger goal.”
The dispute over BATUK has now impacted the legal agreement governing the UK military presence in Kenya.
The 2015 Defence Cooperation Agreement expired in 2021. A replacement was signed that July.
Kenya’s Parliament gave the replacement conditional approval in 2023, requiring that murder be added to the offences over which Kenyan courts hold primary jurisdiction. The UK did not accept the condition, and Kenya has not completed ratification.
The agreement, the parliamentary committee noted last year, is “in limbo” — leaving the legal framework governing the British military’s continuing presence in Kenya contested and unresolved.
Keith, the London barrister, calls Kenya’s demand to add murder to the list of crimes that automatically fall under Kenyan jurisdiction “unusual” and doubts that Britain would ever accept such a provision. In an exceptionally serious case, such as the alleged murder of a civilian, he says
The UK could be expected to permit a local prosecution. But automatically assigning murder to Kenyan jurisdiction in every case would go further, he argues, substantially limiting the jurisdictional protections normally available to British troops stationed abroad. Keith suspects the dispute is tied directly to the “historical issues” between Kenya and BATUK.
The failure to ratify the Defence Cooperation Agreement, Keith adds, means the new agreement was never implemented into domestic law.
In its written statement to the inquiry, the MOD said the defence relationship “is governed by the 2015 DCA”, which is overseen by the joint UK-Kenyan liaison committee, and that Britain “continues to engage with the Kenyan government on the two reservations outlined by the Kenyan Parliament” — which include corporate social responsibility obligations for visiting forces and the inclusion of murder under Kenyan jurisdiction.
Asked by Al Jazeera whether Britain would accept the demand on murder, the MOD said the two governments “are discussing routes to bring the 2021 Defence Cooperation Agreement into force” but that it does not comment on potential amendments proposed during those discussions. Defence cooperation with Kenya, it said, “continues to be governed by the 2015 Defence Cooperation Agreement, which was extended by mutual consent pending entry into force of the 2021 agreement”.
Last year, Kenya's Parliament urged immediate ratification, and the two governments have continued to negotiate. But the dispute over jurisdiction remains unresolved.
Kubai wants the agreement to go further. He points to Cyprus, where the British military runs a permanent claims office allowing residents to walk in and file complaints. The MOD operates similar offices in Germany and elsewhere, but not in Kenya.
“When you come to Kenya, there is no such channel for accountability,” he explains. “Kenyan civilians and their claims have been suppressed for far too long. That cannot continue.”
There is also a stark disparity in the compensation that is paid. In 2018-19, the MOD’s most expensive single payout for farm animal deaths in Cyprus was 5,031 pounds ($6,800) — to a farmer whose pregnant goats miscarried after being panicked by low-flying British aircraft. The payment covered the loss of unborn animals and veterinary fees.
The Lolldaiga settlement — for a fire that burned for two weeks, scorched 12,000 acres, killed one man and left thousands breathing smoke — averaged under 400 pounds ($530) per claimant.
Kubai’s recommendations for BATUK's operations in Kenya are specific. He wants a permanently staffed claims office in Nanyuki, funded through the DCA and modelled after those in Cyprus and Germany, where a family like that of Agnes Wanjiru’s could have reported her missing. He also recommends using the same fund to reimburse pro bono lawyers for the costs of representing victims who cannot afford legal services.
Pressure on BATUK has also moved into the streets. On August 12 , survivors, bereaved families and residents from BATUK-affected communities marched to the Parliament in Nairobi, petitioning lawmakers not to ratify the defence agreement until the documented abuses are addressed.
The odds, however, remain lopsided: a well-funded army with some of the country’s best lawyers on one side, and victims who often cannot afford the bus fare to court on the other.
But Kubai is not deterred and says the odds were even worse for his grandfather.
“At one point, he and the other [Mau Mau] were fighting the colonial government with vastly inferior means against an army that was well equipped and well coordinated,” Kubai says. “The odds were always very much against him. And that has always been the case with me.”
“There hasn’t been one single war that ends all injustices in this world,” he continues. “Then, my grandfather was fighting in the terrain of Mount Kenya. Now, I’m fighting in the corridors of justice.”
“It’s just that the battlefields change,” he says. “But the war remains.”

TEHRAN- The Head of Iran’s Ports and Maritime Organization (PMO) announced the organization’s plan to activate the country’s idle port capacities, develop maritime diplomacy, and use the capacities of the embassies of the Islamic Republic of Iran to expand maritime trade and transport.

Referring to the country’s ports’ nominal capacity of about 302 million tons, he said: “Despite this capacity, in recent years about 50 to 55 percent of the ports’ capacity has been idle, and by introducing the capacities of Iranian ports to target countries, the ground must be provided for greater use of this capacity.”
The Head of the Ports and Maritime Organization added: “Infrastructure development without diplomacy, and diplomacy without infrastructure development, cannot achieve the desired result, and strengthening synergy between domestic bodies and partner countries is essential.”
He also described banking transactions, insurance issues, and investment as important challenges in maritime trade and said: “The embassies of the Islamic Republic of Iran can play an effective role in introducing investment opportunities and the country’s capacities in the North-South and East-West corridors.”

Ghanbari emphasized: “Creating this charter can make the path of joint cooperation clearer and provide the possibility of more precise follow-up of projects and measuring their progress, and it is expected that within the next two months, the framework of cooperations and the implementation path of joint projects will become clearer.”
In this meeting, the ambassadors of the Islamic Republic of Iran abroad also presented their views and proposals on solutions for developing economic and commercial relations with target countries and emphasized strengthening economic cooperation through activating the capacities of the two countries’ private sectors, identifying new investment opportunities, and developing trade interactions.
The ambassadors of the Islamic Republic of Iran also, referring to the existing capacities in their countries of mission, emphasized the necessity of purposefully using the capacity of Iran’s missions to facilitate communication among economic actors, introduce investment capacities, and provide the ground for a more effective presence of Iran’s private sector in foreign markets.

Bundeswehr to Begin Rearmament With New P13 Pistols
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
13:17:13 UTC
22:17:13 KST

The Bundeswehr has completed testing of the new standard-issue P13 pistol, which will begin to be distributed to troops in the coming months and will gradually replace the P8, which has been in service since 1994.
This was announced by the Bundeswehr. The new P13 is based on the Czech CZ P-10 C OR chambered for the 9×19 mm cartridge and is intended to re-equip the German armed forces.
The pistol passed the final series of tests conducted by the Bundeswehr’s Federal Office for Armaments, Information Technology, and In-Service Support. Based on the results, the weapon was deemed suitable for military use, paving the way for mass production.
The P13 has a 15-round magazine, weighs about 760 grams without ammunition, and is equipped with a 102 mm-long barrel. The design also allows for the attachment of optical sights.
One of the main differences from the P8 is the striker-fired trigger mechanism. On the P13, the trigger pull remains approximately the same for each shot and is about 2.3 kg.
By comparison, the P8’s trigger requires a force of about 5.1 kg for the first shot and about 2 kg for subsequent shots. The Bundeswehr expects that a consistent trigger pull will simplify handling of the weapon and increase the likelihood of an accurate first shot.
The pistol also features interchangeable grip panels, allowing it to be adapted to the specific hand of each service member.
According to the Bundeswehr, the P13 is designed for operation in high and low temperatures and under prolonged stress. Its modular design allows it to be adapted for various missions.
The new pistol will be supplied in Flat Dark Earth color. The Bundeswehr notes that this finish, among other things, is intended to reduce the weapon’s infrared signature.
The P13 is set to gradually replace the standard-issue P8, which was adopted by the Bundeswehr in 1994. The P8 is a military version of the Heckler & Koch USP pistol.
Earlier, Militarnyi reported that Germany had selected the Czech CZ P13 pistol as the Bundeswehr’s new standard-issue sidearm.
At that time, the focus was on selecting the system and preparing for the re-equipment of the German military.
The current phase marks the transition from selection and contracting to the actual re-equipment of units: the Bundeswehr has completed testing of the P13 and is preparing for serial deliveries.
The supplier of the new weapons is the German company POL-TEC, which is a partner of the Czech manufacturer Česká zbrojovka. It is CZ that manufactures the base model, the P-10 C OR.
The Bundestag’s Budget Committee approved funding for the program in November 2025, after which a contract was signed for the supply of the new pistols.
The framework agreement provides for the purchase of up to 203,000 P13s, while the initial order covers 65,000 pistols along with related equipment and services.

Russia struck Kyiv’s Northern Bridge with a drone on 3 October, damaging the roadway and overhead trolleybus lines, Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko said. Two people were injured, one of whom was hospitalized.
The strike came one day after repeated Russian drone attacks on the Southern Bridge, which damaged its support structures, road surface and subway infrastructure and forced its closure. The attacks caused severe traffic disruption across Kyiv, with major roads gridlocked and some people reportedly walking across bridges.
Another key bridge targeted
The Northern Bridge connects Kyiv’s Obolon and Troieshchyna districts and is one of the capital’s major routes across the Dnipro.
Damage to its roadway and trolleybus network adds another disruption to Kyiv’s transport system after the attacks on the Southern Bridge. The Northern and Southern bridges are among the capital’s key crossings between its eastern and western banks.
Russia repeatedly attacks bridge connecting Kyiv’s two sides across the Dnipro river, disrupting transport across the capital
Kyiv changes bridge restrictions
Kyiv authorities announced temporary changes to bridge traffic rules following the attacks.
During air raids, traffic on the Southern Bridge will be restricted for 15 minutes in the direction from the right bank to the left bank, while traffic in the opposite direction will remain open. On the Podilskyi-Voskresenskyi Bridge, traffic in both directions will stop for 15 minutes when an air-raid alert is announced or lifted.
The Northern, Darnytskyi, Paton and Metro bridges will operate without restrictions during air raids, according to the Kyiv City Military Administration.
Russia intensifies attacks on Kyiv
The bridge strikes come amid an intensifying Russian aerial campaign against Kyiv. Russian drones and missiles have increasingly targeted the capital in recent weeks, damaging residential buildings, schools and infrastructure and disrupting daily life.
The attacks on the bridges add a different dimension to that campaign, directly disrupting movement between Kyiv’s two banks. With multiple crossings affected within days, the strikes have already translated into major traffic disruptions for the city’s residents.
