‘Sadness, cynicism and deep disappointment’: the Cornell gang-rape case and the failure of #MeToo
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
13:00:01 UTC
22:00:01 KST

Student safety advocates in the US call the start of the fall semester at universities “the red zone”. Fraternities, sororities and off-campus bars throw parties welcoming students back to school. It’s supposed to be fun, but it can also be dangerous: more than 50% of sexual assaults that occur at colleges happen during that six- to 10-week period.
It was mid-October of 2024, during the red zone and just before a deluge of Halloween celebrations, when, a former Cornell University student says, she was gang-raped by a group of fraternity brothers. Recent attention on these allegations sparked widespread outrage this week, reviving a contentious national debate about how authorities respond to allegations of sexual assault on US college campuses.
The anonymous young woman at the center of the story – known as Jane Doe in court documents – filed a civil lawsuit last month, accusing seven men of plying her with drugs and alcohol and assaulting her over the course of seven hours at their fraternity house. The woman originally went to the house to visit a friend; she claims she arrived intoxicated and willingly took the party drug ketamine with the men. Later, she says, she became incapacitated by the drug, which is a dissociative anesthetic, while the men “commanded” her to keep snorting it.
Jane Doe also alleges that the Ivy League university’s ensuing internal investigation was too lenient toward the men. None have ever been charged with a crime. Two were expelled for their misconduct, while five were given lighter punishments: writing an essay, attending a workshop or serving a suspension. Some still attend the school. All seven men denied wrongdoing during Cornell’s investigation.
Public outcry over the case reached a breaking point on Thursday, when the New York governor Kathy Hochul stepped in to appoint a new special prosecutor to investigate the incident, which the original district attorney declined to prosecute. Now, state attorney general Leticia James will decide whether or not to take the case to a grand jury, which would decide whether there was enough evidence to charge the men with a crime.
In a statement, Cornell University defended its investigation of the incident. It closed the fraternity chapter involved and barred the group from campus. “We will continue to examine and strengthen our policies to ensure we are doing all we can to foster a culture where sexual misconduct is never tolerated, those who come forward are supported, and individuals found responsible through our processes are held accountable,” the statement read. (Cornell directed the Guardian to this statement when reached for comment.) After intense public pressure, the university agreed to hire external, independent lawyers to investigate whether its handling of the allegations was appropriate.
Matthew Van Houten, the Tompkins county district attorney, has said that he did not pursue the case two years ago because the woman’s first account to police did not say that she was drugged, incapacitated or forced into sex. He later said he did not read her full interview, only a shorter statement written by campus police and signed by Jane Doe. Her full statement included the sentence: “I can say with 100 percent confidence that I was raped,” but this did not make it into the final statement sent to Van Houten.
In the immediate aftermath of the incident, the woman exchanged friendly messages with some of the men, expressing concern about rumors that were spreading on campus about the event. She also maintains that the alleged assault began as a consensual encounter. It is common for sexual assault survivors to downplay their experiences as a coping mechanism. False rape accusations are incredibly rare.
One of the most damning pieces of evidence in the lawsuit involves screenshots of Snapchat messages sent in a fraternity group chat; at one point, an alleged participant named Jonathan Newell referred to Jane Doe as “free pussy”, advertising the alleged assault as it unfolded.
What upsets many women most about this case is how normalized such actions seem. About one in four undergraduate women experience sexual violence during college; 60% of rapes involving university students involve perpetrators who are known to the victims. Last year, a survey of female undergrads at Cornell found that 35% of respondents experienced “nonconsensual sexual contact involving physical force, threats of force or incapacitation”. That figure was up from 23% in 2023.
“There are so many people in America who find this so familiar,” said Lisa Wade, an associate professor at Tulane and author of American Hookup: The New Culture of Sex on Campus. “Not just the incident itself, but also the response by Cornell.”
As the case plays out in the courts, the so-called “Cornell 7” have become the literal faces of the enduring prevalence of sexual assault on campus, and the institutional failure that allows that behavior to flourish. Their names and images are plastered on social media posts calling for accountability. The Cornell Daily Sun, a student newspaper that has doggedly covered the lawsuit, led the way with an op-ed column titled “Cornell Won’t, We Will”. The piece began by listing the alleged assailants’ names. “We know who you are and we refuse to let you benefit from this University’s concealment,” wrote the editorial board.
A former South Park writer named Toby Morton launched a website detailing the specifics of what Jane Doe alleges each man did to her. Morton wrote on Instagram that he plans to sponsor billboards about the case. The actor Florence Pugh weighed in, pleading on social media for men to be “as horrified and as sickened as us [women]”. She added that “college/schools/universities repeatedly fail women around the world [building] men [who] get taught through time and time again that they can do extreme harm and won’t be harmed in return”.
When content creator and commentator Michael Tracey threatened to release the name and personal details of Jane Doe – going against decades of established journalistic norms for reporting on alleged rape victims – women flooded TikTok in her defense. The Spartacus-style rallying cry of “I’m Jane Doe” hit feeds, with users sharing stories of their own experiences with sexual assault. “All of us women are jane doe, and we will all continue to ban [sic] together for her,” reads the caption of one clip liked more than 267,000 times.
College admissions advisers told the New York Post that some of their high school clients pulled their early decision applications to Cornell because they would not feel safe in the community.
This outpouring recalls the early days of #MeToo, a global hashtag campaign against sexual abuse ignited in the wake of initial allegations against convicted rapist and former film producer Harvey Weinstein. But Wade, the Tulane professor, said she sees this case as “metabolizing the failure of #MeToo”, which promised a so-called reckoning in 2017. Ten years later, manosphere influencers teach their followers to see women as sex objects, and Americans re-elected a man who infamously bragged about grabbing women “by the pussy”.
Sexual assault survivors have long faced victim-shaming. Jane Doe’s narrative is complicated, and the New York Times reported that the alleged victim did not realize she had been raped until she read someone else describe the event as such on a social media forum; she had texted one of the accused that: “At the end of the day non of the sexual stuff was illegal and honestly i really liked being w u and matt.” This is not an unusual trauma response: it is common for victims to continue relationships with their abusers, as it provides some semblance of control over the situation.
But the messy timeline emboldens bad actors and conservative commentators who seek to advance an anti-woman agenda. These young men have not been convicted of a crime, and it would be difficult for prosecutors to convict them of rape due to a New York state legal loophole that does not consider a victim to be incapacitated if she willingly contributes to her own intoxication. (Jane Doe stated she arrived at the fraternity house drunk and willingly took substances with the men, though she also says they coerced her into snorting ketamine.)
The Free Press, a vocally “anti-woke” publication run by Bari Weiss, chastised the “court of public opinion” for “already puni[shing]” the Cornell 7. Dasha Nekrasova, one of the edgelord hosts of the Red Scare podcast, spent much of this week trying to shame Jane Doe and calling women who are upset over the lack of accountability in this case “deranged”.
“There’s a sadness, cynicism and deep disappointment that is also driving the response to this,” Wade said. “#MeToo happened, and nobody cared. Here it is again.”
Elizabeth Armstrong, a professor at the University of Michigan who studies gender inequities in universities, says that there have been “big waves of outrage” over sexual assault on campuses since the 1980s, when Mary Koss first coined the term “date rape”. The last national dialogue took place around 2015, when a Columbia University student carried a mattress around campus for a performance art piece based on her sexual assault.
More than a decade later, the issue has only gotten worse. The Trump administration has gutted Title IX protections, which prohibit sex-based discrimination in universities that receive federal funding, and limited the definition of what constitutes sexual harassment under it. Just this week, Trump announced that universities no longer have to investigate assaults on students that take place off-campus. (The Cornell case occurred at a frat house.) “We have an administration that is actively rolling back protections for student survivors,” said Amanda Walsh, deputy director for external affairs at the Victim Rights Law Center.
But Walsh, who works closely with survivors, says that gen Z women have much less internalized shame over their assaults than previous generations, who were often taught that women invite sexual assault through their actions. “It feels like the focus has shifted away from talking about what the woman did, and more appropriately to exploring the behavior of the men involved,” she said. “I always admire how much they focus on the behavior of the person who harmed them, rather than asking: ‘What could I have done differently? Why did this happen to me? I see college students really pushing back against that.”
The Cornell case has revived discussions on abolishing Greek life, the student social club system that is behind fraternities and sororities in the US. This week, a Vogue article called for universities to “ban frats once and for all”. It’s not unprecedented: the Pennsylvania liberal arts college Swarthmore did so in 2019, after campus publications leaked racist, sexist and homophobic documents written by fraternities. “That would be a really real change, but I doubt that will happen,” said Armstrong.
Elizabeth Allan, who leads the Hazing Prevention Research Lab at the University of Maine, added: “It’s important for everyone [in Greek life] to think how these groups might reflect larger societal norms and expectations and the ways in which [bad] behavior is reinforced.”
Most of all, Walsh worries how all the attention on this case will affect Jane Doe, and the countless other anonymous victims who are sure to come after her. “I’ve been in this field long enough to know that however much support she receives is exactly how much negativity she’ll get on the other side,” Walsh said. “At this point, with the political moment and online response, it almost feels like supporting a survivor of sexual violence feels political or partisan, which is wild.”

Badenoch returns to Conservative conference much stronger than a year ago
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
13:00:01 UTC
22:00:01 KST

A year ago, Tory MPs were braced for the prospect of yet another leadership battle to topple Kemi Badenoch as the party sunk to historic lows of 14-16% in the polls.
At the time, the word “November” was uttered in hushed tones – this being the decisive month when rebels would be able to mount a challenge, Badenoch having served 12 months in office.
But times appear to have changed and – against the odds – the Tories have undergone what has been termed a “Keminisation”, with the leader asserting her style and authority on the party, despite its wider poor performance in the polls.
“Right now, Kemi is the only thing that’s holding them up,” says Luke Tryl, the director of the More in Common thinktank, which conducts focus groups and polling. “If they ditched her, I think they’d be certain for electoral oblivion.”
Badenoch is running a party still discounted as toxic and incompetent by much of the electorate, but polling numbers and focus groups suggest some of them have recently begun to give her more of a hearing.
The party has crept up from the teens to the low 20s – occasionally edging ahead of Reform UK for the first time in almost two years.
“It’s not great for them, but it’s a lot better,” says Tryl. “The problem is the party brand. She is now in our approval ratings net neutral and has been net 1 or net 2. She was in the minus 30s and now only her and Burnham have positive approval.
“Progressives don’t like her, but when you come to those who might conceivably be Tory voters there’s a lot of ‘like her, don’t like the party, she tells it like it is, wish she was in another party’. I do think the Kemi bounce is real. People talk about her having improved and they have seen her PMQs clips.”
Data from the other pollsters backs up the idea that the public is more open to Badenoch than before. James Crouch, the head of policy and public affairs at Opinium, said Badenoch’s approval rating had been rising since May 2025, when she was at -27, to -3 in its latest poll. He said that among 2024 Conservative voters she had the approval of 64%, compared with just 8% who did not approve, while of those who voted Conservative in 2019, 56% approved of her, while 16% did not.
Further research from YouGov this week found four in 10 people used at least one negative term to describe the Tory leader, one of the most common themes being a perceived unpleasantness. But three in 10 included one or more positive terms in their description, strong and intelligent being the main compliments.
Some Tory MPs attribute Badenoch’s improvement over the last year to a willingness to learn and take advice on her performance. This is in spite of her having the preternatural public self-confidence to claim to the FT this weekend that she couldn’t think of any mistakes she had made, saying everyone makes them but “nothing comes to mind”.
But insiders say she has listened to people warning she needs to focus more on the economy and less on culture war talking points, with the party’s conference slogan set as “Stronger economy, stronger country”.
She has also improved her prime minister’s questions appearances, partly with help on preparation from Conservative grandees such as David Cameron.
Tory MPs believe a turning point for Badenoch was the defection of Robert Jenrick and Suella Braverman to Reform – because their departure removed a source of destabilisation on the right, and it gave her an opportunity to show decisiveness in pushing Jenrick before he jumped. She has also been aided by the increasing questions over Nigel Farage and Reform UK’s finances, with the party’s dominance in the polls slipping.
However, the arrival of Andy Burnham on the scene for Labour has changed things.
Giles Kenningham, the former Conservative director of communications who now leads the Trafalgar Strategy advisory firm, says Burnham “raises the bar … he’s a great communicator and comfortable in his own skin”.
“It’s a harder ask now. Starmer was not a great orator or someone who electrified voters … Burnham has had a great conference but all eyes are now on the budget, so her conference needs to be on the economy and welfare. John Healey’s speech didn’t say anything, and there is an opportunity for Badenoch to put pressure on them and drive the agenda.”
Badenoch’s star has also risen further with the membership of the party, the most recent ConservativeHome poll showing she has a 87% net satisfaction rating with the party faithful.
Despite this, a number of Conservative aides and insiders believe that Badenoch’s future is still not totally secure if the party does not start to creep above Reform UK on a sustained basis. One pointed to the Tory selection races – excluding some high-profile former MPs from standing – as a sign of perceived weakness that those around Badenoch are worried about her being challenged. “She is not alone among politicians in not liking tall poppies,” said one Conservative strategist.
“Ultimately, she is not immune from a challenge,” said another. “The shelf life of politicians is getting shorter and shorter. Leaders are much more exposed and the job is precarious. The thing most in her favour is that there are currently no other obvious contenders.”

QinetiQ sets out its role in Scottish warship sinking
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
14:00:01 BST
22:00:01 KST

The decommissioned American frigate sunk during Atlantic Thunder 2026 went down in deep water around 150 miles off the Western Isles, and the company that runs the range from which the exercise was controlled has now set out what it contributed, according to QinetiQ.
The firm operates MOD Hebrides under the Long-Term Partnering Agreement, the arrangement through which it runs most of the Ministry of Defence’s test and evaluation estate. Its staff safeguarded the exercise area from the Range Control and Range Head buildings on South Uist, managing the safety of a large volume of sea and airspace while live weapons were fired into it.
Will Blamey, Chief Executive of QinetiQ UK Defence, said: “Atlantic Thunder is a complex exercise, delivered in partnership with the US Sixth Fleet and Royal Navy to ensure they are warfighting ready.
“Our experts coordinate a range of activity to ensure the exercise is successful for our partners, from managing the safety of a vast area of sea and air space, to planning and overseeing the realistic live-fire scenarios.”
The company also put its own hardware into the air over the range. Banshee Whirlwind uncrewed aerial targets, flown by the Combined Aerial Targets Service, ran sorties over the exercise area to provide realistic threats, and were tracked by an RAF P-8 Poseidon maritime patrol aircraft.
The range at MOD Hebrides, on South Uist and the surrounding islands, is the only place in the United Kingdom where an exercise of this kind can be run, which is the practical reason an American hull was towed across the Atlantic to be sunk off Scotland rather than disposed of closer to home.

Unexploded ordnances left by Israel in Gaza pose a constant danger to Palestinians
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
13:00:00 UTC
22:00:00 KST

On November 23, 2025, Adham al-Firy, 28, from Gaza City’s al-Nasr Neighborhood, found a small object weighing about 1.5 kilograms while working to clear rubble from buildings destroyed during Israel’s genocide in Gaza.
After searching online, it appeared to be a scooter battery, so he decided to take it home and use it for electricity and internet access amid the city’s ongoing electricity blackouts.
At about 7:00 p.m., he brought the object into his family’s second-floor apartment in their four-story building. He placed it on a table in the living room, where nine family members were gathered. Shortly afterward, his 18-month-old son, Yahya, carried the object and walked towards his father, who watched in fear that the child might drop it on himself.
“My son took one step, a second step, and then suddenly the object exploded,” he recalled. My son was thrown into the air before my eyes, and then everything went dark.”
The battery-like trap that killed his son
Adham initially thought that the rubble dust was preventing his vision. The blast threw him into the street and buried him beneath the rubble. He could move his arms and right leg but not his left leg, realizing it had been severely injured.
“I cried out for help until my 30-year-old brother, Muhammad, with the help of some relatives, pulled me out after tying a rope around my sound leg. At that moment, I realized I had lost sight in one eye, as I could not see anything or anyone around me,” he said.
While Adham was being transported by an ambulance to al-Shifa Medical Complex, rescuers found an amputated hand near the area. Medical staff confirmed that none of the injured had a missing limb. It was in that moment that Adham realized the hand belonged to his missing son.
“My family hid the truth of my son’s death from me for three days until my condition improved after my left leg was amputated below the knee,” Adham said. “Then they told me part of the truth — that he had been killed.”
“Two weeks later, I learned the rest from neighbors,” he added. “My son had been torn into pieces scattered around the house, including his hand and rib cage.”
Adham said that everyone inside the apartment was either injured or suffered burns. He lost his left leg and sight in one eye, and doctors warned that his second eye is also at risk.
Lacking experts and proper equipment
Since October 7, 2023, over 200,000 tonnes of explosive ordnance were dropped on the Strip by Israel, with about 70,000 tonnes remaining unexploded, according to Mahmoud Basal, spokesperson for Gaza’s Civil Defence.
Last April, the United Nations Mine Action Service (UNMAS) reported that 1,000 people had been killed due to “indirect conflict from the remnants of war since the start of the attack,” which Basal attributed to the loss of explosive ordnance engineers and the lack of equipment needed to identify and safely dispose of unexploded ordnance (UXO) contaminated in debris.
About 90 percent of those engineers have been killed, he said, either at home or while carrying out what he describes as “humanitarian work”, leaving the city without experts capable of conducting full UXO operations from detection and surveying to safe disposal.
“There are now no experts who know where the explosives are and how to remove them,” he said. “The remaining engineers can handle a small missile or a grenade if people report a UXO remnant, but they can’t handle a high-explosive remnant such as the MK-4 missile because it requires heavy equipment unavailable in Gaza.”
He added that even if experts were available, Gaza lacks the equipment needed to clear UXOs, making the task difficult amid widespread destruction and a high population density in a limited area, with residents living in only about 36 percent of the territory, following the expansion of Israeli military control to around 64 percent of Gaza last March.
As a result, the exact locations of UXO remain largely unknown and are mainly identified only when civilians report suspected objects, according to Basal. They were likely to be concentrated in heavily affected areas, including Gaza City and northern Gaza, where repeated military operations caused massive destruction.
He warned that it poses risks to residents living in or near damaged homes and neighborhoods, as well as to civil defense crews clearing the rubble, with an estimated 50 to 60 million tonnes of rubble that are reportedly contaminated with UXOs.
Basal described these remnants as air-dropped bombs, missiles, and drone munitions, as well as abandoned grenades and explosive devices found in streets, homes, and neighborhoods.
Many of them could be disguised as everyday objects such as cans, juice containers, and children’s toys, which could explode if handled and kill more civilians.
The Humanity and Inclusion organization estimated that clearing UXO in Gaza could take between 20 and 30 years. Basal said that the Israeli authorities should, under international laws, provide detailed information on the UXO locations to support disposal efforts and reduce the risks faced by civilians.
The toy that was not a toy
Yayha and Nabeela al-Shurbasi were among the several victims of another unexploded ordnance incident after finding a suspected object near their home on Gaza’s al-Jalaa Street at about 10:00 a.m., October 24, 2025. They were both six years old.
Yahya, who survived the explosion, told his family that they had found what they thought was a toy in the street while returning from a nearby supermarket after buying some snacks. They took it and played with it near their house.
The object exploded while they were playing with it. Their parents, Muhammad and Nadia, were inside and initially thought a nearby building or passing vehicle had been hit.
When a passerby told them two children had been injured, the family rushed into the street and found Yahya and Nabeela lying on the ground, soaked in blood.
“They were in a terrible condition,” Tawfiq al-Shurbasi, the twins’ grandfather, recounted. “They were bleeding continuously, with torn flesh and missing limbs.”
The twins were taken by car to al-Shifa Hospital, where they underwent multiple surgeries over several weeks.
Yahya lost his right hand, left leg, and a finger on his left hand. His appendix had been removed after shrapnel penetrated his abdomen. His right leg was badly burned, leaving bones exposed. Doctors warned it might need amputation unless he urgently traveled for treatment abroad.
Nabeela had severe fractures to her left leg, lost three fingers, and suffered internal bowel damage, requiring part of her intestine to be surgically removed due to shrapnel injuries.
She died 20 days after the explosion while waiting to be evacuated for treatment abroad.
“Her twin brother Yayha was lucky to be evacuated for treatment in Italy with his parents via Karam Abu Salem on December 7, 2025,” al-Shurbasi said.
“He was hospitalized and underwent several surgeries to save his remaining leg from amputation,” his grandfather added. “He is now receiving rehabilitation before being fitted with prosthetic limbs.”
Losing his legs and his future
Most UXO-related cases arriving at Gaza’s hospitals are children with critical wounds requiring surgical treatment and prolonged stays in intensive care units amid the city’s collapsing health system, according to Dr. Issam Abu Ajwa, a consultant surgeon at the Gaza Baptist Hospital.
“Patients arrive drenched in blood, with limbs missing, severe burns, and at times, partial or complete loss of vision,” Abu Ajwa described.
He said that, despite working with limited resources, medical staff are trying to avoid amputation whenever possible, but it can sometimes become unavoidable, particularly when patients cannot be urgently evacuated to receive treatment outside Gaza.
Nineteen-year-old Daoud Eid lost both legs after a suspected UXO object exploded on November 28, 2025, as he and his cousin returned from Jabalia Refugee Camp.
They had gone to check on their family home after hearing on social media that Israeli forces had withdrawn from the camp. When they arrived, they found the camp completely devastated and their home reduced to rubble.
On their way back to the displacement tent where their families were sheltering in central Gaza, one of them accidentally came into contact with a suspected object that exploded, severely injuring them.
They lay bleeding for nearly three hours before people could safely reach them. During that time, Daoud’s cousin had died, succumbing to his injuries.
Daoud was taken to al-Shifa Hospital with precipitously low hemoglobin levels, and spent two months undergoing multiple surgeries before both of his legs were amputated.
“I missed my Tawjihi exams that year while undergoing several surgeries to save my legs,” Daoud said. “I missed the exams the following year, too, despite scoring above 90 percent during school years.”
Although referred for treatment abroad, Daoud remains unable to leave Gaza, where the destruction of rehabilitation and prosthetics facilities has left artificial limbs unavailable amid restrictions on the entry of medical supplies.
“I dreamed of finishing high school and studying engineering at university,” he said. “Today, my dream is simply to travel outside Gaza and receive artificial limbs.”

Five killed as Kyiv and Moscow trade strikes, Russia hits second bridge
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
12:55:54 UTC
21:55:54 KST

Russia’s ‘new doctrine’ targets civilian sites in Ukraine, Zelenskyy says
Ukrainian president says new intelligence shows Moscow aims to ‘pressure people to leave’ Kyiv and other cities.
At least five people have been killed in a series of long-range strikes carried out by Kyiv and Moscow, as Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy says Ukraine has new evidence that Russia is purposefully targeting civilian infrastructure.
Russia attacked a Liberian-flagged ship in Ukraine’s Odesa region on Saturday, killing one person and injuring three, the Ukrainian Sea Ports Authority said in a statement on Telegram. Another 12 crew members were safely evacuated from the ship. Russia separately hit a cargo ship in Ukraine’s Odesa port, the Interfax news agency reported.
A Russian attack on Kyiv’s Northern Bridge meanwhile injured two people. It is the second bridge Russia has attacked in the Ukrainian capital in the space of two days.
Russia has in effect blockaded Ukraine’s Black Sea ports – formerly a key global source of food exports – by attacking civilian vessels carrying grain and steel, dealing a heavy blow to the Ukrainian economy.
The latest attacks follow days of heavy strikes on Kyiv that have stoked fears across the capital.
Speaking to the Reuters news agency on Saturday, Zelenskyy said Ukrainian intelligence services had reviewed documents revealing Russia’s “new doctrine” of striking roads, schools, hospitals and other civilian sites.
Moscow aims to “pressure people to leave the [Ukrainian] capital, leave different cities”, Zelenskyy said. “This is the goal of the operation.”
Ukraine plans to respond to the change in tactics by Moscow, but not by targeting civilian infrastructure indiscriminately, he added.
“With their attacks on our energy, we have to respond on their energy,” Zelenskyy said in English. “But we will not respond, of course, just like them, on any civilian objects.”
On Saturday, Russia reported casualties from Ukrainian attacks.
Two people were reportedly killed in a Ukrainian strike on the Russia-occupied Luhansk region of Ukraine, according to the Moscow-installed governor.
In the occupied Zaporizhia region, Russian-installed authorities said one person was killed and 10 others injured in a Ukrainian drone attack.
Russian media also reported that one person was killed in a Ukrainian drone attack on Russia’s Belgorod region, which sits just across the border from Ukraine.
Russia warns diplomats, foreigners
Also on Saturday, Russia’s Foreign Ministry issued another warning to diplomats and foreigners in Ukraine’s capital, urging them to leave the city or risk being harmed.
Many foreign embassies are still operating in Kyiv.
Russia’s all-out war on Ukraine is in its fifth year and shows little sign of slowing down.
Russian battlefield gains have slowed to a near-record low. Zelenskyy said a Ukrainian counteroffensive known as “Vivaldi” had recaptured about 140 square kilometres (54 square miles) of Ukraine’s eastern Donbas region, which Russia has claimed it must control as a precondition for any peace deal.
But the Ukrainian leader warned the United States – which has proposed new trilateral talks in the coming weeks in the United Arab Emirates – not to believe in “illusions” that Russia would end the peace deal if it gained control of Donbas.
An exact date and location for any talks has not materialised, Zelenskyy said.
Russia has increased its attacks on civilian infrastructure in recent months, including with the growing use of jet-powered long-range strike drones, which move faster and are harder to shoot down.
Zelenskyy said Ukraine has been forced to rely on its fighter aircraft to down about 60 percent of the Russian jet-powered drones, but supplies of ammunition for the planes are running low.
Kyiv is anticipating the first shipment of small, cheaper air defence missiles in the second half of October.
Ukraine has also engaged in significant long-range strikes, including targeting Russian oil infrastructure and military-industrial facilities deep inside Russian territory.
Recent Ukrainian shelling has damaged external power supply equipment at the Zaporizhzhia nuclear power plant in southeastern Ukraine, the plant said on Saturday.
Russia seized the site in the early weeks of the war in 2022.

US and Russia are negotiating multibillion-dollar deal on Lukoil assets, says NYT
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
15:54:00 EEST
21:54:00 KST

US and Russia are negotiating multibillion-dollar deal on Lukoil assets, says NYT
The US presidential administration's negotiations with Russia to end the war in Ukraine have expanded to include a multibillion-dollar oil deal that could benefit Middle Eastern business executives linked to President Donald Trump's two main negotiators, Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner.
Source: The New York Times, as reported by European Pravda
Details: The deal, which requires approval from the US government and the Kremlin, covers Lukoil's vast global portfolio of oil fields, refineries and petrol stations. Lukoil is one of Russia's largest energy companies.
The leading group seeking to finalise this agreement includes US investor Todd Boehly, who has donated US$2 million to President Trump's political causes; two Middle Eastern groups that have done business with Kushner or Witkoff's family; and a branch of the US government itself.
The negotiations, which have been ongoing for several months, were described to the newspaper by eight people familiar with the matter.
The NYT notes that there is no evidence that Kushner or Witkoff stand to profit personally from the agreement. Still, the proposed deal highlights the close links between personal business interests and geopolitics – even under an administration that routinely dismisses concerns about potential conflicts of interest.
Russian leader Vladimir Putin brought up this deal during a meeting with Witkoff and Kushner at the Kremlin on 5 September, according to three people familiar with the meeting. One of the sources said Putin proposed the agreement to show Russians they can do business with the US.
The Americans replied that they would work on the deal, the source noted. They viewed it as an opportunity to build good relations with the Kremlin while bringing down global energy prices.
This deal is also highly lucrative for the buyers: US approval for the sale would lift American sanctions from the assets, instantly boosting their value.
In Moscow, the decision on the deal is widely considered to be up to Putin, even though Lukoil is officially a private company. Ultimately, the massive transaction, which encompasses assets as diverse as oil fields in Cameroon, refineries in Europe and petrol stations in New Jersey, boils down to decisions made by Putin and Trump.
Trump has been promoting the idea of sealing business deals with Russia since early last year, describing the country as a "tremendous opportunity". This deal once again draws attention to Trump's cryptocurrency company, World Liberty Financial, co-founded by Witkoff. One of the investors in the Lukoil asset deal is also a co-owner of World Liberty.
Background:
- In October 2025, Trump imposed new sanctions on Russia for the first time in his second term, targeting two major oil companies, Rosneft and Lukoil, among others.
- Meanwhile, the US has repeatedly extended the deadline for the sale of assets belonging to sanctioned Russian energy company Lukoil. The latest extension, announced in August, gave potential buyers until 19 September to complete the sale, subject to additional approval from the US Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC).

Two Iranian men identified Manchester synagogue as site for alleged bomb plot, court hears
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
12:53:47 UTC
21:53:47 KST

Two Iranian men identified a Manchester synagogue previously subjected to a fatal terrorist attack as a target for an alleged homemade bomb plot, a court has heard.
Rahman Salehi, 34, from Salford, and Salam Ahmadyan, 36, from Liverpool were charged with preparing to commit an act of terrorism or assisting another to commit an act of terrorism on Friday.
The two men appeared in Westminster magistrates court on Saturday morning. They wore grey overalls in the dock while and, through a Kurdish interpreter, spoke to confirm their names, dates of birth and addresses.
The pair were alleged to have carried out “hostile reconnaissance” within Manchester’s Jewish community and identified a number of potential targets including the city’s Jewish museum and Heaton Park synagogue.
The court heard the pair came to the UK illegally via small boats. Salehi arrived in 2020 before being granted leave to remain in 2023. Ahmadyan came in 2023 and has an outstanding asylum claim.
They were in contact with a third party, believed to be operating from within Iran, who “directed and coordinated” the planned attack and sent them “instructions on how to prepare an explosive device”.
Prosecutor Mark Luckett told the court: “Both defendants are accused of preparing acts of terrorism targeting the Jewish community in Manchester through the use of a homemade explosive device.
“The defendants were observed carrying out, what the prosecution say, is a hostile reconnaissance within Manchester’s Jewish community, identifying attempted targets such as the Jewish Museum and Heaton Park synagogue.”
“They were in contact with a third party who is alleged to have directed and coordinated the planned attack and provided instructions on how to assemble a homemade explosive device,” he said.
“It is assessed this individual is also an Iranian national and most likely operating from within Iran.”
The two men were arrested on 20 September 2026 in broad daylight, just before the festival of Yom Kippur, widely regarded as the holiest day in the Jewish calendar.
Before coming to the UK, Salehi lived in Germany for five years. The men are accused of acquiring a document entitled Steps for Making [a] Powder Chlorine and Car Brake Oil/Fluid Bomb and video material on how to manufacture or assemble an improvised explosive device. They are also accused of acquiring liquids, components and equipment required in order to manufacture or assemble an improvised explosive device.
They are also accused of using the internet to identify and research potential targets, acquiring images, plans and maps of potential targets and conducting reconnaissance of potential locations for attack.
District judge Nina Tempia remanded the two men into custody to appear at the Old Bailey on 23 October

Powerful simulations reveal how the first stars changed the universe
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
12:50:57 UTC
21:50:57 KST

Powerful simulations reveal how the first stars changed the universe
Powerful new simulations are recreating how the first stars lit up the Universe and forged the elements that eventually made planets and life possible.
- Date:
- October 3, 2026
- Source:
- University of Bath
- Summary:
- Ultra-detailed simulations are showing how the first stars lit up the dark Universe and seeded space with elements such as carbon, oxygen, and iron. The MEGATRON project could bridge JWST observations of the earliest galaxies with chemical clues preserved in ancient stars today.
- Share:
Researchers are using extraordinarily detailed computer simulations to reconstruct one of the most transformative periods in cosmic history: the era when the first stars and galaxies began to emerge.
The work is part of the MEGATRON project, led by researchers at the University of Bath in the UK with collaborators at the University of Chicago in the US and the Institut d'Astrophysique de Paris in France. The project is designed to explore how the earliest stars and galaxies illuminated a previously dark Universe and began producing and dispersing the chemical elements that later became essential ingredients of planets, life, and the world around us.
Four studies from MEGATRON, published in the Open Journal of Astrophysics, combine advanced cosmological simulations with detailed models of radiation, chemistry and galaxy formation. Together, they represent the collaboration's first major collection of published results, with additional studies expected in the future.
Connecting JWST With Ancient Stellar Clues
The findings show that researchers need to accurately model the complicated interactions among starlight, gas and newly created elements if they want to connect two different records of the early Universe.
One comes from observations of young galaxies made by the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST). The other comes from chemical signatures preserved in some of the oldest stars in and around the Milky Way - the galaxy that contains our Solar System.
JWST allows astronomers to directly observe galaxies from the Universe's infancy. Ancient stars provide a different kind of evidence, acting as a fossil record of events that occurred billions of years ago. By examining the chemical fingerprints inside these old stars, scientists can infer what the first stars were like and how they began enriching the cosmos with its earliest chemical elements.
The MEGATRON simulations follow a young galaxy as it evolves toward becoming a system roughly comparable in mass to the Milky Way. The models simultaneously track how gas moves, how starlight travels through space and how the concentrations of different chemical elements change over time.
This allows researchers to investigate how generations of stars alter the gas inside and around galaxies across billions of years of evolution.
Simpler Models May Miss Important Physics
The results indicate that less detailed models may underestimate how strongly stellar radiation and complex chemical processes affect the gas surrounding galaxies.
By simulating these effects at exceptionally high resolution, the researchers were able to capture structures in the gas that simpler approaches can miss. That added detail could help astronomers make more accurate predictions for observations being collected now and for those planned in the future.
A Direct Glimpse of the Infant Cosmos
Dr. Martin Rey from the Department of Physics at the University of Bath and a lead contributor to the MEGATRON collaboration said: "The James Webb Space Telescope gives us a direct glimpse of the infant cosmos, while stellar archaeology allows us to study the relics of those earliest times in our own Galactic neighborhood. MEGATRON provides a physical bridge between the two."
The simulations begin with pristine gas containing no heavy elements, reproducing conditions that existed shortly after the Big Bang.
From there, the models follow the formation of the first stars, the radiation those stars release, the supernova explosions that occur at the end of their lives and the spread of newly created elements into later generations of stars and galaxies.
Reconstructing this process could help answer one of astronomy's most fundamental questions: where did the elements that make up the modern Universe come from?
Dr. Rey said: "The elements that make our world and life possible - carbon, oxygen, iron and many others - were forged by stars. To understand where those elements came from, we need to understand how the first stars formed and enriched their surroundings. MEGATRON allows us to test these ideas directly by comparing detailed simulations with observations from JWST and the chemical fingerprints preserved in ancient stars."
Tracing the Origins of Cosmic Elements
As the project moves forward, the researchers plan to use MEGATRON to make even stronger connections between theoretical models and rapidly improving astronomical observations.
JWST continues to reveal new information about some of the earliest known galaxies, while large stellar surveys are producing increasingly detailed measurements of ancient stars in and around the Milky Way. Combining those two sources of evidence could give scientists a much clearer picture of the first generations of stars.
Dr. Rey and his colleagues at Bath are already working on the next generation of MEGATRON simulations.
The project has received 40 million processor hours on the UK's national supercomputers. That amount of computing power is equivalent to running five million laptops at the same time for an entire year.
The additional resources will allow the team to build simulations with even greater resolution and more complete physical models. Researchers will then be able to make increasingly direct comparisons between their simulations, JWST observations and the chemical fossil record preserved in ancient stars.
"MEGATRON provides a common physical framework for interpreting two of astronomy's most exciting new datasets: JWST's view of the earliest galaxies and the stellar fossil record," said Dr. Rey. "Together, these complementary observations allow us to test competing models of the first stars in ways that weren't previously possible."
The MEGATRON project began in 2023 and is scheduled to continue through 2030.
Story Source:
Materials provided by University of Bath. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- Martin Rey, Harley Katz, Corentin Cadiou, Mahsa Sanati, Oscar Agertz, Jeremy Blaizot, Alex J. Cameron, Nicholas Choustikov, Julien Devriendt, Uliana Hauk, Alexander P. Ji, Gareth C. Jones, Taysun Kimm, Isaac Laseter, Sergio Martin-Alvarez, Kosei Matsumoto, Autumn Pearce, Yves Revaz, Francisco Rodriguez Montero, Joki Rosdahl, Aayush Saxena, Adrianne Slyz, Richard Stiskalek, Anatole Storck, Oscar Veenema, Wonjae Yee. MEGATRON: how the first stars can create an iron metallicity plateau in the smallest dwarf galaxies. The Open Journal of Astrophysics, 2026; 9 DOI: 10.33232/001c.169605

Commander of the Unmanned Systems Forces of the Armed Forces of Ukraine Robert (Madiar) Brovdi has urged Ukrainians not to fall for illusions regarding a swift ceasefire and a long-awaited peace, emphasizing that Russia is continuing to escalate the war.
"Pull yourselves together, dear Ukrainians, it's time to turn your brains on," Brovdi wrote on Facebook on Saturday.
According to him, a "weary and frightened people" are currently being targeted with an "illusion about a quick ceasefire and dreamed-of peace" precisely at a time when Russia is raising the level of escalation and threatening other countries.
"Opinions are being shaped virtually in unison with the Valdai chatter," he stated.
Brovdi emphasized that the Russian leadership does not seek peace, but is currently exploiting opportunities to strike Ukraine's rear. "Putin is definitely not about peace. He wants blood, up to completely destroying us. And today he is using the 'jet-shahed' window of opportunity, dismantling the rear specifically, because on the front, to put it mildly, he has had few successes throughout all of 2026," the USF commander wrote.
He stressed that Ukraine must assess the situation rationally rather than relying on expectations of a quick end to the war.
At the same time, he stated that the Defense Forces are working to close the current "window of opportunity" for Russian troops.
"The enemy's current window of opportunity will be closed by the Defense Forces through countermeasures, including re-armament, which takes time. How much? Depends on a number of factors—I won't say more for now," he wrote.
According to Brovdi, the situation at the front remains difficult, but Russian troops are suffering losses. "The front is hard, the worm is pushing and will keep pushing, but it is being destroyed on an escalating scale," the commander stated.
He also urged Ukrainians in the rear to be prepared for a long war and to rely on their own strength.
"The army has hardened, so it's time for the rear to grow up too. Do not believe in illusions and miracles—let's rely on our own strength and on each other; that is the only way we will preserve our statehood and our Motherland. And the shed under a white flag offered by jackals will be burned down on the very first dark night. Adults will understand me," Brovdi emphasized.
Ahead of this, several Ukrainian politicians publicly called for ways to end the war, intensify negotiations with Russia, and find possible compromises.
In particular, MP Oleksiy Honcharenko stated that Ukraine should begin negotiating with Russia step-by-step, addressing individual issues. Kharkiv Mayor Ihor Terekhov stated that Ukraine must simultaneously strengthen its defense capabilities and seek a path to peace that will protect the country from a new attack. Head of the Parliamentary Committee on Finance, Tax, and Customs Policy Danylo Hetmantsev stated that the terms of peace should be determined by the results of combat operations and negotiations, and the final decision on them, in his view, should be made by the people in a referendum.

US delivers latest F-16s to Taiwan
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
12:46:25 UTC
21:46:25 KST

US delivers latest F-16s to Taiwan
The US has delivered Taiwan’s first two newly built F-16 fighter jets, part of an $8 billion order that has repeatedly drawn condemnation from Beijing.
The two aircraft, the modern F-16V Block 70 variant, arrived in Taiwan on Friday. They are the first of 66 new fighters approved for sale by Washington in 2019.
Beijing has long opposed US arms sales to Taiwan, which it considers part of China. The delivery came a week after Chinese President Xi Jinping visited Washington and urged US President Donald Trump to oppose “Taiwan independence” and “handle the Taiwan question with caution.”
The new jets will join Taiwan’s existing fleet of older F-16 variants, which Taipei has operated since the late 1990s. The first aircraft from the 66-plane order were initially expected in 2023, but deliveries were delayed by software development and production issues.
China’s Defense Ministry warned Washington in August to “stop arming Taiwan in whatever form” when asked about the expected delivery.
The US maintains a one-China policy but remains Taiwan’s primary foreign arms supplier.
Under the Trump administration, Washington has approved its largest military packages for Taiwan to date, greenlighting an unprecedented $11 billion in arms last December. Trump has also stalled an even larger $14 billion military package for months, openly describing the sale as a “very good negotiating chip” in talks with Beijing.
Taiwan has remained de facto self-governing since 1949, when nationalist Kuomintang forces retreated to the island after losing to the communists in the Chinese Civil War.
Beijing regards Taiwan as part of its territory under the One China principle, a position recognized in varying formulations by most UN member states, including Russia. China has said it prefers peaceful reunification but has not ruled out the use of force.

Lukashenko Calls Himself, Putin ‘Co-Aggressors’ in Ukraine

Belarusian leader Alexander Lukashenko declared on Friday, Oct. 2, that Belarus will remain unconditionally aligned with Russia in its war against Ukraine, joking that he and Russian President Vladimir Putin routinely debate which of them qualifies as the greater “co-aggressor.”
Speaking in Minsk during a meeting with heads of delegations attending a session of the Eurasian Intergovernmental Council, Lukashenko insisted that while he maintains distinct perspectives on specific dimensions of the conflict, Minsk will execute any decisions adopted by the Kremlin.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“In the end, we are ‘co-aggressors’ with him. We have one question, which we sometimes discuss jokingly: who is more of an ‘aggressor’ – me or him?” Lukashenko stated, according to Belarusian state news agency BelTA.
Lukashenko reiterated that he has directly articulated his analytical assessments of the war to Putin, while assuring the Russian leadership of absolute loyalty regardless of operational developments on the front line.
“I have my own understanding of individual aspects of the conflict in Ukraine, but we will always be committed to our common course,” Lukashenko said. “If you, the leadership of Russia, make a decision, we will always be with you, despite our particular understanding of what is happening there. We have never been traitors.”
Russia Hits Major Pharma Warehouse Near Kyiv
The Belarusian leader repeated his long-standing formulation that Minsk would “never allow anyone to shoot Russia in the back,” defining the geopolitical union between Belarus and Russia as an indivisible territory extending “from Brest to Vladivostok.”
He suggested that other member states of the Eurasian Economic Union (EAEU) could choose whether to integrate deeper into that perimeter, emphasizing that Minsk and Moscow have permanently committed to a unified economic, military, and political space.
Mobilization drills
Lukashenko’s public reaffirmation of solidarity with Moscow follows statements delivered in mid-September in which he balanced threats of domestic military inspections with assertions that Belarus would not initiate an armed assault against neighboring nations.
During a visit to the Obuz-Lesnovsky combined-arms training ground near Baranavichy on Sept. 11, Lukashenko stated that the Belarusian armed forces required comprehensive readiness checks that could extend “up to and including mobilization.”
He instructed Defense Minister Viktor Khrenin to verify that national command structures, civil administration bodies, and territorial defense reserves could deploy rapidly under wartime conditions.
However, during that same military inspection, Lukashenko claimed that launching an offensive against adjacent countries would be suicidal for Belarus.
Describing neighboring states as heavily armed powers positioned along the national frontier, Lukashenko asserted that initiating hostilities would be “tantamount to death,” insisting that Belarusian armed units would fight exclusively to defend domestic territory.
Western military planners and regional analysts view Lukashenko’s dual rhetoric as a calibrated strategy to deter foreign pressure while preserving domestic political leverage, allowing Minsk to display verbal and logistical solidarity with the Kremlin without deploying organic Belarusian ground formations into direct combat in Ukraine.
Enabling Moscow’s invasion
Despite Lukashenko’s recurring disclaimers regarding direct combat participation, Belarus remains Moscow’s primary operational facilitator and regional staging ground in the war against Ukraine.
In February 2022, Minsk permitted Russian forces to utilize Belarusian sovereign territory, rail corridors, and military airfields to launch the initial northern assault directed toward Kyiv.
Russian formations have continuously operated radar stations, training installations, and electronic warfare facilities across Belarus, frequently staging missile strikes and drone overflights from Belarusian airspace.
Belarus shares heavily fortified borders with Ukraine to the south and NATO member states Poland, Lithuania, and Latvia to the west and north.
Minsk’s deepening military integration with Moscow – including the stationing of Russian tactical nuclear weapons on Belarusian soil and recurring joint bilateral maneuvers – has prompted frontline NATO governments to reinforce border fortifications and scale rapid-reaction forces along the alliance’s northeastern flank.

Germany marks 36 years of unity: Why was the country divided and how united is it today?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
12:44:17 UTC
21:44:17 KST

Only 17% of former GDR citizens kept their jobs after the change of system, a legacy still visible in regions short of people and corporate headquarters.
Germany is marking the 36th anniversary of reunification. On 3 October 1990 the former GDR acceded to the Federal Republic, ending a division that had lasted 41 years and making Berlin once again the capital of a united Germany.
In Brandenburg, Steeven Bretz, the leader of the Christian Democratic Union in the state parliament, paid tribute to former Chancellor Helmut Kohl at the Glienicke Bridge in Potsdam, where the border once ran. "We owe him a great deal, above all the fact that unity succeeded," Bretz said, according to his Instagram account. "The fact that we are able to celebrate unity is, I believe, a gift of history."
The bridge, which links Berlin and Potsdam, was blown up in the final year of the Second World War, rebuilt and reopened in 1949 as the "Bridge of Unity". It became famous during the Cold War as a site of international exchanges of agents. Brandenburg's state government, led by Minister-President Dietmar Woidke (SPD), is taking part in the main national celebrations in Bremen.
"A dream will come true"
Kohl, whose term of office ran from 1982 to 1998, is regarded as the "chancellor of unity". In a televised address on 2 October 1990, he said: "In a few hours a dream will come true. After more than forty bitter years of division, Germany, our fatherland, is reunited."
He urged Germans to remember those who had suffered under division. "Families were cruelly torn apart. Political prisoners were locked away in jails. People died at the Wall," he said. He also thanked the East Germans who had fought for their freedom, the former victorious powers and the freedom movements in Central, Eastern and Southern Europe.
German reunification is celebrating its 36th anniversary. On 3 October 1990 the former GDR acceded to the Federal Republic. The date also marks the end of the division of Germany, which had lasted a full 41 years.
How united are Germans today?
The 2026 report by the Federal Government Commissioner for Eastern Germany finds that East and West Germans now assess their living conditions similarly in many respects. Nevertheless, East Germans remain under-represented in senior positions in the top federal authorities, although their share has risen from 13.9 to 16.3 percent since 2022.
The difference is particularly striking in inheritances and gifts: in 2025, 95 percent of the total value of taxable transfers of assets accrued to West Germany, according to the Federal Statistical Office.
One reason lies in the upheaval that followed reunification. Only 17 percent of former GDR citizens kept their job after the change of system, according to a study by the Rockwool Foundation Berlin made available in advance to Reuters. Many companies in the former GDR lost their markets or were closed in the 1990s, while young and well-qualified people moved west. As a result, some regions still lack both population and corporate headquarters.
The federal government is trying to reduce these disparities further, focusing support on structurally weak regions.
Why Germany was divided
After the Second World War, the four victorious powers, the USA, the Soviet Union, Great Britain and France, divided defeated Germany into four occupation zones. Against the backdrop of the emerging Cold War, a conflict developed over the country's political and economic future, and in 1949 the Federal Republic of Germany (FRG) was established in the West and the GDR in the East.
Both were granted sovereignty in 1955, West Germany by the Allies and East Germany by the Soviet Union, but the non-German powers retained special rights. Those rights ended with reunification, the foreign-policy conditions for which were laid down in the Two Plus Four Treaty. In it, the FRG and the GDR recognised the Oder-Neisse line as the border with Poland.
Why 3 October, not 9 November
The Wall fell on 9 November 1989, and that date was initially discussed as a possible national holiday. However, in view of the Reich Pogrom Night of 1938, the decision went against it. The choice fell instead on 3 October 1990, the day the Unification Treaty was implemented.
The treaty, signed on 31 August 1990 by FRG Interior Minister Wolfgang Schäuble and GDR State Secretary Günther Krause, both of the CDU, designated 3 October as the "Day of German Unity" and a public holiday. It replaced 17 June, which commemorated the 1953 popular uprising in the GDR and remains a national day of remembrance.

Greece hands Bulgaria Tsar Samuel’s remains in exchange for 48 relics
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
12:43:37 UTC
21:43:37 KST

ATHENS, October 3. /TASS/. Greece handed Bulgaria the remains of Bulgarian Tsar Samuel (997-1014) in exchange for the return of 48 Greek historical relics taken from Greek monasteries to Sofia during World War I; ERT News aired the exchange ceremony, held at the Museum of Byzantine Culture in Thessaloniki.
Greek Culture Minister Lina Mendoni and Bulgarian Culture Minister Evtim Miloshev signed the relic exchange protocol in the presence of the two countries’ prime ministers, Kyriakos Mitsotakis and Rumen Radev. Mitsotakis said the exchange resulted from almost half a century of negotiations between the two countries.
"The return to Greece and Bulgaria of relics that are important to society transforms difficult moments of the past into ‘bridges’ to a shared future. At the same time, it underscores the strength that two neighboring peoples gain when they courageously choose the path of mutual respect and trust," the prime minister said.
According to Mitsotakis, "48 objects of invaluable cultural, spiritual and emotional significance are returning home." "These are holy icons and crosses, vestments and reliquaries, and even an episcopal throne," he said.
"These relics were removed in 1917, at the height of World War I, from the Holy Metropolis of Serres and Nigrita, as well as from the Timios Prodromos Monastery and the Panagia Eikosifoinissa Monastery. They will initially be housed here, in this magnificent Byzantine Museum, and will then return to where they belong - their historic homes," Mitsotakis emphasized.
He noted that "at the same time, Athens is fulfilling its own duty by handing over to Sofia the remains of Tsar Samuel and other remains from the four sarcophagi discovered in 1964 by Professor Moutsopoulos in the Basilica of St. Achillios."
The Basilica of St. Achillios is an important Byzantine monument on the island of Agios Achillios in Lake Prespa.
The Bulgarian prime minister, in turn, thanked Greece for returning Tsar Samuel’s remains.
Greece and Bulgaria previously agreed to continue negotiations on identifying other historical objects of mutual interest and including them in a subsequent agreement between the two countries. The relics received from Bulgaria will remain on display at the Museum of Byzantine Culture until November 5, 2026.
They will then be transferred, depending on their provenance, to the Holy Monastery of Panagia Eikosifoinissa, the Holy Monastery of Timios Prodromos and the Holy Metropolis of Serres and Nigrita.

The shutdown follows a wave of Russian strikes on the bridge, including an initial strike on Thursday that hit near one of its supports while a metro train was crossing.

Ukraine tests EW system to protect heavy bomber drones and ground robots
The Ukrainian defence company Aura-Ukraine has begun final tests of the Aura 3K mini, an electronic warfare (EW) system designed to protect heavy bomber drones.
Source: Dignitas Fund charity speaking to Ukrainska Pravda
Details: The device provides 360-degree protection through two broadband jammers operating in the 2.1-2.8 GHz range. They can jam Russian FPV drones without interfering with the platform's own Starlink communication link.
The device weighs about 2.4 kg, according to Dignitas Fund, which is working on the EW system alongside the manufacturer. If the system's final tests are successful, it is slated for mass production.
Quote from the press service: "Testing of the system's radiation pattern will begin at the front in the coming days."
Photo: Characteristics and appearance of the Aura 3K Mini EW system. Dignitas
Details: Dignitas Fund said the EW system's operations are planned to be automated. Specifically, the system is to be upgraded with an automatic activation function that will switch it on only when a threat is detected, preventing continuous emissions from giving away the drone's position. There are also plans to adapt the Aura 3K mini for Vampire-type bomber drones.
Background: Ukrainska Pravda previously reported that the Ukrainian company Rebel Group had developed a stationary electronic warfare and reconnaissance system called Brama. It is planned to be officially approved for use by the Ukrainian defence forces.

Leucine does more than build muscle. It powers up your cells
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
12:33:15 UTC
21:33:15 KST

Leucine does more than build muscle. It powers up your cells
- Date:
- October 3, 2026
- Source:
- University of Cologne
- Summary:
- The essential amino acid leucine can boost cellular energy production by protecting key proteins on mitochondria from being destroyed. The discovery reveals a new connection between nutrition and metabolism that could eventually lead to new approaches for metabolic disorders and cancer.
- Share:
Mitochondria are often described as the powerhouses of the cell because they produce much of the energy our bodies need to grow, move, repair tissues, and carry out everyday functions. But they do not operate at a constant pace. Instead, mitochondria continuously adjust their activity depending on how much energy a cell needs and which nutrients are available.
Scientists have long known that nutrition can influence this process. What has been less clear is exactly how individual nutrients send signals that change mitochondrial activity.
Now, researchers led by Professor Dr. Thorsten Hoppe of the Institute for Genetics and the CECAD Cluster of Excellence on Aging Research at the University of Cologne have identified a new mechanism involving the amino acid leucine. Their findings show that leucine can help stabilize important proteins in mitochondria, allowing the organelles to produce energy more efficiently.
The study, published in Nature Cell Biology, is titled "Leucine inhibits degradation of outer mitochondrial membrane proteins to adapt mitochondrial respiration."
How Leucine Helps Mitochondria Produce Energy
Leucine is an essential amino acid, which means the human body cannot make enough of it on its own and must obtain it through food. Amino acids are the building blocks used to make proteins, and leucine is especially abundant in protein rich foods such as dairy products, meat, beans, and lentils.
The researchers found that leucine does more than contribute to protein production. It also helps prevent the breakdown of certain proteins located on the outer surface of mitochondria.
Those proteins play an important role in metabolism because they help move other molecules into mitochondria, where they can be used as part of the cell's energy producing machinery. When leucine helps preserve these proteins, mitochondria can operate more effectively and increase the amount of energy the cell produces.
"We were thrilled to discover that a cell's nutrient status, especially its leucine levels, directly impacts energy production," said Dr. Qiaochu Li, first author of the study. "This mechanism enables cells to swiftly adapt to increased energy demands during periods of nutrient abundance."
A Cellular Quality Control Protein Plays a Key Role
The team traced this effect to a protein called SEL1L, which is involved in cellular quality control.
Cells constantly inspect their proteins because damaged or incorrectly folded proteins can interfere with normal function. SEL1L helps identify proteins that should be removed and directs them toward degradation.
According to the researchers, leucine appears to reduce the activity of SEL1L. That means fewer mitochondrial proteins are broken down, allowing more of them to remain in place and support mitochondrial function.
"Modulating leucine and SEL1L levels could be a strategy to boost energy production," Li added. "However, it is important to proceed with caution. SEL1L also plays a crucial role in preventing the accumulation of damaged proteins, which is essential for long-term cellular health."
That warning is important because increasing energy production is not automatically beneficial in every situation. The same cellular systems that preserve useful proteins also help eliminate defective ones, so changing that balance could have unintended consequences.
Effects on Fertility and Cancer Cells
To explore the broader effects of leucine metabolism, the researchers also studied Caenorhabditis elegans, a tiny roundworm commonly used in biology because many of its cellular processes are similar to those found in more complex organisms.
In the worms, problems with leucine breakdown disrupted mitochondrial function and were linked to fertility problems.
The scientists also examined human lung cancer cells. They found that some mutations affecting leucine metabolism could help cancer cells survive. That observation could be important for future cancer research because treatments that alter leucine related pathways may affect both healthy cells and tumor cells in different ways.
Diet Does More Than Supply Fuel
The findings add to growing evidence that nutrients do more than simply provide raw material for the body. They can also act as signals that influence how cells function.
In this case, leucine appears to help cells adjust energy production according to nutrient availability by protecting key mitochondrial proteins from degradation.
By revealing this previously unknown link between leucine, protein quality control, and mitochondrial metabolism, the researchers have identified potential new targets for diseases in which cellular energy production is disrupted, including cancer and metabolic disorders.
The work was supported by Germany's Excellence Strategy in the framework of CECAD as well as by various Collaborative Research Centres funded by the German Research Foundation (DFG). Additional support was provided by the European Research Council through the ERC Advanced Grant "Cellular Strategies of Protein Quality Control-Degradation" (CellularPQCD), and the Alexander von Humboldt Foundation.
Story Source:
Materials provided by University of Cologne. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- Qiaochu Li, Konstantin Weiss, Fuateima Niwa, Jan Riemer, Thorsten Hoppe. Leucine inhibits degradation of outer mitochondrial membrane proteins to adapt mitochondrial respiration. Nature Cell Biology, 2025; 27 (11): 1889 DOI: 10.1038/s41556-025-01799-3

Hundreds protest against migration in Vilnius, more than 100 hold counter-protest
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
12:33:00 UTC
21:33:00 KST

Protests over Lithuania's migration policy are taking place in Vilnius on Saturday, with more than 300 people demonstrating against what they call mass immigration. Meanwhile, more than 100 people have gathered for a counter-protest to express their opposition to the demonstration.
More than several dozen police vehicles are deployed around Vincas Kudirka Square, near the government building and around the protesters. The demonstrators have been separated by barriers.
More than 240 officers are working at the scene to maintain public order, according to Arūnas Paulauskas, the police chief.
"We are preparing for any scenario and are ready for it, but we genuinely believe that both rallies, although they are taking place close to one another, will pass with mutual respect and without any major incidents," the commissioner told reporters on Saturday.
Concern over scale of immigration
The protest in Vincas Kudirka Square is being organised by the far-right National Alliance party.
Protesters against migration are holding placards reading "Anti-Lithuanian Inga Ruginienė, we need neither Islamists nor Filipinos", "We demand an end to the replacement of Lithuanians with foreigners", and others.
"Lithuania is a Catholic country, a Christian country, we are very different, [...] we are a Catholic country and it would be very difficult for us to imagine pressure from another religion on our faith," said Laima, a 70-year-old Vilnius resident.
Jeronimas Rimkūnas, 29, who travelled from Jonava carrying a Lithuanian flag, told BNS that he saw a threat in the scale of immigration.
"There is a certain sense of anxiety because I have been following the situation in other European Union countries for quite some time. I have been following the news for about 10 years and, seeing that this wave of migration is gradually reaching our country too, I feel a certain sense of concern," he said.
Those attending the protest are demanding stricter deportation of foreigners who commit crimes, the closure of migrant employment centres in foreign countries, known as external service centres, and a reduction in the overall quota for migrants allowed to enter the country.
Anti-racism protest
In response to the National Alliance's initiative, civic activists decided to hold a demonstration against racism at the same time and in the same location, near Vincas Kudirka Square in Vilnius.
The demonstration aims to publicly express opposition to the persecution of migrants and other minorities, as well as racist rhetoric.
According to the organisers, migrants are increasingly portrayed in the public sphere as a threat to society – being associated with crime, taking jobs or wages, and posing a threat to national security.
Gabija, a 26-year-old Vilnius resident who came to oppose the National Alliance's protest, told BNS that the demonstration against migration policy was racist and Islamophobic.
"In my value system, belittling people because of their origin, nationality or religious beliefs is simply unacceptable. These are beliefs rooted in violence, which themselves create insecurity when you regard a particular group as lesser people," she said.
"The data are being interpreted incorrectly to suggest that they [immigrants] have supposedly increased crime," Gabija said, adding that there is no mass immigration in Lithuania.
Laurynas Tomelaitis, 24, one of the organisers of the counter-protest, said he opposed "racism and fascism" and did not see migration as a threat to Lithuania.
"Muslims currently make up 1.5% of Lithuania's population. [...] The Muslim community has always been present in Lithuania, so the fact that the National Alliance is against Muslims is, in part, also opposition to Lithuania," he told BNS.
Third demonstration in Lukiškės Square
Meanwhile, Sienos grupė, a public organisation that advocates for migrants' rights, invited people to Lukiškės Square to discuss migration.
"Migration is not an ideology or a political programme – it is a social phenomenon that has existed throughout history. People have moved because of war, persecution, work, love, family, studies or simply in search of a better life. Therefore, being generally 'for' or 'against' migration is somewhat like being for or against rain," Sienos grupė director Emilija Švobaitė told BNS.
According to the Migration Department, 226,999 foreign nationals held residence permits in Lithuania in September. The largest groups were citizens of Ukraine (80,300), Belarus (47,800), Russia (13,200), Uzbekistan (12,600) and India (9,400).

China takes women's softball silver as Japan claims seventh straight Asian Games gold
China

2026-10-03

Team China encourage each other during the women's gold medal match of softball between China and Japan at the 20th Asian Games Aichi-Nagoya 2026 in Anjo of Aichi Prefecture, Japan, Oct. 3, 2026. (Xinhua/Luo Yuan)
NAGOYA, Japan, Oct. 3 (Xinhua)-- Japan beat China 7-0 in the women's softball final at the 2026 Asian Games on Saturday, claiming a seventh consecutive Asiad title while China took silver.
Both teams had won their first six games in the eight-team round-robin preliminary stage before Japan edged China 7-6 in their final preliminary match.
In the final, Japan opened a 2-0 lead in the second inning, helped by a baserunning interference call and Ayane Nakagawa's sacrifice fly.
Risa Kawamura doubled to start the fourth before Kanna Kudo and Kyoko Ishikawa drove in three more runs to extend Japan's lead to 5-0.
China changed pitchers in the fifth, but Japan loaded the bases on a hit and two walks. With two outs, Rei Fujimoto drove in two runs to make it 7-0, ending the game under the tournament's run-ahead rule.
China's Xi Kailin said the team had improved in both offense and defense during the tournament but needed to acknowledge the remaining gap with Japan.
"Japan had a plan for every pitch," she said. "We need to improve how we deal with different defensive situations while maintaining our progress offensively."
China has brought in Japanese coaches Itsushi Fukuda and Eri Yamada as part of their preparations for the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics.
Fukuda said the silver medal met the team's minimum target, but added that China still lacked match experience, particularly in turning pre-match analysis into effective decisions during games.
Yamada said China had played well against Japan in the preliminary round, but the final showed there was still a gap between the sides.
"We expected Japan to use different locations and different types of pitches, but we were not able to respond well enough," she said, adding that China needed to improve its run-scoring ability.
China won the first three Asian Games women's softball titles in 1990, 1994 and 1998. Japan has won every edition since Busan 2002, with Saturday's victory extending their run to seven straight gold medal. ■

"At dawn today, an exercise involving the launch of intermediate-range strategic missiles toward the east coast of our country was carried out," the statement said.

The DPRK official also addressed assessments of the missiles’ flight range. She noted that South Korea’s Joint Chiefs of Staff reported a range of more than 700 kilometers, while Japan’s Ministry of Defense estimated it at approximately 680 kilometers. Pyongyang views the discrepancy as evidence of the missiles’ distinctive flight characteristics and the limitations of existing surveillance systems.
Kim Yo Jong said the DPRK had observed a similar scenario four times, adding that this, in Pyongyang’s view, confirms the effectiveness of the special flight mode employed by the missiles.
