====================================================================================================

China Focus: A taste of home in orbit: How China keeps its astronauts well-fed
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
20:32:11 CST
21:32:11 KST

by Xinhua writer Yuan Quan
BEIJING, Oct. 3 (Xinhua) -- Although called Tiangong, or "Heavenly Palace," China's space station is becoming less distant and more like home, as astronauts bring the comforting tastes into orbit.
The Chinese space kitchen now serves nearly 200 food items. Alongside dumplings and mooncakes, home-style dishes such as Kung Pao chicken, mapo tofu and fried rice have made it onto the station's menu.
Videos showing astronauts savoring freshly cooked meat and cakes in orbit have gone viral. Their smiling faces and bright eyes make the aroma almost leap off the screen.
Yang Liwei, the country's first astronaut, joked at a recent press conference that he was envious. He said astronauts can now use air-frying equipment in space and enjoy baked chicken wings in orbit. During his Shenzhou-5 mission in 2003, which lasted less than one day, his diet was limited to packaged instant food that could not be heated.
Microgravity, cosmic radiation and the enclosed cabin environment impose strict requirements on space diets. Floating particles and droplets may drift into instruments and trigger malfunctions. Since Yuri Gagarin, the first human to travel into space, paste-like food and compressed energy bars had long served as the standard meals for astronauts.
In June 2013, Wang Yaping, together with two fellow male crewmates, carried out the 15-day Shenzhou-10 space mission. People remembered this female astronaut with a ponytail for her space lecture. At the same time, the image of her floating a "zongzi," a leaf-wrapped rice dumpling, by hand also left a deep impression on the public.
Zongzi is traditionally enjoyed during the Dragon Boat Festival, which happened to coincide with the Shenzhou-10 mission that year. To help the astronauts celebrate, this special snack was added to the spaceship pantry.
Eight years later, Wang spent Spring Festival aboard the Tiangong space station during the Shenzhou-13 mission. It is also China's first six-month-long space stay. Scientists customized the cuisine: for instance, they prepared dumplings with seafood fillings because Wang grew up by the sea, and plenty of spicy food for crew member Ye Guangfu, who was born in chili-obsessed Sichuan Province.
At that time, the core module Tianhe had several sections, including those for working, sleeping, dining and exercising. The videos of Shenzhou-13 crew practicing calligraphy and playing Taichi became social media hits.
China completed the construction of its space station in 2022, with one core module and two lab modules forming a 110-square-meter orbital structure. Oxygen can be fully regenerated, and water recovery exceeds 95 percent.
Since then, long-duration spaceflights have become routine, and the Chinese "space home" can host up to six astronauts in orbit at a time.
Space residency is also set to last even longer. One member of the Shenzhou-23 crew, currently aboard the Tiangong, will conduct a one-year in-orbit stay. Moreover, as China pushes further into deep-space exploration, these extended stays will become the norm, which means astronauts' diets will be more important than ever.
Because weightlessness causes bone calcium loss and muscle atrophy, space food must be high in calcium and protein, low in sodium and balanced in dietary fiber. According to the Astronaut Center of China, researchers have developed space food that counteracts oxidative damage, supports immunity, reduces fatigue and regulates the gut microbiome.
But taste is another problem. In microgravity, blood shifts upward, causing nasal congestion and cutting smell sensitivity by at least 30 percent. Since taste is closely tied to smell, astronauts often find food bland. The center's researchers have responded with adding more strong-flavored dishes, with liquid soy sauce and concentrated chili sauce.
New technology has also played a big role in keeping astronauts well-fed.
The astronaut center, in collaboration with private companies, has upgraded the "space kitchen" with a suite of intelligent appliances for drinking water, food reheating and baking. This allows astronauts in orbit to enjoy hot meals within 20 minutes, rather than waiting longer or eating cold food. Liu Weibo, an expert with the center, gave an example of the hot-air baking oven, which is a pioneering Chinese design for space use that can efficiently remove cooking fumes and allow astronauts to enjoy barbecue in orbit.
During a space lecture for Hong Kong and Macao students last month, Shenzhou-23 crew member Li Jiaying, or Lai Ka-ying in Cantonese, showed freshly baked cakes and said they reminded her of egg waffles, a popular snack from her hometown. She is a Hong Kong local.
Space food supplies have also become more diverse and nutritious, including more fruits and vegetables, as well as frozen steak and chicken wings. The next-generation cargo craft Qingzhou, designed for future in-orbit supply delivery, will have greater cold-chain transport capacity.
However, long-term space residency requires reducing dependence on Earth's supplies, said center expert Bian Qiang. "The controlled ecological life-support tests we are conducting are intended to build an ecosystem in space that regenerates water, air and food on site, to reduce extraterrestrial survival's dependence on Earth resupply and ultimately achieve self-sufficiency."
Since the Shenzhou-16 mission in 2023, China has been growing plants in orbit. It has tested more than 20 varieties from 14 plant species, including lettuce, carrots, potatoes and wheat.
The Shenzhou-18 crew in 2024 was tasked with raising fish in an "aquarium" to study how space affects their growth. Scientists said the work may one day allow astronauts to enjoy fish from their own in-orbit harvests.
China is targeting a crewed lunar landing by 2030. Living on the moon will make resupply much more challenging because of the increased distance from Earth.
"We plan to build a Chinese 'lunar vegetable garden' on the moon," Bian said.
From heating, baking to farming, feeding astronauts well in space is not a luxury. It is part of the mission, bringing a taste of home to the universe. ■

Journalist sues PSNI over alleged surveillance of sources
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
13:30:54 BST
21:30:54 KST

An investigative journalist in Northern Ireland has filed a High Court claim against the Police Service of Northern Ireland, alleging that the force unlawfully obtained their communications in order to identify confidential sources, according to the National Union of Journalists.
The journalist, who reports on serious crime and paramilitary activity, has been granted anonymity and can be identified only as YZL. The claim seeks compensation for misuse of private information, harassment and breaches of the Data Protection Act.
Computer Weekly, which reported the case last month, has set out that the applications for the journalist’s communications data were made by the PSNI in 2014, that the anonymity order was granted on 18 September and that a further hearing is listed for November. The journalist is represented by the solicitor Olivia O’Kane.
Laura Davison, the NUJ general secretary, said: “Allegations that the PSNI attempted to uncover another journalist’s sources are deeply worrying. Journalists have a right to protect their sources and to report without fear or state interference.
“This is not an isolated incident. In recent years the NUJ has supported journalists Barry McCaffrey, Trevor Birney, and Vincent Kearney in exposing unlawful surveillance through the Investigatory Powers Tribunal. In a landmark judgment in July, the Tribunal ordered PSNI and MI5 to pay £10,000 each in damages for breaching Kearney’s right to source protection, which subjected him to considerable risk as a journalist working in a post-conflict society.
“The new Northern Ireland Secretary and the Chief Constable have an opportunity to restore public trust. The NUJ will be monitoring this case and continuing to call for a judge-led inquiry that is broader in scope into unlawful surveillance against journalists, lawyers and human rights defenders in Northern Ireland by police and security forces.”
The claim arrives after a run of findings against the force. An independent review by Angus McCullough KC, published last year, identified 21 cases involving eight journalists in which the PSNI had attempted to identify confidential sources, and concluded that the force’s Code of Practice between 2007 and 2015 had failed to consider whether the authorisations were justified by an “overriding public interest” and that they “must be considered unlawful”. Jon Boutcher, the chief constable, accepted the findings in writing.
Birney and McCaffrey, who made the documentary No Stone Unturned about the 1994 Loughinisland killings, were arrested in 2018 and later succeeded at the Investigatory Powers Tribunal in establishing that they had been unlawfully surveilled. Kearney, now Northern editor at RTÉ and previously the BBC’s home affairs correspondent in Belfast, was awarded a total of £20,000 in July, split evenly between the police and the Security Service, over the obtaining of his phone records.
The NUJ has welcomed the McCullough review while arguing that its terms were drawn too narrowly, and the union wants a public inquiry covering not only the PSNI but other police forces and MI5. Source protection has been a live issue in Northern Ireland for a considerable time, where reporting on paramilitary organisations and on the conduct of the security forces during and after the Troubles has often depended on people who would be at real risk if identified.

The eruption of Anak Krakatau changed the map: two new islands formed near the volcano
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
15:30:52 EEST
21:30:52 KST

The eruption of Anak Krakatau changed the map: two new islands formed near the volcano
Kyiv • UNN
After the September eruption, two new islands formed near Anak Krakatau, and the area of the volcanic island increased by 32.8 hectares. The eruption caused disruptions to nearly 3,000 flights.
Following a powerful eruption of Anak Krakatau volcano in Indonesia, two new island-like landmasses formed nearby. UNN reports this, citing data from Indonesian geological services and satellite observations.
In addition, the area of the volcanic island itself increased by approximately 33 hectares.
Details
The new land areas were detected in satellite images after a powerful phase of the Anak Krakatau eruption that lasted from September 4 to 6. One of the new islands is located approximately 760 meters northwest of the volcano, while the other is roughly 495 meters southeast. Their appearance was also confirmed by observations from sailors.
Experts have not yet established the exact mechanism behind the formation of the new land areas. According to one theory, they may have formed as a result of an underwater eruption, when lava and other volcanic materials accumulated on the seabed until they rose above the water's surface. It is also possible that the new formations consist of ash, rock fragments, and other eruption products.
Geologists note that it is still too early to say whether the new islands will remain permanent. If they consist primarily of loose volcanic material, waves and erosion could destroy them fairly quickly. If, however, their foundation is solidified lava, the new land areas may endure.
The September eruption also changed the shoreline of Anak Krakatau itself. According to estimates by Indonesian specialists, the island's area increased by approximately 32.8 hectares, reaching about 341.5 hectares. During the active phase, the volcano emitted large volumes of ash and lava, while the ash plume rose to approximately 15 kilometers.
The eruption also caused serious disruptions to air traffic. In total, nearly 3,000 flights were canceled, delayed, or diverted, affecting more than 340,000 passengers. Eight airports, including those in the Jakarta area, were temporarily closed. Subsequently, the volcano's activity began to decline, and the danger level was reduced from three to two. At the same time, residents and tourists are prohibited from approaching the main crater closer than two kilometers.
Background
Anak Krakatau is located in the Sunda Strait between the islands of Java and Sumatra and is one of Indonesia's most active volcanoes.
Anak Krakatau itself, whose name translates as "Child of Krakatau," began forming in the late 1920s in the caldera left after the catastrophic 1883 eruption of Krakatau volcano.
In December 2018, the collapse of a significant part of its slope triggered a tsunami in the Sunda Strait. More than 400 people were killed at the time.

Marica Lillemets: It's time to create a cross‑sector life‑course policy
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
12:30:00 UTC
21:30:00 KST

Marica Lillemets: It's time to create a cross‑sector life‑course policy
The lack of meaningful integration between the social welfare and healthcare systems forces people in need to navigate a bureaucratic maze that many older adults cannot manage, writes Marica Lillemets.
Estonia has reached a demographic turning point. Population aging is an everyday reality that requires substantive action. We need a new approach that ensures older people have dignified living conditions, access to healthcare services, and social inclusion. The goal should be to shift from providing social assistance to developing a preventive and empowering life‑course policy.
Despite positive steps in recent years — such as the 2023 care reform and the income‑tax exemption for the average pension — significant shortcomings remain that demand full attention and action.
Older people in Estonia face one of the highest poverty risks in the European Union, as pension growth does not keep pace with rising living costs and healthcare prices. We have special‑pension recipients earning around €4,000 per month and others receiving €400. Unfortunately, healthcare pricing does not sufficiently consider older people's financial capacity, and subsistence support does not cover real‑life needs.
We have also failed to ensure that healthcare services are available everywhere in Estonia. The main reason for service inequality is the drastically different capacities of local governments, which leads to unequal treatment depending on where people live. This particularly affects home‑care services and specialist medical care.
Another striking problem in organizing policy for older adults is institutional fragmentation. There is no substantive integration between social welfare and healthcare. This forces people in need to navigate bureaucratic complexity that many older adults cannot manage.
For example, the modern digital system for accessing family‑doctor services is a barrier for many older people living alone. To overcome it, they must rely on younger relatives or acquaintances — or sit at the doctor's door hoping to be seen.
A unified, person‑centered care fund
As a legislative measure, amendments could be initiated to the Social Welfare Act and the Health Insurance Act to create a unified, person‑centered care fund. This would allow different services — such as home nursing and social transport — to be financed from a single platform. This would reduce pressure on emergency departments and the hospital network. The step would help build an integrated care model, add a preventive component, and increase people's motivation to stay healthy and active for as long as possible.
In addition to physical health, we must focus more on mental and social well‑being. Together, these three components give a person a sufficient sense of being healthy. When one is missing, problems arise.
For example, the digital transition has left some older adults in an information void, deepening loneliness and mental‑health concerns. A more serious consequence is social isolation, which increases the feeling of being excluded from life. I am not calling for resistance to technological development, but for early and age‑appropriate digital‑skills training for older adults. Lifelong learning through "senior universities" would be suitable if conducted in small groups led by trained instructors.
The current widespread practice — where a local librarian or shopkeeper performs necessary digital tasks for an older person when dealing with the state — does not teach independent digital skills. But thanks to these helpers, someone still receives assistance.
The Public Information Act could be supplemented with a provision requiring state institutions and municipalities to maintain accessible physical counseling points for older adults who have missed the digital train entirely. Building digital competence should be the responsibility of individuals, the state, and employers to prevent exclusion in our already small society.
Promoting the "silver economy"
Although our physical capacity decreases with age, our knowledge and dedication often peak later in life. Therefore, employing older adults is a tremendous resource, not a burden. Part‑time or flexible work, age‑appropriate retraining, and valuing life experience make older workers highly valuable.
Unfortunately, not all employers recognize this, and the state's tax laws do not support keeping pension‑age people in the labor market. Yet personal dignity and financial stability are closely linked — not to mention the need to feel socially relevant and contributing to one's own and the country's well‑being.
Tax incentives in the Income Tax Act and Social Tax Act could "nudge" employers toward the silver economy. For example, a lower social‑tax rate could be introduced for employers who hire workers aged 55+ (or 65+) with flexible workloads. This would ease labor shortages and keep older adults socially active.
Estonia's success cannot be measured only by GDP growth. It is also reflected in how we treat our older population. The current reactive and fragmented policy must be replaced with a vision in which aging is a safe and dignified process.
I have not addressed all issues related to older adults or all possible solutions, but the proposals presented here could already justify forming an inter‑ministerial working group and preparing legislative amendments. More proposals will come from stakeholder groups. A cross‑sector life‑course policy is unavoidable.
--
Editor: Kaupo Meiel, Argo Ideon

India proposal among four initiatives
According to Sybiha, four proposals are currently being considered in diplomatic efforts surrounding the war.India's proposal was described by the Ukrainian foreign minister as the most comprehensive.Türkiye and Egypt have separately proposed a grain and agricultural truce in the Black Sea, while the United States has put forward an energy truce proposal.The agricultural and maritime component is particularly important for Egypt, which relies on Ukrainian grain for roughly a third of its supply, according to RBC Ukraine.
The US proposal on an energy truce was also discussed during a meeting between Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy and US President Donald Trump.Kyiv has conveyed its own approach to its partners and wants the energy and Black Sea components to be treated as an interconnected package.Sybiha said the energy component would require a complete halt to attacks on energy infrastructure, including port facilities.Ukraine has also expressed readiness for an unconditional ceasefire along the line of contact. Sybiha said such a ceasefire could potentially emerge from a meeting between Zelenskyy and Russian President Vladimir Putin.The US is currently working actively on this diplomatic track, according to the Ukrainian foreign minister.
Kyiv backs safe Black Sea shipping
The latest Ukrainian position builds on India's earlier engagement with Kyiv over restoring safe navigation in the Black Sea.During last month's UN General Assembly-related engagements, Zelenskyy said Egypt, India and Türkiye had put forward options for a maritime truce between Russia and Ukraine."We are waiting for Russia's response. Ukraine is ready ... to ensure safe shipping and food security in the Black Sea if Russia is ready to take real steps towards de-escalation too. We have to start somewhere," Zelenskyy said at the time.Also read:India's proposal under consideration for safe Black Sea shipping, Zelenskyy saysIndia has been engaging with both Moscow and Kyiv while advocating dialogue and diplomacy.External affairs minister S Jaishankar had said India was in continuous contact with both sides and was exploring ideas that could help mitigate and eventually end the conflict."If India can be of any help, in any manner, we are there," Jaishankar said during his visit to Kyiv last month.During that visit, Jaishankar met Zelenskyy and Sybiha, with discussions covering peace efforts, bilateral cooperation, Black Sea navigation and global food security.Sybiha had also said Ukraine valued India's engagement in efforts to restore freedom of navigation in the Black Sea."Restoring freedom of navigation is critical for global food security. Ukraine is ready to play a constructive role and we value India’s engagement," he said in a post on X.
Russia's position remains key to next steps
While Ukraine has indicated its readiness to consider multiple limited ceasefire arrangements, Russia's response remains central to whether the proposals can move forward.Sybiha's comments come amid differing assessments in Europe over Moscow's willingness to enter substantive peace negotiations.German Chancellor Friedrich Merz recently said Russia was not currently interested in genuine peace negotiations, while German foreign minister Johann Wadephul has expressed expectations that talks to end the war could begin in the near future.
The Kremlin had previously said there were no prerequisites for moving towards a broader peace negotiating track while maintaining that Russia remained open to talks."For now, there are no prerequisites for moving on to a peaceful negotiating track, although we, as the Russian side, remain open to peace talks," Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said.Ukraine's latest position therefore places several limited ceasefire proposals, covering energy infrastructure, Black Sea shipping and agricultural supplies, alongside the possibility of a broader unconditional ceasefire along the line of contact.India's proposal is being considered alongside those initiatives, with Sybiha describing it as the most comprehensive and saying New Delhi has now signalled its readiness to play a role in the process.

Russia Concealed Court Statistics on Missing Persons and Crimes Committed by Military Personnel
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
12:27:05 UTC
21:27:05 KST

The Judicial Department of the Supreme Court of the Russian Federation omitted data from its 2025 statistics regarding citizens declared dead or missing, as well as convicted military personnel and law enforcement officers.
This was reported by Verstka, which analyzed the department’s reports published on October 2.
In particular, the reports no longer specify how many such applications were received by the courts. For comparison, in 2024, the department reported a record 17,500 applications.
Data on convicted military personnel, judges, prosecutors, investigators, police officers, and employees of the Federal Penitentiary Service have also been omitted.
Data on those convicted of treason, disclosure of state secrets, sabotage, organizing an extremist group, and ‘discrediting’ the Russian army have disappeared from the publicly available statistics.
At the same time, the agency retained the figure for the charge of spreading ‘fake news’ about the army: in 2025, 90 people were convicted under this charge. Data on a number of administrative cases has also been redacted, including those involving ‘discrediting’ the army and violations of the rules governing the activities of ‘foreign agents.’
As a reminder, in June 2025, Militarnyi reported, citing Mediazona, that since the beginning of the year, Russian courts had received more than 26,000 applications to declare people missing or deceased. Commanders of specific units were named in nearly 12,000 of these applications, while another 9,000 involved other units of the Ministry of Defence of the Russian Federation.

US Lawmakers Target Serbia's Democratic Backsliding, Ties To Russia, China, Iran
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
12:27:02 UTC
21:27:02 KST

WASHINGTON -- A bipartisan, bicameral group of US lawmakers is pressing for tougher action on what they describe as democratic backsliding, corruption, and growing Russian, Chinese, and Iranian influence in Serbia, just weeks before snap parliamentary elections that could reshape the country's political landscape.
Senators Chuck Grassley (Repubican-Iowa) and Richard Blumenthal (Democrat-Connecticut), along with Representatives Joe Wilson (Republican-South Carolina) and William Keating (Democrat-Massachusetts), have introduced the Supporting the Rule of Law, Building Institutional Justice, and Accountability Act, known as the SRBIJA Act.
The legislation would condition additional US assistance to Serbia on a presidential certification that Belgrade has made "significant and sustained progress" on judicial accountability, media freedom, and alignment with the European Union and NATO.
It would also support sanctions against individuals involved in corruption, serious human rights abuses, or efforts to undermine democratic institutions and regional stability.
The bill comes as Serbia prepares for snap parliamentary elections on October 25, following more than two years of student-led and civic protests and amid mounting concerns over the state of the rule of law, judicial independence, media freedom, and corruption.
The legislation specifically cites the government's response to the protests and the November 2024 collapse of the canopy at the Novi Sad railway station.
Serbian President Aleksandar Vucic resigned from the presidency on September 27, laying the groundwork for a possible move to the prime minister's office if his ruling party wins the October vote, according to the material accompanying the legislation.
Russian, Chinese, Iranian Influence
The bill also focuses heavily on Serbia's relations with Russia and China and calls for a detailed US assessment of their political, economic, energy, and security ties with Belgrade.
It comes after a Serbian cabinet minister traveled to Tehran in July to attend the funeral of former Iranian Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei, joining Russian and Chinese delegations at an event where most European governments were not represented.
"Serbia plays a critical role in preserving peace and security in the Western Balkans. It's critical to prevent Russia, China or Iran from influencing Serbia and destabilizing the region," Senator Grassley said in a statement. He added that the legislation includes accountability measures, including sanctions, aimed at promoting Serbia's return to a strong democracy.
Senator Blumenthal said the US-Serbian relationship should be based on "shared democratic values" and a commitment to combating autocracy.
"Since taking power, the current government in Serbia has deepened its ties to Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping," he noted, adding that the legislation would give the US administration new tools to sanction people who enable democratic backsliding.
Wilson, the Republican co-chairman of the Helsinki Commission who introduced the bill in the House with Keating, told RFE/RL on September 2 that he was grateful for the bipartisan and bicameral backing.
“Congress is unanimous that Serbians deserve free and fair elections," Wilson said. "Serbia is a strategically and culturally important country that could contribute to a peaceful and prosperous region but first democracy and the rule of law must be restored."
The bill would also require the State Department to maintain its participation in the US-Serbia Strategic Dialogue and develop a broader strategy for US engagement with Belgrade. The legislation would expire five years after enactment.
Experts: 'Pressure Matters'
Whether the measure can alter Vucic's behavior is less clear.
Ivana Stradner, a research fellow at the Foundation for Defense of Democracies, told RFE/RL on October 2 that she does not expect Vucic to change his approach.
“Vucic is not going to change behavior, no matter what," Stradner said. "He is going to continue fighting his own policies, which is basically to remain in power for as long as possible.”
But she said the congressional initiative could send an important message to Serbia's opposition and civil society. "This is extremely important because this sends a very clear signal to the opposition that America is watching Vucic's actions," Stradner said.
She argued that Washington should use sanctions against people who threaten individuals close to the Vucic regime and contribute to regional destabilization. She also called for the US and its allies to publicly expose possible efforts to manipulate the elections and, where appropriate, declassify information about such activity in advance.
Stradner characterized Vucic's foreign policy as fundamentally aligned with Russia, China, and Iran, while saying his government continues to rely on European funding and US legitimacy.
Olivia Olson, a project assistant at the Atlantic Council's Europe Center, said the timing was particularly significant.
"With Serbia's elections on October 25 and real energy behind the Student List opposition, Vucic is focused on domestic politics, as his ruling [Serbian Progressive Party] looks to extend years in power," Olson told RFE/RL.
She noted that Vucic's relationship with Washington has historically been closest with the executive branch, pointing to the new US-Serbia strategic dialogue and the Trump administration's interest in Serbia's EXPO 2027 as high points in relations.
“The SRBIJA Act is significant because it's bipartisan," Olson said. "The bill shows both parties are watching Serbia independently of the White House's posture.”
Ilva Tare, a resident senior fellow at the Atlantic Council's Europe Center, called the timing "decisive."
The act is a "rare bicameral, bipartisan signal" arriving three weeks before the elections, she said. It will be the first time, after more than two years of continuous protests, that the student movement's electoral list will face voters.
Tare said protesters' allegations of state capture, deep corruption, and democratic backsliding would now be tested at the ballot box, while the United States, the EU, and other international observers expect a free and fair process.
She cautioned, however, that the legislation alone is unlikely to immediately change Vucic's behavior.
"Will this bill change Vucic's behavior? I believe that will not happen overnight, and not without internal and external pressure," Tare said.

US-Russia Peace Talks Eye Multibillion Lukoil Oil Deal
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
12:20:00 UTC
21:20:00 KST

Negotiations between the US administration and Russia aimed at ending the war in Ukraine have expanded to incorporate a multibillion-dollar oil transaction that could benefit Middle Eastern business figures connected to US President Donald Trump’s primary envoys, Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner.
According to The New York Times, the proposed transaction, which requires formal authorization from both the US government and the Kremlin, concerns the extensive international portfolio of Lukoil, Russia’s second-largest oil producer.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
The assets under discussion encompass oil extraction concessions in Cameroon and Iraq, major European refining complexes in Bulgaria and Romania, and extensive retail fuel station networks across Europe and the US, including filling stations in New Jersey.
The primary consortium seeking to finalize the acquisition includes American financier Todd Boehly – who contributed $2 million to political entities supporting President Trump – alongside two Middle Eastern investment groups that maintain prior commercial ties with Kushner or the Witkoff family, as well as an entity affiliated with the US government.
The negotiations, which have been underway for several months, were described by eight individuals familiar with the proceedings.
While the reporting noted no indications that Kushner or Witkoff would personally profit from the agreement, the transaction demonstrates the close alignment between private commercial networks and geopolitical statecraft within the administration.
Russia Threatens to Strike Defense Plants in NATO Countries
Regulatory hurdles
Russian President Vladimir Putin raised the prospective sale directly during a confidential Kremlin consultation with Witkoff and Kushner on Sept. 5, according to three individuals briefed on the meeting.
Putin reportedly proposed the transaction as a practical vehicle to demonstrate to the Russian business elite and the domestic public that normal commercial engagement with the US remains achievable.
The American negotiators responded that they would facilitate work on the transaction, viewing the commercial bridge as an instrument to cultivate constructive relations with Moscow while exerting downward pressure on international crude oil benchmarks.
For prospective buyers, US regulatory approval represents a substantial financial upside, as clearing the transaction would lift US sanctions restrictions on the assets and immediately elevate their market capitalization.
Although Lukoil operates formally as a publicly traded private enterprise, decisions governing its strategic divestments are widely treated within Moscow as resting directly with Putin. Consequently, the execution of the multi-continent transaction hinges on political determinations made by Trump and Putin.
The commercial discussions align with Trump’s public statements viewing Russia as a vast economic opportunity, which he has promoted as a framework to incentivize peace.
The initiative has also renewed scrutiny over Trump-affiliated business interests, including the cryptocurrency venture World Liberty Financial, which was co-founded by Witkoff and includes an investor who also maintains an equity stake in the proposed Lukoil buyout consortium.

Albanian PM Calls EU Accession Promises to Ukraine ‘a Lie’

Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
12:19:00 UTC
21:19:00 KST

Albanian Prime Minister Edi Rama warned that Western leaders are offering unrealistic promises to Ukraine regarding EU membership, asserting that Kyiv will “never” achieve accession under conventional bureaucratic procedures.
Speaking in an interview with Die Welt, Rama argued that the 27-nation bloc must fundamentally overhaul its enlargement methodology by imposing rigorous performance standards while simultaneously offering candidate states tangible, early integration into institutional mechanisms.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“Look at Ukraine. What they are promising it is a lie. Under the regular accession path, with all criteria, it will never be accepted. Everyone knows this,” Rama stated, contending that European officials privately acknowledge the standard accession framework is ill-suited for a nation fighting a full-scale war.
Rama advocated for a phased integration model where Ukraine and other candidate nations are brought directly into EU working formats and consultative bodies immediately, with formal statutory membership conferred subsequently based on verified reform milestones and tangible results.
Veto reform
The Albanian prime minister also addressed the structural challenges of EU enlargement, warning that expanding the bloc without institutional reforms risks paralyzing decision-making due to unilateral member-state obstruction.
Rama voiced unequivocal support for abolishing the national veto mechanism in European Council voting, arguing that unanimity requirements leave the union vulnerable to tactical blockades by individual capitals.
Switzerland Allocates $162M for 8 Ukraine Recovery Projects
He stressed that in an era of heightened global competition against economic and technological powers such as the US, China, and India, the EU cannot afford procedural gridlock.
“In a world where Europe must compete with China, the US, and India, it is unacceptable that a single member state can block decisions for the entire European Union,” Rama said, pointing to repeated instances where bilateral disputes have stalled accession tracks across the Western Balkans.
Albania itself has navigated protracted EU accession procedures since obtaining official candidate status in 2014, with its negotiating framework repeatedly delayed by regional disputes and institutional reform reviews in Brussels.
Merit-based accession and the 2027 timeline
Rama’s critique coincides with pushback from European officials regarding accelerated membership timetables promoted by Kyiv.
EU Enlargement Commissioner Marta Kos dismissed President Volodymyr Zelensky’s stated target of securing EU entry by Jan. 1, 2027, reiterating that accession remains strictly merit-based. While acknowledging that Russia’s war restored enlargement as a strategic priority, Kos emphasized that calendar targets cannot bypass statutory membership criteria.
The timeline has come under intense scrutiny as Ukraine works to fulfill foundational governance benchmarks.
A September assessment conducted by civil-society coalition Membership Check revealed that implementation of the “Kachka-Kos” priority reform plan – a 10-point emergency blueprint on justice and anti-corruption agreed in December 2025 – remains stalled at 15 percent, with roughly three months remaining before year-end deadlines.
Monitoring groups highlighted unfinished judicial reforms, delays in enhancing the institutional autonomy of the National Anti-Corruption Bureau of Ukraine (NABU) and the Specialized Anti-Corruption Prosecutor’s Office (SAPO), and vulnerabilities in prosecutorial appointment procedures.
Institutional tensions surfaced in September when former Prosecutor General Ruslan Kravchenko issued a notice of suspicion against NABU Director Semen Kryvonos following an internal probe into the Prosecutor General’s Office.
The confrontation prompted parliament to approve Kravchenko’s dismissal, with legal experts warning that recurring executive friction risks undermining the independent oversight institutions required by Brussels.
While Ukraine opened negotiations on the Fundamentals cluster on June 15 and External Relations on July 14, European diplomats emphasize that opening negotiating chapters marks the commencement of technical alignment rather than confirmation that statutory benchmarks have been achieved.

Greece returns remains of Czar Samuel to Bulgaria
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
12:17:00 UTC
21:17:00 KST

Greece returns remains of Czar Samuel to Bulgaria
October 3, 2026
The remains of one of Bulgaria's most important medieval rulers were set to arrive in the Bulgarian capital, Sofia, on Saturday after decades of negotiations with neighboring Greece.
Czar Samuel ruled the First Bulgarian Empire from 997 to 1014, gradually extending his authority over a swathe of the Balkans as far south as Lake Ohrid, now in North Macedonia on the border with Albania.
But Samuel's rule was also characterized by conflict with the Byzantine Empire which ultimately defeated his army at the Battle of Kleidion in 1014.
Samuel is said to have died of shock when thousands of his defeated soldiers returned home having been blinded by order of Byzantine Emperor Basil II, known as Boulgaroktonos – the "Bulgar Slayer."
The Bulgarian lands fell under Byzantine rule four years later but Czar Samuel is still considered a symbol of Bulgarian national identity today, and his remains – discovered in a Greek border area 60 years ago – are set to be received with full state honors.
They are set to be flown to Sofia aboard a military aircraft accompanied by a fighter jet escort before a 21-gun salute and a procession to the Church of St. Sophia, where the public will be able to pay respects.
Free trains to the capital are being provided for the occasion, with some 750 police on duty during the handover ceremony.
Bulgaria: 'Czar Samuel unites us'
"These are items that belong to both our peoples; they constitute our memory and our bond, and our compatriots and future generations deserve and must have the opportunity to pay tribute to their ancestors," said Bulgarian Prime Minister Rumen Radev at a ceremony held at Museum of Byzantine Civilization in Thessaloniki, Greece, ahead of the handover.
Bulgaria officially opened talks on the return of the remains in 2007, and they became a major issue in relations with their southern neighbor.
"If, in the past, Czar Samuel divided us, I can say that today he unites us," said Radev. "He strengthens our strategic cooperation and makes the historical relations between our states and peoples even stronger."
Greece hopes for return of Parthenon Marbles
Greek Prime Minister Kyriakos Mitsotakis, speaking alongside Radev, acknowledged that the remains of Czar Samuel have "incalculable cultural and spiritual but also emotional value" for Bulgaria, adding: "The global community is re-evaluating its long-standing stance on protecting cultural heritage."
In return, Greece is set to receive 48 sentimental objects pillaged by Bulgarian troops from churches and monasteries in northern Greece during the First World War.
Some prominent Greek academics and religious leaders have criticized the exchange as inadequate on the Bulgarian side, but Mitsotakis said he hoped Saturday's ceremony would bolster Greece's international campaign to return the Parthenon Marbles, a collection of 2,500-year-old marble sculptures taken from the Acropolis in Athens and later displayed in the British Museum.
"This shift is embodied by today's initiative, which rests on the obvious principle that monuments and historical heirlooms cannot be treated as spoils of war, nor as the result of circumstances subsequent to their creation."
Czar Samuel: does North Macedonia also have a claim?
However, Bulgaria is not the only country to claim Czar Samuel, who is also celebrated with a huge statue in Skopje, the capital of North Macedonia.
"The bones return, the conflict remains! Samuel once again [contested] between Skopje and Sofia!" declared the Albanian-language newspaper Koha, while Skopje daily Sloboden Pechat called the handover another "battle over history."
In 2022, a bilateral commission recommended that Samuel be presented as the head of a state that "most contemporary historiographers consider to be the Bulgarian Empire" – territory which is now North Macedonia.
"Samuel occupies an important place in the historical narrative both in Bulgaria and in North Macedonia," Dimitar Bechev, a researcher at the Carnegie Europe think tank, told the AFP news agency.
Indeed, history has been playing a major role in the run-up to this month's Bulgarian presidential election, with incumbent President Iliana Iotova, backed by Prime Minister Radev, promoting a more neutral position between the European Union and NATO – both of which Bulgaria belongs to – and Russia.
"Radev is looking to attract the patriotic electorate," said analyst Bechev, adding that the return of the remains to Sofia "aims to underline the Bulgarian character of the Slavic population of Macedonia."

Traffic rules on bridges across the Dnipro River in Kyiv during air raid alerts have been updated, the Kyiv City Military Administration reports.
"South Bridge – during an air raid alert, traffic from the left bank to the right bank operates without restrictions. At the same time, traffic from the right bank to the left bank is restricted for 15 minutes from the moment the air raid alert signal is announced, after which it resumes. Access to the bridge in the direction from the right bank to the left bank is carried out from the side of Stolychne Highway, Naddniprianske Highway, and the Vydubychi bus station," the report on the Telegram channel states.
In addition, on the Podil-Voskresensky Bridge, in the event of an announcement or cancellation of an air raid alert, vehicle traffic will be suspended in both directions for 15 minutes. After that, traffic will resume in full.
On the remaining bridges across the Dnipro, traffic will operate without restrictions.
"We ask you to take this information into account when planning your trips," the Kyiv City Military Administration urged.

Royal Marines seek new ship boarding training facility
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
13:15:26 BST
21:15:26 KST

The Ministry of Defence is looking for a contractor to provide a maritime interdiction operations training facility at Royal Marines Bickleigh, with an option to buy a second one for the Commando Training Centre at Lympstone, according to a tender notice published on Friday afternoon.
Maritime interdiction covers the boarding and searching of vessels at sea, work that runs from counter-narcotics and sanctions enforcement through to stopping a ship suspected of carrying weapons or people. It is physically demanding and unforgiving of poor technique, since teams have to get up the side of a moving hull and through a vessel they do not know, which is why the training for it depends on purpose-built structures ashore.
The notice gives the estimated total value as just over £1.2 million excluding VAT, structured so that the contract starts at a little over £600,000 with an option to double it if the second facility is taken up. Delivery would run from 25 November this year to the end of March 2029.
Navy Commercial at Navy Command Headquarters on Whale Island in Portsmouth is running the competition under the open procedure, which means any supplier may bid. The enquiry deadline falls on 15 October and tenders are due by 10am on 27 October, with an award decision estimated for 10 November. Bidders are being offered a site visit before they submit, and the requirement has been marked as particularly suitable for small and medium-sized enterprises.
No preliminary market engagement notice was issued before the competition opened. The department has explained that decision by reference to the timescales involved and its belief that it already knows the market well enough from previous, similar requirements.
The requirement has been classified under wall and rope climbing equipment, training aids and devices, training facilities building, towers, and training and simulation in warships. It is listed as goods rather than works or services, and the cyber risk profile has been assessed at level one, the lowest tier under the department’s Cyber Security Model.
The department has also reserved the possibility of a future direct award of similar goods or services under paragraph 8 of Schedule 5 to the Procurement Act 2023, the provision covering repeat purchases following an original competed contract. Winning this competition could therefore carry more than the value shown on the notice.
Bickleigh, on the edge of Dartmoor near Plymouth, is home to 42 Commando, the unit that carries the Royal Navy’s maritime boarding role. The Commando Training Centre at Lympstone, further east on the Exe estuary, is where recruits and officers are trained, so a second facility there would put the same equipment in front of marines earlier in their careers.

Three Russian missiles and two drones crossed Moldova’s airspace and exploded on Saturday morning, Moldovan Defense Minister Anatolie Nosatîi told TVR Moldova.
Moldova has seen a dramatic increase in Russian drone incursions in recent weeks as Russia ramps up near-constant drone attacks across Ukraine.
The five incidents occurred between 7:45 and 8:00 a.m., with explosions and debris reported across several districts. Moldova’s Foreign Ministry condemned the airspace violation.
Explosions and debris reported across Moldova
The Moldovan authorities initially said that five drones had crossed the country’s airspace before Nosatîi clarified that the five incidents involved three missiles and two drones. President Maia Sandu said the missiles were Banderol-type missiles, according to NewsMaker.
Nosatîi said the incidents had been documented and that evidence recovered at the sites could be presented to Russia’s ambassador.
Moldova’s Foreign Ministry said Russia’s war against Ukraine continues to create concrete threats for the country and condemned the violation of its airspace.
Moldova counted 39 Russian drone incursions in eight months, against 17 in all of 2025
According to NewsMaker, fragments were found outside Căușeni, near Dubovca in Hîncești District, between Delacău and Puhăceni in Anenii Noi District, and near Crocmaz in Ștefan Vodă District.
Near Crocmaz, an explosion in a vineyard field caused a vegetation fire and damaged windows at a nearby agricultural facility. Fragments were also found near Constantinovca in Căușeni District, where an explosion caused another vegetation fire.
Moldova’s Defense Ministry later reported a sixth unauthorized flight over the country that did not result in an explosion. The object entered Moldovan airspace at 8:04 a.m. from the direction of Udobne, Ukraine, and exited a minute later toward Biliaivka, Ukraine.
Moldova seeks stronger air defenses
Asked why the weapons were not intercepted, Nosatîi said Moldova was taking measures to strengthen its air-defense capabilities and acquire interception systems.
He said the drones are sophisticated and fast, adding that Moldova, like Ukraine, is learning how to defend against them. He also said Moldova needs additional resources to protect its 1,212-kilometer border with Ukraine and monitor its airspace.
Moldova is investing in air defense against the Russian drones crossing from Ukraine—Romania shoots down the ones that reach it
Moldovan authorities urged residents not to approach or touch any fragments they find, but to mark the location and notify police or the military so the area can be secured and the debris neutralized.

Your gut may be making a molecule that raises Alzheimer’s risk
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
12:13:21 UTC
21:13:21 KST

Your gut may be making a molecule that raises Alzheimer’s risk
- Date:
- October 3, 2026
- Source:
- University of Wisconsin-Madison
- Summary:
- Scientists have linked a gut bacterial compound called ImP to greater Alzheimer’s risk, harmful brain protein buildup, and faster cognitive decline. The finding raises the possibility that reducing ImP in the blood could one day help slow or prevent dementia.
- Share:
A molecule made by bacteria in the digestive system may increase the risk of Alzheimer's disease and accelerate cognitive decline in people with dementia, according to new research. The finding could point scientists toward a potential treatment strategy aimed at lowering Alzheimer's risk.
Nearly a decade ago, a research team led by University of Wisconsin-Madison professors Barbara Bendlin and Federico Rey found that the mix of microorganisms living in the intestines differs between people with Alzheimer's disease and healthy individuals.
"Since then, we've been trying to figure out how this difference in the gut perhaps leads to changes in the brain," says Bendlin, a professor of medicine in the UW School of Medicine and Public Health.
A Gut Molecule With Effects Beyond the Intestines
In a recent study published in the journal Nature Communications, Bendlin, Rey and their collaborators focused on imidazole propionate (ImP), a compound produced by certain bacteria in the gut. Their findings suggest that ImP may contribute to brain changes involved in Alzheimer's disease and related forms of dementia.
ImP production varies considerably from person to person. Some people appear to generate relatively large amounts, while others produce very little.
"ImP-producing bacteria are present in a large fraction of people, but they're not very abundant in most people," says Rey, a UW-Madison professor of bacteriology. "But something we have learned over the years is that a microbe doesn't have to be abundant to have an impact on the host."
Once produced in the gut, ImP can enter the circulation and reach other parts of the body. Previous research has linked the compound to type 2 diabetes and coronary artery disease.
The new study suggests that its effects may also extend to the brain. In mice, researchers found that ImP reaching the brain increased the accumulation of abnormal beta amyloid and tau proteins, two major hallmarks associated with Alzheimer's disease.
"That process eventually results in the death of neurons, and in humans is a key feature of Alzheimer's disease," Rey says.
Higher ImP Levels Linked to Faster Cognitive Decline
The researchers then examined blood samples from almost 1,200 people enrolled in the Wisconsin Registry for Alzheimer's Prevention and studies conducted through the Wisconsin Alzheimer's Disease Research Center.
Participants with higher concentrations of ImP in their blood were much more likely to show biological markers associated with abnormal proteins and impaired neuron function in dementia.
Because the volunteers had also completed cognitive testing over time, the researchers were able to compare ImP levels with changes in thinking and memory.
"And because we have the results of cognitive tests these volunteers took over time, we can see that the people with the highest ImP levels also experienced much faster cognitive decline," Rey says.
The team also discovered a genetic variation associated with substantially higher levels of ImP in the bloodstream. About 43% of the people in the study carried this variation.
Researchers suspect the genetic difference may influence how effectively the kidneys remove ImP from the blood, affecting how much of the compound remains in circulation.
"This genetic variation has been associated with increased Alzheimer's risk in large genetic studies before, and now we may understand why it's connected," Rey says.
A Potential New Target for Alzheimer's Prevention
One of the most important possibilities raised by the findings is that ImP itself could become a target for preventing or slowing Alzheimer's disease and related dementias.
However, reducing ImP through diet alone may not be straightforward. Gut bacteria produce the compound while generating energy from histidine, an amino acid that is essential for human health and found in many foods, particularly foods rich in protein.
"Generally improving your diet would probably help," Bendlin says. "But it's not as easy as saying, 'Stop eating eggs' or 'Don't eat so much red meat.' Because you need histidine, and it's all over the place."
Rather than trying to eliminate histidine from the diet, the researchers say the discovery could eventually lead to treatments that specifically reduce ImP levels in the bloodstream.
Identifying a particular molecule and a related genetic variation gives scientists a more precise target to investigate.
"It could be just like cholesterol, where people with elevated cholesterol take a drug, a statin, that reduces their risk for heart disease," Bendlin says. "If we can find an inhibitor that can help decrease the levels of ImP in the blood, that could hopefully reduce the risk of Alzheimer's and the speed of cognitive decline for a significant number of people."
Scientists from the University of California, Los Angeles and the University of Gothenburg also contributed to the study.
This research was supported in part by grants from the Wisconsin Partnership Program and the National Institutes of Health (R01AG070973, R01AG083883, R01AG092220, R21AG089348, R01HL168493, R01DK143650 and U54HL170326) and the U.S. Department of Agriculture (WIS03073).
Story Source:
Materials provided by University of Wisconsin-Madison. Original written by Chris Barncard. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- Vaibhav Vemuganti, Jea Woo Kang, Qijun Zhang, Eric R. McGregor, James R. Hilser, Ruben Aquino-Martinez, Sandra Harding, Joseph Lawrence Harpt, Katharina R. Beck, Hailey Bussan, Jessamine F. Kuehn, Yuetiva Deming, Rachel Studer, Sterling C. Johnson, Sanjay Asthana, Henrik Zetterberg, Kaj Blennow, Corinne D. Engelman, Hooman Allayee, Rozalyn M. Anderson, Tyler K. Ulland, Fredrik Bäckhed, Barbara B. Bendlin, Federico E. Rey. Gut bacterial metabolite imidazole propionate potentiates Alzheimer’s disease pathology. Seventeen EU leaders press Irish presidency to protect farm funding in next budget
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
12:13:19 UTC
21:13:19 KST

With Giorgia Meloni and Nicușor Dan as first signatories, the group also wants cohesion funding preserved, national rebates scrapped and NextGenerationEU loan repaid more slowly to free up fiscal space.
The leaders of 17 European Union countries have sent a letter to Taoiseach Micheál Martin, in his capacity as current president-in-office of the Council of the European Union, calling for agriculture to be given priority ahead of the revision of the Negotiating Box, the document drawn up by the presidency to steer and progressively narrow down negotiations on the EU's long-term budget.
As negotiations on the 2028-2034 Multiannual Financial Framework (MFF) enter a decisive phase, the leaders of Bulgaria, Cyprus, Croatia, Estonia, Greece, Italy, Latvia, Lithuania, Malta, Poland, Portugal, the Czech Republic, Romania, Slovakia, Slovenia, Spain and Hungary have sent "some reflections ahead of the forthcoming revision of the Negotiating Box".
"We fully recognise that the European Union is facing an evolving strategic environment, which brings with it new challenges but also new opportunities for joint European action," reads the letter, whose first signatories are Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni and Romanian President Nicușor Dan.
"The next MFF must enable Europe to seize these opportunities while at the same time responding to growing challenges, including security and defence, competitiveness, connectivity, energy security and resilience. At the same time, this must not come at the expense of treaty-based policies, which remain the backbone of European integration and themselves help to address these new challenges," the European leaders write.
"Therefore, the overall volume set out in the Negotiating Box of the Cypriot presidency remains the relevant basis for dealing effectively with all these financing needs. This is not the time for Europe to lower its ambitions," the heads of state and government add.
The leaders go on to stress that cohesion policy and the Common Agricultural Policy (CAP) are long-standing policies, but that their objectives are more relevant than ever. "They promote convergence between member states and regions, strengthen the single market and support rural and less developed areas. They also contribute to Europe's competitiveness and food security, while providing tangible support to millions of European citizens and demonstrating the added value of common European spending."
In their view, both policies have repeatedly adapted to new economic and social realities while remaining true to their treaty objectives. They also generate direct and indirect benefits for the economies of the entire European Union.
"We therefore believe that overall funding for cohesion policy and the CAP should be preserved in the next MFF. As underlined in our Joint Declaration of 26 May, these policies are already facing real-terms cuts under the Commission's proposal, despite the overall increase in the size of the MFF. A further reduction would not modernise the EU budget; it would merely weaken it and risk undermining public support for the European project. Moreover, the new MFF already entails a fundamental transformation of its structure, programming and spending approach," they explain.
The leaders also argue that Europe's new priorities require appropriate additional resources, while funding for agriculture and cohesion must be safeguarded.
They also say they are ready to work constructively on the revenue side, including on proposals for new own resources that would ease the direct pressure on national budgets. "Such resources should be genuine, fair, simple and non-regressive, in line with our May declaration. We will carefully assess the adjustments to the proposals that the Commission has committed to present," the letter continues.
According to the leaders of the 17 signatory countries, options that should be considered include a more gradual repayment of NextGenerationEU, which could create additional fiscal space in the next MFF, subject to an assessment of its impact on the overall cost of repayment, as well as limited and targeted European debt instruments for clearly identified strategic priorities, in line with the May declaration.
For the leaders, the current system of rebates should have no place in the next MFF. The rebates were intended to address an excessive burden on the contributions of certain member states. The circumstances that originally justified these corrections, they argue, have fundamentally changed. When assessing national contributions, account should be taken not only of their absolute level but also of the differing levels of prosperity of the member states and the relative effort required of each of them, the leaders conclude, saying they remain open to working with the Council presidency.

Scientists just made a superconductor stronger using “empty space”
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
12:03:23 UTC
21:03:23 KST

Scientists just made a superconductor stronger using “empty space”
- Date:
- October 3, 2026
- Source:
- Chinese Academy of Sciences Headquarters
- Summary:
- Researchers have demonstrated that quantum fluctuations in supposedly empty space can strengthen superconductivity, raising the transition temperature of an ultrathin material by as much as 5.4%. The discovery opens the possibility of using specially engineered vacuum environments to control quantum materials without direct contact or external driving.
- Share:
Researchers have demonstrated for the first time that quantum fluctuations in a vacuum can strengthen superconductivity, opening a new path for controlling unusual states of matter.
The study, published in Nature, was led by Profs. Changgan Zeng and Guanghui Cheng of the University of Science and Technology of China of the Chinese Academy of Sciences. The collaboration also included Prof. Qingdong Jiang of Shanghai Jiao Tong University, Prof. Frank Wilczek of the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, and other researchers.
Empty Space Is Not Truly Empty
In everyday language, a vacuum may sound like completely empty space. Quantum physics paints a very different picture.
According to quantum electrodynamics and the Heisenberg uncertainty principle, even the lowest energy state is never perfectly still. Virtual particles continually appear and disappear, producing an ever present background of quantum fluctuations.
These fluctuations are not merely theoretical. Their effects have been observed through well established phenomena such as the Lamb shift, spontaneous emission, and the Casimir effect.
For several years, the teams led by Zeng and Cheng have investigated how these vacuum fluctuations affect condensed matter systems. In an earlier study, the researchers showed that they could directly manipulate vacuum fluctuations by using a magnetic field to reversibly switch the Casimir force between attraction and repulsion.
That result raised a larger question: Could quantum vacuum fluctuations also be used to control macroscopic quantum states?
Turning the Vacuum Into a Control Tool
Jiang's group has approached the same problem from a theoretical perspective, studying how engineered quantum vacuum environments could influence different states of matter.
The researchers introduced the concept of "vacuumronics," in which specially designed vacuum environments are used to control electronic and photonic behavior. That theoretical work helped provide a framework for understanding the superconductivity enhancement observed in the new experiments.
"Vacuum fluctuations in free space are generally too weak to produce observable effects in macroscopic condensed-matter systems," said Prof. Zeng. "To overcome this limitation, we introduced a terahertz split-ring resonator. Such a dark cavity can reshape the electromagnetic environment and substantially amplify vacuum fluctuations."
To test the idea experimentally, the researchers placed the superconductor NbSe2 inside a terahertz dark cavity. This created a coupled system in which the superconducting material interacted with the specially engineered electromagnetic environment inside the cavity.
The team then compared the material's superconducting behavior inside and outside the cavity. The results showed that placing NbSe2 in the cavity significantly increased its superconducting critical temperature, the temperature below which the material enters its superconducting state.
Superconductivity Gets Stronger
"We observed that the critical temperature can increase by up to 5.4% in a six-layer NbSe2 device, while the critical current and critical magnetic field are significantly enhanced near the superconducting transition," said Prof. Cheng. "This represents the first experimental observation of vacuum-fluctuation-enhanced superconductivity."
The researchers conducted a series of control experiments to determine whether the effect could be explained by more conventional changes to the material.
They varied several properties of the setup, including the cavity geometry, characteristic frequency, material thicknesses, dielectric materials, and metallic strips. The results allowed them to rule out explanations involving strain, material degradation, inhomogeneity, and metallic screening effects.
One of the strongest clues came from the relationship between the superconductivity enhancement and the characteristic frequency of the dark cavity. Instead of changing smoothly, the enhancement showed a resonance-like peak at a particular frequency.
"This result, closely tied to the cavity's photonic properties, provides strong experimental evidence of the coupling between the superconducting state and dark-cavity modes," said Prof. Zeng.
Virtual Photons May Explain the Effect
To explain what was happening, Jiang's team and Wilczek developed a theoretical model based on the Ginzburg-Landau framework.
Their interpretation suggests that the superconducting state exchanges virtual photons with the dark cavity. This interaction lowers the energy of the superconducting state, making superconductivity more stable and effectively strengthening it.
"When the characteristic energy of the cavity mode matched the low-energy superconducting fluctuations, the NbSe2 device exhibited resonant enhancement, producing the peak in superconductivity enhancement," said Prof. Jiang.
The result changes the usual way physicists think about the vacuum. Rather than serving only as an empty backdrop, the quantum vacuum can potentially be engineered to influence the behavior of matter itself.
"In most practical physics, the vacuum serves merely as the passive stage on which phenomena play out. This work shows that the background itself can become an actor -- engineered to strengthen superconductivity and reshape the behavior of quantum matter," said Prof. Wilczek.
A New Way To Control Quantum Matter
The approach strengthens superconductivity without directly driving the material with an external energy source. Instead, the researchers reshape the surrounding vacuum environment, providing a noncontact method for influencing a quantum state of matter.
That could eventually make engineered vacuum fluctuations a useful new control mechanism for superconductors and other quantum materials.
"With further optimization of cavity structures and material systems, vacuum-fluctuation coupling may enable more pronounced and widely applicable control of quantum states," said Prof. Zeng.

- Zheyan Wang, Gabriel Cardoso, Liu Yang, Xun Gong, Chi Zhang, Yufei Zhu, Dongbo Zhang, Nan Pan, Hongbing Cai, Yong P. Chen, Qing-Dong Jiang, Guanghui Cheng, Frank Wilczek, Changgan Zeng. Evidence for vacuum-enhanced superconductivity in NbSe2. Nature, 2026; 657 (8133): 912 DOI: 10.1038/s41586-026-11037-x

Bacon has long been a favourite of carnivores, but there is growing consumer concern about the health risks posed by nitrites, chemicals used to cure meats.
While many experts argue there is no evidence processed meat made without nitrites is safer, retailers have responded to consumer concerns by offering “nitrite-free” products to meet demand.
Denhay, the Devon hand- dry-cured bacon specialist, has launched two new back bacon lines in 570 Tesco stores from 21 September – Made Without Nitrites Smoked Back Bacon and Made Without Nitrites Unsmoked Back Bacon (both 200g), both priced at £4.
Waitrose has doubled its Made Without Nitrites range in the past year, with sales up more than 34%. Sales of its British roast and honey roast hams have risen more than 70% since launching in May, and its unsmoked back bacon is up 22%.
Data from Worldpanel by Numerator shows nitrite-free bacon growing steadily while conventional bacon declines, and its share of the fresh bacon category has risen steadily from a small base. In the 52 weeks to 6 September 2026, nitrite-free spend reached £34.8m (up 11.4% year on year) and volumes were up to 2.2m kg (up 8.0%), while spend and volume for conventional bacon was 9.2% and 4.9%, respectively.
Emer Lowry, a nutritionist at Waitrose, said: “As our customers pay closer attention to on-pack ingredient lists, providing options without added nitrites gives shoppers more choice without compromising on flavour and taste.”
Marlene Godwin, the managing director of Denhay, said the move was prompted by retailers and shoppers rather than the producer. “We definitely don’t want to be telling people what to eat. This is about giving bacon lovers choice, not replacement. Retailers were saying customers want this, can you provide it?
She added: “I can’t speak for shoppers, but I think health consciousness is driving it, and consumers are more interested. One of the things people said to me was, why not convert everything? Our customers still love traditional cure, but we’re offering another choice.”
Sodium and potassium nitrates and nitrites are chemicals that are often used to preserve or “cure” meat.
Nitrates, which contain one nitrogen and three oxygens atoms, can be converted by bacteria into nitrites, which contain one nitrogen and two oxygen atoms.
Nitrites help to prevent the growth of microbes, including harmful bacteria, and can enhance the flavour and pink colour of meat products.
People do not consume these chemicals only through eating meat – nitrates are also provided by vegetables, in particular leafy greens.
The Food Standards Agency (FSA) says the key difference is that when nitrates or nitrites are consumed as part of protein-rich foods such as meat, they are converted into chemicals known as nitrosamines, which are thought to be harmful to health.
“Vegetables provide nitrates alongside beneficial nutrients such as vitamin C, polyphenols and fibre. These nutrients help to reduce the formation of harmful nitrosamines,” the FSA adds
The World Health Organization’s cancer agency classes processed meat as a group 1 carcinogen, the same category as tobacco, though the known link between processed meat and cancer cannot be directly attributed to nitrites.
Research suggests eating about 50g of processed meat a day, roughly two rashers of bacon, is linked to a 16% higher relative risk of colorectal cancer.
The FSA says no single component of processed meat has been identified as the cause, and there is no definitive evidence that nitrites directly cause cancer.
The FSA also says there is no evidence that processed meats made without nitrate or nitrite additives are safer. It adds that removing them can create food safety challenges, because they help prevent the growth of dangerous bacteria and must be replaced by other methods of preservation.
Gabriela Peacock, a nutritionist and founder of GP Nutrition, said: “People are much more interested in what is actually in their food now. They are turning packets over, reading ingredient lists and looking for products that feel a little less processed. If someone enjoys bacon or ham but sees an option made without added nitrates, it can feel like a very easy, positive swap, without having to change the way they eat completely.”
Peacock said nitrite-free products are often more expensive. “That may be because they are made by smaller producers, use different curing methods or have a shorter shelf life. They may also use higher-welfare meat or more expensive ingredients. Sometimes, of course, you are paying for the premium positioning and packaging too,” she said.
She added: “The most expensive option is not automatically the healthiest, just as ‘nitrate-free’ does not give a product a magic health halo. Nitrates and nitrites help to preserve meat and control harmful bacteria, and the Food Standards Agency says there is currently no evidence that processed meat made without them is safer.”

“He’s offering what no other politician has offered for a long, long time. He actually feels like he’s one of us,” was how Neil, a geography teacher, described Andy Burnham in our focus group on Thursday night.
Neil wasn’t alone in his praise: this group of Labour 2024 voters – some of whom had drifted to Reform, the Tories and Greens during the Starmer era – provided the most positive reception for a politician since Boris Johnson at the height of his Covid-vaccine bounce.
Talent manager Megan said: “He feels more relatable to people from a working–class background.” Simran, another teacher, added: “He’s obviously better than the others in the short timeframe that he’s been in his position.” Linda, who works in banking, went further, saying: “He actually sounds like a person that’s there, not just for himself, but for all of us, which none of the others prior to him came across that way.”
That praise for Burnham stood in stark contrast to his predecessor Keir Starmer who was, as contracts manager Craig put it, “just a shambles from the moment they won the election up until he left”. None of the group felt it would have been better to keep the former PM in place.
Labour’s conference also seemed to have cut through the noise of the attention economy. Most had picked up at least something from the prime minister’s speech and liked what they had heard. After seeing the clip where Burnham spoke emotionally about the death of his father, the group, in contrast to some online criticism, appreciated a politician willing to show his human side.
But what about two of the substantive proposals in the speech?
On Burnham’s pledge to revisit the UK’s relationship with the EU there was an overwhelming feeling Brexit had been a disaster. Most in this group had voted to remain, but even those like Darren, a field manager at a utility company who had voted Leave, felt cheated: “The amount we got told we were putting into the EU, I thought we could stand on our own two feet … we got told quite a few things, and it didn’t quite happen.”
Interestingly, for most of the group it was less the economic impact of Brexit that worried them but instead the sense of isolation in an increasingly dangerous world and a less reliable US.
But, and here is the caveat, once it came to the specifics of what rejoining may involve the group were far more cautious. Many felt if Britain could rejoin on its old terms it would be a “no brainer”. But the participants now worried that Britain would end up with a worse deal as punishment.
Neil said: “I voted remain, but we’ll get utterly shafted if we rejoin … what do they gain?” Others described feeling 50/50 and nervous about where we’d end up. If this group is anything to go by, Burnham’s biggest fight won’t be in the principle but the details.
What about Burnham’s other, more controversial, pledge that the triple lock would be reformed to pay for social care? The discussion here revealed two things. First the rise in wages is less salient to people than other bits of the lock; most of the group felt as if their wages had not kept up with inflation for a long time anyway, so pensioners would not really lose out. As Linda put it: “My salary has not been increasing that greatly.”
Second, reforming care is a real priority. For Tariq, who works in the pharmaceutical industry, this was an example that “sometimes you need to take hard decisions”.
But the mood definitely shifted when the group were played a clip from Unite leader, Sharon Graham, opposing the move. Suddenly some participants worried this was “taking off pensioners” while others asked “couldn’t the highest earners fund it instead”.
And the group were even more negative when they read former Institute for Fiscal Studies chief Paul Johnson’s analysis that triple lock reform wouldn’t pay for a national care service in the near term and so taxes would have to rise.
None of the group were willing to pay more taxes, personally, for care. Simran said: “If the income tax increases any more, you’re going to find people are going to migrate.” Joanne, who works in dentistry, added: “I feel rather selfish about it because I don’t want to pay any more tax ... people just can’t afford to live a decent life at the moment.”
This led to a wider discussion about the budget and people’s worries that, while Burnham had done some “small things”, was it just going to be, as Linda put it, “robbing Peter and paying Paul”.
If this group is anything to go by, Burnham is impressing the voters who put Labour into office in 2024, and has earned his party a rehearing that Starmer simply could not. But beyond the top line, big questions remain on the details. The Labour leader can be happy with the reception for Tuesday’s speech but definitely cannot afford to rest on a post-conference glow in the battle for public opinion on his plans.
