====================================================================================================

Across China: New paths to lower carbon take shape on China's tropical island
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
19:41:07 CST
20:41:07 KST

HAIKOU, Oct. 3 (Xinhua) -- With a gentle pull of a lever, an operator sends a giant claw plunging into a mountain of waste at a waste-to-energy plant. It scoops up more than five tonnes at a time -- enough to generate the electricity a typical household uses in a year.
The waste is then fed into incinerators burning at over 850 degrees Celsius. The plant in China's southernmost province of Hainan processes some 4,200 tonnes of household garbage daily, generating about 1.7 million kilowatt-hours of power, roughly what more than 200,000 households use in a day.
This transformation of trash into energy is part of a broader low-carbon experiment in Hainan, known for its blue seas, tropical forests and abundant sunshine.
Since 2021, Hainan has closed 16 household waste landfills. With eight waste-to-energy plants now in operation, the province has achieved zero landfilling of untreated household waste, saving precious land resources while reducing the emission of methane, a potent greenhouse gas, generated by landfills.
However, disposing of waste in a more environmentally friendly way is only part of the story. Hainan is also working to reduce waste at its source, beginning with plastic bags.
The change can be seen at a produce market in the provincial capital Haikou. Each of the more than 300 stalls has a digital ledger tracking where their shopping bags were bought, while a system generates green, yellow or red codes daily to flag whether the bags meet environmental requirements.
Since the digital system was introduced in April, the use of fully biodegradable bags has jumped from 18 percent to 81 percent in the market.
The call for biodegradable bags at the market was initially met with skepticism, with some vendors even hiding non-compliant bags from inspectors.
A meat vendor surnamed Wu, who has worked at the market for seven years, was among the skeptics, assuming that greener bags would simply cost more.
"Only after comparing them did I realize that the biodegradable bags here are cheaper than those sold elsewhere or online, and they are more durable," Wu said.
The market is one small piece of a province-wide push. Hainan was the first in China to impose a province-wide ban on non-biodegradable single-use plastic products through legislation.
By the end of 2025, alternatives to such banned plastic products accounted for an average of 80.2 percent at key venues including schools, hospitals, supermarkets and produce markets.
"A 'zero-waste island' is not simply about waste management, but a green transition that runs through the entire operation of a city," said Wang Chenye, deputy head of the Hainan academy of environmental sciences.
Some 100 km away from Haikou, a low-carbon experiment is also underway in the town of Boao. The Boao zero-carbon demonstration zone, China's first project to achieve zero-carbon operation through urban renewal, was created by retrofitting an existing area rather than being built from scratch.
Inside a hotel kitchen on Boao's Dongyu Island, chefs toss woks over sizzling stoves, but there is no flame in sight. Hotel kitchens across the island have been fully electrified.
"An all-electric kitchen alone can cut carbon dioxide emissions by 7.5 tonnes a day," said Luo Hu, an engineer with COSCO SHIPPING Boao Co., Ltd., a company involved in the zero-carbon demonstration zone project. He added that carbon traceability has been introduced for one-fifth of the dishes to help diners better understand the carbon footprint.
Across Dongyu Island in Boao, hotels and conference venues have undergone green renovations, while vehicles and boats have switched to new energy. Altogether, the transformation involved 18 projects spanning green buildings, renewable energy and greener transport, according to Luo.
"Carrying out zero-carbon retrofits with high heat, high humidity and frequent typhoons means there is no ready-made model to follow," said Zeng Youwen, chief engineer of the Hainan branch of the China Academy of Urban Planning and Design.
The effort has paid off. The zone now generates more green electricity than it consumes and has entered sustained zero-carbon operation. Energy-related carbon dioxide emissions from buildings and municipal infrastructure in the zone fell from about 11,350 tonnes in 2019 to just 14.6 tonnes in 2025, a reduction of 99.9 percent.
Hainan is seeking to take such low-carbon practices much further during the 15th Five-Year Plan period (2026-2030).
Under a provincial low-carbon island plan, Hainan aims to complete building a low-carbon island before 2045 and reduce annual CO2 emissions by 70 percent from peak levels. The plan maps out changes across energy, industry, transport and buildings, alongside efforts to strengthen the island's carbon sinks.
The pursuit is already yielding tangible results in Hegui Village in Lingao County. Some 48 hectares of mangroves, long valued for shielding the coast from waves, are estimated to sequester 3,236.05 tonnes of carbon over seven years, potentially bringing over 320,000 yuan (about 47,500 U.S. dollars) to the village collective.
"This mangrove forest not only protects us from waves, but earns money through carbon credits," said Chen Hongwei, an official of the village. "That gives us even more reason to protect it." ■

====================================================================================================

Powerful nuclear attack submarine arrives in Scotland
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
12:40:53 BST
20:40:53 KST

HMS Agamemnon, the sixth of the Royal Navy’s Astute-class hunter-killer submarines, has arrived at her home port of HM Naval Base Clyde for the first time, a week after sailing from the Barrow yard where she was built, according to the Royal Navy.
Members of the Submarine Flotilla lined up to greet her, alongside the Director Submarines, Rear Admiral Andy Perks, the Naval Base Commander Clyde, Commodore Andy Bray, and the Commander of the Submarine Flotilla, Commodore Ben Haskins.
Rear Admiral Perks said: “The arrival of HMS Agamemnon at HM Naval Base Clyde is a significant milestone for the Royal Navy. Her delivery reflects the dedication, skill and collaboration of thousands of people across our Defence Nuclear Enterprise, who have worked together to build one of the world’s most capable attack submarines and deliver a formidable warfighting capability for the United Kingdom.
“As she begins a demanding programme of sea trials and operational preparation, I am delighted to welcome the Submarine and her Ship’s Company to their new home on the Clyde, and I look forward to seeing them join the operational fleet in due course.”
The timing carried a certain weight for the Submarine Service, since the boat came alongside exactly 125 years to the day after the launch of Holland 1, the Royal Navy’s first submarine. Agamemnon left BAE Systems at Barrow on 25 September with around 100 submariners aboard, and the trials that began on passage will run on for weeks and months yet, testing her performance, manoeuvrability, speed and general seaworthiness.
Her commanding officer, Commander John Gabb, said: “It is an enormous privilege to be the first person to command this vessel at sea.
“We will get to know Agamemnon well over the coming months, but this submarine is incredibly quiet, has a world-class Sonar and will be home to us all as we generate for operations.”
The passage north included the boat’s first dive at sea, carried out in the Inner Hebrides Exercise Areas under the watchful eye of a Royal Navy Merlin helicopter. She had been submerged once before, in a trim dive at Devonshire Dock Hall in October 2025, when she went down some 15 metres without leaving the building.
Commander Gabb said of the dive: “The first dive for any submarine is a significant achievement in its generation. While this time we were being supported by a Merlin helicopter, it will not be long before we are conducting realistic pre-operational training using the same aircraft to simulate the enemy.
“Next time we will be pushing the crew and the submarine to its maximum potential to operate undetected.”
Agamemnon’s keel was laid in July 2013 and she was commissioned by the King on 22 September last year, which gives some sense of how long a modern nuclear boat takes to get from the first steel to the open sea. Astute, Ambush, Artful, Audacious and Anson are already in service, and the seventh and final boat of the class, HMS Achilles, is still under construction at Barrow after being renamed from Agincourt in January 2025.
Commodore Haskins said: “Welcoming HMS Agamemnon, the newest submarine of the Flotilla into her new home at HM Naval Base Clyde is a special moment for our Service. To get here the crew have conducted themselves with the professionalism and dedication that is expected from every one of our submariners.
“Today’s milestone marks the first step on a journey which will soon see this outstanding boat delivering high-tempo operations across the globe.”
The Royal Navy describes the Astutes as the largest, most advanced and most powerful attack submarines it has ever operated. They are the first class built without optical periscopes, using high-specification video technology to scan the horizon instead, and the service calls them the quietest submarines ever constructed, able to circumnavigate the globe submerged while making their own oxygen and drinking water.
Their armament runs to the Tomahawk land attack missile, which lets them strike targets hundreds of miles inland, and the Spearfish heavyweight torpedo, which the Royal Navy says can engage at up to 30 miles at low speed.

Moscow has ramped up its pummelling of Kyiv, launching waves of drones at the city, targeting key infrastructure and putting the capital on a near-constant state of alert against attacks.
The strike on the Northern Bridge on the morning of Oct 3 wounded two people and damaged road surface and trolleybus overhead wires, restricting traffic, Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko said.
AFP reporters saw traces of an explosion on a pedestrian walkway and technicians repairing power lines on the bridge.
Hours after the attack, the Russian authorities warned of more strikes, issuing a fresh call for diplomats and foreigners to leave the city and refrain from visiting Ukraine.
“We note with concern that not everyone has heeded these warnings, and that individuals are knowingly exposing themselves to mortal danger,” the Russian Foreign Ministry said in a statement.
The Russian ministry also stated that “responsibility for any potential negative consequences rests entirely with those who ignore this warning.”
Moscow issued a similar warning in May but heads of state and governments from countries backing Ukraine have defied it by travelling to the war-torn country and the capital in show of support.
On Oct 2, Klitschko said the city was in a “very dramatic situation” and should now be on a war footing as the enemy was “tearing Kyiv apart” with strikes on bridges and energy infrastructure.
President Volodymyr Zelensky accused his Russian counterpart, Vladimir Putin, of ripping up the rulebook of armed conflict by sanctioning massive attacks on civilian areas, an accusation the Kremlin has rejected.
Traffic chaos
Kyiv has been increasingly under aerial bombardment in recent months, with the attacks and alerts disrupting daily life and sowing traffic chaos.
Long lines of stationary cars and buses clogged major roads on Oct 2 as commuters sought alternate routes, with some forced to continue their journeys on foot.
Air raid sirens warning of approaching threats sound almost round the clock, urging the city’s estimated three million people to seek shelter.
Strikes across the country in recent days have also caused power outages in several regions in the east, north and centre, with grid operator Ukrenergo urging consumers to limit usage even as demand increases with colder weather.
Ukraine is bracing for another difficult winter. In 2026, heating and power were cut for days on end as temperatures plunged to minus 20 deg C.
The grinding war, which began with Russia’s full-scale invasion in February 2022, has turned into Europe’s bloodiest conflict since World War II.
Ukraine has appeared to stabilise the front in recent months, but depleted air-defence stocks since the start of the US-Israeli war in Iran have left its cities exposed to Russian barrages.
The US-brokered peace efforts are effectively frozen as Moscow has shown no signs of dropping its maximalist conditions to end the war, including a demand that Ukraine cede territory in the east that Russia’s troops have not captured. AFP

Oral, dental health campaign to be held
TEHRAN – The national oral and dental health campaign is scheduled to be held from October 17 to 23 nationwide, focusing on training, self-care, and prevention.
The week-long event will be held under the theme ‘Don’t forget two times two, brushing your teeth for two minutes twice a day’, the health ministry’s website reported.
As the campaign primarily focuses on students, the health ministry, in cooperation with the Ministry of Education, will conduct oral health education at schools to improve the knowledge of children and families about oral health.
With the help of student health ambassadors and healthcare providers at school, they will teach students about proper nutrition and how to brush and floss their teeth correctly.
The health ministry is also planning to benefit from the capacity of dental offices, mass media, and social media to hold educational and preventive programs related to oral health for the promotion of self-care and enhancement of oral health literacy among the public.
In the past Iranian year, the program was held in some 34,000 schools, providing services to more than three million students across the country, IRNA quoted Zahra Qorbani, a health ministry official, as saying in January.
World Oral Health Day (WOHD) is celebrated every year on March 20 to empower people with the tools and knowledge to prevent and control oral diseases, which affect nearly 3.5 billion people worldwide.
It encourages people to look after their oral health by adopting a good oral hygiene routine and managing risk factors.
Themed ‘A Happy Mouth Is… A Happy Life’, WOHD 2026 spotlighted oral health as the foundation of lifelong well-being — from a baby’s first teeth to maintaining a healthy smile in older age.

Trump ruled out a U.S. ban on diesel exports following the G7 decision

Trump ruled out a U.S. ban on diesel exports following the G7 decision
Kyiv • UNN
The G7 will immediately release up to 100 million barrels of oil and diesel over four months. Trump said that the United States would not restrict exports.
U.S. President Donald Trump said on October 2 that the United States would not impose a ban on diesel fuel exports, welcoming the decision by European countries to release fuel from their reserves. UNN reports this with reference to the BBC.
Details
The G7 announced the release of 100 million barrels of oil and diesel fuel to ease supply problems that have caused prices to surge. This includes a "significant release" of diesel fuel over 20 days, as well as discussions on "additional releases of diesel fuel as necessary," according to a statement by G7 leaders.
The G7 will release 100 million barrels of oil amid rising prices02.10.26, 18:33 • 5858 views
The group of advanced economies, including the United States, said the move would begin immediately and last for four months.
Under the measures taken after U.S. President Donald Trump threatened to ban diesel fuel exports, there will be no "export restrictions on energy carriers and energy products" among G7 members.
The G7 comprises the United States, the United Kingdom, Canada, Japan, Germany, Italy, and France; the EU is also represented at its meetings.
Donald Trump warned that he would ban diesel fuel exports from the United States if European countries did not agree to release more of their own reserves onto the market. This would ease price pressure on American consumers ahead of the midterm elections in November, but would lead to higher prices in other countries.
On Friday, October 2, Trump wrote on social media: "Europe has just agreed to release a huge amount of its diesel fuel, of which it has large reserves. The process will begin immediately."
His U.S. Treasury Secretary, Scott Bessent, argued that American farmers, truckers, and businesses "should not bear the burden" of rising prices.
Speaking later at the White House, Trump said that a ban on diesel fuel exports had "never been discussed."
Referring to the G7's decision to release fuel from its reserves, he added that "what Europe did was a great thing."
"Europe has a lot of diesel fuel, and they will make a significant contribution to the global economy—as will we," he said.
And we are not going to impose an export ban; we are going to do what we have to do
Trump initially said he supported a ban on diesel fuel exports at the beginning of last week, and was still considering the issue on Thursday, as his administration pressured Europe to use its reserves.
Diesel is widely used by the transportation industry and in agriculture, meaning that rising fuel costs increase the cost of producing essential goods such as food, the publication notes.
After the G7 leaders' meeting, French President Emmanuel Macron said the bloc had agreed to release reserves of "up to 100 million barrels" over four months under the coordination of the International Energy Agency (IEA).
Macron said the coordinated action would "lower prices for petroleum products, particularly diesel fuel." Referring to the agreement not to impose export bans, Macron said that "President Trump, in particular, expressed himself very clearly on this issue."
In a joint statement, G7 leaders said: "We will fulfill our commitments by coordinating through the IEA the release of 100 million barrels, beginning immediately over four months, including a significant release of diesel fuel during the first 20 days by G7 members and partners."
It remains unclear which partner countries will release their reserves, and how quickly.
What about oil prices
The 100 million barrels are expected to include both diesel fuel and crude oil. The price of the global Brent crude benchmark briefly fell below $100 per barrel, but had risen to approximately $102 by Friday evening. Before the U.S. and Israeli invasion of Iran, it was trading at around $73.
Matt Smith, director of commodity research at Kpler, said that oil prices had risen again due to renewed strikes between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis in Yemen.
"Oil prices fell sharply following the announcement of the release of strategic reserves in Europe, but reversed course amid rumors that Saudi Arabia is planning an offensive in Yemen in an attempt to restore a safe route through Bab el-Mandeb," he said.
The G7 leaders said they would also coordinate maintenance schedules to avoid several refineries being shut down at the same time, while encouraging countries with such capabilities to increase refining, particularly of diesel fuel.

How the brain uses memory to imagine what might have been
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
11:36:39 UTC
20:36:39 KST

A month ago philosopher Felipe De Brigard received a strange phone call. “Are you in a private place where you can have a private conversation?” the voice on the other end asked.
He was on a work retreat surrounded by colleagues. “Just say you need to talk about your taxes,” the caller said. De Brigard excused himself to find a private space, panicking the whole time about his taxes—but it was actually the MacArthur Foundation on the line. De Brigard had been awarded a prestigious “genius grant,” an $800,000 fellowship with no strings attached.
“I just was floored. And I had to put everything back together and walk back in like nothing happened,” says De Brigard, who is a professor at Duke University and originally from Bogotá, Colombia. He is only the second philosopher to be awarded the fellowship in the past 30 years.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
De Brigard would be the first to tell you that his recollection of that day may be flawed. As a philosopher and cognitive scientist, he studies the fallibility of memory. Our brains don’t work like digital cameras recording our experiences to a mental hard drive, he explains. We store only some parts of our experience—gestures, stories, the gist. When we go to retrieve those memories, our brains need to fill in the gaps.
De Brigard’s research shows just how intertwined our brain’s memory is with imagination. We use some of the same mental machinery to reconstruct the past as we do to imagine the future—and to imagine what might have been.
Scientific American spoke with De Brigard about why false memories form, why we dwell on the roads not taken, how forgiveness influences memory and whether we should worry about artificial intelligence becoming conscious.
[An edited transcript of the conversation follows.]
What big question about memory first intrigued you?
I had the huge fortune of being in grad school at a moment in which there were some massive discoveries in episodic memory, or our capacity to remember specific experiences from our past. In 2007 there were three papers that sort of solidified a hunch that the renowned psychologist Endel Tulving had in the 1980s, which was that our capacity to remember the past is also needed for thinking about the future. Tulving had a very famous case report with a patient known as K.C. with hippocampal amnesia. When you asked him to remember an event that happened in his life, he drew a blank. But if you asked him to think about what he was going to do, say, next Christmas, he also drew a blank. It’s not that his imagination was broken across the board—he could imagine lots of things—but things that were part of his personal trajectory, both from the past and the possible future, seemed to be impaired.
So these three papers basically solidified this idea that the hippocampus and the network that we use for episodic recollection are deployed when we think about possible futures. Now, my question was, this is a very asymmetric way of thinking about personal time. When you remember the past, that’s what actually happened. But when you imagine the future, you’re imagining lots of possibilities, right? I started thinking, what if the same mechanisms are required to think about not only what actually happened but also what could have happened in the past? I call that episodic “counterfactual” thinking because it’s contrary to fact. And sure enough, we did a bunch of experiments, and we realized that the hippocampus is required for imaginations about possibilities that pertain to oneself.
Why would memory and imagination would be entwined? Why would we evolve that way?
So, two things: The first one is that you cannot store absolutely every detail of every experience. This suggests your brain needs to employ some computational shortcuts when it’s trying to remember the past. By filling in those gaps at the time of retrieval with the most likely possibility, your memory system can actually be quicker and be more flexible and work online in a timely manner.
The second reason is that you want your memory system and your imagination of possibilities to be highly connected. To use an expression that the philosopher Karl Popper used, we generate hypotheses so that they can die in our stead. We want to imagine alternative ways in which past events could have happened or might happen in the future to hedge future uncertainty. And if we have them really closely connected to our memory mechanisms, then we can store those mental simulations.
There are so many pieces of fiction that exercise this kind of counterfactual thinking, exploring what might have happened—like the alternate history of The Man in the High Castle or even in rom-coms such as Sliding Doors. What do you make of our tendency to dwell on these stories?
I think one of the reasons why fiction is so important in life is precisely because it allows you to inhabit those possibilities and learn from them. Sometimes I give this talk that that I call “The Moral Demands of Imagination.” I think that we are required to employ imagination in all sorts of different tasks in life, and sometimes there are moral demands to imagine things properly. Suppose that you are in jury duty, and they ask you to imagine what the defendant could have done in a particular situation. Suppose that the defendant is like me, a middle-aged Latino who moved to the U.S. in his 20s, and he did something wrong. If they asked me as a juror to imagine what this person could have done instead of what they did, I’m going to have a ton of experiences that I can draw from to generate that mental simulation. By contrast, if someone asks me, “Can you imagine what this Iranian woman in the 1920s would have done?” I have no idea what it would be like to be her. Absent the actual experience, the next best thing is to read about it.
We’ve been talking about the brain a lot like a computer—it runs computations and makes inferences based on probabilities, like large language models do. Is that a superficial similarity to you, or is there a deeper likeness between our brains and AI?
It is actually a really great question because it’s something that I myself have struggled with. Twenty years ago, when I first started thinking about the mind as sort of like the “software of the brain,” I was convinced. I was absolutely convinced that neurons really computed, that they were like biological microchips and that you could sort of reverse engineer the mind like you could a computer.
Someone who has influenced me quite a bit here is a philosopher called Mazviita Chirimuuta. She wrote an extraordinarily beautiful book called The Brain Abstracted. It made me think about how many idealizations [such as the brain as a computer] are super helpful, even if they’re wrong. I think computational models to explain, among other things, memory retrieval are extremely helpful. Whether the model is actually capturing what the neurons do, I don’t know, and I think it actually probably doesn’t. I don’t think that neurons are the only thing that matters for cognition. And I think the jury is still out as to whether neurons are actually computing or if it is best to think of neurons as computers. But many of the computational models that we have are extremely useful—in fact, they are part of the inspiration that we have for AI systems.
You’ve written a lot about consciousness, including criticizing a leading theory as pseudoscience. What do you make of the claims about AI consciousness?
This is interesting. Last semester I taught a class on consciousness and AI, and I didn’t have a view one way or another. I am a little bit more worried about whether AI could be agential, as in agency. In almost everything that we see in the world, agency and consciousness are highly correlated. We tend to think of them together, but I think that they are separable. And it has become pretty clear that there are many AI systems that seem to exhibit something like agency, and that is going to require a set of regulations and rules and ways of interacting with them that are going to be challenging. Whether or not they’re conscious is a little bit irrelevant to the decisions that we have to make right away regarding their agency. I think that that’s the more urgent question.
That makes sense—you don’t need to get bogged down in most the “hard problem” of consciousness and phenomenology to address the urgent questions involving AI right now.
Exactly. I don’t know how apt this comparison is, but I grew up with bullfighting in Colombia, and it seemed like an extraordinarily violent spectacle. Of course the bulls were suffering. But imagine we discover that in order to experience pain you need to have a particular pain receptor, and for whatever reason, the bulls are the only animals on Earth that don’t have it. The whole thing wouldn’t be less monstrous.
I think that it is very hard to separate consciousness and subjectivity from agency, and I think that a similar thing would be probably an exercise that we have to do to understand what to do with AIs that are becoming agents.
Speaking of Colombia, you are currently working on a research project, following the peace agreement reached 10 years ago, on memory and forgiveness with victims of political violence there. Is that what you’ll use the MacArthur Fellowship funds for?
Yes, I think that the majority of the award is going to go toward the memory and forgiveness project in Colombia. So far, the evidence seems to support what we call the emotional fading account: namely that forgiving helps us to modify the [emotional] reactions that we have toward the memories of wrongdoings, without necessarily making us forget the details of the event.
This is very important, especially in the context of postconflict Colombia, because we don’t want to forget what happened. And part of what we are showing is that forgiveness does not involve the forgetting of the memory but the emotional reappraisal of the original memory. Our goal with this award would be to continue that research and to try to explore now strategies in which we can employ emotional reappraisal techniques to bring people closer to forgive and reconcile. I am also profoundly interested in the hippocampus in the brain, and for me it’s still a big puzzle to try to understand exactly how this structure in the brain brings together both space and time. So I have a number of hypotheses and experiments that I want to conduct to try to fully understand the functioning of the hippocampus.
This might seem like an obvious question, but why is forgiveness a good?
I don’t think forgiveness is good all the time. I think that I think that forgiveness is a really efficient strategy to regulate your emotions and your reactive attitudes toward the perpetrators of past wrongdoings. In the case of Colombia, and in particular in the regions of Montes de María, which is where I work, because of the peace process, many of the perpetrators are coming back to live in the same communities with the same victims that they once victimized. It’s very important that we explore ways in which the emotions can be sort of mollified. Forgiveness is an extremely good way of doing that, but it’s not the only way, nor is it mandatory. That also respects the wishes of the participants that would like to have that emotional change without feeling that they need to forgive, because I do believe that there are unforgivable offenses.
How do you facilitate forgiveness?
Where the science of forgiveness has been the most explored is actually in couples therapy. There is this clinician, Everett Worthington, who has a therapy called REACH with steps that people can follow. But it’s very different to forgive your spouse with whom you have had a relationship as opposed to, say, the commander of the battalion of the paramilitary group that killed your brother. You didn’t have a relationship with that person, and you don’t want to have a relationship later.
Contrary to popular belief, forgiveness is not exactly a situation that occurs in a relationship of two, a perpetrator and a victim. Two of my co-investigators in Colombia, Pablo Abitbol and Santiago Amaya, they think that forgiveness in postconflict Colombia actually is a three-party relationship that involves the community as well. It’s part of an ongoing investigation to try to fully understand: Does forgiveness have different concepts depending on the relationship? Is it the same phenomena? That’s what we’re trying to figure out.

St. Petersburg circus unveils water-based show featuring fur seals and chimpanzees

ST. PETERSBURG, October 3. /TASS/. The premiere of Island, a water-based circus show, has taken place at the Great St. Petersburg State Circus. According to Sergey Belyakov, General Director of the state-run circus company Rosgostsirk, the production was inspired by the aquatic program presented by Gaetano Ciniselli at the same venue 125 years ago.
"A water circus is one of the most beautiful and spectacular forms of circus entertainment imaginable. The inspiration for this production was Gaetano Ciniselli’s 'Circus Underwater' program, which drew thunderous applause and amazed audiences in its day," Belyakov said at a press conference ahead of the premiere. He also noted that next year Rosgostsirk’s flagship venue - the Great St. Petersburg Circus, also known as the Circus on Fontanka or Ciniselli Circus - will celebrate its 150th anniversary.
The creators conceived Island as a water-based circus adventure in which a voyage aboard a luxury cruise liner turns into an unexpected journey to a mysterious island. According to the show's director, Daria Kostyuk, the production is among the most multi-genre shows in the circus world. Each act tells a distinct story centered on vivid characters, while performances in the air, on stage, and in the water are complemented by changing scenery, elaborate costumes, and animal acts. The story brings together themes of friendship, courage, and unexpected discoveries.
"There are around 140 tons of water in the Ciniselli Circus today, right in the legendary ring. It provides a setting where not only gymnasts, acrobats, and aerialists can demonstrate their creativity and talent, but animals as well. We have also invited a professional synchronized swimming team," Kostyuk said.
The cast includes trained fur seals and parrots, Lola the chimpanzee, who plays a demanding restaurant customer, and the clown duo Boatswain and Sashka, performed by Sergey Sokolov and Alexander Azhgikhin. The production also features aerial strap artists Olga Legenda and Andrey Kharitonov, as well as a water-based acrobatic vaulting troupe led by Sergey Matyukov, among others.
"We strive to bring unique, one-of-a-kind projects here. I don't think a production quite like this has ever been staged in this ring before. It is fascinating from a technical and directorial standpoint, as well as in terms of the performers' costumes. The best of the best have come to St. Petersburg to showcase their artistry and skill," said Yelena Petrikova, Chief Director of Rosgostsirk.

Protesters across Spain demand action over housing crisis
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
12:35:48 BST
20:35:48 KST

'Anger in the streets': Tens of thousands protest in Spain over housing crisis
- Published
Thousands of protesters have taken to the streets across Spain calling for greater protections for tenants after the government failed to pass emergency housing legislation in parliament on Friday.
About 50 marches took place on Saturday in cities including Madrid, Valencia and Barcelona.
"There is a lot of anger in the streets," a spokesperson for the Valencia Tenants' Union said. Clashes took have taken place between some protesters and police in the city.
The measures put forward by Pedro Sánchez's leftist coalition government on Friday followed public outcry over the eviction of an 87-year-old woman from her home last month after she was unable to afford a sharp rent increase.
Her eviction triggered nationwide protests across Spain with protesters demanding lower rents, an end to evictions, and a ban on investment funds - or "vulture funds" as the government has termed them - buying property.
Sanchez's defeat in Congress on Friday heightens speculation that he might call an early general election, which was not due until next summer.
His coalition government, made up of his ruling Socialist party and junior partner the Sumar alliance, does not command a majority in parliament.
Photographs showed protesters in the east coast city of Valencia clashing with police officers on Saturday near arts centre Palau de les Arts Reina Sofía, which was hosting a real estate summit.
Several protesters removed barriers and threw objects at officers, who responded with rubber bullets, Spanish media reported. Public broadcaster RTVE said nine police officers were injured and five people were arrested.
One of the biggest demonstration is happening in the capital, Madrid. Estimates of the number of participants varied widely, with the city's Tenants' Union putting it at 500,000, while government officials put the figure at 70,000.
Demonstrators held banners reading "There won't be peace for rentism" and "I study to have a future, not to have a tiny apartment". They shook the keys they were holding and chanted: "We have the keys of all the city".
Some have also been camping in one of the city's main squares, Puerta del Sol, for days.
One protester, David, told RTVE ahead of the protest: "We're not here for pleasure or comfort. We're here out of conviction."
Another protester, 26-year-old librarian Marcos Sainz, told AFP news agency that he used to share a two-bedroom flat with friends, paying 900 euros (£766) a month in rent. Today, he said a one-bedroom flat often costs 1,000 euros.
Sainz said he would protest against rent rises "until someone dares to regulate it all", or "we'll all have to leave Madrid".
On Friday night, Madrid's Tenants' Union said that although the government's proposed measures were insufficient, the rejection of the proposed legislation "exacerbates the housing crisis which is costing the working class their lives".
It is calling for a general strike over the housing crisis.
The legislation put forward in Congress on Friday was divided into two separate decrees.
The first decree included the suspension of evictions of vulnerable tenants until 2030, a two-year extension to rental leases due to expire before 2028, tax increases for tourist apartments, and a restriction on the purchase of residential properties by so-called "vulture funds".
The second decree included the automatic renewal of rental contracts, a major demand of many on the left and the Tenants' Union.
MPs rejected the first decree by 178 votes to 172 and voted against the second by 184 to 166.
Prior to the vote, the conservative People's Party (PP) and far-right Vox had already said they would vote against both initiatives, leaving the minority government depending on the support of smaller nationalist parties in Catalonia and the Basque Country.
However, by the eve of the parliamentary session, the centre-right, pro-independence Together for Catalonia (JxCat) had signalled its opposition to both laws, condemning them to failure.
Sánchez's ruling coalition hurriedly drew up the decree laws in an effort to defuse the housing protests that were sparked when 87-year-old Maricarmen Abascal was evicted in September.
The social backlash led to the company that owns Abascal's flat, Urbagestión, negotiating her return to the flat on a low rent. However, protests have continued.
- Dramatic eviction of woman aged 87 highlights Spain's housing shortage 
  - Published23 September
The Bank of Spain estimates the country is short of 700,000 homes, based on the gap between demand and new construction.
House prices have risen by 12.2% in the past year, according to figures for the second quarter of 2026 from national statistics institute INE.
The shortage in rental housing means that costs rose by 8.5% in 2025, according to real estate firm Idealista, with Madrid alone seeing an increase of 9.7% in rents.
It said Barcelona and Madrid were Spain's most expensive cities to rent a home, at €23.80 per square metre and €22.70 per square metre respectively.

The double standards of a failed execution
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
11:32:42 UTC
20:32:42 KST

The double standards of a failed execution
Had Christa Pike faced the death penalty in the Middle East, there would be relentless outrage and condemnations.
Let’s pretend that the Islamic Republic of Iran had undertaken to execute a 50-year-old woman for a crime committed when she was an 18-year-old.
Let’s say the crime was murdering a fellow female student. Let’s also say that the woman slated for execution had suffered rape and sexual abuse since she was a toddler and had been diagnosed with mental illness, later admitting: “It took me numerous years to even realise the gravity of what I’d done.”
A fair amount of international uproar would presumably ensue, alleging Iran’s barbarity in choosing to kill a woman with such a troubled past. The United States would no doubt be at the helm of the criticism.
And yet no such uproar has transpired since Wednesday’s attempted execution in the US state of Tennessee of 50-year-old Christa Pike, to whom all of the above details pertain in reality.
Pike was set to be the first woman executed in Tennessee since 1820 – lest anyone assume US society was advancing rather than regressing. However, the executioners failed in their task, and, when Pike remained alive after being injected with all manner of lethal drugs, the operation was called off and she was rushed to hospital.
Fearing the pain that would attend death by injection, Pike had initially requested to be killed by firing squad – one of various civilised options provided to death penalty victims in some US states. The request had been denied.
According to Pike’s lawyers, the failed execution amounts to “chemical torture”. The degree of brain damage Pike may have sustained due to oxygen deprivation remains to be seen.
Again, one can only imagine the sort of self-righteous denunciations that would be occasioned had Iran not only tried to execute a mentally ill woman but royally messed up the killing, potentially leaving her half-dead instead.
Of course, Iran would not be the only country that would come under fire for such a stunt; plenty of other countries in the Middle East and Africa would be similarly denounced for such savagery.
But it’s all in a day’s work in the US, where the death penalty is legal in more than half of the country’s 50 states.
Among the myriad problems with the death penalty, of course, is the frequency with which innocent folks end up being murdered. The Death Penalty Information Center reported that, “since 1973, at least 203 people who were wrongly convicted and sentenced to death in the U.S. have been exonerated.”
Recalling that capital punishment “served as a tool for controlling Black populations and discouraging rebellion” during the era of slavery in the US, the organisation noted the enduring racialised nature of state killing in the country with Black people “currently comprising 40% of the death row population despite only being 12% of the U.S. population”.
To be sure, it’s hardly shocking that the racist classism that passes for democracy in the US is reproduced in death as well as in life.
After all, what better way to uphold the capitalist hierarchy and maintain elite social control than by disproportionately incarcerating and legally murdering people of colour and the poor?
And while Pike is not Black, her attempted murder still serves the mechanism of control by reminding the nonelite of their dispensability and the ultimate arbitrariness of their fate.
Call it capitalist punishment.
Meanwhile, the state’s monopoly on killing means that many cold-blooded murderers get off scot-free – as in the case of Jonathan Ross, the Immigration and Customs Enforcement officer who fatally shot Renee Good, a 37-year-old mother of three, in Minneapolis, Minnesota, in January.
Ross, it so happens, is a veteran of the war on Iraq, where over the years the US has also engaged in a great deal of killing with impunity. And as in other locations that have had the misfortune to be in the US’s crosshairs, mass slaughter has been cast as just and civilised as long as the US is the one doing the slaughtering.
Indeed, whether it’s committing state-sanctioned execution at home or the extrajudicial killing of fishermen in the Caribbean, the US has yet to be adequately taken to task for barbarism that would have had the US itself up in arms if the tables were turned.
The prevailing double standard goes something like this: When Iran executes people, it’s a moral abomination and a crime. When the US executes people, it’s a legitimate exercise in domestic criminal justice.
As Pike remained unconscious in a Tennessee hospital, the state has paused executions for the remainder of the year as the powers that be ponder what the hell happened during the execution-that-wasn’t.
For his part, President Donald Trump – who ramped up executions during his first term and is busy replicating the feat in his second – reasoned that “it shouldn’t be very difficult” to kill someone by injection, notwithstanding what happened in Tennessee.
But as the US keeps up the killing spree at home and abroad, one can’t help but think that it shouldn’t be that easy.

UK-Iranian man held over airbase incident released on bail: police
A UK-Iranian dual national who was arrested over a murky major incident at a British military airbase was released on bail, counter-terror police said on Saturday.

Five other men who were arrested on suspicion of explosives and terrorism offences on Sunday near the airbase in Gloucestershire were also released on bail earlier this week.
UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham has said there were "strong indications that Iran played a part" in the incident, which Tehran has rejected.
But the source and nature of the threat near the airbase -- used by the US military in its war against Iran -- have remained shrouded in mystery.
Police were called to the base early on Sunday over reports that "suspicious" white vans were heading towards the base, triggering an evacuation of the nearby village and the declaration of a "major incident".
Days later, police said no explosives were found at the scene.
Adding to the mystery, British media reported that officers were alerted to the incident by one of the initial suspects but police have not commented on the reports.
Washington has further muddied waters by criticising the release of the suspects on bail and declaring hostile state involvement early in the investigation.
"The investigation into the circumstances surrounding events in Gloucestershire is continuing," UK police said in the update Saturday.

How to Collect CDs
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
11:30:00 UTC
20:30:00 KST

When I started collecting physical media in 2009 at 13 years old, CDs still dominated the market. Big-box retail stores had music sections with rows and rows of sealed jewel cases, and it was normal to spend $25 on a deluxe album or a box set.
Less than a decade later, streaming had taken over. Vinyl records outsold CDs for the first time in 2022. The Compact Disc began to feel like an afterthought.
But now the CD is enjoying a surge in popularity thanks to cultural shifts like the rise in K-pop, the backlash against the streaming platforms’ policies, and Gen-Zers driving hand-me-down cars without Bluetooth connectivity. When I walked into a record store in July and found a deluxe CD for Madonna’s new album, Confessions II, on sale for $34, more expensive than some of the vinyl pressings, it finally felt like the format was officially back. (And yes, I bought it.)
According to 2026 data from the entertainment industry research firm Luminate, K-pop groups like BTS, Enhypen, and ATEEZ contributed to an overall 16 percent increase in CD sales so far this year, thanks to collectible editions that encouraged fans to buy multiple copies of the groups’ albums. This seems to be the major shift between the old way of buying music and the new normal: CDs are looked at more as merch—collectibles that support the artist—than as necessities to hear the songs. According to the same Luminate report, if K-pop were taken out of the data, disc sales would’ve still increased 6.7 percent.
Though the numbers show solid growth, CDs are nowhere near as hot as they used to be. The music industry sold 16.3 million discs in the first half of this year, a paltry number compared to the CD’s heyday around the turn of the millennium, when annual sales topped 900 million. Still, their collectible physicality has brought them back into fashion.
There really is no right or wrong way to collect CDs. If you keep a CD in its packaging, it will be protected for years to come. But here are some tips if you want to elevate your collecting experience and get more out of your collection, whether you’re new to the format or rescuing an old box of discs from the garage.
Get a CD Player
It might seem that owning a CD player is the obvious first step to collecting CDs. But according to Luminate’s report, only half of millennials and Gen-Zers that collect CDs have a player. Luckily, finding a good CD player is easier and more budget-friendly than buying a record player.
You might even have a CD player without knowing it; a Blu-ray player hooked up to a nice sound bar is a convenient set up to play CDs, since most Blu-ray and DVD players can handle audio discs. Even your Xbox can play them, though the disc drives on Sony PlayStation 4 and 5 consoles weirdly cannot play CDs.
If you need a CD player, the first thing to consider is what kind you want. A personal portable player lets you take your music anywhere. If your record player setup includes a stereo receiver, chances are it has a CD input that you can use to hook up a hi-fi player for at-home listening. This will give you the best audio from your discs. These component players can still be found at big-box retail stores or online music shops like Turntable Lab or RETROSPEKT that specialize in hi-fi systems.
Del Bravo Record Shop, one of the oldest record stores in Texas, has seen an increase in demand for personal CD players that it ships out of its San Antonio store. “They’ve been flying off the shelves,” says Jessica Campa, Del Bravo’s sales associate and social media manager. “We’ve also had about a 12.6 percent increase in CD sales so far this year.”
Bluetooth CD Players are the latest advancement; they let you connect wireless headphones or speakers. If you love the hunt, a thrift store or flea market can be a great place to find a CD player at a great price. Just be sure to test that it works before paying for it. Record stores sometimes keep a variety of used or new CD players as well, depending on their specialty.
The Record Store Is Still Your Friend
Independent record stores are the go-to place to get exclusive vinyl, and many of them still carry CDs. While online shops like Amazon seem like a convenient way to buy these small discs, record stores often receive promotional goodies like posters or stickers that they throw in for free along with your purchase. Oftentimes indie stores will get autographed albums during an artist’s release week to encourage shoppers to come into the store to buy the disc. These are often sold at the regular retail price and not up-charged.
Of course, record stores are great places to buy used discs, and most of the time, the discs are inspected by the staff and you can expect them to play properly and without skips. Stores sometimes even have listening stations so you can preview the used discs.
Track Your Collection
Knowing what music you already have is a great way to prevent accidentally acquiring doubles when you’re out shopping. Thankfully, you don’t need to rely on an Excel spreadsheet. Discogs, an online marketplace and music database for collectors, is well known among vinyl aficionados, but it’s just as helpful as a tool to keep track of your CDs. Not only does the free mobile app feature a barcode scanner that will show you the exact pressing of a CD, it will also show you the current market value of it, in case you come across a rare find in the wild or something that could be overpriced. You can also look up different versions of a CD to find that rare version, like the Japanese pressing with the extra tracks. Discogs will show you a list of the users who own that particular disc who’d be willing to sell it to you for a fair offer.
Inspect Thrifted and Stored CDs
Found that box of old CDs in the garage? Scored a 75-cent copy of Santana’s Abraxas at the thrift store? Be sure to not only check if the disc is actually in the case, but inspect the bottom of the disc—CDs are read by a laser that moves underneath the disc as it spins—for any scratches, discoloration, or spots, which could be a sign of disc rot.
Disc rot is exactly what it sounds like, the deterioration of the reflective layer where a CD’s music data is stored. Sometimes it’s caused by manufacturing defects, but usually it’s the result of improper storage. Over time, heat and humidity can turn these once seemingly indestructible pieces of media into unplayable garbage.
You can score some great finds when thrifting for CDs, but you never know the conditions the discs were stored in before they hit the discount shelf, so learn to spot the most common problems and be discerning. You may even want to bring a portable player with you when you shop so you can test your finds—with the seller’s consent, of course.
Invest in Proper Storage
Similar to a vinyl record, the best way to store a CD is vertically, in its original sleeve, jewel case, or digipack. Any solid shelf makes a good home, but used furniture stores or Goodwill shops will often also have dedicated CD shelving, made of wood or metal, specially designed to fit rows of jewel cases.
About those jewel cases: If they’re damaged or missing pieces, they don’t do as good a job protecting the CDs or artwork inside from spills or scratches. Go the extra step and invest in replacements for cracked jewel cases or damaged interior spindle trays.
If you listen on the move and like to take your discs in the car, a classic CD wallet or CD book is your best solution. You load your disks into the wallet’s plastic pouches and store the jewel case and the artwork somewhere safe, either on the shelf or in a box.
The demand for these nostalgic book-style cases has only increased over the years. “We stocked some recently,” says Steven Alejandro, who has been the general manager at Hogwild Records for over 30 years. “And then the supplier ran out, and now they don’t have any more to sell.”
If you’re lucky to find a case, or you’ve repurposed your parents’ old CD wallets, remember not to leave the case in a hot car, in the sun, or anywhere near a heat source for an extended time.
Keep Your CDs and CD Players Clean
The best way to maintain a physical media collection is to keep everything clean. Found your dream player at a garage sale? Chances are it hasn’t been properly maintained in 20 years. CD players do need to be cleaned every once in a while to ensure the laser lens is free of any debris or fingerprints that can impact playback and audio quality.
On the actual disc, fingerprints, dust, and anything else stuck to the bottom surface can cause audible skips during playback. It's best to use a microfiber cloth and, if necessary, a cleaning solution for extremely dirty CDs. Don’t wipe the disc in a circular motion. Always wipe the disc from the center outward, starting at the hole and pulling the cloth gently toward the outer edge of the disc.
Final Tip
Enjoy your CDs! Rip the contents to your hard drive if you need to, but they sound great when you just give them a spin. There’s a joy in collecting music, because while online streams may be temporary, the physical media we have will always be something we truly own and the actual definition of on-demand.

Prioritizing women’s health ‘a shared responsibility’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
11:29:59 UTC
20:29:59 KST

Prioritizing women’s health ‘a shared responsibility’
TEHRAN – A healthy woman fosters a dynamic family, a strong society, and a bright future. Therefore, prioritizing women’s health and developing a culture of self-care is a shared responsibility among women, families, the healthcare system, and society as a whole.
In this line, the health ministry is holding annual national programs to raise awareness of breast cancer, coinciding with Breast Cancer Awareness Month, observed from October 1 to 31, and highlighting the need to prioritize women’s health.
The programs underline the importance of a healthy lifestyle, early detection, and timely treatment as the three main factors in combating the disease, the health ministry’s website said, quoting Jafar Jandaqi, an official with the health ministry.
Women aged 30 to 69 are invited to benefit from screening and self-care training programs provided at the medical health centers, he added.
Breast cancer is the most common silent cancer among women; increasing women’s knowledge of breast cancer, risk factors, self-examination, related warning signs, and encouraging them to undergo timely breast cancer screening and regular check-ups will help detect the disease at an early stage when the treatment is most effective.
Adopting a healthy lifestyle, such as maintaining a healthy weight, exercising, eating well, and avoiding inactivity, smoking, and alcohol, plays a key role in preventing breast cancer.
October is Breast Cancer Awareness Month, a global opportunity to raise awareness of breast cancer and call for action to improve access to timely diagnosis and quality care.
The theme “Every story is unique, every journey matters” recognizes that every experience of breast cancer is different. Behind every diagnosis is a person, a family, and a unique journey. People may face different challenges depending on their diagnosis, treatment, support networks, and access to care.
Every person affected by breast cancer deserves to be supported and treated with dignity. And everyone, wherever they live, should have access to the care they need.
All countries should aim to reduce breast cancer mortality by 2.5 percent per year, putting the world on track to avert 2.5 million breast cancer deaths by 2040. This is feasible by providing breast cancer services as part of the essential benefit package for universal health coverage and making them available in public facilities.
With the right policies, services and investment, countries can reduce breast cancer deaths and improve survival.
Major inequalities in breast cancer survival persist around the world. 41 percent of women in low-income countries are expected to survive at least five years after a breast cancer diagnosis, compared with 87 percent in high-income countries. Around 70 percent of breast cancer deaths occur in low- and middle-income countries, where access to early detection, timely diagnosis and comprehensive treatment remains more limited.
Everyone, everywhere should have an equal chance to survive breast cancer.
Health ministry to streamline cancer care through national network
The health ministry is set to launch the national cancer care network in early autumn, aiming to integrate fragmented cancer treatment services into a coordinated, team-based, and traceable care pathway.
The initiative aims to ensure that the patients entering the network follow a clear path through the stages of diagnosis, treatment, and follow-up, without the need for patients to go to various centers, ISNA quoted Ali Motlaq, an official with the health ministry, as saying in September.
No new medical center is planned to be built; the network will benefit from available capacities to connect specialized physicians and medical centers. Based on the type of cancer, the center’s capacity, the patient’s place of residence, and other defined criteria, the patients would be referred to the best center and medical team, he noted.
The activities of the network focus on enhancing the quality of care, improving access, and reducing the financial burden of care on patients. Standardization of clinical pathways, systematic referral, teamwork and multidisciplinary decision-making, capacity management of centers, early diagnosis, patient navigation, and the electronic recording and monitoring of care pathways will also be among key components of the program, the official highlighted.
According to Motlaq, free cancer treatment does not mean unconditional access to cancer-related services and all medications free of charge in public and private sectors. The program aims to minimize patients’ out-of-pocket costs for covered services in the public sector, and in specific cases, without paying any money directly.
Recording the information of patients, their referrals and follow-ups, and the received care will help clarify a patient’s current situation, whether they have received required services, and who or what center is responsible for the next step in their treatment, he said.
The official went on to say that the program will also consider incentives for specialists and centers that join the network and accept its standards such as recording essential information, adherence to clinical pathways, participation in patient referral and follow-up, and accountability for the quality of provided services.
The first phase of the program will commence by focusing on breast cancer. The qualified centers and service providers will be identified, and the actual capacity of the services will be determined. After early detection, initial assessment through imaging, biopsy, and pathology, if cancer is confirmed, the treatment will begin, Motlaq said.
Ultimately, the success of the network should not be measured merely by the number of services provided or patients registered. The fundamental question is whether the patient received standard care—at the right time, in the right place, and from the right team, with minimal financial and administrative barriers—and if their journey to the next stage of care was fully traced.
The program aims to cover other top priority cancers in the country by the end of the current Iranian year, March 2027, he added.

Lubinets urges Kazakhstan to prevent extradition of Ukrainian citizen to Russia
According to Ukrinform, Lubinets said this in a Facebook post.
"I received an appeal from Ukrainian citizen Liubov Rozhanska, who was detained in Kazakhstan at the request of the Russian Federation. Liubov arrived in Kazakhstan for humanitarian reasons – to take her minor grandson and return him to Ukraine. Instead, she herself ended up in custody over a criminal case that Russia opened back in 2023," the ombudsman said.
Lubinets said Rozhanska was effectively lured to Kazakhstan through deception. The child's so-called "new" relatives in Russia, working with the Russian Federal Security Service (FSB), contacted the woman and tried to lure her out of Ukraine so that she would come and pick up the child herself. The woman believed them and traveled to Astana, unaware that preparations for her detention were already underway in Russia.
"Handing a Ukrainian woman over to Russian law enforcement agencies would pose a direct and serious threat to her personal safety, health and respect for her fundamental rights. We know all too well what happens to Ukrainians who fall into the hands of the Russian system," Lubinets said.
"Therefore, I immediately appealed to Kazakhstan's Ombudsman Artur Lastayev, urging him to prevent any extradition, handover or forcible transfer of Liubov Rozhanska to Russia. I also held a separate phone call with him," Lubinets said.
He is insisting on an examination of the conditions of Rozhanska's detention and the legal grounds for depriving her of her liberty, as well as ensuring full access to her by Ukrainian diplomatic and consular representatives and her lawyer.
Lubinets noted that the case has another extremely troubling aspect – it concerns a Ukrainian child.
According to available information, the boy's mother took him to Russia back in 2021. In 2022, she obtained Russian citizenship for herself and her child. At the same time, in March 2025, the Supreme Court of Ukraine determined Odesa as the child's place of residence.
The ombudsman clarified that the grandmother traveled to retrieve the Ukrainian child and bring him home, and it was then that she herself was detained in connection with a case initiated by Russia.
"This once again shows how dangerous it is to try to retrieve children who are in Russia on your own," Lubinets said.
He also urged people whose children are in Russia or in temporarily occupied territories not to try to resolve the matter on their own, but to contact official Ukrainian state institutions.
In particular, the Ombudsman's Office facilitates the return of Ukrainian children who have been deported or forcibly transferred, including from foreign countries, in cases where documents are missing or various legal issues are involved. The hotline number is 1678.
Traveling to Russia independently or attempting to retrieve a child through third countries may create serious risks and jeopardize the child's subsequent return, Lubinets said.
The ombudsman also published a video purportedly showing the boy boarding a plane to Kazakhstan. He noted that the video had been deliberately staged to lure the woman out.
Ukrinform reported earlier that Ukrainian citizen Liubov Rozhanska was detained at Astana airport in Kazakhstan at Russia's request after traveling there to retrieve her grandson and take him to his father in Odesa.

Three of the mainland suspects, all men, were illegal immigrants. Another two – a couple – are believed to be the masterminds, who entered Hong Kong on two-way permits, travel documents issued by Beijing authorities for visits to the city or Macau.
A local man arrested in the operation acted as the group’s driver.

King Charles to confront Britain’s slavery past during Caribbean tour
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
11:25:00 UTC
20:25:00 KST

King Charles will confront what Buckingham Palace described as “the darkest days of our past” when he visits the Caribbean later this month, amid renewed calls for Britain to address its role in the transatlantic slave trade.
Charles and Queen Camilla will visit the Bahamas and Guyana before traveling to Antigua and Barbuda, where the king will attend the Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting (CHOGM), scheduled for Nov. 1-4.
The visit comes as Caribbean and African countries intensify calls for Britain and other former colonial powers to pay reparations for their role in slavery. The issue is expected to feature prominently at the Commonwealth summit.
The British government has ruled out reparations, while Charles, who remains head of state of several Caribbean nations, including the Bahamas and Antigua and Barbuda, has previously expressed his sorrow over the legacy of slavery.
“There are important discussions taking place in various fora about colonial legacy and the intergenerational impact of the transatlantic trade in enslaved persons,” a Buckingham Palace spokesperson told reporters, saying the visit was coming at an important time in the relationship between Britain and Caribbean nations.
“The visit program will therefore not shy away from ‘the darkest days of our past,’ as His Majesty has described them, but, in keeping with the wishes of our host nations, it will principally be oriented to the vibrant present and promising future of each country.”
From the 15th to the 19th century, at least 12.5 million Africans were abducted and sold into slavery by European merchants, with Britain responsible for transporting an estimated 3.2 million people, making it the second-most active European nation after Portugal.
Charles, who is head of the Commonwealth, a group of 56 nations, mainly former British colonies, encompassing some 2.7 billion people, has backed research into the British monarchy’s own historical links to the trade.
Last month, the Jamaican government formally asked him to seek legal advice on whether Britain should pay reparations and said it was “encouraged” by Buckingham Palace’s engagement.
“It is important to note here the work His Majesty himself has done over many years both to acknowledge the wrongs of the past and to find creative ways to right inequalities that endure,” the palace spokesperson said.
“As you would therefore expect, opportunities will be found during the visit to reflect and renew his personal, wholehearted and continuing commitment to that process.”
In February, Commonwealth Secretary-General Shirley Botchwey told Reuters she expected its members to make progress toward beginning negotiations on reparations.

New Ukrainian ballistic missile used in combat
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
12:23:51 BST
20:23:51 KST

Ukraine has used a domestically built tactical ballistic missile in combat for the first time, President Volodymyr Zelensky has said, naming the weapon as the FP-7 and signalling that the next task is building it in quantity, according to the president in a post published on Thursday.
Writing on X, Mr Zelensky said: “Ukrainian tactical ballistic missile. FP-7. First combat use. Thank you for the result. Next up: production. Glory to Ukraine!”
No target was given, and Kyiv has declined to say what the missile struck. The brevity of the announcement is itself the point, since a first combat firing is a political statement about Ukrainian industry as much as a military event.
Ukrainian tactical ballistic missile. FP-7. First combat use. Thank you for the result. Next up: production. Glory to Ukraine! pic.twitter.com/IxdjVg51c1
— Volodymyr Zelenskyy / Володимир Зеленський (@ZelenskyyUa) October 1, 2026
The FP-7 is made by Fire Point, the Ukrainian company set up in 2022 that has become one of the more visible names in the country’s wartime weapons industry, and which also produces the FP-1 one-way attack drone and the FP-5 Flamingo cruise missile. The missile is launched from a standard truck trailer rather than a purpose-built transporter erector launcher, an approach that keeps cost down and makes the launch vehicle harder to distinguish from ordinary traffic.
Published figures for the missile vary between sources and none of them have been independently verified. The announced range has been given as between 200 and 300 kilometres, with a warhead variously described as 150 or 200 kilograms, a circular error probable of around 14 metres and a terminal velocity of 1,200 to 1,500 metres a second. Analysts tracking the programme have assessed that the airframe derives from the Soviet 48N6 interceptor used by the S-400 system, rebuilt with composite materials and modern electronics, and the manufacturer has claimed that the resulting speed gives it a better chance of getting through air defences than the Russian Iskander.
Roughly seven months separated the first reported test from this firing, which is fast by any peacetime standard and reflects how much Ukrainian procurement has compressed since 2022.

Delhi landfill garbage mountains shrinking, 100 acres reclaimed in 18 months: CM Rekha Gupta
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
11:22:01 UTC
20:22:01 KST

Delhi CM Rekha Gupta poses for a group picture during an on-site inspection of waste disposal operations near Okhla, in New Delhi
NEW DELHI: Delhi chief minister Rekha Gupta on Saturday said the garbage mountains at the city's landfill sites were steadily shrinking as she reviewed waste disposal work at Okhla and laid the foundation stone for new waste processing facilities at Okhla, Ghazipur and Singhola.Gupta said the Delhi government had reclaimed 100 acres of land across the city's three landfill sites over the past one-and-a-half years, with a large portion of the cleared area also being turned green.She said almost all legacy waste at Okhla that existed before January 2025 had been processed."Today, at Okhla, we have processed almost all the legacy waste that was there before January 2025," Gupta said.
Government targets legacy and fresh waste
Gupta said the government was working on two fronts: clearing the existing garbage mountains while ensuring that fresh waste generated every day did not accumulate into new landfill sites.According to news agency ANI, she said around 3,000-4,000 metric tonnes of fresh waste reaches the sites daily and is being processed round the clock."The garbage currently piled up here is essentially fresh waste generated after January 2025, and that too is being processed round the clock. So, we are fighting on two fronts: one is eliminating waste, and the other is ensuring that the 3,000 to 4,000 metric tons of fresh waste arriving daily is processed immediately, so that new garbage mountains are not formed for future generations," Gupta said.
She said the government was working to reduce the existing garbage mountains to zero."People are seeing that the garbage mountains are continuously shrinking and soon a time will come when they will become zero," Gupta said.Gupta also said she had taken what she described as her "last selfie" with the garbage mountain at Okhla."Today I have taken my last selfie with the garbage mountain; after this I have taken a pledge that this garbage mountain will end soon," she said.Taking a jibe at the Opposition, Gupta added, "I had said - garbage mountain, you will have to go; the opposition mocked. Today I will say the garbage mountain is going; now only its back remains."
New processing plants at three sites
During the programme at the Okhla SLF site, Gupta laid the foundation stone for fresh waste processing plants at Okhla, Ghazipur and Singhola, as well as a biogas facility at Ghazipur. She also inaugurated the M&CW Centre at Kotla Mubarakpur through virtual mode from Okhla.The Okhla plant will be built at a cost of Rs 103 crore and will have a processing capacity of 1,400 metric tonnes per day.The Singhola facility will cost Rs 42 crore and have a capacity of 800 metric tonnes per day, while the Ghazipur plant will have a processing capacity of 700 metric tonnes per day.The facilities are intended to process fresh waste as well as construction and demolition waste. Gupta said the new units would also produce biogas, green energy and manure."Waste should not remain waste; Delhi should use it as wealth," she said, adding that new technologies were being introduced for waste segregation and processing.She said waste and cattle dung would be used to produce biogas and manure as part of efforts to build a technology-driven waste management system.
Gupta said the government was taking up several measures to address pollution, including work on landfill waste, cleaning the Yamuna, dust mitigation, plantation, road infrastructure and waste management."Our government is tackling pollution from a 360-degree perspective to ensure it gradually decreases. We are working on every aspect, be it addressing the mountains of garbage, cleaning the Yamuna, improving road infrastructure, or managing waste, to ensure the people of Delhi enjoy better air quality. Our resolve and policies are absolutely clear, and we are working 24x7 in the public interest," she said.The chief minister also reviewed the progress of waste disposal work with officials and directed them to accelerate the work according to the stipulated timeline.She said the garbage mountains at Bhalswa, Ghazipur and Okhla had caused inconvenience to people travelling through these areas and said the government was continuing efforts to eliminate them.

EU links 2026 Ukraine funding to reforms, rejects request for early advance – FT
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
14:21:39 EEST
20:21:39 KST

The European Union has not supported Ukraine's request for the early provision of additional financing in 2026, emphasizing that the allocation of funds will directly depend on Kyiv's implementation of agreed-upon reforms, the Financial Times reports, citing a letter from European Commissioners Valdis Dombrovskis and Marta Kos to Verkhovna Rada Chairman Ruslan Stefanchuk.
In the summer, Ukraine estimated its additional defense needs at approximately $27 billion and asked the European Commission to prematurely allocate a portion of the funds from the two-year €90 billion Ukraine Support Loan program (€60 billion earmarked for defense, €30 billion for direct budget support). According to the program's parameters, up to €45 billion are to be made available to Ukraine in 2026, with the remaining €45 billion in 2027.
According to FT, the European Commissioners made it clear that access to financing is possible only upon fulfilling an agreed list of commitments. Specifically, this concerns the cancellation of VAT exemptions for small international parcels, the introduction of taxation rules for digital platforms, and proper financial monitoring of politically exposed persons (PEPs), amendments to which raised concerns in Brussels as a departure from the anti-corruption track. According to the publication, meeting these requirements will pave the way for Kyiv to receive about €34 billion in support during 2026.
At the same time, the European Commission emphasized that rejecting the early advance request does not mean halting financial assistance. On October 1, the parties announced the coordination of funding sources for budgetary and defense needs through the end of 2026, confirming the absence of an uncovered financing gap for the current year.
Additionally, on October 2, the European Commission transferred a regular tranche of €2.9 billion to Ukraine under the Ukraine Facility program. Total assistance provided to Kyiv by the EU and member states since the start of Russia's full-scale invasion has reached €227.4 billion.
