High school students in Paris’ deprived suburbs spark national protest movement
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
07:08:15 UTC
16:08:15 KST

High school students in Paris’ deprived suburbs spark national protest movement
- High school students in poor Paris suburbs protest against dilapidated schools, overcrowded classrooms, and teacher shortages, highlighting severe inequalities in education resources.
- Protests spread nationwide with over 1,200 schools involved; police used tear gas and rubber bullets, leading to injuries and arrests amid government budget cuts.
- Experts link unrest to long-term underfunding, government cuts of 3,256 teacher positions, and rising demands on schools, making inequality reduction difficult.
AI generated
AUBERVILLIERS, France – Maisa, a 17-year-old in a poor Paris suburb who aspires to be an English teacher, joined tens of thousands of other students and their supporters this week in protests that spread across France over dilapidated schools, classroom overcrowding and teacher shortages.
At Lycee Le Corbusier school in Aubervilliers, a suburb north of Paris in the Seine-Saint-Denis department, protesters said schools in poor neighbourhoods like theirs faced the worst conditions.
“Last year I took the high school French exam without a French teacher, and teachers have a huge impact,” Maisa said. “These are not conditions to study in.”
As protests raged at more than 1,200 French high schools this week, police responded with tear gas and rubber bullets in some cases. More than 5,000 people were arrested, and some protesters were seriously hurt with eye injuries, broken teeth and blows to the head. Interior Minister Laurent Nunez called it a “climate of unacceptable violence” and called for order.
Amelia, 15, joined Maisa in the crowd outside the school gates and held a sign reading: “Our address should not decide our future.” She said she was demonstrating to demand the same rights as students elsewhere in the country.
“The education authority is not investing enough in the suburbs. It’s classist and racist,” she said.
Ulysse Rabate, a political scientist at Paris 8 University, said the protests show the way that France’s marginalised urban neighbourhoods are increasingly influencing national politics.
“When there is a collapse of the public service, of public education, those who feel it the most, and the most violently, are those at the bottom,” he said.
Political flashpoint
The nationwide demonstrations and blockades, which began last week, have become a political flashpoint at a sensitive moment for the government, which announced a series of deeply unpopular spending cuts in its 2027 budget on Oct 1.
The education budget is set to increase by a below-inflation 1.7% to €65.53 billion (S$94.34 billion), excluding teacher pensions.
Education Minister Edouard Geffray said that education remained a priority and the below-inflation budget increase was due to population decline.
The Education Ministry did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
The protests started in the Parisian suburbs, where poverty levels are high, then spread to Paris itself and other French towns, including Marseille, Strasbourg, Tours and Lille.
At Lycee Le Corbusier, classes including maths, humanities, English and sport have been cancelled since the start of the academic year due to a teacher shortage, according to Karima Kara Ali, an elected parent representative.
In Seine-Saint-Denis, two-thirds of high schools took part in protests on Oct 1, the CGT labour union said. Youth, teachers and parents in four towns complained of unsanitary school conditions and chronic staff shortages, including of nurses and social workers.
Louise Paternoster, a representative for the Seine-Saint-Denis branch of the CGT’s education union, said the area does not get adequate resources for its student population and their educational needs. Two-thirds of schools in the department have unfilled teacher positions, according to a union survey.
Not enough teachers
“Our students are losing out on study time. Some schools don’t have drinking water. We are not equal to other departments,” she said, blaming shortages on government cuts of 3,256 teacher positions nationwide in 2026.
In Pantin, a town on the north-eastern edge of Paris, teacher Dilan Roche joined her students as they protested outside their school this week to support their demands and protect them from the police.
“What they wrote on banners, we wrote in a letter to the local education authority: overcrowded classes, no nurses, no social workers – which is problematic for students with learning difficulties, many living in precarity,” she said.
While France ranks in the middle of Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development countries for spending on education, the average expenditure per secondary school student has remained little changed over the last decade, standing at €11,660 in 2024 and €11,910 in 2010, according to Education Ministry data.
The last nationwide high school protest movement on this scale demanding more funding came in the 1990s. That followed the government sharply expanding access to the baccalaureate, the school-leaving exam that typically paves the way to university, without providing schools with sufficient additional resources, said Clemence Cardon-Quint, a professor at Paul Valery University who researches education funding.
The movement won an increase in funding, but spending per student later stagnated despite growing demands on schools.
Cardon-Quint said students and teachers have taken on additional responsibilities over the years, including navigating Parcoursup, the university admissions system introduced in 2018 and criticised by some students and teachers as opaque and discriminatory.
“In a period of budgetary restraint, it is more difficult to reduce inequalities,” said Cardon-Quint. REUTERS

- The tanks are remotely controlled from a separate crewed vehicle on a tank chassis, with a reported control range of about 3 km.
Russia has used uncrewed tanks from its Shturm heavy robotic assault system in combat drills for the first time, sending remotely controlled T-72-based vehicles to support assault troops during its Tsentr-2026 strategic exercise.
Russian President Vladimir Putin was shown the vehicles at the Chebarkul training range in the Chelyabinsk region, the Russian Defense Ministry said on Oct. 2. The ministry said the machines are built on the T-72B3M tank chassis and have uncrewed fighting compartments, in two versions: one with a tank-type turret and one armed like a BMPT tank support vehicle. During the main stage of the drills, they provided fire support to assault units.
The Shturm system pairs remotely controlled combat vehicles with a crewed control vehicle, all built on T-72 or T-90 tank chassis. The combat vehicles can still be driven by a crew on board if needed. The most visible feature of the main version is a shortened 125 mm gun, designed so the turret can swing freely between buildings in urban fighting. It also carries a bulldozer blade, all-around armor against shoulder-fired anti-tank weapons, and launchers for rocket flamethrowers or other weapons on the turret. A version with a 152 mm gun is reported to be in development.
During the drills, operators controlled the armored group from a safe distance using joysticks, FPV headsets and tablets over a multichannel, jam-resistant link, the Rostec weapons project “Russian Weapons” told Rossiyskaya Gazeta. Russian outlet ANNA News reported that each vehicle was driven by three operators working as commander, gunner and driver, seated in the separate control vehicle.
That control setup is one of the system’s main limitations. The robotic tanks cannot operate on their own. They depend on a dedicated crewed control vehicle, essentially a second tank chassis without a turret, which has to stay close enough to keep the radio link. Earlier Russian reports put the control radius at about 3 km (1.9 miles), meaning the crew still has to work near the fight in an armored vehicle of its own.
The Defense Ministry has not published any data on how the link performs under heavy electronic warfare, the main threat to remote-controlled systems on the battlefield in Ukraine, where both sides jam drones and ground robots daily.
Uralvagonzavod began work on Shturm under a Russian Defense Ministry order around 2018. The first images of a test vehicle appeared in July 2025 at the company’s plant in Nizhny Tagil, with a crew on board. At the time, The National Interest questioned whether the remote control and autonomy features were ready.
The Tsentr-2026 exercise, which ran from Sept. 28 to Oct. 3 and involved more than 47,000 troops, also featured T-14 Armata tanks, the Zarya laser air defense system and other robotic vehicles, according to the Defense Ministry.

More Bulgarians in U.S. want their children to study at Bulgarian universities

Vesela Krasteva
News
More Bulgarians in U.S. want their children to study at Bulgarian universities
Saturday 3 October 2026 09:45
Saturday, 3 October 2026, 09:45
PHOTO Facebook /Bulgarian School St. St. Cyril and Methodius in Los Angeles
Font size
Bulgarian Sunday schools abroad are not simply places where young Bulgarian children learn to read and write far from their homeland. They are places that build community and foster a sense of belonging. This is something modern-day torchbearers—teachers and directors of Bulgarian Sunday schools abroad—have repeatedly emphasized in interviews with Radio Bulgaria.
And in today’s uncertain world, growing up among “one’s own” can sometimes be far more valuable and important to children than any lesson they may learn in the classroom.
While for Bulgarians living in Europe, returning home is only a few hours away by plane or car, there are places around the world that are thousands of kilometers away from Bulgaria, making a return to the homeland a difficult and expensive dream. One such country is the United States.
PHOTO Pexels
According to the latest 2024 data from the U.S. Census Bureau’s American Community Survey, more than 245,000 people in the United States report having Bulgarian ancestry. Many of them are second- and third-generation Bulgarians, who were born and raised there. Yet, as life has shown us time and again, nothing is forever, and returning to the homeland remains an option for many of them. That is why Bulgarian Sunday schools play such an important role in keeping that possibility alive—for both children and adults.
During the current 2026/2027 school year, there are 47 Bulgarian educational centers across the United States, six of them located in the state of California. “Learning the language is the most direct path to preserving one’s connection with the homeland”, says Zhivka Kostova, founder, principal and teacher at the Bulgarian School St. St. Cyril and Methodius in Los Angeles.
Zhivka Kostova
PHOTO Facebook /Bulgarian School St. St. Cyril and Methodius in Los Angeles
“Bulgarians who have chosen to settle America feel their connection to Bulgaria in a very different way. For those living in Europe, that connection remains stronger—they return to their homeland much more often and retain that sense of closeness. But for many of our compatriots living abroad, especially in America, however, that connection gradually weakens, and this is where Sunday schools play a very important role. A school is not simply an institution where we learn. It is also a place where Bulgarians come together and build connections. It is a place where both Bulgarian and American holidays are celebrated. It is a place where we feel like one family”, says Zhivka Kostova.
PHOTO Facebook /Bulgarian School St. St. Cyril and Methodius in Los Angeles
The Bulgarian Sunday School St. St. Cyril and St. Methodius in Los Angeles was founded in 2011 by Zhivka Kostova and a group of like-minded people. Last year, 92 Bulgarian children attended the school, studying in both in-person and online programs. The current school year was officially opened on September 16 at two locations— in Culver City and in Orange County. And despite the smiles, Zhivka Kostova’s team continues to face challenges this year as well.
PHOTO Facebook /Bulgarian School St. St. Cyril and Methodius in Los Angeles
“The challenges are different in every city. Here in Los Angeles, the biggest challenge for us is the distance. It is very difficult for parents to set aside one of their days off to take their children to school. One thing that helps us attract and, above all, retain high school students is the so-called Bulgarian language proficiency exams, which result in a certificate under the Seal of Biliteracy program. The problem is that each school has to strive on its own to obtain this recognition and secure the certificate for its students. Another thing the Bulgarian government could help us with is finding facilities where we can hold our classes. Because for the time being, this is entirely our responsibility.“
A major challenge facing the school in Los Angeles, as well as Bulgarian Sunday schools across North America, is the lack of suitable textbooks and educational materials.
Venelina Dimitrova
PHOTO Facebook /Bulgarian School St. St. Cyril and Methodius in Los Angeles
“The biggest challenge is preparing teaching materials”, says Venelina Dimitrova, who teaches Bulgarian language and literature, history and geography at the St. Cyril and St. Methodius School in Los Angeles, in an interview with Radio Bulgaria.
“It is extremely difficult to work with the textbooks designed for schools in Bulgaria because teaching Bulgarian as a heritage language is very different. The situation becomes particularly challenging at the high school level, after seventh grade, because there are no materials specifically designed for Bulgarian schools abroad. We usually work with three or four textbooks, selecting the material that would be suitable for our children and that they would be able to understand.”
Zhivka Kostova (M) and Venelina Dimitrova (R)
PHOTO Facebook /Bulgarian School St. St. Cyril and Methodius in Los Angeles
Venelina Dimitrova has been part of the team at the Bulgarian Sunday School St. St. Cyril and St. Methodius in Los Angeles for six years now. “Our school is one big family, and I really love spending time with my colleagues and with the children, who are wonderful”, says Venelina Dimitrova. She is adamant that every Bulgarian child who stays at the school through 10th or 11th grade is special. But for that to happen, motivation is essential:
PHOTO Facebook /Bulgarian School St. St. Cyril and Methodius in Los Angeles
“First of all, it is very important to build a community among these children. The most important thing, in my opinion, is for them to have friends and to feel that the adults, teachers and parents are part of a community they belong to. I don’t know if you are aware, but getting into a university here is extremely difficult, and not just because it is expensive. Good universities have many requirements. California’s university admissions system is very competitive and highly sought after, and universities increasingly value a connection to an immigrant culture of this kind. For the children, this is one of the biggest incentives—to show them that attending Sunday school can be an asset when applying to university. Another thing I hear increasingly often from parents is that tuition at American universities is extremely high, and they are unwilling to pay it. More and more parents are considering sending their children to study in Europe or in Bulgaria”, Venelina Dimitrova explains.

Latvians head to the polls amid concerns over rising cost of living and Russia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
07:00:57 UTC
16:00:57 KST

Some 1.5 million people were eligible to cast their ballots in the Saturday parliamentary election, Latvia's 11th since gaining independence from the Soviet Union in 1991.
Exit polls show Latvia's centrist party, United List, prime minister Andris Kulbergs projected to win 35.6% of the vote according to public broadcaster LSM.
"It's remarkably good. I was not expecting such result," Kulbergs said at his party's headquarters in Riga.
Meanwhile, the populist Latvia First party has gained momentum, nearly doubling its 2022 results as exit polls show it in second place with 11.3%.
The pro-Ukrainian leader Kulbergs said on Saturday that he refused to cooperate with any pro-Russian parties precisely mentioning Latvia First.
The polls which opened on Saturday in Latvia's parliamentary election were shaped by concerns over neighbouring Russia and a cost of living crisis.
Some 1.5 million people are eligible to cast ballots in the parliamentary election, Latvia's 11th since gaining independence from the Soviet Union in 1991.
The poll will see 14 parties run for 100 seats in the Saeima using a proportional system.
Partial results are expected on Saturday evening, with preliminary official results due on Sunday.
The Baltic state is a key pillar of NATO's eastern defensive flank, and experts say there is widespread support for Ukraine in the war with Russia.
"The stance towards Russia is the main reason for Latvians' Western, NATO and European anchoring," a Western diplomat in Riga said, adding that it would be hard to imagine major political changes.
Polls predict the centre-right United List, led by Prime Minister Andris Kulbergs, will emerge the largest party in parliament in Saturday's vote.
But his centre-right coalition, which also brings together the centrist New Unity, nationalist National Alliance and the Union of Greens and Farmers, was expected to emerge weakened from the election.
The current governing coalition is made up of United List, New Unity, the Union of Greens and Farmers, and the National Alliance. Polls had suggested the bloc was unlikely to retain power in its current form after the vote.
Security and economy at the top of voters' minds
Security is at the top of voters' minds in a country bordering Russia which was annexed and ruled by Moscow for much of the 20th century.
According to Roberts Kits, an analyst at the Latvian think tank LaSER, "defence and security will be the priority". Apart from a few dissenting voices, he said, there is broad consensus on maintaining military spending at nearly five percent of GDP and on supporting Ukraine.
But the economy is also a major concern for voters.
Latvia is the least affluent of the three Baltic States in terms of living standards, despite catching up since joining the EU in 2004.
Growth is sluggish, with voters pointing to the cost of living, the state of the healthcare system and the difficulties of public finances. Complicating this are major regional disparities.
The gap between Latvia's capital and the rest of the country is stark. Around Riga, GDP per capita reached 101 percent of the European average in 2024, according to a European Commission report. In other regions, the figure does not exceed 50 percent.
The contrast is sharpest in Latgale, Latvia's easternmost region, where depopulation is accelerating and economic opportunity is scarce. The region is home to a large majority of Russian speakers, and its decline is reflected most visibly in Daugavpils, the country's second-largest city, where 90 percent of the population is Russian-speaking.
"The most important thing is the lack of young people and the lack of good jobs," said Aigars Soikants, a 30-year-old Daugavpils resident. "There isn't enough work. People are leaving."
Despite living in a city with a predominantly Russian-speaking population, Soikants says identity is not what will drive his vote. He plans to back "a centrist or right-wing party which acts in the interest of the country."
Rise of populist parties in Latvia
Similar to other parts of Europe, populist parties have benefited from economic worries in the lead-up to the election. The Sovereign Power (Suverena vara, SV) party, critical of aid to Ukraine and increasing military spending, is polling at nine percent and could reach second place in Parliament.
Considered pro-Russian by its critics, the party, led by Julija Stepanenko, emphasises Latvia's economic difficulties. The party, however, is isolated politically and, barring a huge upset, has no chance of entering a future governing coalition.
Carefully avoiding the word "Ukraine", Vjaceslavs Stepanenko, the head of SV's local list in Latgale and husband of the party’s chairwoman, advocates "stopping all aid to any foreign state".
"We are the ones who need help, not the other way around."
Another populist party, Latvia First (LPV), is also at nine percent, and its businessman leader Ainars Slesers is regularly compared to US President Donald Trump.
The party is winning support with a conservative message and promises of economic revival, and unlike SV, it could become an indispensable partner in coalition talks.
"The big question is whether the United List will cooperate with Slesers' party," said political analyst Sigita Struberga.
Can Russian-speaking voters influence the polls?
Long rallied behind the "Harmony" party, Russian speakers, who make up about 35 percent of Latvia's population, no longer vote as a unified bloc.
Harmony, which won several parliamentary elections without ever entering government, disappeared from parliament in 2022 and has very little chance of returning.
Russian-speaking voters should not be treated as a single bloc with uniform behaviour, according to analyst Kits.
While identity politics remain a factor, a growing share of this electorate is now driven by economic and social concerns.
That shift is visible in Daugavpils, where Valentin Trofimov, a 62-year-old watch repairman, says he will vote for Slesers' party.
His reasons are straightforward — the country, he says, "lacks money for everything", including transport, education and medicine. "Wages are too low," he said.

BT accused of ‘bullying’ customers by pausing broadband in digital landline push
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
07:00:52 UTC
16:00:52 KST

BT has been accused of “bullying” customers by temporarily cutting off their broadband to pressure them to upgrade to a digital landline, as providers race to switch households over before the January deadline.
Telecoms companies have so far migrated 16-17m lines from the old copper network to digital voice over internet protocol (VoiP), which uses a broadband connection instead, in the biggest technological upgrade since the early 00s, when analogue TV was switched off.
However, as the date for the retirement of the old public switched telephone network (PSTN) approaches, Openreach, the BT subsidiary that maintains the vast majority of the UK broadband and telephony network, says there are still about 1.3m copper-based landlines yet to be migrated.
To hit the end-of-January deadline telecoms companies have started to ramp up pressure after years of direct customer communications and awareness campaigns – in BT’s case including using personalities including Moira Stuart and Clare Balding – have failed to prompt some to engage in the migration programme.
“I’m getting increasing evidence that there is some bullying behaviour going on in order to try to force people to switch over,” said Dennis Reed, the founder of the campaign group Silver Voices.
“I have heard of cases that some with a contract with BT for broadband, who have not been particularly proactive or cooperative over a date to switch their landline, have been threatened with their internet being cut off. I am also fearful that, because targets have to be met, a lot of people are going to fall through the cracks.”
It is understood that BT did recently “temporarily pause” broadband services for a small group of customers who had not responded to any communications about the copper landline switchover for two years.
They were given five days’ notice of the planned outage to encourage them to contact BT and take action to avoid the “pause” in broadband service. Landline connections and mobile services remained intact, meaning services such as telecare devices remained operational.
More than 80% of the previously unresponsive customers are understood to have subsequently taken the steps needed to switch over.
“Throughout this transformation BT has been raising awareness of the switchover, supported by local events, advertising campaigns and partners – as well as direct communications to our customers,” said a BT spokesperson.
“A small minority of customers are yet to move and haven’t responded to repeated communications about the change. The temporary broadband pause we have introduced for this small minority is intended to help prevent a complete loss of service when the old, analogue network is retired.
“In the final months of the programme, it’s critical that customers take action when contacted about the switchover – failing to do so could result in the loss of their services when the outdated network retires.”
Campaigners are concerned that the 1.3 million households still on copper lines include vulnerable individuals, such as elderly people with only a landline and no internet and those in rural areas with patchy, or no, broadband and variable mobile coverage who worry about being able to call emergency services if there is a power cut.
There are also around 2 million users of telecare services, most commonly personal pendant alarms or buttons that have traditionally relied on copper landlines, which are unaffected if the internet goes down.
In December, Virgin Media was fined £23.8m for leaving thousands of customers, typically older and disabled people, without access to their alarms as it was transitioning customers in 2023.
The issue of vulnerable customers resulted in a pause of non-voluntary migrations to digital landlines, and ultimately resulted in the industry moving the copper landline retirement date from December last year to the end of this coming January.
For most customers, the switch involved just plugging their existing home phone handset into the back of their broadband router rather than into the phone socket on the wall.
Caroline Abrahams, the charity director at Age UK, said: “As the January 2027 deadline gets closer the telecoms providers should commit to ensuring that no older person is cut off if they haven’t yet switched. It should not mark a hard-and-fast cliff edge. We know that older people are overrepresented among those who are yet to switch.”

Brazil’s neck-and-neck election offers test for growing pro-Trump Latin American bloc
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
07:00:35 UTC
16:00:35 KST

Shortly after his controversial speech to the United Nations general assembly in September, Donald Trump gathered a dozen like-minded Latin American leaders and boasted that rightwing candidates had won all seven presidential elections held in the region since he began his second term.
“Everybody I’ve endorsed has won,” the US president said in New York to most of the leaders of the Shield of the Americas, an anti-drug cartel coalition of 15 countries governed by the right or far right.
Those electoral victories – and the US takeover of Venezuela after capturing Nicolás Maduro – have left just six Latin American countries under leftwing governments: regional heavyweights Brazil and Mexico, small Uruguay and Guatemala, and the isolated regimes of Cuba and Nicaragua.
On Sunday, Brazilians go to the polls in a presidential election that many believe will determine more than Latin America’s largest country’s fate for the next four years.
Given Mexico’s geographic proximity and unique economic relationship with the US, analysts see Brazil as perhaps the last country in the region still capable of saying “no” to Trump’s whims – something that could change dramatically depending on the election result.
Polls indicate a neck-and-neck race between Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, the 80-year-old leftist incumbent who is seeking a fourth non-consecutive term, and Flávio Bolsonaro, 45, the far-right senator son of former president Jair Bolsonaro.
“Trump really does take seriously the idea that the Americas should be his back yard,” said Pedro Telles, a professor at the School of International Relations at Brazil’s FGV university.
“Mexico will remain relevant, and its president, Claudia Sheinbaum, is one of the most popular leftwing leaders. But if Flávio wins, it would be a real blow to the left and a major boost to the far-right agenda globally,” added Telles.
“There is a lot at stake,” said Sandra Borda Guzmán, an associate professor of political science at Colombia’s Universidad de los Andes. “Instead of taking the opportunity to expand our region’s autonomy, a far-right victory would align the region unconditionally with the dictates of the US,” she added.
Lula and Bolsonaro differ sharply on the US, including over what has become Trump’s main foreign policy for the region: the so-called “war on drugs” used to justify dozens of airstrikes on boats that have killed more than 230 people and joint operations involving US military personnel on land.
While Bolsonaro has pledged to join the Shield of the Americas and to follow an “iron fist” approach to crime, Lula has raised concerns about sovereignty and said it is “sad to see the inferiority complex of Latin American presidents” who are part of the Trump-created coalition.
Lula and Trump’s relationship has swung between not speaking and public displays of warmth, but it is currently at a low point, with the Brazilian president and Democratic members of the US Congress accusing Washington of trying to interfere in Bolsonaro’s favour.
“Brazil is a big prize,” said Michael Shifter, adjunct professor at Georgetown University’s School of Foreign Service, adding that amid endless conflicts in Iran, Ukraine and Israel-Palestine, “US foreign policy is going very badly in the rest of the world.”
A victory for Bolsonaro in Brazil, he said, would be used “triumphantly” by Trump for producing an “almost completely aligned region”.
At the latest Shield of the Americas meeting, Trump made clear that it was not all about security. The US president also referred to the “tremendous natural wealth” of Latin American countries, which he said could not “be taken over by hostile outside powers” – widely understood as a reference to China.
Privileged access to Brazil’s rare earths and critical minerals was one of the conditions Washington imposed in exchange for not applying tariffs, which Lula rejected. Bolsonaro, on the other hand, has offered those natural resources as the “solution” to help the US “break its dependence on China”.
“Democracy is also kind of on the line here,” added Shifter, noting that Bolsonaro was only running because his father cannot – Jair Bolsonaro is under house arrest after being convicted of attempting a coup to overturn his defeat by Lula in the 2022 election.
“So it’s not just a question of one more country moving to the right, but of a right that has a very problematic relationship with democracy,” he said.
As in recent elections across Latin America, the race includes other candidates but is polarised between two leading candidates. Lula and Bolsonaro have alternated as frontrunners in the final stretch, making the outcome unpredictable; if neither wins 50% plus one of the votes, there will be a runoff on 25 October.
Bolsonaro’s only previous bid for an executive role in government ended ignominiously when he took fourth place in Rio’s 2016 mayoral race. But analysts say there are several reasons why a congressman best known for his family name and corruption allegations – some shelved, others still under investigation – has emerged as a serious challenger to a three-time president.
Unemployment, poverty and inflation have fallen, and average incomes have risen, but so has household debt – something many attribute to online betting, which the older Bolsonaro left unregulated and Lula banned days before the vote.
The incumbent’s campaign has also been hit by corruption allegations – still under investigation – involving his son and a former aide, while a scandal involving supreme court justices with no connection to Lula may have rubbed off on the president.
Many therefore see Bolsonaro’s support as coming both from a simple transfer of his father’s voter base and from an anti-Lula vote.
“I’m going to vote for Flávio, but not because I think he’s the best option,” said Bruna Arguello, 34, a businesswoman from Santana de Parnaíba, whose first choice would be Ronaldo Caiado, a far-right former governor of Goiás, polling at 4%. “Unfortunately, he has no chance of winning, so I’m going with Flávio so we can get Lula out,” she said.
Actor Docy Moreira, 59, will vote for Lula. In 2018, she was so dismayed by Jair Bolsonaro’s election that she decided to leave her home town of Belo Horizonte, where two-thirds of voters backed the far-right leader. “I couldn’t understand how people, including the vast majority of my family, were choosing so much violence and authoritarianism,” she said.
She Googled which cities had given Bolsonaro the lowest share of the vote, chose one about 1,550 miles away and moved north to Luís Correia, in Piauí.
She eventually returned home, and most of her family will now vote for Bolsonaro’s son. Still, Moreira remains confident Lula will win.
“If not, it will be devastating, but I’m not going to move again. I’m stronger now. I’ve learned that I can find refuge within myself,” said Moreira.

Chinese lithium mine registers wider vein, bolstering Beijing’s battery supply
A deposit in Sichuan has registered over 1 million tonnes of lithium carbonate equivalent, adding to China’s stores of the valuable metal
China has announced the expansion of the resource base for a major lithium deposit in the southwestern province of Sichuan by about 70 per cent, strengthening the country’s potential long-term supply for the metal – an essential component in the production of batteries for electric vehicles (EVs) and energy storage.
After recent detection efforts, the Jiada Lithium Mine has registered about 1.05 million tonnes of lithium carbonate equivalent in the deposit, bringing its total resources to 2.53 million tonnes, state news agency Xinhua reported on Thursday. The increase reinforces the mine’s status as a major hard-rock lithium deposit.
Dazhong Mining, the project’s developer, said in a filing that the additional resources had passed review and registration by the Ministry of Natural Resources. They comprise 33.52 million tonnes of ore containing about 423,800 tonnes of lithium oxide, with an average grade of 1.26 per cent.
The addition represents a 70.5 per cent increase from the previously registered 1.48 million tonnes of lithium carbonate equivalent, according to the filing.

‘It finds discarded pizza slices’: Raccoons invade Lithuania’s Curonian Spit
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
07:00:00 UTC
16:00:00 KST

Raccoons are being counted and monitored on the Curonian Spit as authorities prepare a management plan for the invasive species. The animals are likely to start being trapped and hunted as early as next spring.
"The impression is that there are quite a lot of them here, but it is difficult to say exactly how many. I would estimate there could be between 50 and 100 individuals," says Saulius Rumbutis, an employee of the Tadas Ivanauskas Zoological Museum.
Raccoons are nocturnal animals and usually hide during the day.
"They often choose large natural tree hollows or simply a broken-off section of a pine tree. They climb up such a pine and can spend the day there sleeping, then go out at night to look for food," Rumbutis says.
Most raccoons are being observed in Juodkrantė. The omnivorous animals stay close to settlements, where there is plenty of food.
"They crack open mollusc shells and feed on them, find a bird's nest on the ground or in a tree and eat the chicks or eggs. If they find a pizza slice discarded by a tourist in a bin, they will certainly eat that too," says Rumbutis.
On the mainland, only the occasional raccoon is spotted, but they have to face deadly predators, including wolves. On the Curonian Spit, raccoons usually die only after being hit by cars.
"They would run across the road at night while we were driving through the forest. I've seen them," one local woman says.
"They become uncontrollable, and that's the problem. Then they destroy some of our native animals," another woman adds.
The Environment Ministry is preparing a plan to manage raccoons because the problems will increase if nothing is done, according to scientists.
Raccoons are likely to start being hunted as early as next year.
"They can be caught using live traps. They smell the bait, go into the traps and get caught. The problem is that if the traps have not been specially modified, raccoons can easily use their nimble front paws to open the doors of traps and escape," says Rumbutis.
Raccoons may have spread on the Curonian Spit after someone released animals that had been kept in captivity.

NEW YORK – Flydubai flight 1073 was carrying four pilots on its journey from Dubai, United Arab Emirates, to Tel Aviv, Israel. After a co-pilot stabbed the captain, two pilots who were seated in the cabin took control and safely landed the Boeing 737 Max 8 jet in Saudi Arabia.
For the most part, airlines do not intentionally staff shorter flights with a backup flight crew simply as a precaution, because paying two sets of pilots is expensive. However, pilots routinely hitch rides on flights they are not operating – a practice known in the industry as “deadheading” – to position themselves where they are needed next.

Russia has lost around 1,538,950 troops in Ukraine since the beginning of its full-scale invasion on Feb. 24, 2022, the General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine reported on Oct. 3.
The number includes 1,560 casualties that Russian forces suffered over the past day.
According to the report, Russia has also lost 12,391 tanks, 25,477 armored combat vehicles, 156,731 vehicles and fuel tanks, 50,637 artillery systems, 2,178 multiple launch rocket systems, 1,683 air defense systems, 443 aircraft, 356 helicopters, 2,824 unmanned ground vehicles, 35 ships and boats, and two submarines.
Ukraine's General Staff has not revealed its own losses during the full-scale invasion, citing operational secrecy.
Independent Western think-tank reports agree that the Russian casualties significantly surpass Ukraine's losses, with the Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS) estimating the ratio to be "roughly 2.5:1 or 2:1."
A January 2026 CSIS report said Ukraine has likely suffered between 500,000 and 600,000 casualties from February 2022 to December 2025, of which between 100,000 and 140,000 are thought to be killed in action (KIA).
While Ukrainian officials rarely disclose the figure, President Volodymyr Zelensky told France TV on Feb. 4 that at least 55,000 Ukrainian soldiers have been killed in action since the beginning of the full-scale war, in addition to significant numbers who are missing in action.
The intensity of Russian drone attacks and the fighting has made it extremely difficult for Ukraine to retrieve the bodies of fallen soldiers, which are needed for DNA confirmation.

United Hatzalah volunteers rescue Torah scrolls from Jerusalem synagogue fire
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
06:58:29 UTC
15:58:29 KST

Most emergencies are measured in human terms. How many people were injured? How serious are their wounds? How quickly did help arrive?
There are also instances when United Hatzalah volunteers are called upon to help animals affected by an emergency. But the organization is rarely called upon to rescue objects.
That was what happened last week when United Hatzalah volunteers responded to a fire at a synagogue on Sha’arei Pina Street in Jerusalem’s Mea Shearim neighborhood.
A fire is always frightening. Thankfully, there were no injuries. But several Torah scrolls were severely damaged, with United Hatzalah volunteers rushing into the building to help rescue some of the most precious objects in Jewish life.
The timing of the fire, just days after Yom Kippur and shortly before Simchat Torah, carries particular meaning. Simchat Torah marks the completion of the annual cycle of Torah reading. Yet there is almost no pause before the Jewish cycle begins again. Almost in the same breath that the final verses of the Torah are read, we immediately return to the opening words of Genesis.
For volunteers, that sense of continuity is particularly familiar. In emergency medicine, they often begin exactly where someone else left off. Advanced life support medics and paramedics continue the care already provided by an EMT, just as hospital professionals continue the treatment that began in the field.
The principle of Kol Yisrael arevim zeh lazeh, that the Jewish people are responsible for one another, is a value that the organization’s nearly 10,000 volunteers live by every day. This time, however, it was not someone who needed rescuing, but something we all hold dear: Torah scrolls.
Importance of a Torah scroll: Far more than parchment and ink
A Torah scroll is far more than parchment and ink. It carries the story, tradition, and identity of the Jewish people. Its teachings have shaped Jewish life for generations and continue to influence the values by which Jews live today.
Just as Jews devote themselves first and foremost to protecting human life, United Hatzalah also protects sacred objects when they are threatened, as the organization’s workers helped rescue those Torah scrolls from the flames.
For the organization’s volunteers, it is all about that familiar rhythm – one emergency ends, another begins – as they care for and protect what matters most.

Ten years later: How an Israeli surgeon saved three lives in on Yom Kippur - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
06:58:21 UTC
15:58:21 KST

A decade has passed since that Yom Kippur, 2016. I can’t get it out of my mind.
It was the night Ben-Gurion Airport was opened for a matter of life and death.
The Grinfeld family, like so many other Israelis, were taking advantage of the Tishrei holidays and the days off from work and school to take a vacation abroad. Noa and Hanoch Grinfeld and their four children – Yiftach, then 11; Ahinoam, 10; Ivri, seven; and Nevo, five – from the town of Ma’aleh Michmas, northeast of Jerusalem, decided on the Republic of Georgia, with its budget-friendly mix of hiking in the Caucasus Mountains, history, and a vibrant Jewish community with synagogues and kosher food for the holidays.
It sounded perfect.
Travel sites for Georgia highlight Tusheti, a spectacular, high-altitude historic region known for its alpine scenery and pristine beauty.
They also mention the Abano Pass, one of the world’s most notoriously dangerous roads.
That’s where the family was touring when visibility turned bad. Hanoch, then 42, was driving the large four-wheel-drive vehicle they had rented. He inched along at 10 km. an hour. Should they try to pull over or continue to their lodgings?
Suddenly, the jeep’s tires slid off the narrow road. It tumbled into a ravine 80 meters deep.
When the movement stopped, Hanoch at first thought he was dead. It was cold, dark, and silent. Near him, Ahinoam – named in memory of his brother Yehuda, who was killed in Lebanon – was lifeless. So was Nevo.
Then Hanoch heard Ivri’s voice.
“Abba, Abba!” he called.
Yiftach was seriously injured. So was Noa. She couldn’t move her legs.
Hanoch crawled up the abyss, pulling himself over a steep wall. He spotted headlights in the distance – his only hope. In desperation, without a common language, he made the Georgians understand what had happened.
The treacherous rescue began. Then, for hours, they were driven 220 km. over pitted roads to Tbilisi.
The Georgian doctors and nurses were devoted, but Noa and Yiftach needed the more advanced medical care available in Israel, their family in Israel realized. They urgently needed to get home.
But how?
It was the day before Yom Kippur. Ben-Gurion Airport had shut down as the holiday approached. Even the Israeli rescue services were closed.
A resourceful family friend contacted VitalOne, a US medical transport company run by Rabbi Isaac Leider of Monsey, New York. He agreed to undertake the rescue, but warned that they would still have to navigate formidable bureaucratic and diplomatic channels.
They would need permission from the Civil Aviation Authority of Israel, the Airports Authority, the Transport Ministry, and the Prime Minister’s Office. They would need two pilots, a medical team, a plane, and 1,000 gallons of fuel. They needed airport staff on Yom Kippur.
Ben-Gurion Airport hadn’t been open on Yom Kippur for seven years.
Another major obstacle remained. Noa’s cervical spine was detached, and the hospital executives in Georgia were unwilling to let her be transferred, concerned that she would die on the way to the airport.
Her family in Israel sought an orthopedist who could confidently do the transfer and who was willing to fly to the rescue on Yom Kippur eve.
The orthopedist whom they approached was eating seudat mafseket, the meal before the Yom Kippur fast, with his wife and children in Modi’in when his phone buzzed with WhatsApp images of Noa’s neck.
Did he know how to transport such a patient? And would he be willing to fly out if the airport were open and the other bureaucratic hurdles were overcome?
Yes and yes, said the doctor. However, he pointed out that Ben-Gurion Airport was still shut. He promised to take his phone to synagogue, to be available should there be any news.
KOL NIDRE is traditionally recited three times at the opening of the Yom Kippur evening service. During the second repetition, the surgeon felt his phone vibrate.
The flight, he saw, was a go.
'What a beautiful sight to see everyone waiting for the patients'
He asked a friend to tell his wife, on the other side of the crowded synagogue, that he was leaving. He jogged home to get his car. He needed equipment, particularly a kit to stabilize Noa’s neck. He called his Russian-born department head to ask what might be needed in the former Soviet Union.
The highway from Modi’in to Hadassah Medical Center, in Jerusalem’s Ein Kerem, where he worked, had few cars but was filled with bicyclists.
When he finally reached the hospital, he asked for an ambulance to rush him to the airport, where he met the other members of the medical team.
The plane took off at 9:58 p.m.
They landed in Tbilisi close to midnight. The Israeli Consulate arranged an ambulance to take them to the injured family.
Hanoch and Ivri had light injuries. The doctor stabilized Noa’s neck and then asked to see Yiftach, the seriously injured boy. He was across town in a children’s hospital.
The Israeli doctor was distressed by the treatment Yiftach was receiving for a complex fracture and insisted it be changed immediately. The Georgian doctor said he was unfamiliar with the proposed treatment and that the Israeli doctor would have to take responsibility.
“Isn’t that why I’ve come?” asked the Sabra doctor, who took charge.
After five hours on the ground, the team and patients took off.
“I was worried that it would be hard to gather the staff on Yom Kippur, “ the doctor said.”Surgery was urgent.”
But what he found brought relief and a swelling of Zionist pride.
Some of the medical staff had walked to Ein Kerem. Others came by bicycle. Ambulances had worked overtime bringing still others.
“What a beautiful sight to see everyone waiting for the patients,” he said.
I know all these details because the orthopedic surgeon is my son, Prof. Josh Schroeder, now the head of Hadassah’s Spine Unit.
To mark the 10th anniversary, he received a thank-you note from Noa’s family for being among the many good people who took part in this extraordinary rescue. The update included the happy news that Yiftach, who had the complex fracture, had recently married.
On that Yom Kippur, they operated all day.
When they finished, the final prayers were being chanted in the hospital’s Abbell Synagogue under the Chagall Windows.
“Avinu Malkeinu, shlah refuah shleimah l’holei amecha....
“Our Father, Our King, send complete recovery to the sick among Your people.”
And the last: “Be gracious to us and answer us, though we have no worthy deeds...”
I once asked Josh why he had taken part in this mission on Yom Kippur.
He said he didn’t understand my question. Would he or any Israeli doctor ever give up the privilege of helping to secure a place for a patient in the Book of Life on Yom Kippur?
Chag sameach!■
The writer is the Israel director of public relations at Hadassah, the Women’s Zionist Organization of America. Her latest book is A Daughter of Many Mothers.

Russia turns helicopter missile into truck-mounted weapon
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
06:55:14 UTC
15:55:14 KST

- Russia fired its new truck-mounted Izdeliye 347 launcher with a modified LMUR missile at mock artillery positions during the Tsentr-2026 exercise.
- The Defense Ministry says the system can hit stationary and moving targets up to 20 km away, with operator guidance in the final phase.
Russia has fired a guided missile from its attack helicopters off a truck, using a new ground launcher called Izdeliye 347, or “Product 347,” against mock artillery positions during its Tsentr-2026 exercise.
The Russian Defense Ministry said on Oct. 2 that the system carries a modified version of the LMUR light multipurpose guided missile and can hit stationary and moving targets up to 20 km (12 miles) away. During the main stage of the drills at the Chebarkul training range in the Chelyabinsk region, crews used it to strike artillery positions that had been found by aerial reconnaissance.
The ministry said the launcher is mounted on a truck and that an operator can steer the missile onto the target in the final part of its flight. It did not say how many missiles each launcher carries, what chassis it uses, who builds it, or when it could enter service.
The LMUR, also known as Izdeliye 305 and the Kh-39, is built by the KBM design bureau in Kolomna, part of Rostec’s High Precision Systems holding. It weighs about 105 kg (231 pounds) and carries a 25 kg (55-pound) high-explosive fragmentation warhead. The basic version has a stated range of 14.5 km, and a longer-range variant reportedly reaches beyond 25 km.
Russia fields the missile on its Mi-28NM and Ka-52M attack helicopters and has used it widely against Ukrainian forces. Its main advantage is that it does not need to see the target at launch. The missile flies toward given coordinates using satellite navigation, then sends video from its thermal seeker back to the operator, who picks out the target and guides it in. That lets helicopter crews fire from well behind the front, out of range of most Ukrainian short-range air defenses.
A ground version would give Russian units the same kind of long-range, man-in-the-loop strike capability without risking a helicopter. The concept is similar to Israel’s Spike NLOS, which is fired from helicopters, vehicles and ships.
Russia has tried this before. Several years ago, the Defense Ministry worked on a project codenamed Baikal to adapt the LMUR for ground launch. That design used an armored tracked vehicle, similar in concept to the Khrizantema-S anti-tank system, and was also meant to engage slow, low-flying aerial targets. Its fate was never made public.
Izdeliye 347 takes a different approach, putting the missile on an unarmored truck instead of a tracked combat vehicle.
The launcher was one of several new or rarely seen systems Russia showed at Tsentr-2026, which ran from Sept. 28 to Oct. 3 and involved more than 47,000 troops, according to the Defense Ministry.

Flydubai co-pilot attacked pilot with axe, attempted ‘terrorist’ attack, UAE says
DUBAI/JERUSALEM – The co-pilot of flydubai Flight FZ1073 attempted to carry out a terrorist attack during the flight, the United Arab Emirates Attorney-General said on Oct 3, according to the state news agency WAM.
The co-pilot was identified as Hammam al-Hammami, an Omani national, a source with direct knowledge of the matter told Reuters. A second source briefed on the investigation confirmed the co-pilot’s name. The UAE authorities did not immediately respond to a request for confirmation of his identity.
While the Emirati authorities have not publicly identified the co-pilot, Israeli officials have previously said he is an Omani national. Oman has not commented on the incident.
“Investigations into the incident involving flydubai Flight FZ1073 found that the co-pilot had attempted to carry out a terrorist attack,” WAM quoted UAE Attorney-General Hamad Saif Al Shamsi as saying.
The co-pilot attacked the pilot inside the cockpit with a crash axe and attempted to take control of the aircraft, he said.
A crash axe is typically kept in the cockpit for use during emergencies.
Investigations are ongoing to determine the circumstances of the incident, the motives and any related connections, as well as to examine physical and digital evidence, Al Shamsi added. The UAE is leading the investigation. The airline is owned by Dubai’s government.
Al Shamsi’s comments were the first by the Emirati authorities to describe the incident as an attempted terrorist attack.
Disaster was averted on Sept 30 after passengers and crew subdued the co-pilot, who had attacked the captain in what Israeli officials said was an apparent attempt to crash the plane carrying more than 170 passengers and crew.
A reserve flydubai pilot travelling on the flight took control of the aircraft and landed it at Tabuk airport in north-western Saudi Arabia, where the co-pilot was detained by the Saudi authorities. The captain and co-pilot left Saudi Arabia for Abu Dhabi on the morning of Oct 1 after receiving medical clearance, the Saudi Interior Ministry said.
Flydubai said the circumstances surrounding the incident were still under investigation and that it was not in a position to comment further, a spokesperson said.
A source briefed on the investigation told Reuters on Oct 2 that Israeli officials were expected to question the co-pilot in the UAE. The source declined to say which Israeli agency or authority would take part.
An Israeli government official told Reuters earlier that Israeli investigators would take part alongside the Emirati authorities in the UAE-led investigation, which would examine what happened as well as the suspect’s motives and background.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said on Oct 2 that Israel was looking into whether the co-pilot had acted under anyone’s direction, warning that anyone involved would pay a “heavy price”.
Netanyahu said on Oct 1 that the co-pilot had undergone radical Islamist indoctrination and appeared suicidal, though he said a motive had not yet been established. Most of the passengers on board were Israeli nationals.
The aircraft dropped about 16,625 feet in just over 30 seconds while flying over Saudi Arabia on its journey from the UAE to Israel, according to flight-tracking data from Flightradar24. The route is popular among Israeli travellers. REUTERS

Lithuania issues possible air alert warning in Vilnius County, Ukmergė
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
06:52:00 UTC
15:52:00 KST

Lithuania’s authorities have issued an all-clear (code white) following an earlier air alert.
“The Lithuanian Armed Forces inform: AIR ALERT IS OVER (WHITE). You may leave safe places or shelters,” the authorities said in an emergency message.
Previously, at around 09:50, a possible air raid alert (yellow) was issued, indicating that a possibly dangerous object had crossed into Lithuania's airspace. The warning affected Vilnius County in the east of the country. The alert was called off around 50 minutes later.
“It was confirmed that there was no air threat, as the object posed no danger. Whether it was birds or some other object, I cannot say at this time,” NKVC Director Vilmantas Vitkauskas told LRT RADIO on Saturday.
According to the National Crisis Management Centre (NKVC), fighter jets have been scrambled. The controlled airspace around Vilnius Airport has been temporarily closed due to the activity of unidentified flying objects.
“The object has not yet been fully identified; fighter jets have been scrambled and are carrying out that procedure. We are receiving reports from residents that they are observing a possible object already outside the Vilnius area, moving toward Jonava. But we cannot confirm this, as these are reports from residents,” NKVC Director Vilmantas Vitkauskas told LRT RADIO.
He said it is likely that an alert could also be issued in the Kaunas district.
According to him, the speed of the object is relatively slow so it cannot be ruled out that it could be just a flock of birds. Although, according to the NKVC, indications suggest it could be a drone.
Here is a map of shelters across Lithuania:
Vilnius County includes eight municipalities:
- Elektrėnai Municipality
- Šalčininkai District Municipality
- Širvintos District Municipality
- Švenčionys District Municipality
- Trakai District Municipality
- Ukmergė District Municipality
- Vilnius City Municipality
- Vilnius District Municipality

‘Trauma still there’: A decades-old standoff returns to Northern Ireland
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
06:51:09 UTC
15:51:09 KST

‘Trauma still there’: A decades-old standoff returns to Northern Ireland
Families who lived through one of the Troubles’ worst flashpoints fear its legacy is reaching another generation.
Portadown, Northern Ireland – When the summer holidays arrived, Chris Nelson worried about his mother.
At night, he lay awake waiting for her to return. During the day, he rang family members to ask if she was safe. There were threats and letters through the door.
“I was afraid to leave the house,” he told Al Jazeera.
His mother, Rosemary Nelson, was a lawyer representing the Catholic residents opposing the Protestant Orange Order parade along Portadown’s Garvaghy Road in Northern Ireland in the late 1990s.
Every July, as marching season approached, there was a standoff.
Orangemen sought to return from Drumcree church along what they regarded as their traditional route. Residents opposed the passage of the anti-Catholic organisation through a majority Catholic street. In some years, police forced the parade through. In later years, it was blocked.
Rosemary would spend summer evenings alongside the residents on Garvaghy Road. Before leaving home each evening, she told her son that she was going to look after families and make sure their children were okay. She compared them to his friends at primary school.
“She was a big believer in helping the underdog,” said Chris, now 39. “She did a lot of work for free.”
His mother helped people from both sides of the community. When work allowed, the family went to Bundoran, across the border, and for a day the fear would pass.
But one night, during a standoff in 1997 when the state police force, the Royal Ulster Constabulary (RUC), used batons to clear Catholic locals from the road, “she was beaten by the police”, said Chris. “She was spat on”, bruised and bloodied.
“That was very traumatic. I was always thinking something was going to happen to my mum.”
On a Monday in March 1999, nearly a year after the Good Friday Agreement brought an end to the conflict, Rosemary drove away from her home in Lurgan.
As she braked at a nearby junction, a bomb beneath her car exploded. Her eight-year-old daughter, Sarah, was at primary school nearby and heard the blast. The family had spent the previous weekend in Bundoran together.
Chris, 11 at the time, and his older brother were away on a school ski trip when they received a phone call with the news of her death.
“That was hard”, he said, his voice tailing off.
A legacy of loss
Nearly three decades later, another standoff has recast these childhood memories into fears for the next generation, with a renewed attempt by the Protestant Orange Order to march through the Catholic neighbourhood, threatening to unravel a fragile peace.
The Troubles began in the late 1960s as protests by Catholics against discrimination were met by repression and violence. Republican paramilitaries fought for a united Ireland as loyalists and the army battled to preserve British rule, in a conflict that killed more than 3,500 people.
The 1998 Good Friday Agreement established a framework for peace and power-sharing.
Under the agreement, the people of Portadown have lived in relative peace for the past 28 years.
But this was suddenly unsettled by a last-minute decision by the High Court to allow the march. In response, Catholic residents blocked the road. Many camped out as Orange men gathered at the top of the road, awaiting police permission to pass – an image of division that never truly left.
Many of the Garvaghy Road residents are now parents, and fear what their children might inherit from a dispute they hoped had been left behind.
Paul O’Connor, of the Pat Finucane Centre human rights group in Northern Ireland, said Rosemary Nelson is among 21 people whose deaths were linked to the Drumcree dispute.
Many are still being investigated, with families continuing to seek justice and pressing for public inquiries amid concerns about collusion between the British state and loyalist paramilitaries, many of which were members of the Orange Order.
“These murders encompass LVF (Loyal Volunteer Force) killings at that time, and are all linked to the Drumcree disputes. They were responsible for many of the killings around the Mid Ulster area at that time. They were trying to destabilise the peace process, with many riots spreading around, including into Derry,” O’Connor told Al Jazeera.
He worked with Rosemary Nelson and is now seeking a public inquiry into the murder of Sean Brown, another Drumcree-linked case, he believes. The 61-year-old father of six from Bellaghy, County Derry, was abducted and murdered in May 1997.
The following year, the three Quinn brothers – Richard, 10, Mark, nine, and Jason, eight – died after loyalists petrol-bombed their home in Ballymoney, County Antrim, as they slept. Their deaths, during the unrest surrounding Drumcree, brought widespread calls for the Orange Order to end its standoff.
Fear and loathing in Mid Ulster
In Portadown town centre, a Union flag flies among plinths dedicated to the Ulster Defence Regiment, a locally recruited unit of the British army and the Ulster Covenant – a document signed when nearly 500,000 people opposed a form of self-government for Ireland in 1912.
Around the corner, in the Edgarstown housing estate, Ulster Volunteer Force (UVF) flags hang from lampposts, and the kerbs are painted red, white and blue, alongside a mural of a Rangers FC badge.
The area is one of the heartlands of unionism. The Orange Order was founded in 1795 in the village of Loughgall, a few miles from Drumcree.
The Orangemen say they have marched the route through Garvaghy Road since 1807. The parade has been blocked from Garvaghy Road since 1998, but the Orangemen have continued submitting requests to march.
The latest Parades Commission decision permitted 35 men to walk without music. Since then, Orangemen have repeatedly approached the police line before returning to the church.
Irish nationalists have criticised the police assessment underpinning the decision to allow the march, while unionists have denounced police for failing to forcibly remove protesters blocking the route.
Al Jazeera contacted the three main unionist parties – the Democratic Unionist Party (DUP), the Traditional Unionist Voice (TUV) and the Ulster Unionist Party (UUP) – for comment but received no response.
Addressing around 200 supporters in Portadown, loyalist activist Jamie Bryson described protesters as “an unlawful snarling mob”.
He has called for the First Minister, Sinn Fein’s Michelle O’Neill, and police Chief Constable Jon Boutcher to resign, and demands that the Orange men must be allowed to walk the Garvaghy Road.
O’Neill has faced criticism for standing beside the protesters.
At Drumcree Church, the Orangemen were not marching, but sitting down drinking tea and eating crisps. Around six men, one wearing his sash, huddled under a gazebo in the cold.
“We are waiting patiently for the chief constable to apply the law of the land,” Nigel Dawson, the Portadown Orange Order district master, told Al Jazeera.
“Portadown District has never in its history stopped a parade down the road to have a confrontation with its neighbours, ever. So I don’t know where the fear and trepidation comes from.”
Another Orangeman, who requested anonymity, added: “We are determined to get home after Sunday service … We just want to go home.”
‘This community was a ghetto’
Around a mile further down the Garvaghy Road, Irish folk band the Mary Wallopers performed to hundreds of residents and supporters.
Children danced and slid down the embankment, as parents watched from above. Palestine and Ireland flags flew in the wind.
Linda O’Neill, 51, a Garvaghy Road resident, told Al Jazeera the scene would have been unimaginable 30 years ago.
“It was horrendous growing up as a teenager. We stayed in our own community. We didn’t access the town centre … This community was a ghetto. And that was deliberate.”
Another resident, Ciaran O Ferghail, remembered summers spent surrounded by British forces.
“This community was turned into a war zone. There were tanks and British Army everywhere, thousands of RUC. This community was completely under siege every summer, by the Orange Order, the British military, the RUC and loyalist paramilitaries. We were surrounded on every road and in every direction.”
O’Neill said the confrontation changed as residents began asserting their rights.
In 1995, hundreds sat down on Garvaghy Road to block the parade. The ensuing violent standoff between security forces and Orangemen and their loyalist supporters ended in a compromise allowing the march through. Residents say they understood it would be the last.
But the following summer, the parade returned. Police initially blocked it, then reversed course after five days of widespread loyalist attacks. Officers forced residents off the road and beat them, sparking riots in Catholic communities.
In 1997, security forces sealed off the Catholic neighbourhood before dawn and allowed the parade through at midday amid loyalist threats to kill Catholics if it was stopped. Nationalist protests and violence followed. From 1998, the march was banned from Garvaghy Road. But for residents, summers remained marked by the army’s steel barricades until 2000.
Lessons from the past
Chris Nelson, almost 40, is around the same age his mother was when she was killed.
The Garvaghy Road protests mark the first time he has chosen to speak publicly about his mother.
He went on to study law at university, but says his life would have followed a different trajectory if she were still here.
The public inquiry into his mother’s death found no evidence that state security agencies had “directly facilitated” her murder, but it “could not exclude the possibility” that individual members of those agencies had helped the perpetrators.
The inquiry brought the past back repeatedly as he tried to get on with his life. But seeing photographs of families linking arms on Garvaghy Road brought back unavoidable memories of his mother.
“If she were here, that’s where she would be,” he said, “standing with the people of the Garvaghy Road”.
While there has been no violence in Portadown, in Derry’s Waterside, two recent nights of disorder saw petrol bombs and masonry thrown at police. Officers described the crowd on the second night as mostly young people.
The renewed attempt to bring the Orange Order parade through Garvaghy Road risks leaving its mark on children on both sides. With some schools closed, Chris Nelson worries about parents having to explain to their kids what is happening.
“Children don’t forget things“, he said. “They absorb everything.”
He remembers how it felt waiting for his mother each night, and how that worry followed him through the summer holidays. He wants something different for the children growing up now.
“Children shouldn’t grow up knowing the difference between Catholic and Protestant.
“It isn’t something that should be brought into the mind of a child.”

Bosnia-Herzegovina shaped by war, separatism, EU ambitions
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
06:51:00 UTC
15:51:00 KST

Bosnia-Herzegovina shaped by war, separatism, EU ambitions
October 3, 2026
To call Bosnia and Herzegovina a complicated country is an understatement. The country in the Balkan Peninsula divides its economic, administrative and political responsibilities between the multiethnic central government, the self-governing neutral Brcko district and two semi-autonomous entities that, for the most part, operate independently — the Muslim-Croat Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina and the Serb-run Republika Srpska.
Both semi-autonomous entities are further split into several cantons and communities, home to mostly Bosniaks and Bosnian Croats in the central-western federation and Bosnian Serbs in Republika Srpska, to the north and east.
This principle of ethnic nationalism is key to the country's central constitutional and political organization. The Bosnian constitution recognizes Bosniaks, who are predominantly Muslim, the largely Orthodox Bosnian Serbs and primarily Catholic Bosnian Croats as "constituent peoples" with equal rights.
Today, the country has a population of around 3.1 million people. Around half are Bosniaks, while 31% are Serb and 15% are Croat. The rest of the inhabitants belong either to one of the 17 officially recognized minorities, like the Roma and Jews, or chose not to identify with any ethnicity at the last official census. Bosnian, Croatian and Serbian are all recognized as official languages.
The central government is led by rotating three-way presidency, made up of one representative from each of the three main constituent groups. The upper house of parliament and key government offices are also divided according to this principle.
This strict balance between the three groups is always maintained, both politically and socially, often leading to ethnic interests and political gridlock dominating the decision-making process.
Dayton Peace Accords brought an end to war
This complex, convoluted and oft dysfunctional structure was set up during the 1995 Dayton Peace Accords, and then anchored in the constitution. It was intended to bring an end to the Bosnian war — sparked by the breakup of Yugoslavia in the early 1990s — and legally secure the balance of power between the three feuding ethnic groups.
During the war, from 1992 to 1995, the armed forces of the Bosniaks and the Bosnian Croats initially fought each other, before all three groups began to clash. Later, the Bosniaks and the Bosnian Croats joined forces to take on Republika Srpska. Throughout the war, neighboring Serbia and Croatia were actively involved in the fighting.
The fighting devastated wide swaths of the country, and resulted in countless war crimes — among them the nearly four-year siege of Sarajevo and the Srebrenica genocide, in which thousands of Bosniaks were killed at the hands of Serb forces.
By the end of the war, some 100,000 people had been killed. A further 2.2 million were displaced by so-called "ethnic cleansing," forced from their homes by expulsions and violence to flee to other communities or abroad.
The fighting only ended after the international community, especially the United States, stepped up its involvement, culminating in the peace deal agreed at a military base near Dayton, Ohio in November 1995.
International oversight — essential, or no longer relevant?
Although Bosnia and Herzegovina has been recognized on the international stage since the signing of the Dayton agreement, and is also represented at the United Nations, the country itself is still, in effect, only partially independent.
The Office of the High Representative for Bosnia and Herzegovina, an international institution responsible for overseeing the civilian aspects of the Dayton agreement, has been in place since a UN Security Council resolution in 1995.
The high representative — Christian Schmidt of Germany until this past June, and currently filled by acting head Louis J. Crishock of the US — has sweeping powers. He can dismiss elected officials, pass laws, establish new government agencies and overrule all the country's democratic institutions.
This authority is often referred to as the Bonn Powers, as they were negotiated during a meeting of the Peace Implementation Council in Bonn, Germany in December 1997. From 2002 to 2011, the high representative also acted as the EU special representative for Bosnia and Herzegovina.
In recent years, there's been much discussion over whether the office is still relevant. Supporters have said the high representative remains a necessary guarantor of the country's unity and functionality. But critics have pointed out the negative impact on Bosnia-Herzegovina's democratic culture, turning the country into a de facto protectorate that, to an extent, frees local politicians of responsibility for their actions.
Separatist ambitions surface once more
The sharpest criticism has come from the Republika Srpska and Milorad Dodik, its most influential leader. Dodik, in office as prime minister and president of the Serb entity until 2025, views the office and the international backing it provides for a unified Bosnia-Herzegovina as an obstacle to his separatist ambitions.
With strong support from the Serbian capital, Belgrade, Moscow — and, increasingly, the Trump administration — Dodik has flirted with several different scenarios to split his Republika Srpska from Bosnia-Herzegovina. In his interpretation, and that of Republika Srpska's political elite, Bosnia-Herzegovina is highly centralized and unitary, which undermines the independence and sovereignty of the Bosnian Serbs.
A similar sentiment prevails among the political representatives of Bosnia's Croats. Although they aren't considering separation, they are trying to squeeze more independence from the central government in Sarajevo — not least with the creation of a third, Croatian, entity. The plan, incidentally, also has the support of the government in neighboring EU member Croatia.
EU support aims to 'foster regional integration'
A potential path out of the current economic and political paralysis is rapprochement with the European Union — the "European perspective," as it's called in Bosnia-Herzegovina, officially supported by all the relevant political actors.
Bosnia-Herzegovina formally submitted its application for EU membership in 2016, and the European Council gave the green light for negotiations to begin in early 2024. But the actual start of membership talks hinges on the prior implementation of numerous reforms, notably in the areas of rule of law, fighting corruption, the prosecution of organized crime and the functionality of state institutions.
The EU has been financially supporting Bosnia-Herzegovina since 2007 in the framework of pre-accession assistance, and the country is also expected to benefit from the European Commission's Economic and Investment Plan for the Western Balkans. The plan aims to "foster regional integration" — and as a result, infrastructure funding for the Republika Srpska has been partially suspended due to its ongoing separatist rhetoric and policies.
This article was originally written in German.

Montenegro Targets EU Membership by 2028
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
06:49:00 UTC
15:49:00 KST

European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said Montenegro’s accession to the European Union by 2028 is realistic and “within reach” during her official visit to Podgorica, where she met Prime Minister Milojko Spajić and President Jakov Milatović.
The visit was von der Leyen’s third to Montenegro in the past year and was presented as a sign of Brussels’ confidence in the progress achieved by the Balkan country. She said EU enlargement had again become a major geopolitical priority and pointed to Montenegro’s reforms as a positive example for other Western Balkan countries.
Von der Leyen described Montenegro as the region’s undisputed leader, noting that it has completed more than 90 percent of the commitments under the EU Growth Plan.
At a joint news conference with Spajić at Villa Gorica, von der Leyen said the European Commission was preparing additional measures intended to speed up integration. Brussels is expected in the coming days to publish detailed assessments of EU policies to determine the bloc’s internal preparedness for further enlargement.
The Commission will also present individual roadmaps for the most advanced candidate countries, specifying the actions required and their respective deadlines. Von der Leyen stressed that accession remains based on merit, but said progress should not be halted when results are being achieved.
Spajić said Montenegro was entering the “final mile” of its long negotiation process and that his government would not reduce its pace. Most negotiating chapters have already been formally submitted to the European Commission, while Podgorica is ready for detailed reviews and constructive criticism.
The prime minister said he was strongly confident that Montenegro could complete the closure of all negotiating chapters by the end of the year. He also called on the country’s political actors to show consensus and responsibility during the final stage.
Von der Leyen and President Milatović also reaffirmed the accession strategy during their meeting. Milatović presented the country’s plan under the name “28th by '28,” which envisages completing negotiations in 2026, signing the Accession Treaty in 2027 and achieving full EU membership in 2028.
The president said Montenegro was not looking for shortcuts but wanted its achievements to be assessed fairly and for European institutions to provide a predictable path toward membership. He also stressed that Podgorica must prepare for the period after accession by developing sustainable administrative capacity that can immediately turn European funding into infrastructure modernization, investment and improved living standards.
European and Montenegrin officials also discussed potential obstacles to the timetable, including Montenegro’s current political instability. Von der Leyen called for broad political unity and a firm commitment to the European agenda.
The talks also addressed bilateral disputes with neighboring Croatia and the possibility of a veto. Von der Leyen said Brussels was aware of the disputes but expected them to be settled in good faith through bilateral channels.
On safeguard clauses and decision-making procedures, the European Commission president said European law had used comparable mechanisms during previous enlargement rounds, while experts are currently preparing suitable provisions.
Von der Leyen’s Western Balkans tour will end in Skopje on October 2. Serbia and Bosnia and Herzegovina are not part of the itinerary, with the upcoming elections in both countries cited as the official reason.
