Russia shows Pantsir air defense on Belarus-built chassis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
06:46:38 UTC
15:46:38 KST

- Russia showed a Pantsir-S1M air defense system on a Belarusian MZKT-7930-312 chassis during its Tsentr-2026 exercise.
- Belarus reportedly received a 2024 order for 18 such chassis, and Ukraine destroyed one MZKT-based Pantsir near Mariupol in February.
Russia has shown an upgraded Pantsir-S1M air defense system mounted on a Belarus-built MZKT-7930-312 chassis during its Tsentr-2026 strategic exercise, the first official confirmation that the gun-and-missile system now rides on the heavy Minsk-built chassis.
Until now, the configuration was known only from a leaked supply contract and from a single vehicle that Ukrainian drone operators destroyed near Mariupol in February. Russian officials did not say how many Pantsirs have been built on the new chassis, which units operate them, or whether the switch will extend across the fleet.
Tsentr-2026 ran from Sept. 28 to Oct. 3, with its main stage held on Oct. 2 at the Chebarkul training range in Russia’s Chelyabinsk region. President Vladimir Putin watched part of the drills on Oct. 1. Russia’s Defense Ministry said more than 47,000 troops and over 2,000 pieces of equipment took part. Rostec’s “Russian Weapons” project told Rossiyskaya Gazeta that Pantsir systems were demonstrated during the exercise.
The Pantsir combines short-range surface-to-air missiles with twin 30 mm cannons and its own radar. Russia uses it as the inner layer of its air defense, protecting long-range S-300 and S-400 batteries, airfields and other key sites from aircraft, cruise missiles and drones. The standard version sits on an 8×8 KamAZ-6560 truck, with export versions on the German MAN SX45 and some units on Russia’s BAZ-6309.
The MZKT-7930 is a heavy 8×8 military platform built by the Minsk Wheeled Tractor Plant in Belarus. Russia already uses it for some of its most important systems, including the Iskander ballistic missile launcher, the Bastion coastal defense system and elements of the S-400. A Pantsir on the MZKT-7930 first appeared only as a display mock-up at the MAKS air show near Moscow in 2009.
In early 2024, the Belarusian plant received an order from Russia for 18 MZKT-7930-312 chassis to carry Pantsir systems, according to an investigation reported in April by Ukrainian outlet Obozrevatel. That summer, Pantsir maker KBP, based in Tula, reported successful tests of the chassis. The documents showed the trucks would carry the 72V6 combat module used by Russia’s own armed forces, and the investigation said some vehicles may have been finished as an MZKT-7930-415 version with an armored cab and a different windshield layout.
The first visual evidence of the pairing came from the battlefield. In late February, Ukraine’s Unmanned Systems Forces struck a Pantsir-S1 mounted on an MZKT-7930 near the former Azovstal steel plant in Mariupol, The Defence Blog reported. The vehicle carried add-on screens meant to protect it from drone strikes.
Ukraine has made Pantsirs a priority target. Open-source tracking group Oryx had recorded at least 52 Russian Pantsir systems destroyed or damaged, and Ukrainian officials have claimed that about half of Russia’s deployed Pantsirs have been knocked out, a figure that has not been independently verified.

The way you speak could reveal early signs of brain ageing
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
06:40:59 UTC
15:40:59 KST

The way we speak may reveal how quickly we are ageing, with older-sounding speech linked to dementia and brain changes.
The way someone speaks can reveal more about their health and ageing than previously thought, a new study using an automated computer tool called a "speech clock" found. A person's speech age isn't just about vocal style; researchers say it reflects what is happening inside the body, and they hope this could be a low-cost, non-invasive, automated alternative for measuring biological ageing.
“Our voice appears to contain much more information about aging than we previously recognised,” said Agustín Ibáñez, senior author of the study at Trinity College Dublin.
An automated computer calculated a person’s speech age and compared it to their actual birth age, revealing whether their speech sounds younger, average, or older than expected, and offering clues about healthy ageing.
“It captures both the passage of chronological time and signals coming from cognition, the brain, systemic biology, and even our accumulated social environment,” he added.
The researchers analysed audio recordings of nearly 3,000 Spanish-speaking adults across Latin America. Participants completed a range of tasks, including narrating a short animated film, retelling a story after a 20-minute gap and naming items within given categories.
Using machine learning, the team examined hundreds of features capturing how people speak and what they say, such as speech rate and pauses, pitch, emotional content, vocabulary, and semantic precision, to estimate chronological age and generate an individual “speech age gap”.
What "older" speech shows
The speech clock distinguished healthy individuals from people with dementia. Healthy participants showed the lowest speech age gaps, while progressively wider gaps were seen in people with Alzheimer’s disease and forms of frontotemporal dementia.
People whose speech appears older than expected for their chronological age showed signs of accelerated ageing across several biological and clinical systems. MRI brain scans indicated greater loss of brain structure and altered brain activity.
Older speech scores were also tied to higher levels of p-Tau217, a key protein in the blood linked to Alzheimer's disease.
Participants with older speech scores performed worse on tests of memory, focus, and problem-solving. This link was present not only for language-related tasks, but also for non-verbal tasks like visual memory.
“The broader finding is nevertheless striking in that a person’s voice may provide a remarkably compact readout of multiple dimensions of aging,” added Ibáñez.
Factors such as chronological age, brain ageing, cognition, and Alzheimer's and dementia phenotypes are traditionally measured with very different and often expensive tools, yet they appear to converge in the way someone speaks, he said.
The authors noted that many current measures of biological ageing require MRI scanners, blood samples or specialised clinical assessments. By contrast, the “speech clock” offers a low-cost, non-invasive, automated alternative that can be carried out remotely on standard devices without specialist medical staff.
The researchers stressed, however, that the speech clock is not yet a diagnostic test for dementia and it cannot establish whether an older-appearing speech profile predicts who will subsequently develop cognitive decline.

Teenagers are editing phone screens to bypass age checks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
06:30:00 UTC
15:30:00 KST

Teenagers are editing phone screens to bypass age checks
Minors in Estonia are using the state portal Eesti.ee to change their personal data in a web browser and thereby gain access to bars and clubs. The Information System Authority (RIA) is aware of the scheme but cannot do anything to stop it.
Programmer Krister Viirsaar said that any browser allows a phone user to change what appears on their screen. A browser lets users view and search web pages. Changing one's data this way does not mean anything changes in a database or state system — only the text displayed on the phone screen is altered.
If a minor decides to go to nightlife venues, they can change their personal identification code on Eesti.ee and pretend to be older. They then show the altered screen to a security guard, who may not notice anything is wrong.
Changing the data can take only ten seconds
Viirsaar said that on a computer, such data alteration can take just ten seconds. "I haven't tried it on a phone, but it's simple and does not qualify as hacking," he said. Instructions for doing it can easily be found online.
Veiko Raime, owner of Möku bar in Tallinn, said that although visitors generally present a physical ID, security staff also accept identity verification through the Eesti.ee portal.
Rumors about minors' schemes came as a surprise to him. "We don't turn a blind eye to this," he assured.
RIA's head of technology development, Õie‑Mari Aasmäe, explained that personal data on Eesti.ee is meant primarily for people to view their own information and use state e‑services. She added that the portal's web view is not intended for proving one's age or identity. It is also not permitted by law.
Eesti.ee is not allowed — but the Eesti app is
"Service providers such as shops, bars, or clubs should not use the state portal's web view on a person's phone as a document for proving identity or age," Aasmäe said.
If a visitor has left their ID card or passport at home, they can use the Eesti app, a national mobile application in which users cannot change their date of birth or age. Age verification in the app is based on a QR code.
However, using the Eesti app is voluntary for service providers. If a nightlife venue does not wish to check age through the app, it may ask the person to present a physical identity document.
Aasmäe said that showing personal data on a phone screen is essentially treated the same as stating it verbally.
Möku bar owner Raime noted that the entire issue with nightlife venues may stem from poor communication. Conversations with security staff revealed that they may not distinguish between Eesti.ee and the Eesti app.

Yemen sees widest escalation in 3 weeks as displacement nears 200,000
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
06:28:21 UTC
15:28:21 KST

Yemen witnessed its widest military escalation in three weeks in recent hours between government forces and the Houthi group, as the displacement crisis caused by the fighting continued to worsen.
Clashes were concentrated in the southwestern provinces of Taiz and Lahej, marking the most intense escalation since Sept. 10, when the Houthis took control of the strategic city of Mokha, according to Anadolu’s monitoring.
Amid the escalation on the ground, the number of people displaced since military operations intensified in July approached 198,000, according to government data.
The army said Thursday that it foiled a major Houthi attack on several fronts in Taiz and Lahej, while carrying out airstrikes on the group’s positions and vehicles.
“The armed forces’ warplanes carried out six airstrikes on positions and vehicles belonging to the Houthi militia,” the army’s Tor Al-Baha military axis said in a statement, noting that forces “thwarted a large-scale Houthi attack on all fronts of the Tor Al-Baha axis and eliminated all its attacking formations.”
The strikes targeted positions “on the Al-Akboush, Al-Ahkoum and Hayfan fronts south of Taiz province,” it added, without providing details.
The Tor Al-Baha axis operates in Taiz and Lahej provinces, according to an Anadolu correspondent.
The Taiz military axis said in a statement that army forces “are engaged in fierce battles in the Bani Bakari area of Jabal Habashi district, the Himyar front in Maqbanah district in western Taiz, and the Al-Aqroud front in the southeast of the province.”
It added that army forces “inflicted casualties and equipment losses on the Houthi militia,” without providing details.
In a separate development, a military source told Anadolu that government forces foiled a Houthi attack on the Sharie area in the Sama’a district, southeast of Taiz.
The source, speaking on condition of anonymity, said the Houthis attacked the area but resistance forces thwarted the assault, resulting in deaths and injuries on both sides.
The attack was the first launched by the Houthis on the district since 2014, according to Anadolu’s monitoring.
Yemen’s Executive Unit for Internally Displaced Persons Camps Management said Thursday that the number of people displaced by the escalation since July had risen to nearly 198,000.
The government unit said that “waves of forced displacement caused by the continued military escalation, direct shelling and deteriorating security conditions have worsened, posing serious threats to the lives and safety of civilians.”
It said the number of people registered as displaced since the military escalation resumed in July stood at 29,519 families, comprising 197,906 people.
Taiz topped the list of provinces hosting displaced people, with 13,925 families comprising 97,529 people distributed in 15 districts.
Lahej ranked second, hosting 7,179 families with 50,253 people in nine districts, most arriving from conflict areas in Taiz and Al-Hudaydah.
The temporary capital, Aden, received 3,741 families comprising 17,782 people, while Abyan recorded 2,097 families with 14,679 people.
In Al-Hudaydah, 1,471 families comprising 10,297 people were registered in the districts of Hays and Al-Khokha, with indications of secondary displacement toward Aden, according to the statement.
Yemen’s Human Rights Ministry warned Wednesday of the growing presence of children recruited by the Houthis amid the latest military escalation.
The ministry said it documented the deaths of at least 100 children recruited by the Houthis during fighting in September, based on names, information and photographs it was able to obtain following their deaths.
It stressed that the figure does not represent the total number of recruited or killed children, but only a limited number of cases it was able to identify and verify, adding that field information indicated the actual number was much higher.
It also said it had documented cases of children being abducted or recruited in several provinces under Houthi control before being transferred to mobilization camps and deployed to battlefronts, and later returned to their families as bodies.
In a related development, the government filed a complaint with the UN Security Council, warning of “a serious Houthi threat to the safety of civil aviation.”
It came in a letter sent by the government to the council that was published early Thursday by the Foreign Ministry and Expatriates.
The government warned of “a serious threat to the safety and security of international civil aviation over the southern Red Sea, due to the use by the Houthi terrorist militia of Iranian-origin weapons launched from areas under its control in Al-Hudaydah province toward international air routes.”
The government urged the Security Council “to take urgent international action to confront this threat and enforce the arms embargo imposed on the militia.”
It said the weapons “use heat-tracking systems that track heat sources without distinguishing between military and civilian targets.”
It warned that “launching these weapons near international air routes poses a direct and serious threat to civilian aircraft and their passengers, including UN and humanitarian flights operating in Yemen and the region.”
The complaint came one day after military escalation between government forces and the Houthis on several fronts, including Taiz, Lahej, Marib, Al-Jawf and Al-Bayda, alongside the army’s announcement that it carried out hundreds of strikes against the group’s positions and members.
The Houthis, meanwhile, reported dozens of airstrikes and missile attacks on areas under their control.
The escalation coincided Wednesday with a military meeting in Aden to discuss strengthening readiness and implementing directives from Presidential Leadership Council Chairman Rashad Al-Alimi on general mobilization.
Saudi Arabia also announced Wednesday its full support for the government in extending its authority in the country and restoring stability.
The developments are part of the escalation that began in early July and is considered the widest since the relative calm that followed an April 2022 truce.
Fighting intensified in September, leading to the Houthis seizing several vital areas in Al-Hudaydah and Taiz provinces, including Mokha, and eventually Mayyun Island overlooking the international Bab al-Mandeb maritime strait.
Yemen has been mired in conflict since the Houthis seized the national capital, Sanaa, and several provinces in 2014, prompting a Saudi-led coalition to intervene in 2015 in support of Yemen's internationally recognized government.

Famous half-millennium-old Holei Sea Arch in Hawaii collapsed into the ocean
Kyiv • UNN
The Holei Sea Arch in Hawaii Volcanoes National Park collapsed during a tropical storm. The formation had been damaged by earthquakes and waves.
The picturesque Holei Sea Arch, which is estimated to have formed approximately half a millennium ago, collapsed into the ocean in Hawaii, US. UNN reports this, citing NBC News.
Details
The red marker on Google Maps identifying Holei Sea Arch—a stark 27-meter dome formed by 550-year-old lava flows and sculpted over time by the salty Pacific Ocean—now says: "Permanently closed."
On Thursday, the US National Park Service reported that the picturesque arch in Hawaiʻi Volcanoes National Park on the Big Island collapsed sometime between September 23 and Sunday, around the time a tropical cyclone caused significant swells along the coast.
"The exact time of the collapse is unknown and may have occurred when the park was temporarily closed during Tropical Storm Nolo," the Park Service said in a statement.
The Park Service expressed regret over the collapse of the natural feature, which, it said, formed from lava flows approximately half a millennium ago and was then gradually shaped by the pounding of the turbulent sea.
It was also reported that some people seeking to see the remains of Holei Sea Arch came too close to the edge of the surrounding cliffs—as seen in photographs on social media.
The National Park Service warned tourists to maintain a safe distance from the crumbling shoreline, where they could "put themselves and rescuers at great risk of falling and drowning on the turbulent coast washed by waves."
"Visitors are strongly advised to stay away from unstable edges of coastal cliffs that drop vertically into the ocean and pose a serious fall hazard," the statement said.
The collapse had been a long time coming, the National Park Service said, because the 2018 eruption of Kīlauea volcano shook the ground so intensely that it damaged the cliffs adjacent to the arch.
New cracks in the arch itself and the surrounding area in early 2020 prompted staff at Hawaiʻi Volcanoes National Park to move the Holei Sea Arch viewpoint farther inland, the National Park Service said. "Later that year, powerful waves from Tropical Storm Darby broke off a piece of rock from the lower part of the arch," the statement said.

====================================================================================================

China Focus: Beyond mining tunnels: China's coal-rich province accelerates smarter, greener energy transition
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
14:24:16 CST
15:24:16 KST

TAIYUAN, Oct. 3 (Xinhua) -- From intelligent coal mines to digital power-grid management, north China's Shanxi Province is accelerating its energy transition and maintaining stable coal supplies.
As one of China's major coal-producing provinces and a key national energy base, Shanxi is seeking to make its energy system smarter, more diversified and more efficient.
The province is upgrading its traditional coal industry through smarter technologies and cleaner production, while expanding wind and solar power to diversify its energy mix. Backed by increasingly flexible power management, these efforts are reshaping how Shanxi produces, supplies and uses energy as China pursues greener development.
AUTOMATED COAL MINING
For 50-year-old Zhao Huacheng, deputy head of a fully mechanized mining team at Huayang New Material Technology Group Co., Ltd., a major coal mining enterprise in Shanxi, the transformation of coal mining is evident in his daily work.
Zhao has worked in the industry for nearly 30 years, taking on almost every frontline role in his team, from coal miner and powered-support operator to safety officer.
Huayang's No. 1 Mine, with an annual production capacity of 8.5 million tonnes, is among China's first batch of intelligent demonstration coal mines. Its intelligent mining faces use 5G technology and automated equipment to enable remote control and reduce the need for underground workers.
The number of workers required underground for a shift at Zhao's team has already fallen from 24 to 16.
Operating a coal-cutting machine was once one of the toughest jobs. Three operators had to work together, with one controlling the machine from a platform and the other two observing the terrain from the front and rear.
When the machine started up, clouds of coal dust often made it nearly impossible to see, and flying chunks of coal posed a real risk of injury. Zhao still has a scar near his right eye as a reminder.
"With advances in technology, the operator in the middle is no longer needed. The operators in front and behind can control the machine remotely from six meters away, reducing the risks," Zhao said. "We used to get bumped and bruised almost constantly. Now, such incidents are rare."
Today, intelligent equipment has taken over most labor-intensive tasks. Clean mine tunnels, dust-suppression systems and enclosed control rooms have replaced the once dusty and hazardous working conditions.
Productivity has also seen a sharp increase. A production shift that once yielded about 3,000 to 4,000 tonnes of coal can now produce 5,000 to 6,000 tonnes, according to Zhao.
The transformation at Zhao's workplace is part of a broader push to make coal mining smarter and cleaner in Shanxi. By the end of November 2025, the province had built 369 intelligent coal mines, accounting for more than one-third of the national total, as well as 75 demonstration mines for green mining.
On the national level, China aims to make virtually all types of coal mines intelligent by 2035 by leveraging advanced technologies, according to the National Development and Reform Commission.
DIVERSIFIED ENERGY SUPPLY
While making coal production smarter and cleaner, Shanxi is also reshaping its energy mix, with renewable energy becoming an increasingly important source of new capacity and power generation.
At Shanxi Jinnan Steel Group Co., Ltd. in Quwo County, Linfen City, photovoltaic panels cover unused spaces ranging from rooftops and south-facing walls to hillside slopes and areas near an artificial lake.
The company produces nearly 6 million tonnes of steel annually. Over the past five years, it has invested heavily in clean energy projects to reduce the carbon intensity of its energy consumption.
Three months ago, the company partnered with PowerChina New Energy Group Co., Ltd. to develop green electricity by tapping the region's mountainous and valley resources. The two sides plan to use a "green electricity direct supply" model to better match the company's energy needs.
"We have developed photovoltaic projects with a combined capacity of 550 megawatts, generating more than 1 billion kWh of electricity annually," said Zhang Tianfu, president of Shanxi Jinnan Steel Group Co., Ltd.
Green electricity currently accounts for 15 percent of the company's power consumption. Zhang said the company will continue expanding its renewable energy portfolio and plans to raise the share to 50 percent by 2029.
The company's growing investment in green electricity comes as renewable energy has become the main source of newly added power generation capacity and electricity generation in Shanxi.
By the end of June this year, the province's installed capacity of wind and solar power had exceeded 80 million kW. In 2020, roughly one in every seven kWh generated in Shanxi came from renewable sources. Today, despite a substantial increase in total power generation, the share has risen to one in every four kWh.
A historic shift has taken place in Shanxi's energy mix. By the end of September last year, installed capacity of new and clean energy sources accounted for 54.55 percent of the province's total, marking a historic shift from a fossil-fuel-dominated energy mix toward one led by clean energy.
SMARTER POWER MANAGEMENT
As wind and solar power generation expands, Shanxi faces a new challenge: how to accommodate increasingly variable renewable generation while keeping the power grid stable.
Virtual power plants are emerging as one solution.
Shanxi Fengxingcekong Co., Ltd. operates China's first virtual power plant participating in the electricity spot market. Nan Dou, deputy general manager of the company, said the spot market generates a new electricity price every five minutes.
The virtual power plant aggregates scattered electricity-consuming resources and dispatches them through a digital platform, using algorithms to adjust the power loads of participating enterprises in response to changes in electricity prices and grid demand.
"When electricity prices are low and renewable power generation is high, we encourage enterprises to consume more electricity, maximizing the use of renewable power. When prices are high and the grid is under pressure, we organize enterprises to reduce their loads during peak periods, helping ensure safe and stable grid operation," Nan said.
"This benefits all three sides by ensuring power supplies, facilitating renewable power consumption and reducing energy costs for enterprises," he added.
From August 2023 to June 2026, the virtual power plant helped facilitate the consumption of 350 million kWh of renewable electricity, equivalent to reducing carbon dioxide emissions by about 350,000 tonnes, the operators said. It also saved about 210 million kWh of electricity.
Over the three years since entering the electricity market, the company's ability to aggregate and dispatch resources has continued to improve. The number of users on its platform has risen from five to more than 60, while its aggregated capacity has jumped from 80,000 kW to 2.282 million kW.
"The most important improvement is that our control success rate has risen from 33 percent to 80 percent. Only by improving the quality of regulation can we achieve the desired results," Nan said.
As of September 2026, 14 virtual power plants in Shanxi had participated in market trading, aggregating 1,459 users. Their combined capacity in the Shanxi electricity market had reached 6.4548 million kW, with a maximum adjustable load of 1.545 million kW.
Traditional coal-fired power plants are also undergoing flexibility upgrades in response to market signals. The upgrades allow them to reduce output when wind and solar generation is abundant, creating more room for renewable power, and quickly ramp up output when renewable generation falls short, helping ensure electricity supplies.
More than half of Shanxi's coal-fired power generating units have completed such flexibility upgrades.
"Guided by market needs, Shanxi's renewable electricity utilization rate has remained above 90 percent," said Zhang Chao, an official in charge of the spot market at the Dispatching and Control Center of State Grid Shanxi Electric Power Co., Ltd. ■

A crash axe is a tool kept in a cockpit to help pilots cut through the plane in emergencies.
The plane carrying 174 passengers was on its way from the UAE’s Dubai to Israel’s Tel Aviv on Wednesday when a co-pilot wounded Indian pilot Smit Machchhar who opened the cockpit to seek help.
The attacker was not officially identified, but media reports quoting unnamed sources claimed he was Omani national Hamam al-Hammami.
The aircraft briefly plunged about 17,000 feet (5,180 metres) before it was brought back under control by a second paid of new pilots after passengers and crew subdued the attacker.
The flight was diverted and forced to make an emergency landing at Prince Sultan bin Abdulaziz International Airport in Tabuk in northwestern Saudi Arabia.
The co-pilot was arrested by Saudi authorities and handed over to the UAE as it leads the probe.
Machchhar was also returned to the UAE.

Russia has rejected accusations that the country is planning to attack NATO. Western officials have said that Russia is not capable of carrying out a direct attack.
Nevertheless, security concerns have played a major role in the election campaign in Latvia.
Opinion polls have given Andris Kulbergs’ centrist United List a lead with around 14 percent of the votes – closely followed by the pro-Russian Sovereign Power.
The 47-year-old Kulbergs, who is a businessman and amateur rally driver, came to power in May.
This happened after the previous coalition government collapsed over its handling of incidents in which military drones flew into Latvia unnoticed.
Although the drones were Ukrainian, officials have accused Russia of causing them to deviate from their flight paths.
– We need to give Ukraine everything necessary right now so that they can gain the upper hand and win, Kulbergs told the Reuters news agency last month.
During the election campaign, he has promised to strengthen Latvia’s capacity to counter drones and maintain defense spending at five percent of the gross domestic product.
His pro-Russian opponents believe, however, that Latvia should stop all support for Ukraine and instead focus on cost-of-living issues, particularly among the Russian-speaking minority.
– Our voters want peace, to avoid having to seek safety, and to no longer experience air raid alarms, Sovereign Power party leader Julia Stepanenko told Reuters.
– The war must not be encouraged in any way, not even by financing it. Ukraine must win, but through peace negotiations.
Polling stations open at 08:00 Saturday morning – 07:00 Danish time – and close at 20:00.
The first results are expected within a few hours, while the final result is expected to be clear after midnight.
The 100 members of the Saeima, which is the country’s parliament, are elected for a four-year term.
Opinion polls show that at least two other parties may enter parliament.
This includes Latvia First, which according to Reuters is populist and resembles the MAGA movement in the United States, and The Progressives, which is a left-wing party that attracts younger voters.
Kulbergs’ ability to form a coalition will largely depend on how many votes the parties receive and how many other parties cross the five percent threshold.
Latvia has 1.9 million inhabitants. It is located between the Baltic Sea and the EU and NATO countries Estonia and Lithuania to the north and south, as well as Russia and Belarus to the east.
RITZAU/Reuters

Judge blocks border wall in Texas national park

2026-10-03
06:16:19 UTC
15:16:19 KST

A federal judge in the US on Friday issued a temporary injunction preventing President Donald Trump’s administration from constructing a border wall between the US and Mexico through Big Bend National Park in the state of Texas.
The Reuters news agency reports this during the night before Saturday Danish time.
The injunction is to remain in effect while the courts hear an environmental lawsuit challenging the project.
Friday’s ruling comes nearly seven weeks after Rodney Scott, who is commissioner of the US Customs and Border Protection agency, CBP, paused construction.
That occurred due to criticism of the project and its potential impact on the national park’s landscape and wildlife.
In August, construction workers began clearing areas in Big Bend National Park, sparking demonstrations and lawsuits demanding a halt to the work.
Scott stated that he wanted to pause the project until he could visit the area, “make a personal assessment”, and speak with some of the affected parties.
Friday’s preliminary injunction was issued by Federal District Judge Kathleen Cardone.
In practice, this prevents Rodney Scott from changing his mind, writes Reuters.
The ruling states that the government “may not construct a border barrier or related infrastructure or conduct construction activities involving ground disturbance” unless it complies with environmental legislation.
The lawsuit was filed by the organizations Center for Biological Diversity and Friends of the Ruidosa Church, as well as a person who works as a river guide in the national park and owns land in the Big Bend area.
Judge Cardone states in her ruling that the plaintiffs are likely to prevail on at least some of their claims once the lawsuit has been fully considered.
The plaintiffs believe that Trump’s administration, including Secretary of Homeland Security Markwayne Mullin, had unjustifiably granted a comprehensive waiver from environmental legislation to expedite the project in Big Bend National Park.
The Republican Donald Trump has long argued for strengthening the border along the southern US to deter illegal immigration into the country.

The governor of the US state of New York, Kathy Hochul, said on Friday that she wants to close a legal loophole that makes it harder to prosecute rape cases if the victims were voluntarily intoxicated.
The announcement comes after a case concerning an alleged gang rape at Cornell University, located in New York, has received significant attention.
The complainant in the case has filed a civil lawsuit regarding the alleged assault at the university in 2024. This has directed a sharp spotlight onto the prosecution’s decision not to bring charges at that time.
The investigation into the incident was reopened on Monday, and Hochul has appointed state Attorney General Letitia James as special prosecutor.
At the same time, frustrations over the case have grown in the US, with accusations that Cornell did not hold the men sufficiently accountable.
In her civil lawsuit, the woman writes that she was drugged with the drug ketamine, assaulted, and raped by seven members of the student fraternity Chi Phi.
It is a social fraternity for male students.
– It should not matter whether the person chose to take drugs or drink alcohol. Voluntary intoxication is not a permission for sexual assault or gang rape. Period, Kathy Hochul said on Friday.
– I support closing this loophole and will work with New York’s legislature to get it done.
Several US states, including New York, have provisions in their legislation that make it harder for prosecutors to bring a case against a person who has had sex with someone who was voluntarily so intoxicated that the person could not genuinely give or withhold consent.
– It is quite simply astonishing that this loophole still exists, says Shiwali Patel, who is senior director of education justice at the American organization National Women’s Law Center.
– It is of great significance for cases at universities, because the reality is that a significant portion of sexual assaults at universities involve alcohol and drugs.

Russia strikes second major bridge in Kyiv, mayor says
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
07:13:22 BST
15:13:22 KST

Russia hits second major bridge in Ukraine's capital Kyiv
- Published
A Russian strike has hit a second major bridge in Kyiv, Mayor Vitaliy Klitschko has said, as Moscow ramps up attacks on critical infrastructure in Ukraine's capital.
The attack on Saturday morning injured two people, and damaged the road surface and overhead trolleybus wires on the Pivnichnyi (Northern) Bridge, Klitschko said, causing traffic jams.
It comes after the Pivdennyi (Southern) Bridge was hit multiple times by Russian drones this week, with Klitschko warning that "the enemy is tearing Kyiv apart".
Russia said its drones had hit the two bridges used to transfer Ukrainian troops and military cargo. Moscow again urged foreign citizens, including diplomats, to leave Kyiv.
The two Kyiv bridges across the Dnipro River link the western and eastern parts of the capital and had not been hit before Thursday.
The Russian strikes have severed road, rail and trolleybus links across the wide river. The ongoing drone threat means restrictions on other routes, bringing traffic jams to the city's roads for a second day - though Friday's gridlock has not been repeated to the same level.
Many of the city's residents - which number about three million - rely on the metro to travel across the city every day. The fear is this new Russian tactic will result in sustained attacks which could effectively cut the city in two.
Writing on Telegram on Saturday morning, Klitschko said "emergency services are on their way" after the Pivnichnyi Bridge was hit.
"Traffic on the bridge from the left to the right bank is currently blocked," he added.
Earlier attacks on the Pivdennyi Bridge prompted Kyiv's defence council to hold a crisis meeting on Friday.
Klitschko warned afterwards that the city was now in a "very dramatic situation" as Moscow was battering its "critical infrastructure, logistics, housing" and other key facilities.
Experts say Russian drones are unlikely to bring down the bridges - but repeated attacks will force their closure and risk weakening their structure, making them unusable.
More powerful weapons could collapse the bridges, some of which are reported to be in poor condition after years carrying heavier traffic than they were designed for.
It was reported that Ukrainian lawmakers discussed the state of Kyiv's bridges in a recent meeting, setting out contingency plans to use ferries or temporary pontoon bridges to keep the city connected in the event of any bridges being destroyed.
Russian President Vladimir Putin has said Russia is acting in response to Ukraine's strikes on Russian energy facilities, despite the fact that it was Moscow that had first launched such attacks.
After the Pivdennyi Bridge was attacked, passengers described how dust from a blast wave entered their carriage through the ventilation system.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said Putin had decided that there were "no rules now" when attacking Ukraine.
In an interview with the Financial Times, he said: "The Russians have failed to occupy us. So now they are carrying out massive attacks and mass killings."
He added: "They want to destroy our bridges... our data centres, the internet, mobile networks, hospitals, kindergartens, schools, universities - everything. They want people to flee their cities."
Putin on Thursday insisted that Russia's attacks on Ukrainian economic targets were a direct response to Ukraine's strikes on Russia's oil refineries and its ships in the Black Sea.
"Now from every direction we're receiving calls 'let's stop'. But they started it," Putin said after a wide-ranging speech at the Valdai foreign policy forum.
The Kremlin leader admitted Kyiv had "got some results" from its refinery attacks and Russia had lost about 1% of its GDP. Ukraine maintains it began attacking Russian oil infrastructure because it helps the Kremlin finance the war.
Russia has targeted Ukrainian energy infrastructure, ramping up attacks every winter since Putin launched a full-scale invasion in February 2022.
In other developments on Saturday:
- A sailor on a Liberia-flagged civilian ship was killed and another three crew members injured in a Russian attack on Ukraine's Black Sea port in the Odesa region, the Ukrainian port authorities said
- At least 12 people were injured in overnight Russian strikes on Ukraine's Dnipropetrovsk, Kharkiv and Kyiv regions, local officials said
- Two people were killed and three injured in a Ukrainian drone attack in the country's eastern Luhansk region occupied by Russia, the Moscow-installed regional head said
- Moldova, Ukraine's south-western neighbour, summoned the Russian ambassador after saying that five Russian drones and missiles had crossed its border and exploded near "several localities in four districts". No injuries were reported

Greenland municipality imposes temporary alcohol ban
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
06:09:54 UTC
15:09:54 KST

The Greenlandic government, Naalakkersuisut, has introduced a temporary ban on the sale and serving of alcohol in the southern Greenlandic municipality of Kujalleq.
Naalakkersuisut writes this on Friday, when the ban took effect, in a press release.
The ban comes following a request from the municipal council in Kujalleq.
– The purpose of the temporary closure of alcohol sales and serving is to eliminate the threat to children’s welfare and the safety of the population.
– Furthermore, Kommune Kujalleq has expressed concern and insecurity among the municipality’s population in recent times as a result of the fatal incidents that are a direct consequence of alcoholic beverages, the press release states.
It is not specified further which alcohol-related incidents have taken place in the municipality.
Malene Vahl Rasmussen, who is mayor of Kujalleq, confirms in a post on Facebook that she has asked Naalakkersuisut to temporarily halt the sale of alcohol in the municipality.
– Based on the negative consequences that alcohol consumption has on our surroundings, we can no longer defend the way we use alcohol, she writes.
In a press release, according to the Greenlandic media outlet Sermitsiaq, she elaborates further.
– We can no longer stand passively by and watch the negative consequences that alcohol consumption has on our surroundings, and merely wait for another serious incident to happen in our society, the mayor writes according to the media outlet.
The ban on the sale and serving of alcohol will last until the executive order is repealed, it is stated.
Thus, it is not clear how long the ban will remain in effect.
It is not the first time that an alcohol ban has been introduced in parts of Greenland.
At the beginning of the coronavirus pandemic, a ban was introduced for a period on the serving of alcohol with an alcohol percentage above 2.25 percent in Nuuk, Kapisillit, and Qeqertarsuatsiaat.
At that time, it happened with the justification that they wanted to protect children who were at home during the pandemic.

RITZAU
Professor: Old IT makes universities hacking targets
Danish universities hold vast amounts of personal data while some continue to rely on ageing IT systems that may not meet modern security standards, a cybersecurity professor warns following the major attack on DTU.
Old IT systems combined with large amounts of sensitive personal data make Danish universities particularly vulnerable to cyberattacks, according to Jens Myrup Pedersen, professor of cybersecurity at Aarhus University.
His warning comes after the Technical University of Denmark (DTU) revealed Friday that hackers had gained access to its user database and extracted a large amount of data.
“Universities possess a very large amount of personal data,” Pedersen told Ritzau.
“And then it is my impression that several universities have quite a few older systems that probably do not have the security level one can expect in 2026.”
Pedersen stressed that he cannot comment specifically on the quality of DTU’s IT security.
But he said the attack raises important questions about how universities protect access to sensitive information.
“The question is which accounts have had access to all this personal data, and how well they are protected,” he said.
Another key question, according to Pedersen, is whether university IT systems can detect when unusually large amounts of data are being extracted and trigger an alarm before the damage becomes more extensive.
Universities face a ‘very high’ cyber threat
The problem extends beyond DTU.
Danish universities have been targeted by hackers several times in recent years, while a 2025 assessment from the Danish Agency for Societal Security (Styrelsen for Samfundssikkerhed) rated the cybercrime threat against Danish universities as “very high”.
Universities can be attractive targets because they combine extensive personal databases with large and complex IT environments used by thousands of students, researchers and employees.
The latest attack has brought renewed attention to whether security measures have kept pace with that complexity.
More than 200,000 potentially affected at DTU
As previously reported by The Copenhagen Post, more than 200,000 people could be affected by the DTU attack.
Unauthorised parties compromised several DTU user profiles and used them to access the university’s user database. DTU says a large amount of data was extracted and that the information involved could include CPR numbers, home addresses and telephone numbers.
The university has not yet determined exactly what information was taken or how many people are affected.
The incident has been reported to the Danish Data Protection Agency (Datatilsynet), while the National Special Crime Unit (NSK) is in contact with DTU about the case.
It has not been disclosed who is suspected of carrying out the attack.
Source: Ritzau
G7 releases oil reserves – could it bring down Denmark’s record-high diesel prices?
Diesel prices in Denmark have climbed to record levels. Now the G7 countries are releasing up to 100 million barrels of diesel and crude oil from emergency reserves in an attempt to ease pressure on global energy markets.
Danish motorists could see some relief from record-high diesel prices after the G7 countries agreed to release emergency fuel reserves.
The move was announced Friday following a meeting of G7 leaders and will see up to 100 million barrels of diesel and crude oil released over the next four months.
The release will be coordinated through the International Energy Agency and is intended to increase supply and help stabilise energy prices.
For Denmark, the move could take some of the pressure off diesel prices, according to Jens Nærvig Pedersen, senior commodities analyst at Danske Bank.
But motorists should not expect prices to return to normal immediately.
“It is not the grand solution that can cause prices to fall again,” Pedersen told Ritzau.
“It does not solve the supply crisis in the oil market, which is primarily due to the conflict in the Middle East.”
Diesel has hit a Danish record
The price of diesel at Danish filling stations reached a record DKK 19.19 per litre in September.
The additional supplies from G7 reserves could help cushion the market, Pedersen said, but they cannot fully replace the supplies currently missing from the Middle East.
“For us to get lower and more normal prices again, a solution must be found to the current supply crisis,” he said.
The G7 announcement has already had an impact on international energy markets, with oil prices beginning to fall following the decision.
Why is the G7 releasing its reserves?
The decision follows mounting concern about global fuel supplies and sharply rising prices linked to the conflict in the Middle East.
It also comes after US President Donald Trump raised the possibility of stopping US diesel exports to Europe.
Europe is heavily dependent on imported diesel, making any restriction on US exports potentially significant for European supplies and prices.
Following the G7 agreement, Trump said Friday that he would not impose a diesel export ban.
The G7 countries have also agreed not to introduce restrictions on energy exports between member countries.
What happens to Danish fuel prices now?
The release of emergency reserves increases the amount of oil and diesel available on the market and could therefore put downward pressure on prices.
But the underlying problem remains the shortage of supply caused by the conflict in the Middle East.
That means Danish motorists could see some relief at the pump without necessarily seeing a return to the prices that prevailed before the current energy crisis.
The G7 consists of Canada, France, Germany, Italy, Japan, the United Kingdom and the United States.

World Cup assault suspect convicted in separate case
Next week, a 31-year-old man is to appear in court in a case concerning violence against a Swedish man, who later died, at a big-screen event at Islands Brygge.
However, that is not the only case of violence the 31-year-old is involved in.
On Friday, at the Court in Svendborg, he was sentenced to three months of unconditional imprisonment for violence against another inmate in Nyborg State Prison in 2022.
B.T. and TV 2 report this.
In the case, two men of similar age have also been convicted. They have likewise received three months in prison, writes B.T.
The three men were charged with having assaulted an inmate in the prison with numerous punches and kicks to the face.
The victim suffered a concussion and broke both his nose and a rib, according to the indictment.
The three men were charged under the severe violence section, but were only found guilty under the mild violence provision – section 244.
It is also under this section that the 31-year-old man is charged when he appears in court next week in the case from Islands Brygge.
In that case, he is charged with having struck a 32-year-old Swedish man with a powerful punch.
The Swede died three days later.
The violence took place at a big-screen event at Islands Brygge in Copenhagen on 30 June at around 20:45. A screening of the football World Cup was held here.
According to the case’s indictment, the 31-year-old man at one point stood up on a bench, from where he, with a powerful overhand throw, threw two beer cans in the direction of a group of people – including the 32-year-old Swede.
Immediately after, the 31-year-old man dealt the Swede the powerful blow.
The blow hit the Swede on the left side of the head/neck, after which he fell to the ground.
Because of the blow, the Swede suffered, among other things, a rupture of the artery, which meant that the man later died.
In the case, charges have also been brought under section 247 of the penal code, which pertains to the 31-year-old man having previously been convicted of crimes against the person. Among other things, he has a conviction for attempted murder.
If one is convicted under section 247, the sentence can be increased by up to half.
A prosecutor in the case has previously stated that the man charged with violence faces between eight and ten months in prison.

Lidl to invest more than 100 million DKK renovating all Danish stores
Lidl plans to renovate all its supermarkets in Denmark under a new store concept, investing more than 100 million DKK over the coming business years.

Changes will include allocating more space for products on shelves.
Lidl has tested the concept through renovations at several locations. The first store to open after the official introduction of the concept began operating in Holbæk on September 27.

Individual supermarkets will close completely while renovation work is underway.
Lidl has more than 170 stores across Denmark and expects the full renovation program to take between two and four years.
The chain also plans to continue opening locations as it works toward having more than 200 supermarkets in Denmark.
Lidl opened its first Danish store in 2005.

Universities can be attractive and vulnerable targets for cyberattacks because they store large amounts of personal information and may rely on outdated computer systems, a Danish cybersecurity expert said.
Jens Myrup Pedersen, a cybersecurity professor at Aarhus University, spoke after the Technical University of Denmark, known as DTU, reported a data breach Friday.
“Universities hold a very large amount of personal data,” Pedersen said.
He added that several universities appeared to use older systems that might not meet the level of security expected in 2026.
More than 200,000 current and former DTU users could be affected by the attack, the university said.
Unauthorized people compromised several DTU user profiles to gain access to its database and retrieved “a larger amount” of information.
The exposed data could include CPR numbers, which are Denmark’s personal identification numbers, as well as home addresses and telephone numbers.

Danish online banking fraud cases fall 51 percent from 2023 peak
Reported online banking fraud in Denmark has fallen sharply as banks improve detection and customers become more aware of scams.
Banks registered 2,571 cases during the first half of 2026, according to Finans Danmark, the main association representing Danish banks.
That was 51 percent fewer than during the first half of 2023, when reported online banking fraud reached its highest level.
Scammers attempted to steal 74.7 million DKK during the first six months of 2026. Actual losses totaled 38.1 million DKK, almost 16 percent less than during the previous six months.
More than half of the reported cases caused no financial loss.
Jens Myrup Pedersen, a cybersecurity professor at Aarhus University, linked the decline to stronger fraud detection and greater public awareness.
He said banks had become better at identifying suspicious transactions and limiting the amount customers could transfer.
More than half of the cases involved contact fraud. In these scams, criminals call or otherwise contact victims while pretending to represent a bank, the police or another authority.
Consumers should remain alert when callers pressure them to act quickly, said Malene Gøttge Rasmussen.
“If you are just the slightest bit skeptical, hang up,” she said. “Better once too often.”

More than half of Denmark’s school classes experienced physical violence between students during a school year, a government report found.
Research firms Epinion and Als Research prepared the report for the Ministry of Children and Education.
The problem was most common in early primary school, covering kindergarten through third grade, and in classes where students had additional support needs.
Three-quarters of early primary classes reported violence or disruptive behavior among students during the year.
Physical violence most often occurred outside lessons when games, sports or jokes got out of control, the report said. Only seven percent of incidents involved deliberate and planned violence.
In many classes, one or two students were responsible for the physical violence.
The report also examined threats and harassment, including insulting language and threats delivered verbally or digitally.
Verbal or digital threats of violence occurred at least once a month in 34 percent of school classes.
“The extent of violence in primary and lower secondary school is worrying, to say the least,” Education Minister Magnus Heunicke of the Social Democrats said.
“School must not be a place where either students or teachers fear to be,” he added.
Heunicke said some children had not received the support they needed. The government plans to propose legislation giving teachers more options to intervene.

Denmark’s regions are taking responsibility for treating 18- to 24-year-olds with mild to moderate anxiety and depression under a new patient right taking effect today.
Young people in the target group who are referred by their doctor must now have treatment started within 30 days.
The change was passed by the Folketing, Denmark’s parliament, in December 2025 as part of an agreement on a 10-year plan for psychiatric care.
Previously, young people could receive a referral for free treatment from a psychologist with a provider number, but waiting times varied considerably.
“Some had to wait half a year to be seen, while others could be seen the next day,” said Jane Alrø Sørensen, secretary general of Bedre Psykiatri, a Danish association for people affected by mental illness and their relatives.
“By introducing it as a patient right, everyone is guaranteed help within 30 days,” she said.
The regions can provide treatment at their own facilities or through private providers with which they have agreements. Treatment can include individual psychologist sessions, group programs or online courses.
Sørensen said offering different types of treatment could better meet patients’ individual needs.
“Mental illness can develop just as quickly as any other illness. So early intervention is the key to thriving,” she said.
Bedre Psykiatri plans to monitor whether patients receive treatment within the required 30 days and whether the treatment is at least as good as under the previous system.
Region Østdanmark has previously estimated that around 9,500 young people in its future area will be referred for treatment each year.

A record 17.5 percent of Danes who reached the state pension age worked enough to qualify for the first senior bonus in 2025, according to ATP.
ATP, Denmark’s statutory pension and labor market pension administrator, said 11,351 people received the first senior bonus last year. That was up from 9,592 people in 2024.
In previous years, around 14 to 15 percent of people reaching the state pension age qualified for the first bonus.
“The state pension age is not necessarily the time when one stops working, and we can see that a larger share continues after that age,” ATP Group Director Maria Damborg Hald said.
Employment Minister Ane Halsboe-Jørgensen welcomed the increase.
“It is great that so many seniors want to keep contributing. We need that if we are to continue to create growth and prosperity in Denmark,” she told Ritzau in a written statement.
The senior bonus is a tax-free lump sum available to people who continue working after reaching the state pension age. Generally, a person must work at least 1,560 hours over 12 months to qualify.
The first-year bonus is 56,327 DKK, while people who continue working sufficiently during the second year can receive 33,517 DKK.
ATP paid 546.4 million DKK in first-year bonuses in 2025, compared with 446.3 million DKK in 2024.
Just under 6,775 people also received the second senior bonus in 2025, almost 3,400 more than the previous year.
In 2029, the two bonus amounts will increase to just under 65,900 DKK and 39,100 DKK, respectively.
Denmark has reached 100 organ donors using a method introduced three years ago, exceeding initial expectations for the number of people who would donate this way.
The method, known as donation after circulatory death, or DCD, allows organs to be retrieved after a person’s heart has stopped beating and breathing has ceased, the Danish Health Authority said.
Since its introduction in 2023, 100 people have donated 210 organs through DCD. Authorities had expected the method to result in about 35 additional donors annually once fully implemented.
“This involves several hundred organs that would not otherwise have been able to be donated,” Danish Health Authority chief physician Camilla Krogh told Ritzau.
Previously, major organs could only be donated in Denmark by people who had been declared brain-dead and were being kept alive artificially. New technology has made donation possible from some patients who cannot be declared brain-dead but whose ventilator treatment is discontinued.
Of the 210 organs donated through DCD since 2023, 187 were kidneys.
During the first half of 2026, 46 people donated organs after being declared brain-dead, while 20 donated through DCD.
Between 400 and 500 patients have been on Denmark’s organ transplant waiting list each year over the past decade, with most waiting for a kidney.
By the end of June 2026, 1.9 million Danes had actively registered their position on organ donation.
Under a consent model introduced last year, everyone over 18 is automatically included in the Organ Donor Register, but individuals must still actively record their decision on whether to donate.

The Danish government and Naalakkersuisut, Greenland’s government, agreed to launch the investigation in June 2022.

The investigation will examine major decisions and events since World War II and their consequences for Greenland’s population. Its stated purpose is to provide a basis for reconciliation with the past.
Possible areas of research mentioned earlier included the closure of Greenlandic settlements, adoptions and Greenlandic children sent to Denmark.
The investigation is based at Ilisimatusarfik, the University of Greenland, and citizens are expected to be involved in the work.
Denmark originally allocated 45 million DKK to the project. Under the terms of reference, the investigation should, as far as possible, be completed within five years of the agreement between the university and the research leader.
Danish economy grew 0.9% in second quarter after sharp upward revision
Denmark’s economy grew by 0.9% in the second quarter of the year, according to new figures from Statistics Denmark.
The estimate was revised upward by 0.6 percentage points compared with the previous calculation for the quarter, published in August. Statistics Denmark said the change followed an update to the data used in the calculation.
Gross domestic product, or GDP, measures the size of a country’s economy. Denmark’s GDP was 5.7% higher in the second quarter than a year earlier.
Las Olsen, chief economist at Danske Bank, said the revision puts Denmark’s annual growth rate at the high end compared with other countries.
“This largely reflects a strongly increasing production among Danish companies abroad, and this is of course not least Novo, which is producing significantly more medicine than previously,” he wrote in a comment.
Erik Bjørsted, chief economist at Dansk Metal, a Danish trade union representing workers in industry and related sectors, also pointed to strong economic activity but said employment is a better measure of the economy’s health.
“The GDP figures can fluctuate a lot from quarter to quarter and are subject to considerable uncertainty,” he wrote.
“But when companies continue to hire more employees, it is a clear sign that the Danish economy continues to do well.”
Employment increased by 0.2% in the second quarter, according to Statistics Denmark.

Danish prisons reach record overcrowding as inmate numbers exceed capacity
Danish prisons are more overcrowded than ever, with 4,650 inmates currently held in facilities designed for 4,300 people, according to Fængselsforbundet, the Danish prison officers’ union.
The average occupancy rate has reached a record 105.4%, up from 102.7% last year.
Overcrowding means prisons have to create additional capacity by installing bunk beds in cells or converting hobby rooms, visiting rooms and offices into accommodation.
Vejle Arrest, a remand prison, has recorded an average occupancy rate of 135% this year.
Jan Bruun, a union representative at the prison, said the situation is putting pressure on the facility as cells fall increasingly into disrepair.
“We spend a lot of time finding room for inmates, swapping around when a double cell does not work between two inmates, and moving again when some have letter and visiting controls lifted,” he said in the union’s statement.
Hillerød Arrest has had an occupancy rate of 140% in recent months, placing additional demands on staff. At Randers Arrest, occupancy has averaged 115% this year, with the local union representative reporting more conflicts among inmates.
The pressure could increase further as tougher sentences introduced under Denmark’s penal reform take effect.
Half of the increased penalties for violence and rape came into force in February, while further increases are due to take effect in January.

Higher winter electricity tariffs set to take effect across Denmark
Many households in Denmark will pay higher electricity grid tariffs during peak evening hours from Thursday as the country’s grid companies switch to winter rates.
The higher tariffs apply between 5 PM and 9 PM, when demand puts the greatest strain on the electricity grid. The aim is to encourage customers to move flexible electricity use to other times of the day.
“Electricity consumption in Danish households is significantly higher in the winter period, and we feel that in the power grid. Therefore, with the tariffs, we give customers an incentive to use electricity wisely,” said Lise Bering, CEO of grid company N1.
N1, which is owned by Danish energy company Norlys, supplies electricity to more than 800,000 households and businesses.
Its grid tariff between 5 PM and 9 PM will rise to 99 øre per kilowatt-hour until March 2027, compared with 43 øre during the summer period. Between midnight and 6 AM, the tariff remains at 11 øre.
Bering recommends moving flexible electricity use, such as charging an electric car or running a washing machine, away from peak hours.
Doing so can reduce individual electricity bills while easing pressure on the grid, she said.
“The more efficiently we can operate the existing power grid, the smaller the need becomes for new investments in the electricity grid, which are ultimately paid for by the consumers,” Bering said.
Winter tariffs vary between grid companies. At Cerius, which operates much of the electricity grid east of the Great Belt, the tariff between 5 PM and 9 PM will be 129.75 øre per kilowatt-hour from October 1.
Denmark introduces new measures to crack down on phone scams
Danish telecom companies will be required to block calls from abroad that falsely appear to come from Danish phone numbers under new rules expected to take effect in 2027.
The Danish Agency for Digital Government announced the planned rules as part of efforts to make it harder for fraudsters abroad to disguise their calls.
The practice, known as spoofing, involves manipulating caller ID so that a call appears to come from a different phone number. Fraudsters can use the method to make calls originating abroad look as though they come from Denmark.
According to the agency, the number of such calls has increased in recent years. It said Danish phone numbers can create greater trust among recipients than foreign numbers.
Under the new rules, telecom companies will be able to determine whether the Danish phone number displayed by the caller is actually located in Denmark.
If the number is located in Denmark but the call using it can be traced to another country, the caller ID will be considered falsified and the call must be blocked.
The agency said the system will not detect and stop every scam call.
“But it is expected to make it significantly harder for the fraudsters to pretend to call with Danish numbers,” the agency wrote.
The executive order containing the new rules has been sent for consultation and is expected to take effect on January 1, 2027.
Telecom companies will then be required to introduce the necessary technical measures in their systems to comply with the rules.
September records Denmark’s highest raw electricity prices since December 2022
Low wind and limited sunshine combined with high gas prices pushed Denmark’s raw electricity prices to their highest monthly level in nearly four years, according to energy company OK.
The average raw electricity price in September was 1.07 DKK per kilowatt-hour east of the Great Belt and 1.05 DKK west of it. VAT, taxes and tariffs are added to those prices.
By comparison, prices averaged 0.62 DKK east of the Great Belt and 0.54 DKK west of it in September last year.
“Unfortunately, there has not been enough wind and sun to push prices down in September,” said Troels Skipper, commercial manager at OK.
He said high gas prices caused by geopolitical unrest had influenced electricity prices for much of the month.
Despite the increase, OK said Danish consumers’ bills will not be higher than last year because the electricity tax has been reduced to the EU’s minimum rate in 2026 and will remain there next year.
Prices also varied significantly during September. On September 14, electricity cost more than 5 DKK per kilowatt-hour for short periods, while several weekend days had hours when prices were around zero.
Skipper encouraged consumers to follow electricity prices and adjust their consumption when possible.
“This will also be important over the winter, where we will see more large fluctuations in the electricity price. But the fluctuations thus also provide an opportunity to lower one’s electricity bill,” he said.
The average electricity price has exceeded 1 DKK per kilowatt-hour during four weeks so far in 2026, including two weeks in September.

The package would also raise the maximum prison sentence for the most serious animal welfare offenses from two years to six. It will cost 160 million kroner annually once fully phased in.
“It is no secret that it has not been good enough as it has been until now. Therefore, we are presenting a series of initiatives,” Justice Minister Nicolai Wammen said at a news conference at his ministry.

Denmark’s government and several parties in parliament have agreed to provide an additional 5.6 billion kroner in operating support for a planned hydrogen pipeline from Jutland to Germany, while easing financial requirements for producers.
The funding comes on top of 10.9 billion kroner already allocated to the project. The agreement means the state will take on more of the financial risk while the hydrogen market is still developing.
“We are entering the project with open eyes. The hydrogen market is still immature, and a hydrogen pipeline is a large project with several risks,” Climate, Energy and Utilities Minister Samira Nawa said in a press release.

Germany has committed to supporting five hydrogen projects in Denmark with a total of 12 billion kroner in German state and European Union funding. The public support is intended to help the industry develop.
Pioneering Spirit, the world’s largest ship by gross tonnage, passed under Denmark’s Great Belt Bridge at 12:55 p.m. Tuesday, nearly three hours later than planned as it waited for a required gap in other southbound traffic.
The construction vessel traveled at 5.4 kilometers per hour during the passage.
“Apart from us just needing to have a few pieces in place, everything went according to plan,” said Jimmy Westermann, head of VTS Storebælt, the vessel traffic service for the Great Belt.
The ship had been scheduled to pass at 10 a.m., but needed a two-hour window clear of other southbound traffic under the bridge before it could proceed.
Before the passage, Westermann said the vessel had already been lowered in the water using ballast to reach the required draft, the distance between the waterline and the bottom of the hull.
“The ship is ballasted down to the draft it needs to have and is ready out there, so it is the two-hour clearance window we are missing,” he said.
Registered in Malta, Pioneering Spirit is 382 meters long and 124 meters wide. It is built to transport, install and remove offshore oil drilling platforms.
Its gross tonnage is 403,342. Gross tonnage measures the volume of a ship’s enclosed spaces.
Planning the passage involved checking both the ship’s draft and its height above the water to ensure it could pass safely beneath the bridge, which has a clearance of 65 meters. The vessel had a draft of 19.9 meters during Tuesday’s passage. It also passed under the bridge in 2018.
The ship’s next destination is Rostock, Germany, according to the ship-tracking website VesselFinder. Its previous port call was at Rotterdam Maasvlakte four days earlier.

Gender pay gap in Denmark narrows for first time in three years
The pay gap between men and women in Denmark narrowed last year for the first time in three years, according to new figures from Statistics Denmark.
In 2025, women earned on average 12.3 percent less than men, compared with 12.9 percent in 2024.
Statistics Denmark has tracked the pay gap since 2004, when the difference was 16 percent. It fell to 11.9 percent in 2020, but then widened again in 2023 and 2024 before declining last year.
Mads Moberg Reumert, chief economist at pension company Danica, said the development also matters for retirement savings.
“Salary is the factor that matters most for the size of pension savings,” he said. “Therefore, the development in pay gaps is also one of the most important things to keep an eye on if you want less economic inequality between men and women as retirees.”
Helle Dalsgaard, head of advisory services at pension company Sampension, also called the decrease positive, while stressing that women still earn “significantly less than men.”
She said women’s growing educational advantage over men could support higher wages over time. She also pointed to rules on earmarked parental leave, which have led more men to take leave, as another factor that could improve women’s finances.
“After a few years with bumps in the road, the development once again went in the right direction last year,” Dalsgaard said.
German military drone makes first test flight of its kind over Denmark
A German military surveillance drone is flying over Jutland on Tuesday in what the Danish Defence says is the first test flight in Danish airspace involving an unmanned military aircraft of its size.
The German Heron TP weighs more than five tons, is 13 meters long and has a wingspan of 26 meters. It is flying at an altitude of about seven kilometers, sharing airspace with manned aircraft.
The drone belongs to the German air force, the Luftwaffe, and is being remotely controlled by a pilot at a military base in Schleswig, Germany.
The roughly two-hour flight begins at the Danish-German border in South Jutland, continues over eastern Jutland to Aalborg and then returns to Germany over western Jutland.
During the flight, the German pilot remains in contact with Naviair, which manages air traffic in Danish airspace. Denmark’s Civil Aviation and Railway Authority has approved the safety procedures for flying the drone beyond visual range, including procedures for a possible loss of control or radio connection.
The test is part of preparations for the Danish air force to receive its own General Atomics MQ-9B unmanned aircraft in 2028. They will operate from Aalborg Air Base under Squadron 729 and will be used, among other tasks, for patrol and surveillance over Greenland and the North Atlantic.
Brigade Commander Hans Peter Andersen called the flight “yet another important step toward receiving our own unmanned aircraft in the coming years.”

Electric cars above DKK 366,000 could become more expensive in Denmark from 2027
Electric cars costing more than DKK 366,000 could become more expensive in Denmark from 2027 if the government allows a current registration tax exemption to expire.
The proposal is part of the financing for the government’s upcoming budget bill, four ministers told Berlingske.
Electric cars currently benefit from lower registration taxes than petrol and diesel cars. A gradual increase in the tax was originally planned from January 2026, but the previous government and the Conservatives postponed it by one year.

Study finds young women more likely than young men to cross sexual boundaries due to pressure to perform
Young women are more likely than young men to take part in sexual acts they do not want because of pressure to perform, according to a new Danish study.
Sex & Samfund, the Danish Family Planning Association, conducted the study with polling company Voxmeter among people aged 15 to 25.
More than one in three young women said they had pretended to enjoy a sexual act more than they actually did because they felt pressure to perform.
One in six said that pressure had led them to do something they did not want to do.
“We know from previous studies that many young women are afraid to say no during sex because they are afraid of the reaction they will be met with,” Sex & Samfund Secretary General Majbrit Berlau said.
Among young men, fewer than one in 10 said they had shown more enjoyment during sex than they actually felt. About 4.7 percent said they had agreed to do something they did not want to do.
According to Berlau, most young people understand that sex requires consent and should be mutual, but they can still struggle to express and respect boundaries in practice.
“You can be so focused on doing well for the other person or living up to certain expectations that your own desire and your own boundaries fade into the background,” she said.
Sex & Samfund said the findings show a need for better knowledge about sex and sexuality.
Sex education is one of young people’s preferred sources of information, but one in three said they did not find the teaching useful.
Young people also rely heavily on friends and social media for information about sex, while one in three cited pornography as a source.
