Higher winter electricity tariffs set to take effect across Denmark
Many households in Denmark will pay higher electricity grid tariffs during peak evening hours from Thursday as the country’s grid companies switch to winter rates.
The higher tariffs apply between 5 PM and 9 PM, when demand puts the greatest strain on the electricity grid. The aim is to encourage customers to move flexible electricity use to other times of the day.
“Electricity consumption in Danish households is significantly higher in the winter period, and we feel that in the power grid. Therefore, with the tariffs, we give customers an incentive to use electricity wisely,” said Lise Bering, CEO of grid company N1.
N1, which is owned by Danish energy company Norlys, supplies electricity to more than 800,000 households and businesses.
Its grid tariff between 5 PM and 9 PM will rise to 99 øre per kilowatt-hour until March 2027, compared with 43 øre during the summer period. Between midnight and 6 AM, the tariff remains at 11 øre.
Bering recommends moving flexible electricity use, such as charging an electric car or running a washing machine, away from peak hours.
Doing so can reduce individual electricity bills while easing pressure on the grid, she said.
“The more efficiently we can operate the existing power grid, the smaller the need becomes for new investments in the electricity grid, which are ultimately paid for by the consumers,” Bering said.
Winter tariffs vary between grid companies. At Cerius, which operates much of the electricity grid east of the Great Belt, the tariff between 5 PM and 9 PM will be 129.75 øre per kilowatt-hour from October 1.
Denmark introduces new measures to crack down on phone scams
Danish telecom companies will be required to block calls from abroad that falsely appear to come from Danish phone numbers under new rules expected to take effect in 2027.
The Danish Agency for Digital Government announced the planned rules as part of efforts to make it harder for fraudsters abroad to disguise their calls.
The practice, known as spoofing, involves manipulating caller ID so that a call appears to come from a different phone number. Fraudsters can use the method to make calls originating abroad look as though they come from Denmark.
According to the agency, the number of such calls has increased in recent years. It said Danish phone numbers can create greater trust among recipients than foreign numbers.
Under the new rules, telecom companies will be able to determine whether the Danish phone number displayed by the caller is actually located in Denmark.
If the number is located in Denmark but the call using it can be traced to another country, the caller ID will be considered falsified and the call must be blocked.
The agency said the system will not detect and stop every scam call.
“But it is expected to make it significantly harder for the fraudsters to pretend to call with Danish numbers,” the agency wrote.
The executive order containing the new rules has been sent for consultation and is expected to take effect on January 1, 2027.
Telecom companies will then be required to introduce the necessary technical measures in their systems to comply with the rules.
September records Denmark’s highest raw electricity prices since December 2022
Low wind and limited sunshine combined with high gas prices pushed Denmark’s raw electricity prices to their highest monthly level in nearly four years, according to energy company OK.
The average raw electricity price in September was 1.07 DKK per kilowatt-hour east of the Great Belt and 1.05 DKK west of it. VAT, taxes and tariffs are added to those prices.
By comparison, prices averaged 0.62 DKK east of the Great Belt and 0.54 DKK west of it in September last year.
“Unfortunately, there has not been enough wind and sun to push prices down in September,” said Troels Skipper, commercial manager at OK.
He said high gas prices caused by geopolitical unrest had influenced electricity prices for much of the month.
Despite the increase, OK said Danish consumers’ bills will not be higher than last year because the electricity tax has been reduced to the EU’s minimum rate in 2026 and will remain there next year.
Prices also varied significantly during September. On September 14, electricity cost more than 5 DKK per kilowatt-hour for short periods, while several weekend days had hours when prices were around zero.
Skipper encouraged consumers to follow electricity prices and adjust their consumption when possible.
“This will also be important over the winter, where we will see more large fluctuations in the electricity price. But the fluctuations thus also provide an opportunity to lower one’s electricity bill,” he said.
The average electricity price has exceeded 1 DKK per kilowatt-hour during four weeks so far in 2026, including two weeks in September.

Pioneering Spirit, the world’s largest ship by gross tonnage, passed under Denmark’s Great Belt Bridge at 12:55 p.m. Tuesday, nearly three hours later than planned as it waited for a required gap in other southbound traffic.
The construction vessel traveled at 5.4 kilometers per hour during the passage.
“Apart from us just needing to have a few pieces in place, everything went according to plan,” said Jimmy Westermann, head of VTS Storebælt, the vessel traffic service for the Great Belt.
The ship had been scheduled to pass at 10 a.m., but needed a two-hour window clear of other southbound traffic under the bridge before it could proceed.
Before the passage, Westermann said the vessel had already been lowered in the water using ballast to reach the required draft, the distance between the waterline and the bottom of the hull.
“The ship is ballasted down to the draft it needs to have and is ready out there, so it is the two-hour clearance window we are missing,” he said.
Registered in Malta, Pioneering Spirit is 382 meters long and 124 meters wide. It is built to transport, install and remove offshore oil drilling platforms.
Its gross tonnage is 403,342. Gross tonnage measures the volume of a ship’s enclosed spaces.
Planning the passage involved checking both the ship’s draft and its height above the water to ensure it could pass safely beneath the bridge, which has a clearance of 65 meters. The vessel had a draft of 19.9 meters during Tuesday’s passage. It also passed under the bridge in 2018.
The ship’s next destination is Rostock, Germany, according to the ship-tracking website VesselFinder. Its previous port call was at Rotterdam Maasvlakte four days earlier.

Gender pay gap in Denmark narrows for first time in three years
The pay gap between men and women in Denmark narrowed last year for the first time in three years, according to new figures from Statistics Denmark.
In 2025, women earned on average 12.3 percent less than men, compared with 12.9 percent in 2024.
Statistics Denmark has tracked the pay gap since 2004, when the difference was 16 percent. It fell to 11.9 percent in 2020, but then widened again in 2023 and 2024 before declining last year.
Mads Moberg Reumert, chief economist at pension company Danica, said the development also matters for retirement savings.
“Salary is the factor that matters most for the size of pension savings,” he said. “Therefore, the development in pay gaps is also one of the most important things to keep an eye on if you want less economic inequality between men and women as retirees.”
Helle Dalsgaard, head of advisory services at pension company Sampension, also called the decrease positive, while stressing that women still earn “significantly less than men.”
She said women’s growing educational advantage over men could support higher wages over time. She also pointed to rules on earmarked parental leave, which have led more men to take leave, as another factor that could improve women’s finances.
“After a few years with bumps in the road, the development once again went in the right direction last year,” Dalsgaard said.
German military drone makes first test flight of its kind over Denmark
A German military surveillance drone is flying over Jutland on Tuesday in what the Danish Defence says is the first test flight in Danish airspace involving an unmanned military aircraft of its size.
The German Heron TP weighs more than five tons, is 13 meters long and has a wingspan of 26 meters. It is flying at an altitude of about seven kilometers, sharing airspace with manned aircraft.
The drone belongs to the German air force, the Luftwaffe, and is being remotely controlled by a pilot at a military base in Schleswig, Germany.
The roughly two-hour flight begins at the Danish-German border in South Jutland, continues over eastern Jutland to Aalborg and then returns to Germany over western Jutland.
During the flight, the German pilot remains in contact with Naviair, which manages air traffic in Danish airspace. Denmark’s Civil Aviation and Railway Authority has approved the safety procedures for flying the drone beyond visual range, including procedures for a possible loss of control or radio connection.
The test is part of preparations for the Danish air force to receive its own General Atomics MQ-9B unmanned aircraft in 2028. They will operate from Aalborg Air Base under Squadron 729 and will be used, among other tasks, for patrol and surveillance over Greenland and the North Atlantic.
Brigade Commander Hans Peter Andersen called the flight “yet another important step toward receiving our own unmanned aircraft in the coming years.”

Residents of Vesterbro who have parking permits for areas outside the zero-emission zone will also be able to apply for exemptions allowing them to drive and park fossil-fuel cars inside the zone.
The adjusted zone will cover Inner Vesterbro, apart from the areas that have been exempted.
The proposal must now be approved by the Danish Environmental Protection Agency before it can go to Copenhagen’s Borgerrepræsentation, the city council, for final approval.
A final vote is expected by the end of 2026.

Study finds young women more likely than young men to cross sexual boundaries due to pressure to perform
Young women are more likely than young men to take part in sexual acts they do not want because of pressure to perform, according to a new Danish study.
Sex & Samfund, the Danish Family Planning Association, conducted the study with polling company Voxmeter among people aged 15 to 25.
More than one in three young women said they had pretended to enjoy a sexual act more than they actually did because they felt pressure to perform.
One in six said that pressure had led them to do something they did not want to do.
“We know from previous studies that many young women are afraid to say no during sex because they are afraid of the reaction they will be met with,” Sex & Samfund Secretary General Majbrit Berlau said.
Among young men, fewer than one in 10 said they had shown more enjoyment during sex than they actually felt. About 4.7 percent said they had agreed to do something they did not want to do.
According to Berlau, most young people understand that sex requires consent and should be mutual, but they can still struggle to express and respect boundaries in practice.
“You can be so focused on doing well for the other person or living up to certain expectations that your own desire and your own boundaries fade into the background,” she said.
Sex & Samfund said the findings show a need for better knowledge about sex and sexuality.
Sex education is one of young people’s preferred sources of information, but one in three said they did not find the teaching useful.
Young people also rely heavily on friends and social media for information about sex, while one in three cited pornography as a source.

Next week, a 31-year-old man is to appear in court in a case concerning violence against a Swedish man, who later died, at a big-screen event at Islands Brygge.
However, that is not the only case of violence the 31-year-old is involved in.
On Friday, at the Court in Svendborg, he was sentenced to three months of unconditional imprisonment for violence against another inmate in Nyborg State Prison in 2022.
B.T. and TV 2 report this.
In the case, two men of similar age have also been convicted. They have likewise received three months in prison, writes B.T.
The three men were charged with having assaulted an inmate in the prison with numerous punches and kicks to the face.
The victim suffered a concussion and broke both his nose and a rib, according to the indictment.
The three men were charged under the severe violence section, but were only found guilty under the mild violence provision – section 244.
It is also under this section that the 31-year-old man is charged when he appears in court next week in the case from Islands Brygge.
In that case, he is charged with having struck a 32-year-old Swedish man with a powerful punch.
The Swede died three days later.
The violence took place at a big-screen event at Islands Brygge in Copenhagen on 30 June at around 20:45. A screening of the football World Cup was held here.
According to the case’s indictment, the 31-year-old man at one point stood up on a bench, from where he, with a powerful overhand throw, threw two beer cans in the direction of a group of people – including the 32-year-old Swede.
Immediately after, the 31-year-old man dealt the Swede the powerful blow.
The blow hit the Swede on the left side of the head/neck, after which he fell to the ground.
Because of the blow, the Swede suffered, among other things, a rupture of the artery, which meant that the man later died.
In the case, charges have also been brought under section 247 of the penal code, which pertains to the 31-year-old man having previously been convicted of crimes against the person. Among other things, he has a conviction for attempted murder.
If one is convicted under section 247, the sentence can be increased by up to half.
A prosecutor in the case has previously stated that the man charged with violence faces between eight and ten months in prison.

In a press release, according to the Greenlandic media outlet Sermitsiaq, she elaborates further.

Professor: Old IT makes universities hacking targets
Danish universities hold vast amounts of personal data while some continue to rely on ageing IT systems that may not meet modern security standards, a cybersecurity professor warns following the major attack on DTU.
Old IT systems combined with large amounts of sensitive personal data make Danish universities particularly vulnerable to cyberattacks, according to Jens Myrup Pedersen, professor of cybersecurity at Aarhus University.
His warning comes after the Technical University of Denmark (DTU) revealed Friday that hackers had gained access to its user database and extracted a large amount of data.
“Universities possess a very large amount of personal data,” Pedersen told Ritzau.
“And then it is my impression that several universities have quite a few older systems that probably do not have the security level one can expect in 2026.”
Pedersen stressed that he cannot comment specifically on the quality of DTU’s IT security.
But he said the attack raises important questions about how universities protect access to sensitive information.
“The question is which accounts have had access to all this personal data, and how well they are protected,” he said.
Another key question, according to Pedersen, is whether university IT systems can detect when unusually large amounts of data are being extracted and trigger an alarm before the damage becomes more extensive.
Universities face a ‘very high’ cyber threat
The problem extends beyond DTU.
Danish universities have been targeted by hackers several times in recent years, while a 2025 assessment from the Danish Agency for Societal Security (Styrelsen for Samfundssikkerhed) rated the cybercrime threat against Danish universities as “very high”.
Universities can be attractive targets because they combine extensive personal databases with large and complex IT environments used by thousands of students, researchers and employees.
The latest attack has brought renewed attention to whether security measures have kept pace with that complexity.
More than 200,000 potentially affected at DTU
As previously reported by The Copenhagen Post, more than 200,000 people could be affected by the DTU attack.
Unauthorised parties compromised several DTU user profiles and used them to access the university’s user database. DTU says a large amount of data was extracted and that the information involved could include CPR numbers, home addresses and telephone numbers.
The university has not yet determined exactly what information was taken or how many people are affected.
The incident has been reported to the Danish Data Protection Agency (Datatilsynet), while the National Special Crime Unit (NSK) is in contact with DTU about the case.
It has not been disclosed who is suspected of carrying out the attack.
Source: Ritzau
G7 releases oil reserves – could it bring down Denmark’s record-high diesel prices?
Diesel prices in Denmark have climbed to record levels. Now the G7 countries are releasing up to 100 million barrels of diesel and crude oil from emergency reserves in an attempt to ease pressure on global energy markets.
Danish motorists could see some relief from record-high diesel prices after the G7 countries agreed to release emergency fuel reserves.
The move was announced Friday following a meeting of G7 leaders and will see up to 100 million barrels of diesel and crude oil released over the next four months.
The release will be coordinated through the International Energy Agency and is intended to increase supply and help stabilise energy prices.
For Denmark, the move could take some of the pressure off diesel prices, according to Jens Nærvig Pedersen, senior commodities analyst at Danske Bank.
But motorists should not expect prices to return to normal immediately.
“It is not the grand solution that can cause prices to fall again,” Pedersen told Ritzau.
“It does not solve the supply crisis in the oil market, which is primarily due to the conflict in the Middle East.”
Diesel has hit a Danish record
The price of diesel at Danish filling stations reached a record DKK 19.19 per litre in September.
The additional supplies from G7 reserves could help cushion the market, Pedersen said, but they cannot fully replace the supplies currently missing from the Middle East.
“For us to get lower and more normal prices again, a solution must be found to the current supply crisis,” he said.
The G7 announcement has already had an impact on international energy markets, with oil prices beginning to fall following the decision.
Why is the G7 releasing its reserves?
The decision follows mounting concern about global fuel supplies and sharply rising prices linked to the conflict in the Middle East.
It also comes after US President Donald Trump raised the possibility of stopping US diesel exports to Europe.
Europe is heavily dependent on imported diesel, making any restriction on US exports potentially significant for European supplies and prices.
Following the G7 agreement, Trump said Friday that he would not impose a diesel export ban.
The G7 countries have also agreed not to introduce restrictions on energy exports between member countries.
What happens to Danish fuel prices now?
The release of emergency reserves increases the amount of oil and diesel available on the market and could therefore put downward pressure on prices.
But the underlying problem remains the shortage of supply caused by the conflict in the Middle East.
That means Danish motorists could see some relief at the pump without necessarily seeing a return to the prices that prevailed before the current energy crisis.
The G7 consists of Canada, France, Germany, Italy, Japan, the United Kingdom and the United States.

Reported online banking fraud in Denmark has fallen sharply as banks improve detection and customers become more aware of scams.

That was 51 percent fewer than during the first half of 2023, when reported online banking fraud reached its highest level.
Scammers attempted to steal 74.7 million DKK during the first six months of 2026. Actual losses totaled 38.1 million DKK, almost 16 percent less than during the previous six months.

Ilyas Dogru, chief consultant at FDM, Denmark’s main car owners’ association, said Tesla traditionally registers imported Model 3 vehicles at the end of a quarter.
He said Tesla’s offer of zero-percent financing also increased demand by giving buyers savings worth tens of thousands of kroner.
Mobility Denmark, the Danish automotive industry association, criticized government plans to raise taxes on some electric cars in 2027.
Electric cars currently face tax above a price of 419,300 DKK. The proposed threshold is 366,200 DKK.
Under the proposed budget, a car costing 400,000 DKK would face a tax of almost 25,000 DKK from New Year.
FDM expects some buyers to complete purchases before the higher tax takes effect, potentially increasing sales during the final three months of the year.

Legislation for departure centers outside the EU is now in place, says Immigration Minister Morten Bødskov
European Union countries will adopt legislation Thursday allowing the creation of departure centers outside Europe, Danish Immigration Minister Morten Bødskov said.
“Europe must strengthen the external borders,” Bødskov of the Social Democrats said before an EU ministerial meeting in Luxembourg.
The centers would hold rejected asylum seekers sent from Europe while authorities arrange their return. Denmark, Germany, the Netherlands, Austria and Greece are seeking agreements with non-EU countries to begin transfers next year.
Bødskov said the five countries had made progress during talks Thursday morning.
EU ministers will also discuss a sudden arrival of migrants in Ceuta, a Spanish territory in North Africa.

He said the EU remained vulnerable to sudden large arrivals and needed stronger external borders.
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen and Migration Commissioner Magnus Brunner recently proposed measures including closer cooperation with neighboring countries, improved monitoring and stronger action against human smugglers.
The plan would also strengthen deportations and allow visa restrictions or economic pressure against countries refusing to accept the return of their citizens. Bødskov said departure centers could support that effort.
More than half of Danish school classes report student violence during school year
More than half of Denmark’s school classes experienced physical violence between students during a school year, a government report found.
Research firms Epinion and Als Research prepared the report for the Ministry of Children and Education.
The problem was most common in early primary school, covering kindergarten through third grade, and in classes where students had additional support needs.
Three-quarters of early primary classes reported violence or disruptive behavior among students during the year.
Physical violence most often occurred outside lessons when games, sports or jokes got out of control, the report said. Only seven percent of incidents involved deliberate and planned violence.
In many classes, one or two students were responsible for the physical violence.
The report also examined threats and harassment, including insulting language and threats delivered verbally or digitally.
Verbal or digital threats of violence occurred at least once a month in 34 percent of school classes.
“The extent of violence in primary and lower secondary school is worrying, to say the least,” Education Minister Magnus Heunicke of the Social Democrats said.
“School must not be a place where either students or teachers fear to be,” he added.
Heunicke said some children had not received the support they needed. The government plans to propose legislation giving teachers more options to intervene.

Denmark’s regions are taking responsibility for treating 18- to 24-year-olds with mild to moderate anxiety and depression under a new patient right taking effect today.
Young people in the target group who are referred by their doctor must now have treatment started within 30 days.
The change was passed by the Folketing, Denmark’s parliament, in December 2025 as part of an agreement on a 10-year plan for psychiatric care.
Previously, young people could receive a referral for free treatment from a psychologist with a provider number, but waiting times varied considerably.
“Some had to wait half a year to be seen, while others could be seen the next day,” said Jane Alrø Sørensen, secretary general of Bedre Psykiatri, a Danish association for people affected by mental illness and their relatives.
“By introducing it as a patient right, everyone is guaranteed help within 30 days,” she said.
The regions can provide treatment at their own facilities or through private providers with which they have agreements. Treatment can include individual psychologist sessions, group programs or online courses.
Sørensen said offering different types of treatment could better meet patients’ individual needs.
“Mental illness can develop just as quickly as any other illness. So early intervention is the key to thriving,” she said.
Bedre Psykiatri plans to monitor whether patients receive treatment within the required 30 days and whether the treatment is at least as good as under the previous system.
Region Østdanmark has previously estimated that around 9,500 young people in its future area will be referred for treatment each year.
Danish jewelry company Pandora is expanding production beyond Thailand for the first time in decades with a new facility in Ho Chi Minh City.
The factory opens Thursday following an investment of just under 1 billion DKK. Once fully operational, it is expected to employ 7,000 people and increase Pandora’s current production capacity by 50 percent.
The facility will eventually be able to produce 60 million pieces of jewelry annually, although production will be increased gradually as demand grows. Around 700 of the potential 7,000 positions have initially been filled.
Pandora CEO Berta de Pablos-Barbier said the company chose Vietnam partly to reduce its dependence on a single production market.
“The reason why we are looking toward markets other than Thailand is that we want to create greater resilience and flexibility and avoid being dependent on a single market,” she said.
She added that Vietnam, like Thailand, has a strong tradition of jewelry manufacturing, giving Pandora access to workers with relevant skills.
Pandora makes its jewelry by hand, making access to employees who can be trained to meet the company’s craftsmanship standards important, de Pablos-Barbier said.
“We have not built the factory with a view to the next quarter, but instead with a view to the next decade,” she said.
The company expects to add employees and equipment as demand increases.
De Pablos-Barbier said she particularly expects future growth from consumers in the U.S. and Asia. The U.S. is currently Pandora’s largest individual market, while Asia is among its fastest-growing markets.
A record 17.5 percent of Danes who reached the state pension age worked enough to qualify for the first senior bonus in 2025, according to ATP.
ATP, Denmark’s statutory pension and labor market pension administrator, said 11,351 people received the first senior bonus last year. That was up from 9,592 people in 2024.
In previous years, around 14 to 15 percent of people reaching the state pension age qualified for the first bonus.
“The state pension age is not necessarily the time when one stops working, and we can see that a larger share continues after that age,” ATP Group Director Maria Damborg Hald said.
Employment Minister Ane Halsboe-Jørgensen welcomed the increase.
“It is great that so many seniors want to keep contributing. We need that if we are to continue to create growth and prosperity in Denmark,” she told Ritzau in a written statement.
The senior bonus is a tax-free lump sum available to people who continue working after reaching the state pension age. Generally, a person must work at least 1,560 hours over 12 months to qualify.
The first-year bonus is 56,327 DKK, while people who continue working sufficiently during the second year can receive 33,517 DKK.
ATP paid 546.4 million DKK in first-year bonuses in 2025, compared with 446.3 million DKK in 2024.
Just under 6,775 people also received the second senior bonus in 2025, almost 3,400 more than the previous year.
In 2029, the two bonus amounts will increase to just under 65,900 DKK and 39,100 DKK, respectively.
Denmark has reached 100 organ donors using a method introduced three years ago, exceeding initial expectations for the number of people who would donate this way.
The method, known as donation after circulatory death, or DCD, allows organs to be retrieved after a person’s heart has stopped beating and breathing has ceased, the Danish Health Authority said.
Since its introduction in 2023, 100 people have donated 210 organs through DCD. Authorities had expected the method to result in about 35 additional donors annually once fully implemented.
“This involves several hundred organs that would not otherwise have been able to be donated,” Danish Health Authority chief physician Camilla Krogh told Ritzau.
Previously, major organs could only be donated in Denmark by people who had been declared brain-dead and were being kept alive artificially. New technology has made donation possible from some patients who cannot be declared brain-dead but whose ventilator treatment is discontinued.
Of the 210 organs donated through DCD since 2023, 187 were kidneys.
During the first half of 2026, 46 people donated organs after being declared brain-dead, while 20 donated through DCD.
Between 400 and 500 patients have been on Denmark’s organ transplant waiting list each year over the past decade, with most waiting for a kidney.
By the end of June 2026, 1.9 million Danes had actively registered their position on organ donation.
Under a consent model introduced last year, everyone over 18 is automatically included in the Organ Donor Register, but individuals must still actively record their decision on whether to donate.

Green groups challenge government claim that 2035 climate target is on track
Environmental groups and climate experts are challenging the Danish government’s claim that it has demonstrated a path to meeting its 2035 climate target.
Climate Minister Samira Nawa has said the government considers the path to an 85% emissions reduction by 2035 to be demonstrated, even though current measures are projected to deliver only an 80% reduction.
“It is demonstrated because there is enough time to make the decisions, and because there is enough time to handle the risks that may arise on the way towards 2035,” Nawa said.
Greenpeace and green think tank Concito argue that this differs from how the term has previously been used in Danish climate policy.
“That is stretching the definition of demonstrated,” Concito chief economist Torsten Hasforth said.
Greenpeace political campaign lead Christian Fromberg said additional policy would be needed before the target could be considered demonstrated.
“Of course, that target has not been demonstrated yet. That will require new policy,” he said.
The Climate Council has previously assessed possible pathways toward an 85% reduction target, while stressing that reaching a higher target would require additional measures beyond policies already adopted.
The government has proposed an 85% target for 2035, which would go beyond Denmark’s current 2030 target of a 70% reduction.
Enhedslisten climate spokesperson Rasmus Vestergaard Madsen also said the final 5 percentage points still needed to be backed by concrete measures.
4 years on, Danish-Greenland history projects unveiled
More than four years after Denmark and Greenland agreed to examine their historical relationship, researchers have presented the first four subprojects in the investigation.
The projects will focus on adoptions, people who were legally registered without a father, school and language policies, and settlement and working conditions, Greenlandic broadcaster KNR reported.
“We are beginning with four important projects, which each shed light on concrete decisions and their consequences,” research leader Tenna Jensen said in a press release cited by KNR.
The Danish government and Naalakkersuisut, Greenland’s government, agreed to launch the investigation in June 2022.
The decision came after reporting by Danish broadcaster DR on the so-called IUD case, in which thousands of Greenlandic women and girls had contraceptive devices fitted without their knowledge or consent.
The investigation will examine major decisions and events since World War II and their consequences for Greenland’s population. Its stated purpose is to provide a basis for reconciliation with the past.
Possible areas of research mentioned earlier included the closure of Greenlandic settlements, adoptions and Greenlandic children sent to Denmark.
The investigation is based at Ilisimatusarfik, the University of Greenland, and citizens are expected to be involved in the work.
Denmark originally allocated 45 million DKK to the project. Under the terms of reference, the investigation should, as far as possible, be completed within five years of the agreement between the university and the research leader.

Higher winter electricity tariffs set to take effect across Denmark
Many households in Denmark will pay higher electricity grid tariffs during peak evening hours from Thursday as the country’s grid companies switch to winter rates.
The higher tariffs apply between 5 PM and 9 PM, when demand puts the greatest strain on the electricity grid. The aim is to encourage customers to move flexible electricity use to other times of the day.
“Electricity consumption in Danish households is significantly higher in the winter period, and we feel that in the power grid. Therefore, with the tariffs, we give customers an incentive to use electricity wisely,” said Lise Bering, CEO of grid company N1.
N1, which is owned by Danish energy company Norlys, supplies electricity to more than 800,000 households and businesses.
Its grid tariff between 5 PM and 9 PM will rise to 99 øre per kilowatt-hour until March 2027, compared with 43 øre during the summer period. Between midnight and 6 AM, the tariff remains at 11 øre.
Bering recommends moving flexible electricity use, such as charging an electric car or running a washing machine, away from peak hours.
Doing so can reduce individual electricity bills while easing pressure on the grid, she said.
“The more efficiently we can operate the existing power grid, the smaller the need becomes for new investments in the electricity grid, which are ultimately paid for by the consumers,” Bering said.
Winter tariffs vary between grid companies. At Cerius, which operates much of the electricity grid east of the Great Belt, the tariff between 5 PM and 9 PM will be 129.75 øre per kilowatt-hour from October 1.
Denmark introduces new measures to crack down on phone scams
Danish telecom companies will be required to block calls from abroad that falsely appear to come from Danish phone numbers under new rules expected to take effect in 2027.
The Danish Agency for Digital Government announced the planned rules as part of efforts to make it harder for fraudsters abroad to disguise their calls.
The practice, known as spoofing, involves manipulating caller ID so that a call appears to come from a different phone number. Fraudsters can use the method to make calls originating abroad look as though they come from Denmark.
According to the agency, the number of such calls has increased in recent years. It said Danish phone numbers can create greater trust among recipients than foreign numbers.
Under the new rules, telecom companies will be able to determine whether the Danish phone number displayed by the caller is actually located in Denmark.
If the number is located in Denmark but the call using it can be traced to another country, the caller ID will be considered falsified and the call must be blocked.
The agency said the system will not detect and stop every scam call.
“But it is expected to make it significantly harder for the fraudsters to pretend to call with Danish numbers,” the agency wrote.
The executive order containing the new rules has been sent for consultation and is expected to take effect on January 1, 2027.
Telecom companies will then be required to introduce the necessary technical measures in their systems to comply with the rules.
September records Denmark’s highest raw electricity prices since December 2022
Low wind and limited sunshine combined with high gas prices pushed Denmark’s raw electricity prices to their highest monthly level in nearly four years, according to energy company OK.
The average raw electricity price in September was 1.07 DKK per kilowatt-hour east of the Great Belt and 1.05 DKK west of it. VAT, taxes and tariffs are added to those prices.
By comparison, prices averaged 0.62 DKK east of the Great Belt and 0.54 DKK west of it in September last year.
“Unfortunately, there has not been enough wind and sun to push prices down in September,” said Troels Skipper, commercial manager at OK.
He said high gas prices caused by geopolitical unrest had influenced electricity prices for much of the month.
Despite the increase, OK said Danish consumers’ bills will not be higher than last year because the electricity tax has been reduced to the EU’s minimum rate in 2026 and will remain there next year.
Prices also varied significantly during September. On September 14, electricity cost more than 5 DKK per kilowatt-hour for short periods, while several weekend days had hours when prices were around zero.
Skipper encouraged consumers to follow electricity prices and adjust their consumption when possible.
“This will also be important over the winter, where we will see more large fluctuations in the electricity price. But the fluctuations thus also provide an opportunity to lower one’s electricity bill,” he said.
The average electricity price has exceeded 1 DKK per kilowatt-hour during four weeks so far in 2026, including two weeks in September.

The package would also raise the maximum prison sentence for the most serious animal welfare offenses from two years to six. It will cost 160 million kroner annually once fully phased in.

Wammen said livestock owners would pay for the strengthened inspections. Visits will generally involve two inspectors instead of one, and more will take place without advance notice.
Although recent scrutiny has focused on conditions at Danish pig farms, the measures also cover other livestock, including cattle and poultry.

Responsibility for animal welfare inspections moved to the Justice Ministry when the new government took office. The ministry will establish an independent agency to carry out inspections, with more staff intended to help clear the backlog and improve enforcement.
Denmark’s government and several parties in parliament have agreed to provide an additional 5.6 billion kroner in operating support for a planned hydrogen pipeline from Jutland to Germany, while easing financial requirements for producers.
The funding comes on top of 10.9 billion kroner already allocated to the project. The agreement means the state will take on more of the financial risk while the hydrogen market is still developing.
“We are entering the project with open eyes. The hydrogen market is still immature, and a hydrogen pipeline is a large project with several risks,” Climate, Energy and Utilities Minister Samira Nawa said in a press release.
The pipeline would run from Esbjerg through Veerst, near Egtved, to the German border. Its route resembles the number seven, giving the project its Danish name, Syvtallet, or “The Figure Seven.”
It is intended to allow Danish companies to produce green hydrogen using renewable energy and sell it to German businesses. German industrial companies could use the hydrogen to reduce carbon dioxide emissions from their production processes.
Germany has committed to supporting five hydrogen projects in Denmark with a total of 12 billion kroner in German state and European Union funding. The public support is intended to help the industry develop.
Pioneering Spirit, the world’s largest ship by gross tonnage, passed under Denmark’s Great Belt Bridge at 12:55 p.m. Tuesday, nearly three hours later than planned as it waited for a required gap in other southbound traffic.
The construction vessel traveled at 5.4 kilometers per hour during the passage.
“Apart from us just needing to have a few pieces in place, everything went according to plan,” said Jimmy Westermann, head of VTS Storebælt, the vessel traffic service for the Great Belt.
The ship had been scheduled to pass at 10 a.m., but needed a two-hour window clear of other southbound traffic under the bridge before it could proceed.
Before the passage, Westermann said the vessel had already been lowered in the water using ballast to reach the required draft, the distance between the waterline and the bottom of the hull.
“The ship is ballasted down to the draft it needs to have and is ready out there, so it is the two-hour clearance window we are missing,” he said.
Registered in Malta, Pioneering Spirit is 382 meters long and 124 meters wide. It is built to transport, install and remove offshore oil drilling platforms.
Its gross tonnage is 403,342. Gross tonnage measures the volume of a ship’s enclosed spaces.
Planning the passage involved checking both the ship’s draft and its height above the water to ensure it could pass safely beneath the bridge, which has a clearance of 65 meters. The vessel had a draft of 19.9 meters during Tuesday’s passage. It also passed under the bridge in 2018.
The ship’s next destination is Rostock, Germany, according to the ship-tracking website VesselFinder. Its previous port call was at Rotterdam Maasvlakte four days earlier.

“There is something we need to have a little less of, so that in return we can invest in the community, in welfare, in security, and in a competitive business sector,” he told Berlingske.
Economic and Interior Affairs Minister Pia Olsen Dyhr said support for Ukraine would continue to form part of defense spending in the coming years.
“This is both about defending Denmark and Europe, while at the same time we also protect welfare. The Danish economy is strong enough to do both,” she said.
Taxation and Growth Minister Jakob Engel-Schmidt said continued donations to Ukraine would require support from the Folketing, Denmark’s parliament.
NATO members agreed in 2025 to increase the alliance’s military spending target to at least 3.5 percent of GDP, replacing the previous 2 percent target.

Gender pay gap in Denmark narrows for first time in three years
The pay gap between men and women in Denmark narrowed last year for the first time in three years, according to new figures from Statistics Denmark.
In 2025, women earned on average 12.3 percent less than men, compared with 12.9 percent in 2024.
Statistics Denmark has tracked the pay gap since 2004, when the difference was 16 percent. It fell to 11.9 percent in 2020, but then widened again in 2023 and 2024 before declining last year.
Mads Moberg Reumert, chief economist at pension company Danica, said the development also matters for retirement savings.
“Salary is the factor that matters most for the size of pension savings,” he said. “Therefore, the development in pay gaps is also one of the most important things to keep an eye on if you want less economic inequality between men and women as retirees.”
Helle Dalsgaard, head of advisory services at pension company Sampension, also called the decrease positive, while stressing that women still earn “significantly less than men.”
She said women’s growing educational advantage over men could support higher wages over time. She also pointed to rules on earmarked parental leave, which have led more men to take leave, as another factor that could improve women’s finances.
“After a few years with bumps in the road, the development once again went in the right direction last year,” Dalsgaard said.
German military drone makes first test flight of its kind over Denmark
A German military surveillance drone is flying over Jutland on Tuesday in what the Danish Defence says is the first test flight in Danish airspace involving an unmanned military aircraft of its size.
The German Heron TP weighs more than five tons, is 13 meters long and has a wingspan of 26 meters. It is flying at an altitude of about seven kilometers, sharing airspace with manned aircraft.
The drone belongs to the German air force, the Luftwaffe, and is being remotely controlled by a pilot at a military base in Schleswig, Germany.
The roughly two-hour flight begins at the Danish-German border in South Jutland, continues over eastern Jutland to Aalborg and then returns to Germany over western Jutland.
During the flight, the German pilot remains in contact with Naviair, which manages air traffic in Danish airspace. Denmark’s Civil Aviation and Railway Authority has approved the safety procedures for flying the drone beyond visual range, including procedures for a possible loss of control or radio connection.
The test is part of preparations for the Danish air force to receive its own General Atomics MQ-9B unmanned aircraft in 2028. They will operate from Aalborg Air Base under Squadron 729 and will be used, among other tasks, for patrol and surveillance over Greenland and the North Atlantic.
Brigade Commander Hans Peter Andersen called the flight “yet another important step toward receiving our own unmanned aircraft in the coming years.”

Electric cars costing more than DKK 366,000 could become more expensive in Denmark from 2027 if the government allows a current registration tax exemption to expire.

Study finds young women more likely than young men to cross sexual boundaries due to pressure to perform
Young women are more likely than young men to take part in sexual acts they do not want because of pressure to perform, according to a new Danish study.
Sex & Samfund, the Danish Family Planning Association, conducted the study with polling company Voxmeter among people aged 15 to 25.
More than one in three young women said they had pretended to enjoy a sexual act more than they actually did because they felt pressure to perform.
One in six said that pressure had led them to do something they did not want to do.
“We know from previous studies that many young women are afraid to say no during sex because they are afraid of the reaction they will be met with,” Sex & Samfund Secretary General Majbrit Berlau said.
Among young men, fewer than one in 10 said they had shown more enjoyment during sex than they actually felt. About 4.7 percent said they had agreed to do something they did not want to do.
According to Berlau, most young people understand that sex requires consent and should be mutual, but they can still struggle to express and respect boundaries in practice.
“You can be so focused on doing well for the other person or living up to certain expectations that your own desire and your own boundaries fade into the background,” she said.
Sex & Samfund said the findings show a need for better knowledge about sex and sexuality.
Sex education is one of young people’s preferred sources of information, but one in three said they did not find the teaching useful.
Young people also rely heavily on friends and social media for information about sex, while one in three cited pornography as a source.

Industrial robots working in factories surpass 5M worldwide
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
06:06:20 UTC
15:06:20 KST

Bahattin Gonultas and Emir Yildirim
03 October 2026•Update: 03 October 2026
The ever-growing developments in artificial intelligence (AI) and supply chains drove global factory automation adoption to historic highs, with the global active industrial robot inventory surpassing 5 million last year, according to a report.
The International Federation of Robotics said the operational robot stock rose 9% on an annual basis and global installations jumped 11% to more than 600,000 units.
China boasts an overwhelming dominance in the field, expanding annual robot installations by 20% to 354,000 units, making up 59% of the global deployment, while domestic firms secured 55% of the market share in the country.
Japan’s installations fell 19% to 36,219 units, falling from second place to be replaced by the US, which posted a 12% surge to 38,500 robots.
South Korea maintained its fourth position with 30,200 annual robot installations, followed by Germany with an 8% decline to 24,800. India had a 15% surge to 10,500.
Germany’s growth decelerated while accounting for 41% of all EU installations, alongside contractions in Italy, France, and Spain.
The global robot demand is expected to rise in the coming years, with installations climbing to 655,000 units this year and 806,000 by 2029.
Persistent labor shortages in advanced economies, supply chain reshoring and AI-focused technologies lowering deployment costs for small- and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) drove the expansion in robot installations.
At the same time, Türkiye ranked 17th in the global robot market last year, while robot installations declined 9% to 3,194 units, down from its record of 4,429 units in 2023.
Türkiye’s operational stock rose 7% to a record of 30,990 units, ranking 15th worldwide in the robot fleet.
The country’s metal industry remained the top automation buyer among other sectors, as installations rose 8% to 990 units to capture 31% of the market, with 6,774 robots in active duty.
The Turkish auto sector’s robot inventory climbed 3% to 889 units, accounting for 28% of new installations and maintaining 11,017 active units.
Demand weakened in other sectors, with annual robot installations in the electrical/electronics sector, including home appliances and electrical machinery, falling 37% to 136 units, while adoption in the food products, beverages and tobacco products segment saw annual robot installations plummet by 40% to 144 units.
Some 59% of all new robots were deployed for handling operations/machine tending and 16% for welding and soldering, the report showed.
The report added that the robot density remains quite low, with 52 units per 10,000 workers in the manufacturing industry, while the density was better in the auto sector, reaching 374 per 10,000 workers, compared to a rate of 35 units per 10,000 workers in other industries.

Latvia votes in parliamentary election amid rising costs

Latvia: Ruling party leads in exit polls amid populist gains
Published October 3, 2026last updated October 3, 2026
The party of Latvian Prime Minister Andris Kulbergs took a comfortable lead in parliamentary elections on Saturday, exit polls showed.
Kulbergs' centerist, pro-Ukraine party, United List, was projected to win 35.6% of the vote, according to an exit poll by public proadcaster LSM.
"It's remarkably good. I was not expecting such result," Kulbergs said at his party's headquarters in Riga.
The exit poll put the the populist Latvia First party in second place with 11.3% — nearly double its share at the last election in 2022. It had courted the country's substantial ethnic Russian minority.
Kulbergs said on Saturday night that he would not cooperate with any pro-Russian parties and specifically ruled out forming a coaltition with Latvia First.
Some 1.5 million people were eligible to vote in the country's 11th parliamentary election since independence from the Soviet Union in 1991.
The election, which saw 100 seats in the Saeima being contested by 14 parties using a proportional system, has been dominated by rising living costs and national security concerns in the small Baltic country which borders both Russia and Belarus.
Kulbergs, has only been in office since May after the previous government collapsed over a dispute about Ukrainian drones. Despite his party leading opinion polls, his coalition is expected to emerge weakened as populist parties gain.
Latvia vote shaped by Russia concerns
Russia's ongoing invasion of Ukraine is seen as a direct threat to national security in Latvia which, like Ukraine, is a former Soviet state with a sizeable ethnic Russian and Russian-speaking minority.
Unlike Ukraine, however, Latvia is a member of both the European Union and NATO.
Riga is one of Kyiv's closest partners and supporters, having committed itself by law to spending at least 5% of GDP on defense – leaving less room for spending elsewhere.
Many Latvians complain of high prices and low wages, the economy is sluggish, the health system is under strain, and emigration and an ageing population remain persistent challenges.
Populist movements such as the Sovereign Power/Young Latvians Alliance and the Latvia First party have attempted to exploit discontent by taking a less stringent line towards Moscow and arguing that a complete economic decoupling from Russia is damaging.
German Eurofighter jets in Latvian airspace
Nevertheless, no parties are proposing any major deviation from Latvia's clear foreign policy alignment with the EU and NATO.
Indeed, four German Eurofighter jets have been deployed to protect Latvian airspace during the election in response to a request from Riga.
Once ballots are counted, attention is likely to shift quickly to coalition negotiations, which could prove lengthy and complex.
Partial results are expected on Saturday evening, with preliminary official results due on Sunday.

Eating with someone you love could help your body regulate blood sugar, Israeli study finds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
06:02:23 UTC
15:02:23 KST

We know that being near someone we love can make us feel good. A new study discovers why: it helps the body work better.
Researchers have previously shown that people who live together or share the same workplace often adopt similar sleep-wake schedules, light exposure, and screen-time habits. Roommates, close couples, or tight-knit office teams often experience stress spikes, anxiety, or low moods simultaneously during major shared events.
If one person yawns in a room full of close friends or family members, several others will often yawn shortly after. Even dogs, which are pack animals, do this. It’s an involuntary neurological response tied to empathic connections and mirrors neuron activity in the brain. And people living in the same home often report having similar meal schedules, eating identical foods, and even experiencing synchronized bathroom habits.
Now, researchers at the Hebrew University of Jerusalem (HUJI) and Sheba Medical Center at Tel Hashomer have found another physiological connection – blood glucose after a meal is lower when eating in companionship, compared with when eating alone. After the same standardized carbohydrate meal, participants had smaller glucose spikes and quicker glucose recovery in the social condition.
They published it in the prestigious journal Science Advances under the title “Social Physiology: Human homeostasis is more efficient in social proximity.” The research was led by HUJI Prof. Shir Atzil and her PhD student Monia Masalha, with Dr. Shai Fuchs from Sheba. They and six students in her lab worked on the project for three years.
They call this principle “social physiology”: the human body regulates itself more efficiently in the presence of social partners. “We used to think of the body as an isolated system that regulates itself,” Atzil told The Jerusalem Post.
“Our findings show that human physiology is inherently social. Being close to someone you love lowers the physical energy your body spends on regulating itself. This gives us a direct metabolic benefit to being together and reveals a core evolutionary reason why humans form bonds in the first place: our bodies run better together.”
In their article, they noted: “This discovery has two key implications; the first concerns evolution. Although attachment theory and social neuroscience have provided valuable insights into how close relationships are formed and maintained, they don’t resolve a central paradox.
“Why are social animals motivated to invest considerable cognitive and physical effort, and accept risks of competition, conflict, and aggression to engage in social interactions?… Addressing this discrepancy requires identifying immediate gains that make social interaction worthwhile in the moment yet can also accumulate into long-term fitness benefits.”
Atzil asserted that “what we discovered was not known at all. Nobody else has studied it.”
Benefits of social proximity
The experiment consisted of a standardized carbohydrate-meal test, in which participants consumed 50 grams of carbohydrates contained in 102 gr. of a standardized white-wheat bread. Their glucose levels after eating were sampled over 120 minutes.
The effect even extended beyond blood sugar. Social proximity also improved temperature regulation during cold exposure and reduced stress responses in adults and infants. The benefits appeared even without physical touch and were not explained by reduced stress. Across preregistered experiments, the evidence suggests that social physiology is a domain-general principle of human physiology.
At a time when blood sugar regulation is a growing global health concern, the findings suggest that metabolic health may be shaped not only by what is on the plate, but also by who is at the table.
“Blood sugar regulation is not just about what we eat, but who we eat with,” says Atzil. “Our relationships have an active biological role in our physical wellbeing.”
The research, which was supported by a European Research Council Starting Grant awarded to Atzil, offers a new way to understand human connection. Relationships may not only support our emotional lives; they may help regulate the body’s most basic systems.
The researchers emphasized that social closeness is not a substitute for medical care, nutrition, or exercise. But the study points to a powerful and overlooked factor in health: the people beside us.
Atzil is director of HUJI’s Bonding Neuroscience Laboratory, where she focuses on the neural and behavioral mechanisms that form and sustain close human bonds. She earned her bachelor’s degree in biology and master’s degree in psychobiology from Tel Aviv University, followed by a doctorate at Bar-Ilan University and postdoctoral work in neuroscience at Harvard University.
With this multidisciplinary expertise and extensive experience working with parents, infants, and romantic partners, she developed a novel theoretical framework to understand the neural and behavioral processes that underpin intimate human bonds and their developmental consequences.
“For the experiments, we used a room in our lab that looks like a living room. They were all connected to electrodes. They didn’t have to sit together at a table. We let them do whatever they wanted,” recalled Atzil. “I thought touch would be a strong indicator, but it wasn’t.”
The average change in the glucose level was 23%. “Overall, it was a significant effect, but there was a huge variation. Some had a big benefit, while others had much less. I can’t say now what caused the differences,” she continued.
“There were no differences between men and women. We controlled for age, gender, body-mass index, metabolic health, how much they touched, stress levels, and more. We looked for strongest-connection partners and mothers and children.
“The study is preliminary, and there is a lot more to learn. Our next step will be to study siblings and strangers.”
Asked what she thought was actually causing the improved glucose level, Atzil suggested: “I think it’s the brain, whose most important job is to keep the body up and running. A baby is dependent on caregivers and can’t eat by themselves.
“Gradually, as they grow older, their brains develop with close human bonds. It doesn’t even have to be its parents. Anybody who takes care of an infant with sensitivity and a positive input affects the baby, who learns to regulate its body through social interaction.”
The team hasn’t tested glucose levels of diabetics or those who have pre-diabetes, but Atzil said that “this is the obvious direction of our research. Asked if the findings have implications for older adults who eat alone, hospital patients, people living alone, or people in nursing homes, she commented that “it could be if social physiology has a real effect. It should be studied.”
“We still have a lot of questions, but its significance among our participants makes us believe the effect. We still have to characterize it much more to discover how generalizable it is.”

Can young diabetics safely observe Jewish fasts? Insulin pump tweaks can help, Israeli study finds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
06:01:53 UTC
15:01:53 KST

A first-of-its-kind study has found that more than 70% of young participants completed a 25-hour fast without significant complications when they adjusted their insulin pumps in advance, thus raising the likelihood of success eightfold.
With two major fasts and four minor ones in the Jewish calendar, many people with type 1 diabetes will regularly face a difficult question: Is it possible to observe the fast without putting their health at risk? The new research was conducted jointly by researchers at the Jerusalem College of Technology (JCT) and Shaare Zedek Medical Center. Offering encouraging findings, it showed that advanced diabetes technologies can make it possible for many people with type 1 diabetes to fast safely.
The study, conducted by the diabetes clinic team at Shaare Zedek Medical Center and led by Dr. Floris Levy-Khademi of Shaare Zedek and Dr. Eliyahu Heifetz, a lecturer and researcher at JCT, examined whether automated insulin delivery (AID) systems could enable adolescents and young adults with type 1 diabetes to safely complete prolonged Jewish fasts.
There are two major Jewish fasts commonly observed in the calendar: Yom Kippur (a 25-hour fast, including both food and drink; Tisha B’Av (essentially the same food-and-drink restriction, from before sunset until after nightfall); and four minor fasts (all from dawn to nightfall) – 17 Tammuz, the fast of Gedaliah, 10 Tevet, and the fast of Esther.
The team decided to carry out the study only for the major fasts, even though some religious young people don’t eat or drink on the minor fasts as well. “They could endanger their health; they mustn’t do it without consulting their doctor,” Levy-Khademi asserted.
Levy-Khademi is the director of Shaare Zedek’s pediatric endocrinology unit, which diagnoses and treats a wide array of hormonal and metabolic conditions in children and adolescents, not only those with type 1 diabetes but also those with puberty disorders, pediatric obesity, and more. Heifetz is a lecturer and scientific researcher at the JCT’s Faculty of Management.
It was published in the Journal of Diabetes Science and Technology under the title “Automated insulin delivery systems are safe during prolonged religious Jewish fasting among adolescents and young adults with type 1 diabetes.”
Fasting despite having an exemption
The purpose of religious fasting is “to gain self-restraint, arouse spiritual consciousness, and better understand the poor and hungry,” they wrote. “Traditionally people with type 1 diabetes were exempted from fasting by the medical and religious authorities, due to a fear of hypoglycemia, hyperglycemia, and dehydration.
“Despite medical recommendations, many individuals with the condition from various religious backgrounds choose to fast; it makes them feel equal, mature and capable of fulfilling their religious obligations.”
The researchers analyzed 109 fasts undertaken by 80 adolescents and young adults with type 1 diabetes on Yom Kippur and Tisha B’Av, in 2023 and 2024. All participants used automated insulin delivery systems that combine an insulin pump with a continuous glucose monitor. The findings showed that 71.5% of participants successfully completed the fast without significant complications.
The mean age of participants was 17.4 ± 4.1 years; 47.5% were male, and the average duration of diabetes was 7.2 ± 4.3 years. A total of 67.6% of participants modified their AID system settings during the fasting period, with the most common modification being a change in the target glucose level, the researchers reported.
“The most important finding of the study is that there were no life-threatening complications among the participants, with no cases of severe hypoglycemia or diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA), the two major complications that raise concerns during prolonged fasting,” said Levy-Khademi.
Another notable finding was the importance of advance preparation and consultation with the patient’s medical team. “About 68% of participants adjusted their pump settings ahead of the fast, either by raising their glucose target or reducing their insulin dosage,” said Levy-Khademi. “Among those who made adjustments, 84.5% successfully completed the fast, compared with just 40% of those who did not.”
Statistical analysis showed that adjusting pump settings before the fast increased the likelihood of successfully completing it eightfold,” she noted. “This is the first study to examine the use of automated insulin delivery systems during prolonged Jewish fasts,” she continued
Heifetz, whose son was diagnosed with autoimmune diabetes as a child and has observed full fasts since age 13, including in the years before today’s advanced technologies became available.
The researchers said that participants’ blood sugar control actually improved during the fast. Participants remained within their target glucose range 80.7% of the time during the fast, compared with approximately 72% during the week leading up to it. The amount of time participants experienced low blood sugar was also relatively limited.
Levy-Khademi explained that “most patients completed the fast successfully, but of the 28.5% who did not, some thought that if they gave themselves less insulin, they would be OK. We told them to be careful, that if they saw their blood sugar was going down significantly, they should stop fasting.
“We monitored them not only during the fast, but also a week before and a week after. We carried out the study because they knew that some religious diabetics were doing dangerous things without consulting anyone.”
The researchers noted that this is the first study to examine the use of automated insulin delivery systems during prolonged Jewish fasts.
“The findings indicate that this technology may enable some people with type 1 diabetes to fast safely, but only with individualized adjustments to their system settings and appropriate medical guidance,” the researchers said.
They didn’t include older people with type 1 diabetes, or those who already had complications of the disease. The team members plan to continue the study next year, focusing on ketones, which are chemical substances that the liver produces when it breaks down fat for energy instead of using sugar because it doesn’t get enough carbohydrates from food.
They cautioned, however, that the findings should not be interpreted to mean that everyone with type 1 diabetes can safely fast.
“The study participants were relatively young and had good glucose control. The decision about whether to fast therefore needs to be made on an individual basis, based on the recommendation of the treating physician and in consultation with the appropriate halachic authority,” the researchers said.

Ukrainian Mirage 2000 Downs Russian Cruise Missile With Cannon
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
06:01:00 UTC
15:01:00 KST

A Ukrainian Air Force Mirage 2000-5F multi-role fighter jet has intercepted and destroyed a Russian S8000 “Banderol” compact cruise missile using its onboard 30mm automatic cannon, marking the first confirmed gun kill of the munition type by the French-supplied aircraft.
The close-range interception was reported by French Aid to Europe, an open-source research initiative monitoring Western military assistance delivered to Kyiv, with defense portal Militarnyi independently detailing the engagement.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
According to military monitoring data, the Ukrainian fighter pilot bypassed conventional guided air-to-air missiles, relying instead on one of the aircraft’s two internal 30mm DEFA 554 automatic cannons.
Each cannon carries an onboard ammunition capacity of 125 rounds and can fire at a rate of up to 1,800 rounds per minute, giving the aircraft rapid close-in ballistic engagement capabilities against low-flying targets.
Downing an aerial target with automatic cannon fire demands close visual proximity and aggressive maneuvering compared to engaging targets at standoff ranges with guided missiles.
According to manufacturer specifications, the Russian Banderol maintains an operational cruising speed between 520 and 560 kilometers per hour, with maximum dash speeds reaching 620 to 650 kilometers per hour across an operational flight range of up to 500 kilometers.
Close-range gun engagement
Military analysts noted that neutralizing high-speed targets with gun rounds offers substantial cost efficiency by conserving scarce and expensive air-to-air munitions.
Russian Ballistic Missiles and Drones Hit Kyiv, Killing 1
At the end of September, France delivered a fresh consignment of MICA heat-seeking and radar-guided air-to-air missiles alongside specialized 30mm high-explosive incendiary rounds to maintain operational readiness across Ukraine’s Mirage fleet.
The S8000 Banderol, developed by Russian defense contractor Kronshtadt, is engineered as a low-cost, compact cruise missile tailored for saturation barrages against urban logistics, transportation hubs, and utility facilities.
The weapon is propelled by a Chinese-manufactured Swiwin micro-turbojet engine and carries a high-explosive fragmentation warhead weighing more than 114 kilograms, containing roughly 49.5 kilograms of high-grade explosive filler.
Its small radar cross-section, low-altitude flight profile, and turbine velocity have posed operational hurdles for mobile ground-based gun crews, requiring the Ukrainian Air Force to commit combat aircraft to patrol interception sectors.
Late-night information: the Mirage 2000-5F was the first western fighter aircraft to destroy a Russian S8000 Banderol cruise missile with the cannon. In 2025, France took 4️⃣ Mirage 2000-5F from its Air Force’s stocks and transferred them to Kyiv. pic.twitter.com/rtg8LMeocP
— French Aid to Europe 🇨🇵 🇪🇺 (@aidefranceukr) October 1, 2026
French fighter fleet
France delivered its initial batch of renovated Mirage 2000 fighters to Ukraine in early 2025, fulfilling commitments announced by French President Emmanuel Macron to reinforce Ukrainian airspace defenses following the earlier supply of American-built F-16 fighters.
Independent defense estimates place the Ukrainian Air Force’s operational Mirage fleet between 12 and 15 airframes.
The delta-wing French aircraft have been integrated into Ukraine’s layered territorial air defense network, tasked with intercepting cruise missiles and loitering munitions while retaining strike capacity to deploy Western standoff ordnance such as SCALP-EG cruise missiles.
In March 2025, a Ukrainian Mirage 2000 recorded its first confirmed operational victory by intercepting a Russian Kh-101 strategic cruise missile.
The fleet has sustained operational strains amid continuous air patrols. In July 2025, a Ukrainian pilot safely ejected from a Mirage 2000 after experiencing an in-flight equipment failure during a defensive sortie, resulting in the loss of the airframe without causing casualties on the ground.

London Labour council warns it may raise council tax by 150%
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
06:00:53 UTC
15:00:53 KST

A flagship Labour authority has warned it may have to impose a 150% council tax rise on residents to maintain current services following central government cuts under a new funding settlement.
Hammersmith and Fulham council’s cabinet has concluded in a report due to be published on Monday that such a rise would cost Band D households an additional £29.11 a week in 2027/28.
The west London council has said it is losing more than half of its government grant under Labour’s “fair funding” review, which was introduced last year to redirect cash from affluent areas to places hit hardest by austerity.
Ministers have argued that the review will mean that local authorities with “historically low” council tax levels will have the cash they receive from Whitehall slashed, forcing them to bring bills into line with national averages to make up shortfalls.
Hammersmith and Fulham, along with Westminster, Kensington and Chelsea, Wandsworth, City of London, and Windsor and Maidenhead councils, have been given powers to raise bills above the 5% cap next year to balance its budget in the wake of cuts.
A household in Band D currently pays £1,519 annually, including the £510.51 City Hall surcharge, known as the Greater London Authority (GLA) precept.
In a document seen by the Guardian, the councillor Rowan Ree, serving as cabinet member for finance and reform, said the council was “facing the biggest financial challenge in living memory” under the new funding formula. The council received £150.5m in government funding in 2025/26, but this will be cut by more than half to £72.4m over the next four years.
“Various scenarios in this report show the deep extent that Hammersmith and Fulham council could be required to raise its element of the council tax (which excludes the GLA precept) during 2027/28,” he said.
Scenarios include:
- A 100% increase in the Hammersmith and Fulham council tax element – £2,018 a year at Band D – leaving a budget shortfall of £46.1m. “For a family in a Band D property that would mean an increase of £19.40 a week,” the document said.
- A 125% increase in the Hammersmith and Fulham council tax element – £2,270.25 a year at Band D – leaving a budget shortfall of £20.6m. For a family in a Band D property that would be an increase of £24.25 a week.
- A 150% increase in the Hammersmith and Fulham council tax element – £2,522.50 a year at Band D – which would broadly balance the budget on current assumptions. According to the document, a family in a Band D property would pay an increase of £29.11 a week.
Under rules set by Angela Rayner at the start of last year, cash was supposed to be redirected from affluent rural areas to urban councils hit hardest by austerity. Ministers said the changes put in place a fairer system that recognised the extra needs and weaker council tax-raising powers of councils in “left-behind” areas.
But Hammersmith and Fulham’s Labour councillors argue that they have kept bills low with “ruthless” cost cutting in a borough that has significant areas of deprivation. They claim that the council’s inclusive economic growth strategy, Upstream London, has attracted more than £6bn of investment into the borough and created 17,200 jobs.
London boroughs affected by the formula argue that flawed deprivation measures risk undermining the government’s aim of ensuring funding follows need.
In a letter to Andy Burnham in August, the Conservative leaders of Kensington and Chelsea, Westminster and Wandsworth councils urged a rethink of the proposals.
A spokesperson for the Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government said: “Local authorities decide the level of council tax they wish to set, but we are clear that in doing so they should put taxpayers first.
“We’ve made over £78bn available for council finances next year, with the majority of money unringfenced so local leaders can decide how best to spend on their local priorities.”
