‘It’s shocking really’: Devon community tracks River Dart sewage spills
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
06:00:53 UTC
15:00:53 KST

The easy thing for the people who live on the banks of the River Dart in Devon might have been to grumble and groan about the sewage spills that blight their beloved waterway.
Instead, citizen environmentalists in the area have created a unique online platform that flags up spills in real time, highlights spots that are repeatedly polluted, and sets out where improvement work is planned – and where it isn’t.
Friends of the Dart (FOD), an independent, not-for-profit organisation, says its River Hub is the first platform to pull together, overflow by overflow, such a sweep of granular detail about how one British river is being polluted.
It argues it should be up to water companies or the Environment Agency to provide this sort of information in a user-friendly way – but claims they don’t – so it has done the digging and provided what it believes is a vital service.
Rob Worthington, one of the designers of the platform, said there was a lot of justified anger about sewage. “We built River Hub to help channel that constructively: to show where the problems are and why, so communities can help decide what gets fixed first.”
The launch comes in the week that South West Water (SWW) was fined almost £8m for sewage spills, including in Cornwall’s River Camel, which like the Dart rises on the moors and plunges down to cherished tourist hotspots.
It also coincides with the prime minister, Andy Burnham, telling the Labour conference that water was a symbol of what had gone wrong with Britain and promising to reverse Margaret Thatcher’s “ideological ban” on the public ownership of water companies.
Worthington told the Guardian about River Hub while sitting on a bench at Steamer Quay on the Dart in the market town of Totnes. This is a designated bathing water spot – but Worthington says he would not swim there, knowing about what goes on a little farther upstream.
The hub has a page that people can check to find out where spills are happening right now and where they stopped in the last 12 hours. There is also information about “dry spills” – discharges when there was no or little rain.
Worthington acknowledged other independent sewage maps, such as Top of the Poops, also do this job. “But River Hub takes this a lot further,” he said.
A section called Why it keeps happening? probes issues such as whether sewage treatment works have the capacity to deal with the sewage produced by the size of the population it serves. The hub concludes that not all do.
In Who is fixing it?, the hub spells out works that are taking place or planned, with the dates they are due to be completed, and also draws attention to problem spots where there is no planned remedial work.
A lengthy How we know? section sets out the hub’s methodology – for example, where the rainfall data it uses to classify each dry spill comes from.
Much of the data used, such as SWW spill information and permits, is in the public domain but some of it can be difficult to spot, and FOD had to extract some through freedom of information requests.
Worthington has worked on the hub alongside his day job as a business analyst and accepted that the picture the platform provided was incomplete and there could be inaccuracies. He and the rest of the team are happy to be corrected when they have got something wrong.
They are offering the model for free to any groups who want to do the same thing on their local river. Organisations FOD has links with have already shown an interest.
People who live in and around Totnes tell tales of falling ill after swimming in the Dart and its tributaries.
Emma Roberts, an interfaith minister and theatre director, said she ended up in hospital with an E coli infection after a dip. “It’s shocking really. The river is alive and we should all be protecting it, not putting poo into it.”
She is not a member of FOD but thinks the hub will help. “The more information people have, the more pressure that we can put on.” A quick check of the hub reveals that place where she got ill was close to a treatment work that FOD believes does not have sufficient capacity.
Olivia Doherty, who works in children’s rights and participation, said her son Seamus, 17, recently suffered stomach problems after swimming in the Dart.
She said the United Nations had made it clear that young people had a right to safe spaces. “For me that includes our rivers. Getting into the river is a big thing for children here. It’s so wrong if they miss out because it’s too dirty.”
Ben Brierley, who runs kayak tours and courses on the Dart, said the hub could help him work out where and when it was safe for his clients to be submerged in the river.
Brierley expressed frustration that water companies have been given a deadline of 2035 by the UK government to reduce sewage flowing into bathing water and areas of ecological importance, and 2050 for other places. “It’s bonkers that we’ll be putting sewage into our rivers until 2050,” he said.
SWW said it welcomed people taking an interest in rivers’ health. A spokesperson said its WaterFit Live site provided customers with a wide range of information, including near real-time storm overflow data, bathing water information and details about investment programmes.
The spokesperson said: “We are committed to making information accessible and continue to develop the platform to help customers better understand our work to improve river health.”
An Environment Agency spokesperson said it was taking action to tackle pollution on the Dart and welcomed the initiative from local communities to use data to raise standards.
The agency said: “100% of storm overflows are now monitored and the data is publicly available. As part of the government’s storm overflows reduction plan, a record £10.2bn is also being invested over the next five years to improve more than 2,500 storm overflows in England. We will continue to hold water companies to account where performance falls short.”
Hannah Pearson, a healer, coach and a founding director of FOD, said the hub built on other initiatives such as water monitoring and installing river “guardians” in parishes along the Dart.
Pearson was keen to stress that they met dedicated professionals who wanted to do the right thing within organisations such as SWW and the Environment Agency. “But they are working in a dysfunctional system,” she said.
She said the idea of the hub and other FOD projects was to find a way to bring about change, not to moan. “We’re not saying: ‘This is terrible.’ We’re taking responsibility and saying: ‘What can we do?’”

What is Zionism and why do some critics describe it as racist?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
06:00:51 UTC
15:00:51 KST

Zack Polanski has described himself as an anti-Zionist as his party prepares to debate the motion at its conference. Photograph: Sean Smith/The Guardian View image in fullscreen Zack Polanski has described himself as an anti-Zionist as his party prepares to debate the motion at its conference. Photograph: Sean Smith/The Guardian Explainer What is Zionism and why do some critics describe it as racist? Green party debate over the motion ‘Zionism is racism’ comes amid renewed arguments over the meaning and history of a contested term Zack Polanski, the leader of the Green party, has said he is an anti-Zionist. As his party conference prepares to debate a motion that “Zionism is racism”, what precisely is Zionism and what is the history of the claim that it is racist? What is Zionism? Modern Zionism developed in the late 1800s out of several strands of thinking on the future of Jewish collective and cultural identity, emerging from a millennia-old religious yearning to return to Zion, which runs through Jewish holy texts. The term came, however, to be most associated with Theodor Herzl’s brand of political Zionism, the movement for Jewish self-determination and statehood in the context of rising European antisemitism. Although Zionism tends to be seen by critics as a monolithic political idea, its history has encompassed multiple, often contradictory, intellectual strands including the notion – proposed by the philosopher Martin Buber before the foundation of Israel – of a binational Arab-Jewish state in Palestine. Since the foundation of the state of Israel in 1948, the debate over Zionism inside the country has largely centred on liberal and rightwing, or “revisionist”, camps – the latter represented by Benjamin Netanyahu’s Likud party. Issues such as settlement, occupation and whether Israel should be defined as an ethno-nationalist Jewish state moved to the core of political contest. However, as Dov Waxman, a professor of Israel studies at the University of California, wrote in the Conversation last month, the issue is further complicated by the fact that, despite contested definitions, the idea of Zionism for many Jews represents something more amorphous: “Jewish liberation and sovereignty, a safe haven from persecution, a revival of the Hebrew language, and a renewed sense of collective pride, especially after the Holocaust.” What is the criticism of Zionism? One critique of Zionism – used as a shorthand for the state of Israel – is that it is a “colonial” project. Those critics, in parts of the left, in the wider Arab world and among some anti-Zionist Jews such as Polanski, would point to three pieces of evidence. First, the violent displacement of Palestinians during the Nakba, or “catastrophe” for Palestinians, that accompanied the founding of the Jewish state. Second, they argue Israel has created an apartheid system of unequal rights in the occupied territories that denies Palestinian ambitions to statehood and their own self-determination and, third, that within Israel those of Palestinian origin are discriminated against. Before the establishment of Israel in 1948, Palestinians had a vibrant society across British Mandatory Palestine, but their connection to historical Palestine has often been dismissed or diminished by significant strands of Zionist thinking. At the heart of academic debate is how widespread the use by some early Zionists was of the notion of a “land without people” for a “people without land”, which critics have used as evidence that Zionism was a colonial enterprise at its very beginning. In contrast, Zionists point to the evidence of a historical presence of Jews in the Holy Land, as well as for many a promised biblical patrimony in a homeland from which Jews were displaced and that many hold up as a refuge in a hostile world. What is the history of the claim that ‘Zionism is racism’? The argument that Zionism is racism, while controversial, is not new. The phrase came to particular prominence during the cold war, when the UN passed resolution 3379 in 1975. The so-called “Zionism as racism” resolution compared “the racist regime in occupied Palestine” to apartheid South Africa. Sponsored’ by the Arab League and promoted by the Soviet Union, it passed with support from countries in the developing world but was later revoked in 1991 under pressure from the then US president, George HW Bush. Proponents of the argument say Zionism privileges the rights of Jews in Israel over non-Jews via a discriminatory system. Opponents of the framing describe it as antisemitic as it singles out Jews as a group to deny them alone the right to self-determination. They argue that, by delegitimising the basis for Israel’s founding as a Jewish homeland, it acts as a cover for antisemitism. The war in Gaza has intensified arguments about the nature of Zionism, in part driven by the overtly racist framing of senior Israeli political figures towards Palestinian society after the 7 October deadly Hamas attack on southern Israel in 2023. What does British law say about the argument that Zionism is racist? An employment tribunal two years ago found that the views of David Miller, a former professor of political sociology who was sacked by the University of Bristol in 2021, that “Zionism is and always has been a racist, violent, imperialist ideology premised on ethnic cleansing” amounted to a protected philosophical belief under the 2010 Equality Act, a case upheld on appeal. A highly controversial figure, Miller has also argued in social media posts that Zionists have worked as “infiltrators and subversives”, gained access to not just all UK political parties but also “the media, entertainment industries, the law, financial institutions, sports and all sorts of apparently obscure parts of the UK”. Miller is a key figure in the anti-Zionist Movement and has links to Greens for Palestine, which is proposing the Green party motion on Zionism is racism. From the Bayeux tapestry to Glastonbury: top tips and tricks to grab the hottest tickets
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
06:00:51 UTC
15:00:51 KST

Whether your passion is the battle of the bands or the Battle of Hastings, what are probably Britain’s hottest cultural tickets are about to go on sale – and to be in with a shout of going, there are insider tips that will get you a good spot in the queue.
General admission tickets to the Glastonbury festival next June go on sale online at 9am on Sunday, while the next tranche of tickets to view the Bayeux tapestry at the British Museum will be released to members on Tuesday 6 October before a public on-sale on 21 October.
If you are planning to try your luck, get your fastest finger ready and check out our tips for how to increase your chances of bagging tickets for the most in-demand events.
Join the club
Membership of an organisation or venue often includes priority booking, giving you early access to tickets. However, the cost will be beyond many people’s budgets.
The next member priority booking window for the Bayeux tapestry – for slots from 1 January to 31 March 2027 – opens on Tuesday 6 October at noon. That is for members who joined up to 16 September. If you join now, you can book before the public in January for April to July 2027 dates. However, standard individual membership starts at £82.
Sometimes you don’t have to pay to get priority booking for hot-ticket events. Some theatres (such as those run by the LW Theatres group) and gig promoters (such as Live Nation) offer presale access to people who sign up for email alerts or newsletters.
Assemble your squad
Planning to try for Glastonbury tickets? One person can book up to six per transaction, and this year, when the sale begins, everyone who is already on the glastonbury.seetickets.com page will be assigned a place in a queue to access the booking process.
The six-ticket limit means that if there are a lot of you who want to go, the best way to maximise your chances is to split into one or more groups of six. They need to all be logged on before 9am.
The festival says you only get five minutes on the booking page, and there’s a lot of information to input.
If and when one of the six people gets through, they will need the registration details, including postcodes, of everyone in their party in order to book tickets. (Registration for this year is now closed.) Everyone should check their registration details are still correct ahead of the sale.
So, before things kick off, get a spreadsheet going with everyone’s details on it that everyone can access, and set up a group chat on WhatsApp or wherever so you can message each other instantly. To speed up the checkout process, everyone should consider having their debit or credit card details saved in their browser.
For the Glastonbury general admission sale, you pay a £100 deposit a person now, so everyone needs to have enough cash in their account, or a big enough credit limit on their card, to pay for all the tickets. They must have their mobile phone charged and ready to approve the payment by entering a code if necessary.
Multiple devices and browsers?
In theory you can increase your chances of getting a good spot in the queue for in-demand tickets by using multiple web browsers or several devices. However, ticket websites often warn there is a risk you will be identified as an automated bot and blocked from making a purchase.
The ticketing company AXS is known to be particularly strict about this sort of thing.
Crucially, it appears that for this year, Glastonbury ticket hunters must enter their registration number before entering the queue. They then get a unique queue ID linked to that. So it appears that means one queue spot only per person, and means the end of being able to use multiple devices and/or browsers for Glastonbury.
Be ready
If it says the tickets go on sale at 9am, don’t log on to the site at 8.58am. Go on at perhaps 8am or even earlier. It means you are in the website, just in case it starts to buckle later when everyone else tries to log on.
Some ticketing and venue websites will let you create an account and add your address and payment card details in advance. That will mean a quicker checkout if you get through.
Hold your nerve
So the tickets for that gig or show, etc went on sale at 9am but a few minutes later the website says it is sold out.
Don’t give up: keep refreshing the page for at least a few minutes. In that 9am scramble, some people’s purchases won’t have gone through. Perhaps there was a technical glitch or they took too long inputting their details and were “timed out”, or their bank card was rejected.
In such cases, their tickets will go back on sale – maybe immediately or a little while later.
Once you’re done, don’t hang around
You got through, and the tickets are in your basket. Pay for your tickets and get out quick. Don’t tempt fate by hanging around: sometimes websites crash when they are overloaded, causing people to lose the tickets in their basket.
Resale sites and ‘wait lists’
Did you end up missing out? Secondary ticketing websites such as Viagogo and StubHub are not popular with everyone.
However, there are more palatable options – notably Twickets, an “ethical” fan-to-fan marketplace enabling people to sell spare tickets at no more than face value (plus fees). Twickets is an app and website and is well worth checking regularly if you are hunting for tickets for a gig, show or sporting event.
Some venues such as the Royal Albert Hall in London use Twickets as their official ticket resale partner.
Meanwhile, you may be able to join a waiting list for tickets that have been returned by people who can no longer attend a sold-out event. Some theatres operate waiting lists, as does the gig tickets app Dice. On Dice, if something is sold out, it will usually say “Wait list” under the event information. Once you join this, you will be sent an email or push notification if tickets become available, and you will have a short window to buy them.
Get help from AI
According to Ticketmaster, music fans “are increasingly using AI assistants to discover live events, compare options and make purchasing decisions”.
If you have your eye on a gig or event that is sold out, a tool such as ChatGPT can now “work in the background” and check the relevant ticketing or venue website from time to time. So you could ask it to alert you if tickets become available or extra ones are released (or if prices fall below a specific amount).
For example, if it’s an arena or stadium event, extra “production seats” – also known as “production holds” – are often released nearer the time, when they have got the staging finalised. Similarly, theatres will sometimes only put certain seats (such as the front row) on sale once they have sorted out the staging and sightlines.

‘People are deserting it’: why are London mansions struggling to sell?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
06:00:50 UTC
15:00:50 KST

An elegant Georgian facade, a full-width balcony and an exclusive address in South Kensington just steps from the Natural History Museum and the V&A. Yet the listing price of this west London flat at Queen’s Gate Gardens has dropped by nearly £1m since last year, to £4.4m.
It is far from an isolated case. A nearby house originally listed at £20m was slashed to £14m this year, says a local estate agent. In neighbouring Notting Hill, a stucco-fronted property that came to market two years ago at £16m is now being offered for less than £14m, they said.
London’s premium property market is stuck in a rut. While borrowing costs and stretched affordability weigh on everyday buyers, the city’s richest residents are also making deep cuts to the prices of their multimillion-pound homes.
This market is a world away from the rest of the UK property market – where the average house price was just under £275,000 in September, according to Nationwide. The well-heeled neighbourhoods also present a stark contrast with much of the capital, where Londoners struggle to get on to the housing ladder, face rising rents and a lack of affordable housing, and estate agents report the market for flats is now “dead”.
But neighbourhoods such as Knightsbridge, bordering Hyde Park and home to Harrods, are also feeling the pinch, said Harry Dawes, a buying agent based in Belgravia.
“There is a flat on Pont Street, a five-minute walk from Harrods, which sold at £4.4m in 2014, then sold at £3.5m. It can now be bought at £2.5m.”
Deflating the bubble
For decades, London’s property prices raced ahead of the national average. But that gap has been slowly narrowing: while the average price of a UK home rose by about 2% in the year ended in June, prices in inner London boroughs fell by 8.3%, according to the Office for National Statistics.
That drop has been particularly pronounced in Westminster – which includes areas such as Marylebone, Belgravia and Mayfair – with prices down 25.4% year on year. In the City, prices slumped by 20.4%, and in Kensington and Chelsea, prices fell 14.7%.
Properties in the capital became overvalued in the mid-2010s after a period of rapid price growth, said Anthony Payne, the chief executive of the data analyst LonRes. London was then hit hard by Brexit, the Covid pandemic, higher property taxes and a surge in borrowing costs.
Now, owners who bought at the peak now face losses of as much as 25% if they choose to sell, according to estimates from the estate agent Savills.
“London benefited dramatically from international investment and buyers wanting property here as a store of wealth and a way of making money,” Payne said. “These are the people that inflated the market, but now more and more of them are deserting it.”
Jeremy Gee, the managing director at the super-prime estate agent Beauchamp Estates – whose portfolio includes a £42m sub-penthouse overlooking Hyde Park – said the decline had also been driven partly by the exit of super-wealthy groups from the UK, especially after the abolition of the non-dom tax regime.
“There is a section of society who have left the UK recently for lots of reasons, but mainly because of tax,” he said.
“When there are not that many buyers and lots of properties, the prices are going to be softer. Many of our sellers have decided that enough is enough – let’s just sell the property and move on.”
Tax changes have put sellers on edge, too, he added. Last year, the former chancellor Rachel Reeves announced plans for a “mansion tax” on homes worth more than £2m.
This nervousness has triggered a slowdown across the higher tiers of London’s market. Prime properties spent an average of 186 days on the market in the first half of 2026, up from 178 days in the first half of 2025, according to LonRes. Over the same period, the average discount to asking price widened from 8.3% to 10.4% – sellers have grown more likely to accept lowball offers.
Sellers, who normally own these properties for at least a decade, “don’t like it but have to accept it,” said Dawes.
“If they are older, they have to take a lifetime view on their property and accept that from a profit and loss perspective, this last trade might not look good.
“We bought three flats for a client’s kids last year – two in Chelsea and one in Notting Hill – and every seller was selling at a loss.”
A divided market
Even with multimillion pound discounts propping up on the market, Stuart Bailey, the head of super-prime London sales at the estate agent Knight Frank, said there were still buyers willing to pay above the asking price for “the very best in class” properties.
“A fabulous address, lovely views, immaculate style and newly refurbished,” he said. “It is a matter of premium or discount, retail or trade, brand new or not, and there is nowhere in between. It’s the discounted properties dragging the market down.
“Sellers are more and more realistic about moving on,” he added. “They do not see material price growth on the horizon.”
“With a Labour government the concern is always that there’s going to be some kind of wealth tax somewhere,” he said.
“But many wealthy people also just accept the cost of taxation and that London is simply an expensive city to live in.”
Camilla Dell, a buying agent, said demand is still strong from a wide base of international buyers, including Americans, Singaporeans and Nigerians. Politics, she said, rarely comes up in conversation.
“Most people accept that the UK does not have the best political stability but they want to live here,” she said. “And actually, it helped that Andy Burnham ruled out an overhaul of property taxes in the next budget.”
Sluggish prices in London are in stark contrast with the likes of San Francisco and Lisbon (a hub for Europe’s digital nomads). Both cities have benefited from booming wealth in the tech sector, with prices rising by 4.8% and 3.3%, respectively, in the first half of this year. Tokyo has been the global standout, with prices up 7% as international buyers have swooped on a weak yen and snapped up luxury properties already in low supply.
Berlin’s prime market, which was the worst performer in Europe, has suffered under the weight of rising borrowing costs and meagre economic growth.
London’s trophy homes
While the multimillionaires’ tier of the property market is being squeezed, the billionaire “super-prime” end of the market is buzzing with activity.
This year, billionaire Reform donor Nick Candy sold his Chelsea home for more than £270m, which is believed to the UK property market’s biggest single house sale in history. Meanwhile, the Holme, the 40-bedroom mansion inside Regent’s Park, is reportedly nearing a £190m sale, less than two years after it was sold for £139m in 2024.
“There have been some very big transactions in super-prime – those are people buying long-term family homes and trophy assets,” Dawes said.
For agents, their cut on these deals – typically about 2% – can run into the millions, and business is thriving. The sale of homes priced at £10m or more climbed 50% in the three months ended in June, compared with the same quarter in 2025, according to the property developer JLL. Meanwhile, Savills found that transactions in the £15m to £20m bracket rose by almost 40%, also in the second quarter of this year compared with last.
The rise of newly minted multimillionaires from the world of tech and social media is driving new renovation trends, too – with more calls for home cinemas, steam rooms, saunas and dedicated yoga and meditation spaces, according to the interior designer Nu Projects.
Still, many of the wealthy are waiting on the sidelines. Beauchamp says that seven out of 10 of its ultra-prime clients are now choosing to rent rather than buy, because they want to save on maintenance, stamp duty, service charges and property taxes – as well as anxiety over whether the government will introduce higher taxes on property, wealth and pensions.
It is pushing prime rental stock into scarce supply. Prices in this market rose 1.6% in the year ended in June, according to Savills. Super-expensive tenancies, where tenants hand over at least £5,000 a week – were up 17% last year, according to Knight Frank.
A buyers’ market
Such intense competition for “best in class” properties mean that even in a fragile market, the most discerning buyers can still face stiff competition, advisers said.
“There’s still demand from overseas buyers who want to buy best-in-class trophy assets,” Gee says. “American and Middle Eastern buyers are underpinning that market.
“But then there is everything beneath that. Anything secondhand, needing a bit of work, where you might normally find a domestic buyer, that is where it is a bit stickier.”
The outlook for the broader prime market remains less rosy. The estate agent Strutt & Parker has downgraded its forecast for prime central London price growth to 4.4% by 2030, compared with an estimate of 9% to 12% at the start of the year.
For now, the balance of power remains with buyers in London, Payne said.
“I look at some of the stuff that’s coming on the market and you just think to yourself, ‘My God, this is such unbelievably good value’,” he added.
“Hand on my heart, I do not think we are at the bottom of the market yet.”

Hungarian restaurants struggle: costs match Europe but revenues lag behind
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
06:00:32 UTC
15:00:32 KST

A new study says tourist traps create competition that squeezes quality restaurants, as foreign visitor numbers fall and most Hungarians cannot afford to eat out regularly.
Across the EU, the number of hospitality venues is falling fastest in Hungary. Between 2021 and 2024 the decline was 6 percent, while 22 member states recorded growth. Looking at the past ten years, the situation is even more dramatic: 18.5 percent of hospitality businesses have disappeared.
According to a recently published study (source in Hungarian), one reason for the worsening trend is that cheap, poor-quality lángos and goulash bars, geared towards foreign tourists and working with high margins, are pushing quality restaurants out of the market. This segment primarily attracts low-spending visitors, such as stag party tourists, which is problematic for the country’s image as well.
"I dare say that we are the only country in the world where you can get lángos with Greek salad, lángos with beef stew, and I could go on. There is nothing wrong with a simple dish being good. That is not a problem at all. The problem is when we try to serve this simple dish in a way that means it is no longer that dish, and on top of that we try to attach a gastronomic culture to it," said Áron Reményik, author of the study and communications expert at Raconteur Agency.
Hungary becoming expensive
Tourism was at its highest in 2025, but even that failed to really give hospitality a boost. This year, the problems have multiplied: after the election, the strengthening of the forint has made Budapest 12–14 percent more expensive for tourists paying in euros, and nation-branding campaigns have also been halted. In August, 14 percent fewer foreign tourists came to Hungary than a year earlier.
As a result, Hungarian restaurants face huge competitiveness problems, according to the founder of Eventrend Group, a corporate group that operates 35 hospitality venues.
"We have reached European price levels in almost every cost category. We pay almost the same for energy and wages. Today, it is cheaper to employ hospitality workers in southern Italy or southern Spain than in Hungary. In Austria, it may still be a little more expensive, but overall, there is not much difference. Raw material prices are almost at the same level," explained Zoltán Kőrössy to Euronews.
Few Hungarians can afford to eat out regularly
While costs — and therefore often prices — are at a Western European level, revenues are not. In Austria, for example, there is a similar number of hospitality venues, but the sector’s turnover is twice that of Hungary. And this depends not only on tourists but also on domestic guests.
Economist Zoltán Pogátsa recently pointed out (source in Hungarian) that two-thirds of Hungarian society live on less money than the EU’s lower middle class. Yet without a broad, solvent middle class, restaurants that rely on returning guests cannot operate.
It is no surprise that, since measurements began, the number of hospitality venues in the capital fell below 8,000 for the first time in 2024, and by the end of 2025, the Central Statistical Office recorded only 7,778.
According to Reményik, one possible solution would be to extend the certification and inspection system for Hungarikums and authentic Hungarian cuisine to the street-food segment as well.
It would also help if the number of purely tourist-oriented street-food outlets in the busiest tourist zones were limited. That will not, of course, give Hungarians more money to eat out, but the likely fall in rents caused by weaker competition might put struggling quality restaurants in a slightly better position.

Officials defend new rules requiring healthier school snacks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
05:50:00 UTC
14:50:00 KST

Officials defend new rules requiring healthier school snacks
If schools restrict snack bar offerings but children start buying snacks from nearby shops instead, their diet will not become healthier, school caterers say. The Ministry of Social Affairs, however, believes there is no reason to assume that all students will rush to shops instead of the school snack bar because of the new requirements.
New rules for food offered in childcare institutions took effect last September, with a one‑year transition period. At the start of this school year, all changes entered into force, and they now apply not only to school cafeterias but also to food sold in school snack bars.
The Health Development Institute (TAI) guidelines (link in Estonian) require that at least 80 percent of items offered in school snack bars must be health‑supporting — high‑fiber products with low added sugars, salt, and saturated fats.
Examples include fruits and vegetables, porridges, high‑fiber bread and rolls, kama, unprocessed fish, seafood, poultry, eggs, cold cuts, nuts, seeds, pesto, and hummus. The guidelines also consider unsweetened dairy products, cheeses, and plant‑based drinks used as milk alternatives to be healthy options.
Up to 20 percent of the selection may consist of "conditionally suitable" products — foods with added sugar, honey, syrup, jam, or similar ingredients. This group includes juices, smoothies, galettes, muesli and muesli bars, sweetened dairy products, salad dressings, red meat, canned fish, ham, dumplings, pâté, and sausages.
Most highly processed foods — such as sweet and salty snacks and sweetened drinks — are considered unsuitable. Deep‑fried foods, instant noodles, powdered mashed potatoes, and foods containing certain colorants or sweeteners are also prohibited.
Children go to shops instead of the school snack bar
Baltic Restaurants Estonia CEO Aaro Lode said that of course school snack bars should offer healthier options, but the real question is whether the new rules change children's behavior — or simply change where they buy their snacks.
"If we restrict the snack bar's assortment but purchases simply move outside the school building, the child's diet does not become healthier. Shifting the problem is not solving the problem," Lode said, adding that the success of the change should not be measured by formal compliance alone.
P. Dussmann Eesti also highlights this risk. The company's catering development manager, Inga Paenurm, raised concerns with TAI, several ministries, and other relevant institutions, arguing that the situation has become the opposite of what the guidelines intended.
"Students leave the school and buy products from nearby shops that are not sold inside the school," Paenurm said, adding that the child's food choices do not change — only the place where they buy food.
Lode emphasized that he does not oppose the guideline's goals and agrees that children should have healthy options at school. However, Baltic Restaurants' experience does not show that removing certain products from the snack bar automatically leads children to choose healthier alternatives.
He added that many healthy options — fruits, vegetables, nuts, and sometimes unsweetened dairy products — are already available for free as part of school meals. Therefore, it is difficult to assume that children will start buying items from the snack bar that they already receive at no cost.
Rules alone are not enough
Dussmann wants TAI to provide guidelines with precise examples of affordable products available on the market. Paenurm stressed the need for national communication, as each new requirement means concrete changes in ingredients, preparation, workflow, staffing, and ultimately price. Students also need education to understand why the offerings are changing.
Lode agrees that simply introducing a new rule is not enough: schools, parents, contracting authorities, and caterers must understand why the change is being made and what it aims to achieve.
"If adults themselves do not understand why the rule exists, unrealistic expectations and conflicts arise quickly, and the caterer is left alone to explain why something has changed," Lode said.
He added that discussions often focus on whether today's food tastes bland, but far less on how many healthy years of life children gain from proper eating habits.
Paenurm said that for children and parents, the most important questions are simple: *What can I buy? How much does it cost? Is it appealing?*
"If these aspects are not explained, the snack bar's selection may become healthier according to the guidelines, but students simply will not buy these products," she said. This, in turn, increases food waste — contradicting environmental and climate goals.
Baltic Restaurants' experience has not yet shown that the new guidelines have increased food waste or made food significantly more expensive, Lode said, but these risks exist and should be monitored.
"What the guidelines need is clear logic. For example, it must be obvious how the 80/20 ratio is calculated and what to do when healthy products run out during the day," Lode said. "Our goal is not to defend any specific product on the snack bar shelf. The goal should be that children actually make healthier choices."
Ministry: Responsibility lies with all adults
Ingrid Põldsaar, adviser at the Ministry of Social Affairs' public health department, said that TAI's guidelines focus on the basics of healthy eating, and these principles have not changed over the years.
"It is important that what children learn about healthy eating — both in human studies classes and elsewhere — aligns with what is actually offered at school. Ensuring this is a shared responsibility of all adults," Põldsaar said.
According to her, a more health‑supporting school environment does not necessarily mean that students will start going to shops more often instead of staying at school.
"Although we cannot influence the choices children make outside of school, we can shape the school environment so that healthy choices are as easy and accessible as possible," Põldsaar said, adding that behavioral sciences show people often choose the options that require the least effort and are supported by their surroundings.
"If healthy food is easily accessible and well presented at school, children are more likely to choose it," she added.
Equally important, in Põldsaar's view, is the school's role in shaping habits and attitudes, because school is a social environment where children learn and develop shared routines. She noted that some schools have agreed on common principles — for example, that students stay on school grounds during breaks and do not leave the premises.
"If students want to leave school to buy sweets and soda from a shop, the solution is not to make those same products more easily available at school. Instead, attention should be paid to what influences those choices and how students' eating habits develop," the adviser said. "The choices adults offer children — and the example they set — also shape children's eating habits."
Therefore, both the home and school environments should support what children are taught about healthy eating. Põldsaar added that there is no reason to assume that all students will start buying food outside school because of the new requirements.
"Previous studies show that the vast majority of students eat school lunch. Some students may buy food elsewhere, but that does not diminish the school's role in creating a health‑supporting food environment. The school can give every child the opportunity to make a healthy choice as easily as possible and help develop good eating habits," she said.
Healthy does not have to be expensive
Põldsaar noted that the requirement for food to meet children's energy and nutrient needs, be health‑supporting and varied, and be prepared from minimally processed ingredients already existed before. Healthier food should not necessarily mean higher prices for school snack bars, she said.
"Micronutrient requirements were previously described in detail, but there was no clarity on how to meet them in everyday catering. Now the emphasis is more on practical dietary principles and balance between food groups. Childcare and educational institutions that already met earlier requirements and provided health‑supporting food can generally meet the new requirements with existing resources, without needing significant additional costs," she said.
At the same time, she acknowledged that food and service prices have risen significantly since 2022. According to Põldsaar, this was taken into account when drafting the regulation, and the requirements were designed so that existing catering practices could continue without unjustified extra costs, avoiding price pressure on caterers.
"For example, more expensive food groups — such as nuts and seeds — were left out of the regulation because they would have increased catering costs. Requirements for fish were also eased. Previously, only fresh fish could be used, but now frozen fish is allowed as well. It is nutritionally valuable, often cheaper, and more accessible," she said.
Health Board will focus first on guidance
A separate question is how the ministry will monitor compliance with the requirements in schools.
Olga Gurjanova, head of the Health Board's education and social services health safety division, said the school year has only just begun and everyday practices related to the new requirements are still developing. Therefore, at this stage, the agency considers cooperation and clarification of requirements to be most important.
"The Health Board supervises compliance with the requirements, but for now the main focus is on advising and cooperating to support schools in developing suitable practices. If necessary, the Health Board will also use appropriate supervisory measures," Gurjanova said.
The school principal has the authority to decide what food is offered in the snack bar, but must follow the requirements.
"The school community can also contribute to shaping the selection. The school board has the right to make proposals to the principal about the snack bar's offerings, based on the recommendations in the guidelines," Gurjanova noted.

Ostend launches second edition of popular ‘Lichtgolf’ light walk
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
05:46:00 UTC
14:46:00 KST

The seaside resort of Ostend (West Flanders) is pulling out all the stops this winter with the second edition of ‘Lichtgolf’ (Light Wave). This time, the light walk route uses the story of two sea-glow algae that end up in Ostend to link seven light installations scattered throughout the city centre. Actors Wim Opbrouck and Sien Eggers provide the voices for the story. “This year, the story fits in better with the installations,” says Rob Jonckheere of the Ostend Tourism Office, following criticism last year.
This year’s story centres on a young sea sparkle called Noxi, who sets foot ashore in Ostend for the first time and discovers the city alongside the 101-year-old sea sparkle Sola. Sea sparkles are tiny, single-celled marine organisms that create a glowing blue-green light in the ocean when disturbed by movement. “It’s a maritime story that truly brings out Ostend's DNA,” explains Rob Jonckheere.
“As a trusted guide Wim Opbrouck guides visitors through a magical interplay of light, sound and memories, whilst Sien Eggers plays the role of Sola,” he adds. During the 4-kilometre route, they guide you past seven light installations scattered throughout the city centre.
According to Jonckheere, more attention is being paid this year to the link between the story and the light installations, following criticism on this point last year. “That’s why we’ve made adjustments to ensure there’s also a connection between the installations and the story being told,” says Jonckheere.
Light installation at the station
Some venues from the first edition are returning, such as the Kursaal and St Peter and St Paul’s Church. New this year is an installation in the historic station concourse, in collaboration with rail company NMBS. The NMBS is celebrating its 100th anniversary this year.
100 deckchairs will be placed in the ticket hall, where visitors can watch a video projected onto the ceiling.
Changes following criticism
Last year, the first edition of Lichtgolf attracted 25,000 visitors – a clear success. However, there were also some points of criticism. As well as a lack of a genuine link between the narrative and the installations, there were technical issues, including problems with the synchronisation of sound and light. “These were resolved on the spot each time, but we are now looking for long-term solutions,” says Jonckheere.
The West Flemish accent of narrators also meant, that at times last year, the story was not clearly understandable for visitors from outside the coastal shire. Sien Eggers says she is speaking “her best Dutch” this year, whilst Wim Opbrouck still uses a touch of West Flemish. “But that West Flemish touch does, of course, add to its charm,” emphasises Jonckheere.
The ‘Lichtgolf’ light walk runs from 27 November to 3 January. A ticket costs 8 euros, but anyone booking before 16 November pays 5 euros. Tickets will soon be available via the Ostend Tourism website.

The EU insists on further reforms for new funding for Ukraine - FT
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
08:44:31 EEST
14:44:31 KST

The EU insists on further reforms for new funding for Ukraine - FT
Kyiv • UNN
Brussels has not approved additional support, demanding reforms to unlock around €34 billion. The conditions include changes to VAT and platform taxation.
Brussels rejected Ukraine’s request for additional financial support this year, demanding that Kyiv implement the promised reforms before receiving further funding from the EU. This is reported by the Financial Times, writes UNN.
Details
The decision was reportedly made against the backdrop of intensified Russian attacks on Ukraine’s civilian infrastructure, while its parliament is attempting to adopt the reforms necessary to unlock support from the EU and other donors.
The discussion about additional funding arose after Kyiv identified an additional $27 billion in military needs this summer and asked the European Commission to help cover the gap by allocating tranches from the EU’s €90 billion loan, agreed at the end of last year, the publication writes.
Only €15.7 billion of this amount has been paid out this year. The sum was divided into two parts of €45 billion each for 2026 and 2027, partly due to delays in meeting the reform requirements, the publication writes.
"Brussels rejected the request for funding for 2027, instead insisting that Kyiv fulfill the conditions that could unlock around €34 billion in EU support this year," the publication says.
In a joint statement on Thursday, Ukraine and the European Commission said they had "identified means to cover Ukraine’s budgetary and defense needs for 2026. We also confirmed the steps necessary to ensure their timely disbursement."
The reforms Ukraine must carry out to receive the funds include abolishing the VAT exemption for small parcels and introducing new tax rules for digital platforms.
"Both measures were approved by parliament, but they include a controversial amendment that weakens the rules governing politically exposed persons (PEPs), which was an EU requirement for strengthening anti-corruption efforts. If signed into law, this amendment could jeopardize Ukraine’s compliance with the conditions attached to EU funding," the publication says.
European Commissioners Valdis Dombrovskis and Marta Kos wrote a letter to the speaker of the Ukrainian parliament, emphasizing that additional financial assistance for 2026 remains available to Ukraine if it implements the reforms that were requested.
"Avoiding any weakening of Ukraine’s policy framework on politically exposed persons" is "critically important," they wrote in the letter seen by the FT.
In an interview with the FT on Thursday, Zelenskyy denied media reports of tense discussions with European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen over the reform conditions.
The European Commission, the publication writes, is also assessing Ukraine’s as-yet-unidentified financial needs for 2027, which officials say could amount to around €70 billion in military and budgetary support. The assessment is expected to be presented to EU leaders at a meeting in mid-October.
Ukraine is negotiating with the IMF over further disbursements under its $8 billion program, the review of which is due to be conducted later this year. These disbursements depend on financing agreements with the EU and Ukraine’s other allies, which will help cover Ukraine’s financial needs in 2027, the publication writes.

Gaza voters want jobs and security as Palestinian elections approach
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
05:39:29 UTC
14:39:29 KST

Gaza voters want jobs and security as Palestinian elections approach
Ahead of first Palestinian national elections in 20 years, people in Gaza hope to rebuild after Israeli destruction.
Deir el-Balah, Gaza Strip – Ahmad Mohsen, 24, sits in a shop selling prepaid internet access cards in Deir el-Balah. Three years ago, before Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza started, he imagined a different future. He had graduated with a degree in nursing and was preparing to complete the procedures required to obtain his professional licence. He dreamed of working in a hospital, pursuing a master’s degree or taking specialised courses.
But the war pushed him onto a different path.
During the first months of the war, Mohsen worked as a volunteer at Al-Aqsa Martyrs Hospital in Deir el-Balah, amid large numbers of wounded and dead, before the lack of pay led him to look for other work.
“I got tired, and I wasn’t being paid for my efforts, so I started looking for another job that would give me at least a small income,” he said.
The upcoming Palestinian legislative elections, scheduled for November 28, would be Mohsen’s first national vote, and the first Palestinian legislative election since 2006. Mohsen has his priorities: he wants candidates to address problems facing his generation, including unemployment, security, housing, education and healthcare.
“The first thing I want is to be able to find a stable job with a decent salary so I can support myself and my family, and the second thing is to have security,” he said.
Mohsen’s concerns are common among Palestinians in Gaza, where unemployment sits at about 80 percent. The enclave’s economy has been destroyed following years of Israeli blockade and its war that has killed more than 74,000 Palestinians.
His family owns land east of Gaza’s Salah al-Din Street, in an area Israel restricts access to, leaving him unable to reach it. He hopes that, in accordance with the October 2025 ceasefire agreement, Israel will soon withdraw from the area and allow for reconstruction to begin in the devastated territory.
For Mohsen, elections are not enough if they do not translate into improvements in people’s lives.
“A candidate should put themselves in the people’s place and speak with the people’s voice, not someone else’s voice. They should speak for us, the young people who have been wronged for 20 years through wars and destruction. There needs to be an end to this,” he said.
Democratic memories
Unlike Mohsen, Ghassan Marwan, 53, carries memories of the 2006 elections, which were won by Hamas.
Marwan previously worked as a goldsmith and established a factory that became his family’s source of income.
When he went to the polls in 2006, he hoped the elections would help improve people’s lives, provide security and jobs, and give his children a more stable future. He remembers voting at a school in Nuseirat for a list headed by the independent politician Mustafa Barghouti, and says the experience was transparent and fair.
“I witnessed a great deal of transparency and integrity. It was like a democratic celebration. But unfortunately, that experience was not repeated over the past 20 years,” Marwan said.
Twenty years later, his life has completely changed. He lost his home and his factory in January 2024, during the war. More than 30 years of work can no longer guarantee the stability he had sought for his family.
“After losing your home and your source of income, what else do you want? All you hope for is reconstruction, calm and security in the country,” he said.
What hurts Marwan most, he said, is seeing his children living among tents instead of in the stable home he had hoped to provide. The war has also brought him back to tasks he never imagined he would face after years of work, such as searching for water and carrying it over long distances.
“After all these years, I am carrying water from far away. Am I going to remain in this situation? I am 53 today. In 10 years, I will be in my 60s, and I will not be able to carry this burden,” he said.
Marwan believes these circumstances have also affected people’s interest in politics.
“Our interest in politics has declined, not because it does not concern us, but because of all the frustration and despair that have accumulated. People have become preoccupied with how to get by and secure their daily bread,” he added.
The prospect of elections amid the widespread destruction and displacement around him nevertheless leaves him torn between hope and scepticism.
“Sometimes I feel that talking about elections is almost a joke, because there are no clear conditions for holding them,” he said.
Recovery is priority
The Palestinian Central Elections Commission is preparing to hold the vote in the occupied West Bank, occupied East Jerusalem and Gaza. It estimates that about 1.24 million Palestinians in Gaza will be eligible to vote.
According to Jamil al-Khalidi, the commission’s regional director in Gaza, the process faces logistical and security challenges because of the scale of destruction in the territory and the mass displacement that has occurred since Israel’s war started. The commission has prepared contingency plans to produce election materials locally in case Israel restricts the entry of supplies into Gaza.
For Gaza-based political analyst and writer Iyad al-Qarra, the war has not eliminated Palestinians’ interest in politics, but has instead changed what they expect politics to deliver.
After nearly three years of displacement, destruction and lost livelihoods, he argued that political demands from Palestinians in Gaza have become directly linked to the ability of future leaders to restore a normal life, rather than simply administer institutions or offer political slogans.
Al-Qarra says that the priority is a leadership capable of representing people and meeting their basic needs, foremost among them rebuilding Gaza, restoring infrastructure and the health and education sectors, and creating conditions that allow people to regain their lives and livelihoods.
“There is a widespread desire for leadership that puts Gaza’s recovery at the top of its priorities, given the heavy price the Strip has paid,” al-Qarra said.

OpenAI says its review into hacks, including on Australian government sites, is costing $500,000 a day
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
05:39:22 UTC
14:39:22 KST

OpenAI says its review in response to the Medicare and Hugging Face agent attacks is costing the company more than US$500,000 per day, as it deploys AI to examine data that would take a human 66m years to read.
The company has warned the review is ongoing, and more organisations may be informed they’ve been targeted in the near future.
On Friday evening, OpenAI revealed agents had hacked into a New South Wales government website in June and accessed historical non-public data on bushfires without authorisation.
It is the sixth government website in Australia to be notified by the AI giant since last month of agent activity on their services, after the prime minister, Anthony Albanese, announced OpenAI’s agents had hacked into Services Australia’s Medicare statistics portal.
The reason for the delay compared to the revelation of the Medicare attack is due to the sheer volume of data OpenAI needs to review.
In a blog post this week the company revealed the large amount of work involved in reviewing its agents’ activity.
OpenAI said it has to review 50 petabytes of data – roughly 50m gigabytes.
“We’re working back through the records month by month, looking for potential unintended activity beyond the cases we’ve already found,” the company said.
“To put that in perspective, if that were all plain English text, it would take one person about 66 million years to read it at 240 words a minute, reading nonstop without ever sleeping or taking a break.”
The company is searching records for where models accessed and changed websites, or took actions involving passwords, application programming interface (API) access or other sensitive credentials.
AI is being used to help sift through the records, and it was costing the company more than half a million US dollars per day to go through. OpenAI said it also plans to increase its computing power as the process is refined.
As of late last month, more than 100 organisations had been notified of having being targeted by OpenAI’s agents, but the company said notifying an organisation does not mean private information was accessed or that their system was compromised.
OpenAI said it expects to find more cases and notify more organisations about events that may have occurred months ago.
Organisations will be informed privately if they need to investigate and address potential security issues, and OpenAI has said it will publicly report findings about agent behaviour and identified weaknesses in safeguards for the broader AI sector.
“We err on the side of notification when our models’ activity exposes a potential security vulnerability, even in cases where it is unclear if the information accessed was intended to be public, so the organization can investigate and take appropriate action,” OpenAI said.
OpenAI discovered the latest NSW government website breach on Tuesday, and informed the state government and the Australian Signals Directorate after a 48-hour review.
The Medicare breach has prompted the Australian government to require departments and agencies to undertake a stocktake of legacy technology to reduce the number of ageing systems within government and reduce the cybersecurity risk they may present in the event of an AI agent attack.
Executives from OpenAI, Anthropic, Microsoft and Google will front a joint parliamentary committee on artificial intelligence in Sydney on Tuesday.

The morning strike on the North Bridge follows days of systematic aerial targeting directed against Kyiv’s strategic river crossings, severely constraining vehicular and rail mobility across the Dnipro River.
On Friday, persistent Russian drone bombardments forced municipal authorities to completely close the South Bridge and impose severe traffic restrictions on both the Paton and Metro bridges, triggering gridlock across the capital.
Russian unmanned systems had repeatedly struck the South Bridge over the preceding 48 hours, damaging roadway sections, bridge piers, and structural barrier systems engineered to protect municipal metro infrastructure.
The recurring hits have placed immense strain on Kyiv’s surviving transport arteries, forcing hundreds of thousands of daily commuters to funnel through limited bypass corridors as municipal authorities work to reinforce critical transit nodes against standoff strikes.
Deadly overnight barrage
The strike on the river crossing occurred hours after a coordinated Russian ballistic missile and drone assault targeted the Ukrainian capital ealry Saturday morning, killing one person and injuring two others.
Mayor Klitschko reported that falling missile debris triggered structural fires across non-residential areas in the Sviatoshynskyi and Obolonskyi districts, while another fire ignited within a commercial garage cooperative in Sviatoshynskyi.
One man was killed in the bombardment, while emergency medical personnel hospitalized one wounded resident and treated a second victim on-site.

North Korea fired a ballistic missile towards the sea on Saturday, South Korea and Japan said, a day after it rejected Seoul’s accusation of its mines wounding soldiers.
The missile was launched from the Wonsan area at about 6.30am towards the East Sea – also known as the Sea of Japan – and flew more than 700km (434 miles), the South Korean military said. Seoul and Washington were analysing the test for details, it added.
Japan’s coast guard, citing the defence ministry, said the object may have been a ballistic missile and appeared to have come down, warning ships to take precautions.
South Korea’s military said it heightened its monitoring of any further missile tests and would share intelligence with the US and Japan. The South Korean presidential office’s national security council convened an emergency meeting on Saturday to assess the situation.
Pyongyang’s Kim Yo-jong, the powerful sister of ruler Kim Jong-un, issued a statement on Friday that dismissed Seoul’s demand for an apology for what it said were North Korean mines that seriously wounded South Korean soldiers in the demilitarised zone – the heavily guarded buffer between the two Koreas.
South Korea’s president, Lee Jae Myung, had urged Pyongyang on Thursday to return to dialogue, despite his military demanding an apology a day earlier. Kim Yo-jong responded by calling Seoul “really despicable” and ridiculing Lee’s latest overture, calling it “the climax of the farce that everyone should watch”.
Kim also warned that Pyongyang was “ready for anything” Seoul might do over the mine blast – remarks followed the next morning by North Korea’s ballistic missile launch.
South Korea said this week that North Korean mines caused the blast that injured three South Korean soldiers on a reconnaissance mission inside the 4km-wide buffer zone that stretches across the Korean peninsula.
The missile test might be an attempt by Pyongyang to draw a response from South Korea to the sister’s statement, said Cheong Seong-chang, vice-president at the Sejong Institute in Seoul, a research centre on North Korean affairs. North Korea might also have tested a new type of missile, he added.
North Korea has launched missile tests on more than 10 occasions so far this year. Some came after North Korea protested against joint military drills between Seoul and Washington.
North Korea has ramped up hostility against the South in recent years, disavowing unification as a national goal and calling South Korea its “primary foe”.

Latvia elects its 15th Saeima today
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
05:24:19 UTC
14:24:19 KST

Latvia’s 15th Saeima election takes place today, with 1,428 candidates from 14 political party lists competing for 100 seats in parliament.
There are five electoral districts in the Saeima election – Riga with 38 seats, Vidzeme with 26, Latgale with 12, Kurzeme with 11 and Zemgale with 13. Voters abroad cast their ballots for candidate lists in the Riga electoral district. As before, voters will be able to cast their ballots at any polling station in Latvia.
Data from the Central Election Commission (CVK) show that an average of 14.3 candidates are competing for each Saeima seat in this election. Competition has decreased compared with the 14th Saeima election, when an average of 18.3 candidates competed for each seat in 2022.
This time, 14 candidate lists with a total of 1,428 candidates have been submitted for the election – five fewer lists and 398 fewer candidates than in the previous parliamentary election.
The Sovereign Power/Young Latvians alliance will appear under number one on the ballot in the 15th Saeima election, while the Progressives drew the final number, 14.
We Are Changing the Rules will run under number two, Harmony Centre under number three, the Union of Greens and Farmers (ZZS) under number four, the National Alliance (NA) under number five, Gobzems’ List under number six and the United List (AS) under number seven.
Latvia First (LPV) will have number eight, New Unity (JV) number nine and the New Conservative Party (JKP) number ten. Latvia’s Development will run under number 11, Rising Sun for Latvia under number 12 and Stability! under number 13.
Seven political forces have fielded the maximum possible number of candidates across all five electoral districts – 125 each. They are the National Alliance, Latvia First, the Progressives, New Unity, the United List, the Union of Greens and Farmers and Sovereign Power/Young Latvians.
The remaining lists have fewer candidates: Harmony Centre has 105, JKP 85, Latvia’s Development 84, We Are Changing the Rules 77, Rising Sun for Latvia 75, Gobzems’ List 73 and Stability! 60.
The largest number of candidates is running in the Riga electoral district, where 527 people are competing for 38 seats. In Vidzeme, 347 candidates are competing for 26 seats; in Zemgale, 207 for 13 seats; in Latgale, 180 for 12 seats; and in Kurzeme, 173 for 11 seats.
At the same time, competition relative to the number of seats is highest in Zemgale and Kurzeme, while Riga has lower competition despite having the largest number of candidates.
LETA’s analysis of CVK data shows that candidates in the 15th Saeima election are older and more highly educated than in the previous election. The average age of candidates is 48.5 years, compared with 46.6 years in the previous election.
A total of 78.7% of candidates have reported having higher education, compared with 74.6% in 2022.
Of all candidates, 34% are women and 66% are men. The highest proportion of female candidates is in the Latgale electoral district, where women account for almost 40% of candidates. Meanwhile, 74.3% of candidates have identified themselves as Latvian and 7.6% as Russian.
Of all 1,434 candidates, 475, or one-third, also ran in the previous Saeima election, while around two-thirds are new candidates or at least did not stand in the 2022 parliamentary election.
A total of 933 in-person polling stations will operate in Latvia for this Saeima election, 15 fewer than in the previous election. At the same time, several municipalities plan to expand the network of mobile polling stations.
This year, voters can also cast their ballots at unconventional locations not previously used for voting, including Riga Airport, Riga Zoo, hospitals and shopping centres. Mobile polling stations will also operate at various locations across Latvia.
More than 83% of all polling stations will be accessible to people with reduced mobility.
Polling stations across Latvia will be open on Saturday from 08:00 to 20:00. Voters can cast their ballots at any polling station in Latvia regardless of their declared place of residence. Latvian citizens living abroad will vote for candidate lists in the Riga electoral district.
Preliminary election results will become available after polling stations close and the votes are counted.
At the polling station, each voter will receive a set of ballot papers and a stamped ballot envelope. Alone in a voting booth or screened-off area, the voter must select one candidate list.
The ballot can be left unchanged, or the voter can mark individual candidates by filling in the oval in the “for” column if they particularly support the candidate’s election, or in the “against” column if they do not support the candidate. Candidates’ names and surnames do not need to be crossed out.
The selected ballot paper must then be placed in the election envelope, which must be sealed and deposited in the ballot box.
Voters who are unable to visit a polling station due to their health, as well as people caring for someone who is ill, can apply to vote at their current location.
The CVK encourages voters to submit a written application in good time, preferably by 12:00 on 3 October. Applications received later will be fulfilled by the polling station commission if it is possible to reach the voter before voting ends.
If a voter previously deposited a ballot for safekeeping but chooses to vote again on election day, only the most recently cast ballot will be counted.
After voting ends, polling station commissions will begin counting the ballots. Votes will be counted manually during open commission meetings, which may be observed by authorised observers and media representatives.
Preliminary results will be published gradually as vote-counting data are received from polling stations.

The Disney generation: What unites Baby Boomers, millennials and Gen Z
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
05:20:48 UTC
14:20:48 KST

Disney stories may be aimed at children, but their lessons can last a lifetime. A study by SWPS University in Poland found that values such as friendship, loyalty, family, courage, resilience and being yourself can stay with us well into adulthood.
Some stories stay with us long after childhood is over. With time, details of the plot, the order of the songs and even the characters’ names may fade. What remains are the emotions and the ideas these stories gave us about the world.
For decades, Disney has been part of childhood for generations of Poles. Research by SWPS University found that 84% of adult Poles regularly watched Disney films and animations as children, while 82% still have a soft spot for them.
But it is not just about nostalgia. Our attachment to these stories is also linked to values that can stay with us well into adulthood.
The values mentioned most often were friendship and loyalty, cited by 46% of respondents. They were followed by the triumph of good over evil (43%), overcoming difficulties (32%) and family (31%).
Money, fame and prestige did not feature among the most frequently mentioned values, nor did the drive to be the best. For adult Poles, Disney is associated above all with relationships, kindness, personal growth, loyalty and responsibility.
In other words, it seems to be less about what we achieve and more about who we share our lives with and the kind of people we want to be.
Friendship before success
In Disney stories, heroes rarely make it on their own. Friends, family and sometimes unexpected allies are there to support them, helping them through their toughest moments.
It is therefore no surprise that friendship and loyalty rank among the values most strongly associated with Disney.
The message remains relevant at any age. Some 89% of Poles say kindness towards others matters, while the same proportion believe in the value of being yourself. Courage is valued by 87%, family by 86%, and 84% agree that love can help us overcome difficulties.
The differences between generations are relatively small.
This could help explain why Disney continues to resonate with people who grew up at different times. The characters may change, but the need for connection, friendship and the sense that we are not alone remains the same.
Each generation sees these stories differently
Sharing the same core values does not mean that every generation sees these stories in quite the same way.
For Baby Boomers (born between 1945 and 1965), the idea that the world should have clear rules seems particularly strong. Some 54% say the triumph of good over evil is one of the values reflected in Disney stories. Their responses also highlight honesty, hope, perseverance and a belief in justice.
Generation X (born between 1965 and 1980) are more likely to associate Disney stories with responsibility, growing up and dealing with adversity. For 74% of respondents in this group, Disney also offered a glimpse of the Western world.
Millennials (born between 1980 and 1995) place more emphasis on authenticity, acceptance and the freedom to live life on their own terms. Characters such as Mulan, Elsa and Vaiana do not simply try to meet other people’s expectations. Their stories are about discovering who they are and finding their place in the world.
“I have the right to be myself”
This shift is most apparent among the youngest participants.
Self-acceptance is mentioned by 12% of the oldest respondents, compared with 29% of Gen Z (born between 1995 and 2010). Independence and diversity show a similar pattern, rising from around 10% among the oldest respondents to 18% among Gen Z.
The difference is even more striking when it comes to pursuing dreams: 14% of Baby Boomers mention this, compared with 38% of Gen Z.
The pattern is reversed when it comes to the belief that good triumphs over evil. This is cited by 54% of the oldest respondents, compared with 24% of the youngest.
This does not mean that younger people have stopped believing in good. Rather, what they expect from a hero appears to have changed.
Simply defeating evil and restoring order is no longer enough. What also matters is whether a hero can choose who they want to be and the path they want to take.
For Gen Z, self-realisation, identity, belonging and acceptance of diversity are particularly important. The key message can be summed up simply: find your own path.
The classics still matter
It might seem that a generation with almost unlimited choice of content would be ready to leave classic Disney behind. Yet Gen Z are not rejecting its core values. Instead, they want to see them combined with a more contemporary approach to storytelling.
Almost half of Gen Z respondents (46%) favour combining Disney classics with modern ideas.
The picture is similar across all respondents. A large majority (87%) want Disney’s classic values to be preserved. Of these, 45% would like them to remain unchanged, while 42% would prefer to see them combined with modern values. Only 4% would like Disney to fully adapt its values to current social trends.
Contemporary stories are also well received, particularly when they focus on overcoming difficulties (75%), working together (74%) and perseverance (72%).
So the choice is not really between classic Disney and modern storytelling. It is about holding on to values that still resonate while telling stories in a way that reflects the world we live in today.
Lessons from childhood stay with us
This may be why Disney has become a shared experience for so many generations. Not because everyone remembers the same films and characters, but because each generation has found something of its own in these stories.
Baby Boomers remember justice, honesty and hope. Generation X associate Disney with responsibility, perseverance and the strength to overcome adversity. Millennials value authenticity and the freedom to live life on their own terms. Gen Z place more emphasis on self-realisation, identity and the courage to find their own path.
Yet beneath these differences, the same values come through: friendship, loyalty, family, courage, kindness and perseverance.
They are not new or particularly fashionable. But perhaps that is why they have lasted.
Disney has never been only about castles, crowns and happy endings. Its stories have also taught generations the value of having people they can trust, the strength to get through difficult times and the freedom to choose their own path.
Growing up does not necessarily mean leaving these stories behind. We may forget some of the details, but the lessons can stay with us long after childhood is over.
