White House filing claims president has authority to bar news outlets
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
04:25:00 UTC
13:25:00 KST

White House filing claims president has authority to bar news outlets
Erik Wemple
In a court filing on Oct 2, the White House again argued that its move in September to bar CNN, MS NOW and Politico from its grounds was squarely within the bounds of presidential authority and asked a federal judge to deny a motion from the media outlets for a court order extending their access.
Throughout US history, the government’s filing contended, presidents “have long decided which journalists should receive privileged access, which has varied substantially from administration to administration”.
The court battle began after US President Donald Trump announced on Sept 18 that he would bar CNN, MS NOW and Politico from entering the White House grounds.
The media organisations quickly sued to regain their access and a federal court issued a two-week order requiring the White House to restore their press passes. The order expires on Oct 8 and this week, the three news outlets asked the court for a longer reprieve.
The government’s latest filing aligns with the Trump administration’s legal arguments in other access battles with the media.
The filing said “the mere denial of special access is not an adverse action that would objectively chill” reporting on the White House.
The media outlets have said the ban violated their First Amendment rights because Trump made it clear that he had instituted it because he objected to their reporting.
The White House’s filing on Oct 2 said the administration would have “taken the same action anyway”, without regard to the outlets’ criticism of Trump.
The White House claims that the barred outlets failed to meet professional standards and that they have threatened national security or spread falsehoods with their reporting – claims vigorously opposed by the companies.
Asked this week whether it would reimpose its ban if the court declined to continue blocking it, the White House responded with a statement praising Trump’s accessibility.
Even after the court restored the journalists’ access to the White House, Trump twice excluded CNN from fulfilling its role in the TV pool that covers him. It is one of five networks that rotate the work and share the costs of following the President from event to event.
When CNN has been excluded, the other networks have banded together in a show of support and declined to substitute for the network, leaving the President with no pool coverage on those occasions.
The government’s filing on Oct 2 said the “decision to deny special, privileged access to the press pool or to the White House complex would not deter a reasonable reporter”.
It also noted that the media outlets had not contested their access revocation directly to the White House, which imposed a deadline of Sept 25 for doing so.
As a result, the White House’s decision became “final”, according to the government filing, though the court’s temporary order blocked it from taking effect.
The media outlets have argued that the White House imposed the ban against them and only later “got to work backfilling contrived justifications for it”.
Judge Timothy Kelly of the US District Court in Washington, who issued the temporary order, has indicated that he will rule “expeditiously” on the media outlets’ request. NYTIMES
- This article originally appeared in The New York Times.

UK man charged over Farage terror plot
The man accused of murdering former UK Conservative minister Ann Widdecombe has also been charged with preparing a terrorist attack on Reform UK leader Nigel Farage.
Joshua Kerry, 28, of Rotherham, South Yorkshire was charged on Friday under the Terrorism Act 2006 and will appear in court on Wednesday, police said. The new charge relates to activities that allegedly took place May 31 to July 8.
“We have been running a hugely intensive and complex investigation for some time. The charge announced today is a result of the tireless work of investigators across the Counter Terrorism Policing network,” Vicki Evans, the senior national coordinator for counter terrorism policing, said.
“My profound sympathies are with Nigel Farage and his family. Let no one make any mistake: an attack on anyone in politics is an attack on us all,” Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood wrote on X. She added that the case “raises serious questions about the security of those in public life.”
Kerry was arrested shortly after Widdecombe’s body was found on July 9 at her rural home in southwest England. Prosecutors allege that the suspect struck the 78-year-old politician 21 times with a hammer in an attack that was caught on camera. No motive has yet been made public.
A Conservative MP for more than two decades, Widdecombe served as employment minister and later as prisons minister. From 2019 to 2020, she was a member of the European Parliament for the Brexit Party, which Farage co-founded.
She was known for her socially conservative views, opposing same-sex marriage and abortion. In 2019, a theater show featuring Widdecombe was canceled after critics accused her of endorsing conversion therapy, the controversial practice of attempting to change a person’s sexual orientation or gender identity. Widdecombe argued that her comments were misconstrued.
Farage, one of the leading campaigners for Leave during the 2016 Brexit referendum, has long faced death threats and has repeatedly been targeted during public appearances.
He was doused with milkshakes while campaigning in 2019 and again in 2024, and has also had eggs and other objects thrown at him.
In April 2025, a suspected incendiary device was pushed through the letterbox of his home and burned itself out. Counter-terrorism police reopened the investigation this year after identifying a previously missed line of inquiry. No one has been charged over the incident.
Reform UK said Farage’s publicly funded security was cut by 75% last year, forcing the party and private donors to fund additional protection. Parliamentary authorities have declined to confirm the figure, citing security concerns.

Recycling as an educational mission and business in Bulgaria
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
04:22:34 UTC
13:22:34 KST

Author
Diana Tsankova
Saturday 3 October 2026 06:05
Saturday, 3 October 2026, 06:05
PHOTO vavakada.com
Font size
Two
young people realized early on their mission to give a second chance
- they transform waste into value, giving it a new meaning in the
home and in the urban environment. Daniela Kostova
and Vladislav Kostov created a start-up for the production of
furniture and interior elements from recycled plastic in their
hometown of Silistra. Even as children, the brother and sister were
interested in the topic of environmental protection and want to make
the planet a cleaner and greener place through a personal
contribution.
After
high school, Vladislav realized that the waste problem was the path
to follow and began educating himself through various online sources.
When Daniela returned from Germany with a degree in architecture, she
proposed starting a business together. The two focused on utilizing
plastic bottle caps, building their own machinery, including a press,
to achieve this. He handled the technical aspects, while she managed
design and communications.
PHOTO Facebook / Vavakada RE
"We produce panels from the recycled plastic," Daniela Kostova says. "From these we create various interior elements, such as small tables, chairs, lighting fixtures, or really anything we can think of, as the possibilities for use are endless. We’ve received some fascinating inquiries from clients, including a request to design bench backrests - a project we realized in collaboration with street artist Aleksi. The material’s durability and recyclability are of utmost importance. When elements made from recycled plastic are introduced into public spaces, people will say: 'So it does get recycled after all!' There is a widespread myth that all waste ends up in the same truck and no one knows what happens to it."
PHOTO vavakada.com
The business model is built entirely on circular economy principles. "We generate zero waste," Daniela says. By utilizing waste donated by a local depot that is nearing capacity, and employing innovative 3D printing technology, the entrepreneurs create products that are entirely eco-friendly.
PHOTO vavakada.com
In
addition to production, Daniela and Vladislav devote time to
educational activities. For example, few people know that there are
many different types of plastics and each of them must be disposed of
separately.
"Educating
the people
is crucial because they
have the desire to recycle but aren't aware of all the nuances,"
Daniela Kostova says.
"They assume that simply tossing an item into a recycling bin
ensures it gets recycled, but the reality is far more complex. That
is why education is so important. It
is something we have prioritized since the workshop was first
established. We regularly visit schools and universities to give
presentations on recycling, as our goal isn't merely to create
products from recycled plastic, but to change
people's way
of thinking."
PHOTO vavakada.com
The
young entrepreneurs will continue to demonstrate that recycled
plastic is a new "noble“ material and to present their
production process as a form of modern craftsmanship. They believe
that change begins with how we perceive the resources around us,
especially when
the
material can be transformed into a bold, colorful, and valuable
element of contemporary interior design. Yet, their cause goes beyond
achievements, evolving into a global dream: to 
find themselves out of work one day because the problem they are currently
addressing has been solved. They hope to live to see the day when
humanity has fully overcome the issue and plastic pollution has
become a thing of the past.

Diana Tsankova (Based on an interview by Alexandra Ilieva from BNR’s
Radio Sofia)

Europe’s Approach to Climate Is Entering a New Era
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
04:08:38 UTC
13:08:38 KST

For decades, the European Union has led the world in implementing policies designed to cut emissions, creating the world’s most important price on carbon and crafting the rules of the road for a wide range of regulatory efforts. Now, as the costs of climate change become increasingly difficult to ignore, the bloc is increasingly focusing on adaptation.
In a Sept. 8 interview, Teresa Ribera, who oversees climate policy in the EU as executive vice-president of the European Commission, told me that the growing costs of the effects of climate change mean that policymakers need to consider adaptation as a key focus of economic policy.
“There is no public budget that can support all of this. There is no private insurance that can cope with all these costs,” she said when we met at the EU Delegation office in New York. “We need to invest to reduce these impacts and this cost.”
The EU’s turn to adaptation is an important marker of this climate moment. Most obviously, it signals the harsh reality that global emission reductions efforts have failed to forestall the effects of climate change. It's also a wake-up call. A focus on adaptation from policymakers in Europe—and eventually elsewhere—should help protect the economy from the growing risks of climate change. But it will also force businesses and governments to confront costs they have largely been able to defer. This is good for long-term economic wellbeing, but it may come as an immediate shock for the unprepared.
At the heart of the EU’s approach is a new adaptation framework due for release later this month. At first glance, it can sound like just another white paper identifying approaches to dealing with climate risk. It calls for a common approach for member states to measure climate risk, principles to ensure that infrastructure is built with future climate conditions in mind, and efforts to identify the most vulnerable places in Europe.
Yet, looking at what EU authorities have released in advance, it is worth underlining that this will not be just a white paper. The package is expected to include proposed legislation that, among other things, could require EU member states to develop climate resilience plans as a prerequisite to funding. And, Ribera says, the framework may eventually serve as the basis for more prescriptive future regulation. “There may be certain regulations that could be increasingly tougher,” she told me.
While the EU’s adaptation work has been long coming, this past summer provided additional public attention and pressure. Record heat swept much of the continent, leading to tens of thousands of excess deaths. Wildfires encroached on major European cities, a once unthinkable threat. Meanwhile, drought conditions made fires harder to fight. It was “quite a shocking experience,” says Ribera.
The aggregate numbers are just as shocking. Between 2021 and 2024, climate-related extreme events led to more than €200 billion in economic losses in the EU, according to figures from the European Environment Agency. Much of those losses were uninsured, leaving the losses to be absorbed by governments, businesses, or households. Without intervention, those numbers will only grow as extreme events worsen. Ribera says the EU is working with insurers to expand coverage where it makes sense while also using public and private financing to cover risks that cannot be covered by insurance alone.
In many circles, the first mention of climate policy in the EU tends to be a discussion about backtracking. It’s a convenient excuse for those who want to train their attention elsewhere. Earlier this year, the EU softened its corporate sustainability disclosure rules and adjusted its carbon pricing framework. This week, the bloc said it was considering delaying implementation of elements of the rules meant to curb methane emissions.
Ribera insists that this misunderstands the European perspective. The long-term goals remain the same. Indeed, earlier this year the EU created a legally binding 2040 emissions reduction target. “There is this strong temptation from some to say, ‘Okay, let’s give up,’ or ‘Let’s lower the bar,’” she told me. But, she argued, Europe instead needs to proceed in a “humble and flexible manner” while “keeping the sense of direction, the commitments, [and] the principles.”
Perhaps more importantly, the bloc is incorporating climate into the core of its economic planning. Decisions about industrial policy, infrastructure, public spending, and competition increasingly have to account not only for emissions but climate risk. Sustainability is moving into “the real heart of the economy,” Ribera told me.
Anyone who trains their eyes too closely on one policy adjustment risks missing the forest for the trees.

3-MIN READ3-MIN

Phoebe Zhangin Shenzhen
For the first time in a decade, China has returned to the top 100 out of 145 economies in an annual global report assessing gender equality.
China closed 69.9 per cent of its gender gap in 2025, rising to 96th place from 103rd the previous year and increasing 1.3 percentage points, according to the 2026 Global Gender Gap Report published by the World Economic Forum (WEF), an international non-profit organisation based in Switzerland.
It marks the first time China has been ranked in the top 100 since 2016, when it placed 99th.
This year, China ranked higher than a few major economies in the region, including South Korea (101), Japan (117) and India (131).

US judge dismisses DOJ lawsuit that used abortion clinic access law against protesters
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
03:58:14 UTC
12:58:14 KST

US judge dismisses DOJ lawsuit that used abortion clinic access law against protesters
WASHINGTON, Oct 2 - A US judge dismissed a lawsuit against pro-Palestinian organizations and protesters that President Donald Trump's administration brought last year under a law traditionally used against people blocking access to abortion clinics.
US District Judge Katharine Hayden in New Jersey said the government's complaint did not adequately plead violations of the statute. She dismissed the claims without prejudice, saying the government can file an amended complaint within 30 days.
The case was brought under the Freedom of Access to Clinic Entrances Act, or FACE Act, a 1994 law that prohibits the use of force and physical obstruction to interfere with people at reproductive health centers or houses of worship.
In September 2025, the Justice Department sued pro-Palestinian activists that it accused of intimidating attendees during a November 2024 protest against an event at a synagogue in New Jersey.
The event was billed by organizers as a spiritual service and real estate fair. It promoted the sale of property in Israeli settlements in the Israeli-occupied West Bank.
The lawsuit said the protest escalated into violence, alleging the demonstrators physically assaulted some worshippers and chanted and used vuvuzelas - plastic trumpets sometimes used by soccer fans - to disrupt the event.
The Justice Department has brought several cases against protesters who have obstructed abortion clinics, but the case appeared to be the first time the law was used to allege interference with religious worship, according to Harmeet Dhillon, the head of the Justice Department's Civil Rights Division.
The Justice Department under Trump has curtailed the use of the FACE Act in abortion-related cases, alleging that past criminal prosecutions represented an improper politicized use of law enforcement. Dhillon said those restrictions do not apply to cases related to houses of worship. Last year, Trump pardoned several people prosecuted under the law.
Trump has attempted to deport foreign pro-Palestinian protesters, threatened funding freezes for universities where protests were held, expanded social media screening of immigrants and imposed sanctions on some of Israel's critics.
His administration says pro-Palestinian protesters are antisemitic and support extremists. Demonstrators say their criticism of Israeli attacks on Gaza and of Israel's occupation of Palestinian territories does not amount to antisemitism, and their advocacy for Palestinian rights should not be equated with supporting extremism. REUTERS

Ukraine loses 2 mln tonnes of metallurgical output by end-September — TASS calculations
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
03:57:30 UTC
12:57:30 KST

MOSCOW, October 3. /TASS/. Ukraine lost 1.96 million tonnes of metallurgical output between June and the end of September 2026 due to explosions and fires at steel plants, according to TASS calculations.
Compared to June, the peak production month in 2026, Ukraine’s losses included 690,800 tonnes of steel, 670,600 tonnes of pig iron, and 599,800 tonnes of rolled metal.
Based on European market prices, these losses are valued at approximately $580.2 million per month for steel, $274.9 million for pig iron, and $449.9 million for rolled products. Metallurgical products, shipped primarily to Europe, were Ukraine's second-largest source of foreign currency export revenue in the first half of 2026.
Currently, the production of steel, pig iron, and rolled metal has ground to a complete halt following a series of explosions at Ukraine's largest metallurgical facilities. On September 25, ArcelorMittal announced it would be unable to resume operations at ArcelorMittal Kryvoy Rog, Ukraine's largest steel plant, following explosions on the nights of September 12 and September 21. It was the country's last major steel plant that had not previously shut down. On September 22, the Interpipe Steel pipe-rolling plant announced a halt in operations, following reported shutdowns at Zaporozhstal and Kametstal on September 18. Another major enterprise, the Dnepr Metallurgical Plant, had effectively ceased operations earlier due to financial difficulties (the plant suspended operations in January 2022, and insolvency proceedings began in 2026) explosions also hit the facility in early September.

Two Iranians charged over alleged plot targeting Jewish community in UK
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
03:56:10 UTC

Two Iranians charged over alleged plot targeting Jewish community in UK
Two Iranian men are accused of preparing to commit attack in Manchester on or before Yom Kippur.
Two Iranian nationals charged with planning an attack against the Jewish community in northern England have appeared in a London court.
The UK Crown Prosecution Service (CPS) said on Friday that Rahman Salehi, 34, and Salam Ahmadyan, 36, were charged with “preparing to commit or assisting another to commit an act of terrorism” in Manchester “on or before” Yom Kippur, the Jewish Day of Atonement, which began at sundown on September 20.
After appearing in Westminster Magistrates’ Court on Saturday, the men who did not enter a plea were remanded into custody. Their next hearing is set at London’s Old Bailey court for October 23.
“It is alleged that the two men were in contact with an overseas third-party who may be in Iran in relation to the plot,” police said in a separate statement on Friday.
Details of the alleged plot have not been released, but police have confirmed its “disruption”.
Counterterrorism police said Salehi and Ahmadyan, both arrested in Manchester on September 20, allegedly tried to acquire components and equipment to make an improvised explosive device and conducted reconnaissance on potential targets for attack.
Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood said Salehi and Ahmadyan arrived in the UK on a small boat from Europe several years ago. One of the men had been granted asylum and the other had a live asylum claim, the Home Office said.
“It is no secret that this country faces a range of serious threats from the Iranian regime,” she said in a statement.
“They target our Jewish communities and try to silence their critics overseas, often through proxies and criminal networks to hide their involvement,” she added.
Iran has denied similar accusations.
The charges come a year after two people were killed in a knife and gun attack by a British citizen of Syrian descent at the Heaton Park Hebrew Congregation Synagogue in northern Manchester on October 2, 2025.
Heightened tensions
“I’m aware that the news of this alleged plot coming during the High Holy day period has caused a great deal of concern to the Jewish community, as well as with the wider public,” Deputy Assistant Commissioner Vicki Evans, senior national coordinator for counterterrorism policing, said on Friday.
“It also coincides with the anniversary of the devastating terrorist attack last year at Heaton Park synagogue and comes in a wider context of increasing antisemitic incidents across the UK.”
Detectives said there was no connection between Friday’s charges and the suspected plot involving the RAF Fairford air base, over which a dual UK-Iranian national was arrested on Thursday, according to the Reuters news agency.
Britain said Tehran had been involved in an alleged plot earlier this week targeting an airbase used by the US to launch attacks against Iran.
Iran denied any involvement in the RAF Fairford plot and said speculation would “fuel Iranophobia propaganda”.

Co-pilot on Flydubai flight was banned from flying by Oman
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
03:52:00 UTC
12:52:00 KST

Flydubai co-pilot attempted 'terrorist attack,' UAE says
Published October 3, 2026last updated October 3, 2026
The co-pilot accused of stabbing his captain during Flydubai Flight 1073 was wielding a crash ax and attempted to carry out a "terrorist attack," UAE investigators said Saturday, according to Emirati state news agency WAM.
A crash ax is typically stored in the plane's cockpit for use in case of an emergency.
According to a Reuters media report based on unnamed sources familiar with the matter, the suspect is an Omani national.
The Wall Street Journal reported on Friday that the co-pilot had been barred from flying by Oman over concerns that he had adopted radical ideological views.
What happened on the Flydubai flight?
The attack that took place on a flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv has raised many questions about how the incident unfolded as well as about background checks in aviation hiring.
There were 182 people on board, including four pilots.
After the co-pilot stabbed the captain in an apparent attempt to crash the plane, two other pilots in the cabin took control and landed the aircraft safely in Tabuk, Saudi Arabia.
Anwar Gargash, an Emirati presidential adviser, referred to the Flydubai incident on X, saying the latest "terrorist operation" showed the Mideast region's "fight against extremism continues."
Flydubai co-pilot was barred from flying by Oman over security concerns
The Wall Street Journal report said the co-pilot was hired by Flydubai despite the ban by Oman, allowing him to fly the jet on a sensitive route connecting the UAE and Israel.
Israel and the UAE, which includes Dubai, signed the Abraham Accords normalizing relations in 2020.
The newspaper said it could not be determined whether Oman shared concerns about the pilot's radicalization with other countries or airlines.
The nature of his radicalization was also not clear.
US broadcaster CNN cited two sources saying the co-pilot was removed from a job at Oman's national airline last year over concerns about extremist views.
Saudi broadcaster Al Arabiya, also citing an informed source, reported that Omani authorities determined that the co-pilot held extremist views.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said Thursday in a video statement that they know the co-pilot "underwent Islamist radical indoctrination" and intended to crash the jet.
Netanyahu also said they were also looking into whether the co-pilot had acted under anyone's direction, warning that whoever was involved would pay a "heavy price."
The investigation is ongoing. A Gulf diplomat, in comments to AP, said authorities were attempting to find out whether the Omani co-pilot was a "lone wolf or has any connection with any extremist groups."

12:45:39 KST

BEIJING, Oct. 3 (Xinhua) -- China has launched an anti-dumping investigation into imports of p-Nitrotoluene from the European Union (EU), the Ministry of Commerce said Saturday.
The investigation was initiated following an application from the domestic industry, a spokesperson for the ministry said in response to a media query.
Preliminary evidence submitted by the applicants showed that the volume of p-Nitrotoluene imports from the EU remained at a high level from 2022 to 2025, while prices fell by nearly 60 percent cumulatively over the period. The dumped imports from the EU caused damage to the production and operations of China's domestic industry, the spokesperson noted.
The spokesperson said the application met the requirements for initiating an anti-dumping investigation under Chinese law and World Trade Organization rules, adding that China will conduct the investigation in accordance with relevant laws and regulations and fully protect the rights of all interested parties.
P-Nitrotoluene, also known as 4-Nitrotoluene, is mainly used to produce chemicals that are widely applied in dyes, pigments, pesticides and pharmaceuticals, according to the ministry. ■

‘I was not going to let others die’: Flydubai pilot recounts cockpit attack
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
03:32:37 UTC
12:32:37 KST

Zehra Nur Çelik
03 October 2026•Update: 03 October 2026
The Indian pilot of a Flydubai flight who was stabbed by his co-pilot spoke publicly for the first time on Friday about the attack, saying he was determined not to let the passengers and crew die as the aircraft rapidly lost altitude.
Capt. Smit Machchhar said he was lying injured on the floor and still being attacked when he realized the plane was descending and made a final effort to open the cockpit door.
“When I fell, I could tell the plane was going down. I told myself to give it one last push to open the door from inside,” Machchhar said during a video call with Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi.
“I was still getting injured. But I managed to open the door and the others came in, and they also played a big role,” he said.
“I was of course trying to protect myself but at the same time I knew I was not going to let others die,” he added.
Machchhar said his 17 years of flying experience, including 11 as a captain, helped him understand what was happening to the aircraft.
“I can tell what is happening to the plane even with my eyes closed,” he said.
Flydubai flight FZ1073 was traveling from Dubai to Tel Aviv with 174 passengers early Wednesday when an altercation broke out in the cockpit.
The aircraft plunged more than 17,000 feet (5,200 meters) two-and-a-half hours into the flight before diverting to Prince Sultan bin Abdulaziz International Airport in Tabuk, Saudi Arabia.
Flydubai said an “altercation occurred in the flight deck” and that crew members secured the aircraft before it landed safely.
The captain and first officer were taken to hospital with injuries, while all passengers and crew members were reported safe.
Modi praised Machchhar’s “courage, patience and quick decision-making,” saying his actions saved many lives.

Stubb: Every Russian Threat Should Bring More Support for Ukraine
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
03:02:08 UTC
12:02:08 KST

Finnish President Alexander Stubb said Friday that Russia’s escalating hybrid campaign against Europe should trigger the opposite of what Moscow seeks – more support for Ukraine – as the leaders of Finland, Moldova and Ukraine delivered stark warnings in Helsinki about the long-term threat posed by Russia.
“The more you intimidate, the more you threaten, the more we’re going to end up supporting Ukraine,” Stubb told the fifth annual Helsinki Security Forum.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“I do think that’s the right approach.”
Speaking alongside Moldovan President Maia Sandu, with President Volodymyr Zelensky joining the forum remotely, Stubb argued that Europe must stop viewing cyberattacks, sabotage and information operations as isolated incidents.
“What we have to understand is that these are not one-off attempts from the Russian side, but they are actually a campaign,” Stubb said.
“The aim of that campaign is to destabilize us mentally and otherwise, to make sure that we don’t support Ukraine.”
The Helsinki Security Forum, held Oct. 2–4 under the theme “Layers of Security,” brings together European policymakers and security experts against the backdrop of Russia’s continuing war against Ukraine and growing concern over hybrid operations elsewhere in Europe.
Stubb described the dividing line between war and peace in Europe as increasingly blurred.
Ukraine Records Nearly 227,000 Russian War Crimes Since Full-Scale Invasion
“The warfare that Russia is conducting in Ukraine is kinetic, traditional warfare, but what it’s conducting in Europe is hybrid,” he said.
That campaign, Stubb said, includes daily cyberattacks, sabotage attempts and information warfare.
He pointed to recent incidents in Germany and Estonia, where authorities have attributed suspected sabotage operations to Russia or Russian-linked actors.
Stubb said governments cannot protect themselves completely against such attacks, particularly because Moscow frequently relies on proxies.
The answer, he argued, is attribution, resilience and consequences.
Some responses can be public, while others should be delivered privately through diplomatic channels, he said.
But the broader message to Moscow should remain unmistakable: increased pressure against Europe will translate into stronger backing for Kyiv.
Stubb: Putin’s war achieved the opposite of its objectives
Looking beyond the immediate conflict, Stubb argued that Russia’s full-scale invasion has already produced strategic consequences directly opposed to Moscow’s original goals.
“The aim of [Russian President Vladimir] Putin and Russia? The aim was to deny the independence of Ukraine and make it Russian. Well, it became European,” Stubb said.
“The aim was to prevent NATO from enlarging. Well, Finland and Sweden would have never joined had the full-blown attack not taken place.”
Finland joined NATO in 2023 and Sweden followed in 2024 after both countries abandoned decades of military non-alignment following Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
Stubb also pointed to rapidly rising European defense expenditure.
“The aim was to reduce the defense budgets of European states. And look what’s happened. We’re moving towards 5%,” he said.
The cumulative result, according to Stubb, will be a fundamentally altered European security balance after the war.
“I think the power balance in Europe will be very different after the war is over to what it is now,” he said.
Central to that new balance will be Ukraine.
“And on top of that, we have the most modern and effective and experienced army in Ukraine,” Stubb said.
“So that means that the whole security scene of Europe will have changed, probably in a way in which Russia did not want.”
Stubb cautioned, however, against assuming that Russia will emerge from the war militarily weakened or incapable of presenting another threat.
“The Russian military was not capable of modern warfare when this war began, but now they are,” he said.
“They are also going to be much stronger when they regroup after the war.”
Europe will therefore have to preserve a favorable balance of power while deciding what form any eventual relationship with Moscow might take.
Stubb said some future dialogue with Russia would ultimately be necessary, particularly for Finland, which shares a 1,340-kilometer border with its eastern neighbor.
But he stressed that any future engagement with Russia would depend on what kind of Russia emerges after the war, with trust shattered by Moscow’s invasion of Ukraine.
Zelensky: Putin wants all of Ukraine
Zelensky warned that Putin’s ambitions go far beyond Donbas, saying Moscow still seeks control over all of Ukraine and wants to restore the influence once wielded by the Soviet Union.
“His goal is not the east of Ukraine. His goal is not Donbas. His goal is the occupation of our entire country,” Zelensky said.
He warned that such ambitions also threaten the Baltic states and other countries bordering Russia, and rejected attempts to seek a neutral middle ground between Moscow and Kyiv.
“The role of the experts, with all due respect, is not to be in the middle between good and evil, between the occupier and the victim,” Zelensky said.
“Nobody needs mediation between life and death, between those who want to live in democracy and autocracy.”

Interview: Global humanitarian body sees China as key partner in building resilient African communities, says official
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
10:53:16 CST
11:53:16 KST

Pierre Kremer, deputy regional director for Africa at the International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies (IFRC), speaks at the opening ceremony of the Seminar on Resilient Community Building for Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies under the China-Africa Cooperation Framework in Beijing, capital of China, Sept. 10, 2026. (Xinhua/Zhang Yuwei)
BEIJING, Oct. 3 (Xinhua) -- The International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies (IFRC) sees China as an important partner in building durable solutions and community resilience in Africa, drawing on China's experience in poverty alleviation and community development, a humanitarian official said.
Pierre Kremer, deputy regional director for Africa at IFRC, made the remarks in a recent interview with Xinhua on the sidelines of the Seminar on Resilient Community Building for Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies under the China-Africa Cooperation Framework in Beijing.
Twenty-six representatives from national Red Cross and Red Crescent societies from 19 African countries, along with representatives of the IFRC, attended lectures, field visits and interactive discussions during the two-week seminar, exchanging experience and learning about China's practices in disaster risk reduction, community resilience and sustainable development.
Hosted by the Training Center of the Red Cross Society of China and supported by the IFRC, the seminar provides a valuable platform for Chinese and African national Red Cross and Red Crescent societies to exchange expertise, share best practices and strengthen cooperation, said Kremer.
Reviewing past cooperation between African national Red Cross and Red Crescent societies and Chinese partners, Kremer highlighted the Accelerating Malaria Elimination in The Gambia project as an effective example of partnership.
The project was launched to accelerate malaria elimination in The Gambia by strengthening community-based prevention, early care-seeking and case management, alongside the procurement and distribution of seasonal malaria chemoprevention medicines for children under five.
Kremer, who worked in China in 2021, said he had seen firsthand how community health systems could reach people effectively at the grassroots level. "I believe this experience could be valuable in building effective, people-centered and integrated community health workforces and systems in Africa."
The malaria project also reflects a broader area of convergence between China's development cooperation in Africa and the IFRC's approach to humanitarian action: building local capacity and supporting sustainable development.
The IFRC's Africa Zero Hunger initiative, for example, calls for a shift from short-term assistance toward longer-term resilience, with a focus on durable, locally led solutions that can be sustained and scaled up, he said.
China's poverty alleviation efforts have offered another source of inspiration for this approach. "China's experience in building community resilience is even more valuable than funding," Kremer said, highlighting its know-how, multi-level leadership and consistent implementation.
Looking ahead, the IFRC could provide a multilateral platform to help scale up effective China-Africa partnership programmes while strengthening and streamlining capacity-building efforts, particularly those aimed at developing the next generation of young leaders, he said.
Youth leadership and entrepreneurship are areas where Kremer sees particular potential for cooperation. According to him, the IFRC's Africa region has around 4 million volunteers, 80 to 90 percent of whom are young people. Many of them work on the front lines of emergencies and take significant risks to serve their communities.
"We want to give back by creating opportunities for them," Kremer said. "There is strong potential for cooperation with China in this area. We see an opportunity to combine the IFRC's network with China's expertise to support youth leadership and entrepreneurship in Africa."
Digital transformation and renewable energy are other potential areas for cooperation, Kremer underlined.
The IFRC is seeking to accelerate the digital transformation of its 16,000 branches across Africa, but only about 23 percent are currently connected. The goal is to connect all branches, particularly those in remote or conflict-affected areas, to strengthen emergency response and enable them to develop their own community information systems.
"We want them to be fully self-reliant, autonomous and able to make decisions for themselves," Kremer said.
Solar panels and other equipment are part of the solution, and so is building the capacity of volunteers to collect and use data from their own communities, said Kremer, noting that China could be a valuable partner in this effort, given its experience in community-level digital transformation and its globally competitive renewable energy technologies.
"In the future, we look forward to further cooperation with Chinese partners through IFRC as a multilateral platform to scale up sustainable China-Africa cooperation projects to more countries," Kremer said. ■
The Seminar on Resilient Community Building for Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies under the China-Africa Cooperation Framework is held in Beijing, capital of China, Sept. 10, 2026. (Xinhua/Zhang Yuwei)

DR Congo says Ebola outbreak eases in areas despite death toll topping 4,000
China
Unknown Publisher

11:53:07 KST

KINSHASA, Oct. 3 (Xinhua) -- Health authorities in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) said Friday that the Ebola outbreak has eased in some areas with no new cases reported in more health zones for weeks despite that the total death toll has surpassed 4,000.
"We are no longer talking about outbreaks at the provincial level, but outbreaks concentrated in individual health zones," Health Minister Roger Kamba told a press briefing in Kinshasa.
Data released Friday showed that the outbreak has claimed 4,018 lives among 8,300 confirmed cases across seven provinces, with an overall case fatality rate of 48.4 percent. A total of 2,162 patients have recovered.
Of the 63 health zones affected across seven provinces since the outbreak began, 12 have reported no new cases for 42 days, Kamba said.
"The situation remains highly variable, but we can see that the number of health zones reporting cases has decreased," he said.
Despite signs of localized improvement in the DRC's Ebola outbreak situation, international medical charity Medecins Sans Frontieres warned Thursday that the actual toll was likely higher than officially reported due to gaps in disease surveillance and case detection.
The Ebola outbreak declared in May has become the largest and deadliest ever recorded in the DRC and the second largest Ebola outbreak worldwide, after the 2014-2016 one in West Africa. ■

The common viral infections that are responsible for one in eight cancers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
02:52:21 UTC
11:52:21 KST

in brief
- A new global analysis has revealed that 12 per cent of cancer is caused by pathogenic infection.
- Just four viruses and one bacteria are responsible, opening new pathways for cancer prevention.
Roughly one in every eight cancer cases diagnosed worldwide is triggered by common viral and bacterial infections, rather than inherited genetics or lifestyle factors.
A major global analysis by the World Health Organization body, the International Agency for Research on Cancer, has found that an estimated 2.3 million new cancer cases in 2024 were directly caused by 12 carcinogenic pathogens.
While developing cancer is often viewed as unpredictable, the findings highlight the fact that millions of cases worldwide come from transmissible infections — which are largely preventable.
In an analysis for The Conversation, Dr John La Marca and Dr Sarah Diepstraten, senior research officers at Australia's Walter and Eliza Hall Institute, noted that the vast majority of these cancer diagnoses are driven by just a handful of pathogens.
"Four viruses and one bacteria were responsible for 12% of the world's cancer cases in 2024," they wrote.
News that makes sense
Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
Kate Broun, deputy chair of Cancer Council’s Cancer Screening and Immunisation Committee, told SBS News that vaccinations and screenings can reduce the risk of cancers.
How does an infection cause cancer?
Cancer is a group of diseases in which abnormal cells grow out of control instead of dying, and is one of the leading causes of death worldwide.
The Australian Institute of Health and Welfare estimates that around 170,000 new cases of cancer are diagnosed each year in Australia. Roughly 40 per cent of the population will receive a cancer diagnosis by the age of 85.
The disease is caused when normal cell functions are disrupted, something that a virus or a bacterium can trigger.
Certain viruses, like human papillomavirus (HPV), insert their own genetic material directly into human DNA, hijacking cells and deactivating tumour-suppressing proteins. This allows the cells to divide uncontrollably.
"HPV can cause several cancers and other diseases in people of all genders," Broun said. "It is responsible for cases of cervical cancer, anal cancer, vaginal cancer, vulvar cancer, and penile cancer."
Other pathogens, like Helicobacter pylori in the stomach or hepatitis B and C in the liver, operate through persistent, chronic inflammation.
Decades of continuous tissue damage, cell death, and forced regeneration significantly increase the probability of copying errors, which eventually turn healthy cells malignant.
Others still, like HIV, weaken the immune system's natural surveillance mechanisms, which gives other, dormant viruses in the body the chance to activate and trigger tumours.
Which viruses cause cancer?
The report, published in Lancet Oncology, found that four primary pathogens were responsible for the vast majority of infection-driven cancers in 2024.
They were:
- H. pylori: A common stomach bacterium responsible for 760,000 cases annually, mainly non-cardia gastric cancers.
- HPV: Responsible for 750,000 cases, with cervical cancer making up 600,000 of those diagnoses.
- Hepatitis B and C: Driven by chronic liver infections, these caused 360,000 and 160,000 cases of liver cancer, respectively.
- Epstein-Barr Virus (EBV): The virus responsible for glandular fever also drove 260,000 cases, with more research needed into its role in throat and stomach cancers, as well as various lymphomas.
Despite being the primary cause behind a substantial number of cancer cases, public awareness of the role pathogens play in the disease is limited.
La Marca and Diepstraten attribute this to the fact that many people carry these pathogens without knowing it.
"These infections can cause more than 20 different types of cancer, including stomach, liver, blood and cervical cancers," they wrote, noting that there is a long delay between infection and cancer onset, which blurs the link.
Preventing future cancer diagnoses
Despite the considerable global figures, researchers emphasise that infection-driven cancers represent the most preventable type on the planet.
Several successful public health interventions for many of these primary pathogens already exist.
HPV and hepatitis B immunisations offer anti-cancer protective properties, while hepatitis C antivirals and antibiotic treatment for H. pylori can eliminate chronic risks before issues develop.
"The HPV vaccine is safe and effective at protecting against HPV-related cancers and diseases," Broun said. "It is recommended and free for Australians aged 12 to 25 years of age."
"Even if you’re vaccinated against HPV, we encourage you to screen."
She added that people uncertain if they have been vaccinated against hepatitis B can speak with their GP about a blood test.
While there is no preventative vaccine against EBV, clinical trials are underway.
"Because these infections are largely preventable or treatable," La Marca and Diepstraten wrote, "scaling up global access to existing vaccines, screening, and antimicrobial therapies offers one of our most direct routes to cutting global cancer rates".

Ten people have been injured, one critically, after a car crashed into a crowd of people in Newcastle waiting to farewell the Knights team bus before the NRL grand final.
New South Wales police said a five-year-old girl remained in a critical but stable condition in an induced coma after the crash on Saturday morning.
Initially a 67-year-old man was also in a critical. The man is now in a serious but stable condition.
John Hunter hospital provided an update to Australian Associated Press on Saturday night confirming five other patients were in a stable condition and three others had been discharged.
The injured were treated on the scene by NSW ambulance paramedics, before being taken to hospital.
Police said the P-plate driver was an 18-year-old man who was arrested at the scene and taken to hospital for mandatory testing and subsequently charged with nine offences including dangerous driving occasioning grievous bodily harm, negligent driving and causing bodily harm by misconduct.
He was refused bail to appear in court on Sunday.
Assistant Commissioner Dave Waddell said two other people allegedly in the car were escorted from the crash scene after the crowd turned on them.
Police did not believe the incident was deliberate but declined to comment on reports the vehicle was allegedly being driven erratically before the accident.
“I’ll let the investigators from the crash investigation unit deal with that,” Waddell told reporters.
The police minister, Yasmin Catley, said so many lives had been affected by a split-second decision, as she urged other drivers to take care over the NSW long weekend.
“We have already started Saturday morning with this devastation,” she said.
“Nobody can comprehend what has happened with this terrible tragedy.”
The roads minister, Jenny Aitchison, said the incident could have been worse, with more than 1,000 people gathered in the area where it occurred.
Emergency services were called to Newcastle Link Road at the Transfield Drive roundabout in Wallsend about 9.30am on Saturday after reports a vehicle struck multiple people in a crowd.
“Several people have been injured and are currently receiving treatment at the scene,” police said.
“Police have commenced an investigation into the circumstances surrounding the incident, with initial inquiries indicating it is not believed to be terror related.”
Gavin Morris, the mayor of Newcastle, told the ABC that the driver, who he said was a Knights fan, lost control while revving his car shortly before the team arrived.
“I’ve spoken to the authorities, a number of which, and look, first of all, it is under investigation, and the young driver is now with police, so it appears that he was revving the car in some form. He was excited. He was a supporter. He was, you know, a fan,” Morris said.
“It appears that he’s lost control of the car, and he’s gone … sideways into the crowd.”
Footage posted on social media appeared to show a car being driven quickly around a roundabout shortly before the crash.
Other images showed it had careened off the road soon afterwards.
A witness to the incident, Dylan Prior, told ABC News that the car was “revving a bit” before it ran into a group of people.
“I saw some young kids go flying, and people running to help the victims,” he said.
“Everyone was yelling and hysterical, yelling at the driver.
“They were screaming for help.”
The Newcastle Link Road was closed in both directions, leading to the diversion of the Knights grand final procession.
The club confirmed in an Instagram post that it had changed its route, apologising to fans who may have missed farewelling the team but saying “public safety is our priority”.
Police appealed for fans to leave the area.
“Police acknowledge many loyal supporters may have missed the opportunity to see the team and show their support.

“My thoughts are with everyone injured or involved in the horrible incident this morning in Newcastle,” Albanese said in a statement. “I want to acknowledge and thank emergency services and police for responding so quickly, and their ongoing work in treating the injured.
“Rugby league brings people together, and this should have been a weekend of excitement and pride for Newcastle fans.”
Multiple fundraisers were launched on Saturday afternoon by friends and loved ones of injured fans, including for a five-year-old child who was placed in an induced coma after suffering serious injuries.
The child has already required multiple operations, according to organiser Ashleigh Gibbs.
“Their mum was also seriously injured and will require multiple operations and a long period of recovery,” the fundraising page says.
“Both mum and child now have a long road ahead of them, with ongoing surgeries, hospital stays, rehabilitation.”

Sandu: Russia Will Remain Major Threat to Europe Even After Ukraine War Ends
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
02:47:32 UTC
11:47:32 KST

Moldovan President Maia Sandu warned Friday that Russia will remain a major source of instability in Europe long after the war in Ukraine ends, regardless of whether Russian President Vladimir Putin remains in power, urging Europe to strengthen militarily, accelerate EU enlargement and treat Ukraine as a central pillar of the continent’s future security.
Speaking alongside Finnish President Alexander Stubb at the fifth annual Helsinki Security Forum, Sandu described Moldova’s experience confronting Russian hybrid warfare – from political financing and voter bribery to cyberattacks, disinformation, energy pressure and repeated violations of Moldovan airspace.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“Moldova enjoys peace today thanks to the courage of the Ukrainian people, of the Ukrainian leadership, and thanks to the support that you and many other friends of Ukraine have been providing,” Sandu told the forum.
The Moldovan president argued that her small country also plays a significant security role because preventing Moscow from gaining political control over Moldova protects Ukraine’s southwestern flank.
“If we would have allowed Russia to get to control power in Moldova, you could imagine what the situation would look today, given that Moldova has a pretty long border with Ukraine – 1,200 kilometers – and you can imagine what Russia could have done to Ukraine using the Russian proxies in Moldova,” Sandu said.
Ukraine Records Nearly 227,000 Russian War Crimes Since Full-Scale Invasion
Russia’s hybrid war against Moldova
Sandu described a wide-ranging Russian campaign against Moldova that has intensified around elections.
She said Moscow has used energy blackmail, illicit political financing, attempts to bribe voters, cyberattacks, false bomb threats and large-scale disinformation.
“We do not depend on Russian gas anymore,” Sandu said. “We do not depend on Russian trade, but at some point we had quite a big share.”
When those traditional tools of economic pressure became less effective, she said, Moscow shifted toward other methods.
“In our case, this was dirty money to try to corrupt politicians, to try to finance political campaigns. These were attempts to even bribe voters. This was cyberattacks. This was trying to shut down [voting through] false bomb alerts during the day of the election, and then of course a lot of disinformation and manipulation.”
Sandu said one of Moldova’s most effective responses has been exposing the mechanisms of Russian interference publicly rather than allowing them to operate in the shadows.
“What we did, we exposed it together with the press, so it was a whole-society response,” she said.
But combating Russian money in elections requires much more than public messaging, Sandu stressed.
“You need to have everybody: the agency for fighting money laundering. You need to have the intelligence service. You need to have the tax inspectorate. You need to have the police,” she said.
“It has to be a very well-coordinated effort by all the institutions, and it has to be very good communication for the people to see the risks. Because if they don’t see the risks, then it’s very difficult for them to protect themselves and their votes.”
‘Seven or eight’ Russian drones in one week
Sandu said the pressure on Moldova is not confined to information warfare.
“In addition to all the problems and the bigger number of violations of our airspace, just in the last week we had seven or eight Russian drones violating our airspace,” she said.
The Moldovan president said such incidents, combined with high energy prices and Russia’s war against neighboring Ukraine, have created immediate security concerns for Chisinau.
But she warned Europe not to mistake those pressures for a temporary problem that disappears when fighting eventually stops.
“I think it’s very clear that Russia will continue to be a major source of instability for many years to come, regardless of whether Putin is still there or not after this war,” Sandu said.
“This is not just a short-term challenge or a mid-term challenge.”
Europe, she argued, must emerge from the war substantially better prepared than it was before Russia launched its full-scale invasion.
“This means Europe needs to be strong militarily,” Sandu said.
“We should all understand that Ukraine is going to be a very important pillar of the security in Europe.”
Any eventual dialogue with Russia, she added, should come “from the position of strength, with one voice,” while ensuring Moscow is held accountable for crimes committed against Ukraine.

Teva said it was disappointed by the decision and criticized what it described as the politicization of Britain's healthcare system.

In 2023, Teva agreed to pay $225 million to resolve U.S. Justice Department charges related to price-fixing involving three drugs.
A Teva spokesman said in response that "as one of the largest suppliers of medicines in the U.K., we value our long-standing partnership with the RCN and the opportunity we've had to support healthcare workers and their patients."
"We are disappointed by the RCN's decision to end this collaboration and wish to continue dialogue with them," he added. "The healthcare system functions best when it is focused on patient well-being and not politicized."
Teva also told TheMarker that its commitment to supporting healthcare professionals and patients "remains unchanged," adding: "Although we disagree with the decision, we will continue to operate with integrity and focus on what matters most: helping patients access the medicines they need."

Taiwan allocates NT$99.5 billion to improve public-sector compensation since 2025
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
02:43:21 UTC
11:43:21 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Taiwan has allocated NT$99.5 billion (US$3.1 billion) from 2025 to date to raise pay and improve benefits for military personnel, public servants, and education personnel, the Cabinet said.
Of the total, about NT$34.6 billion has been used to improve compensation for 168,831 military personnel. Measures include higher allowances for volunteer service, combat duties, and specialized work such as air and sea traffic control, electronic intelligence, and cyber warfare, according to CNA and LTN.
Another NT$13.1 billion has been allocated to improve compensation for police officers and firefighters, including higher allowances for demanding and hazardous duties and criminal investigation work. The government has also expanded eligibility for work bonuses and allowances for late-night and hazardous duties, benefiting 80,947 personnel.
Compensation for other civil servants and education personnel has also been adjusted based on the demands of their respective jobs. For civil servants, 17 types of compensation have been increased, including professional allowances, position and duty allowances, and bonuses, benefiting 11,783 people.
For education personnel, six types of compensation have been adjusted, including position allowances, hourly pay, and bonuses. These measures have benefited 362,399 people.
The Cabinet said compensation adjustments take into account the financial burden on central and local governments, as well as differences in the risks and workloads of different positions. Rather than applying uniform increases, the government has adjusted compensation based on these differences.
Looking ahead, the Cabinet has approved a plan for further compensation increases for public-sector personnel in 2027. The plan includes a 4% across-the-board pay increase, along with NT$2,000 increases in professional allowances, including teachers' academic research allowances, as well as supervisory position allowances.

EU will not provide Ukraine with additional funds until promised reforms are implemented – FT
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher

05:42:00 EEST
11:42:00 KST

EU will not provide Ukraine with additional funds until promised reforms are implemented – FT
Brussels has rejected Ukraine's request for additional financial support this year. The European Union is demanding that the Ukrainian authorities first implement the promised reforms in order to unlock further funding.
Source: Financial Times
Details: In the summer, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy estimated Ukraine's additional defence needs at US$27 billion. The government asked the European Commission to help cover the shortfall by releasing funds early from the two-year Ukraine Support Loan programme worth €90 billion.
The loan is intended to cover Ukraine's financial needs in 2026-2027. The programme provides for up to €45 billion in annual funding, subject to the implementation of reforms. However, Ukraine has received only €15.7 billion this year because of delays in implementing these reforms.
Brussels has rejected a request for early disbursement of the funds earmarked for 2027. Instead, the EU is insisting that the Ukrainian government fulfil its commitments, which would unlock around €34 billion in support before the end of this year. These include scrapping the exemption for small international parcels and introducing new tax rules for digital platforms. The European Commission also separately stressed that Ukraine must not backtrack on previously implemented commitments, citing as an example the easing of requirements concerning politically exposed persons (PEPs).
European Commissioners Valdis Dombrovskis and Marta Kos stressed in a letter to Verkhovna Rada Chairman Ruslan Stefanchuk that additional assistance for 2026 is still available if the necessary reforms are implemented.
Background:
- Prime Minister Serhii Koretskyi said that Ukraine risked losing part of the US$29.5 billion in international funding because of delays in the required votes.
- During a meeting with European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen on 24 September, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said that because of the war, the Verkhovna Rada (Ukrainian parliament) was unable to operate as normal and swiftly adopt all the necessary legislation. The European Commission stressed in response that access to funding depended solely on the timely implementation of reforms.
- At a meeting of the Ukraine Donor Platform in Brussels on 29 September in Brussels, EU Commissioner for Enlargement Marta Kos said that the Ukrainian government, the Verkhovna Rada and other institutions must join forces to advance the reforms necessary for Ukraine's European future and to secure European funding.
- On 1 October, the European Commission and Ukraine said they had identified ways to cover Ukraine's budget and defence needs for 2026, as well as the steps required to ensure the timely provision of the relevant funding.

Early Saturday, "our military detected a ballistic missile launched from the Wonsan area of North Korea toward the East Sea," Seoul's Joint Chiefs of Staff said, referring to the body of water also known as the Sea of Japan.

Seoul and the US-led United Nations Command found that last month's explosion inside the DMZ, the heavily mined buffer dividing the two Koreas since their 1953 armistice, was caused by North Korean mines laid on the South side of the border.

Kim also warned Pyongyang was "ready for anything" Seoul might do over the mine blast – remarks followed the next morning by North Korea’s ballistic missile launch.
'Escalating' tensions
Analysts said the launch would be viewed as a show of force in response to the South Korean government's diplomatic efforts, effectively rejecting engagement.
"Seoul called for easing tensions, but Pyongyang answered by escalating them," Yang Moo-jin, former president of the University of North Korean Studies in Seoul, told AFP.
"The message is that the North is pursuing ... confrontation in response to goodwill," he added.
South Korea's defence minister said on Tuesday the military had "a range of necessary measures at our disposal, and we will implement them in stages" to respond to the DMZ incident, without providing further detail.

Saturday 3 October 2026 05:35
Saturday, 3 October 2026, 05:35
PHOTO BNT
Font size
More than a thousand years after his death, Tsar Samuil (Samuel) (997-1014) is returning home, to Bulgaria, to whose freedom and independence he devoted his life. The remains of one of Bulgaria’s most renowned medieval rulers will be handed over to the Bulgarian state today at an official ceremony at the Museum of Byzantine Culture in Thessaloniki, in the presence of Prime Minister Rumen Radev and Greek Prime Minister Kyriakos Mitsotakis, the government press service reports.
Later, Bulgaria will welcome the remains of its tsar with a state ceremony at Prince Alexander I Square in Sofia.
After entering Bulgarian airspace, the Spartan military transport aircraft carrying Tsar Samuil’s remains will be intercepted and escorted by two pairs of MiG-29 and F-16 fighter jets. The formation will fly over Prince Alexander I Square at around 12:30 p.m. The fighter jets will make a second flyover after the Spartan transport aircraft has landed.
Tsar Samuil’s remains will then be carried by the Bulgarian Armed Forces from Vasil Levski Airport in Sofia to Prince Alexander I Square.

Gang rape case at Cornell University exposes sexual violence at US colleges
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
02:40:00 UTC
11:40:00 KST

Gang rape case at Cornell University exposes sexual violence at US colleges
NEW YORK – An alleged gang rape at Cornell University, detailed in a graphic lawsuit last month, has provoked fury in the United States over sexual violence on campuses and colleges’ failure to stamp out the behaviour.
The accuser has said that in 2024, she was drugged with ketamine, assaulted and raped by seven members of the Chi Phi fraternity, a social club for male students.
Her allegations fell within what activists call the “red zone”, a period at the start of the academic year when a large share of assaults happen, often at parties fuelled by drugs and alcohol.
An estimated one in four female students and one in 14 male students experience rape or sexual assault at some point during their undergraduate studies, according to a 2020 study by the Association of American Universities.
Mental health non-profit the Jed Foundation has reported that men in fraternities – which are routinely criticised for shielding sexism – are more likely to commit sexual violence.
The accused students in the Cornell case were members of the Chi Phi fraternity, one of several “Greek life” organisations common across US colleges.
Meanwhile, the accuser was part of a sorority for female students. Sorority members are statistically more likely than their non-affiliated peers to suffer from sexual assault.
Consent
For Jennifer Freyd, a psychology professor at the University of Oregon, the Cornell case and the Ivy League college’s response are “so typical of other universities”.
Following the initial allegations in 2024, Cornell closed the fraternity and temporarily suspended the students allegedly involved, several of whom were later expelled.
Meanwhile, the district attorney declined to prosecute because he said the victim’s police testimony did not establish a lack of consent.
The investigation was reopened after the complainant’s civil lawsuit fuelled allegations that prosecutors and the elite college had failed to hold the men accountable.
Observers have noted that severe punishments like full expulsions are rare for fraternity members as they are often connected to elite networks and represent a key source of revenue for universities.
Freyd added that there should be a wider institutional approach of respecting whistleblowers when they come forward with accusations.
“That doesn’t mean they believe them without investigation, but it means that they take it seriously, and that they acknowledge the bravery involved,” she said.
Sex education
A further challenge in the Cornell case is a legal provision that makes it harder to prosecute rape cases in New York and several other US states if accusers were willingly intoxicated.
In response to growing public anger, New York Governor Kathy Hochul has vowed to work with lawmakers to close that loophole.
“Voluntary intoxication is not a licence for sexual assault or gang rape. Period,” Hochul said.
The Democrat has also appointed Attorney General Letitia James, who has battled with President Donald Trump, as a special prosecutor for the Cornell case.
Shiwali Patel, of the National Women’s Law Center, said she backed closing the legal loophole and added that better sex education was also crucial.
“One of the most effective ways of prevention is to have comprehensive sex education that is age-developmentally appropriate from a young age, that includes talking about consent,” Patel said.
“But we are not seeing these changes being implemented, and so this issue is happening over and over again.” AFP

The first Israeli repatriation flight from Dubai following the attempted attack aboard a Flydubai flight landed at Ben Gurion Airport shortly after 1:20 a.m. Saturday, after authorities resolved a dispute that had delayed efforts to bring stranded Israelis home.
The Arkia flight departed Dubai on Friday night after Emirati authorities had earlier demanded that a cargo aircraft accompany passenger flights bound for Israel in order to transport travelers’ luggage separately.
The issue was eventually resolved, allowing the Arkia aircraft to depart. Another flight operated by Israir was expected to follow.
Arkia had earlier been forced to delay sending an empty aircraft to Dubai after the UAE imposed the baggage requirement. The airline initially agreed to dispatch a separate cargo plane, but Emirati authorities sought to apply the procedure to subsequent flights as well.
Arkia said the operation involved close coordination with Israeli authorities and significant security and operational preparations. It was the airline’s first such operation from Dubai following the aviation disruption triggered by the Flydubai incident.
Flydubai, meanwhile, has suspended all flights to and from Israel while authorities investigate the attempted attack aboard Flight FZ1073 from Dubai to Tel Aviv. The airline said the suspension was coordinated with the relevant authorities and would remain under review as the investigation progresses.
Etihad Airways has continued operating between Abu Dhabi and Tel Aviv under tightened security arrangements and announced additional flights intended to help passengers return.
Emirati source accuses Israel of politicizing crisis
The flight disruptions have also exposed tensions between Israel and the UAE over how the aftermath of the incident has been handled.
A source close to the government in Abu Dhabi accused Israel of using the attempted attack for political purposes and delaying the restoration of Flydubai services.
“They are talking about ‘repatriation flights’ as though there is a war in the country. There is no war,” the source told ynet.
The source argued that if Israeli passengers could be flown home aboard Arkia, there was no reason Flydubai should not be allowed to resume carrying passengers to Israel under enhanced security procedures.
“Who is stopping the flights? Israel,” the source claimed. “If passengers can board an Arkia flight, why not Flydubai?”
The source also objected to Israel’s use of the term “repatriation” or “rescue” flights, arguing that it falsely suggested the UAE was experiencing a war or emergency.
“Rescue from what? From whom? From where?” the source said.
A separate report citing a source close to the UAE government similarly said Emirati officials believed Israel was exploiting the Flydubai incident for political purposes amid Israel’s election campaign. That remains an allegation by the Emirati source rather than an established fact.
The source said the UAE was prepared to strengthen security procedures and increase screening of flight crews, while accusing Israel of slowing efforts to restore normal aviation links.
“Obviously there was a failure,” the source acknowledged, referring to the attempted attack. But the source argued that Israeli officials did not appreciate the effect the dispute was having on the UAE-Israel relationship.
“We are going crazy over Israel’s behavior,” the source said. “It doesn’t seem like the Israeli government understands what it is doing.”
Emirati authorities are conducting their own investigation into the Omani co-pilot accused of attempting to crash the Flydubai aircraft and have said they are cooperating with other governments as the probe continues.
The source also alleged that Emirati officials believed Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu was seeking to connect the incident to Iran for political reasons ahead of Israel’s election. Israeli security officials have said that, at this stage, they have found no indication that the co-pilot was directed by an outside actor, though all possibilities remain under investigation.
The dispute unfolded after Flydubai suspended Israel service following the cockpit attack, leaving aviation links between the two countries sharply reduced and prompting Israeli carriers to arrange flights for stranded passengers.

Thirty Palestinians have been killed in attacks by Israeli occupiers across the occupied West Bank since the beginning of 2026, official Palestinian figures showed on Friday.
In a statement, the Palestinian Colonization and Wall Resistance Commission said the number of Palestinians killed by occupiers had reached 30 as of Oct. 2, exceeding the annual toll recorded in any year since 2022.
The 2026 toll, with the year still ongoing, is already more than double the total for all of 2025, an increase of around 114%, it said.
The commission described the figures as "a dangerous escalation in the deadly consequences of attacks by occupiers."
According to the commission, the deaths were heavily concentrated in the Ramallah and Al-Bireh and Nablus provinces. It recorded 15 deaths in Ramallah and Al-Bireh Governorate and seven in Nablus, accounting for around 73% of the total.
Three Palestinians were killed in Hebron, two each in Jerusalem and Salfit, and one in Qalqilya.
The commission said Israeli forces and occupiers carried out 2,051 attacks against Palestinians and their land and property across the West Bank in September.
Of those, occupiers carried out 647 attacks, killing three Palestinians during the month.
The commission said occupiers carried out 5,561 attacks from the beginning of 2026 through the end of September. The attacks damaged 14,600 trees in September, including 9,334 olive trees.
Israeli authorities also demolished 254 Palestinian structures during the month, including 89 inhabited homes. The demolitions directly affected 320 Palestinians, including 164 children and 64 women.
Occupiers also attempted to establish 21 new illegal outposts across the West Bank in September.
Meanwhile, Israeli authorities advanced 16 plans for the construction of 3,821 illegal settlement units last month.
The commission said Israeli authorities seized around 6,635 dunams (1,640 acres) of Palestinian land since the start of 2026.
Official Palestinian figures estimate that around 750,000 Israeli occupiers live in the West Bank, including occupied East Jerusalem, in 194 illegal settlements and 400 outposts.
In June, 14 UN special rapporteurs warned that the sharp rise in "settler terrorism," with support and complicity from the Israeli state in the occupied Palestinian territory, posed an existential threat to Palestinian communities.
