Israeli air attack on Gaza City apartment kills at least five
Multiple Israeli attacks leave a total of eight people dead across the Gaza Strip.
Israeli air attack on residential apartment in Gaza kills 5 Palestinians
An Israeli air attack on a residential apartment in western Gaza City has killed at least five people and severely wounded several others, according to Gaza’s Civil Defence agency and staff at al-Shifa Hospital.
A total of eight Palestinians died across Gaza on Saturday, hospital sources told Al Jazeera, including one killed in Beit Lahiya in northern Gaza and two who succumbed to wounds sustained in earlier Israeli attacks.
The Gaza City strike hit the al-Asala building in the Remal neighbourhood while residents were asleep in the early hours of Saturday. It came without prior warning, Al Jazeera’s Hani al-Shaer said, reporting from Gaza.
Remal is one of Gaza City’s most crowded residential areas, home to thousands of displaced people sheltering in makeshift camps.
“We heard fighter jets getting louder, then three strikes followed, hitting the apartment and killing those inside,” al-Shaer said.
The attack penetrated the targeted apartment and tore through the floors below, causing further destruction throughout the multistorey building.
‘Terrifying night’
Reporting from Gaza City later on Saturday, Al Jazeera’s Hind Khoudary described yet “another terrifying night”.
“Around 2am [on Saturday, 11:00 GMT on Friday], two huge explosions shook the al-Haid roundabout. We later learned that the Israeli army targeted a building with two explosive drones, killing at least three women, a child and a young man”.
Fires burned for at least an hour before Palestinian Civil Defence crews managed to put them out.
Al-Shaer described the scene as “horrific”, while Khoudary said “the whole neighbourhood was shaken”, as people were buried under the rubble as they slept.
Civil Defence crews were still searching the site for missing people and bodies, al-Shaer said, as Israeli drones continued flying over the area and fighter jets were heard flying low across Gaza.
The Israeli military said it targeted the building in an attempt to kill Ali al-Amoudi, whom it described as the deputy chairman of Hamas’s political bureau in Gaza, claiming the apartment was “used by Hamas”.
The military said the results of the attack were still “under review” and did not confirm whether al-Amoudi was killed.
Christian mother and daughter killed
Among those killed were two Christian women, Maysa Khader Ibrahim Abu Daoud (Ayyad) and her daughter Mary Hafez Michel al-Najjar (Abu Daoud), the Palestinian Wafa news agency reported, citing a statement from the head of the Higher Presidential Committee for Church Affairs in Palestine, Ramzi Khoury.
Friends and relatives gathered for their funeral at the Church of Saint Porphyrius in Gaza City on Saturday.
“Today is essentially the worst day of my life. I lost my mother and my grandmother today,” said Fouad Al-Najjar.
Cardinal Pierbattista Pizzaballa, the Latin patriarch of Jerusalem, expressed his “deep sorrow and grief” over their “tragic” killing.
He also extended “his heartfelt condolences and sympathy to the families of the deceased and to the Christian community in Gaza”.
In a statement later on Saturday, the Greek Orthodox Patriarchate of Jerusalem mourned the women and extended condolences to their family.
“We pray for an end to the war and bombardment, for the protection of civilian lives, and for a just peace in which the people of Gaza can feel secure for their children and loved ones. May their memory be eternal,” the Patriarchate said.
‘Very hard to save lives’
“This is not the first ceasefire violation, or the first attack, in the past 24 hours,” Al Jazeera’s Khoudary said, as an Israeli drone strike killed a Palestinian man and wounded several others in southern Gaza on Thursday.
“According to doctors, it is very, very hard to save the lives of those who are injured, because Israel continues to restrict medical supplies and instruments,” Khoudary said. “A lot of people are queueing to leave the Gaza Strip through the Rafah crossing.”
Bordering Egypt in the south of Gaza, the Rafah crossing is only opened by Israeli forces for limited movements of people, especially patients needing medical treatment abroad, the World Health Organization (WHO) said.
Repeated delays in bringing life-saving medicines, prosthetics and other supplies from Israel into Gaza are having “devastating consequences” for Palestinians who urgently need them, the WHO said on Saturday.
Since Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza began on October 7, 2023, at least 74,000 Palestinians have been killed and 175,000 injured, according to the enclave’s Health Ministry. The true toll is likely much higher, as many people are still missing beneath the rubble.
Since last year’s “ceasefire”, at least 1,400 people have been killed and nearly 5,000 injured.

The Australian Embassy in Brasilia also said it was closing on Friday, citing the US alert and advising Australians to avoid US diplomatic missions.

What to know about Brazil's heated election
The news comes at a tense time in US-Brazil relations.
Brazilians are headed to the polls this Sunday for what will likely be the first round of the presidential elections that has effectively shaped up to be a rematch of the 2022 contest.
Surveys show the contest is a statistical tie between left-wing President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva, who is seeking a fourth term, and right-wing Senator Flavio Bolsonaro, the son of former President Jair Bolsonaro.

Trump has not endorsed a candidate, but there are fears that he may be too deeply involved in the outcome of the election results.
US Democratic lawmakers, for example, in late September expressed "grave concern" in a letter to Secretary of State Marco Rubio over what they said was the administration's "coordinated effort to threaten our strategic alliance with Brazil and undermine the Western Hemisphere’s second-largest democracy ahead of its upcoming presidential election."
Lula and his allies have warned of foreign interference in the election, pointing to tariffs and an effort this summer by Washington to send US officials to Brazil to "discuss electoral integrity."
When asked at the White House whether he would support Bolsonaro in the election, Trump said: "Well, we're looking at that whole thing, and we're watching that election very closely."
Brazil is surrounded by neighbors who've swung to the right and the election outcome — which could be determined on October 25th when the country advances into runoff if no candidate secures a majority of the vote this Sunday — will determine the direction of the country's foreign policy.

color-shifting light sculpture suspends above orchestra at walt disney concert hall
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
02:10:59 UTC
11:10:59 KST

color-shifting light sculpture suspends above orchestra at walt disney concert hall
rope-like LED tubing produces the installation’s changing illumination in synchronization with the performance.
RADIANCE Translates Fire Into Light at Walt Disney Concert Hall
RADIANCE is a light sculpture installation by Grimanesa Amorós, commissioned by the Los Angeles Philharmonic and presented at Walt Disney Concert Hall across three consecutive performances. Conceived to accompany Alexander Scriabin’s Prometheus: The Poem of Fire, Op. 60 (1910), the work takes fire as its subject, resolving into the form of a pulsing spark suspended above the orchestra.
The installation draws on two cultural references: Prometheus, who gave fire to humanity, and Viracocha, the Incan creator deity. Together, they frame light as a carrier of knowledge and a medium of transformation. Amorós, a Peruvian-born American artist, has worked with light as both material and language since 2002, with RADIANCE extending this approach to an architectural scale.
Programmable LED Light Sculpture Responds to the Orchestra
Measuring 60 × 35 × 5 feet (18.29 × 10.67 × 1.52 meters), the installation is constructed from reflective material, color-shifting rope-like LED tubing, and custom electrical hardware. A lighting sequence written specifically for the work controls its changing illumination.
A central aspect of the commission is the integration of the sculpture with Walt Disney Concert Hall’s existing house lighting. Artist Grimanesa Amorós programmed both systems as a single lighting environment, connecting the suspended sculpture with the architecture and the performance rather than treating it as an isolated object within the space.
The sequence was composed second by second in relation to the orchestra and develops through six major synchronized moments. The lighting of the sculpture, the concert hall, and the performance therefore progress as a coordinated system throughout the work.
project info:
name: RADIANCE
artist: Grimanesa Amorós | @grimanesaamoros

commissioned by: LA Philharmonic
dimensions: 60 × 35 × 5 feet (18.29 × 10.67 × 1.52 meters)

Ukraine’s National Police has opened nearly 227,000 war-crimes proceedings since Russia launched its full-scale invasion, documenting a vast catalogue of crimes committed by Russian troops and their accomplices across the country.
As of Oct. 2, investigators had opened 243,982 criminal proceedings linked to crimes committed on Ukrainian territory by Russian servicemen and their accomplices, according to the National Police. Of those, 226,766 are being investigated as war crimes under Article 438 of Ukraine’s Criminal Code.

Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
The figures illustrate the scale of the legal and investigative burden Ukraine continues to face more than four years into Russia’s invasion, as authorities document killings, attacks on civilian infrastructure, forced deportations, sexual violence and other violations.
Nearly a quarter-million criminal proceedings
According to the latest National Police figures, Ukrainian investigators have opened:
- 226,766 proceedings involving war crimes;
- 9,412 proceedings over encroachment on Ukraine’s territorial integrity and inviolability;
- 4,781 proceedings involving collaboration;
- 452 proceedings involving treason.
The latest tally is higher than the 243,435 criminal proceedings recorded by police on Sept. 26, including 226,221 war-crimes cases, showing that hundreds of new cases continue to be added within days.
Russian war takes devastating toll on Ukrainian children
The National Police update also highlights the continuing toll on Ukrainian children.
As of Oct. 2, official data showed 749 children killed and 2,924 wounded since the start of the full-scale invasion.
Another 2,365 children remained missing, while 20,651 had been recorded as deported to Russia. Ukraine has returned 2,651 children, while 59,462 have been located, according to the figures cited by police from the Children of War database.
Putin Ally Schröder Takes Russian Business Post After Kremlin Floated Him as Ukraine Mediator
The figures remain incomplete because authorities cannot fully verify cases in areas of active fighting and Ukrainian territories under Russian occupation.
Sexual violence investigations
Ukrainian authorities have also opened 153 criminal proceedings involving sexual violence committed by Russian military personnel.
Sexual violence has been among the categories of Russian crimes documented by Ukrainian investigators and international organizations throughout the war.
Ukraine has repeatedly stressed that the scale of such crimes may be significantly greater than the number of formal cases, particularly because many victims remain in occupied territories or may be unable or unwilling to report abuse.
International Legal Ramifications
In late August, police reported 236,528 criminal proceedings, including 219,335 war crimes. By Oct. 2, the total had risen by more than 7,400 proceedings, while the number classified as war crimes had increased by more than 7,400 as well.
The meticulously cataloged metrics compiled by the National Police are intended to serve a purpose far beyond domestic reporting.
Every logged war crime, forced transfer of a minor, and act of systemic violence is being documented in compliance with international legal standards.
This evidentiary database is being prepared to form the bedrock of prosecutions within both Ukrainian courts and future international tribunals to ensure accountability for both high-ranking Kremlin officials and frontline perpetrators.

The arrests come nearly a year after a deadly knife and gun attack on the Heaton Park Hebrew Congregation Synagogue in northern Manchester, where worshipers had gathered for Yom Kippur, the holiest day in the Jewish calendar. Two people died in that Oct. 2, 2025, attack.
U.K. Metropolitan Police said in a news release that 36-year-old Salam Ahmadyan of Liverpool and 34-year-old Rahman Salehi of Salford, both Iranian nationals, were arrested in Manchester on Sept. 20.
"It is alleged that the two men were in contact with an overseas third-party who may be in Iran in relation to the plot," the Met wrote.
The Associated Press reported that the third party provided instructions on making a homemade chlorine bomb.
"We do not believe there to be any ongoing threat to the public in relation to this matter," Deputy Assistant Commissioner Vicki Evans said in a statement.
"This news will be deeply distressing for our Jewish communities, coming so soon after Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur," British Home Minister Shabana Mahmood said in a statement. "I know this will be especially true in Manchester, as we mark one year since the terrorist attack at Heaton Park Synagogue."
Mahmood also added in her statement that "both suspects" had "arrived by small boat several years ago," which she said was a "reminder of the importance of our relentless work to tackle illegal migration into this country." Salehi was granted asylum and Ahmadyan has a pending asylum claim, the Associated Press reported.
The past year has seen a spate of attacks in the British capital targeting Jewish or Israel-linked locations.
This also comes after five British nationals, all men in their mid-20s, were arrested on Sept. 27 in a southwest English village near the British air force base RAF Fairford on suspicion of preparing a terrorist act. The base has been used by American bombers to launch attacks on Iran during the war in the Middle East. The men were later released on bail.
On Thursday, British authorities arrested a 25-year-old dual U.K.-Iranian national in London on suspicion of plotting a terror attack near the RAF Fairford air base. He was also released on bail Saturday, the U.K. Counter Terrorism Policing agency announced.
U.K. Prime Minister Andy Burnham said that the British government believes Iran "played a part" in the Sept. 27 incident. Iran's government has denied any involvement.

‘We guarded the cockpit’: passenger recounts tense hour after Flydubai attack was stopped
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
02:03:25 UTC
11:03:25 KST

For Opher Dubrovsky, the ordeal aboard the Flydubai flight did not end when passengers subdued the co-pilot accused of trying to crash the plane.
Dubrovsky, who was returning to Israel after a trip to Kathmandu, was seated in 8C near the front of the aircraft. He fell asleep after takeoff and woke to shouting as the crisis unfolded.
In an interview with the YouTube channel Captain Steve, he described the struggle inside the cockpit, the unexpectedly smooth emergency landing in Saudi Arabia, his wife’s efforts to calm panicked passengers and how he later bought SIM cards for Israelis who were unable to contact their families.
“Everything was normal until that moment,” Dubrovsky recalled.
“Luckily, the woman sitting in front of me went to the bathroom at the front of the plane, heard shouting and said to the flight attendant, ‘What’s going on? We have to check.’ They opened the cockpit door and saw blood everywhere. She started screaming. That got everyone moving, especially her husband, who ran toward her. People around me rushed forward, and I joined them to help. We immediately understood that the co-pilot had stabbed the captain.”
Captain Steve Scheibner, a former U.S. Navy and American Airlines pilot who hosts the YouTube channel, said Boeing cockpit doors are relatively easy to open from inside but considerably harder, though not impossible, to open from the passenger cabin.
Dubrovsky said passengers pulled the wounded captain out of the cockpit and overpowered the co-pilot.
“He was a big guy. Three people managed to subdue him,” he said. “At first, someone tied his hands with headphones, and then the cabin crew brought plastic restraints and tied him up. About 30 seconds later, the plane started diving.”
Flight data showed the aircraft descending roughly 5,500 meters, or about 18,000 feet, in around 30 seconds.
Scheibner said it was possible, though not yet known for certain, that the co-pilot had damaged or manipulated the flight controls in a way that disengaged the autopilot and triggered the dive.
According to Scheibner, Israeli fighter jets were scrambled after a hijacking alert code was transmitted from the aircraft. He said the replacement pilots aboard the flight were apparently not permitted to land in Israel and, after what appeared to be communication with the Israeli jets, diverted toward Saudi Arabia.
Dubrovsky said that even after control of the aircraft had been restored, passengers remained deeply uneasy.
“The story wasn’t over after the struggle and after the plane was stabilized,” he said. “We still had about another hour of flying, and we were worried that someone from the cabin crew might be cooperating with the co-pilot.”
“We, the passengers, secured the cockpit and placed guards on the flight attendants,” he continued. “Someone accompanied them wherever they went. It wasn’t based on any concrete suspicion, but better to apologize than regret it.”
Some passengers were struggling to remain calm.
“Some of the passengers panicked,” Dubrovsky said. “My wife is a psychiatrist, and she went over to them together with several other people and calmed them down. So until we landed in Saudi Arabia, everyone was tense, but calm.”
Dubrovsky said he pressed his phone against the window and used GPS data to determine that the aircraft was heading toward Saudi Arabia.
“I wondered why it was taking us so long to land,” he said. “The captain was seriously injured, but we circled several times. At the time, we didn’t understand that the rear of the aircraft had been damaged.”
The landing itself, he said, was surprisingly smooth.
“I complimented the replacement pilot afterward,” Dubrovsky recalled. “He told me, ‘Thank Boeing for that. The nose wheel did the job it was supposed to do.’”
When the aircraft landed, emergency services were waiting.
“At the airport there were ambulances, fire engines and soldiers, because apparently the place is also used by the military,” Dubrovsky said. “They put us in an isolated area and took care of us. They brought us food and water. Everyone was really nice.”
But the unexpected landing created another problem: many of the Israeli passengers could not connect their phones and tell relatives back home that they were safe.
“I spoke to someone and asked him to open a hotspot so I could order a SIM card,” Dubrovsky said. “I ordered one for myself and bought SIM cards for another 20 people so they could speak to their loved ones.”
The uncertainty continued when Flydubai sent a replacement crew to Saudi Arabia.
According to Dubrovsky, the crew had been instructed to fly there without being told what had happened aboard the original flight.
“They landed and asked us to get on the plane, which looked exactly like the previous plane, and they asked us to sit in the same seats,” he said. “People were very stressed by that.”
Dubrovsky said he spoke directly with the new pilots and explained what had happened.
“I think for them it was no less stressful, thinking that a colleague could have stabbed them,” he said. “They were very patient with the passengers. They spoke with them and asked them to board, but they didn’t pressure anyone.”
He ultimately tried to reassure fellow passengers that the replacement crew could be trusted.
“I spoke to people and told them the crew was great,” Dubrovsky said. “What’s amazing about this whole story is that everyone on that plane contributed something in that situation.”

FIFA report on World Cup identifies counter-pressing as defining trend
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
10:02:15 CST
11:02:15 KST

GENEVA, Oct. 2 (Xinhua) -- FIFA published a post-tournament report of the 2026 World Cup on Friday, saying the tournament showed the trend of counter-pressing and a redefined role of the goalkeepers.
The report, compiled by FIFA's Technical Study Group and the FIFA Football Performance Insights Department, analyzed all 104 World Cup matches to find tactical innovation, evolving player roles and new pathways to success at the highest level.
According to FIFA, counter-pressing is a double-edged asset identified as one of the competition's defining trends. "The top teams regularly succeeded in turning a loss of possession into an immediate attacking opportunity," it said.
Goalkeepers are increasingly used as active participants in the build-up phase and as a solution in the quest to overcome the opposition's press, FIFA said.
FIFA said the analysis showed there is no single winning formula, describing it as "contrasting routes to success" - from aggressive high presses to disciplined low blocks and rapid transitions.
The report also explored the game across every phase of play to raise nine key topics, including building with a back three, wide-player rotations, exploiting inside channels, progression through key players, high pressing, counter-pressing, defensive blocks, attacking transitions, and the evolving role of the goalkeeper.
"The objective is not simply to describe what happened, but to understand why it happened: how teams created and controlled space, how they attacked and defended, how individual roles evolved, and how the decisions of players and coaches influenced the different moments of the game," said FIFA chief of global football development, Arsene Wenger. ■

Latvian PM faces bittersweet victory in election backdropped by Russia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
02:00:00 UTC
11:00:00 KST

RIGA — Latvia’s populist Prime Minister Andris Kulbergs will face his first electoral test Saturday — but his head start in the polls is unlikely to shield him from coalition headaches in a contest where Ukraine and Russia are looming large.
After a campaign partially fought in Brussels’ corridors, Kulbergs could see two of his allied parties fail to reach the 5% threshold to get seats. And if his centrist allies fail to make it into parliament, the pro-Ukraine prime minister might struggle to get enough backing.
In this worst-case scenario, he may even need to open talks with Ainārs Šlesers, a right-wing veteran of Latvian politics who opposed restrictive tariffs on Russia.
Advertisement
But Kulbergs, who took office in May after his predecessor, Evika Siliņa, was engulfed in backlash over stray Ukrainian drone strikes, dismissed this idea as speculation, as he is aiming to keep Latvia among the EU’s Russia hawks.
Latvian politics spilled into Brussels last week, when a push from France, Luxembourg and Slovakia to delist two Russian billionaires from the EU sanctions list turned into a standoff between Paris and Riga.
Latvia was the last holdout in a decision requiring agreement from all 27 member countries. Kulbergs filmed social media vlogs ranting about the proposed delistings, which would free up the European holdings of the men in question and allow them to travel to the bloc.
Despite the tycoons being delisted, the overall sanctions regime with almost 3,000 listings is now locked in for three years — a massive achievement considering EU capitals hitherto had to agree every six months. Latvia also said it would start negotiating with France on enhancing military cooperation and initiate talks on Paris’ nuclear deterrence initiative.
Kulbergs’ expected win on Saturday might be just as bittersweet, despite his right-wing United List party polling in first place at around 20% — a good showing in Latvian parliamentary politics.
Advertisement
His center-right partners, New Unity, are struggling to cross the 5% electoral threshold, which would be a floundering performance for a party that has been home to many Latvian prime ministers, including current European Commissioner Valdis Dombrovskis.
But for the party’s prime ministerial candidate and ex-Finance Minister Arvils Ašeradens, the low polling numbers are simply the “political pendulum which shifts from one way to the other,” he told POLITICO in Riga last month.
During the last election in 2022, New Unity was the major beneficiary of a rally-round-the-flag moment as Russia had just launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine. But in 2026, voters seem frustrated with Latvia’s high inflation, the ongoing uncertainty surrounding national airline airBaltic and instrumentalized migration orchestrated by Russia and Belarus.
The prime minister may need to open talks with Ainārs Šlesers, a right-wing veteran of Latvian politics. | Robert Hegedus/EPA
Kulbergs’ other coalition partner, the agrarian Union of Greens and Farmers (known as ZZS), is also polling below the threshold. And if neither party manages to scrape by, it might force Kulbergs to work with the controversial businessman Šlesers, who carefully advocated expanding trade with Russia.
Kulbergs has dismissed this possibility — “as it is given now: no,” he told POLITICO in early September — because he does not trust the people Šlesers has surrounded himself with. Just weeks earlier, however, he had been less definitive, telling POLITICO in July: “I have to see what chess pieces I will get … to make a coalition.”
Šlesers has been a central figure in Latvian politics for decades, most notably as a local “oligarch” who, via family holdings, exerts influence over the Port of Riga. The capital’s harbor has seen its largely Russian and Belarusian hinterland slowly carved off by EU sanctions. And after Kulbergs slapped 300% tariffs on transited Russian grain this month , Šlesers told Latvian national TV such transit should be allowed, though he supports Ukraine’s EU accession.
Advertisement
Šlesers had distanced himself from politics for a time, after he was caught on tape plotting to divvy up influential posts with fellow oligarchs about 15 years ago. But he has now captured part of the Russian-speaking vote with his conservative-populist rhethoric.
For Latvian political scientist Una Bergmane at the University of Helsinki, there is a clear scenario where Šlesers, a former transport minister, ends up in government. “There is a possibility: If ZZS makes it into the parliament then there might be a temptation [for Kulbergs] to do something with ZZS and Šlesers.”
But it’s not all doom and gloom for the prime minister. Last week’s sanctions standoff could prop him and his New Unity partners up, said Bergmane. “[Foreign Minister Baiba] Braže is the most positively recognizable New Unity member, so everything she does helps the party, but at this point Kulbergs gets most visibility anyway,” she explained.
Kulbergs’ short time in office could play in his favor too. The prime minister and his party, Bergmane said, are in “this very, very comfortable place where they haven’t been in power for a long time” but still hold the most influential office in the country of 1.9 million.

Holei Sea Arch, a centuries-old Hawaii wonder, crumbles into the Pacific
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
01:58:00 UTC
10:58:00 KST

Holei Sea Arch, a centuries-old Hawaii wonder, crumbles into the Pacific
Neil Vigdor
- The Holei Sea Arch, a 90-foot lava rock formation in Hawai’i Volcanoes National Park, collapsed into the ocean around late September during Tropical Storm Nolo.
- The arch had stood for over 500 years but was always expected to erode and disappear due to natural coastal processes.
- The National Park Service shared before-and-after photos, urged caution near cliffs, and noted the arch's collapse amid a series of storms linked to El Nino warming.
AI generated
NEW YORK – For more than half a millennium, one of Hawaii’s most cherished geological marvels, an arch about 27m high composed of lava rock, withstood a battering from the Pacific and evoked a sense of awe.
But that formation, the Holei Sea Arch at Hawai’i Volcanoes National Park, is now gone from the coastline on the Big Island, having crumbled into the ocean around the same time that a tropical storm brought strong winds and heavy rain to Hawaii in late September, the National Park Service said on Oct 1.
A cascade of tributes and vacation photos quickly began pouring in from those who have hiked the park’s rugged coastline over the years, many of them lamenting the landmark’s demise.
The park service posted before-and-after photos of the coastline on social media on the night of Oct 1, along with a crying face emoji.
“Yes, it’s true,” it wrote. “RIP Holei Sea Arch.”
Google Maps labelled the tourist attraction as “permanently closed”.
The arch was still standing as at Sept 23 but had collapsed by the night of Sept 27, according to park officials, who urged people to stay away from unstable cliff edges.
“The exact time of the collapse is unknown and could have occurred when the park was temporarily closed during Tropical Storm Nolo,” the park service wrote.
The storm, propelled by El Nino-warmed waters in the Pacific, passed about 233km south of the Big Island on Sept 26 and brought heavy rain and powerful wind gusts.
It shifted between a tropical storm and a hurricane, part of a procession of storms that have inundated Hawaii since August.
Before that climatological cycle, park officials foreshadowed the disappearance of the sea arch, which they said in an online description was named for Holei, a small endemic plant in the milkweed family.
“This formation is beautiful, but temporary, and has a limited life span,” the description said. “The sea arch will eventually crumble into the sea. However, others will replace it as the cliff slowly migrates inland.”
According to the park service, the sea arch “was cut into the cliff of an ancient lava flow from about 550 years ago”.
The arch’s destruction recalled the collapse in February of another famed rock formation in Italy that was known as the Lover’s Arch. The landmark, a popular backdrop for wedding proposals on the Adriatic coast in Puglia, crumbled on Valentine’s Day after a storm. NYTIMES
- This article originally appeared in The New York Times.

Noah’s Ark? Researchers claim radar scan reveals 'man-made' structure at Turkey site
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
01:54:19 UTC
10:54:19 KST

A new radar survey of Turkey’s controversial Durupinar Formation by Noah’s Ark Scans (NAS) has identified what the organization claims could be a man-made structure buried beneath the site, renewing the long-running debate over whether the formation could be connected to the biblical Noah’s Ark.
“Dr. Khosrow Bakhtar’s preliminary report CONFIRMS that the Durupinar Formation is NOT geological, and that an ‘extraordinary’ man-made structure lies beneath the surface,” NAS wrote in a Wednesday post to social media.
The findings have not yet been independently verified or peer-reviewed.
Discovered first by a Kurdish shepherd and then rediscovered by Turkish Army Captain Ilhan Durupinar in 1959, the site became associated with the biblical ark due to its unique shape and proximity to Mount Ararat.
Since the 1960s, researchers have attempted to prove the theory of the site’s biblical origin to no avail. While the site’s length has been measured to be nearly exact to the size described in the Tanach, no other definitive archaeological or scientific evidence has been found at the site.
“A natural rock formation near Dogubayazit, Turkey, has been misidentified as Noah's Ark,” wrote American salvage expert David Fasold and geologist Lorence Collins in a 1990s paper on the topic. “Microscopic studies of a supposed iron bracket show that it is derived from weathered volcanic minerals.”
Turkish government approves deeper investigation of Durupinar site
But in 2026, the Turkish government gave NAS permission to begin more invasive and comprehensive geological and archaeological excavations at the Durupinar formation.
The preliminary findings come from this new investigation, which used BakhtarRadar, a subsurface imaging system developed by engineer Dr. Khosrow Bakhtar.
According to NAS, the survey detected linear features, angular intersections, layered structures and possible voids beneath the formation. Researchers interpret these features as possible corridors, compartments, and multiple internal levels, rather than geological abnormalities.
However, as the findings are preliminary, they have yet to be peer-reviewed.
As part of the 2026 investigation, NAS began drilling into the formation in order to extract samples from the soil to test for organic material, such as wood, that could serve as a jumping off point for further research.
“This is the most significant finding for 40 years or 45 years of my career. I have never seen this kind of anomalies before. I have never in my life,” said Bakhtar in a video shared on NAS’ social media.
“If these anomalies were not important, we would have seen them at all, but the fact that they showed so clearly indicates that they come from something. I am 100% sure that they come from the same original object. What that original object was, a ship or a spacecraft or what, I do not know.”
Noah's Ark Scan begins drilling into formation
Earlier this week, NAS shared footage taken by a “gopher” robot sent down into the carefully drilled hole in order to attempt to map the abnormalities within.
According to NAS, it hit no rock or bedrock.
Additionally, soil samples from the formation’s exposed sides and rims were taken by researchers and are undergoing laboratory analysis to check for remnants of petrified wood or anything man-made.
“As we entered the boat, we identified a very strong interface, which is a very dark line going all the way down,” Bakhtar said. “If you look at the strength of a signature, it does not matter what depth you are looking at. They all have the same strength, and we can quantify that.”
“Repeated anomalies that when you connect them, they form corridors. Because of that, I think all the anomalies are related to one particular object.”
However, until that evidence is available and independently evaluated, the Durupinar Formation remains neither a confirmed archaeological vessel nor a proven location of Noah’s Ark.

Saudi Arabia preparing massive Yemen offensive – Reuters
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03

Saudi Arabia preparing massive Yemen offensive – Reuters
Saudi Arabia is planning a major offensive in civil war-torn Yemen, hoping to reverse gains made by the Iranian-backed Houthi rebels, who seized a strategic Red Sea chokepoint last month, Reuters reported on Friday, citing Gulf and Yemeni officials and Western diplomats.
More than 100,000 Yemeni government troops could be mobilized for the offensive, depending on the scale, according to Reuters. The operation would be overseen by Saudi Arabia and supported by Saudi airstrikes. The US and other Western countries providing intelligence and material support to Riyadh are not expected to take part in combat operations.
According to Reuters, the Saudis are considering two options: an attack focused on recapturing the coastal area around the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, which connects the Red Sea with the Gulf of Aden and the Indian Ocean, or a broader offensive involving synchronized attacks on multiple fronts in Al-Bayda, Marib, Taiz, and Al-Jawf.
Saudi Arabia first intervened in Yemen in 2015 to support the internationally recognized government, which the Houthis had driven from the capital, Sanaa, the previous year. Large-scale fighting decreased significantly following a UN-brokered truce in 2022.
The fighting escalated again last month, with the Houthis accusing Riyadh of imposing an illegal siege on Yemen. The rebels have since captured the strategic port of Mokha and Perim Island in the Bab el-Mandeb Strait.
The Houthis said on Friday that Saudi forces carried out 94 strikes on areas under their control over the previous 24 hours. Omar al-Bukhaiti, a spokesman for the Houthi-run government in Sanaa, accused the kingdom of deliberately targeting civilian sites, including schools and health facilities.
The group earlier fired drones and missiles at Saudi Arabia, targeting energy facilities, but denied striking a power station in Medina, one of Islam’s holiest cities, dismissing the Saudi claim as a “lie.”
The escalation in Yemen comes amid the ongoing US-Iran war, with the Strait of Hormuz remaining closed to most shipping and US-Iranian talks on ending the conflict stalled.
Several Saudi allies have stepped up military support for the kingdom. Britain has agreed to provide air-to-air refueling for Saudi warplanes, while France is sending troops, radar, and air-defense systems to help protect the Red Sea oil hub of Yanbu.
Pakistan has deployed 30,000 to 40,000 troops to Saudi Arabia to help defend its borders and intercept missiles and drones, Reuters reported, citing a Pakistani official. Islamabad has also supplied air-defense systems, artillery, drones, and anti-drone equipment, while Pakistani military advisers are working alongside Saudi personnel supporting Yemeni forces. Pakistan has not, however, decided to send troops into Yemen for combat operations.

US charges Hamas terrorists, 3 Americans in alleged $1.7 million terror funding scheme
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
01:37:17 UTC
10:37:17 KST

U.S. authorities have charged an alleged Hamas operative in Gaza and three American men in connection with an international fundraising network that prosecutors say collected more than $1.7 million for Hamas while presenting the campaigns as humanitarian aid for Palestinian families.
The Justice Department said Saleem Alzaq, 45, of Gaza, and his associates raised the money through purported charitable campaigns beginning in January 2020. At least $626,000 came from donors based in the United States.
Prosecutors allege the campaigns told donors their money would provide food, winter supplies and other humanitarian assistance to Palestinians in Gaza, while funds were instead directed to Hamas.
Alzaq, who remains in Gaza and has not been arrested, is alleged by U.S. prosecutors to be a Hamas member and a deputy in a battalion of the Izz al-Din al-Qassam Brigades, Hamas’ armed wing. The Justice Department says he also worked in the media apparatus of Hamas’ Shujaiyya Brigade and posted propaganda supporting the organization online.
Three alleged co-conspirators in the United States have been arrested: brothers Abdel Adhami, 35, and Omar Adhami, 33, of Covington, Louisiana, and Raed Yousef, 56, of Lutz, Florida.
According to prosecutors, Abdel Adhami contributed approximately $94,000 to Alzaq’s network between 2021 and September 2026, while his brother Omar contributed about $11,000. Yousef allegedly provided nearly $50,000.
French authorities also arrested three of Alzaq’s alleged associates in a coordinated operation, according to the Justice Department.
Prosecutors say Alzaq operated an international fundraising network involving the United States and France, with associates helping collect money and transfer it to Gaza.
After the Oct. 7, 2023, Hamas attack on Israel, Alzaq allegedly launched another fundraising campaign claiming to assist Gazans injured that day. The campaign operated for several days, until around Oct. 12.
The indictment alleges that Alzaq knew money collected through the campaigns was reaching Hamas and took steps to prevent fundraising accounts from being shut down.
He allegedly instructed supporters not to mention Hamas when transferring money and, in October 2024, told donors using his PayPal accounts not to write phrases including “Free Palestine” or “long live Hamas.”
Prosecutors also said an undercover law enforcement operation provided evidence that Alzaq knew where the money was going. According to the indictment, Alzaq told an undercover officer posing as a Hamas supporter that he regularly helped people send money to “the Green,” a term prosecutors said referred to Hamas.
Alzaq faces charges including conspiracy to provide material support to Hamas, conspiracy to violate the International Emergency Economic Powers Act, conspiracy to commit money laundering and conspiracy to defraud the United States.
The Adhami brothers face charges including providing and conspiring to provide material support to a foreign terrorist organization, wire fraud conspiracy and money laundering conspiracy.
Yousef faces charges including conspiracy and attempts to provide material support to a foreign terrorist organization, money laundering offenses and passport fraud.
“Anyone who finances or assists terrorist organizations responsible for the deaths of American citizens should expect to be prosecuted by the Department of Justice,” Attorney General Todd Blanche said.
Blanche said the Justice Department would continue pursuing terrorist financing networks and seeking to hold those involved accountable.
The Justice Department stressed that the charges are allegations and that all defendants are presumed innocent unless proven guilty in court.

The joint U.S.–Ukraine Reconstruction Investment Fund (URIF) unveiled several investment projects on Oct. 2, including the first-ever critical minerals deal with Ukrainian company BGV Group Management.
Spearheaded by U.S. President Donald Trump, Ukraine signed the so-called "minerals deal" with the U.S. in April 2025, which established a joint investment fund in Ukraine and gives the U.S. favorable access to investment projects in Ukraine. The fund is one of several bilateral investment arrangements that Kyiv has set up since the start of Russia's full-scale invasion and has since broadened beyond minerals.
The long-awaited critical minerals project will see URIF develop a "joint investment platform" with BGV Group — a firm founded by Ukrainian billionaire Hennadii Butkevych — which will "build a diverse portfolio of early-stage mining projects across Ukraine," according to a press release. The initial focus will be on identifying rare earths, beryllium, and zirconium deposits in Ukraine, URIF said.
While the press release did not specify the details of the investment, Reuters reported, citing a top U.S. official, that the deal will be worth around $30 million.
In addition to the critical minerals deal, two new investments also focused on energy projects ahead of yet another harsh winter amid Russia's anticipated onslaught of attacks on energy infrastructure.
According to Reuters, the first will add, and provide "access to capital if damages arise," to a previously announced 85 million euro ($97 million) loan to Ukraine’s biggest private energy firm, DTEK, for a critical battery storage project.
DTEK opened the battery storage facility last September with American energy firm Fluence Energy Inc., which provided 698 Gridstack batteries. Together, the batteries form a 200-megawatt system that can power 600,000 Ukrainian homes for two hours — reducing blackout risks and helping to stabilize the grid in Kyiv and Dnipropetrovsk oblasts.
URIF will separately participate in an equity investment in a combined heat and power (CHP) cogeneration platform intended to construct and operate "community-scale energy hubs" to restore energy supply to homes impacted by Russian energy attacks.
Oleksii Sobolev, deputy head of Ukraine's Presidential Office, said in a statement that the new investments give "investors' confidence in Ukraine."
"We want to see more Ukrainian companies develop through this partnership and create new opportunities for the Ukrainian economy," Sobolev added.
U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said that the investments "represent the continued realization of the vision behind the novel agreement" reached in April 2025.
Total funding for the new investments sits around $70 million, officials said.
For the first 10 years of the fund's agreement, all profits will be directly reinvested into Ukraine. U.S. military assistance could also be considered as contributions to the fund.
Ukraine has received hundreds of billions of dollars in financial assistance from allies since Russia's full-scale invasion in 2022, which has helped support the military and keep the country's economy afloat.

Abdual El-Sayed’s ‘genocide’ charge revives the oldest antisemitic libel - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
01:35:44 UTC
10:35:44 KST

On the Raging Moderates podcast, Scott Galloway laid out the case for Abdul El-Sayed, Michigan’s Democratic Senate nominee.
The Holocaust murdered two-thirds of European Jewry, including more than 90% of Poland’s Jewish population. Rwanda’s genocide killed about 70% of the Tutsis; the Khmer Rouge slaughtered about a quarter of Cambodia’s population.
Galloway then listed what Israel did in Gaza that no genocidal regime ever has done: distributed polio vaccinations, food aid, evacuation corridors, leaflets, and phone calls warning civilians out of buildings Hamas had made military targets.
El-Sayed’s response amounted to a confession: the point of the word “genocide” is not to wait “until the crime is that big again.” Its “power is in naming a thing before it gets that big.”
Translation: the charge need not be accurate, only useful. El-Sayed conflates when genocide must be stopped with what must be proven before it is alleged. That is a theory of libel, not genocide.
Clips spread on the far-left and anti-Israel woke right with a familiar argument since October 2023: Why quibble over the word? More than 70,000 are dead. Call it whatever you want. Just stop the killing.
This poses as rising above semantics. It is the opposite. First, that death toll comes from Hamas’s Health Ministry, which doesn’t separate combatants from civilians, and whose own statistics chief admitted that natural deaths were being counted as war deaths.
Second, most of those who recite it never demanded what would have ended the war on October 8: Hamas’s surrender and the hostages’ return. Third, if the word “genocide” didn’t matter, nobody would fight so hard to keep it.
History of antisemetic libels
The word matters because antisemitic libels always have. In Norwich in 1144, a dead boy spawned the first recorded ritual-murder charge. In Blois, France, in 1171, the charge – without a body – resulted in over 30 Jews being burned alive at the stake.
During the 1348 Black Death, claims that Jews poisoned wells caused the annihilation of hundreds of Jewish communities. In 1648, Cossacks branded Jews as Poland’s instruments of oppression and killed over half of Ukraine’s Jewish population.
In 1903, newspapers in Kishinev blamed Jews for a murdered boy in Dubossary; weeks later, a Kishinev Easter mob slaughtered 49 Jews.
The Land of Israel got its own version. In 1929, Haj Amin al-Husseini’s circle spread the lie that Jews planned to seize or destroy al-Aqsa Mosque. The ensuing pogroms killed more than 130 Jews – 67 in Hebron alone – with hundreds wounded, and mobs committing mass rapes of Jewish women. Ninety-four years later, Hamas named its October 7 mega-massacre “Al-Aqsa Flood.”
How Many knew they were inciting murder is unknowable. Surely, some believed they were naming a crime “so we could do something about it,” as in El-Sayed’s framing. But antisemitic libels are never about vocabulary. They’re a license. They tell ordinary people that the Jews among them are doing or abetting something so monstrous that anything done to stop them is justified.
“Genocide” is the modern ritual-murder charge, the one crime so absolute it suspends every moral limit. Galloway warned El-Sayed the word implies the accused has earned a genocide in return. El-Sayed waved it off.
That license to kill has already been redeemed. On May 21, 2025, Elias Rodriguez shot dead Yaron Lischinsky and Sarah Milgrim outside the Capital Jewish Museum in Washington. His manifesto declared the “perpetrators and abettors” of genocide had “forfeited their humanity.”
Eleven days later, in Boulder, Mohamed Soliman firebombed people marching for the hostages. Karen Diamond, 82, died of her burns.
As a lawyer, I can supply what El-Sayed, a physician, admits he lacks. “Neither you nor I are scholars on genocide,” he told Galloway, after years of leveling the charge.
In fact, the Genocide Convention requires specific intent to destroy, in whole or in part, a protected group as such. Where intent is inferred from conduct, the International Court of Justice held in Bosnia vs Serbia, and Croatia vs Serbia, that it must be the only reasonable inference. Galloway’s list points the other way.
El-Sayed’s standard doesn’t fail that test. It abolishes it, turning the word “genocide” – coined in 1944 by Raphael Lemkin from the ashes of the Holocaust – into a weapon against the Jewish state.
Michigan has seen where this leads. On March 12, Ayman Ghazali rammed a pickup loaded with gasoline and fireworks into Temple Israel in West Bloomfield, with 140 children in its preschool, and opened fire with an AR-style rifle. Only armed guards stood between him and those children.
El-Sayed condemned the attack, then gutted the condemnation by saying: “Hurt people hurt people.”
On August 5, newly nominated, El-Sayed claimed his commitment to Jewish safety was “the same as the commitment I have to the safety of my own daughters.”
Asked that day if he regretted his “hurt people” comment, he stood by it. Only on August 29, before the state party’s Jewish caucus, did he manage to say: “If my statement caused pain, I’m sorry,” while insisting the “context” could still come “in the fullness of time.”
No decent father rationalizes the man who tried to murder his daughters. The rationalization came free. The half-apology came when politically necessary.
The “daughters line” also has a geography problem. Nearly half the world’s Jews live in Israel. El-Sayed opposes US arms sales to it, even Iron Dome interceptors, after years of Iranian ballistic missiles and Hezbollah rockets. He calls Israel’s war against Hamas – whose official Ghazi Hamad vowed to repeat October 7 “again and again” until Israel is destroyed – a “genocide.”
El-Sayed’s concern may extend to the Jews whose votes he needs. It stops at the Jews defended by a Jewish army. A man willing to disarm half of world Jewry has told you what their safety is worth.
Galloway and co-host, Jessica Tarlov, pushed harder than most, yet still treated this as an electability problem. Tarlov asked only for “bare minimum acknowledgment” of Jewish concerns.
Galloway even allowed that Israel may have committed war crimes, as if that were genocide-lite. It isn’t. The two are legally distinct, and war crimes do not establish genocidal intent. Few modern wars have lacked them, and Hamas built its entire war on them: fighting out of uniform; using child soldiers; hiding next to, behind, and beneath human shields.
This is how moderation launders a libel: it treats the charge as a messaging problem and haggles over tone. You don’t negotiate with a libel. You demand its retraction. El-Sayed is not a friend with a different view on foreign policy. He is the latest purveyor of the world’s oldest hatred.
El-Sayed argues “genocide” needn’t wait for all the facts. On that, he is right. Antisemitic libels never have. In Norwich, in Kishinev, in Hebron, and in Washington, the libel came first, and the killers followed. Name it, without equivocation, for the dangerous lie it is, before it buries more Jews.
The writer is an attorney, former IDF soldier, and former NYPD officer. He writes widely on Israel, Zionism, antisemitism, and Jewish history. He serves on the board of Herut North America.

Zohran Mamdani’s antisemitism plan is political warfare, not protection of Jews - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
01:35:43 UTC
10:35:43 KST

New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani responded three times after Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu called him “the antisemitic mayor of New York” from the podium of the UN General Assembly on September 24.
First came the planting of olive trees for Gaza. Then came a statement dismissing the prime minister’s speech as baseless lies meant to sanitize a “genocide.” Then came money: a plan to raise the budget of the city’s Office for the Prevention of Hate Crimes from $3 million to $29 million a year.
The sequence matters. The plan is more than a budget line. It is a political-warfare maneuver, and Jews on both sides of the Atlantic should read it that way. The money is real. So is the maneuver.
Let us be fair. Security for synagogues, Holocaust education, and support for victims of hate crimes are worth funding. Jews comprise roughly 10% of New York’s population, yet according to New York City Police Department data, they were the target of 57% of reported hate crimes in 2025. Any mayor who ignored that would deserve condemnation.
But note what the plan leaves out. It fails to adopt a working definition of antisemitism. On taking office in January, Mamdani revoked the prior Adams administration’s order adopting the International Holocaust Remembrance Alliance (IHRA) definition of antisemitism along with its restrictions on New York City boycotts of Israel. The new plan does not mention Israel at all.
The Anti-Defamation League emphasized the point in its harsh criticism of Mamdani, noting:
“He [Mamdani] turned a blind eye when flags glorifying terrorist organizations were flown outside synagogues – a deliberate act intended to intimidate families walking inside to pray – and when crowds gathered outside houses of worship and expressed support for those same organizations.
“At the same time, he continues to prioritize his anti-Israel agenda over the basic promises he made to Jewish New Yorkers.”
That omission of Israel is the point. The plan protects Jews as a religious minority while sidelining the Jewish people’s connection to the Jewish state, leaving it outside the definition of what counts as hatred and antisemitism.
Mamdani has labeled Israel’s war on the Iranian regime-backed Hamas in Gaza “genocide,” has backed BDS, and supported legislation targeting nonprofits linked to pro-Israel causes. The same mayor now offers to protect the city’s Jews from harassment and violence provided nobody asks whether demonizing the Jewish state is itself part of the problem.
A wedge strategy
This is the classic new antisemitism’s “3D” architecture of delegitimization, demonization and double standards against Jews, and the Jewish state, as former Israeli deputy prime minister and prisoner of Zion Natan Sharansky labeled it:
Separate “good” Jews from “bad” Zionists. Fund the former. Treat the latter as a legitimate political target. Recast a national debate, whether the Jewish people may have a state, as an issue on which Jews may “disagree,” so that the dispute between Jews and their critics becomes a conflict between Jews. Drive a wedge between Diaspora Jews in New York and sovereign Jews in Israel.
For most Jews, Zionism is not a policy position. It is the historically rooted national sovereignty movement of the Jewish people grounded in the doctrine that Jews have the right to self-determination in their 3,600-year-old ancestral homeland.
A line drawn between antisemitism and anti-Zionism therefore slices through the Jewish community itself. The city’s message amounts to this: you are safe to the extent that you disown a central part of who you are.
The impulse to divide the Jewish community was visible in its reaction to the mayor’s cunning offer. Some Jewish leaders welcomed the funding; others insisted that Zionist Jews must also be free to speak without fear. That is exactly the right demand, and the plan as written does not meet it.
Not a local story
The Jerusalem Center for Security and Foreign Affairs has tracked this divide-and-conquer pattern for more than 25 years.
PLO founder, chairman, and 20th-century arch-terrorist Yasser Arafat first employed Mamdani’s strategy in the early 1970s, when he embraced progressive leaders of the Jewish community in New York. Arafat’s successor, Mahmoud Abbas, pursued the same strategy, openly embracing the far-left J Street while nazifying the Jewish state.
Mamdani’s victory similarly reflects the convergence of a revolutionary Left worldview and Islamist anti-Western currents, a “Red-Green” assault that reshapes the language of civil rights to serve an anti-Israel, anti-Western agenda.
Commentators favorable to the Islamic Republic’s regime in Tehran celebrated his election as a crack in pro-Israel hegemony. His campaign’s populist economic message also recalls Hamas’s 2006 campaign against the ruling Fatah faction of the Palestinian Authority, which paired economic grievance with radical Islamic themes.
Political warfare works through institutions. It wins not by frontal attack but by redefining terms, controlling the moral vocabulary, and offering concessions that cost the adversary nothing while advancing its long-term aim. A large budget announcement, issued days after a global confrontation, is a very efficient instrument of that kind.
What New York’s Jews, and Israel, should do
First, accept the funding and demand the IHRA definition. Security money should come with a clear statement that targeting Jews for their connection to Israel is antisemitism in line with the IHRA standard the mayor discarded.
Second, refuse the wedge. Jewish communal leaders must openly declare that the differentiation between “protected Jews” and “Zionist Jews” is false and should be labeled another form of warfare. Jewish unity on this point is essential.
Third, recognize that Israel’s critics cannot be fended off by rebuttal alone. The contest here is a classic example of what is known as the “eighth front” in Israel – the non-military yet equally existentially dangerous political warfare front over narrative and legitimacy.
This war must be fought with the same seriousness, aggressiveness, and determination as any other counterterrorism strategy.
Given his statements, it may be hard to believe that Mamdani is sincere about protecting Jewish New Yorkers from antisemitism. But a mayor who seeks credit for fighting antisemitism cannot exempt the most common form it takes today - the multidimensional, multi-front war against the existence of the only nation-state of the Jewish people.
Until the plan includes the IHRA definition of and commits to fighting this new genocidal antisemitism targeting the Jewish state, Mamdani’s $29m. is best understood as a down payment on a political platform, not a solution to metastasizing Jew hatred.
The writer is president of the Jerusalem Center for Security and Foreign Affairs and, since 2010, has directed its Counter-Political Warfare Initiative.

Former US congressman sentenced to 10 years in prison for secretly lobbying for Venezuela
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
01:35:41 UTC

Former US Congressman David Rivera was sentenced to 10 years in prison on Friday for illegally lobbying US officials to ease pressure on ousted Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro's government.
Rivera, a Republican who represented southern Florida in the US House of Representatives from 2011 to 2013, was convicted at trial in May of lobbying US officials on Venezuela's behalf in 2017 without registering as a foreign lobbyist as required by the Foreign Agents Registration Act (FARA).
US District Judge Melissa Damian handed down the sentence at a hearing in federal court in Miami.
Prosecutors with the Miami US Attorney's Office had urged Damian to impose a "significant term of incarceration." They said Rivera acted on behalf of a "hostile foreign government" and was paid $20 million by the US subsidiary of Venezuela's state oil company.
Rivera pleaded not guilty to charges
Rivera, 61, pleaded not guilty, and his lawyers said he should be spared prison time. They argued he had been working to help Venezuela's opposition remove Maduro from power, not benefit his government.
Rivera was charged in 2022, during former US president Joe Biden's administration, and defense lawyers noted that US President Donald Trump has deemphasized FARA cases since taking office in January 2025.

CBS releases messages sent between victim, defendant

'Switzerland of the Middle East': What is Oman’s relationship with Israel, if any?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
01:35:38 UTC
10:35:38 KST

The Omani pilot who allegedly tried to hijack and crash a flydubai flight bound for Tel Aviv has drawn new attention to his native country. Oman, sometimes dubbed the “Switzerland of the Middle East,” has long sought to balance its relations with the West and Iran. Its strategic location, combined with its distinctive diplomatic approach, has made it an unusual player in the Middle East.
Oman is located on the southeastern corner of the Arabian Peninsula, bordering Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates and Yemen. It sits alongside the Strait of Hormuz, the strategically important maritime passage through which roughly one-fifth of the world’s oil supply passes.
Until recently, Oman wasn’t a Middle Eastern country used to making international headlines. But it has emerged as a key player in recent months after long serving as a central mediator between Washington and Tehran. Its neutral posture, along with its close ties to both the United States and Iran, placed it in an important position during the talks between the two sides before the outbreak of the US-Iran war earlier this year.
When Omani mediation failed to prevent the conflict, Oman condemned the joint US-Israeli military campaign launched in February, saying it had “deep regrets at the military operations launched by Israel and the United States of America against the Islamic Republic of Iran” and that it “considers this action to be in contravention of the rules of international law.”
Even after Iran itself attacked Oman, which hosts three US military bases, as part of Tehran’s campaign to pressure countries in the region and deter US President Donald Trump, Muscat did not abandon its neutral stance. The targets Iran struck in Oman included a port and oil infrastructure, although the attacks were limited compared with those on other countries in the region.
Relations between Washington and Muscat have become further strained as the war has continued. In an opinion article published in The Economist, Oman’s foreign minister described the war as “unlawful” and said the United States “has lost control of its foreign policy.”
Trump, meanwhile, threatened to bomb Oman, telling reporters in August, “I don’t think they behaved very well, but we’d handle them very easily just like we do others.” The Wall Street Journal reported that senior US officials had privately accused Oman of being “a duplicitous actor” that largely sides with Iran rather than seeking the best possible deal between Washington and Tehran.
While the Gulf state maintains significant ties with Washington, it does not have formal diplomatic relations with Israel. The two countries once maintained commercial relations, but those ties were cut in 2000 amid a deterioration in the Israeli-Palestinian conflict. Contacts between the countries later continued quietly, and Netanyahu visited Oman in 2018 in a rare public meeting between an Israeli prime minister and an Omani sultan.
The two countries have discussed establishing formal relations, but those efforts have not come to fruition to date. Oman’s position has remained broadly similar to that of Saudi Arabia, which talked openly about the possibility of normalization with Israel but has conditioned that recognition on a clear, irreversible path toward a Palestinian state.
Omani support for Abraham Accords
Oman has also expressed support for the Abraham Accords, which normalized relations between Israel, the United Arab Emirates and Bahrain in 2020 and have since been signed by a handful of other Muslim countries.
Oman’s rhetoric toward Israel has grown harsher since Oct. 7, 2023, and relations between the countries have cooled. Omani officials have strongly criticized Israel’s conduct in Gaza and have been particularly critical of Israel’s war against Iran.
Ahmed bin Hamad al-Khalili, Oman’s grand mufti, described Israel’s attack on Iran as “treacherous American-Zionist aggression against Iran.”
A strategic Gulf state
Much of Oman’s geographic importance comes from its position along bodies of water through which large quantities of oil transit. Its land, by contrast, is covered by desert, with a coastal plain home to a significant share of the country’s population of roughly 5.5 million.
That population is distinctive in the Muslim world: A significant portion of its citizens belong to the Ibadi branch of Islam, a tradition separate from both Sunni and Shiite Islam. The country is also home to a large expatriate population from different religious backgrounds.
Oman is a sultanate, meaning the sultan holds extensive powers. The current ruler, Sultan Haitham bin Tarik Al Said, took office in January 2020 following the death of his cousin, Sultan Qaboos, who had ruled the country for nearly 50 years.
Oil underpins a significant part of Oman’s economy, although the country has sought to diversify. Its strategic location and extensive coastline have also made it a gateway for international trade between Europe and Asia.
Oman has so far not issued an official response to the incident or publicly confirmed the identity or nationality of the pilot who allegedly carried out the flydubai attack. But Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and international media outlets have described the pilot as Omani.
In a statement, Netanyahu said that “the perpetrator underwent Islamist radicalization. He came to crash the plane. We are now investigating whether he was sent, and whoever sent him will pay a very heavy price.”

Why a film about a dictator has South Korea at war with itself
A blockbuster about the 1974 assassination attempt of former president Park Chung-hee is causing a political backlash
Like many films released during Chuseok, South Korea’s national mid-autumn harvest festival, The Assassin(s) shot right to the top, selling more than a million tickets in its first four days.
But the box-office success of the film about the 1974 assassination attempt on former president and military leader Park Chung-hee was quickly overshadowed by calls to halt screenings, as well as a police complaint against the film’s director and producers.
Park loyalists and conservative politicians are claiming the film, directed by acclaimed filmmaker Hur Jin-ho, distorts history and defames Park and his administration.
Park, who came to power after a 1961 military coup, remains one of the most divisive figures in South Korean history. His authoritarian rule coincided with one of the world’s fastest periods of industrialisation, but his government was also marked by political repression and restrictions on civil liberties.

The Organization of American States (OAS) approved a resolution on Friday that urged Nicaragua to guarantee human rights, hold free and fair elections and unconditionally release political prisoners.
The measure was adopted during the organization's 31st Meeting of Consultation of Ministers of Foreign Affairs, convened in Washington to address the country's political and human rights situation.
It urged authorities to restore fundamental freedoms, while establishing conditions for free, fair and inclusive elections and releasing people detained for political reasons.
The statement also called for the restoration of the separation of powers, the disclosure of the whereabouts of forcibly disappeared people and the restoration of nationality to those who were deprived of it.

Nicaragua left the OAS in 2023, saying it had become a tool for US interventionism.

US appeals court blocks Minnesota law barring ‘nudified’ photos in xAI lawsuit
WASHINGTON - Elon Musk’s xAI on Oct 2 persuaded a US federal appeals court to halt Minnesota’s first-in-the-nation ban on AI-generated fake nude images as the technology and social media company pursues a lawsuit alleging that the law is unconstitutional.
The St Louis-based 8th US Circuit Court of Appeals in its order put the law on hold for now, granting a request for an injunction by xAI. A lower court judge last month had rejected Musk’s bid for an order stopping the law.
The state’s anti-“nudification” law, which took effect on Aug 1, prohibits website operators, software developers and others from allowing users to create realistic images depicting an intimate body part that is not shown in an original photo of an identifiable individual.
xAI alleges the measure restricts free speech protected by the US Constitution.
Minnesota and xAI did not immediately respond to requests for comment.
US District Judge Donovan Frank ruled last month that xAI had not shown it would suffer irreparable harm while challenging the law and said the company had waited too long to seek emergency relief.
In its appeal, xAI disputed the judge’s finding that it delayed bringing the suit. The company also said its Grok Imagine tool includes “rigorous protections” against creating nudified or sexualized images of real people.
xAI has begun suing users whom it alleges are evading Grok’s technological blockers to create sexual images of people without their consent.
Minnesota had urged the appeals court not to block the law. The state has said it adopted the measure this year to combat the spread of what it called a “staggering amount (of) child sexual abuse material that AI products like Grok Imagine generate.” REUTERS

NSW Ambulance has confirmed that ten people were injured and have been transported to John Hunter Hospital.
NSW Police said a five-year-old girl and a 67-year-old man are in critical condition. The remaining eight, including a second five-year-old girl and a two-year-old girl, are in stable condition.
Police told the ABC that the driver was an 18-year-old man on his P-plates. Following his arrest, the man was taken to hospital for mandatory drug and alcohol testing before being taken to a police station where he is expected to be charged.

NSW Police assistant commissioner David Waddell told reporters two other people in the car were escorted from the scene after the crowd turned on them.

The Newcastle Knights bus was diverted via an alternate route in response to the incident, and the team has now left Newcastle ahead of the grand final in Sydney on Sunday.
"Due to a major incident, the team bus has been diverted from the planned route," the Newcastle Knights said in a post to social media.

Incident follows elation of Knights reaching grand final
The elation of the Knights reaching Sunday's NRL decider prompted an avalanche of fan support in Newcastle over recent days.
Diehards waited in the rain for the return of the team bus from Sydney last weekend after a 22-14 qualifying win over Penrith.
Thousands also showed up for team training during the week, while other Knights enthusiasts have even gone to the trouble of painting their houses in team colours.

What is celebrated on October 3 in Ukraine and around the world
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
04:04:15 EEST
10:04:15 KST

What is celebrated on October 3 in Ukraine and around the world
Kyiv • UNN
On October 3, international and national holidays are celebrated, including Sobriety Day, German Unity Day, and the foundation of South Korea. Believers commemorate Dionysius the Areopagite according to the new calendar and Eustace Placidus according to the old calendar.
On October 3, the world observes World Temperance Day and the Day Against Alcoholism, German Unity Day, and the Foundation of the State Day in South Korea. According to the new-style church calendar, the day honors Hieromartyr Dionysius the Areopagite, Bishop of Athens, while according to the old style, it commemorates Saint Great Martyr Eustathius Placidas and his family, UNN writes.
World Temperance Day and the Day Against Alcoholism (World Temperance Day)
An unofficial international observance dedicated to preventing alcohol dependence, promoting a healthy lifestyle, and raising awareness of the medical and social consequences of alcohol abuse. The observance has its roots in the 19th-century temperance movement and calls on governments, public organizations, and medical institutions to strengthen educational efforts, provide psychological and addiction-treatment assistance to those affected, and foster a culture of sober living in society.
German Unity Day (Tag der Deutschen Einheit)
The main national and only official public holiday of the Federal Republic of Germany at the federal level. It was established to commemorate the official reunification of West Germany (FRG) and East Germany (GDR) on October 3, 1990, in accordance with the Unification Treaty. This event marked the end of more than 40 years of the division of the German nation following World War II, the fall of the Berlin Wall in 1989, and became one of the key stages in the end of the "Cold War" in Europe.
Foundation of the State Day in South Korea
An official public holiday, "Gaecheonjeol" ("the Day the Heavens Opened"), commemorating the legendary founding of the first Korean state, Gojoseon, in 2333 BCE by Dangun Wanggeom—the mythical founder of the Korean nation. The holiday is accompanied by solemn ceremonies on Mount Manisan on Ganghwado Island, where, according to tradition, Dangun offered sacrifices to Heaven, as well as national cultural events throughout the country.
The Day Commemorating Hieromartyr Dionysius the Areopagite
According to the new calendar, Orthodox and Greek Catholic believers honor the memory of Hieromartyr Dionysius the Areopagite, Bishop of Athens, as well as the martyrs Rusticus the presbyter and Eleutherius the deacon. Dionysius was an Athenian thinker and a member of Athens' highest judicial body—the Areopagus. Converted to Christianity by the Apostle Paul during his preaching in Athens, Dionysius became the first Bishop of Athens. He later went on a mission to Gaul, where, during the reign of Emperor Domitian in the 1st century, he was tortured and executed by beheading on a hill that later became known as Montmartre.
According to the old calendar, believers honor the memory of Saint Great Martyr Eustathius Placidas, his wife Theopista, and their sons Agapius and Theopistus. Eustathius was a distinguished Roman military commander under Emperors Trajan and Hadrian. After converting to Christianity following a miraculous vision of a cross between the antlers of a deer while hunting, he and his family endured severe trials, the loss of their property, and separation. For refusing to sacrifice to pagan gods after a military victory, Eustathius and his family were tortured and executed in Rome in the 2nd century.

Brazil probes alleged US funding plan for far-right causes
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
01:01:12 UTC
10:01:12 KST

Brazil's attorney general has requested an investigation into an alleged US government funding programme that targeted the Supreme Federal Court (STF), days before the presidential election.
Attorney General Jorge Messias said that foreign political interests seeking to interfere in Brazilian institutions or influence decisions belonging to Brazilian voters "cannot be tolerated."
The request followed a report by The Guardian newspaper that the administration of US President Donald Trump planned to direct funds toward a campaign opposing the top court.
The report said a $1 million US grant was allocated to a "Countering Lawfare and Censorship in Brazil" project to support civil society groups opposing judicial overreach and censorship by the court.
Messias described the reported initiative as "an important alert for Brazilian sovereignty" and said the issue was particularly sensitive because of the electoral process.
The attorney general's office asked the Federal Police and federal prosecutors to examine the origin, destination and purpose of the funds, and determine whether they could constitute foreign interference in Brazil's political or electoral process.
The reported $1 million grant is part of a broader package of more than $175 million from a US State Department human rights fund for projects worldwide, according to The Guardian.
The project comes amid tensions between supporters of former President Jair Bolsonaro and the Supreme Court, particularly Justice Alexandre de Moraes.
Bolsonaro was sentenced to 27 years in prison after he was convicted of attempting to overturn the result of the 2022 presidential election.
Brazil is set to hold a presidential election on Sunday, with President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva seeking another term. Flavio Bolsonaro, the former president's son, is among the candidates.
The US has not publicly confirmed that the reported funding was intended to interfere in the election.

Hongkongers lose HK$220 million to customer service scams in August
Scammers are taking real-time control of victims through direct calls or tricking them into installing malicious apps, police warn
Scams involving fraudsters posing as customer service officers caused losses of over HK$220 million (US$28.2 million) in August in Hong Kong, more than triple the monthly average in the first seven months of the year, police have said.
The police force also warned that scammers had shifted their modus operandi from using phishing links to taking real-time control of victims through direct calls and screen sharing, or tricking them into installing a malicious app that turned mobile phones into a credit card reader.
Hong Kong recorded 29,670 scam cases in the first eight months of 2026, up 4.5 per cent from 28,379 in the same period a year earlier, with losses rising by 3.8 per cent to HK$5.2 billion.
About 17 per cent, or around 5,000 cases, were customer service scams, which incurred total losses of nearly HK$700 million.

In FocusChina has dominated tungsten for decades. Can US cash in Central Asia loosen its grip?
Kazakhstan is at the centre of US efforts to build a new supply chain for the metal, but analysts say China’s lead will be difficult to overcome
The race to loosen China’s grip on tungsten is moving to Kazakhstan, where United States-backed mining projects are attempting to compete in an industry where Chinese investment already has an operating foothold.
The supply squeeze has reached US oilfield equipment makers, which are redesigning one of their most important tools as the global shortage raises the cost of making drill bits.
According to Ulterra Drilling Technologies, the cost of manufacturing drill bits had risen by as much as 50 per cent over the past year. The company is responding by shifting production towards steel-bodied models, even as bits containing more tungsten typically last longer when cutting through hard, abrasive rock.
